entities.histo: Malignant cutaneous tumours of the breast skin are primary skin cancers rather than mammary carcinomas, and should be classified according to WHO Skin Tumours. Basal cell carcinoma, rare on the nipple and areola, shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, stromal retraction clefts and a mucinous stroma. It is positive for BerEP4 and negative for EMA, and may clinically mimic Paget disease. Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin, including Bowen disease, shows atypical keratinocytes and must be distinguished from metaplastic squamous carcinoma of the breast by its epidermal origin and the absence of a deep parenchymal tumour. Melanoma of the breast skin shows atypical melanocytes that are SOX10-positive, Melan-A-positive and HMB45-positive. Melanoma in situ must be separated from pigmented Paget disease, which is CK7-positive. Extramammary-type adnexal carcinomas, such as porocarcinoma and microcystic adnexal carcinoma, and Merkel cell carcinoma (CK20 perinuclear dot, neuroendocrine markers, MCPyV) are rare. The main differentials are cutaneous metastasis or direct skin involvement by breast carcinoma (GATA3-positive and TRPS1-positive) and mammary Paget disease.
entities.cyto: Malignant cutaneous tumours of breast skin, such as basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, may be aspirated or scraped. Basal cell carcinoma shows cohesive basaloid clusters with peripheral palisading; squamous cell carcinoma shows atypical keratinising cells; melanoma shows dyscohesive cells with prominent nucleoli, intranuclear inclusions and pigment; DFSP shows storiform bland spindle cells (CD34 positive). The main challenge is to distinguish skin tumours from breast carcinoma infiltrating the skin and Paget disease; clinical appearance and immunochemistry help. Reported descriptively, as malignant (Yokohama Category 5) where appropriate.
entities.ihc: Malignant cutaneous tumours of the breast skin are classified per the WHO skin volume, and IHC helps separate them from mammary carcinoma and Paget disease. Basal cell carcinoma of the nipple-areola is BerEP4 positive, BCL2 positive and EMA negative. Squamous cell carcinoma is p63, p40 and CK5/6 positive, and CK7 and GATA3 negative. Melanoma is S100, SOX10, Melan-A and HMB-45 positive, and keratin negative. Merkel cell carcinoma shows paranuclear dot CK20, is synaptophysin positive and INSM1 positive, and is MCPyV (CM2B4) positive. Extramammary-type Paget disease and dermal invasion of breast carcinoma are GATA3, CK7 and often HER2 positive. Post-radiation angiosarcoma (ERG, CD31, MYC) should also be considered.

entities.remarks: Not separately classified by WHO 5th; infiltrative malignant tumour of purely myoepithelial phenotype, often spindle cell; overlaps with spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma; triple-negative. Not listed as a separate entity in WHO 6th ed (beta) TOC.
entities.histo: Myoepithelial carcinoma (malignant myoepithelioma) is a rare malignant tumour of purely myoepithelial phenotype. WHO 5th edition does not classify it separately, considering it within the spectrum of metaplastic carcinoma and adenomyoepithelioma with carcinoma. It presents as an enlarging mass, usually in older women. Microscopically, the tumour is infiltrative and consists predominantly of atypical spindle cells in fascicles, sometimes with epithelioid or clear cells, and often with myxoid or collagenous stroma. Nuclear pleomorphism, increased mitoses and necrosis are present. The cells are positive for p63, SMA, calponin, SMMHC, CK5/6, S100 and often keratin, and are triple-negative for ER, PR and HER2. The tumour overlaps with spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma, which is also p63-positive and keratin-positive, and many pathologists group the two together. A residual adenomyoepithelioma component supports carcinoma arising in AME. Differentials include myoepithelioma, malignant phyllodes tumour, leiomyosarcoma, fibromatosis and other sarcomas. Haematogenous metastases occur, and treatment follows that of metaplastic carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Myoepithelial carcinoma (malignant myoepithelioma) yields cellular aspirates of atypical spindle, epithelioid or clear cells, singly and in fascicles or loose clusters, with nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, mitoses and sometimes necrosis or myxoid matrix, without a luminal epithelial component. The cytology overlaps substantially with spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma, malignant phyllodes tumour, sarcomas and malignant adenomyoepithelioma. Cell block immunochemistry shows myoepithelial markers (p63, SMA, calponin, S100) with high-molecular-weight cytokeratin, and the tumour is usually triple negative. Exact classification requires histology. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), malignant spindle cell neoplasm, or Category 4 when limited.
entities.ihc: Myoepithelial carcinoma (malignant myoepithelioma) is an infiltrative, triple-negative malignant tumour with a purely myoepithelial phenotype. IHC shows p63 positivity, CK5/6 and CK14 positivity, positivity for broad keratins (AE1/AE3, 34βE12), variable SMA, calponin and SMMHC, and often S100 positivity. EGFR is often positive and Ki-67 is high. ER, PR and HER2 are negative. Its phenotype overlaps almost completely with spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma, and many authors classify it as such. The distinction from benign myoepithelioma rests on atypia, necrosis, mitoses and infiltration. Malignant phyllodes tumour (adequate sampling for leaf-like architecture, CD34+ stroma) and sarcomas (keratin-negative, p63-negative) are excluded with the keratin and p63 panel. PD-L1 testing applies as for TNBC.

entities.remarks: Not separately classified by WHO 5th; very rare invasive carcinoma (often poorly differentiated, solid) arising from cystic hypersecretory DCIS; thyroid colloid-like secretions in the cysts. Not listed as a separate entity in WHO 6th ed (beta) TOC.
entities.histo: Invasive cystic hypersecretory carcinoma is a very rare invasive carcinoma arising from cystic hypersecretory DCIS. WHO 5th edition does not classify it separately. The in situ component shows cysts filled with dense, eosinophilic, colloid-like secretion resembling thyroid follicles, lined by micropapillary or stratified atypical epithelium. The invasive component is often poorly differentiated, with solid sheets or nests of high-grade tumour cells. It may lack the cystic hypersecretory features of the in situ component, so its origin is recognised from the associated DCIS. Receptor status is variable, with many tumours ER-negative or HER2-variable. The secretions are PAS-positive and thyroglobulin-negative, and the tumour cells are GATA3-positive and TTF-1-negative, which helps exclude metastatic thyroid carcinoma. Differentials include cystic hypersecretory DCIS without invasion, cystic hypersecretory hyperplasia, metastatic thyroid carcinoma, secretory carcinoma (ETV6::NTRK3) and IBC-NST. Thorough sampling of cystic hypersecretory lesions is advised to detect invasion, and the invasive component is graded, measured and staged as for IBC-NST.
entities.cyto: Invasive cystic hypersecretory carcinoma is very rare and arises from cystic hypersecretory DCIS. Aspirates show abundant dense, homogeneous colloid-like secretion with cracking artefact, foamy macrophages, and malignant epithelial cells, often poorly differentiated in solid groups and singly, with nuclear pleomorphism and prominent nucleoli, sometimes alongside micropapillary groups from the in situ component. The colloid-like material may suggest metastatic thyroid carcinoma or mucinous lesions; thyroglobulin and TTF-1 negativity on cell block helps. Invasion cannot be assessed cytologically. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), carcinoma, or Category 4 when cells are scanty or less atypical.
entities.ihc: Invasive cystic hypersecretory carcinoma is a very rare, often poorly differentiated, solid invasive carcinoma that arises from cystic hypersecretory DCIS with thyroid colloid-like secretions. IHC confirms invasion by the absence of myoepithelial cells (p63, SMMHC, calponin) around the solid nests, while the background in-situ cysts keep their myoepithelium. Breast origin is supported by CK7 positivity and GATA3 positivity, and negativity for TTF-1, PAX8 and thyroglobulin excludes metastatic thyroid carcinoma, which is the key differential given the colloid-like material. The invasive component is frequently ER-negative or ER-low and high grade with a high Ki-67, so ER, PR and HER2 per ASCO/CAP should be reported. Because the data are limited, the profile is described from case reports.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; intermediate features: well-defined to focally permeative border, moderate stromal cellularity/atypia, 2.5 to <5 mitoses/mm² (5–9/10 HPF), focal or absent stromal overgrowth; may recur, rarely metastasise. Not all criteria need to be present. WHO 6th ed (beta) lists a single entity 'Phyllodes tumour', graded benign/borderline/malignant.
entities.histo: Borderline phyllodes tumour is a fibroepithelial neoplasm with features intermediate between benign and malignant phyllodes tumour, and not all criteria need to be present. It presents as an enlarging mass, often larger than a fibroadenoma. Microscopically, there is leaf-like architecture with periductal stromal condensation and moderate stromal hypercellularity with moderate nuclear atypia. Mitoses number 2.5 to fewer than 5 per mm², about 5 to 9 per 10 HPF. The border is well defined to focally permeative, and stromal overgrowth is focal or absent, with no malignant heterologous elements. Borderline tumours have a higher risk of local recurrence than benign phyllodes tumours, especially with positive margins, but metastasis is rare. Grading should be based on the most cellular and atypical areas, so generous sampling is required. Classification on core biopsy is often provisional. Differentials include benign phyllodes tumour, malignant phyllodes tumour (marked atypia, 5 or more mitoses per mm², overgrowth, permeative border), cellular fibroadenoma, and spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma, which is keratin-positive and p63-positive. Excision with clear margins is recommended.
entities.cyto: Borderline phyllodes tumour aspirates show a fibroepithelial pattern with epithelial sheets, myoepithelial cells and bare bipolar nuclei, together with hypercellular stromal fragments and numerous single stromal spindle cells showing moderate nuclear atypia and occasional mitoses. Distinction from benign or malignant phyllodes tumour and from cellular fibroadenoma is not possible on cytology, as grading depends on histological criteria including stromal overgrowth, borders and mitotic count. Stromal-predominant smears with atypia should raise concern. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or Category 4 (Suspicious), fibroepithelial lesion with cellular stroma, recommending excision.
entities.ihc: Borderline phyllodes tumour is defined by intermediate morphological features: moderate stromal cellularity and atypia, 5–9 mitoses per 10 HPF, focally permeative borders and no stromal overgrowth. IHC doesn't determine grade. Stromal Ki-67 is intermediate, p53 is patchy, and CD34 may be partly lost, but these markers only support the grade. Broad-spectrum keratins and p63 are needed in any atypical spindle-cell tumour to exclude metaplastic carcinoma, and focal keratin can occur in phyllodes. MED12 and TERT promoter mutations are common. Additional TP53, RB1, NF1 or EGFR alterations suggest progression to malignant phyllodes. Margin status is key for management.

entities.remarks: Regarded as a variant/form of phyllodes tumour (WHO 5th): non-circumscribed stromal proliferation around open tubules lacking leaf-like pattern; grade as phyllodes. Not listed as a separate entity in WHO 6th ed (beta) TOC.
entities.histo: Periductal stromal tumour is a rare biphasic lesion now regarded as a form of phyllodes tumour and graded in the same way. It usually presents as a mass in perimenopausal women. Microscopically, it is a non-circumscribed, infiltrative proliferation of spindle stromal cells that condenses around open, non-compressed ducts and tubules with a two-cell layer, forming cuffs of hypercellular stroma, and the stroma infiltrates the surrounding fat. Unlike a classic phyllodes tumour, the leaf-like intracanalicular pattern with elongated clefts and broad fronds is absent. The stromal cells show variable atypia and mitotic activity, and some lesions contain heterologous elements. Stromal cells are CD34-positive and may be CD117-positive, and are negative for keratins and p63. Because some cases progress to typical phyllodes tumour or recur, the lesion should be graded using phyllodes criteria and excised with clear margins. Differentials include benign phyllodes tumour, fibroadenoma, PASH, juvenile hypertrophy, and spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma (keratin-positive).
entities.cyto: Periductal stromal tumour is a rare biphasic tumour with stromal proliferation around open ducts, regarded as part of the phyllodes spectrum. There are no specific cytological criteria. Aspirates would show bland ductal epithelial groups with myoepithelial cells and a population of spindle stromal cells with mild to moderate atypia and mitoses, overlapping with phyllodes tumour, fibroadenoma and spindle cell lesions. Definitive diagnosis requires histology showing periductal cuffing without leaf-like architecture. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or Category 4 (Suspicious), spindle cell or fibroepithelial lesion, with excision.
entities.ihc: Periductal stromal tumour is regarded as a form of phyllodes tumour in WHO 5th edition. It's a stromal proliferation around ducts without leaf-like architecture. The stromal cells are CD34 positive and often CD117 positive and BCL2 positive, with a variable Ki-67, and negative for keratins and p63, which excludes metaplastic carcinoma. Myoepithelial markers show the benign epithelial component. Grading follows phyllodes criteria for atypia and mitoses. Morphology, not IHC, separates it from PASH (CD34+, PR+, slit-like spaces) and myofibroblastoma (desmin+, RB1 loss). Molecular studies show MED12 and TERT alterations similar to phyllodes.

entities.variants: Lymphatic type; vascular (blood-vessel) type
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; post-radiation cutaneous vascular proliferation (circumscribed, superficial dermis, no multilayering/significant atypia); MYC not amplified; small risk of progression to angiosarcoma — complete excision & follow-up.
entities.histo: Atypical vascular lesion (AVL) arises in the skin of the breast after radiotherapy, usually several years after breast-conserving treatment. It presents as small, often multiple, flesh-coloured to erythematous papules or vesicles under 1 cm within the radiation field. Microscopically, it is a circumscribed, superficial, dermal proliferation of thin-walled, dilated, sometimes anastomosing vessels. The vessels are lined by a single layer of bland or slightly hyperchromatic endothelial cells, sometimes hobnail, without multilayering, significant atypia or mitoses, and they do not involve subcutaneous fat. The lymphatic type, the commonest, shows irregular dilated lymphatic channels that are D2-40-positive, often with stromal lymphocytes. The vascular (blood vessel) type shows capillary-sized vessels with red cells and pericytes. MYC is not amplified, and MYC IHC is negative, which is the key distinction from post-radiation angiosarcoma. Angiosarcoma shows infiltration of the deep dermis and fat, endothelial multilayering and atypia, and MYC amplification. AVL carries a small risk of progression to angiosarcoma, so complete excision and clinical follow-up are recommended. Differentials also include haemangioma, lymphangioma and recurrent carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Atypical vascular lesion arises in irradiated breast skin and is diagnosed by punch biopsy rather than FNA. Scrapes or aspirates, if obtained, show blood and a few bland or mildly atypical endothelial cells, without the cellularity or pleomorphism of angiosarcoma. Cytology cannot reliably distinguish AVL from well-differentiated postradiation angiosarcoma, for which MYC amplification on histology helps. The lesion is important as a possible precursor or mimic of angiosarcoma. A cytological specimen would be reported as non-diagnostic or Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), with biopsy recommended.
entities.ihc: Atypical vascular lesion (AVL) is a post-radiation cutaneous vascular proliferation, of lymphatic or blood-vessel type. IHC shows endothelial markers: CD31 and ERG positive, D2-40 and PROX1 positive in the lymphatic type, and CD34 variable. The key test is MYC: AVL is MYC negative by IHC and lacks MYC amplification by FISH, whereas post-radiation angiosarcoma shows diffuse nuclear MYC staining and amplification. Ki-67 is low in AVL. Because sampling may be limited and AVL can coexist with or precede angiosarcoma, complete excision and MYC testing are recommended. FLT4 co-amplification is seen only in angiosarcoma.

entities.variants: Sporadic; post-surgical/post-implant; FAP (Gardner) associated
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; locally aggressive, non-metastasising; infiltrative long sweeping fascicles of bland myofibroblasts entrapping ducts/lobules; nuclear β-catenin (CTNNB1 or APC mutation); keratin negative (vs fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma).
entities.histo: Desmoid fibromatosis of the breast is a locally aggressive, non-metastasising myofibroblastic neoplasm that arises from the pectoral fascia or within the breast parenchyma. It may be sporadic, follow surgery or implant placement, or occur in familial adenomatous polyposis (Gardner syndrome), and it presents as a firm, irregular mass that mimics carcinoma clinically and on imaging. Grossly it is a firm, grey-white, trabeculated lesion with poorly defined, infiltrative margins. Microscopically, long, sweeping fascicles of bland, uniform spindle myofibroblasts with pale nuclei and small nucleoli lie in collagenous stroma with thin-walled vessels. The fascicles infiltrate fat and entrap ducts and lobules at the periphery, and lymphoid aggregates are present at the advancing edge. Mitoses are few, and necrosis is absent. Nuclear beta-catenin is positive, reflecting CTNNB1 or APC mutations, and the cells are SMA-positive and negative for keratins, p63, CD34 and S100. Differentials include fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma (keratin-positive and p63-positive clusters), scar, nodular fasciitis, myofibroblastoma and low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma. Management increasingly favours active surveillance or systemic therapy rather than radical surgery.
entities.cyto: Desmoid fibromatosis of the breast, often arising from the pectoral fascia, yields hypocellular aspirates with scattered bland spindle cells with oval to elongated nuclei, fine chromatin and small nucleoli, singly and in small fascicles, together with fragments of collagenous stroma and sometimes trapped skeletal muscle or breast tissue. Epithelial cells are absent. Low-grade fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma is the most important differential, requiring cytokeratin and p63 on cell block; nuclear beta-catenin positivity supports fibromatosis. Scar, nodular fasciitis and phyllodes stroma are other mimics. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), bland spindle cell lesion, with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Desmoid fibromatosis of the breast consists of long fascicles of bland spindle cells that infiltrate fat and parenchyma. IHC shows nuclear β-catenin in most cases, reflecting CTNNB1 mutation (sporadic) or APC mutation (FAP/Gardner), together with SMA positivity, variable desmin and negative keratins, p63, CD34 and S100. The key differential is fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma, which is keratin positive (often focal, so use a broad panel including 34βE12 and CK5/6) and p63 positive. Nodular fasciitis (USP6) and myofibroblastoma (CD34+, desmin+) should also be considered. Post-implant and post-surgical cases occur, and CTNNB1 sequencing can help.

entities.remarks: WHO 5th; intermediate (rarely metastasising); myofibroblasts with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate; ALK rearrangement (ALK IHC+) in ~50%, also ROS1/NTRK fusions. Not listed as a separate entity in WHO 6th ed (beta) TOC.
entities.histo: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour (IMT) of the breast is a rare intermediate (rarely metastasising) neoplasm of myofibroblastic spindle cells with a prominent inflammatory infiltrate. It presents as a painless, well-defined or irregular mass. Microscopically there are three patterns, which often coexist. The myxoid or vascular pattern resembles nodular fasciitis, with loose spindle cells and inflammation. The compact spindle cell pattern shows fascicles with a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. The hypocellular fibrous pattern shows scar-like collagen. The spindle cells have vesicular nuclei and small nucleoli, and the inflammation consists of plasma cells, lymphocytes and eosinophils. About half the cases harbour ALK rearrangements and show ALK IHC positivity, and other cases have ROS1, NTRK or other kinase fusions that may be targetable. The cells are SMA-positive and variably positive for desmin and keratin, which is a pitfall. Differentials include IgG4-related mastitis, nodular fasciitis (USP6-positive), desmoid fibromatosis (nuclear beta-catenin), spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma (strong keratin and p63 positivity), and lymphoma. Complete excision is the treatment.
entities.cyto: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour of the breast is rare and yields aspirates of moderate cellularity with plump spindle or stellate myofibroblasts with oval nuclei, small nucleoli and abundant cytoplasm, in a myxoid or collagenous background, admixed with lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils. Mild atypia may be seen. Differentials include nodular fasciitis, IgG4-related mastitis, granulomatous mastitis, fibromatosis and spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma. ALK immunopositivity on cell block or ALK rearrangement supports the diagnosis, along with SMA. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical), spindle cell lesion with inflammation, with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour of the breast consists of myofibroblastic spindle cells in a lymphoplasmacytic background. IHC shows SMA positivity, variable desmin and keratin, and ALK positivity in about half of cases, reflecting ALK rearrangement (various partners), confirmed by FISH or NGS. ROS1, NTRK, PDGFRB or RET fusions occur in ALK-negative cases and can be targeted. The epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma variant shows nuclear membrane or perinuclear ALK staining (RANBP2-ALK). Separate it from IgG4-related mastitis (IgG4 ratio), nodular fasciitis (USP6), fibromatosis (nuclear β-catenin) and spindle-cell metaplastic carcinoma (strong keratins, p63+).

entities.entity: Other intermediate soft-tissue tumours in breast
entities.variants: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (breast skin; COL1A1::PDGFB, CD34+); solitary fibrous tumour (NAB2::STAT6, STAT6 nuclear); atypical lipomatous tumour / well-differentiated liposarcoma (MDM2 amplification); giant cell tumour of soft tissue
entities.remarks: Rare in breast; classify per WHO Soft Tissue & Bone Tumours 5th ed; ALT component in phyllodes does not by itself upgrade to malignant phyllodes. Not listed as a separate entity in WHO 6th ed (beta) TOC.
entities.histo: Other intermediate soft-tissue tumours of the breast are rare and are classified according to WHO Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans of the breast skin shows uniform spindle cells in a tight storiform pattern infiltrating subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern, with CD34 positivity and a COL1A1::PDGFB fusion. Its fibrosarcomatous transformation shows herringbone fascicles. Solitary fibrous tumour is a circumscribed tumour of bland spindle cells in a patternless arrangement with staghorn haemangiopericytoma-like vessels, positive for CD34 and nuclear STAT6, reflecting NAB2::STAT6. Atypical lipomatous tumour or well-differentiated liposarcoma shows atypical stromal cells within mature fat, with MDM2 amplification. When it occurs as a component of a phyllodes tumour, it does not by itself make the tumour malignant. Giant cell tumour of soft tissue shows nodules of mononuclear cells with osteoclast-like giant cells. Differentials include myofibroblastoma (desmin-positive, RB1 loss), metaplastic carcinoma, phyllodes tumour, lipoma and benign fibrous histiocytoma, so thorough sampling and IHC are needed.
entities.cyto: Other intermediate soft tissue tumours in breast, such as solitary fibrous tumour, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma and Kaposi sarcoma, are rare. Aspirates show variable bland to mildly atypical spindle cells in collagenous, myxoid or haemorrhagic backgrounds, features that are non-specific and overlap with phyllodes tumour stroma, metaplastic carcinoma and benign spindle cell lesions. Cell block immunochemistry (STAT6 for SFT, CD34 for DFSP, MUC4 for LGFMS, HHV-8 for Kaposi) and molecular tests are used for classification, which usually requires histology. Reported as Yokohama Category 3 (Atypical) or Category 4 (Suspicious), spindle cell lesion, with core biopsy.
entities.ihc: Other intermediate soft tissue tumours of the breast are classified per the WHO soft tissue volume. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans in the breast skin is CD34 positive (diffuse), factor XIIIa negative, and carries COL1A1-PDGFB fusion (FISH or RT-PCR), which predicts response to imatinib. Solitary fibrous tumour is STAT6 nuclear positive and CD34 positive (NAB2-STAT6). Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma is MUC4 positive (FUS-CREB3L2). Kaposiform and other vascular tumours are ERG and CD31 positive. In each case, metaplastic carcinoma should first be excluded with broad keratins and p63, and phyllodes tumour by adequate sampling for an epithelial component.

entities.entity: Metastases to the breast (and secondary tumours)
entities.variants: Contralateral breast carcinoma; melanoma (commonest extramammary source in many series); lung carcinoma (adenocarcinoma, small cell); ovarian (high-grade serous) carcinoma; gastric/colorectal adenocarcinoma; renal cell carcinoma; neuroendocrine tumours (GI, lung); thyroid carcinoma; sarcomas; alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (adolescents); haematolymphoid (leukaemia/lymphoma) secondary involvement; mesothelioma (direct/metastatic)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th; ~0.5–2% of breast malignancies; clues: lack of in situ component, unusual morphology, multiple well-circumscribed nodules; IHC: GATA3, TRPS1, SOX10, mammaglobin, GCDFP-15 (breast) vs TTF-1/napsin A (lung), PAX8/WT1 (ovary), CDX2/SATB2 (GI), SOX10/S100/HMB45/Melan-A (melanoma). TRPS1 highly sensitive for breast including TNBC/metaplastic.
entities.histo: Metastases to the breast account for about 0.5 to 2% of breast malignancies. The commonest sources are the contralateral breast, melanoma, lung carcinoma (adenocarcinoma and small cell), ovarian high-grade serous carcinoma, gastrointestinal and renal cell carcinomas, neuroendocrine tumours, thyroid carcinoma and sarcomas, and alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma in adolescents. Haematolymphoid malignancies also occur, as does mesothelioma. Clinical clues include a known primary, multiple well-circumscribed nodules and rapid growth. Histological clues include the absence of an in situ component, unusual morphology for breast carcinoma (clear cell, serous papillary or mucinous intestinal types) and prominent lymphovascular involvement. IHC is essential. GATA3, TRPS1, mammaglobin, GCDFP-15 and ER support a breast primary, with TRPS1 being highly sensitive, including in triple-negative and metaplastic tumours. TTF-1 and napsin A suggest lung, PAX8 and WT1 suggest ovary, and CDX2, SATB2 and CK20 suggest the gastrointestinal tract. PAX8 and CA-IX suggest kidney, and SOX10, S100, HMB45 and Melan-A suggest melanoma. Accurate distinction is important because treatment differs fundamentally.
entities.cyto: Metastases to the breast are uncommon, most often from contralateral breast carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma, lung carcinoma, ovarian serous carcinoma, gastrointestinal, renal and neuroendocrine tumours, and rhabdomyosarcoma in children. Aspirates show malignant cells whose morphology may suggest the primary, such as pigment and intranuclear inclusions in melanoma, psammoma bodies and papillae in ovarian carcinoma, clear cells in renal carcinoma or small round cells in rhabdomyosarcoma. Absence of DCIS and clinical history are clues. Cell block immunochemistry (GATA3, ER, TTF-1, PAX8, WT1, CDX2, SOX10) is essential to avoid misdiagnosis and inappropriate surgery. Reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant), with a comment on the likely primary.
entities.ihc: In metastases to the breast, IHC is central to identifying the primary site. Primary breast carcinoma is typically GATA3+, ER+ (in most cases), mammaglobin+ and SOX10+ (in TNBC), and TRPS1+, which is the most sensitive and specific marker, including in TNBC and metaplastic carcinoma. Melanoma is S100, SOX10, Melan-A and HMB-45 positive. Lung is TTF-1 and napsin A positive. Ovarian serous carcinoma is PAX8 and WT1 positive. GI is CDX2, CK20 and SATB2 positive. Renal is PAX8 and CAIX positive. Neuroendocrine tumours are synaptophysin positive, and lymphoma is CD45 positive. A lack of in-situ carcinoma and an unusual morphology are clues. Pitfalls: GATA3 is also positive in urothelial and other carcinomas, and SOX10 is shared with melanoma.

entities.entity: Hereditary breast cancer predisposition - overview and other associations (Lynch syndrome, Carney complex)
entities.variants: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (BRCA1 — TNBC/basal-like, medullary pattern; BRCA2 — luminal, male breast cancer); PALB2; Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53; HER2+ early-onset); Cowden / PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome (hamartomas, multiple papillomas); hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (CDH1 — lobular carcinoma); Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11); ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM); CHEK2; NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1); Lynch syndrome (mismatch-repair genes, minor); Carney complex (myxoid fibroadenomas, ductal adenoma)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes. WHO 5th chapter on genetic tumour syndromes of the breast; listed for completeness (not single histological entities); germline testing per guidelines; BRCA-associated tumours eligible for PARP inhibitors. Not listed as a separate entity in WHO 6th ed (beta) TOC. The individual syndromes listed in WHO 6th ed (beta) now have their own rows; this row keeps the overview and the associations not listed there (Lynch syndrome, Carney complex).
entities.histo: Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes are covered in a WHO 5th edition chapter. They are not single histological entities, but recognising their associated morphology can prompt germline testing. BRCA1-associated carcinomas are typically high-grade, triple-negative and basal-like, often with a medullary pattern, pushing borders and abundant TILs. BRCA2-associated carcinomas are usually luminal, ER-positive tumours and account for a significant proportion of male breast cancers. PALB2 resembles BRCA2. Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53) causes early-onset, frequently HER2-positive carcinomas. Cowden or PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome is associated with multiple hamartomas, papillomas and fibroadenomas. Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (CDH1) predisposes to invasive lobular carcinoma. Peutz-Jeghers (STK11), ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM), CHEK2, NF1 and Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair genes) confer moderate risk. Carney complex is associated with myxoid fibroadenomas and ductal adenomas. Germline testing follows established clinical criteria, and BRCA-associated tumours may be eligible for PARP inhibitor therapy. Pathologists can flag suggestive morphology, especially triple-negative carcinoma with a medullary pattern in young women and carcinoma in men.
entities.cyto: Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes, such as BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53, PALB2, PTEN and CDH1, are a genetic diagnosis made by germline testing, not by cytology. Cytology of lesions in these patients is reported in the same way as in sporadic cases. BRCA1-associated carcinomas are often high-grade, triple-negative NST carcinomas with marked pleomorphism, necrosis and lymphocytic infiltrate on FNA, while CDH1-associated tumours are lobular. In high-risk patients a benign or atypical cytology should be correlated carefully with MRI and imaging, and there should be a low threshold for core biopsy. Yokohama categories apply to the lesion sampled, not to the syndrome.
entities.ihc: Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes are diagnosed by germline testing, not IHC, but tumour phenotype can suggest them. BRCA1-associated tumours are usually high grade, triple-negative and basal-like (CK5/6+, EGFR+), with medullary-like features and dense TILs. BRCA2 and PALB2 tumours are usually ER-positive. CDH1 germline variants give lobular carcinoma (E-cadherin loss) and diffuse gastric cancer. TP53 (Li-Fraumeni) tumours are often HER2-positive at young age. PTEN (Cowden) tumours may show PTEN loss on IHC. MMR deficiency (Lynch) can be screened with MLH1, PMS2, MSH2 and MSH6 IHC. Germline BRCA testing guides PARP inhibitor therapy (olaparib).

entities.variants: BRCA1-associated (triple-negative, basal-like, high grade); BRCA2-associated (luminal, ER-positive; male breast cancer); associated ovarian, prostatic and pancreatic cancers
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: covered within the single row 'Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes'. WHO 6th ed (beta) lists it as a separate genetic tumour syndrome entity. Highest-penetrance hereditary breast cancer genes; lifetime breast cancer risk roughly 60-70%; tumours eligible for PARP inhibitors; risk-reducing surgery specimens may show occult carcinoma or in situ disease.
entities.histo: BRCA-related cancer predisposition is caused by germline pathogenic variants in BRCA1 or BRCA2, which impair homologous recombination DNA repair. Carriers have a high lifetime risk of breast cancer and also risks of ovarian, fallopian tube, prostatic and pancreatic cancer. BRCA1-associated carcinomas are typically high-grade invasive carcinomas of no special type with a solid, syncytial growth pattern, pushing margins, geographic necrosis, high mitotic activity and prominent tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, often with medullary-like features, and they occur at a young age. BRCA2-associated carcinomas resemble sporadic luminal tumours, are usually ER-positive, and account for a large share of male breast cancers. Risk-reducing mastectomy specimens are sampled carefully and may reveal occult DCIS, lobular neoplasia or small invasive carcinomas. Pathologists play a role by recognising suggestive triple-negative morphology in young women and recommending germline testing.
entities.cyto: Cytology does not diagnose BRCA status, which is established by germline testing. FNA of BRCA1-associated carcinoma typically shows highly cellular smears of large, markedly pleomorphic cells in syncytial groups and singly, with high mitotic activity, necrosis and many lymphocytes, which can resemble lymphoma or medullary-type carcinoma. BRCA2-associated tumours resemble sporadic luminal carcinomas, with dyscohesive groups of moderately atypical cells. In carriers under high-risk surveillance, small MRI-detected lesions are usually sampled by core biopsy, and benign or atypical FNA results need careful correlation with imaging. Lesions are categorised in the Yokohama system according to what is sampled, typically Category 5 (Malignant) for carcinoma.
entities.ihc: No immunostain identifies a germline BRCA variant, but the phenotype is a useful pointer. BRCA1-associated carcinomas are usually triple-negative (ER, PR and HER2 negative) and basal-like, expressing CK5/6, CK14, CK17 and EGFR, with diffuse p53 aberration and a high Ki-67 index, while dense CD3/CD8-rich lymphocytic infiltrates are common. BRCA2-associated carcinomas are mostly ER-positive and PR-positive and HER2-negative. Loss of BRCA1 protein on IHC is not reliable and is not used clinically. Homologous recombination deficiency assays and germline sequencing are the definitive tests, and confirmed carriers with HER2-negative early or metastatic disease may receive PARP inhibitors such as olaparib.

entities.variants: Cowden syndrome; Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome; breast hamartomas, multiple intraductal papillomas, fibroadenomas and fibrocystic change; dense fibrous stromal lesions
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: covered within the single row 'Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes'. WHO 6th ed (beta) lists it as a separate genetic tumour syndrome entity. Germline PTEN variants; lifetime breast cancer risk up to about 85% in some series; also thyroid, endometrial and renal cancer, trichilemmomas and macrocephaly; multiple benign breast lesions can be a clue.
entities.histo: PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome results from germline loss-of-function variants in PTEN, a negative regulator of the PI3K-AKT pathway. It includes Cowden syndrome and Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome. The breast is commonly affected, with multiple and bilateral benign lesions such as hamartomas, intraductal papillomas, fibroadenomas, adenosis, apocrine metaplasia and dense hyalinised fibrous nodules, sometimes called Cowden-associated stromal lesions, often at a young age. The risk of breast carcinoma is high, and both invasive carcinoma of no special type, often with apocrine features, and DCIS occur. Other features include thyroid follicular neoplasms and carcinoma, endometrial carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps, mucocutaneous trichilemmomas, papillomatous papules and macrocephaly. Pathologists should consider the syndrome when they see multiple hamartomatous or papillary breast lesions in a young patient, especially with a relevant personal or family history.
entities.cyto: There is no specific cytological marker of PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome. Aspirates of its benign breast lesions resemble their sporadic counterparts: fibroadenomas give cohesive staghorn sheets, bare nuclei and stromal fragments, papillomas give papillary clusters with foamy macrophages, and hamartomas give a mixture of benign ductal epithelium, fat and fibrous stroma that can be read as nondiagnostic or benign. Apocrine cells are frequent. Because these patients have multiple lesions and a high cancer risk, any atypical or suspicious finding warrants core biopsy. Lesions are categorised in the Yokohama system on their own merits, usually Category 2 (Benign) for the hamartomatous lesions.
entities.ihc: PTEN immunohistochemistry can show complete loss of PTEN protein in the lesions of affected patients, with retained staining in internal controls such as endothelial and stromal cells, and loss in both benign and malignant lesions supports a germline cause. However, PTEN loss is also common in sporadic carcinomas, so it is a screening clue rather than a diagnosis, and germline sequencing is required. Breast carcinomas in Cowden syndrome are usually ER-positive and PR-positive, and some show apocrine differentiation with AR and GCDFP-15 positivity. Myoepithelial markers help to confirm the benign nature of papillary and sclerosing lesions. Interpretation of PTEN staining should use validated antibodies and careful control assessment.

entities.entity: Ataxia-telangiectasia and ATM-related breast cancer predisposition
entities.variants: Biallelic ATM (ataxia-telangiectasia: cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, lymphoma/leukaemia); monoallelic heterozygous ATM carriers (moderate breast cancer risk)
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: covered within the single row 'Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes'. WHO 6th ed (beta) lists it as a separate genetic tumour syndrome entity. Moderate-penetrance gene in heterozygotes (about 2-fold risk, roughly 20-30% lifetime); tumours mostly ER-positive; radiosensitivity concerns in biallelic patients; included in standard multigene panels.
entities.histo: ATM encodes a kinase that senses DNA double-strand breaks and activates checkpoint and repair pathways. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause ataxia-telangiectasia, a childhood disorder with progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, radiosensitivity and a high risk of lymphoid malignancies. Heterozygous carriers, who are far more common, have a moderately increased risk of breast cancer, and also of pancreatic and prostatic cancer. ATM-associated breast carcinomas have no distinctive morphology. Most are invasive carcinomas of no special type, often ER-positive, luminal and of intermediate to high grade, and lobular carcinomas also occur. DCIS is frequent in carriers undergoing screening. The diagnosis is genetic, made through multigene panel testing, and pathology is reported in the usual way. Some evidence suggests a higher risk of contralateral cancer in carriers.
entities.cyto: ATM status cannot be determined by cytology. Breast lesions in carriers are aspirated and reported as for sporadic disease. Carcinomas usually resemble luminal invasive carcinoma of no special type, with dyscohesive groups, single intact atypical cells, moderate pleomorphism and no bare bipolar nuclei, while lobular carcinomas give small, single, discohesive cells and intracytoplasmic lumina. In patients with ataxia-telangiectasia, lymphadenopathy or breast masses may represent lymphoma, so lymphoid-rich aspirates should be sent for flow cytometry. Yokohama categories apply to the sampled lesion, and core biopsy is preferred for receptor testing.
entities.ihc: There is no validated immunostain for ATM-related predisposition in routine breast pathology. ATM protein loss on IHC has been studied in research but is not used clinically, and germline sequencing establishes the diagnosis. Carcinomas in heterozygous carriers are mostly ER-positive and PR-positive, with variable HER2 status, and are tested with standard ER, PR, HER2 and Ki-67 according to ASCO/CAP guidance. Triple-negative tumours are less frequent than in BRCA1 carriers. In patients with biallelic ATM deficiency, lymphoid lesions require a full lymphoma panel, including CD3, CD20, CD10, BCL6, TdT and Ki-67, together with flow cytometry and clonality studies.

entities.variants: Classic Li-Fraumeni syndrome; Li-Fraumeni-like syndrome; early-onset breast cancer (often HER2-positive); associated sarcomas, adrenocortical carcinoma, brain tumours, leukaemia; phyllodes tumour association reported
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: covered within the single row 'Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes'. WHO 6th ed (beta) lists it as a separate genetic tumour syndrome entity. Germline TP53; breast is the most common cancer in female carriers, often under 35 years; HER2-positive enriched; avoid radiotherapy where possible (radiation-induced second cancers); consider testing in very early-onset breast cancer.
entities.histo: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germline pathogenic TP53 variants and confers a very high lifetime cancer risk from childhood. The core tumours are breast carcinoma, soft tissue and bone sarcomas, adrenocortical carcinoma, brain tumours and leukaemia. Breast cancer is the most common malignancy in female carriers and typically appears before the age of 35. The carcinomas are usually invasive carcinomas of no special type, high grade, and they are frequently HER2-amplified, with a high frequency of associated DCIS, which is often also HER2-positive. Phyllodes tumours and sarcomas of the breast have also been reported. Because carriers are highly sensitive to radiation-induced cancers, mastectomy is often preferred over breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy. Pathologists should suggest germline testing when HER2-positive breast cancer occurs at a very young age or with a personal or family history of sarcoma or other core cancers.
entities.cyto: Li-Fraumeni syndrome cannot be recognised on cytology. Breast carcinomas in carriers give cellular aspirates of high-grade, pleomorphic malignant cells in dyscohesive groups and singly, with necrosis and mitoses, and are usually reported as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant). Spindle cell or pleomorphic aspirates in a carrier should raise the possibility of a sarcoma or malignant phyllodes tumour, which need histology. Because of the young age of patients, benign mimics such as fibroadenoma and lactational change are common, and any atypia should lead to core biopsy. Ancillary studies are performed on core material.
entities.ihc: Germline TP53 status is not determined by immunohistochemistry, although p53 staining of the tumour may show an aberrant pattern, either diffuse strong nuclear overexpression or complete null staining, reflecting somatic or germline alteration. This is not specific for the syndrome, since sporadic high-grade carcinomas show the same patterns. The characteristic finding is frequent HER2 positivity, so HER2 testing by IHC and in situ hybridisation according to ASCO/CAP is particularly important, alongside ER, PR and Ki-67. Associated DCIS is often HER2-positive as well. Germline sequencing confirms the diagnosis, and carriers need lifelong whole-body surveillance.

entities.variants: CHEK2 c.1100delC and other truncating variants; missense variants (lower risk); associated male breast, prostatic, colorectal and thyroid cancers
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: covered within the single row 'Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes'. WHO 6th ed (beta) lists it as a separate genetic tumour syndrome entity. Moderate-penetrance gene (about 2- to 3-fold risk for truncating variants); tumours predominantly ER-positive; higher risk of contralateral cancer; risk modified by family history and polygenic score.
entities.histo: CHEK2 encodes a checkpoint kinase activated by ATM in response to DNA damage. Germline truncating variants, especially the c.1100delC founder allele common in Northern and Eastern Europe, confer a moderate increase in breast cancer risk, while missense variants confer a smaller increase. CHEK2-associated breast carcinomas have no specific morphology. They are mostly invasive carcinomas of no special type, usually ER-positive and luminal, with a tendency toward higher grade than sporadic luminal tumours, and invasive lobular carcinomas also occur. There is an increased risk of bilateral and contralateral breast cancer and of male breast cancer. The diagnosis is made by germline multigene panel testing. Pathology reports follow the standard format, and management integrates the variant type with family history and polygenic risk.
entities.cyto: Cytology cannot identify CHEK2 carriers. Breast carcinomas in these patients are aspirated and categorised as for sporadic tumours, and most resemble luminal invasive carcinoma of no special type, with dyscohesive clusters, single intact atypical epithelial cells and an absence of bare bipolar nuclei. In men with CHEK2 variants, subareolar masses must be distinguished from gynaecomastia, which gives cohesive sheets with myoepithelial cells. Yokohama categories apply to the sampled lesion, and core biopsy is preferred for prognostic markers.
entities.ihc: There is no immunohistochemical marker of CHEK2 status. Carcinomas in CHEK2 carriers are predominantly ER-positive and PR-positive and HER2-negative, so a luminal phenotype on standard ER, PR, HER2 and Ki-67 testing is typical, and triple-negative tumours are uncommon. Testing follows ASCO/CAP guidelines. Unlike BRCA1/2 and PALB2, CHEK2 is not currently an established indication for PARP inhibitor therapy. The diagnosis rests on germline sequencing, ideally with variant classification by an accredited genetics laboratory.

entities.entity: Hereditary diffuse gastric and lobular breast cancer syndrome (CDH1, CTNNA1)
entities.variants: CDH1 germline (hereditary diffuse gastric cancer and invasive lobular breast cancer); CTNNA1 germline (mainly diffuse gastric cancer); hereditary lobular breast cancer without gastric cancer; LCIS in carriers
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: covered within the single row 'Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes'. WHO 6th ed (beta) lists it as a separate genetic tumour syndrome entity. Germline CDH1 confers a lifetime lobular breast cancer risk around 40%; consider testing in bilateral or early-onset ILC or with a family history of diffuse gastric cancer; prophylactic gastrectomy is discussed with carriers.
entities.histo: This syndrome is caused by germline pathogenic variants in CDH1, which encodes E-cadherin, or less often CTNNA1, which encodes alpha-E-catenin. Both genes are essential for cell-cell adhesion. Carriers have a high risk of hereditary diffuse (signet ring cell) gastric cancer, and female CDH1 carriers have a substantial risk of invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast, often bilateral and diagnosed at a younger age. Some families have lobular breast cancer without gastric cancer. The breast carcinomas show classic or pleomorphic lobular morphology, with small discohesive cells in single files and targetoid arrays and frequent intracytoplasmic lumina, often accompanied by lobular carcinoma in situ, which may be extensive. Pathologists should consider the syndrome in bilateral or early-onset invasive lobular carcinoma, or in lobular carcinoma with a personal or family history of diffuse gastric cancer, and recommend germline testing and gastric surveillance or prophylactic gastrectomy.
entities.cyto: Cytology does not establish the germline diagnosis. Aspirates of lobular carcinoma in carriers are often only moderately cellular, with small, monotonous, discohesive cells singly and in loose groups, eccentric nuclei, intracytoplasmic lumina or signet ring forms, and a few bare nuclei, which leads to frequent under-calling. Pleomorphic lobular carcinoma gives larger, more atypical cells. In a known carrier, small-cell discohesive aspirates should be regarded as suspicious, and metastatic gastric signet ring cell carcinoma should be excluded in the axilla or breast. Most cases are reported as Yokohama Category 4 (Suspicious) or Category 5 (Malignant), with core biopsy for confirmation.
entities.ihc: E-cadherin immunohistochemistry is central to the diagnosis of lobular neoplasia: it shows complete loss of membranous staining in lobular carcinoma and LCIS, with aberrant cytoplasmic p120 catenin and loss of membranous beta-catenin staining. In CTNNA1-related cases, E-cadherin may be retained while alpha-catenin staining is lost. These findings confirm lobular differentiation but do not distinguish germline from somatic alterations, so germline sequencing is needed. The carcinomas are usually ER-positive and PR-positive and HER2-negative, with low Ki-67 in classic cases. GATA3 and TRPS1 support breast origin against metastatic gastric signet ring cell carcinoma, which is usually CDX2-positive and CK20-positive and lacks ER.

entities.variants: PALB2 truncating variants (heterozygous); biallelic PALB2 (Fanconi anaemia complementation group N); associated pancreatic, ovarian and male breast cancer
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: covered within the single row 'Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes'. WHO 6th ed (beta) lists it as a separate genetic tumour syndrome entity. High- to moderate-penetrance gene (lifetime breast cancer risk about 35-50%, higher with strong family history); tumours often triple-negative or ER-positive high grade; carriers may benefit from PARP inhibitors.
entities.histo: PALB2 encodes a partner of BRCA2 that links BRCA1 and BRCA2 in homologous recombination repair. Heterozygous pathogenic variants confer a breast cancer risk approaching that of BRCA2, together with increased risks of pancreatic, ovarian and male breast cancer, while biallelic variants cause a severe form of Fanconi anaemia. PALB2-associated breast carcinomas are mostly invasive carcinomas of no special type, often of high grade. Many are ER-positive, but triple-negative tumours are over-represented compared with sporadic cancer, and some show the solid growth, pushing borders and lymphocytic infiltrate also seen in BRCA1-related tumours. There is no pathognomonic morphology, and the diagnosis is made by germline testing. Pathologists may prompt testing in young patients with triple-negative or high-grade carcinoma, male breast cancer, or a family history of pancreatic cancer.
entities.cyto: Cytology cannot identify PALB2 carriers. Carcinomas in these patients are aspirated and reported as for sporadic disease. High-grade tumours give cellular smears of large pleomorphic cells in syncytial groups and singly, with mitoses, necrosis and lymphocytes, whereas luminal tumours give smaller dyscohesive groups of moderately atypical cells. Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant) is typical for carcinoma, and core biopsy is obtained for receptor and HER2 status. In men, gynaecomastia remains the main benign differential of a subareolar mass.
entities.ihc: There is no immunostain for PALB2. Carcinomas in carriers are tested with standard ER, PR, HER2 and Ki-67 according to ASCO/CAP guidance, and show either a luminal phenotype (ER-positive, often high grade with high Ki-67) or a triple-negative phenotype, which may be basal-like (CK5/6, EGFR positive). Germline sequencing establishes the diagnosis, and homologous recombination deficiency testing may be positive. Confirmed carriers with HER2-negative disease may be considered for PARP inhibitor therapy under current guidelines and trial data.

entities.variants: Germline STK11 (LKB1); gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps; mucocutaneous pigmentation; breast cancer (mostly IBC-NST, ductal); sex-cord tumour with annular tubules, adenoma malignum of cervix, Sertoli cell tumours
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: covered within the single row 'Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes'. WHO 6th ed (beta) lists it as a separate genetic tumour syndrome entity. Autosomal dominant; lifetime breast cancer risk about 30-50%, comparable to BRCA2; earlier onset; surveillance from early adulthood; breast tumours have no specific morphology.
entities.histo: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by germline pathogenic variants in STK11, also called LKB1, a serine-threonine kinase that regulates cell polarity and the mTOR pathway. It is characterised by hamartomatous polyps of the gastrointestinal tract with arborising smooth muscle, mucocutaneous melanin pigmentation of the lips and buccal mucosa, and a high lifetime risk of several cancers. These include gastrointestinal, pancreatic, breast, ovarian (sex cord tumour with annular tubules), cervical (gastric-type adenocarcinoma) and testicular (large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumour) cancers. Breast cancer risk is substantial, and it often appears at a younger age than sporadic cancer. The breast carcinomas are mostly invasive carcinomas of no special type and DCIS, without a distinctive histological signature. The diagnosis rests on the clinical criteria and germline testing, and the pathologist's role is to recognise the syndrome from its extramammary lesions.
entities.cyto: There are no specific cytological features of breast lesions in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Breast carcinomas in carriers give the usual findings of invasive carcinoma of no special type: dyscohesive groups, single intact atypical cells, nuclear pleomorphism and absence of bare bipolar nuclei, with reporting as Yokohama Category 5 (Malignant) when diagnostic. Because carriers are younger and under surveillance, benign lesions such as fibroadenoma are frequent in the differential. Atypical results should lead to core biopsy, and cytology has no role in confirming the syndrome itself.
entities.ihc: No immunostain is used routinely to diagnose Peutz-Jeghers syndrome in breast pathology. Loss of LKB1 protein has been described in some tumours, but this is a research finding and germline sequencing of STK11 establishes the diagnosis. Breast carcinomas in carriers are characterised with standard ER, PR, HER2 and Ki-67 testing according to ASCO/CAP guidelines, and most are hormone receptor positive. GATA3 and TRPS1 help to confirm breast origin when a metastasis from another syndrome-associated site, such as pancreas or ovary, is a possibility.

entities.variants: Germline NF1; breast carcinoma (often before 50, higher grade, more ER-negative and HER2-positive than sporadic); neurofibromas of breast skin and nipple; malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour; GIST and phaeochromocytoma
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: covered within the single row 'Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes'. WHO 6th ed (beta) lists it as a separate genetic tumour syndrome entity. Moderate risk (about 3- to 5-fold under 50 years); earlier onset and worse survival reported; screening from age 30 recommended in many guidelines; neurofibromas may complicate imaging.
entities.histo: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by germline loss-of-function variants in NF1, which encodes neurofibromin, a negative regulator of RAS signalling. Clinical features include café-au-lait macules, axillary and inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules, cutaneous and plexiform neurofibromas, optic gliomas, and risks of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour, gastrointestinal stromal tumour and phaeochromocytoma. Women with NF1 have a moderately increased risk of breast cancer, especially before the age of 50, and their carcinomas tend to be of higher grade, with a higher proportion of ER-negative and HER2-positive tumours than sporadic cancer. The breast carcinomas are mostly invasive carcinomas of no special type, without specific morphology. Neurofibromas of the breast skin, nipple and areola are common and can mimic other masses. The diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by genetic testing, and somatic NF1 alterations are also found in some sporadic, treatment-resistant breast cancers.
entities.cyto: Cytology does not diagnose NF1, but it helps separate the common benign lesions from carcinoma. Aspirates of neurofibroma give scant cellularity with wavy, bland spindle cells in a myxoid or fibrillary background, and they may be read as nondiagnostic or benign, whereas pleomorphic or mitotically active spindle cells should raise concern for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour. Breast carcinomas in NF1 give the usual dyscohesive groups and single atypical epithelial cells, often high grade. Yokohama categories apply to the lesion sampled, and core biopsy is recommended for any atypical or suspicious result.
entities.ihc: There is no routine immunostain for germline NF1 status. Breast carcinomas in NF1 patients are characterised with ER, PR, HER2 and Ki-67 according to ASCO/CAP guidance, and are more often ER-negative or HER2-positive and of higher proliferative index than sporadic carcinomas. Associated neurofibromas are S100-positive and SOX10-positive in a subset of cells, with CD34-positive fibroblasts and neurofilament-positive axons. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour shows patchy or lost S100 and SOX10 and loss of H3K27me3 in many cases. Germline sequencing confirms the syndrome.

entities.entity: Polygenic component of breast cancer susceptibility
entities.variants: Polygenic risk score (PRS) from common low-risk SNPs; combination with moderate-penetrance genes (CHEK2, ATM) and family history; ER-positive and ER-negative specific scores
entities.remarks: WHO 5th: covered within the single row 'Hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes'. WHO 6th ed (beta) lists it as a separate genetic tumour syndrome entity. Not a histological entity; hundreds of common variants each with small effect combine into a PRS that stratifies risk; used in research and some clinical risk models (e.g. CanRisk/BOADICEA); listed for completeness.
entities.histo: The polygenic component of breast cancer susceptibility refers to the combined effect of many common genetic variants, each conferring a very small increase in risk, which together account for a sizeable proportion of familial breast cancer not explained by high- or moderate-penetrance genes. Genome-wide association studies have identified hundreds of such single nucleotide polymorphisms, and their weighted sum forms a polygenic risk score. Women in the highest percentiles of the score have a risk comparable to carriers of moderate-penetrance variants, and the score also modifies the risk in BRCA2, CHEK2 and ATM carriers. There is no associated morphology. Breast carcinomas arising in women with high polygenic risk are histologically indistinguishable from sporadic tumours, with a predominance of ER-positive invasive carcinoma of no special type and lobular carcinoma, and they are reported in the standard way. The concept matters for risk prediction models and screening.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in assessing the polygenic component of breast cancer susceptibility. Lesions in women with high polygenic risk scores are aspirated and categorised exactly as in the general population, using the Yokohama system for the specific lesion sampled. High-risk status may lower the threshold for core biopsy of indeterminate imaging findings, but cytological criteria do not change. The polygenic risk score is derived from germline DNA genotyping, usually from blood or saliva, not from tumour or cytology samples.
entities.ihc: There is no immunohistochemical correlate of polygenic breast cancer risk. Carcinomas in women with a high polygenic risk score are tested with ER, PR, HER2 and Ki-67 according to ASCO/CAP guidelines, as for any breast cancer, and most are ER-positive. Separate polygenic scores have been developed for ER-positive and ER-negative disease, but these are germline genotype measures and are not inferred from tumour staining. IHC is relevant only for the characterisation of the individual tumour.

entities.entity: Carcinoma of unknown primary presenting with axillary nodal metastasis (occult breast primary)
entities.remarks: Axillary nodal adenocarcinoma with occult breast primary (GATA3/TRPS1/ER/mammaglobin+); MRI breast; managed as stage II breast cancer. Not listed as a separate entity in WHO 6th ed (beta) TOC.
entities.histo: Carcinoma of unknown primary presenting with axillary nodal metastasis is diagnosed when an adenocarcinoma or poorly differentiated carcinoma is found in axillary lymph nodes without a clinically or mammographically detectable breast primary. In women this usually represents an occult breast carcinoma. Microscopically the node shows metastatic carcinoma, often IBC-NST-like, sometimes lobular, apocrine or poorly differentiated, with possible extranodal extension. IHC supports a breast origin when GATA3, TRPS1, ER, PR, mammaglobin or GCDFP-15 are positive, and HER2 status is assessed for treatment. Exclusion of other primaries requires markers such as TTF-1 (lung), PAX8 (ovary or kidney), CDX2 (gastrointestinal tract) and SOX10 (melanoma), as well as consideration of lymphoma and skin adnexal carcinoma. Breast MRI detects the primary in a substantial proportion of cases. Mastectomy or whole-breast radiotherapy specimens may reveal small or multifocal carcinomas, and careful sampling is required. Management follows that of node-positive (stage II) breast cancer, with axillary dissection, systemic therapy and breast treatment.
entities.cyto: In carcinoma of unknown primary presenting with axillary nodal metastasis (occult breast primary), FNA of the axillary node shows malignant epithelial cells, often in dyscohesive groups and single cells, with morphology resembling breast carcinoma NST or lobular carcinoma, sometimes with intracytoplasmic lumina, in a lymphoid background. Cell block immunochemistry is essential: GATA3, ER, PR, mammaglobin, SOX10 and TRPS1 support a breast origin, while TTF-1, PAX8, CDX2 and others help exclude alternatives; HER2 testing is also possible. Breast MRI is used to search for the primary. Reported as malignant, metastatic carcinoma consistent with breast origin, using the Sydney System for lymph node cytology.
entities.ihc: For carcinoma of unknown primary presenting with axillary nodal metastasis, IHC is used to confirm an occult breast primary. Breast origin is supported by TRPS1 positivity, GATA3 positivity, ER and PR positivity, mammaglobin and GCDFP-15 positivity, CK7 positivity and CK20 negativity, with SOX10 often positive in triple-negative tumours. Lung (TTF-1, napsin A), melanoma (S100, SOX10, Melan-A), skin adnexal carcinoma and ovarian (PAX8, WT1) primaries must be excluded. Apocrine tumours are AR+ and GCDFP-15+. ER, PR and HER2 testing per ASCO/CAP and Ki-67 on the nodal metastasis guide treatment as for breast cancer, and breast MRI usually localises the primary. CK5/6 or p40 positivity raises the possibility of squamous carcinoma.

entities.variants: Rosai-Dorfman disease (S100+ histiocytes showing emperipolesis); Langerhans cell histiocytosis; Erdheim-Chester disease
entities.remarks: Rare; Rosai-Dorfman disease of breast mimics carcinoma or mastitis clinically; classified as histiocytic neoplasms in WHO Haematolymphoid 5th ed. Not listed as a separate entity in WHO 6th ed (beta) TOC.
entities.histo: Histiocytic neoplasms of the breast are rare and are classified according to WHO Haematolymphoid Tumours, 5th edition. Rosai-Dorfman disease is the commonest. It presents as a firm, painless breast mass, with or without lymphadenopathy, and mimics carcinoma or mastitis clinically. Microscopically, it shows alternating pale and dark areas. The pale areas are sheets of large histiocytes with abundant pale cytoplasm and round vesicular nuclei with nucleoli, which show emperipolesis of lymphocytes and plasma cells. The dark areas are lymphoid aggregates and plasma cells, accompanied by fibrosis. The histiocytes are positive for S100, CD68, CD163 and OCT2, and negative for CD1a and langerin, and plasma cells may be IgG4-rich. Langerhans cell histiocytosis shows Langerhans cells with grooved, folded nuclei and eosinophils, positive for CD1a, langerin and S100, often with BRAF V600E mutations. Erdheim-Chester disease shows foamy CD68-positive, CD1a-negative and S100-negative histiocytes with Touton giant cells and fibrosis, and is BRAF-mutated. Differentials include fat necrosis, granulomatous mastitis, IgG4-related mastitis, granular cell tumour, lymphoma and histiocytoid carcinoma, which is keratin-positive.
entities.cyto: Histiocytic neoplasms of the breast are rare. In Rosai-Dorfman disease, aspirates show numerous large histiocytes with abundant pale cytoplasm and round vesicular nuclei, showing emperipolesis of lymphocytes and plasma cells, in a lymphoplasmacytic background; the histiocytes are S100 and CD68/CD163 positive and CD1a negative. Langerhans cell histiocytosis shows grooved, folded Langerhans cells with eosinophils (CD1a, langerin, S100 positive). Erdheim-Chester disease shows foamy histiocytes with Touton giant cells and fibrosis. Differentials include granulomatous mastitis, fat necrosis, lymphoma and lipid-rich carcinoma. Reported as Yokohama Category 2 (Benign) or Category 3 with a comment suggesting the entity, and immunochemistry on cell block.
entities.ihc: Histiocytic neoplasms of the breast are diagnosed with IHC. Rosai–Dorfman disease shows large histiocytes with emperipolesis that are S100 positive, CD68 positive, CD163 positive and OCT2 positive, with nuclear cyclin D1, CD1a negativity and langerin (CD207) negativity, in a plasma-cell-rich background in which IgG4-positive cells may be increased. Langerhans cell histiocytosis is CD1a positive, langerin positive and S100 positive, and often BRAF V600E mutated (VE1 IHC). Erdheim–Chester disease shows foamy histiocytes that are CD68+, CD163+ and factor XIIIa+, with CD1a and S100 negative or weak, and BRAF V600E or MAP2K1 mutations. All are keratin negative, which separates them from histiocytoid or lobular carcinoma, the key clinical and morphological mimic.

entities.variants: Stages: congestion; red hepatisation; grey hepatisation; resolution. Organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae (commonest); Klebsiella pneumoniae; Legionella; Haemophilus influenzae (less often lobar). Complications: abscess, empyema, organisation (carnification), bacteraemia
entities.remarks: Consolidation of a whole lobe or large part of it; classic community-acquired pattern; Gram stain and culture, urinary antigen; autopsy rather than biopsy diagnosis.
entities.histo: Lobar pneumonia is a confluent fibrinosuppurative consolidation of a large part or all of a lobe, classically caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. Grossly the lobe passes through four stages. In congestion the lung is heavy, red and boggy, with vascular engorgement, intra-alveolar oedema fluid and scattered neutrophils and abundant bacteria. In red hepatisation the lobe is red, firm and airless like liver, and alveoli are packed with neutrophils, red cells and fibrin. In grey hepatisation red cells lyse and the cut surface turns grey-brown and dry, with a persisting fibrinosuppurative exudate. In resolution the exudate is digested enzymatically and cleared by macrophages, restoring normal architecture because the alveolar walls remain intact. Overlying fibrinous pleuritis is common. Failure to resolve gives organising pneumonia (carnification) with Masson bodies, and complications include abscess, empyema and bacteraemic spread. Differentials include bronchopneumonia (patchy, bronchiolocentric), Legionella pneumonia, invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma presenting as lobar consolidation, and organising pneumonia.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. Sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) shows abundant neutrophils, fibrin and necrotic debris, sometimes with Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci on Gram stain. Reactive bronchial cells and type II pneumocytes with enlarged nuclei and nucleoli can be atypical and must not be overcalled as carcinoma in an inflammatory background. Material should go for Gram stain and culture. Persistent consolidation in a non-resolving pneumonia should prompt cytological or histological exclusion of invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (acute inflammation), with microbiology correlation.
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role in lobar pneumonia, and diagnosis rests on morphology, Gram stain and culture. Tissue Gram stain (Brown-Brenn or Brown-Hopps) highlights Gram-positive diplococci; GMS and Ziehl-Neelsen help exclude fungi and mycobacteria in atypical cases. Pneumococcal antigen detection is done on urine rather than tissue. In a non-resolving consolidation, TTF-1, CK7, CK20 and mucin stains on a biopsy help to exclude invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma (usually TTF-1 negative, CK7 positive, often CK20 and HNF4-alpha positive).

entities.variants: Community-acquired bronchopneumonia; hospital-acquired (nosocomial) pneumonia; ventilator-associated pneumonia; terminal bronchopneumonia; confluent bronchopneumonia. Organisms: Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Gram-negative bacilli (Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Escherichia coli, Acinetobacter), Bordetella pertussis
entities.remarks: Patchy, bronchiolocentric, often bilateral and basal consolidation; extremes of age, debility, aspiration, ventilation; common autopsy finding.
entities.histo: Bronchopneumonia is patchy consolidation centred on bronchioles and spreading into adjacent alveoli, usually bilateral and basal, reflecting dependent distribution. Grossly there are multiple firm, grey-red to yellow, slightly raised nodules 3 to 4 cm across, which may become confluent (confluent bronchopneumonia). Microscopically bronchioles and surrounding alveoli contain a neutrophil-rich exudate with fibrin, oedema and haemorrhage, with intervening relatively spared lung. Bronchiolar walls are inflamed and may ulcerate. Staphylococcal and Gram-negative infections (Klebsiella, Pseudomonas) are prone to necrosis and microabscesses, and Pseudomonas may show vasculitis with bacterial cuffing of vessel walls. Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia often coexists with diffuse alveolar damage, aspiration and organisation. Pertussis gives necrotising bronchiolitis. Healing occurs by resolution or organisation. Differentials include aspiration pneumonia (food particles, mixed flora), lobar pneumonia (uniform lobar involvement), diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes, and haemorrhagic or neoplastic consolidation.
entities.cyto: Sputum, endotracheal aspirate and BAL show many neutrophils with debris, bacteria and fibrin. Quality is judged by the ratio of neutrophils to squamous cells (many squamous cells indicate oral contamination). Reactive bronchial epithelium and repair atypia may mimic carcinoma; cohesive flat sheets with orderly nuclei and an inflammatory background favour a reactive process. Microbiology (Gram stain, culture with sensitivity) drives management. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (acute inflammatory process), or Atypical when repair changes are marked.
entities.ihc: IHC has no routine diagnostic role. Tissue Gram stain separates Gram-positive cocci (staphylococci, streptococci) from Gram-negative bacilli; GMS and acid-fast stains exclude fungi and mycobacteria, and Warthin-Starry or Dieterle silver stains can show Legionella. Viral IHC (CMV, HSV, adenovirus) is helpful when inclusions or necrotising bronchiolitis suggest viral co-infection, especially in ventilated or immunocompromised patients. Molecular panels on BAL have largely replaced tissue stains for organism identification.

entities.variants: Post-influenza staphylococcal pneumonia; community-acquired MRSA necrotising (Panton-Valentine leukocidin) pneumonia; septic (haematogenous) pulmonary emboli from right-sided endocarditis; nosocomial; pneumatocoeles in children
entities.remarks: Necrotising bronchopneumonia with abscesses and pneumatocoeles; complicates influenza; PVL-positive strains cause haemorrhagic necrotising pneumonia in young adults.
entities.histo: Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia is a necrotising bronchopneumonia that typically complicates influenza, intravenous drug use (septic emboli), cystic fibrosis or hospitalisation. Grossly the lungs show multiple confluent haemorrhagic consolidations with small abscesses, cavitation and, in children, thin-walled pneumatocoeles; empyema and pyopneumothorax are common. Septic emboli produce multiple peripheral, wedge-shaped haemorrhagic infarcts that cavitate. Microscopically the bronchioles and alveoli are filled with neutrophils and Gram-positive cocci in clusters, with liquefactive necrosis destroying alveolar walls, haemorrhage and fibrin. Panton-Valentine leukocidin-positive strains cause extensive haemorrhagic necrosis of the airway mucosa and alveoli with relatively few neutrophils because the toxin kills leucocytes. Post-influenza cases may show coexisting diffuse alveolar damage and necrotising tracheobronchitis. Differentials include other necrotising pneumonias (Klebsiella, anaerobes, Pseudomonas), invasive fungal infection, GPA and septic emboli from other organisms.
entities.cyto: Cytology is not used for diagnosis but sputum, BAL or aspirates from abscesses show purulent material with abundant neutrophils, necrotic debris and Gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters, often intracellular. Lack of malignant cells and a purely suppurative background distinguish it from necrotic carcinoma, although squamous cell carcinoma with cavitation can coexist with infection, so atypical keratinised cells must be assessed carefully. Culture and sensitivity (MRSA screening) are essential. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (acute inflammation/abscess material).
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role. Gram stain on tissue shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters within necrotic exudate; GMS and Ziehl-Neelsen are used to exclude fungal and mycobacterial infection in cavitating lesions. Influenza A IHC can confirm viral co-infection in fatal post-influenza cases. Elastic stains show destruction of alveolar walls in necrotising areas. Keratin and p40 staining help only when a cavitating squamous cell carcinoma is a differential diagnosis.

entities.entity: Klebsiella, Pseudomonas and other Gram-negative bacillary pneumonias
entities.variants: Klebsiella pneumoniae (Friedlander pneumonia; lobar with bulging fissure, mucoid exudate); Pseudomonas aeruginosa (nosocomial, ventilator, cystic fibrosis, neutropenia; necrotising vasculitic pneumonia); Escherichia coli; Acinetobacter baumannii; Enterobacter; Serratia; Stenotrophomonas; Haemophilus influenzae; Moraxella catarrhalis
entities.remarks: Common in alcoholics, diabetics, ventilated and neutropenic patients; necrosis, abscess and cavitation frequent; Pseudomonas shows perivascular bacterial cuffing and vascular necrosis.
entities.histo: Gram-negative bacillary pneumonias are largely hospital-acquired, affecting ventilated, neutropenic, diabetic or alcoholic patients and those with cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis. Klebsiella pneumoniae causes a lobar or bronchopneumonic consolidation with a thick, gelatinous, mucoid exudate due to the capsule, bulging of fissures and rapid necrosis and abscess formation; healing often leaves fibrosis. Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces a necrotising bronchopneumonia with haemorrhagic nodules; a characteristic feature in neutropenic patients is a necrotising vasculitis in which bacilli massively cuff the adventitia and media of vessels, with surrounding coagulative necrosis and haemorrhage and a sparse neutrophil response. In cystic fibrosis, mucoid Pseudomonas forms biofilms in bronchiectatic airways. Acinetobacter and other Enterobacterales give bronchopneumonia with microabscesses. Differentials include staphylococcal and anaerobic necrotising pneumonia, angioinvasive aspergillosis or mucormycosis (hyphae within vessels), and infarcts.
entities.cyto: Cytology is rarely diagnostic. Respiratory specimens contain neutrophils, necrotic debris and Gram-negative rods; Klebsiella may produce thick mucoid material. In ventilated patients, endotracheal aspirates are dominated by inflammatory cells and reactive bronchial epithelium with repair atypia, which is a frequent pitfall for overcalling atypia or malignancy. Quantitative cultures guide antibiotic therapy. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (acute inflammation), or Atypical if reactive changes cannot be separated from neoplasia.
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role and microbiology is the key investigation. Tissue Gram stain shows Gram-negative bacilli, conspicuously cuffing vessel walls in Pseudomonas vasculitis. GMS is essential to exclude angioinvasive moulds that cause similar haemorrhagic infarct-like nodules, and acid-fast stains exclude mycobacteria. Elastic stains highlight vessel wall destruction. No specific immunostains are used routinely; PCR panels on BAL or tissue may identify organisms and resistance genes.

entities.variants: Legionnaires disease (pneumonic); Pontiac fever (non-pneumonic, self-limited); Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 (most common); L. micdadei and others (immunocompromised)
entities.remarks: Water-borne (cooling towers, plumbing); intracellular Gram-negative bacillus; acute fibrinopurulent pneumonia with leukocytoclasis; urinary antigen detects serogroup 1 only.
