entities.histo: Legionella pneumonia is acquired by inhalation of contaminated aerosols from water systems and affects older smokers, those with chronic lung disease and the immunosuppressed. Grossly there is lobar or multilobar consolidation, often with small abscesses and pleuritis. Microscopically alveoli are filled with fibrin, neutrophils and macrophages, with conspicuous leukocytoclasis (nuclear dust from degenerating neutrophils) that gives a dirty, granular exudate. Alveolar walls may undergo necrosis, and there is often accompanying necrotising bronchiolitis, vasculitis, diffuse alveolar damage and later organisation. The organisms are small intracellular and extracellular Gram-negative bacilli seen poorly on routine Gram stain. Differentials include other bacterial pneumonias (more bronchocentric, less karyorrhectic), Mycoplasma and viral pneumonias, and acute fibrinous and organising pneumonia; organisms are best confirmed by culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar, urinary antigen and PCR.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. BAL shows neutrophils, macrophages, fibrin and much nuclear debris. The organisms are not visible on Papanicolaou or Giemsa stains, and the specimen is mainly useful for culture, direct fluorescent antibody testing and PCR. Reactive pneumocytes can appear atypical. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, with recommendation for microbiological correlation.
entities.ihc: Routine IHC is not used, but Legionella-specific immunohistochemistry or immunofluorescence can confirm the organism in tissue where available. Silver impregnation stains (Warthin-Starry, Dieterle) show the slender bacilli within macrophages and exudate far better than Gram stain, on which they stain poorly. GMS and acid-fast stains help exclude fungi and mycobacteria. Molecular methods (PCR) on lavage or tissue are the most sensitive approach and also detect non-pneumophila species not covered by the urinary antigen test.

entities.entity: Atypical pneumonia - Mycoplasma pneumoniae and related organisms
entities.variants: Mycoplasma pneumoniae (walking pneumonia, outbreaks in young adults); Chlamydia (Chlamydophila) pneumoniae; Chlamydia psittaci (psittacosis); Coxiella burnetii (Q fever); viral atypical pneumonias (see viral rows)
entities.remarks: Interstitial (atypical) pneumonia with cold agglutinins (Mycoplasma); lymphoplasmacytic bronchiolitis and interstitial inflammation; rarely biopsied; serology and PCR.
entities.histo: Atypical pneumonia refers to an interstitial and bronchiolar inflammatory process with little alveolar exudate. Mycoplasma pneumoniae infects ciliated airway epithelium and causes a cellular bronchiolitis with a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in bronchiolar walls, intraluminal neutrophils and mucus, and peribronchiolar extension into alveolar septa, which become widened and oedematous with mononuclear cells. Organising pneumonia, diffuse alveolar damage and occasionally constrictive bronchiolitis or bronchiectasis may follow severe cases. Chlamydia pneumoniae and psittacosis cause a similar patchy interstitial pneumonia with alveolar exudates, and Q fever (Coxiella) can produce inflammatory pseudotumour-like nodules with necrosis and granulomas. Grossly the lungs show patchy red-blue congested areas without lobar consolidation. Differentials include viral pneumonias (look for cytopathic effects), hypersensitivity pneumonitis (poorly formed granulomas, chronic course), cellular NSIP and follicular bronchiolitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology is not diagnostic in Mycoplasma and other atypical pneumonias. BAL is typically lymphocyte and macrophage rich with variable neutrophils, and reactive bronchial cells, sometimes with ciliocytophthoria (detached ciliated tufts), may be seen. The organisms are not visible microscopically. The role of cytology is mainly to exclude other infections such as Pneumocystis and to send material for PCR. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC has no routine role. Mycoplasma and Chlamydia are diagnosed by PCR on respiratory samples and serology (cold agglutinins and specific antibodies). Tissue sections are used to exclude other causes: GMS for Pneumocystis and fungi, viral IHC (CMV, HSV, adenovirus, influenza) for viral pneumonias, and acid-fast stains for mycobacteria. CD3, CD20 and CD138 may be used only when a lymphoid-rich infiltrate needs separating from a lymphoproliferative disorder.

entities.variants: Chemical aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome, gastric acid); bacterial aspiration pneumonia (oral anaerobes and mixed flora); particulate (food/vegetable) aspiration pneumonia with granulomas; pill fragment aspiration (crospovidone, microcrystalline cellulose, cellulose); diffuse aspiration bronchiolitis; barium or contrast aspiration; exogenous lipoid pneumonia (separate row)
entities.remarks: Risk factors: impaired consciousness, dysphagia, alcohol, neurological disease; dependent segments (posterior upper lobe, superior lower lobe, right side); foreign material with giant cells is diagnostic.
entities.histo: Aspiration injury depends on what is aspirated. Acid gastric content causes chemical pneumonitis with oedema, haemorrhage and diffuse alveolar damage within hours. Oropharyngeal bacteria, especially anaerobes, cause a necrotising bronchopneumonia that often progresses to abscess, mainly in dependent segments (posterior segments of the upper lobes and superior segments of the lower lobes, more often on the right). Particulate aspiration of food produces a bronchiolocentric acute and organising pneumonia with foreign-body giant cells and granulomas around vegetable matter, which has thick cellulose walls, skeletal muscle fibres or pill excipients. Crospovidone appears as coral-like basophilic material, microcrystalline cellulose as birefringent rod-like crystals, and barium as fine grey-green granules. Diffuse aspiration bronchiolitis shows bronchiolitis with foreign material and giant cells in chronic aspirators. Differentials include infectious granulomatous disease, intravenous talc granulomatosis (intravascular and perivascular particles), sarcoidosis and organising pneumonia of other causes.
entities.cyto: BAL or sputum may show neutrophils, lipid-laden macrophages, vegetable matter with rigid cellulose walls, skeletal muscle, squamous cells and bacterial colonies. Vegetable cells and degenerating food material can mimic atypical or keratinised malignant cells, which is an important pitfall; their refractile walls and lack of nuclear detail help recognition. Lipid-laden macrophages support but do not prove aspiration. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (inflammatory, aspirated material present).
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role in aspiration. Diagnosis relies on recognising foreign material on H&E, polarised light (pill fillers and some excipients are birefringent) and special stains: PAS highlights vegetable cellulose walls, GMS and Gram stains show mixed bacteria and fungi, and oil red O on fresh material shows lipid. Pill fragments are distinguished by their morphology and staining (crospovidone is basophilic and non-birefringent; microcrystalline cellulose is strongly birefringent). Keratin and CD68 only help when separating squamous debris or histiocytes from neoplasia.

entities.variants: Primary (aspiration, anaerobic, mixed flora); secondary (obstruction by tumour or foreign body, septic emboli, post-pneumonic necrotising pneumonia of S. aureus or Klebsiella, extension from subphrenic or liver abscess, infected bulla or cyst); acute vs chronic abscess; amoebic abscess (see parasites)
entities.remarks: Localised suppurative necrosis with cavity; right lung, dependent segments; always exclude underlying carcinoma (especially squamous) in adults.
entities.histo: A lung abscess is a localised area of suppurative necrosis that forms a cavity, typically 2 to 6 cm, often with an air-fluid level. Aspiration of mixed anaerobic oral flora is the commonest cause, so abscesses usually lie in dependent segments of the right lung. Other causes include necrotising pneumonia, septic emboli (multiple, peripheral), bronchial obstruction by tumour or foreign body, and spread from adjacent sites. Grossly the cavity contains pus and necrotic debris and is lined by a shaggy wall. Microscopically there is central liquefactive necrosis surrounded by neutrophils, then granulation tissue and, in chronic abscesses, a thick fibrous wall with chronic inflammation, foamy macrophages and surrounding organising pneumonia. Bronchial communication allows drainage. Complications include empyema, bronchopleural fistula, haemorrhage and brain abscess. The key differential is a cavitating carcinoma (most often squamous cell carcinoma), so walls should be sampled for tumour; other differentials are cavitating tuberculosis, fungal infection, GPA and infected cysts or sequestration.
entities.cyto: FNA or aspirated pus shows abundant neutrophils, necrotic debris, histiocytes and bacteria, often mixed. The main role of cytology is to exclude malignancy in the abscess wall and to provide material for culture. Degenerated squamous cells or reactive, keratinised squamous metaplasia in the wall can mimic squamous cell carcinoma, while necrotic carcinoma can masquerade as abscess. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign if purulent material only, Atypical when atypical squamous cells are present, or Malignant when diagnostic tumour cells are seen.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used for abscess diagnosis. Gram stain, GMS, Ziehl-Neelsen and modified acid-fast stains (for Nocardia) on the wall and contents identify organisms. When malignancy is suspected in the wall, p40, CK5/6 and TTF-1 help classify atypical epithelial cells, remembering that reactive squamous metaplasia is also p40 positive, so morphology must drive the diagnosis. Elastic stain may show destroyed lung architecture.

entities.variants: Pulmonary nocardiosis (N. asteroides complex, N. farcinica, N. nova); disseminated nocardiosis (brain, skin); immunocompromised hosts (transplant, steroids, HIV) and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
entities.remarks: Branching, beaded, weakly acid-fast filamentous bacteria; suppurative necrotising pneumonia and abscesses; brain abscess frequent in dissemination.
entities.histo: Pulmonary nocardiosis is an opportunistic infection caused by aerobic actinomycetes, typically in immunocompromised patients and in those with pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. It presents as nodules, consolidation or cavitating masses that mimic tumour or tuberculosis. Microscopically there is a suppurative necrotising pneumonia with abscesses containing neutrophils and necrotic debris, surrounded by granulation tissue and histiocytes; well-formed granulomas are uncommon. The organisms are thin (about 1 micrometre), beaded, branching filaments seen at the edges of abscesses; they are poorly visible on H&E and lack the sulphur granules typical of Actinomyces, although small granules can occasionally form. Dissemination to brain, skin and kidneys is common. Differentials include actinomycosis (granules, strictly anaerobic, non-acid-fast), tuberculosis and atypical mycobacteria (acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen, granulomas), fungal abscesses and septic emboli.
entities.cyto: Sputum, BAL or FNA shows purulent material with neutrophils and necrotic debris. Thin, beaded, branching filaments may be seen on Papanicolaou or Giemsa stains and are better shown with Gram or modified acid-fast stains on smears. FNA of a nodule can therefore establish a rapid diagnosis and exclude malignancy. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (infectious organisms identified), with culture confirmation.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. The organisms are Gram-positive, beaded, branching filaments that are GMS positive and partially acid-fast with the modified Ziehl-Neelsen (Fite or Kinyoun) stain, which separates them from Actinomyces (acid-fast negative). Standard Ziehl-Neelsen is usually negative. Culture is slow, so the laboratory should be alerted, and molecular methods (16S rRNA sequencing, MALDI-TOF on isolates) identify the species, which matters for antibiotic choice.

entities.variants: Thoracic actinomycosis (A. israelii and others); endobronchial actinomycosis (often with aspirated foreign body or broncholith); chest wall extension with sinus tracts
entities.remarks: Anaerobic Gram-positive filamentous bacteria forming sulphur granules; aspiration of oral flora, poor dentition; mimics carcinoma radiologically; crosses fissures and chest wall.
entities.histo: Pulmonary actinomycosis follows aspiration of oropharyngeal flora in patients with poor dental hygiene, alcohol use or impaired swallowing. It produces a chronic suppurative and fibrosing consolidation or mass that characteristically crosses fissures and can spread to the pleura, chest wall and skin with draining sinus tracts, closely mimicking lung cancer. Microscopically there are abscesses filled with neutrophils surrounding characteristic sulphur granules: rounded basophilic colonies of radiating filaments with eosinophilic club-shaped peripheral fringes (Splendore-Hoeppli material). The abscesses are surrounded by granulation tissue, foamy macrophages, plasma cells and dense fibrosis. Endobronchial disease is often associated with aspirated foreign material. Differentials include nocardiosis (no granules, partially acid-fast), botryomycosis (granules formed by cocci or bacilli), fungal infection, and carcinoma with obstructive pneumonia; isolated colonies of Actinomyces in tonsillar or aspirated debris without tissue reaction should not be called actinomycosis.
entities.cyto: FNA or BAL may show neutrophils with sulphur granules, seen as dense tangled clusters of filaments with radiating peripheral clubs, best appreciated on Papanicolaou and Gram stain. Oral contaminant Actinomyces colonies in sputum are common and are not diagnostic of infection without a tissue reaction. Cytology is helpful mainly to exclude carcinoma in a mass lesion. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (infectious organisms present).
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. Gram stain shows Gram-positive branching filaments within the granules, and GMS also highlights the filaments. Modified acid-fast stains are negative, unlike Nocardia. PAS shows the eosinophilic Splendore-Hoeppli fringe. Anaerobic culture is often negative because of prior antibiotics, so morphology with special stains is frequently diagnostic. Keratin and p40 or TTF-1 may be needed in biopsies where carcinoma is a differential.

entities.variants: Rhodococcus equi infection (HIV, transplant, immunosuppression); E. coli and other organisms
entities.remarks: Sheets of von Hansemann histiocytes with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies; cavitating mass in immunocompromised patients; defective macrophage bacterial killing.
entities.histo: Pulmonary malakoplakia is a rare chronic granulomatous response caused by defective lysosomal killing of bacteria by macrophages, most often due to Rhodococcus equi in HIV-infected or transplant patients. It presents as a cavitating mass or consolidation, often in the upper lobes, that mimics tuberculosis or tumour. Microscopically, sheets of large histiocytes (von Hansemann cells) with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm replace the lung, admixed with neutrophils, lymphocytes and plasma cells, abscesses and fibrosis. The pathognomonic Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are round, laminated, targetoid basophilic inclusions within and between histiocytes, representing calcified and iron-encrusted bacterial debris. Gram-positive coccobacilli may be seen within histiocytes. Differentials include mycobacterial infection (especially Mycobacterium avium complex in HIV, with foamy histiocytes full of acid-fast bacilli), Whipple disease, xanthogranulomatous inflammation, granular cell tumour, and histiocyte-rich tumours.
entities.cyto: FNA shows numerous histiocytes with abundant granular to foamy cytoplasm and occasional intracytoplasmic round laminated Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, together with neutrophils and debris. Recognition of the inclusions allows diagnosis and avoids misinterpreting histiocyte sheets as a tumour. Culture should be requested. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (specific inflammatory process).
entities.ihc: IHC confirms the histiocytic nature: CD68 and CD163 positive, keratin negative, S100 negative (versus granular cell tumour, which is S100 and SOX10 positive). Michaelis-Gutmann bodies stain with von Kossa (calcium), Perls Prussian blue (iron) and PAS (diastase resistant). Gram stain and modified acid-fast stain show the Rhodococcus coccobacilli (weakly acid-fast), and Ziehl-Neelsen helps exclude MAC infection, which shows large numbers of bacilli.

entities.variants: Acute septicaemic melioidosis with pneumonia; subacute and chronic cavitating (TB-like) pulmonary melioidosis; Burkholderia pseudomallei; endemic in South and Southeast Asia including India (Odisha, coastal Karnataka) and northern Australia
entities.remarks: Soil and water-borne Gram-negative bacillus; diabetics and rice farmers in monsoon season; necrotising pneumonia, abscesses and granulomas; mimics tuberculosis.
entities.histo: Melioidosis is an infection by Burkholderia pseudomallei, an environmental Gram-negative bacillus endemic in tropical Asia including many parts of India, affecting diabetics, alcoholics and agricultural workers during the rainy season. Acute disease causes a septicaemic necrotising pneumonia with multiple abscesses in lungs, liver and spleen. Chronic pulmonary melioidosis produces upper lobe cavitating consolidation that closely mimics post-primary tuberculosis. Microscopically acute lesions show suppurative necrosis with neutrophil-rich abscesses, karyorrhectic debris and haemorrhage, while chronic lesions show central suppurative necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells and fibrosis, producing necrotising granulomas. Small intracellular Gram-negative bacilli may be visible within macrophages, sometimes forming globi-like clusters. Differentials include tuberculosis (caseous granulomas, acid-fast bacilli), other necrotising bacterial pneumonia, fungal infection, and GPA; culture is essential and the laboratory should be warned because of biosafety risk.
entities.cyto: Aspirates of abscesses show purulent material with neutrophils, necrotic debris and histiocytes, sometimes with epithelioid cells and giant cells in chronic lesions. Bacilli are small and rarely seen; bipolar safety-pin staining may be visible on Gram or Wayson stains of smears. Cytology mainly excludes malignancy and directs culture. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (inflammatory or granulomatous process) with microbiology correlation.
entities.ihc: IHC has no routine role, although specific antibody staining and immunofluorescence for B. pseudomallei exist in reference laboratories. Gram stain may show small Gram-negative bacilli within histiocytes. Ziehl-Neelsen, GMS and PAS are needed to exclude tuberculosis and fungal infection, which are the main histological mimics. Culture with selective media (Ashdown agar), latex agglutination and PCR confirm the diagnosis.

entities.entity: Pulmonary zoonoses and other uncommon bacterial infections
entities.variants: Tularaemia (Francisella tularensis); inhalational anthrax (Bacillus anthracis, haemorrhagic mediastinitis); pneumonic plague (Yersinia pestis); psittacosis (Chlamydia psittaci); Q fever (Coxiella burnetii); leptospirosis (pulmonary haemorrhage syndrome); brucellosis; Bartonella (bacillary angiomatosis in HIV); pertussis; Rhodococcus (see malakoplakia); botryomycosis
entities.remarks: Rare, often occupational or animal exposure; patterns range from haemorrhagic pneumonia (anthrax, plague, leptospirosis) to necrotising granulomas (tularaemia, brucellosis); public health notification for some.
entities.histo: Zoonotic and uncommon bacterial lung infections are acquired from animals, vectors or the environment and usually present to pathologists at autopsy or in unexplained necrotising pneumonia. Inhalational anthrax causes haemorrhagic mediastinal lymphadenitis and mediastinitis with oedema and haemorrhagic pleural effusions rather than a primary pneumonia, and large boxcar Gram-positive bacilli are present. Pneumonic plague gives a fulminant haemorrhagic, necrotising lobular pneumonia packed with Gram-negative coccobacilli. Tularaemia and brucellosis produce necrotising pneumonia or nodules with suppurative necrosis evolving to necrotising granulomas. Psittacosis and Q fever cause patchy interstitial and alveolar pneumonia, and Q fever may form inflammatory pseudotumours with doughnut granulomas. Leptospirosis causes severe bland diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with little inflammation. Bartonella causes bacillary angiomatosis with lobular capillary proliferations and neutrophils. Botryomycosis forms bacterial granules resembling actinomycosis. Differentials include tuberculosis, fungal infection, GPA and other causes of alveolar haemorrhage.
entities.cyto: Cytology rarely contributes. Respiratory specimens show non-specific acute inflammation, haemorrhage or necrotic debris, and organisms are seldom visible except in plague (bipolar staining coccobacilli) or anthrax (large Gram-positive rods). Biosafety precautions are essential when these organisms are suspected. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, with urgent microbiology and public health referral as appropriate.
entities.ihc: IHC is mainly available in reference laboratories, where specific antibodies for Bacillus anthracis, Yersinia pestis, Francisella, Coxiella, Leptospira and Bartonella can identify organisms in tissue. In routine practice Gram stain, Warthin-Starry silver stain (Bartonella, Leptospira, Legionella), Giemsa and acid-fast stains are used, together with serology, culture and PCR. Iron and elastic stains are not helpful. Results should be correlated closely with exposure history.

entities.variants: Primary tuberculosis (Ghon focus, Ghon complex, Ranke complex); progressive primary TB; secondary (post-primary, reactivation) apical cavitary TB with Simon foci; tuberculoma; tuberculous (caseous) bronchopneumonia; miliary (haematogenous) TB; endobronchial TB and tracheobronchial stenosis; tuberculous lymphadenitis compressing airways; TB in HIV (poorly formed granulomas); silicotuberculosis; drug-resistant (MDR, XDR) TB
entities.remarks: Caseating epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells; Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex; high burden in India; ZN, auramine, GeneXpert/CBNAAT, culture; cavitation, haemoptysis, Rasmussen aneurysm; differentials fungi, NTM, sarcoid.
entities.histo: Pulmonary tuberculosis results from inhaled Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Primary infection gives a small subpleural Ghon focus near the interlobar fissure with caseating hilar nodes (Ghon complex), which usually heals by fibrosis and calcification (Ranke complex); in children and the immunosuppressed it can progress to primary progressive disease. Secondary tuberculosis arises by reactivation or reinfection and localises to the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes and superior segments of the lower lobes, forming caseous foci that cavitate and erode bronchi, producing spread (tuberculous bronchopneumonia) and endobronchial disease. Cavities have an inner layer of caseous necrosis, a middle zone of epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans giant cells, and an outer fibrous wall; an exposed artery may form a Rasmussen aneurysm. Tuberculomas are circumscribed caseous nodules with fibrous capsules. Miliary tuberculosis shows innumerable 1 to 2 mm yellow-white nodules of granulomas. In advanced HIV infection granulomas are poorly formed with necrosis rich in bacilli. Differentials include fungal granulomas (histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis), NTM infection, sarcoidosis (non-necrotising, lymphangitic), GPA (geographic basophilic necrosis, vasculitis), rheumatoid nodules and aspiration.
entities.cyto: FNA, BAL and sputum show epithelioid histiocyte clusters (granulomas) with elongated footprint-shaped nuclei, Langhans giant cells, and granular amorphous caseous necrosis, often with lymphocytes. Necrosis alone with neutrophils occurs in immunocompromised patients. Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine-rhodamine staining of smears and molecular testing (GeneXpert MTB/RIF or CBNAAT and line probe assays) on the material provide diagnosis and rifampicin resistance status. Pitfalls include squamous cell carcinoma with necrosis and keratin mimicking caseation, and granulomatous reactions to tumour, so a careful search for malignant cells is needed. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (granulomatous inflammation, with or without necrosis); a dedicated microbiology sample should always be sent.
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role. Ziehl-Neelsen (or auramine-rhodamine fluorescence) on tissue shows beaded acid-fast bacilli, usually scant and found in necrosis or at its edge; immunohistochemistry for mycobacterial antigens (MPT64) can increase sensitivity in paucibacillary lesions where available. GMS and PAS exclude fungal granulomas, and reticulin shows preserved framework in necrosis. Molecular tests on formalin-fixed tissue (PCR, Xpert) help when cultures are not sent. CD68 confirms histiocytes and keratin stains exclude carcinoma in necrotic masses.

entities.variants: Fibrocavitary (upper lobe, TB-like) disease in men with COPD; nodular bronchiectatic disease (Lady Windermere syndrome) in older women; hot tub lung (hypersensitivity-like, M. avium complex); disseminated MAC in advanced HIV; organisms: M. avium complex, M. kansasii, M. abscessus, M. xenopi, M. malmoense, M. fortuitum, M. chelonae; NTM in cystic fibrosis
entities.remarks: Environmental mycobacteria; necrotising and non-necrotising granulomas in bronchiectatic airways; culture needed for species and susceptibility; hot tub lung shows bronchiolocentric non-necrotising granulomas.
entities.histo: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria are environmental organisms that cause chronic lung disease in patients with structural lung damage, cystic fibrosis, or immune defects. Fibrocavitary disease resembles reactivation tuberculosis with upper lobe cavities and caseating granulomas. Nodular bronchiectatic disease, typically in thin, older, non-smoking women, shows bronchiectasis of the middle lobe and lingula with peribronchiolar necrotising and non-necrotising granulomas, bronchiolitis and organising pneumonia. Hot tub lung is caused by inhaling aerosolised Mycobacterium avium complex and shows well-formed, non-necrotising granulomas within bronchiolar lumens and walls with organising pneumonia, resembling hypersensitivity pneumonitis but with more prominent granulomas. In advanced HIV, disseminated MAC produces sheets of foamy histiocytes stuffed with bacilli and poorly formed or absent granulomas. Differentials include tuberculosis (indistinguishable histologically, culture or PCR required), fungal infection, sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and aspiration.
entities.cyto: Cytology mirrors histology: epithelioid granulomas, giant cells and necrosis in fibrocavitary disease, and histiocytes with foamy or striated cytoplasm containing negative images of bacilli on Romanowsky stains in immunosuppressed patients. Morphology cannot separate NTM from tuberculosis, so material should be sent for mycobacterial culture and molecular identification. Repeated positive sputum cultures are needed to distinguish disease from colonisation. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (granulomatous inflammation).
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role. Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine stains show acid-fast bacilli, often longer and more numerous than in tuberculosis, and plentiful in HIV-associated MAC; rapidly growing mycobacteria may be poorly acid-fast. NTM organisms are also PAS and GMS positive in heavy infections. Speciation requires culture, line-probe assays or sequencing; M. tuberculosis-specific IHC (MPT64) is negative in NTM, which can help separate the two in reference settings. CD68 marks histiocytes; keratin excludes carcinoma.

entities.variants: Influenza A (seasonal, H1N1 pandemic, avian H5N1 and H7N9); influenza B; primary viral pneumonia; secondary bacterial pneumonia (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae); necrotising tracheobronchitis
entities.remarks: No viral inclusions; necrotising tracheobronchitis, bronchiolitis and diffuse alveolar damage with haemorrhage; bacterial superinfection drives much mortality.
entities.histo: Influenza virus infects ciliated respiratory epithelium. Mild disease causes tracheobronchitis with epithelial necrosis, oedema and lymphocytic inflammation, while severe pandemic or avian disease produces primary viral pneumonia with heavy, haemorrhagic lungs. Microscopically there is necrotising tracheitis, bronchitis and bronchiolitis with sloughing of epithelium and later squamous metaplasia, together with diffuse alveolar damage showing hyaline membranes, intra-alveolar oedema and haemorrhage, and later type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and organisation. Microthrombi are common. Unlike many viruses, influenza does not produce visible nuclear or cytoplasmic inclusions. Secondary bacterial pneumonia, especially due to Staphylococcus aureus, adds neutrophilic bronchopneumonia and abscesses. Reparative squamous metaplasia with atypia in the bronchiolar epithelium can be striking and should not be mistaken for squamous carcinoma. Differentials include other viral pneumonias with DAD (COVID-19, adenovirus with smudge cells, CMV with inclusions), drug-induced DAD and acute interstitial pneumonia.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a supportive role. Nasopharyngeal and BAL specimens show ciliocytophthoria (detached ciliated tufts and degenerate ciliated cells), reactive bronchial cells, and later atypical reparative squamous metaplasia and reactive type II pneumocytes, which may be mistaken for carcinoma. No inclusions are seen. Diagnosis rests on rapid antigen tests and RT-PCR. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical when reparative atypia is marked.
entities.ihc: Influenza A and B antigen IHC on tissue confirms infection, particularly at autopsy, staining infected bronchial and alveolar epithelium, but RT-PCR on swabs or tissue is the main test. Gram stain shows secondary bacteria. TTF-1, napsin A and p40 may be needed to show that atypical cells are reactive pneumocytes or metaplastic squamous cells rather than carcinoma, using morphology, a low Ki-67 and the clinical context. Other viral IHC (CMV, HSV, adenovirus) excludes co-infection.

entities.variants: COVID-19 pneumonia (acute phase diffuse alveolar damage; organising and fibrotic phase; acute fibrinous and organising pneumonia pattern; microvascular thrombosis); post-COVID fibrosis; COVID-associated pulmonary aspergillosis and mucormycosis; SARS (2003); MERS
entities.remarks: Diffuse alveolar damage with prominent microthrombi and endothelial injury; no reliable viral inclusions; superinfection with fungi (CAPA, mucormycosis, notable in India); RT-PCR confirms.
entities.histo: COVID-19 pneumonia, caused by SARS-CoV-2, produces heavy, firm, congested lungs at autopsy. The dominant pattern is diffuse alveolar damage: exudative phase hyaline membranes, oedema and type II pneumocyte hyperplasia with reactive atypia and multinucleated pneumocytes, evolving to an organising phase with interstitial and intra-alveolar fibroblastic proliferation, squamous metaplasia and eventually fibrosis. Distinctive features include frequent microthrombi and larger thrombi in pulmonary arteries, endothelial injury (endothelialitis) and alveolar haemorrhage. Acute fibrinous and organising pneumonia and organising pneumonia patterns are also seen. Superimposed bacterial bronchopneumonia and fungal infection (COVID-associated aspergillosis and, especially in India, mucormycosis) are important complications. SARS and MERS caused similar DAD with multinucleated pneumocytes. Post-acute disease may leave organising pneumonia or fibrotic lung. Differentials are other causes of DAD (influenza, drugs, sepsis), acute exacerbation of ILD, and acute interstitial pneumonia.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a minor role. BAL and respiratory specimens show reactive type II pneumocytes, sometimes multinucleated, reactive bronchial cells, macrophages and variable neutrophils. Marked reactive atypia can mimic adenocarcinoma, especially when cell clusters are three-dimensional. Material should be handled with biosafety precautions and tested by RT-PCR. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical (reactive changes).
entities.ihc: IHC for SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid or spike protein and RNA in situ hybridisation can show virus in pneumocytes and macrophages in early disease, though signal declines with time; RT-PCR on tissue is more sensitive. GMS and PAS are important to detect superimposed Aspergillus or Mucorales. CD61 or CD42b can highlight platelet-rich microthrombi. Keratin, TTF-1 and a low Ki-67 index together with morphology help distinguish reactive pneumocytes from adenocarcinoma.

entities.variants: CMV pneumonitis in transplant (stem cell and solid organ, including lung allograft), HIV and chemotherapy patients; congenital CMV; miliary nodular, diffuse interstitial and haemorrhagic forms
entities.remarks: Cytomegalic cells with large owl-eye intranuclear inclusions and granular cytoplasmic inclusions in pneumocytes, endothelium and macrophages; interstitial pneumonitis, DAD, haemorrhagic nodules.
entities.histo: CMV pneumonitis is an opportunistic infection mainly in transplant recipients and other immunosuppressed patients. Patterns include a miliary form with small haemorrhagic and necrotic nodules, a diffuse interstitial pneumonitis with lymphocytes and oedema, and diffuse alveolar damage with haemorrhage. The diagnostic feature is cytomegaly: infected cells (alveolar pneumocytes, endothelial cells, macrophages and bronchial epithelium) are greatly enlarged and contain a single large, dense amphophilic to basophilic intranuclear inclusion separated from the nuclear membrane by a clear halo (owl-eye), and often multiple small basophilic granular cytoplasmic inclusions. Infected cells may be few and require careful search. Coexisting infections (Pneumocystis, fungi, other viruses) are frequent. In lung transplant patients CMV can mimic acute rejection with perivascular lymphocytes. Differentials include HSV and VZV (multinucleation, moulding, Cowdry A inclusions, necrosis), adenovirus (smudge cells without cytomegaly), measles (multinucleated giant cells), and reactive pneumocytes with large nucleoli.
entities.cyto: BAL may show enlarged cells with characteristic large intranuclear inclusions with a halo and cytoplasmic inclusions, though sensitivity is low and the cells are rare. Reactive type II pneumocytes with macronucleoli can mimic CMV inclusions and vice versa. Quantitative PCR in BAL and blood is more sensitive, and IHC on cell blocks can confirm. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (viral cytopathic effect present).
entities.ihc: CMV IHC (early and immediate-early antigen) is the most useful confirmatory test and also highlights infected cells without classic inclusions, increasing sensitivity in transplant biopsies; in situ hybridisation is an alternative. GMS should be performed to exclude Pneumocystis and fungal co-infection, and HSV-1/2, VZV and adenovirus IHC help with the differential of viral cytopathic effect. In lung allografts, CD3 and CD20 characterise perivascular infiltrates when rejection is in the differential.

entities.entity: Herpes simplex virus tracheobronchitis and pneumonia
entities.variants: Necrotising herpetic tracheobronchitis (intubated, burns); focal (airway-centred) HSV pneumonia from aspiration of oral virus; diffuse haematogenous HSV pneumonia (disseminated, neonates, immunosuppressed); HSV-1 and HSV-2
entities.remarks: Necrotising ulcerative tracheobronchitis and necrotising pneumonia with multinucleated cells showing the 3 Ms (multinucleation, margination of chromatin, moulding) and Cowdry A inclusions.
entities.histo: HSV infection of the lower respiratory tract occurs in intubated, burned, immunocompromised and neonatal patients. Airway disease is a necrotising ulcerative tracheobronchitis with sloughed epithelium, fibrinopurulent exudate and inflammation. Pneumonia may be focal and airway-centred following aspiration of oral virus, or diffuse and haematogenous in disseminated infection, the latter producing miliary haemorrhagic necrotic nodules. Microscopically there is extensive necrosis with nuclear debris, haemorrhage and fibrin, together with diffuse alveolar damage. Infected epithelial cells show ground-glass nuclei with margination of chromatin, nuclear moulding and multinucleation, and eosinophilic Cowdry A inclusions surrounded by a halo. Necrosis may be so extensive that only rare viable infected cells remain at the edges. Differentials include VZV (morphologically identical), CMV (cytomegaly, owl-eye inclusions), adenovirus (smudge cells), bacterial necrotising pneumonia and Aspergillus tracheobronchitis.
entities.cyto: Bronchial brushings, washings and BAL show multinucleated epithelial cells with ground-glass nuclei, moulding, chromatin margination and Cowdry A inclusions, with necrotic debris. These features are fairly characteristic but do not separate HSV from VZV. Viral cytopathic change in squamous cells must not be mistaken for squamous carcinoma or high-grade atypia. PCR or IHC confirms. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (viral cytopathic effect).
entities.ihc: HSV-1 and HSV-2 IHC confirms the diagnosis and highlights infected nuclei and cytoplasm at the edges of necrosis; cross-reactivity between HSV-1 and HSV-2 antibodies is common and of little clinical importance. VZV IHC is needed to separate VZV, which looks identical. CMV and adenovirus IHC exclude other viruses. Gram stain and GMS look for bacterial and fungal co-infection. PCR on BAL or tissue is highly sensitive.

entities.variants: Primary varicella pneumonia (adults, pregnancy, smokers); disseminated zoster in immunosuppressed; healed varicella pneumonia with miliary calcified nodules
entities.remarks: Miliary necrotic and haemorrhagic nodules with Cowdry A inclusions and multinucleation, identical to HSV; healing gives diffuse tiny calcified nodules on imaging.
entities.histo: VZV pneumonia complicates primary varicella in adults, particularly pregnant women and smokers, and disseminated zoster in immunocompromised patients. It appears two to six days after the rash. Grossly the lungs are heavy, with numerous small haemorrhagic and necrotic nodules scattered throughout. Microscopically there are foci of necrosis with haemorrhage, fibrin and nuclear debris involving alveolar walls, bronchioles and vessels, accompanied by an interstitial lymphocytic pneumonitis and diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes. Cells at the edges of necrosis show multinucleation, nuclear moulding, chromatin margination and Cowdry A inclusions, indistinguishable from HSV. After recovery, the necrotic foci heal by fibrosis and may calcify, producing diffuse miliary calcified nodules 1 to 3 mm in size on imaging. Differentials include HSV pneumonia, disseminated fungal infection, miliary tuberculosis and other causes of DAD.
entities.cyto: BAL and brushings may contain multinucleated cells with moulded ground-glass nuclei and Cowdry A inclusions, with necrotic debris, morphologically identical to HSV. PCR or IHC separates them. Viral changes in reactive squamous and bronchial cells should not be interpreted as malignant. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (viral cytopathic effect).
entities.ihc: VZV-specific IHC confirms the virus and separates it from HSV, which shows identical cytopathic effects; HSV-1/2 IHC should be negative. PCR on BAL, blood or tissue is the most sensitive test. GMS, Gram stain and acid-fast stains help exclude other causes of miliary nodules and necrosis. No other immunostains are routinely useful.

entities.variants: Necrotising bronchiolitis and bronchopneumonia (children, military recruits); disseminated adenovirus in transplant and immunosuppressed patients; sequelae: constrictive bronchiolitis, bronchiectasis, Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome (unilateral hyperlucent lung)
entities.remarks: Smudge cells: enlarged nuclei with dark, smudgy basophilic inclusions obscuring chromatin; necrotising bronchiolitis with karyorrhexis; serious in immunocompromised and children.
entities.histo: Adenovirus causes a necrotising bronchiolitis and bronchopneumonia, especially in infants, young children, military recruits and immunocompromised hosts. Grossly the lungs show patchy consolidation and haemorrhage. Microscopically there is necrosis of bronchiolar epithelium with extension into peribronchiolar alveoli, abundant nuclear debris, fibrinous exudate, haemorrhage and diffuse alveolar damage. Infected epithelial cells show two inclusion types: early eosinophilic Cowdry A-like inclusions with a halo, and the characteristic smudge cells, in which the nucleus is enlarged and filled by a dark basophilic to amphophilic homogeneous inclusion that obscures the nuclear membrane and chromatin. Multinucleation is not a feature. In survivors, particularly children, healing can lead to constrictive bronchiolitis, bronchiectasis and Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome. Differentials include CMV (cytomegaly with owl-eye inclusions and cytoplasmic inclusions), HSV and VZV (multinucleation and moulding), measles (giant cells), and degenerating cells mimicking smudge cells.
entities.cyto: Cytology of BAL or brushings can show smudge cells, which are enlarged bronchial or alveolar cells with dark, homogeneous, glassy nuclear inclusions, together with necrotic debris and degenerating ciliated cells. Degenerate pyknotic cells can mimic smudge cells. Confirmation by IHC or PCR is advisable. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (viral cytopathic effect).
entities.ihc: Adenovirus IHC is the confirmatory test of choice and stains nuclei of smudge cells and early infected cells; PCR on BAL and blood quantifies viral load in transplant patients. CMV, HSV and VZV IHC help in the differential of viral cytopathic effects. GMS and Gram stain exclude co-infections. Morphology with a positive adenovirus stain is diagnostic.

entities.entity: Respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza and human metapneumovirus infections
entities.variants: Acute viral bronchiolitis of infancy (RSV commonest); croup (parainfluenza laryngotracheobronchitis); RSV and parainfluenza pneumonia in transplant and elderly patients (giant cell pneumonia); human metapneumovirus; rhinovirus; enteroviruses (EV-D68); hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (non-cytopathic oedema)
entities.remarks: Paramyxovirus/pneumovirus family; acute bronchiolitis with epithelial necrosis and mucus plugging in infants; syncytial giant cells with eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in immunocompromised hosts.
entities.histo: RSV, parainfluenza viruses and human metapneumovirus are common causes of lower respiratory infection in infants and are important in transplant recipients and the elderly. In infant bronchiolitis, small airways show epithelial necrosis and sloughing, peribronchiolar lymphocytic infiltrate, oedema and plugs of mucus, fibrin and cell debris that cause air trapping and patchy atelectasis. Pneumonia shows an interstitial mononuclear infiltrate, alveolar exudate and diffuse alveolar damage. A characteristic feature in severe or immunocompromised cases is multinucleated syncytial giant cells (giant cell pneumonia), formed from bronchiolar and alveolar epithelium, containing eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions with a halo; nuclear inclusions are unusual. Parainfluenza viruses cause croup in children with subglottic oedema. Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome shows severe non-cardiogenic oedema with few hyaline membranes and immunoblasts but no cytopathic effects. Sequelae include constrictive bronchiolitis and possibly later wheeze. Differentials include measles (giant cells with nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions), adenovirus and other causes of bronchiolitis.
entities.cyto: Nasopharyngeal aspirates and BAL may show ciliocytophthoria, degenerated ciliated cells, and occasionally multinucleated syncytial cells with eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions. Morphology is non-specific and diagnosis relies on multiplex PCR or antigen tests. Reactive bronchial cell clusters are common. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC for RSV, parainfluenza and metapneumovirus antigens is available in some laboratories and confirms infection in biopsy and autopsy tissue, but multiplex PCR on respiratory specimens is the standard. Measles IHC helps when giant cells are present. Other viral IHC (CMV, adenovirus, HSV) and GMS exclude co-infection in immunocompromised patients. Hantavirus is diagnosed by serology and PCR, with IHC in reference centres.

entities.variants: Primary measles giant cell pneumonia (Hecht pneumonia) in malnourished or immunocompromised children; secondary bacterial pneumonia; post-measles bronchiectasis; atypical measles
entities.remarks: Warthin-Finkeldey-type multinucleated giant cells with both nuclear and cytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions; may occur without rash in immunodeficient hosts; vaccine-preventable but still relevant in India.
entities.histo: Measles virus causes interstitial pneumonitis in many infected children, and severe giant cell pneumonia in malnourished, immunodeficient or leukaemic children, sometimes without the typical rash. Microscopically there is interstitial lymphocytic inflammation, bronchiolitis and diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes. Characteristic multinucleated giant cells, containing up to dozens of nuclei, line alveoli and bronchioles; they contain eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions with halos and eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions. Squamous metaplasia of bronchiolar epithelium is common. Secondary bacterial pneumonia is a frequent cause of death, and healing may lead to bronchiolitis obliterans and bronchiectasis. Lymphoid tissue may show Warthin-Finkeldey cells. Differentials include RSV and parainfluenza giant cell pneumonia (cytoplasmic inclusions only), HSV and VZV (necrosis, moulding), giant cell interstitial pneumonia due to hard metal (bizarre giant cells in alveoli with cobalt exposure history), and foreign-body giant cells.
entities.cyto: Respiratory cytology may show multinucleated epithelial giant cells with numerous nuclei and both nuclear and cytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions. These must not be mistaken for malignant giant cells or for HSV effect. Diagnosis is confirmed by serology and RT-PCR. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (viral cytopathic effect).
entities.ihc: Measles virus IHC confirms infection in giant cells, and RT-PCR on respiratory samples or tissue is definitive. Keratin staining shows that the giant cells are epithelial, distinguishing them from histiocytic foreign-body giant cells (CD68 positive). Other viral IHC and GMS exclude co-infections. In hard metal disease the history and lack of viral inclusions are decisive.

entities.variants: Opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, tuberculosis, MAC, CMV, cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, talaromycosis, bacterial pneumonia); lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia (children); HIV-associated pulmonary hypertension (plexiform arteriopathy); HIV-associated neoplasms (Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas including primary effusion lymphoma and DLBCL, lung carcinoma); immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome; nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis
entities.remarks: Spectrum depends on CD4 count; multiple co-existing processes common; always perform special stains for organisms on lung biopsies from HIV patients.
entities.histo: HIV infection predisposes to a wide spectrum of pulmonary diseases whose likelihood depends on the CD4 count. At higher counts bacterial pneumonia and tuberculosis (classic caseating granulomas) predominate; below 200 cells per microlitre Pneumocystis pneumonia, cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, talaromycosis and tuberculosis with poorly formed granulomas occur; below 50 cells CMV and disseminated MAC appear. Children develop lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia with dense interstitial lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates and lymphoid follicles. HIV-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension shows plexiform lesions identical to idiopathic PAH. Kaposi sarcoma involves the airways and lymphatic routes, and lymphomas include DLBCL and primary effusion lymphoma; the incidence of lung carcinoma is also increased. Immune reconstitution after antiretroviral therapy can provoke florid granulomatous inflammation. Nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis with mild lymphocytic infiltrates is also described. Multiple processes often coexist, so a single finding should not end the search.
entities.cyto: BAL is central in HIV-related lung disease: it detects Pneumocystis (foamy alveolar casts), Cryptococcus (budding yeast with capsules), Histoplasma and Talaromyces (small intracellular yeasts), CMV cytopathic change, mycobacteria and Kaposi sarcoma rarely. Lymphocytosis suggests LIP. Malignant cells from lymphoma or carcinoma can be identified and triaged for flow cytometry or IHC. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign for infections, or Suspicious or Malignant for neoplasms.
entities.ihc: IHC and special stains are complementary. GMS, PAS, mucicarmine and Ziehl-Neelsen are routinely needed to detect organisms; CMV IHC confirms viral infection; HHV-8 (LANA-1) confirms Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma; CD20, CD3, CD138, kappa/lambda and EBER separate LIP and reactive infiltrates from lymphoma. Lung carcinomas in HIV are worked up as usual with TTF-1, p40 and predictive markers.

entities.variants: Angioinvasive aspergillosis (target lesions, haemorrhagic infarcts; neutropenia, stem cell transplant); airway-invasive aspergillosis (Aspergillus bronchiolitis, bronchopneumonia); ulcerative and pseudomembranous Aspergillus tracheobronchitis (lung transplant anastomosis); COVID-19 and influenza-associated aspergillosis; disseminated aspergillosis; species: A. fumigatus, A. flavus, A. niger, A. terreus
entities.remarks: Septate hyphae 3 to 6 micrometres with regular acute-angle (45 degree) dichotomous branching; vascular invasion with infarction; galactomannan and culture support diagnosis.
entities.histo: Invasive aspergillosis occurs in profoundly immunosuppressed patients, especially with neutropenia, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, high-dose steroids or after severe viral pneumonia. Angioinvasive disease produces nodular haemorrhagic infarcts with a central necrotic core and a haemorrhagic rim (target lesions, halo sign on CT) and may cavitate (air-crescent sign) on neutrophil recovery. Microscopically, hyphae invade and permeate vessel walls, causing thrombosis and coagulative necrosis of the surrounding lung, often with few inflammatory cells. The hyphae are narrow, uniform (3 to 6 micrometres), septate and branch dichotomously at acute angles, often radiating in parallel arrays. Airway-invasive disease involves bronchi and bronchioles with necrotising bronchitis and peribronchiolar consolidation, and Aspergillus tracheobronchitis forms pseudomembranes of fibrin, necrotic debris and hyphae, particularly at lung transplant anastomoses. Calcium oxalate crystals suggest A. niger. Differentials include mucormycosis (broad pauciseptate ribbon-like hyphae, right-angle branching), Fusarium and Scedosporium (morphologically similar hyalohyphomycetes, need culture), Pseudomonas vasculitis and bland infarcts.
entities.cyto: BAL, brushings or FNA show septate hyphae with acute-angle branching, sometimes with conidial heads in cavities, within necrotic debris and neutrophils. Calcium oxalate crystals may accompany A. niger. Morphology alone does not distinguish Aspergillus from other hyaline moulds, and colonisation versus invasion cannot be determined on cytology, so correlation with culture, galactomannan and imaging is needed. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (fungal organisms identified).
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role, but Aspergillus-specific immunostains and in situ hybridisation are available in some centres and can help separate Aspergillus from mimics. GMS and PAS (with diastase) highlight the hyphae and are essential in every necrotic nodule from an immunocompromised patient; elastic stain shows vascular invasion. Fontana-Masson is negative (unlike dematiaceous fungi). Panfungal PCR or species-specific PCR on fresh or paraffin tissue confirms identity, and culture determines antifungal susceptibility.

entities.variants: Simple aspergilloma (fungus ball in pre-existing cavity, e.g. healed TB, sarcoid, bullae); chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis; chronic fibrosing pulmonary aspergillosis; Aspergillus nodule; subacute invasive (chronic necrotising) pulmonary aspergillosis
entities.remarks: Occurs in non-immunocompromised or mildly immunocompromised hosts with structural lung disease; post-tuberculous cavities are a key setting in India; haemoptysis is the main complication.
entities.histo: Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis comprises a spectrum of non-angioinvasive Aspergillus disease in patients with pre-existing cavities or structural lung damage, most commonly healed tuberculosis. A simple aspergilloma is a fungus ball of tangled hyphae, fibrin, mucus and debris lying free within a cavity whose wall shows fibrosis, chronic inflammation and sometimes granulation tissue or squamous metaplasia, but no tissue invasion. Haemoptysis from bronchial arteries in the wall is the main risk. Chronic cavitary aspergillosis shows multiple expanding cavities with or without fungus balls, thick inflamed walls, granulomas and pleural thickening, and chronic fibrosing disease leads to extensive fibrosis of a lobe. An Aspergillus nodule is a necrotic nodule with peripheral granulomatous reaction resembling a tuberculoma. Subacute invasive (chronic necrotising) aspergillosis occurs in mildly immunosuppressed patients and shows slow tissue invasion with necrosis and granulomas. Differentials include mycetomas due to other fungi, tuberculosis cavities, cavitated carcinoma and infected bullae.
entities.cyto: Sputum, BAL or aspiration of cavity contents may show tangled septate hyphae with acute-angle branching and sometimes fruiting heads (conidiophores) because of air exposure, with calcium oxalate crystals for A. niger. Cytology cannot establish invasion and the wall is not sampled. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (fungal organisms).
entities.ihc: IHC is generally not required. GMS and PAS outline the hyphae in the fungus ball and are used on the cavity wall to check for tissue invasion. Ziehl-Neelsen helps exclude active tuberculosis in post-tuberculous cavities. Aspergillus IgG serology and precipitins are the main diagnostic tests for chronic pulmonary aspergillosis; culture or PCR confirms species.

entities.entity: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis
entities.variants: ABPA (asthma, cystic fibrosis); allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis due to other fungi (Bipolaris, Curvularia, Candida); mucoid impaction of bronchi; bronchocentric granulomatosis (associated pattern); eosinophilic pneumonia component; allergic fungal sinusitis association
entities.remarks: Hypersensitivity to colonising Aspergillus in asthmatics and CF; central bronchiectasis, mucus plugs with allergic mucin, raised IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE.
entities.histo: ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction (type I and type III) to Aspergillus colonising the airways of patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis. Proximal bronchi become filled with thick, tenacious mucus plugs that cause central (proximal) bronchiectasis and fleeting infiltrates. Microscopically the plugs are allergic mucin: layered, lamellated mucus containing numerous eosinophils, many degenerating, with Charcot-Leyden crystals and scant fragmented septate hyphae that do not invade tissue. Bronchial walls show asthmatic changes with eosinophils, basement membrane thickening and goblet cell hyperplasia. Associated lesions include bronchocentric granulomatosis (necrotising granulomas replacing bronchiolar walls), eosinophilic pneumonia, mucoid impaction and, in late disease, fibrosis. Diagnosis rests on clinical criteria including asthma, raised total IgE, Aspergillus-specific IgE or skin test, precipitins and imaging. Differentials include mucoid impaction from other causes, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, chronic eosinophilic pneumonia and invasive aspergillosis.
entities.cyto: Sputum or BAL may show mucus with abundant eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals, Curschmann spirals and occasional fragmented hyphae, which in the right clinical context supports ABPA. Expectorated brown plugs can be examined directly. Fungal elements alone do not distinguish colonisation, hypersensitivity or invasion. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. GMS reveals sparse fragmented hyphae within allergic mucin, and Giemsa or Congo red can highlight eosinophils; Charcot-Leyden crystals are seen on H&E. Serology (total IgE, Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG) and skin testing are the principal investigations. Fontana-Masson can identify dematiaceous fungi in allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis caused by non-Aspergillus moulds.

entities.variants: Rhizopus, Mucor, Lichtheimia (Absidia), Rhizomucor, Cunninghamella; angioinvasive pulmonary mucormycosis; rhino-orbito-cerebral with pulmonary spread; COVID-associated mucormycosis (prominent in India); diabetic ketoacidosis, neutropenia, iron overload (deferoxamine) settings; Entomophthorales (Basidiobolus, Conidiobolus) rare
entities.remarks: Broad (6 to 25 micrometres), ribbon-like, pauciseptate hyphae with irregular right-angle branching; marked angioinvasion and infarction; rapidly fatal; surgical debridement plus amphotericin.
entities.histo: Pulmonary mucormycosis is an aggressive angioinvasive infection caused by fungi of the order Mucorales, seen in uncontrolled diabetes (especially ketoacidosis), neutropenia, haematological malignancy, transplantation, iron overload and, prominently in India, after COVID-19 treated with steroids. It produces haemorrhagic infarcts, consolidation and cavitation, with a reversed halo sign on CT, and may erode into the mediastinum, chest wall or pulmonary artery causing fatal haemorrhage. Microscopically there are broad, thin-walled, ribbon-like hyphae with few or no septa, irregular diameters and non-dichotomous branching at wide (often right) angles, frequently appearing folded or twisted and with empty-looking cross-sections. They invade vessel walls massively, producing thrombosis, infarction and haemorrhagic necrosis with a neutrophilic or granulomatous reaction and occasional perineural invasion. Differentials include aspergillosis (narrow, septate, acute-angle hyphae), which may coexist, and other moulds; distinguishing the two matters because voriconazole is ineffective for Mucorales.
entities.cyto: BAL or FNA may show broad, ribbon-like pauciseptate hyphae with right-angle branching in necrotic debris, often fragmented. They stain weakly with Papanicolaou stain and may appear as pale ghost outlines. Cytology provides rapid diagnosis but culture is often negative because hyphae are damaged by tissue grinding, so mince rather than homogenise for culture. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (fungal organisms identified), with urgent clinical notification.
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role; Mucorales-specific antibodies and in situ hybridisation are available in reference centres. GMS and PAS stain the hyphae, though often less intensely than Aspergillus, and H&E alone often shows them well. Elastic stains highlight angioinvasion. Fontana-Masson is negative. Molecular identification (PCR targeting Mucorales genes) from fresh or paraffin tissue is valuable because cultures frequently fail.

entities.variants: Haematogenous (disseminated) candidiasis with miliary microabscesses; aspiration (bronchopneumonic) Candida pneumonia (rare); Candida tracheobronchitis; colonisation of airways (common, not disease); C. albicans, C. glabrata, C. tropicalis, C. auris
entities.remarks: True Candida pneumonia is rare; mostly part of disseminated candidiasis in neutropenic or ICU patients; yeasts with pseudohyphae; sputum or BAL growth usually represents colonisation.
entities.histo: Candida species commonly colonise the oropharynx and airways, and their recovery from sputum or BAL rarely indicates pneumonia. True pulmonary candidiasis occurs mainly as part of haematogenous dissemination in neutropenic, ICU, intravenous catheter or total parenteral nutrition patients, and rarely through aspiration. Haematogenous disease produces multiple small microabscesses and haemorrhagic nodules distributed randomly, often perivascular, with central necrosis, neutrophils and organisms. Aspiration produces bronchopneumonia centred on airways. The organisms are oval budding yeasts 3 to 5 micrometres in diameter with pseudohyphae (elongated, constricted chains) and true hyphae; C. glabrata forms only small yeasts without pseudohyphae, resembling Histoplasma. Candida tracheobronchitis shows mucosal plaques and ulceration. Differentials include Aspergillus (true septate hyphae with dichotomous branching), Histoplasma and Torulopsis-like small yeasts, Trichosporon, and other causes of miliary microabscesses.
entities.cyto: Sputum and BAL frequently contain Candida yeasts and pseudohyphae due to oropharyngeal contamination, which is not diagnostic of infection. Recognition helps avoid confusion with other fungi, and invasion can only be shown histologically. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (fungal organisms, likely contaminant unless clinically correlated).
entities.ihc: IHC has no routine role, though Candida-specific antibodies exist. GMS and PAS highlight budding yeasts and pseudohyphae; Gram stain shows yeasts as Gram positive. Culture with species identification (including C. auris) and susceptibility testing is essential. Beta-D-glucan supports invasive fungal infection but is not specific for Candida.

entities.variants: Cryptococcus neoformans (pigeon droppings; HIV) and C. gattii (eucalyptus; immunocompetent); cryptococcoma (granulomatous nodule) in immunocompetent hosts; diffuse pneumonia with gelatinous mucoid lesions and minimal inflammation in immunosuppressed; capsule-deficient variants; disseminated disease with meningitis
entities.remarks: Round yeasts 4 to 10 micrometres with narrow-based budding and a thick mucopolysaccharide capsule; granulomatous nodule mimicking carcinoma or gelatinous pneumonia; always assess for CNS involvement.
entities.histo: Pulmonary cryptococcosis follows inhalation of Cryptococcus neoformans or C. gattii. In immunocompetent patients it often presents as single or multiple peripheral nodules (cryptococcomas) found incidentally and mistaken for lung cancer. These show granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells containing many yeasts, sometimes with central necrosis, and surrounding fibrosis and lymphoplasmacytic inflammation. In immunosuppressed patients, particularly with HIV, the yeasts fill alveolar spaces and septa with little inflammation, giving gelatinous, mucoid, slimy lesions resembling soap bubbles. The organisms are round to oval yeasts of variable size with narrow-based budding and a thick capsule that appears as a clear halo on H&E. Capsule-deficient forms may mimic Histoplasma or Blastomyces. Differentials include histoplasmosis (smaller uniform intracellular yeasts), blastomycosis (broad-based budding, thick refractile wall), Pneumocystis, and mucinous adenocarcinoma in gelatinous forms.
entities.cyto: FNA, BAL or sputum show round yeasts with clear halos (capsules), narrow-based buds and variable size, either free or within histiocytes and giant cells in a granulomatous background. Mucicarmine and India ink highlight the capsule, and cryptococcal antigen testing on fluid or serum is highly sensitive. Mistaking yeasts for degenerated cells or mucinous material is a pitfall. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (fungal organisms identified).
entities.ihc: IHC is rarely needed, although Cryptococcus-specific antibodies are available. The capsule stains with mucicarmine and Alcian blue, and Fontana-Masson stains the cell wall melanin, which helps identify capsule-deficient forms. GMS and PAS stain the yeast wall. Cryptococcal antigen (serum, BAL, CSF) and culture are key, and lumbar puncture is advised for disseminated or immunosuppressed cases.

entities.variants: Histoplasma capsulatum var. capsulatum; acute pulmonary histoplasmosis; histoplasmoma (healed calcified nodule); chronic cavitary pulmonary histoplasmosis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (HIV); fibrosing mediastinitis; broncholithiasis; Indian endemic foci (Gangetic plains, West Bengal)
entities.remarks: Small (2 to 4 micrometres) intracellular yeasts with narrow-based budding in macrophages; necrotising granulomas with calcification; mimics tuberculosis and carcinoma; urinary and serum antigen useful.
entities.histo: Histoplasmosis is caused by inhalation of Histoplasma capsulatum spores from soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings. Most infections are subclinical and heal as calcified nodules and hilar lymph nodes. Acute pulmonary histoplasmosis produces patchy pneumonia with granulomas. Histoplasmomas are well-circumscribed nodules with a central area of caseous necrosis, often concentrically laminated and calcified, surrounded by a fibrous capsule with granulomatous inflammation, closely mimicking tuberculomas and carcinoma radiologically. Chronic cavitary disease in emphysematous lungs resembles tuberculosis. Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis in HIV and other immunosuppressed states shows sheets of macrophages packed with tiny yeasts rather than well-formed granulomas. Mediastinal lymph node involvement can lead to fibrosing mediastinitis and broncholithiasis. The yeasts are uniform, oval, 2 to 4 micrometres, with narrow-based buds, mainly within macrophages, and in old necrotic granulomas may be sparse and degenerate. Differentials include tuberculosis, cryptococcosis, Talaromyces (transverse septum, no budding), Pneumocystis, Leishmania (kinetoplast) and C. glabrata.
entities.cyto: FNA or BAL shows granulomatous inflammation, necrosis or, in disseminated disease, macrophages containing numerous tiny yeasts with a clear halo-like artefact. Giemsa and Diff-Quik stains show them well. They must be distinguished from Leishmania, Talaromyces and Pneumocystis. Antigen detection in BAL and urine is helpful. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (granulomatous inflammation or fungal organisms identified).
entities.ihc: IHC is seldom needed; Histoplasma-specific immunostains and in situ hybridisation exist in reference centres. GMS is the most important stain and reveals small yeasts in necrotic centres of old granulomas where they are often invisible on H&E; PAS is less sensitive. Mucicarmine is negative and Fontana-Masson is negative, helping separate capsule-deficient Cryptococcus. Ziehl-Neelsen excludes tuberculosis. Antigen tests, serology and culture complete the diagnosis.

entities.variants: Coccidioides immitis and C. posadasii (American Southwest, Mexico, South America; travel-associated); acute pneumonia (valley fever); coccidioidal nodule; chronic cavitary coccidioidomycosis; disseminated disease
entities.remarks: Large spherules (30 to 100 micrometres) with thick walls containing endospores; necrotising granulomas with eosinophils; non-endemic in India, so travel history is key; laboratory hazard in culture.
entities.histo: Coccidioidomycosis is acquired by inhaling arthroconidia from soil in endemic semi-arid areas of the Americas. Most infections are self-limited, but some produce persistent nodules, thin-walled cavities or disseminated disease to skin, bone and meninges, particularly in immunocompromised patients, pregnant women and some ethnic groups. Histology shows necrotising granulomas with central caseous necrosis and peripheral epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells, often with eosinophils and a mixed suppurative response when endospores are released. The diagnostic structures are large, thick-walled spherules 30 to 100 micrometres across containing numerous round endospores 2 to 5 micrometres in size; empty or collapsed spherules and free endospores also occur. In cavities with air exposure, hyphae and arthroconidia may form. Differentials include Rhinosporidium (larger sporangia, mucicarmine positive), Emmonsia adiaspores (thick-walled but without endospores), Blastomyces, myospherulosis and tuberculosis.
entities.cyto: FNA or BAL can show spherules with endospores, free endospores, granulomatous inflammation, eosinophils and necrosis. Recognition of spherules on Papanicolaou or Diff-Quik is diagnostic, but free endospores can be mistaken for small yeasts such as Histoplasma. Culture is hazardous and the laboratory must be warned. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (fungal organisms identified).
entities.ihc: IHC has little role, although Coccidioides-specific antibodies exist in reference laboratories. GMS and PAS stain the spherule walls and endospores clearly; mucicarmine is negative (unlike Rhinosporidium). Serology (complement fixation, EIA, immunodiffusion) and PCR support the diagnosis, and Ziehl-Neelsen helps exclude tuberculosis.

entities.variants: Blastomyces dermatitidis and B. gilchristii (North America; rare reports from India and Africa); acute pneumonia; chronic pneumonia or mass lesion; disseminated (skin with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, bone, prostate)
entities.remarks: Yeasts 8 to 15 micrometres with thick refractile double-contoured walls and broad-based single budding; pyogranulomatous inflammation; pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia may mimic squamous carcinoma.
entities.histo: Blastomycosis is an endemic mycosis acquired by inhalation, presenting as acute pneumonia, chronic pneumonia or a mass that mimics lung cancer, with frequent dissemination to skin and bone. Histologically the hallmark is pyogranulomatous inflammation: microabscesses of neutrophils within and around granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells, often with necrosis and fibrosis. The organisms are round yeasts 8 to 15 micrometres across with a thick, refractile, double-contoured wall, multiple nuclei and characteristic single broad-based buds, found within giant cells and in microabscesses. Bronchial mucosa and skin may show pseudoepitheliomatous squamous hyperplasia overlying the abscesses, which can be mistaken for squamous cell carcinoma in small biopsies. Differentials include Cryptococcus (narrow-based budding, capsule), Paracoccidioides (multiple buds, ship's wheel), Coccidioides endospores, Histoplasma (much smaller) and squamous cell carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology from BAL, sputum or FNA shows neutrophils, epithelioid histiocytes and large thick-walled yeasts with broad-based budding, which are readily visible on Papanicolaou stain and are diagnostic. Reactive squamous atypia is a pitfall for overdiagnosis of carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (fungal organisms identified).
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed routinely. GMS and PAS highlight the thick-walled yeasts and their broad-based buds; mucicarmine is negative or only weakly positive. Culture (biphasic) or PCR and urine antigen testing confirm. In biopsies with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, p40 and keratin will stain both reactive and malignant squamous cells, so careful morphology and fungal stains are crucial.

entities.variants: Pneumocystis jirovecii; classic HIV-associated PCP with foamy alveolar exudate; non-HIV PCP (transplant, steroids, chemotherapy; more acute, more DAD); atypical patterns: granulomatous PCP, diffuse alveolar damage, interstitial fibrosis, cavitary nodules, calcification, vascular invasion, minimal-change; extrapulmonary pneumocystosis
entities.remarks: Foamy eosinophilic intra-alveolar casts containing cysts (4 to 7 micrometres, cup or crescent shaped on GMS with central dot); bilateral ground-glass; important in HIV with CD4 below 200.
entities.histo: Pneumocystis jirovecii is a fungal organism causing pneumonia in HIV infection with low CD4 counts and in patients receiving immunosuppressive therapy. Grossly the lungs are heavy and airless. The classic histology is a foamy, frothy, eosinophilic, honeycomb-like exudate filling alveoli, composed of masses of organisms and surfactant debris, accompanied by mild interstitial lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and type II pneumocyte hyperplasia. On GMS the cysts are round to cup-shaped, 4 to 7 micrometres, often crushed into crescent or helmet shapes, with characteristic central or paired intracystic dots. Atypical patterns occur in up to a third of cases, including diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes, granulomatous inflammation with few organisms, interstitial fibrosis, cavitation, calcification and vascular invasion, and sometimes minimal changes. Differentials include pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (granular PAS-positive material with cholesterol clefts, no organisms), pulmonary oedema, Histoplasma (budding yeasts within macrophages), and DAD of other causes.
entities.cyto: BAL or induced sputum is the main diagnostic specimen. On Papanicolaou stain the organisms form characteristic foamy, alveolar casts with a honeycomb appearance and tiny dots; on Giemsa or Diff-Quik the trophic forms show small purple nuclei within the cast. GMS on smears shows the cysts. Proteinaceous material in PAP and mucus can mimic casts. Immunofluorescence and PCR increase sensitivity. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (organisms identified).
entities.ihc: IHC for Pneumocystis (and direct immunofluorescence on BAL) is more sensitive than GMS, particularly in non-HIV cases with low organism burden. GMS shows the cysts with their typical intracystic dots, and Toluidine blue O is an alternative. PAS stains the foamy exudate. Beta-D-glucan in serum and PCR on BAL are supportive. CMV IHC should be done because co-infection is common.

entities.entity: Other fungal infections of the lung
entities.variants: Paracoccidioidomycosis (Paracoccidioides brasiliensis; ship's wheel multiple budding); talaromycosis (Talaromyces marneffei; HIV, North-East India and Southeast Asia; intracellular yeasts with transverse septum); sporotrichosis; hyalohyphomycosis (Fusarium, Scedosporium/Lomentospora, Paecilomyces); phaeohyphomycosis (dematiaceous moulds: Exophiala, Cladophialophora, Bipolaris, Alternaria); emergomycosis and adiaspiromycosis (Emmonsia); Trichosporon; chromoblastomycosis (rare); rhinosporidiosis of trachea (rare)
entities.remarks: Rare mycoses; morphology suggests genus but culture or molecular methods are needed; talaromycosis is AIDS-defining and endemic in Manipur and neighbouring regions.
entities.histo: This group covers uncommon fungal infections that the pathologist should recognise morphologically. Paracoccidioidomycosis, endemic in South America, produces granulomatous pneumonia and fibrosis with large yeasts showing multiple peripheral buds (pilot's or ship's wheel). Talaromycosis, endemic in Southeast Asia and North-East India, occurs in advanced HIV and causes granulomatous, suppurative or anergic necrotising lesions with macrophages packed with 3 to 5 micrometre oval or sausage-shaped yeast-like cells that divide by fission and show a transverse septum, unlike Histoplasma. Hyalohyphomycetes such as Fusarium and Scedosporium cause angioinvasive disease indistinguishable from aspergillosis, sometimes with adventitious sporulation in tissue. Phaeohyphomycetes produce brown-pigmented septate hyphae and yeast-like forms in necrotising granulomas. Emmonsia adiaspiromycosis shows large thick-walled adiaspores without endospores in granulomas. Sporotrichosis forms granulomas with asteroid bodies and rare yeasts. Differentials depend on morphology: histoplasmosis, aspergillosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis and tuberculosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology may show the characteristic fungal forms within histiocytes or in necrotic debris: multiple budding large yeasts in paracoccidioidomycosis, septate yeast-like cells in talaromycosis, pigmented hyphae in phaeohyphomycosis. Precise identification requires culture or molecular testing. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (fungal organisms identified).
entities.ihc: IHC is limited to reference laboratories. GMS and PAS stain all these fungi; Fontana-Masson highlights melanin in dematiaceous fungi (and is weakly positive in some hyaline moulds); mucicarmine helps exclude Cryptococcus. The transverse septum of Talaromyces is best seen on GMS. Culture and panfungal PCR with sequencing are needed for genus and species identification and antifungal choice.

entities.variants: Larval migration with Loeffler-like eosinophilic pneumonitis; hyperinfection syndrome and disseminated strongyloidiasis (steroids, HTLV-1, transplant) with alveolar haemorrhage and Gram-negative sepsis
entities.remarks: Strongyloides stercoralis filariform larvae in alveoli and airways; hyperinfection in corticosteroid-treated patients is often fatal; endemic in India; screen before immunosuppression.
entities.histo: Strongyloides stercoralis is a soil-transmitted nematode whose larvae migrate through the lungs. In normal hosts, migration produces transient eosinophilic infiltrates (a Loeffler-like syndrome). In hyperinfection, typically triggered by corticosteroids, HTLV-1 infection or transplantation, autoinfection produces enormous numbers of filariform larvae that pass through the lungs, causing diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, acute pneumonia, diffuse alveolar damage and secondary Gram-negative bacteraemia from gut organisms carried with the larvae. Microscopically, larvae 400 to 500 micrometres long and about 15 micrometres wide, with a notched tail, lie within alveoli, airways and capillaries, often with surprisingly little eosinophilia in immunosuppressed patients. Adult worms and eggs are occasionally seen in the airways in heavy infection. Differentials include other migrating helminths (Ascaris, hookworm, Toxocara), eosinophilic pneumonia of other causes and bacterial pneumonia.
entities.cyto: Sputum, BAL or bronchial washings can show the filariform larvae, which are long, slender worms with a notched tail and a short buccal cavity, often accompanied by eosinophils, haemorrhage and Charcot-Leyden crystals. Finding larvae in respiratory specimens indicates hyperinfection and is a critical result requiring immediate communication.
