WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (parasites identified), urgent clinical notification.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. The larvae are visible on H&E and Papanicolaou stains. Gram stain and cultures detect accompanying enteric bacteria. Serology, stool examination and agar plate culture support diagnosis, and HTLV-1 testing is recommended in hyperinfection. Ivermectin treatment should begin promptly.

entities.variants: Echinococcus granulosus (cystic echinococcosis); intact, complicated (ruptured, infected) cysts; daughter cysts; alveolar echinococcosis (E. multilocularis, rare in lung); endemic in India
entities.remarks: Second commonest site after liver; laminated acellular membrane with germinal layer and protoscolices with hooklets; rupture may cause anaphylaxis; avoid FNA if suspected.
entities.histo: Pulmonary hydatid disease results from the larval stage of Echinococcus granulosus, acquired from dogs, and is endemic in India and many sheep-rearing regions. Lung cysts are often single, in the lower lobes, and can reach a large size, growing faster than liver cysts. The cyst has three layers: an outer host-derived fibrous pericyst with chronic inflammation, a middle thick, acellular, eosinophilic, lamellated (laminated) membrane, and an inner thin nucleated germinal layer producing brood capsules containing protoscolices with refractile hooklets. Daughter cysts may be present. Rupture into a bronchus produces expectoration of salty fluid and membranes (hydatid vomica), secondary infection, a cavity with the water lily sign, or anaphylaxis; rupture into pleura gives secondary hydatidosis. Collapsed or infected cysts show only the laminated membrane fragments with inflammation and necrosis. Differentials include other cystic lung lesions (bronchogenic cyst, abscess, CPAM) and rare alveolar echinococcosis (infiltrative small vesicles).
entities.cyto: Sputum or fluid may contain fragments of laminated membrane, protoscolices and refractile hooklets, which are diagnostic. Although FNA has been performed, it is generally avoided because of the risk of anaphylaxis and dissemination. Hooklets are acid-fast and birefringent. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (parasite identified).
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. The laminated membrane is strongly PAS positive and GMS positive, which helps identify fragments in degenerated or infected cysts. Hooklets are acid-fast on modified Ziehl-Neelsen and birefringent under polarised light. Serology (ELISA, indirect haemagglutination) supports the diagnosis, and imaging is usually characteristic.

entities.variants: Paragonimus westermani and other species (lung fluke); endemic in North-East India (Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh), East Asia; acquired from raw crabs and crayfish; pleuropulmonary disease; cerebral and ectopic forms
entities.remarks: Often misdiagnosed as tuberculosis; haemoptysis with rusty sputum; worm cysts and burrows with eosinophilic necrosis; operculated golden-brown eggs in sputum.
entities.histo: Paragonimiasis is caused by lung flukes acquired from undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish. Juvenile flukes migrate from the gut through the diaphragm and pleura into the lungs, where they mature in fibrous cysts or burrows near bronchi. Patients present with chronic cough, rusty or chocolate-coloured sputum and haemoptysis, mimicking tuberculosis, and pleural effusion and pneumothorax are common. Pathologically there are cystic cavities 1 to 2 cm across containing one or two adult worms, brown fluid and eggs, surrounded by a fibrous wall with eosinophils, histiocytes and Charcot-Leyden crystals, and tracks of eosinophilic necrotising inflammation. Eggs evoke granulomatous inflammation with foreign-body giant cells. The eggs are oval, yellow-brown, 80 to 120 micrometres long, thick-shelled and operculated, with a thickened abopercular end. Differentials include tuberculosis, other causes of eosinophilic pneumonia, Strongyloides, schistosomiasis (eggs with spines) and lung cancer.
entities.cyto: Sputum, BAL and pleural fluid can show the characteristic operculated golden-brown eggs, often with eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals; finding them is diagnostic. Microscopy of sputum in suspected tuberculosis that is smear negative should include a search for eggs in endemic regions. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (parasite identified).
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. The eggs are visible on H&E and Papanicolaou stains and are weakly acid-fast, which can cause confusion on Ziehl-Neelsen smears. Serology (ELISA, immunoblot) is useful when eggs are not found. Eosinophilia and raised IgE support the diagnosis.

entities.variants: Dirofilaria immitis (dog heartworm) causing pulmonary coin lesion; D. repens (subcutaneous and ocular in India, rare in lung)
entities.remarks: Solitary peripheral coin lesion from a dead worm embolised to a pulmonary artery branch, causing infarct; mimics carcinoma; diagnosed at resection.
entities.histo: Pulmonary dirofilariasis follows the bite of a mosquito carrying Dirofilaria immitis, a canine heartworm. In humans the immature worm cannot mature, dies and embolises to a small pulmonary artery, causing a localised infarct. The result is usually a solitary, well-circumscribed peripheral subpleural nodule 1 to 3 cm, a coin lesion suspicious for carcinoma, found incidentally and excised. Microscopically there is a spherical zone of coagulative necrosis (infarct) surrounded by a granulomatous rim of epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils and fibrosis. Within a thrombosed artery in the centre lie cross sections of a degenerating nematode with a thick multilayered cuticle, prominent lateral cords, internal longitudinal ridges and musculature. Differentials include tuberculoma, fungal granulomas, GPA and pulmonary infarct of other causes; identifying the worm in the vessel is diagnostic.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a minimal role. FNA of the nodule usually yields necrotic debris and histiocytes and is rarely diagnostic; fragments of the worm are only occasionally sampled. The main value is excluding malignancy. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (necrosis and granulomatous inflammation), or Non-diagnostic when only necrosis is obtained.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. Elastic stains (Verhoeff-van Gieson) show the worm lies within a pulmonary artery branch, and trichrome highlights the cuticle and musculature. GMS and Ziehl-Neelsen exclude fungal and mycobacterial causes of necrotising granulomas. Species identification relies on morphology or PCR.

entities.entity: Other parasitic infections of the lung
entities.variants: Amoebic lung abscess (Entamoeba histolytica, extension from liver); toxoplasmosis (immunocompromised); schistosomiasis (granulomas and pulmonary hypertension; eggs with spines); ascariasis and hookworm larval migration (Loeffler syndrome); visceral larva migrans (Toxocara); cryptosporidiosis of airways (AIDS); trichomonads; leishmaniasis (rare); microsporidia; Pentastomiasis (rare); filarial (tropical pulmonary eosinophilia, see eosinophilic row)
entities.remarks: Rare; mostly in endemic or immunocompromised settings; morphology of organisms in tissue or cytology is key; eosinophilia frequent in helminth infections.
entities.histo: Several other parasites affect the lung. Amoebic abscesses usually arise by direct extension from a right-lobe liver abscess through the diaphragm, forming a right lower lobe cavity with anchovy-sauce necrotic material and trophozoites at the edge, which have foamy cytoplasm and ingested red cells. Toxoplasmosis in immunosuppressed patients causes necrotising pneumonitis with tachyzoites and cysts in cells. Schistosomiasis (S. mansoni, S. haematobium, S. japonicum) produces granulomas around eggs within or near pulmonary arteries and can lead to plexiform pulmonary hypertension. Migrating larvae of Ascaris, hookworms and Toxocara cause transient eosinophilic pneumonitis (Loeffler syndrome) with eosinophil-rich alveolar exudates and occasionally larvae in granulomas. Cryptosporidium can coat the airway epithelium in AIDS. Trichomonads and microsporidia are rare. Differentials include eosinophilic pneumonia of other causes, bacterial abscess, tuberculosis and fungal infection.
entities.cyto: Cytology can identify organisms: amoebic trophozoites with ingested red cells in aspirates, toxoplasma tachyzoites, schistosome eggs with terminal or lateral spines, helminth larvae, and cryptosporidia as small spherules on epithelial surfaces. Eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals suggest helminth infection. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (parasites identified).
entities.ihc: IHC is useful for Toxoplasma (specific antibody confirms tachyzoites and cysts) and can help with Entamoeba in reference laboratories. PAS highlights amoebic trophozoites, modified acid-fast stain shows Cryptosporidium, and Ziehl-Neelsen stains the lateral-spined S. mansoni egg shell. Serology, stool microscopy and PCR complement tissue findings.

entities.variants: Pulmonary sarcoidosis (Scadding stages 0 to IV); nodular sarcoidosis; necrotising sarcoid granulomatosis; endobronchial sarcoidosis; fibrotic (stage IV) sarcoidosis with honeycombing and upper lobe fibrosis; Lofgren syndrome; sarcoid-like reactions (drug-induced including checkpoint inhibitors, tumour-associated, CVID)
entities.remarks: Multisystem disease with tight, well-formed non-necrotising granulomas in lymphangitic distribution (bronchovascular bundles, septa, pleura); hilar nodes; diagnosis of exclusion (TB is key differential in India); EBUS-TBNA useful.
entities.histo: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem disorder of unknown cause characterised by non-necrotising granulomas, with the lungs and hilar or mediastinal lymph nodes involved in most patients. The granulomas are tight, well formed and compact, composed of epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells with a rim of lymphocytes and concentric lamellar fibrosis, and they coalesce into nodules. Their distribution is characteristically lymphangitic, along bronchovascular bundles, interlobular septa and the pleura, which explains the high yield of transbronchial and endobronchial biopsy. Giant cells may contain asteroid bodies, Schaumann bodies (laminated calcified concretions) and calcium oxalate crystals, none specific. Granulomatous vasculitis of vessel walls is common. Small foci of fibrinoid necrosis can occur, but caseation is not a feature. Advanced disease shows hyalinised fibrotic nodules, upper lobe predominant fibrosis and honeycombing. Necrotising sarcoid granulomatosis shows confluent granulomas, large zones of necrosis and granulomatous vasculitis. Differentials include tuberculosis and fungal infection (necrosis, organisms), hypersensitivity pneumonitis (poorly formed, bronchiolocentric granulomas), berylliosis (identical, exposure history), drug-related and tumour-associated sarcoid-like reactions, GLILD, aspiration and talc granulomatosis.
entities.cyto: EBUS-TBNA of hilar and mediastinal nodes is a key diagnostic method. Aspirates show cohesive clusters of epithelioid histiocytes with elongated, curved, bland nuclei and pale cytoplasm, multinucleated giant cells and a background of lymphocytes, without necrosis. BAL shows lymphocytosis, often with a raised CD4:CD8 ratio (above 3.5 supports the diagnosis). Granulomas in cytology do not exclude tuberculosis, lymphoma or a sarcoid reaction to carcinoma, so microbiology and careful screening for malignant cells are needed. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (granulomatous inflammation, non-necrotising).
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role and serves mainly to exclude alternatives. CD68 highlights histiocytes, and CD4 and CD8 flow cytometry on BAL can support the diagnosis. Ziehl-Neelsen, GMS and PAS should be performed on granulomas to exclude mycobacteria and fungi, and polarisation detects foreign material and oxalate crystals. When granulomas occur in nodes from patients with known cancer, keratins, CD30, CD15 and CD20 help exclude metastatic carcinoma and lymphoma (especially Hodgkin lymphoma) associated with a sarcoid reaction.

entities.variants: Non-fibrotic (cellular, previously acute or subacute) HP; fibrotic HP (UIP-like, fibrotic NSIP-like, bronchiolocentric fibrosis patterns); antigens: bird fancier's lung, farmer's lung (thermophilic actinomycetes), hot tub lung (MAC), humidifier lung, mushroom workers, isocyanates, metal-working fluids, moulds; acute exacerbation
entities.remarks: Immune-mediated response to inhaled antigens; triad of cellular bronchiolitis, interstitial lymphocytic pneumonitis and poorly formed non-necrotising granulomas; BAL lymphocytosis; fibrotic HP has worse prognosis.
entities.histo: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immunologically mediated interstitial lung disease caused by repeated inhalation of organic antigens or low molecular weight chemicals. Non-fibrotic HP shows a characteristic triad centred on small airways: cellular chronic bronchiolitis with lymphocytes and plasma cells, a diffuse but bronchiolocentric interstitial lymphocytic pneumonitis that expands alveolar walls, and poorly formed, loose, non-necrotising granulomas or scattered multinucleated giant cells in the interstitium and peribronchiolar areas, often containing cholesterol clefts or Schaumann bodies. Foci of organising pneumonia and foamy macrophages in alveoli are common. Fibrotic HP shows fibrosis in a UIP-like pattern with honeycombing, a fibrotic NSIP-like pattern, or peribronchiolar fibrosis with bronchiolar metaplasia (peribronchiolar metaplasia, lambertosis) and bridging fibrosis between bronchioles and septa, with residual granulomas and lymphoid inflammation suggesting the diagnosis. Hot tub lung shows more compact intraluminal granulomas. Differentials include sarcoidosis (lymphangitic tight granulomas), NSIP, UIP/IPF, LIP, aspiration, drug reactions, mycobacterial infection and connective tissue disease-associated ILD.
entities.cyto: Cytology contributes mainly through BAL, which typically shows marked lymphocytosis, often above 30 to 40 percent, with mast cells and foamy macrophages; the CD4:CD8 ratio is usually low or normal but variable. Granulomas are rarely sampled. BAL findings support but do not establish the diagnosis, which requires multidisciplinary discussion of exposure, imaging and histology. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role in hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Special stains are used to exclude infection (Ziehl-Neelsen and GMS on granulomas, particularly to rule out mycobacteria in hot tub lung), and CD3, CD20 and light chains may be used when a dense lymphoid infiltrate raises the question of lymphoma. Elastic stains help assess airway-centred fibrosis and bronchiolar obliteration. Serum specific IgG (precipitins) supports antigen exposure.

entities.variants: Classic systemic GPA; limited (lung-predominant) GPA; airway GPA (subglottic and tracheobronchial stenosis, ulcerative tracheobronchitis); patterns: necrotising nodules, diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with capillaritis, organising pneumonia-like, bronchocentric, eosinophil-rich variants
entities.remarks: ANCA-associated (PR3-ANCA usually) necrotising granulomatous vasculitis of upper and lower respiratory tract and kidneys; triad of parenchymal necrosis, vasculitis and granulomatous inflammation.
entities.histo: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is an ANCA-associated, usually PR3-positive, necrotising granulomatous inflammation of the respiratory tract with necrotising vasculitis of small and medium vessels and often glomerulonephritis. In the lung it typically forms multiple cavitating nodules or masses. The diagnostic triad is geographic parenchymal necrosis, vasculitis and granulomatous inflammation. The necrosis has irregular serpiginous outlines with basophilic, dirty debris from neutrophil karyorrhexis, and is rimmed by palisading histiocytes. Microabscesses with neutrophils, scattered multinucleated giant cells and loose granulomas are seen, but well-formed sarcoid-like granulomas are unusual. Vasculitis affects arteries, veins and capillaries, with acute, chronic or granulomatous inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall. Capillaritis with diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, organising pneumonia and airway involvement (subglottic stenosis, ulcerative tracheobronchitis) also occur. Differentials include mycobacterial and fungal infections (organisms, caseous rather than basophilic necrosis), EGPA (asthma, eosinophilia), lymphomatoid granulomatosis (atypical EBV-positive B cells), rheumatoid nodules, necrotising sarcoid granulomatosis and infarcts.
entities.cyto: Cytology is non-specific. FNA or BAL of nodules shows necrotic debris, neutrophils, scattered histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells, sometimes with haemosiderin-laden macrophages in haemorrhage. Reactive atypical cells and necrosis may raise concern for carcinoma. BAL showing progressively bloodier aliquots and siderophages supports alveolar haemorrhage. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (necrotising inflammation), with ANCA serology and histological correlation advised.
entities.ihc: IHC plays a limited role. Elastic stains (EVG) are very useful to show vessel wall destruction, and GMS and Ziehl-Neelsen must be negative to exclude infection, which is essential before diagnosing GPA. CD20, CD3 and EBER help exclude lymphomatoid granulomatosis when there are atypical lymphoid cells and angiocentric infiltrates. Iron stain shows haemosiderin in alveolar haemorrhage. Serum PR3-ANCA (cytoplasmic pattern) or MPO-ANCA is the key laboratory correlate.

entities.entity: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg-Strauss syndrome)
entities.variants: Prodromal (asthma, rhinosinusitis), eosinophilic (eosinophilic pneumonia) and vasculitic phases; ANCA-positive (MPO) and ANCA-negative subsets; leukotriene antagonist or omalizumab unmasking
entities.remarks: Asthma, blood eosinophilia and necrotising vasculitis; eosinophilic pneumonia, eosinophil-rich vasculitis and extravascular necrotising granulomas with eosinophils; cardiac involvement main cause of death.
entities.histo: EGPA is a systemic small to medium vessel vasculitis occurring in patients with asthma and blood eosinophilia, with about 40 percent being MPO-ANCA positive. Lung involvement includes eosinophilic pneumonia, asthmatic bronchitis and vasculitis. Histologically the classic triad is eosinophil-rich infiltrates (often eosinophilic pneumonia with alveoli filled with eosinophils and macrophages), necrotising vasculitis of small arteries and veins with numerous eosinophils, and extravascular necrotising granulomas in which a central eosinophilic necrotic core (with degranulated eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals) is surrounded by palisading histiocytes and giant cells. All three are seldom present together in a biopsy, and treatment with steroids may mask features. Airways show the changes of asthma. ANCA-positive patients tend to have glomerulonephritis and alveolar haemorrhage, while ANCA-negative patients have more cardiac and lung parenchymal disease. Differentials include chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (no vasculitis), ABPA, parasitic infection, drug reactions, GPA (fewer eosinophils, basophilic necrosis) and hypereosinophilic syndrome.
entities.cyto: BAL in EGPA typically shows marked eosinophilia, often more than 25 percent, with Charcot-Leyden crystals, supporting eosinophilic lung disease but not distinguishing EGPA from chronic eosinophilic pneumonia or parasitic causes. FNA is rarely used. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC has no specific role. Elastic stains highlight vasculitis and destruction of vessel walls, and Congo red or Giemsa stains can accentuate eosinophils. GMS, Ziehl-Neelsen and parasite search exclude infection. Serology for MPO-ANCA, blood eosinophil count and IgE are key, and clinical criteria (ACR/EULAR 2022) are used for classification.

entities.variants: Microscopic polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA); isolated pauci-immune pulmonary capillaritis; capillaritis in SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, IgA vasculitis, drugs (propylthiouracil, hydralazine, levamisole-adulterated cocaine), Behcet disease; MPA-associated fibrotic ILD (UIP pattern)
entities.remarks: Necrotising small-vessel vasculitis without granulomas; neutrophilic capillaritis with diffuse alveolar haemorrhage; pulmonary-renal syndrome; MPO-ANCA positive interstitial fibrosis may precede vasculitis.
entities.histo: Microscopic polyangiitis is an ANCA-associated, usually MPO-positive, necrotising small-vessel vasculitis without granulomatous inflammation, most often presenting with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (pulmonary-renal syndrome). The lung lesion is neutrophilic capillaritis: alveolar septa are infiltrated by neutrophils with nuclear dust, fibrinoid necrosis of capillary walls and fibrin thrombi, with red cells, fibrin and haemosiderin-laden macrophages filling alveoli. Neutrophils may spill into alveolar spaces. Small arterioles and venules can show fibrinoid necrosis. Repeated episodes leave interstitial haemosiderin and fibrosis. A subset of MPO-ANCA positive patients has fibrotic interstitial lung disease, usually a UIP pattern. Isolated pulmonary capillaritis is a pauci-immune capillaritis limited to the lung. Differentials include anti-GBM disease (linear IgG on immunofluorescence), lupus and other immune-complex capillaritis, GPA (granulomatous inflammation, necrotising nodules), bland haemorrhage (no neutrophils in septa) and diffuse alveolar damage with haemorrhage.
entities.cyto: BAL showing progressively bloodier returns in sequential aliquots, many haemosiderin-laden macrophages (over 20 percent siderophages) and neutrophils supports diffuse alveolar haemorrhage but does not identify the cause. Cytology also excludes infection. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (haemorrhage and haemosiderin-laden macrophages).
entities.ihc: IHC is not routinely useful. Perls iron stain shows haemosiderin-laden macrophages and interstitial iron, and elastic stains outline damaged small vessels. Immunofluorescence on fresh lung (or more often kidney) helps separate pauci-immune vasculitis from anti-GBM linear IgG deposition and lupus granular immune complexes. ANCA serology (MPO, PR3) and anti-GBM antibodies are essential. Special stains for organisms exclude infection-related haemorrhage.

entities.variants: Anti-GBM disease with pulmonary haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis; lung-limited presentation; double-positive (anti-GBM and ANCA) disease; triggers: smoking, hydrocarbon exposure
entities.remarks: Autoantibodies to the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen; diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with linear IgG along alveolar and glomerular basement membranes; young men, smokers.
entities.histo: Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease is an autoimmune disorder in which antibodies against the non-collagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen bind alveolar and glomerular basement membranes, causing pulmonary haemorrhage and crescentic glomerulonephritis. It affects young men, often smokers, and older patients, and pulmonary haemorrhage is more common in smokers because injury exposes the antigen. Grossly the lungs are heavy and red-brown. Microscopically the alveoli are filled with fresh blood, fibrin and haemosiderin-laden macrophages, and the alveolar septa may be slightly thickened, with type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and occasional mild capillaritis; recurrent episodes lead to interstitial haemosiderosis and fibrosis. Immunofluorescence shows linear deposition of IgG (and sometimes C3) along alveolar capillary basement membranes, although this is technically difficult in lung and the kidney is usually biopsied. Differentials include ANCA vasculitis, lupus pneumonitis, idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis and other causes of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage.
entities.cyto: BAL shows haemorrhage with numerous haemosiderin-laden macrophages and increasing blood in sequential aliquots, confirming alveolar haemorrhage but not its cause. Cytology mainly excludes infection. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (haemorrhage).
entities.ihc: Direct immunofluorescence on fresh tissue for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and light chains shows linear IgG along basement membranes, which is diagnostic; the kidney biopsy is the usual source. Perls stain demonstrates haemosiderin. Serum anti-GBM antibodies and ANCA (double positivity in about a third) are essential. Routine IHC on paraffin is not diagnostic.

entities.variants: Behcet disease (pulmonary artery aneurysms, thrombosis); Takayasu arteritis and giant cell arteritis involving pulmonary arteries; isolated pulmonary arteritis; IgA vasculitis; polyarteritis nodosa (bronchial arteries, rare); cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis; drug-induced and infection-associated vasculitis; necrotising sarcoid granulomatosis (see sarcoidosis); Hughes-Stovin syndrome
entities.remarks: Large and variable vessel vasculitides rarely biopsied; pulmonary artery aneurysm in Behcet disease is a major cause of fatal haemoptysis; secondary vasculitis is common in infections and should not be overinterpreted.
entities.histo: Several systemic vasculitides involve pulmonary vessels. Behcet disease, a variable-vessel vasculitis, causes pulmonary artery aneurysms and thrombosis due to lymphocytic and neutrophilic inflammation of the vasa vasorum and media with destruction of elastic laminae, leading to massive haemoptysis; Hughes-Stovin syndrome is a related disorder. Takayasu arteritis and giant cell arteritis can involve elastic pulmonary arteries with granulomatous panarteritis, giant cells, intimal fibrosis and stenosis, producing pulmonary hypertension or perfusion defects. IgA vasculitis and cryoglobulinaemia occasionally cause capillaritis and haemorrhage. Polyarteritis nodosa rarely affects bronchial arteries. Secondary vasculitis is common in infections (fungal, mycobacterial, Pseudomonas), within inflammatory nodules and adjacent to tumours, and should not be diagnosed as primary vasculitis without clinical support. Differentials include chronic thromboembolic disease, intimal sarcoma of the pulmonary artery, pulmonary hypertension and infectious arteritis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has essentially no role in large and medium vessel pulmonary vasculitis. BAL may show haemorrhage when capillaritis is present and is mainly used to exclude infection. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Non-diagnostic.
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role. Elastic stains demonstrate destruction and fragmentation of elastic laminae, aneurysm formation and intimal proliferation, and trichrome shows fibrosis. CD3, CD20 and CD68 characterise inflammation. In large vessel involvement, IgG4 staining helps exclude IgG4-related arteritis, and MDM2 IHC or FISH helps exclude intimal sarcoma in obstructive pulmonary artery lesions. Special stains for organisms exclude infectious arteritis.

entities.variants: Asthmatic (eosinophil-rich, associated with ABPA) and non-asthmatic (neutrophil-rich; associated with infection, rheumatoid arthritis, GPA, ankylosing spondylitis) forms
entities.remarks: A pattern rather than a disease: necrotising granulomatous destruction of bronchi and bronchioles; search for fungi and mycobacteria; asthmatic cases relate to ABPA.
entities.histo: Bronchocentric granulomatosis is a descriptive histological pattern in which necrotising granulomatous inflammation replaces the mucosa and wall of bronchi and bronchioles. Affected airways are filled with necrotic debris and lined by palisading epithelioid histiocytes, with giant cells, chronic inflammation and destruction of the wall, while adjacent pulmonary arteries may show secondary vasculitis. In asthmatic patients the lesion is usually a manifestation of ABPA or allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis, with numerous eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals, allergic mucin and fragmented fungal hyphae, and is often accompanied by eosinophilic pneumonia and mucoid impaction. In non-asthmatic patients the infiltrate is rich in neutrophils and plasma cells, and the pattern may be due to mycobacterial or fungal infection (especially Histoplasma), rheumatoid arthritis, GPA or aspiration. Differentials include tuberculosis and fungal infection (organisms, caseous necrosis), GPA (vasculitis, parenchymal geographic necrosis), aspiration (foreign material) and EGPA.
entities.cyto: Cytology is non-specific. BAL or sputum may show eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals and fungal hyphae in asthmatic cases, or neutrophils and necrotic debris in non-asthmatic forms. Epithelioid histiocytes may be seen. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. Special stains are essential: GMS and PAS for fungi (often sparse and fragmented), Ziehl-Neelsen and auramine for mycobacteria, and Gram stain for bacteria. Elastic stain helps recognise destroyed airway walls adjacent to pulmonary arteries. Serology (IgE, Aspergillus-specific IgE, ANCA, rheumatoid factor) is used for clinical correlation.

entities.entity: Intravenous drug use-related pulmonary granulomatosis (talc and excipient granulomatosis)
entities.variants: Talc (magnesium silicate) granulomatosis; microcrystalline cellulose, crospovidone and starch embolisation from injected crushed tablets; cotton fibre emboli; secondary panlobular emphysema (methylphenidate, talc); pulmonary hypertension; septic emboli and endocarditis-related abscesses
entities.remarks: Injection of crushed oral tablets deposits birefringent filler particles within and around small arteries and in the interstitium with foreign-body giant cells; can cause pulmonary hypertension and lower lobe emphysema.
entities.histo: People who inject crushed oral tablets intravenously embolise insoluble excipients such as talc, microcrystalline cellulose, crospovidone and starch into the pulmonary circulation. These lodge in small arteries and arterioles and migrate into the perivascular and interstitial tissue, provoking foreign-body granulomas with multinucleated giant cells containing the particles. Talc forms plate-like, needle-shaped, strongly birefringent crystals; microcrystalline cellulose appears as elongated, rod-like birefringent fibres; crospovidone appears as coral-like basophilic non-birefringent particles; and starch shows Maltese-cross birefringence. Chronic deposition leads to intimal fibrosis, thrombotic arteriopathy and pulmonary hypertension, sometimes with plexiform lesions, and conglomerate fibrotic masses resembling progressive massive fibrosis. Methylphenidate and talc injection are associated with panlobular, lower-lobe emphysema. Septic emboli, abscesses and endocarditis are additional complications. Differentials include aspiration of pill fragments (bronchiolocentric rather than angiocentric), sarcoidosis, silicosis and other pneumoconioses, and infection.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a minor role. BAL may contain macrophages with birefringent particles, which can suggest the diagnosis, and FNA of conglomerate masses shows histiocytes, giant cells and polarisable material. Polarised light examination of smears is helpful. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (granulomatous inflammation with foreign material).
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. Polarised light microscopy is the key adjunct, showing birefringent talc and cellulose particles; PAS and GMS stain cellulose and starch (and fungi), crospovidone is highlighted by mucicarmine and Congo red artefactually, and elastic stain shows the intravascular location and vascular remodelling. Energy-dispersive X-ray analysis can identify mineral composition. Ziehl-Neelsen and GMS exclude infectious granulomas.

entities.variants: Large airway disease (tracheobronchitis, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, subglottic stenosis); small airway disease (bronchiolitis, granulomatous bronchiolitis); interstitial lung disease (organising pneumonia, NSIP, granulomatous ILD); necrobiotic nodules; drug toxicity (mesalazine, sulfasalazine, methotrexate, anti-TNF agents with infections); thromboembolism
entities.remarks: Airways are the commonest site, especially in ulcerative colitis; granulomas suggest Crohn disease; exclude drug toxicity and infection, particularly tuberculosis on anti-TNF therapy.
entities.histo: Lung involvement in inflammatory bowel disease reflects the shared embryological origin of gut and airway epithelium and is more often seen in ulcerative colitis, sometimes after colectomy. The commonest manifestation is large airway disease, with chronic bronchitis or tracheobronchitis showing dense mucosal and submucosal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, mucosal ulceration and bronchiectasis, and occasionally subglottic stenosis. Small airway disease includes cellular bronchiolitis, granulomatous bronchiolitis (in Crohn disease) and constrictive bronchiolitis. Parenchymal disease includes organising pneumonia, NSIP, eosinophilic pneumonia, non-necrotising granulomatous interstitial disease and rare necrobiotic (sterile neutrophilic) nodules. Drug toxicity from aminosalicylates, methotrexate and biologics must always be considered, and anti-TNF therapy increases the risk of tuberculosis and fungal infection. Differentials include infection, sarcoidosis, drug reaction, GPA (for necrobiotic nodules) and asthma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. BAL may show lymphocytosis or neutrophilia, and is used mainly to exclude infection, especially in patients on immunosuppression. Granulomatous material may be seen. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. Special stains (Ziehl-Neelsen, GMS, PAS) are important to exclude infection, particularly mycobacterial infection in patients on anti-TNF agents. CD3 and CD20 characterise lymphoid infiltrates when needed. Diagnosis relies on clinical correlation and exclusion of drug toxicity.

entities.variants: GLILD in common variable immunodeficiency; components: LIP, follicular bronchiolitis, nodular lymphoid hyperplasia, non-necrotising granulomas, organising pneumonia; association with lymphoma risk
entities.remarks: Seen in 10 to 20 percent of CVID patients; combination of granulomatous and lymphoproliferative changes; worse prognosis; exclude infection and lymphoma.
entities.histo: Granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease is a pulmonary complication of common variable immunodeficiency and related primary antibody deficiencies. Imaging shows nodules, ground glass and lymphadenopathy, often with splenomegaly. Histologically it combines lymphoid proliferations and granulomas: dense peribronchiolar and interstitial lymphoid infiltrates with reactive germinal centres (follicular bronchiolitis and nodular lymphoid hyperplasia), lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia with expansion of alveolar septa by small lymphocytes, and scattered non-necrotising, often poorly formed granulomas in the interstitium. Organising pneumonia and interstitial fibrosis may be present. Plasma cells are characteristically scant or absent, reflecting the antibody deficiency, which is a useful clue. Differentials include sarcoidosis (tight, lymphangitic granulomas, plasma cells present in surrounding tissue), hypersensitivity pneumonitis, infection, LIP of other causes, and lymphoma, particularly MALT lymphoma, to which these patients are predisposed.
entities.cyto: BAL shows lymphocytosis and is mainly used to exclude infection, which is frequent in CVID. Cytology cannot distinguish GLILD from other lymphoid or granulomatous processes. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is helpful in characterising the infiltrate: CD3 (T cells predominate, often CD4 more than CD8), CD20 highlighting B-cell follicles, and CD138 showing a paucity of plasma cells. Kappa and lambda in situ hybridisation and B-cell clonality studies help exclude MALT lymphoma. Special stains for organisms (GMS, Ziehl-Neelsen) are essential given immunodeficiency. EBER can be helpful to exclude EBV-driven lymphoproliferations.

entities.variants: Interstitial lung disease (UIP pattern commonest, NSIP, organising pneumonia, LIP, DAD); airway disease (follicular bronchiolitis, constrictive bronchiolitis, bronchiectasis, cricoarytenoid arthritis); rheumatoid (necrobiotic) nodules; Caplan syndrome (rheumatoid pneumoconiosis); pleuritis and effusion; drug toxicity (methotrexate, leflunomide, biologics) and infection
entities.remarks: Lung disease is a major cause of mortality in RA; multicompartment involvement with lymphoid follicles with germinal centres and plasma cells is a clue; rheumatoid nodules have central fibrinoid necrosis with palisading histiocytes.
entities.histo: Rheumatoid arthritis affects every compartment of the lung. Interstitial lung disease most commonly shows a UIP pattern with patchy subpleural fibrosis, fibroblast foci and honeycombing, but compared with IPF there are more lymphoid follicles with germinal centres, plasma cells and pleural involvement. NSIP, organising pneumonia, LIP and acute DAD (acute exacerbation) also occur. Airway disease includes follicular bronchiolitis with hyperplastic lymphoid follicles along bronchioles, constrictive bronchiolitis with concentric submucosal fibrosis narrowing bronchioles, and bronchiectasis. Rheumatoid nodules are subpleural or parenchymal necrobiotic nodules with central eosinophilic fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes and an outer zone of lymphocytes and plasma cells, which can cavitate. Caplan syndrome is the development of multiple rheumatoid-like nodules with dust rings in coal workers or silica-exposed patients with RA. Pleuritis and effusions are common. Differentials include IPF, drug toxicity (methotrexate pneumonitis with granulomas), infection (tuberculosis on biologics), GPA and necrotising granulomas of infection.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. Pleural fluid in rheumatoid pleuritis shows a characteristic triad of elongated or spindle-shaped histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells and granular necrotic background, with low glucose, and BAL may show lymphocytosis or neutrophilia. FNA of nodules yields necrotic debris and palisading histiocytes. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. Special stains (GMS, Ziehl-Neelsen) must be performed on necrobiotic nodules to exclude infection. CD20 and CD3 show reactive follicles, and kappa and lambda staining or ISH can exclude lymphoma in lymphoid-rich biopsies. Elastic stain is useful to identify obliterated bronchioles in constrictive bronchiolitis. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are clinical correlates.

entities.variants: Fibrotic NSIP (commonest), UIP pattern, organising pneumonia; pulmonary arterial hypertension (vasculopathy, also PVOD-like lesions); aspiration from oesophageal dysmotility; increased lung cancer risk
entities.remarks: ILD and PAH are the leading causes of death in systemic sclerosis; anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) associated with ILD, anti-centromere with PAH.
entities.histo: Interstitial lung disease affects most patients with systemic sclerosis and is a leading cause of death. The usual histological pattern is fibrotic NSIP, with temporally uniform interstitial fibrosis and mild chronic inflammation diffusely expanding alveolar walls, preserved architecture and few fibroblast foci, mainly in the lower lobes. A UIP pattern is less common and carries a worse prognosis. Pulmonary vascular disease is the other major complication, with intimal fibrosis, medial hypertrophy and concentric laminar intimal proliferation of small arteries, and occasionally venous and capillary involvement similar to PVOD; plexiform lesions are uncommon. Chronic aspiration from oesophageal dysmotility can add bronchiolocentric organising pneumonia with foreign material. There is an increased risk of lung carcinoma in fibrotic lungs. Differentials include idiopathic NSIP, IPF, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug toxicity and other connective tissue disease-associated ILDs.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role, with BAL showing neutrophilia or eosinophilia in active disease and being used mainly to exclude infection. FNA or cytology is used if a carcinoma develops. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic for SSc-ILD. Trichrome and elastic stains help assess interstitial fibrosis and vascular remodelling, including venous involvement. Special stains exclude infection. Serology (anti-Scl-70, anti-centromere, anti-RNA polymerase III) and clinical features establish the association. Any carcinoma arising in fibrotic lung is worked up with standard lung carcinoma panels.

entities.entity: Other connective tissue disease-associated lung diseases
entities.variants: Systemic lupus erythematosus (acute lupus pneumonitis with DAD, diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with capillaritis, shrinking lung syndrome, pleuritis, NSIP); polymyositis, dermatomyositis and antisynthetase syndrome (NSIP, OP, DAD; anti-Jo-1, anti-MDA5 rapidly progressive ILD); Sjogren syndrome (LIP, follicular bronchiolitis, cysts, amyloid, MALT lymphoma, NSIP); mixed connective tissue disease; undifferentiated CTD; ankylosing spondylitis (apical fibrobullous disease)
entities.remarks: Each CTD has a typical pattern set; multicompartment involvement (pleura, airway, interstitium, vessels) suggests CTD; Sjogren syndrome carries risk of MALT lymphoma and amyloid.
entities.histo: Several connective tissue diseases have characteristic pulmonary patterns. SLE causes pleuritis most commonly, and also acute lupus pneumonitis showing diffuse alveolar damage, diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with or without capillaritis and immune complex deposits, chronic NSIP-like fibrosis, and shrinking lung syndrome due to diaphragmatic dysfunction. Inflammatory myopathies, especially antisynthetase syndrome and anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis, produce NSIP, organising pneumonia, combined NSIP with OP, or rapidly progressive DAD with high mortality. Sjogren syndrome shows lymphoid lesions including follicular bronchiolitis, lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia with thin-walled cysts, nodular amyloid and light chain deposition, NSIP, and an increased risk of MALT lymphoma. Mixed and undifferentiated CTD show NSIP and pulmonary hypertension. Ankylosing spondylitis causes apical fibrobullous disease, sometimes with aspergilloma. Differentials include idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, drug reactions, infection, and lymphoma in Sjogren syndrome.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. BAL shows lymphocytosis, neutrophilia or haemorrhage depending on the pattern, and excludes infection. Pleural fluid in lupus may show LE cells. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic but helps in specific contexts. In Sjogren syndrome, CD20, CD3, CD43, kappa and lambda ISH and clonality studies help separate LIP and follicular bronchiolitis from MALT lymphoma, and Congo red confirms amyloid. Immunofluorescence for immune complexes may support lupus capillaritis. Special stains exclude infection. Serology (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Ro/La, myositis panel including anti-Jo-1 and anti-MDA5) establishes the CTD.

entities.variants: Patients with ILD and features of autoimmunity not meeting criteria for a defined CTD; histological domain features: NSIP, OP, NSIP with OP overlap, LIP, interstitial lymphoid aggregates with germinal centres, diffuse lymphoplasmacytic infiltration
entities.remarks: Research classification combining clinical, serological and morphological domains; multidisciplinary diagnosis; some patients evolve into a defined CTD.
entities.histo: Interstitial pneumonia with autoimmune features describes patients with interstitial lung disease who have some clinical or serological features of autoimmune disease but do not fulfil criteria for a specific connective tissue disease. The classification uses three domains: clinical (for example Raynaud phenomenon, mechanic's hands, inflammatory arthritis), serological (specific autoantibodies) and morphological, which includes imaging and histological patterns. Histological features that count in the morphological domain are NSIP, organising pneumonia, NSIP with organising pneumonia overlap, LIP, interstitial lymphoid aggregates with germinal centres, and diffuse lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with or without follicles; multicompartment involvement (pleural, airway, vascular) also contributes. A UIP pattern alone is not a morphological criterion but may be seen with other features. IPAF is not a final disease entity but a framework for research and follow-up, and some patients later develop a defined CTD. Differentials include idiopathic NSIP, IPF, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and drug-related lung disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. BAL may show lymphocytosis and is used to exclude infection and alternative diagnoses. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. CD20, CD3 and CD138 can characterise lymphoid aggregates and plasma cells, and special stains exclude infection. Autoantibody serology is the key correlate. Diagnosis requires multidisciplinary discussion.

entities.variants: Idiopathic acute eosinophilic pneumonia; smoking initiation or resumption (cigarettes, e-cigarettes); drug-induced (daptomycin, minocycline, NSAIDs); dust exposure (World Trade Center); infection-related
entities.remarks: Acute febrile respiratory failure in a young adult, often after starting smoking; diffuse alveolar damage with interstitial and alveolar eosinophils; BAL eosinophils over 25 percent; rapid steroid response.
entities.histo: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia presents as acute respiratory failure with bilateral infiltrates, typically in young adults who have recently started or resumed smoking, or after drug or dust exposure. Peripheral blood eosinophilia is often absent at onset. Histologically there is acute and organising diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes, interstitial oedema and type II pneumocyte hyperplasia, accompanied by numerous eosinophils in alveolar septa and alveolar spaces, intra-alveolar fibrin and macrophages, and occasionally eosinophilic microabscesses. Eosinophilic infiltration may also involve bronchioles, vessels and pleura. Vasculitis and granulomas are absent. Recovery with steroids is rapid and complete, without relapse. Differentials include acute interstitial pneumonia and other causes of DAD (lacking eosinophils), chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (subacute, no DAD), EGPA (vasculitis, asthma), drug reaction, parasitic infection, and vaping-associated lung injury.
entities.cyto: BAL is the key diagnostic test, showing eosinophils usually over 25 percent of cells, with macrophages and lymphocytes; this in the right clinical context avoids the need for biopsy. Infection must be excluded by appropriate stains and cultures. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (eosinophilic inflammation).
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. Eosinophils are recognised on H&E and can be accentuated with Congo red or Giemsa; Charcot-Leyden crystals may be seen. GMS, Ziehl-Neelsen and parasite examination exclude infectious causes. Drug and smoking history are essential correlates.

entities.variants: Idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia; secondary forms (drugs, ABPA, parasites, EGPA overlap); associated asthma in about half
entities.remarks: Subacute illness in middle-aged women, often asthmatic; peripheral photographic-negative-of-pulmonary-oedema infiltrates; alveolar eosinophils and macrophages; relapses on stopping steroids.
entities.histo: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia is a subacute to chronic illness, more frequent in middle-aged women and asthmatics, presenting with cough, fever, weight loss and peripheral, upper-zone predominant infiltrates that classically resemble the photographic negative of pulmonary oedema. Blood eosinophilia is usual. Histologically alveolar spaces are filled with eosinophils and macrophages, which are often multinucleated, together with fibrin, and alveolar septa are thickened by eosinophils, lymphocytes and plasma cells with type II pneumocyte hyperplasia. Eosinophilic microabscesses (necrotic eosinophils surrounded by histiocytes), Charcot-Leyden crystals and organising pneumonia are frequent; a mild non-necrotising vasculitis can occur. Diffuse alveolar damage is absent. The disease responds quickly to steroids but relapse is common. Differentials include EGPA (necrotising vasculitis, systemic disease), ABPA, parasitic infection, drug reaction, Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophils with Langerhans cells), organising pneumonia without eosinophils, and acute eosinophilic pneumonia.
entities.cyto: BAL shows marked eosinophilia, typically over 25 percent and often over 40 percent, with eosinophils, macrophages and Charcot-Leyden crystals, which supports the diagnosis when clinical and radiological features fit. Parasitic and fungal infections must be excluded. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (eosinophilic inflammation).
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role. CD1a and langerin can be used to exclude Langerhans cell histiocytosis when eosinophils are prominent and Langerhans cells are suspected. GMS and parasite search exclude infection. Elastic stain helps evaluate vessels if vasculitis (EGPA) is a concern. ANCA serology and IgE support clinical classification.

entities.variants: Parasitic (Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides larval migration); drug-induced; idiopathic
entities.remarks: Transient migratory infiltrates with blood eosinophilia and mild symptoms; resolves spontaneously within weeks; rarely biopsied.
entities.histo: Simple pulmonary eosinophilia, or Loeffler syndrome, is characterised by transient, migratory pulmonary infiltrates and peripheral blood eosinophilia with mild or absent symptoms that resolve within about a month. It is most often caused by larval migration of helminths such as Ascaris and hookworms through the lungs, and less often by drugs. When sampled, the lungs show interstitial and alveolar eosinophil-rich infiltrates with oedema and macrophages, similar to a mild eosinophilic pneumonia, sometimes with larvae in granulomas or alveoli. Organising pneumonia and vasculitis are absent or minimal. Stool examination for ova is usually negative in the early migratory phase and becomes positive weeks later. Differentials include chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (persistent, more severe), tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (filarial), ABPA, drug reactions and EGPA.
entities.cyto: Sputum or BAL shows eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals, and occasionally larvae. Cytology supports the diagnosis of eosinophilic lung disease but is rarely required because the condition is self-limited. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (eosinophilic inflammation).
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. Eosinophils are seen on routine stains, and larvae are recognised morphologically. Stool microscopy, parasite serology and drug history establish the cause.

entities.variants: Filarial hypersensitivity to Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi microfilariae trapped in lungs; acute, subacute and chronic fibrotic stages; endemic in India
entities.remarks: Nocturnal cough and wheeze, very high blood eosinophil count (often over 3000 per microlitre), raised IgE and filarial antibodies; responds to diethylcarbamazine; untreated disease leads to fibrosis.
entities.histo: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia is an immunological hyperresponsiveness to microfilariae of Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi that are cleared from the blood and trapped in the pulmonary vasculature. It is common in endemic areas of India and presents with nocturnal cough, wheeze, very high blood eosinophilia, high IgE and high filarial antibody titres, while microfilariae are usually absent from blood. Histological changes evolve with time: early disease shows histiocytic infiltration of alveoli; the subacute phase shows eosinophilic bronchopneumonia, interstitial eosinophilic infiltrates, eosinophilic abscesses and granulomas, occasionally around degenerating microfilariae; and chronic untreated disease shows interstitial fibrosis with a mixed infiltrate that can be permanent. Diagnosis is clinical and serological, with rapid response to diethylcarbamazine. Differentials include asthma, ABPA, chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, EGPA, Loeffler syndrome and Strongyloides infection.
entities.cyto: BAL shows striking eosinophilia, often far above that of other eosinophilic pneumonias, with Charcot-Leyden crystals; microfilariae are rarely seen. Cytology supports the diagnosis in an endemic setting with compatible serology. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (eosinophilic inflammation).
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. Microfilariae, if present, are recognised on H&E or Giemsa. Filarial antibody serology, antigen tests, blood eosinophil count and IgE support the diagnosis, and the therapeutic response to diethylcarbamazine is confirmatory.

entities.variants: Atopic (extrinsic, allergic) asthma; non-atopic (intrinsic) asthma; aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease; occupational asthma; exercise-induced; eosinophilic vs neutrophilic (T2-high vs T2-low) phenotypes; status asthmaticus and fatal asthma; asthma with mucoid impaction or ABPA
entities.remarks: Reversible bronchoconstriction from chronic airway inflammation; eosinophils, mucus plugs with Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals, thickened basement membrane, smooth muscle and gland hypertrophy (airway remodelling).
entities.histo: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways producing episodic, reversible bronchoconstriction, airway hyperresponsiveness and mucus hypersecretion. In fatal asthma (status asthmaticus) the lungs are overdistended and fail to collapse, and bronchi and bronchioles are occluded by thick, tenacious mucus plugs. Microscopically the plugs contain mucus, eosinophils, shed epithelial cells in clusters (Creola bodies), Curschmann spirals (coiled mucus casts of small airways) and Charcot-Leyden crystals derived from eosinophil galectin-10. Airway remodelling includes thickening of the subepithelial basement membrane zone by collagen deposition, submucosal oedema and an inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils, mast cells and lymphocytes, goblet cell hyperplasia, enlargement of submucosal glands, and hypertrophy and hyperplasia of bronchial smooth muscle. Epithelial damage with denudation is common. Neutrophil-predominant inflammation occurs in some severe and occupational cases. Differentials include chronic bronchitis (neutrophils and lymphocytes, glandular hypertrophy, less basement membrane thickening), EGPA, ABPA and eosinophilic bronchitis.
entities.cyto: Sputum cytology in asthma shows Curschmann spirals, Charcot-Leyden crystals, eosinophils and Creola bodies, which are clusters of reactive ciliated and columnar bronchial cells that can be papillary and three-dimensional. Creola bodies are a classic pitfall mimicking adenocarcinoma; the presence of cilia or terminal bars and the clinical setting are key. Induced sputum eosinophil counts help phenotype asthma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role in asthma. Eosinophils can be highlighted with Giemsa or Congo red, mast cells with tryptase or CD117, and the thickened basement membrane with trichrome. Creola bodies retain cilia, so careful morphology rather than IHC distinguishes them from adenocarcinoma; reactive cells can be TTF-1 positive, so TTF-1 alone is not helpful. Serum IgE, blood eosinophils and FeNO are clinical biomarkers guiding biologic therapy.

entities.variants: Simple chronic bronchitis (mucus hypersecretion); chronic mucopurulent bronchitis; chronic obstructive bronchitis (with COPD); chronic asthmatic bronchitis; industrial bronchitis (dust exposure); smoking-related; biomass smoke-related (common in rural Indian women)
entities.remarks: Clinical definition: productive cough for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years; mucous gland hypertrophy with Reid index above 0.4, goblet cell hyperplasia and squamous metaplasia; overlaps with emphysema in COPD.
entities.histo: Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically by persistent productive cough for at least three months in two consecutive years, most often due to cigarette smoking or exposure to biomass and occupational dusts. The bronchial mucosa is grossly hyperaemic and swollen, with mucinous or mucopurulent secretions. The cardinal histological feature is hypertrophy of submucosal mucous glands, measured by the Reid index (ratio of gland thickness to wall thickness between epithelium and cartilage), which exceeds 0.4 in chronic bronchitis compared with about 0.4 or less in normal airways. There is goblet cell hyperplasia extending into bronchioles, mucus plugging, chronic inflammation with lymphocytes, macrophages and neutrophils, squamous metaplasia, basal cell hyperplasia and sometimes dysplasia. Small airway changes (chronic bronchiolitis, goblet cell metaplasia, peribronchiolar fibrosis and narrowing) contribute most to airflow obstruction. Differentials include asthma (eosinophils, thick basement membrane, muscle hypertrophy), bronchiectasis (permanent dilatation), cystic fibrosis and diffuse panbronchiolitis.
entities.cyto: Sputum and bronchial washings show abundant mucus, neutrophils, macrophages and goblet cells, with reactive bronchial cells, squamous metaplastic cells and occasionally atypical metaplastic cells. Smokers may show pigmented macrophages. Atypical squamous metaplasia must be distinguished from squamous dysplasia and carcinoma, and keratinised atypical cells warrant further evaluation. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical when squamous atypia is present.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role. PAS and Alcian blue highlight goblet cell hyperplasia and mucus, and the Reid index is measured on H&E. In biopsies with squamous metaplasia and atypia, p40 and Ki-67 may help grade dysplasia, but the decision remains morphological. Infection stains are used when there is mucopurulent exacerbation.

entities.variants: Viral tracheobronchitis (influenza, adenovirus, RSV, HSV); bacterial tracheitis (S. aureus, membranous croup); diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae pseudomembrane, still reported in India); pertussis; pseudomembranous and ulcerative Aspergillus tracheobronchitis; inhalational injury (smoke, burns, toxic gases); post-intubation tracheitis
entities.remarks: Mucosal inflammation, ulceration and pseudomembrane formation of trachea and bronchi; diphtheritic pseudomembrane causes airway obstruction and toxin-mediated myocarditis.
entities.histo: Acute tracheobronchitis is inflammation of the trachea and bronchi, most often viral. Viral infection causes mucosal oedema, hyperaemia, epithelial necrosis with sloughing of ciliated cells and a lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrate, with characteristic inclusions in HSV and adenovirus. Bacterial tracheitis, often staphylococcal, produces purulent exudate and membranes in children. Diphtheria forms a tough, adherent grey pseudomembrane composed of fibrin, necrotic epithelium, neutrophils and Gram-positive club-shaped bacilli over ulcerated mucosa, which can dislodge and obstruct the airway, while exotoxin damages heart and nerves. Aspergillus tracheobronchitis in immunosuppressed and lung transplant patients shows pseudomembranes containing hyphae with mucosal invasion. Inhalational injury from smoke or toxic gases causes epithelial necrosis, fibrin casts and soot deposition. Healing may lead to squamous metaplasia, fibrosis and stenosis. Differentials include GPA airway disease, relapsing polychondritis, amyloidosis and tracheobronchial tumours causing ulceration.
entities.cyto: Brushings and washings show inflammatory cells, necrotic debris, degenerating ciliated cells with ciliocytophthoria, reactive bronchial cells and, depending on cause, viral inclusions, fungal hyphae or bacteria. Reparative changes in bronchial cells may appear atypical. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical for marked reactive atypia.
entities.ihc: IHC is used selectively for viral identification (HSV, CMV, adenovirus, influenza). Gram stain shows bacteria including Corynebacterium in diphtheritic membranes, which must be confirmed by culture and toxin testing. GMS highlights fungi in pseudomembranous tracheobronchitis. No tumour markers are needed unless a mass is present.

entities.variants: Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome after lung transplant (see CLAD) and after HSCT (GVHD); post-infectious (adenovirus, Mycoplasma; Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome); inhalational injury (nitrogen dioxide silo-filler's disease, diacetyl popcorn lung, sulphur mustard, military burn pit exposure); rheumatoid arthritis and other CTD; drugs (penicillamine, gold); DIPNECH-associated; idiopathic; Stevens-Johnson syndrome
entities.remarks: Concentric submucosal fibrosis narrowing or obliterating bronchioles; irreversible obstruction with mosaic attenuation and air trapping on expiratory CT; easily missed on biopsy (needs elastic stain).
entities.histo: Constrictive bronchiolitis, also called obliterative bronchiolitis, is a fibrotic small airway disease in which concentric subepithelial fibrosis progressively narrows and finally obliterates the lumen of membranous and respiratory bronchioles. Causes include lung and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, viral and Mycoplasma infection in childhood, toxic inhalations, connective tissue disease (especially rheumatoid arthritis), drugs and DIPNECH. Histologically, early lesions show lymphocytic bronchiolitis with submucosal fibrosis between the epithelium and smooth muscle, while late lesions show complete replacement of the bronchiole by a fibrous scar, recognisable only as a nodule of scar next to a pulmonary artery branch of similar size (an orphan artery). Smooth muscle hypertrophy, mucostasis, bronchiolectasis and mucus plugs may be seen, and the lung parenchyma between airways is often normal, so the changes are subtle and patchy. Differentials include proliferative bronchiolitis or organising pneumonia (intraluminal polypoid fibroblast plugs, reversible), asthma, respiratory bronchiolitis and peribronchiolar metaplasia.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role. BAL may show neutrophilia in transplant-related disease and is used to exclude infection. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Non-diagnostic.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role. Elastic stains (EVG, Movat) are essential to identify obliterated bronchioles by demonstrating residual elastic lamina and smooth muscle around fibrous scars adjacent to arteries, and trichrome highlights submucosal collagen. Special stains exclude infection in transplant patients. Synaptophysin and chromogranin should be applied when DIPNECH is suspected (neuroendocrine cell proliferation in affected airways).

entities.variants: Predominantly East Asian (HLA-B54); associated chronic sinusitis; Pseudomonas colonisation in late disease; responds to long-term macrolides
entities.remarks: Chronic progressive bronchiolitis of respiratory bronchioles with interstitial foamy macrophages in walls; centrilobular nodules and tree-in-bud on CT; rare in India but should be recognised.
entities.histo: Diffuse panbronchiolitis is a chronic inflammatory disorder of respiratory bronchioles described mainly in Japan, Korea and China, associated with chronic sinusitis and progressive obstruction, and later colonisation by Pseudomonas. Grossly there are diffuse yellow centrilobular nodules. Microscopically the walls of respiratory bronchioles and adjacent alveolar ducts are thickened by a transmural and peribronchiolar infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells and, characteristically, sheets of foamy macrophages that accumulate in the interstitium of the bronchiolar wall and adjacent alveolar septa. Lymphoid follicles may be present. Neutrophils fill the airway lumen, and proximal bronchiolectasis develops in later stages. The disease responds strikingly to long-term low-dose macrolide therapy. Differentials include follicular bronchiolitis (lymphoid follicles without foamy interstitial macrophages), aspiration bronchiolitis, cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, NTM infection, and endogenous lipoid pneumonia (foamy macrophages in alveoli rather than bronchiolar walls).
entities.cyto: Cytology has no specific role. BAL typically shows neutrophilia and sometimes lymphocytosis, and cultures may grow Haemophilus or Pseudomonas. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used for diagnosis. CD68 confirms that the interstitial foam cells are macrophages, and special stains exclude mycobacteria and fungi. Diagnosis rests on clinical, radiological and histological correlation.

entities.variants: Primary/idiopathic; secondary to rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren syndrome and other CTD; immunodeficiency (CVID, HIV); hypersensitivity; infection; part of GLILD spectrum
entities.remarks: Hyperplastic lymphoid follicles with reactive germinal centres along bronchioles; polyclonal; overlaps with LIP and nodular lymphoid hyperplasia; exclude MALT lymphoma.
entities.histo: Follicular bronchiolitis is a reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue in which numerous hyperplastic lymphoid follicles with reactive germinal centres lie along the walls of bronchioles and, to a lesser extent, bronchi, sometimes compressing the airway lumen. It occurs in connective tissue diseases, particularly rheumatoid arthritis and Sjogren syndrome, in congenital and acquired immunodeficiency, and in hypersensitivity reactions, and occasionally without an identifiable cause. The interstitium away from the airways shows little or no infiltrate, distinguishing it from LIP, although the two overlap. Mild lymphoplasmacytic bronchiolitis and peribronchiolar lymphoid aggregates without follicles may accompany it. Imaging shows small centrilobular and peribronchial nodules and ground glass. Differentials include LIP (diffuse interstitial infiltrate), nodular lymphoid hyperplasia (localised mass), MALT lymphoma (lymphangitic spread with sheets of monocytoid or marginal zone B cells, lymphoepithelial lesions, Dutcher bodies and light chain restriction), hypersensitivity pneumonitis and diffuse panbronchiolitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. BAL may show lymphocytosis, and FNA, if performed, shows a polymorphous lymphoid population with tingible body macrophages, consistent with reactive hyperplasia. Flow cytometry helps exclude a clonal B-cell population. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (reactive lymphoid population), or Atypical if a lymphoproliferative disorder cannot be excluded.
entities.ihc: IHC confirms the reactive nature: CD20 marks follicles with BCL2-negative germinal centres, CD3 highlights interfollicular T cells, CD21 or CD23 shows intact follicular dendritic cell meshworks, and kappa and lambda ISH shows polytypic plasma cells. MALT lymphoma, by contrast, shows sheets of CD20-positive, CD5-negative, CD10-negative B cells outside follicles, lymphoepithelial lesions highlighted by keratin, and light chain restriction. Molecular B-cell clonality studies are helpful in borderline cases.

entities.variants: Idiopathic LIP (rare); secondary LIP in Sjogren syndrome, other CTD, HIV (paediatric), CVID, autoimmune disorders, EBV, drug reactions; cystic LIP; LIP with amyloid or light chain deposition
entities.remarks: Diffuse polyclonal lymphoplasmacytic infiltration of alveolar septa with follicles; thin-walled cysts on CT; most cases are secondary; must exclude low-grade lymphoma.
entities.histo: Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia is a rare interstitial lung disease in which alveolar septa are diffusely and markedly expanded by a dense infiltrate of small lymphocytes, plasma cells and histiocytes, often with scattered lymphoid follicles with germinal centres and loose non-necrotising granulomas. The infiltrate is interstitial throughout the lobule rather than lymphangitic, and architecture is preserved, although thin-walled cysts form, probably through bronchiolar obstruction. Most cases are associated with Sjogren syndrome, other autoimmune diseases, HIV infection (especially in children) or immunodeficiency, and idiopathic LIP is now regarded as rare; many cases previously called LIP were cellular NSIP or lymphoma. Amyloid or light chain deposits may accompany Sjogren-associated disease. Differentials include cellular NSIP (milder, more uniform infiltrate), hypersensitivity pneumonitis (bronchiolocentric, poorly formed granulomas), follicular bronchiolitis, GLILD and MALT lymphoma, which shows lymphangitic spread, sheets of atypical B cells, pleural involvement and light chain restriction.
entities.cyto: BAL in LIP shows lymphocytosis, and cytology cannot reliably distinguish LIP from lymphoma or other lymphoid processes; flow cytometry or cell block immunophenotyping is helpful to exclude a clonal B-cell population. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical when a lymphoproliferative disorder is suspected.
entities.ihc: IHC is essential to support a reactive process: a mixed population of CD3-positive T cells (often predominant) and CD20-positive B cells, reactive follicles with BCL2-negative germinal centres, CD21 or CD23 follicular dendritic meshworks, and polytypic plasma cells on kappa and lambda ISH. Keratin shows no destructive lymphoepithelial lesions. Light chain restriction, aberrant CD43 coexpression on B cells and monoclonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangement favour MALT lymphoma. Congo red identifies associated amyloid.

entities.variants: Solitary or multiple lymphoid nodules; formerly pseudolymphoma; association with Sjogren syndrome and IgG4-related disease in some cases
entities.remarks: Localised reactive lymphoid mass with numerous reactive germinal centres and interfollicular plasma cells; diagnosis requires exclusion of MALT lymphoma and IgG4-related disease.
entities.histo: Pulmonary nodular lymphoid hyperplasia is a rare reactive lymphoproliferative lesion that presents as one or a few well-circumscribed nodules, usually discovered incidentally. Microscopically the nodule is composed of numerous reactive lymphoid follicles with prominent germinal centres, separated by sheets of mature plasma cells, small lymphocytes and variable fibrosis, with mild extension along lymphatic routes at the periphery. Russell bodies may be present but lymphoepithelial lesions, Dutcher bodies and amyloid are absent, and the alveolar architecture is effaced only within the nodule. Many cases historically labelled pseudolymphoma were in fact MALT lymphomas, so strict exclusion is required. Some cases have increased IgG4-positive plasma cells and may represent IgG4-related disease. Differentials include MALT lymphoma, IgG4-related disease, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour, follicular bronchiolitis and Castleman-like lesions.
entities.cyto: FNA shows a polymorphous population of small and large lymphocytes, plasma cells and tingible body macrophages, consistent with a reactive lymphoid process; flow cytometry or IHC on cell block is needed to exclude lymphoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical when lymphoma cannot be excluded on limited material.
entities.ihc: IHC shows CD20-positive follicles with BCL2-negative reactive germinal centres, intact CD21 and CD23 meshworks, a CD3-positive interfollicular population and polytypic plasma cells on kappa and lambda ISH. Lack of CD43 coexpression on B cells and absence of keratin-highlighted lymphoepithelial lesions support hyperplasia. IgG4 and IgG staining exclude IgG4-related disease. B-cell clonality PCR is negative, unlike MALT lymphoma.

entities.variants: Laryngotracheobronchial involvement with tracheomalacia and stenosis; systemic RP (auricular, nasal, joint); association with myelodysplasia and VEXAS syndrome (UBA1 mutation)
entities.remarks: Autoimmune inflammation and destruction of cartilage; airway disease spares the posterior membranous trachea; airway collapse and pneumonia cause death.
entities.histo: Relapsing polychondritis is an immune-mediated disease causing recurrent inflammation of cartilaginous structures, including the ear, nose, joints and the laryngotracheobronchial tree, which is involved in up to half of patients and is a major cause of mortality. CT shows thickening of the anterior and lateral walls of the trachea and bronchi with sparing of the posterior membranous wall, and later tracheobronchomalacia and stenosis. Biopsy shows perichondrial inflammation by lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils and histiocytes infiltrating the cartilage edge, loss of basophilia of cartilage matrix (chondrolysis) and progressive replacement of cartilage by granulation tissue and fibrosis. The overlying mucosa may be oedematous or normal. In older men, association with VEXAS syndrome (somatic UBA1 mutations) and myelodysplasia should be considered. Differentials include GPA (granulomatous inflammation, necrosis, vasculitis, involves posterior wall), tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica (submucosal bone and cartilage nodules without inflammation), amyloidosis and infection.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role in relapsing polychondritis. Airway samples are used only to exclude infection. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Non-diagnostic.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. Alcian blue and toluidine blue show loss of cartilage proteoglycans at the inflamed edges, and special stains exclude infection. Elastic and trichrome stains show fibrosis replacing cartilage. ANCA serology helps exclude GPA. In suspected VEXAS, bone marrow examination with vacuolated myeloid and erythroid precursors and UBA1 sequencing are needed.

entities.variants: Cellular NSIP; fibrotic NSIP; idiopathic NSIP; secondary NSIP (connective tissue disease, especially systemic sclerosis and myositis; hypersensitivity pneumonitis; drugs; IPAF; familial); NSIP with organising pneumonia overlap
entities.remarks: Temporally uniform interstitial inflammation and/or fibrosis with preserved architecture; few or no fibroblast foci or honeycombing; better prognosis than UIP; often a marker of CTD.
entities.histo: Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia is a pattern of diffuse interstitial lung disease characterised by uniform involvement of alveolar walls that appears to be of the same age throughout the biopsy. In cellular NSIP the alveolar septa are expanded by a mild to moderate infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells with type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and little fibrosis. In fibrotic NSIP the septa are thickened by uniform, homogeneous collagen deposition with variable inflammation, preserving the lung architecture, with few if any fibroblast foci and no or minimal honeycombing. Lymphoid aggregates, focal organising pneumonia and peribronchiolar accentuation can be present, but prominent granulomas, extensive organising pneumonia, eosinophils or hyaline membranes suggest other diagnoses. Imaging shows bilateral lower-zone ground glass and reticulation with subpleural sparing and traction bronchiectasis. Many cases are associated with connective tissue disease, hypersensitivity pneumonitis or drugs, so idiopathic NSIP requires multidisciplinary exclusion. Differentials include UIP (spatial and temporal heterogeneity, fibroblast foci, honeycombing), hypersensitivity pneumonitis, LIP, organising pneumonia and DIP.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. BAL in NSIP typically shows lymphocytosis, and occasionally neutrophilia in fibrotic disease, which supports an inflammatory ILD and helps exclude infection but is not diagnostic. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role. Trichrome and elastic stains help evaluate the uniformity of fibrosis and architectural preservation versus remodelling. Special stains exclude infection when inflammation is prominent. In lymphoid-rich cases, CD20, CD3 and light chain studies help exclude lymphoma. Serology for connective tissue disease is the most important correlate.

entities.variants: Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (formerly idiopathic BOOP); secondary OP (infection, aspiration, drugs, connective tissue disease, radiation, transplant, immune checkpoint inhibitors, inhalational injury, adjacent to abscess, tumour or infarct); focal nodular (mass-forming) OP; fibrosing OP; OP pattern in COVID-19
entities.remarks: Polypoid plugs of loose fibroblastic tissue (Masson bodies) in alveolar ducts, alveoli and bronchioles with preserved architecture; patchy migratory consolidations; steroid responsive; common nonspecific reaction in biopsies.
entities.histo: Organizing pneumonia is a reparative response to alveolar injury in which loose, pale-staining fibroblastic tissue in a myxoid matrix forms polypoid plugs (Masson bodies) that fill alveolar ducts, alveoli and often respiratory bronchioles (proliferative bronchiolitis), sometimes connecting adjacent alveoli through pores of Kohn in a butterfly pattern. The process is patchy and of uniform age, the underlying lung architecture is preserved, and there is mild chronic interstitial inflammation, type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and foamy macrophages in alveoli from obstructed airways. Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia is diagnosed only after exclusion of secondary causes, which are numerous and include infection, aspiration, drugs, connective tissue diseases and immunotherapy. In small biopsies, OP is frequently a nonspecific finding at the edge of abscesses, granulomas, infarcts or carcinoma, and the pathologist should mention that a more significant lesion may not have been sampled. Differentials include organising DAD (diffuse, hyaline membranes), AFOP (fibrin balls), NSIP, fibroblast foci in UIP (flat, in interstitium) and organising infection.
entities.cyto: Cytology is not diagnostic. BAL typically shows a mixed cellularity with lymphocytosis, often with neutrophils and eosinophils, and a low CD4:CD8 ratio, which supports but does not establish OP. FNA of mass-like OP may yield reactive pneumocytes and fibroblasts, a pitfall for overcalling malignancy. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical if reactive atypia is prominent.
entities.ihc: IHC has no specific role. Special stains for organisms (GMS, Ziehl-Neelsen, Gram) are performed to exclude infection, and the presence of foreign material on polarisation suggests aspiration. Keratin, TTF-1 and morphology help distinguish reactive pneumocyte hyperplasia from adenocarcinoma in nodular OP, and Ki-67 is generally low in reactive cells. Elastic stains show preserved architecture.
