entities.variants: Idiopathic AFOP; secondary AFOP (infection including COVID-19 and Acinetobacter, drugs, connective tissue disease, haematological malignancy and HSCT, transplant); fulminant and subacute courses
entities.remarks: Intra-alveolar fibrin balls with organising tissue, without hyaline membranes; patchy distribution; overlaps with DAD and OP; prognosis between OP and DAD.
entities.histo: Acute fibrinous and organizing pneumonia is a histological pattern of acute lung injury characterised by intra-alveolar fibrin deposits in the form of balls, accompanied by organising pneumonia, in a patchy distribution. The fibrin fills alveolar spaces as dense eosinophilic aggregates, often with loose fibroblastic tissue growing into it, while hyaline membranes, which define diffuse alveolar damage, are absent or minimal. Alveolar walls show mild oedema, acute and chronic inflammation and type II pneumocyte hyperplasia, but eosinophils, abscesses and granulomas are absent. Clinically, a fulminant form behaves like DAD with high mortality and a subacute form resembles organising pneumonia with better survival. Causes include infections, drugs, connective tissue disease and haematological disorders. Differentials include DAD (hyaline membranes, diffuse), organising pneumonia (no fibrin balls), eosinophilic pneumonia (eosinophils with fibrin), and infectious pneumonia (neutrophils, organisms), and AFOP may represent a sampling of DAD in small biopsies.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role. BAL is used to exclude infection and may show fibrin, neutrophils and reactive pneumocytes. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role. Fibrin stains (MSB, PTAH) highlight intra-alveolar fibrin balls if needed, and special stains (GMS, Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen) and viral IHC exclude infection. Eosinophil-rich cases should be reconsidered as eosinophilic pneumonia.

entities.variants: Smoking-related DIP; non-smoking DIP (marijuana, occupational dusts, drugs, connective tissue disease, surfactant mutations in children); DIP-like reaction around other lesions
entities.remarks: Diffuse uniform filling of alveoli by pigmented macrophages with mild septal thickening; mostly current or former smokers; good response to smoking cessation and steroids.
entities.histo: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia, now often called alveolar macrophage pneumonia, is a smoking-related interstitial lung disease in which alveolar spaces throughout the lobule are diffusely and uniformly filled with macrophages containing fine granular golden-brown smoker's pigment. The alveolar septa are mildly thickened by fibrosis and a sparse infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells, with type II pneumocyte hyperplasia; lymphoid aggregates and eosinophils may be present. The process is uniform and lacks the bronchiolocentric limitation of respiratory bronchiolitis, and fibroblast foci and honeycombing are minimal. In children, DIP can be due to surfactant gene mutations, and non-smoking adult cases occur with dust exposure and drugs. A DIP-like reaction is frequently seen around other lesions, including Langerhans cell histiocytosis, UIP and tumours, and should not be overinterpreted. Differentials include RB-ILD (bronchiolocentric), Langerhans cell histiocytosis, hard metal disease (giant cells), eosinophilic pneumonia, PAP and haemosiderin-laden macrophages in chronic haemorrhage.
entities.cyto: BAL shows abundant pigmented alveolar macrophages with fine brown particulate pigment that is weakly positive for iron, consistent with smoking-related macrophage accumulation; this is nonspecific and seen in many smokers. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. CD68 confirms macrophages, and CD1a or langerin helps exclude Langerhans cell histiocytosis when smoking-related lesions coexist. Perls iron shows faint dusty staining in smoker's macrophages, unlike the coarse refractile iron of haemosiderin. PAS is negative for the PAP-type material.

entities.entity: Respiratory bronchiolitis and respiratory bronchiolitis-associated ILD (RB-ILD)
entities.variants: Respiratory bronchiolitis (incidental, almost universal in smokers); RB-ILD (symptomatic, with interstitial disease); smoking-related interstitial fibrosis overlap (see separate row); vaping-associated macrophage changes
entities.remarks: Pigmented macrophages within respiratory bronchioles and adjacent alveoli with mild peribronchiolar fibrosis; RB-ILD is the clinical syndrome; histologically indistinguishable from RB.
entities.histo: Respiratory bronchiolitis is an almost universal histological finding in cigarette smokers, consisting of clusters of lightly pigmented macrophages containing fine brown particulate pigment within the lumens of respiratory bronchioles and adjacent alveolar ducts and alveoli, with mild chronic inflammation and fibrosis of the bronchiolar walls. When patients have symptoms, physiological impairment and imaging abnormalities (centrilobular nodules and ground glass), the condition is called respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease, which is histologically identical to RB but more extensive, and the diagnosis is clinicopathological. Peribronchiolar alveolar septa may be mildly thickened and lined by hyperplastic cuboidal epithelium. Coexisting smoking-related diseases are common, including centrilobular emphysema, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and smoking-related interstitial fibrosis. Differentials include DIP (diffuse, not bronchiolocentric), hypersensitivity pneumonitis (lymphocytic bronchiolitis, granulomas), Langerhans cell histiocytosis and haemosiderosis.
entities.cyto: BAL shows many pigmented macrophages with fine granular pigment, typical of smokers and not diagnostic of RB-ILD. Cytology helps exclude infection and other processes. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. Perls iron gives faint, dusty staining in smoker's macrophages, CD68 marks macrophages and CD1a or langerin excludes coexisting Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Elastic and trichrome stains assess peribronchiolar fibrosis.

entities.variants: Patterns: DAD (bleomycin, busulfan, cyclophosphamide, gemcitabine), NSIP (methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin), OP (amiodarone, bleomycin, statins), eosinophilic pneumonia (daptomycin, minocycline, NSAIDs, sulfasalazine), granulomatous and sarcoid-like (methotrexate, BCG, interferon, checkpoint inhibitors, anti-TNF), HP-like, DAH (anticoagulants, propylthiouracil, cocaine), pulmonary oedema (opioids, cytarabine), pulmonary hypertension and PVOD (dasatinib, mitomycin, anorexigens), constrictive bronchiolitis (penicillamine); immune checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis; targeted therapy (EGFR TKIs, mTOR inhibitors)
entities.remarks: Any pattern of lung injury can be caused by drugs; diagnosis is by exclusion and temporal association; pneumotox.com resource; checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis increasingly common.
entities.histo: Drug-induced lung disease encompasses a wide range of histological patterns, none specific, and the diagnosis rests on temporal association with a drug, exclusion of infection and other causes, and improvement on withdrawal. Cytotoxic drugs such as bleomycin, busulfan, gemcitabine and cyclophosphamide cause diffuse alveolar damage, often with marked cytological atypia of type II pneumocytes, and later fibrosis. Methotrexate typically produces cellular interstitial pneumonia with poorly formed granulomas and eosinophils. Nitrofurantoin causes acute hypersensitivity or chronic NSIP-like fibrosis. Many drugs cause organising pneumonia or eosinophilic pneumonia, and some cause diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, pulmonary oedema, vasculopathy or PVOD, sarcoid-like granulomas and constrictive bronchiolitis. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, anti-CTLA-4) cause pneumonitis with OP, NSIP, cellular interstitial pneumonia, DAD or sarcoid-like granulomas. Eosinophils, granulomas and pneumocyte atypia are helpful clues but none is diagnostic. Differentials include infection, underlying disease (connective tissue disease, tumour progression), radiation pneumonitis and idiopathic interstitial pneumonias.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a supportive role. BAL may show lymphocytosis (often CD8 predominant in hypersensitivity-type reactions), eosinophilia, foamy macrophages (amiodarone) or haemorrhage, and its main role is to exclude infection. Drug-induced atypia of pneumocytes, especially after bleomycin or busulfan, can be marked and must not be mistaken for carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical if reactive atypia is marked.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role. Special stains and viral IHC exclude infection, which is the main differential in immunosuppressed patients. In checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis CD3, CD4 and CD8 can characterise the T-cell infiltrate, and tumour markers are needed only when distinguishing tumour progression. Perls iron and fibrin stains support haemorrhage or DAD patterns. PD-L1 status of the tumour does not predict pneumonitis.

entities.variants: Chronic interstitial pneumonitis with foamy macrophages; organising pneumonia; DAD (acute, especially after surgery); pulmonary nodules or masses (amiodarone pneumonitis); pleural disease; hyperattenuating lung on CT due to iodine
entities.remarks: Foamy macrophages and foamy pneumocytes with lamellar inclusions (phospholipidosis) indicate exposure but not necessarily toxicity; toxicity needs interstitial pneumonitis, OP or DAD.
entities.histo: Amiodarone, an iodinated antiarrhythmic drug, causes pulmonary toxicity in a small percentage of patients, related to dose and duration. All exposed patients accumulate drug-induced phospholipidosis, seen as foamy, finely vacuolated alveolar macrophages and type II pneumocytes, and these alone indicate exposure rather than toxicity. Toxicity is manifested by chronic interstitial pneumonitis with septal lymphocytic inflammation, fibrosis, type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and abundant intra-alveolar foamy macrophages, by organising pneumonia, by mass-like nodules of organising pneumonia with foamy cells, and by acute diffuse alveolar damage, which may follow surgery or angiography and carries high mortality. Pleural effusion and pleuritis also occur. CT may show high-attenuation consolidation and increased liver density due to iodine. Differentials include other causes of foamy macrophages (endogenous lipoid pneumonia from obstruction, exogenous lipoid pneumonia, storage disorders), hypersensitivity pneumonitis, infection and heart failure.
entities.cyto: BAL shows numerous foamy macrophages with fine vacuolation, often accompanied by lymphocytosis with a low CD4:CD8 ratio when toxicity is present. Foamy macrophages alone confirm exposure, not toxicity. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role. CD68 confirms histiocytic nature of foam cells, and oil red O on fresh material is less strongly positive than in exogenous lipoid pneumonia. Electron microscopy, if done, shows lamellar osmiophilic inclusions typical of phospholipidosis. Special stains exclude infection.

entities.variants: Acute radiation pneumonitis (DAD, 1 to 6 months); chronic radiation fibrosis (6 to 12 months onward); radiation recall; sporadic (out-of-field) OP after breast irradiation; stereotactic body radiotherapy changes
entities.remarks: Field-limited injury after thoracic radiotherapy (lung, breast, lymphoma, oesophagus); atypical fibroblasts and pneumocytes with large bizarre nuclei; vascular hyalinisation; recurrence of tumour is main differential.
entities.histo: Radiation-induced lung injury follows thoracic radiotherapy and is usually limited to the radiation field, with straight margins not following anatomical boundaries. Acute radiation pneumonitis develops one to six months after treatment and shows diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes, oedema and fibrin, accompanied by striking cytological atypia of type II pneumocytes and bronchiolar epithelium, with enlarged, hyperchromatic and sometimes bizarre nuclei but low nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio and smudged chromatin. The chronic phase, beyond six to twelve months, shows dense interstitial and pleural fibrosis, loss of alveoli, traction bronchiectasis and atypical radiation fibroblasts with large hyperchromatic nuclei. Vessels show intimal fibrosis, foamy intimal macrophages, myointimal proliferation and medial hyalinisation. Organising pneumonia, sometimes outside the field (after breast radiotherapy), also occurs. Differentials include recurrent or residual carcinoma, drug toxicity (often combined chemoradiation), infection and other causes of DAD.
entities.cyto: Cytology may show markedly atypical reactive pneumocytes and bronchial cells with nuclear enlargement, multinucleation, vacuolated cytoplasm and smudged chromatin, which is a major pitfall for recurrent carcinoma. Low N:C ratio, cytoplasmic vacuolation and lack of a discrete malignant population favour radiation change. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical; Malignant only when unequivocal tumour cells are present.
entities.ihc: IHC is used mainly to separate radiation atypia from recurrent tumour. Reactive pneumocytes are keratin and TTF-1 positive, like adenocarcinoma, so these markers alone do not help; low Ki-67, absence of p53 overexpression or null pattern and lack of tumour-type markers (p40 for squamous carcinoma) favour reactive change, but morphology and pattern of infiltration are decisive. Trichrome and elastic stains show fibrosis and vascular changes. Special stains exclude infection.

entities.variants: Solid nodular (inflammatory pseudotumour-like); bronchovascular; alveolar interstitial; round-shaped ground glass; tracheobronchial; pleural; associated mediastinal fibrosis and lymphadenopathy
entities.remarks: Dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4 plasma cells, storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis/arteritis; spread along lymphatic routes; raised serum IgG4 in many; steroid responsive.
entities.histo: IgG4-related lung disease is a manifestation of IgG4-related disease, usually in older men, often with involvement of pancreas, salivary glands or other organs. Radiologically it presents as solid nodules, bronchovascular thickening, interstitial disease or ground glass, and pleural thickening. Histologically there is a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with many plasma cells, often with eosinophils, accompanied by storiform fibrosis with whorled fibroblasts and collagen, and obliterative phlebitis and arteritis, in which vessels are infiltrated and occluded by inflammation; arteritis without necrosis is more common in the lung than elsewhere. The process tends to follow lymphatic routes along bronchovascular bundles, interlobular septa and pleura. Necrosis, neutrophilic abscesses, granulomas and vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis are not features. The diagnosis requires morphology, increased IgG4 plasma cells and correlation with serum IgG4 and clinical features. Differentials include inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour (ALK or ROS1 positive spindle cells), MALT lymphoma, Castleman disease, GPA, nodular lymphoid hyperplasia, Rosai-Dorfman disease and inflammatory reactions near carcinoma, many of which can have increased IgG4 cells.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. FNA shows lymphocytes, plasma cells and fibroblastic fragments, and cell block IHC for IgG4 may suggest the diagnosis, but histology is required. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical when a lymphoproliferative or spindle cell neoplasm cannot be excluded.
entities.ihc: IHC for IgG4 and IgG is central: typical thresholds in lung are more than 50 IgG4-positive plasma cells per high-power field in surgical specimens (more than 20 in small biopsies) and an IgG4:IgG ratio over 40 percent. Elastic stains highlight obliterative phlebitis. ALK and ROS1 exclude inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour, kappa and lambda ISH and CD20 exclude MALT lymphoma, S100 excludes Rosai-Dorfman disease, and special stains exclude infection. Raised IgG4 counts alone are not specific.

entities.entity: E-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury (EVALI)
entities.variants: Patterns: acute fibrinous pneumonitis, DAD, organising pneumonia, AFOP, acute eosinophilic pneumonia, lipoid pneumonia (rare); associated with THC products and vitamin E acetate
entities.remarks: Acute lung injury in vaping users; foamy vacuolated macrophages and pneumocytes, bronchiolocentric acute injury; diagnosis of exclusion with vaping history.
entities.histo: EVALI is an acute or subacute lung injury occurring in users of electronic cigarettes and vaping devices, strongly associated with THC-containing products adulterated with vitamin E acetate. Patients present with respiratory, gastrointestinal and constitutional symptoms and bilateral ground glass, often with subpleural sparing. Histologically the patterns are those of acute lung injury, including acute fibrinous pneumonitis, diffuse alveolar damage, organising pneumonia and AFOP, often bronchiolocentric, accompanied by numerous foamy or finely vacuolated macrophages and vacuolated pneumocytes. True exogenous lipoid pneumonia with large lipid vacuoles is rare. Eosinophilic pneumonia is occasionally reported. There are no specific features, and diagnosis requires vaping history and exclusion of infection. Differentials include infectious pneumonia, acute eosinophilic pneumonia, DAD of other causes, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and amiodarone toxicity.
entities.cyto: BAL in EVALI frequently shows numerous lipid-laden or foamy macrophages on oil red O staining, together with neutrophils, but these findings are not specific. The main role of BAL is to exclude infection. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. Oil red O on BAL or fresh tissue can highlight lipid-laden macrophages, and special stains exclude infection. Clinical and exposure history are decisive.

entities.entity: Acute cellular rejection of lung allograft
entities.variants: ISHLT grading: A0 none, A1 minimal, A2 mild, A3 moderate, A4 severe perivascular rejection; small airway inflammation (lymphocytic bronchiolitis) B0, B1R low grade, B2R high grade, BX ungradable; large airway lymphocytic bronchitis
entities.remarks: Perivascular mononuclear infiltrates around small vessels and lymphocytic bronchiolitis on transbronchial biopsy; at least 5 pieces of alveolated lung recommended; must exclude infection (CMV, Pneumocystis).
entities.histo: Acute cellular rejection is a T cell-mediated alloimmune reaction in the lung allograft, most common in the first year. Diagnosis is made on transbronchial biopsies containing at least five pieces of alveolated parenchyma. The defining lesion is perivascular mononuclear infiltration around small blood vessels, mainly venules, graded by the ISHLT system: A1 minimal rejection shows scattered infrequent perivascular infiltrates two to three cells thick; A2 mild shows more frequent and thicker cuffs with endothelialitis and eosinophils; A3 moderate shows dense cuffs extending into adjacent alveolar septa; and A4 severe shows diffuse infiltrates with pneumocyte damage, hyaline membranes, haemorrhage and necrosis. Airway inflammation is graded separately: B1R low-grade shows lymphocytes in the submucosa of bronchioles, and B2R high-grade shows larger, activated lymphocytes with epithelial infiltration, damage and necrosis. Differentials include infection (CMV, Pneumocystis, respiratory viruses), PTLD (atypical B cells, EBV positive), bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue, aspiration and antibody-mediated rejection.
entities.cyto: Cytology does not grade rejection. BAL is performed with biopsies to exclude infection, with lymphocytosis being nonspecific. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is used to exclude mimics: CMV IHC, GMS for Pneumocystis and fungi, and EBER with CD20 for PTLD. CD3, CD4 and CD8 characterise perivascular infiltrates but do not alter grading. C4d staining is performed when antibody-mediated rejection is suspected. Elastic stains help identify small airways and vessels.

entities.variants: Hyperacute rejection (preformed antibodies, rare); acute AMR (clinical, subclinical; definite, probable, possible); chronic AMR contributing to CLAD
entities.remarks: Diagnosis combines donor-specific antibodies, allograft dysfunction, histology (capillary neutrophilic margination, capillaritis, DAD, AFOP) and C4d deposition; multidisciplinary consensus required.
entities.histo: Antibody-mediated rejection in lung transplantation is an alloimmune injury caused by donor-specific antibodies against HLA or non-HLA antigens. Diagnosis requires integration of clinical allograft dysfunction, circulating donor-specific antibodies, compatible histology and C4d deposition, after exclusion of other causes, with a consensus categorisation into definite, probable and possible AMR. Histological patterns are nonspecific and include neutrophilic margination in alveolar capillaries, neutrophilic capillaritis with septal necrosis and haemorrhage, endothelialitis, diffuse alveolar damage, AFOP, organising pneumonia and high-grade acute cellular rejection. Hyperacute rejection from preformed antibodies causes immediate graft failure with thrombosis and haemorrhage and is now rare. Chronic AMR is thought to contribute to chronic lung allograft dysfunction. Differentials include infection, acute cellular rejection, primary graft dysfunction and drug toxicity.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role. BAL is used to exclude infection. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: C4d IHC or immunofluorescence showing diffuse linear subendothelial staining of alveolar septal capillaries (more than 50 percent) supports AMR, though interpretation is difficult because of background staining. CD68 and myeloperoxidase may highlight capillary leucocytes. Special stains and viral IHC exclude infection. Donor-specific antibody testing is the essential correlate.

entities.variants: Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS; obstructive, constrictive bronchiolitis histology); restrictive allograft syndrome (RAS; pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis histology); mixed phenotype; chronic vascular rejection (graft vasculopathy)
entities.remarks: Main limitation of long-term survival after lung transplant; BOS shows constrictive bronchiolitis; RAS shows PPFE-like fibrosis; transbronchial biopsy insensitive.
entities.histo: Chronic lung allograft dysfunction is a persistent decline in lung function after transplantation and affects about half of recipients within five years. The bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome phenotype corresponds histologically to constrictive (obliterative) bronchiolitis, with dense eosinophilic hyaline submucosal fibrosis concentrically narrowing or completely obliterating membranous and respiratory bronchioles, sometimes preceded by lymphocytic bronchiolitis, leaving fibrous scars beside pulmonary arteries. Bronchiectasis and mucostasis may be present. The restrictive allograft syndrome phenotype shows pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis with intra-alveolar fibrosis and septal elastosis beneath a thickened pleura, often upper lobe predominant, with or without constrictive bronchiolitis and acute fibrinoid organising changes. Chronic vascular rejection shows fibrointimal thickening of arteries and veins. Risk factors include acute rejection, AMR, infections and gastro-oesophageal reflux. Transbronchial biopsy is insensitive because lesions are patchy. Differentials include infection, recurrent native disease, aspiration and other causes of fibrosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role in CLAD. BAL neutrophilia is associated with BOS and is used together with cultures to exclude infection. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. Elastic stains (EVG, Movat) are essential to identify obliterated bronchioles and to demonstrate elastosis in RAS-type PPFE, and trichrome shows submucosal fibrosis. Special stains and viral IHC exclude infection. C4d may be relevant when chronic AMR is suspected.

entities.entity: Pulmonary complications of haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (including lung graft-versus-host disease)
entities.variants: Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (lung chronic GVHD, constrictive bronchiolitis); idiopathic pneumonia syndrome (DAD); diffuse alveolar haemorrhage; engraftment syndrome; organising pneumonia; pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis (late); pulmonary veno-occlusive disease; peri-engraftment respiratory distress; post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (see lymphoma rows); infections
entities.remarks: Lung is a major target after allogeneic HSCT; BOS is the only diagnostic lung manifestation of chronic GVHD; infections must always be excluded.
entities.histo: Recipients of haematopoietic stem cell transplantation develop a range of non-infectious pulmonary complications in addition to frequent infections. Early complications include idiopathic pneumonia syndrome with diffuse alveolar damage, diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, engraftment syndrome with capillary leak and peri-engraftment respiratory distress. Late complications include bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome, which is the pulmonary manifestation of chronic graft-versus-host disease and shows lymphocytic bronchiolitis progressing to constrictive bronchiolitis with concentric submucosal fibrosis and obliteration of bronchioles, organising pneumonia, interstitial fibrosis, pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis and pulmonary veno-occlusive disease. Histologically these patterns are identical to their idiopathic counterparts. Drug toxicity from conditioning agents (busulfan, cyclophosphamide, BCNU) adds atypical pneumocytes and DAD. Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder may also arise. Differentials always include CMV, adenovirus, respiratory viruses, Pneumocystis and invasive fungal infection.
entities.cyto: Cytology contributes mainly through BAL, used to exclude infection (viral cytopathic effect, Pneumocystis, fungi) and to confirm diffuse alveolar haemorrhage by haemosiderin-laden macrophages. Drug-induced pneumocyte atypia can be marked. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical for marked reactive atypia.
entities.ihc: IHC is used mainly for infection: CMV, adenovirus, HSV and respiratory virus antigens, plus GMS and Ziehl-Neelsen. EBER and CD20 help diagnose PTLD. Elastic stains are essential for constrictive bronchiolitis and PPFE, and iron stain confirms haemorrhage. No marker is specific for GVHD in the lung.

entities.entity: Mucous membrane plasmacytosis of the trachea and airway
entities.variants: Plasma cell orificial mucositis-type tracheitis; plasmacytosis mucosae involving larynx, trachea and bronchi; idiopathic or associated with chronic irritation
entities.remarks: Rare benign polyclonal plasma cell infiltrate of airway mucosa causing nodular or cobblestone thickening and stenosis; must be distinguished from plasmacytoma, MALT lymphoma and IgG4-related disease.
entities.histo: Mucous membrane plasmacytosis is a rare, benign, idiopathic condition in which the mucosa of the upper aerodigestive tract, including the larynx, trachea and main bronchi, is infiltrated by dense sheets of mature plasma cells, producing a nodular, cobblestone or velvety mucosal thickening that can narrow the airway and cause hoarseness, stridor or dyspnoea. It is thought to represent an exaggerated reaction to chronic irritation or an unknown antigen and usually follows a chronic, relapsing course. Microscopically the lamina propria contains a band-like or diffuse infiltrate of mature plasma cells with occasional Russell bodies, scattered lymphocytes and dilated capillaries, beneath an intact or hyperplastic, sometimes ulcerated, respiratory or squamous epithelium, without lymphoepithelial lesions, atypia or amyloid. Differentials include extramedullary plasmacytoma and MALT lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation (both monoclonal), IgG4-related disease, syphilis, rhinoscleroma (Mikulicz cells and bacilli), granulomatosis with polyangiitis and relapsing polychondritis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no practical role; brushings, if taken, show non-specific inflammatory cells and plasma cells. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (inflammatory) or Non-diagnostic; biopsy is required.
entities.ihc: IHC confirms that the plasma cells are CD138 and MUM1 positive and polyclonal, with a balanced kappa to lambda ratio on IHC or ISH, which excludes plasmacytoma and MALT lymphoma; CD20 shows only scattered B cells without a monotonous infiltrate. IgG4 and IgG staining help exclude IgG4-related disease. Warthin-Starry, Treponema IHC and PAS stains help exclude syphilis and rhinoscleroma, and Congo red excludes amyloid.

entities.entity: Rhinoscleroma of the trachea and bronchi (tracheobronchial scleroma)
entities.variants: Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis infection; catarrhal (exudative), granulomatous (proliferative) and sclerotic (fibrotic) stages; subglottic and tracheal stenosis; usually extension from nasal scleroma
entities.remarks: Chronic granulomatous infection by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, endemic in parts of Africa, Central America, Eastern Europe and South Asia; airway involvement causes nodules and stenosis; Mikulicz cells with bacilli are diagnostic.
entities.histo: Rhinoscleroma is a chronic, progressive granulomatous infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae subspecies rhinoscleromatis, which usually begins in the nasal cavity but can extend to the larynx, trachea and bronchi in a minority of patients, producing mucosal nodules, crusting and eventually subglottic or tracheal stenosis. It is endemic in parts of Africa, Central and South America, Eastern Europe and South Asia, including India. The disease passes through three stages. In the catarrhal stage there is non-specific chronic inflammation with squamous metaplasia. In the granulomatous stage the submucosa is replaced by a dense infiltrate of plasma cells with Russell bodies, lymphocytes and characteristic large vacuolated histiocytes (Mikulicz cells) with foamy, pale cytoplasm containing numerous gram-negative bacilli, beneath often pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplastic epithelium. The sclerotic stage shows dense fibrosis with few Mikulicz cells, causing stenosis. Differentials include mucous membrane plasmacytosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, leprosy, tuberculosis, fungal infections, Rosai-Dorfman disease, xanthogranulomatous inflammation, plasmacytoma and squamous cell carcinoma (pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia).
entities.cyto: Cytology has little role, though smears or brushings may show foamy histiocytes and plasma cells; culture of tissue or secretions on MacConkey agar may grow the organism. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (inflammatory, infection suspected) or Non-diagnostic.
entities.ihc: IHC is not usually needed for diagnosis; Mikulicz cells are CD68 and CD163 positive and S100 negative (which helps exclude Rosai-Dorfman disease), and plasma cells are polyclonal. Special stains are key: Warthin-Starry or other silver stains, Giemsa and PAS highlight the bacilli within Mikulicz cells, and Gram stain shows gram-negative rods. Immunostaining with antibodies to Klebsiella or PCR from tissue confirm the organism. Ziehl-Neelsen and GMS stains exclude mycobacterial and fungal infections.

entities.variants: X-linked (CYBB) and autosomal recessive (NCF1, CYBA, NCF2, NCF4) forms; Aspergillus (including A. nidulans), Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia, Serratia and Nocardia infections; mulch pneumonitis; non-infectious granulomatous inflammation; pulmonary infections in other primary immunodeficiencies
entities.remarks: Inherited defect of NADPH oxidase in phagocytes, leading to recurrent bacterial and fungal pneumonias with necrotising granulomas, abscesses and fibrosis; pigmented lipid-laden macrophages may be seen; diagnosis by DHR flow test.
entities.histo: Chronic granulomatous disease is an inherited primary immunodeficiency in which mutations in subunits of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase prevent the respiratory burst, so neutrophils and macrophages cannot kill catalase-positive organisms, leading to recurrent, severe infections and exaggerated granulomatous inflammation beginning in childhood. The lungs are the most frequently affected organ, with recurrent pneumonias, abscesses, empyema and progressive fibrosis or bronchiectasis. Typical organisms include Aspergillus species (A. fumigatus and the characteristic A. nidulans), Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia cepacia complex, Serratia marcescens and Nocardia, and acute fulminant mulch pneumonitis follows heavy inhalation of fungal spores. Microscopically there are necrotising and non-necrotising granulomas, microabscesses with central neutrophils surrounded by palisading histiocytes and giant cells, organising pneumonia and fibrosis, and sometimes macrophages containing golden-brown, lipofuscin-like pigment. Fungal hyphae or bacteria may be scanty, so cultures are essential. The diagnosis is confirmed by abnormal dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry or nitroblue tetrazolium tests and genetic testing. Differentials include tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, invasive aspergillosis in other immunodeficiencies, GLILD and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
entities.cyto: BAL or FNA shows neutrophils, histiocytes, granulomatous fragments and sometimes fungal hyphae or bacteria, which should be sent for culture. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (inflammatory, with infection suspected) or Non-diagnostic.
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role; CD68 highlights histiocytes in granulomas. Special stains (GMS, PAS, Gram, modified Ziehl-Neelsen for Nocardia, Ziehl-Neelsen for mycobacteria) are applied to look for organisms, and cultures, fungal PCR and galactomannan are important. The diagnosis of the immunodeficiency is made with DHR flow cytometry and genetic testing for CYBB and autosomal recessive genes.

entities.variants: Agenesis (no lung or bronchus); aplasia (rudimentary bronchus, no lung); hypoplasia (primary or secondary to congenital diaphragmatic hernia, oligohydramnios/renal agenesis or Potter sequence, thoracic dystrophies, neuromuscular disease, trisomies); alveolar simplification (deficient alveolarisation; prematurity, Down syndrome); acinar dysplasia and congenital alveolar dysplasia
entities.remarks: Reduced lung weight (lung:body weight ratio below about 0.012 at term) and radial alveolar count; secondary hypoplasia is far commoner than primary; usually an autopsy diagnosis.
entities.histo: Pulmonary agenesis is complete absence of a lung and its bronchus, aplasia is absence of lung tissue with a rudimentary bronchial stump, and hypoplasia is an incomplete development of a lung that is reduced in weight, volume and number of airways, acini and alveoli. Hypoplasia is usually secondary to space-occupying lesions in the chest (congenital diaphragmatic hernia, effusions, masses), oligohydramnios (renal agenesis, prolonged rupture of membranes), small thoracic cage or reduced fetal breathing (neuromuscular disease). At autopsy the lungs are small, with a lung to body weight ratio below about 0.012 at term (0.015 before 28 weeks) and a reduced radial alveolar count; microscopically the lungs appear immature for gestational age with fewer, simplified airspaces and thick septa. Alveolar simplification with enlarged, poorly septated airspaces is seen in prematurity, chronic neonatal lung disease and Down syndrome. Acinar dysplasia is a severe arrest of lung development at the pseudoglandular or early canalicular stage, often linked to TBX4 or FGF10 variants. Differentials include bronchopulmonary dysplasia, alveolar capillary dysplasia and normal immaturity of preterm lungs.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in pulmonary agenesis, aplasia or hypoplasia, which are anatomical diagnoses made at imaging, surgery or autopsy. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Diagnosis relies on weight ratios, radial alveolar counts and morphometry. In suspected acinar dysplasia or other developmental disorders, genetic testing (TBX4, FGF10, FOXF1) is more informative than any stain, and CD31 can help evaluate capillary development when alveolar capillary dysplasia is a differential.

entities.variants: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula with oesophageal atresia (types A to E, commonest Gross type C); laryngotracheo-oesophageal cleft; tracheal agenesis and atresia; congenital tracheal stenosis with complete cartilaginous rings; tracheomalacia and bronchomalacia; tracheal bronchus (pig bronchus); bronchial isomerism; tracheobronchomegaly (Mounier-Kuhn syndrome); Williams-Campbell syndrome (bronchial cartilage deficiency); vascular rings and pulmonary artery sling; tracheal diverticulum and paratracheal air cysts
entities.remarks: Structural airway malformations presenting with stridor, feeding difficulty or recurrent infection; diagnosed by bronchoscopy and imaging; pathology mainly at surgery or autopsy.
entities.histo: Congenital airway anomalies result from errors in the separation of the foregut and in tracheobronchial branching and cartilage formation. Tracheo-oesophageal fistula with oesophageal atresia, most commonly a blind upper oesophageal pouch with a distal fistula between trachea and lower oesophagus, presents with drooling, choking and aspiration in neonates. Laryngotracheo-oesophageal clefts are incomplete septation defects. Congenital tracheal stenosis is often due to complete cartilaginous O-shaped rings lacking a posterior membranous wall, and may accompany a pulmonary artery sling. Tracheomalacia and bronchomalacia reflect soft, deficient cartilage, either primary or secondary to compression by vessels or fistulae. Mounier-Kuhn syndrome is marked dilatation of the trachea and main bronchi due to atrophy of elastic fibres and smooth muscle with diverticula, and Williams-Campbell syndrome is deficiency of cartilage in subsegmental bronchi producing bronchiectasis. Histology of resected segments shows abnormal cartilage, sometimes heterotopic oesophageal tissue, inflammation and squamous metaplasia. Differentials include acquired stenosis from intubation and inflammatory airway diseases.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in congenital tracheobronchial anomalies. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Histological assessment of resected airway segments relies on H&E, with elastic stains useful in Mounier-Kuhn syndrome to show loss of elastic tissue and Alcian blue or toluidine blue to evaluate cartilage. Diagnosis is primarily endoscopic and radiological.

entities.variants: Segmental (commonly apicoposterior left upper lobe) or lobar bronchial atresia; association with CPAM, sequestration and congenital lobar overinflation
entities.remarks: Focal interruption of a segmental bronchus with distal mucocele (bronchocele) and hyperinflated segment; may underlie many congenital cystic lesions.
entities.histo: Bronchial atresia is a focal obliteration of a segmental or lobar bronchus, most often in the left upper lobe, with normal development of the distal airways, which become filled with inspissated mucus (mucocele or bronchocele) and ventilated by collateral air drift through pores of Kohn, so the segment is hyperinflated. Grossly a mucus-filled dilated bronchus ends blindly near the hilum, surrounded by overinflated, emphysema-like parenchyma. Microscopically the dilated bronchus is lined by respiratory epithelium and contains mucus, with surrounding alveoli that are enlarged or show simplification, and sometimes CPAM-like changes. Bronchial atresia is thought to be a common underlying mechanism of several congenital lung malformations, including CPAM type 2, intralobar and extralobar sequestration and congenital lobar overinflation, and examination of resection specimens should include dissection of the airways. Differentials include acquired obstruction by tumour or foreign body, bronchogenic cyst and mucoid impaction in ABPA.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in bronchial atresia. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed. H&E examination with careful airway dissection is diagnostic, and mucin stains are rarely required.

entities.variants: Type 0 (acinar dysplasia, tracheobronchial; incompatible with life); type 1 (large cyst, bronchial/bronchiolar, commonest; mucinous cell clusters, KRAS-mutated, risk of mucinous adenocarcinoma); type 2 (small cysts, bronchiolar, often with sequestration or other anomalies); type 3 (solid-appearing, bronchiolo-alveolar, adenomatoid); type 4 (large peripheral thin-walled alveolar/acinar cysts; overlaps with type I pleuropulmonary blastoma, DICER1); hybrid lesions with sequestration
entities.remarks: Stocker classification; formerly congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation; prenatal ultrasound detection; type 1 mucinous cell clusters and type 4 overlap with pleuropulmonary blastoma are key oncological issues.
entities.histo: Congenital pulmonary airway malformations are developmental hamartomatous lesions of the airways classified by Stocker into five types based on cyst size and presumed level of origin. Type 0 is acinar dysplasia, with small solid lungs composed only of bronchial-type airways, and is lethal. Type 1 is commonest and has one or several large cysts over 2 cm lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, with smooth muscle and elastic tissue in the walls and smaller cysts nearby; clusters of mucinous (goblet) cells along the cyst lining are present in a proportion, harbour KRAS mutations and can give rise to invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma later in life. Type 2 has multiple uniform small cysts up to 2 cm lined by cuboidal to columnar bronchiolar epithelium, sometimes with striated muscle, and is frequently associated with sequestration and other anomalies. Type 3 is a bulky, solid-appearing lesion of small bronchiolar and alveolar duct-like structures resembling the canalicular-stage lung. Type 4 consists of large, thin-walled peripheral cysts lined by flattened alveolar epithelium with loose mesenchymal septa, and its distinction from type I (cystic) pleuropulmonary blastoma, which has a cambium layer of primitive cells and is associated with DICER1 mutation, is critical. Differentials include bronchogenic cyst, sequestration, congenital lobar overinflation, bronchial atresia and pleuropulmonary blastoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has essentially no role; CPAM is diagnosed on imaging and resection. Cyst fluid, if aspirated, contains macrophages and benign bronchial cells. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is generally not required. Mucinous cell clusters in type 1 CPAM are CK7 and CK20 positive with variable MUC5AC and lack TTF-1 or show weak expression, similar to invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma; KRAS testing is not routinely needed. In type 4 CPAM versus pleuropulmonary blastoma, desmin and myogenin can highlight rhabdomyoblastic cells in the cambium layer of PPB, and DICER1 germline testing is advised when PPB is suspected. TTF-1 and Ki-67 add little.

entities.variants: Intralobar sequestration (within visceral pleura of a lobe, usually left lower lobe; recurrent infection; often acquired-appearing); extralobar sequestration (own pleural covering, infants, associated anomalies such as CDH; may be subdiaphragmatic); hybrid lesions with CPAM type 2; bronchopulmonary foregut malformation (communication with GI tract)
entities.remarks: Non-functioning lung tissue without normal bronchial connection, supplied by systemic artery (often from aorta); feeding vessel must be identified and ligated at surgery.
entities.histo: Bronchopulmonary sequestration is a mass of non-functioning lung tissue that lacks a normal connection to the tracheobronchial tree and receives its blood supply from an anomalous systemic artery, usually arising from the thoracic or abdominal aorta. Intralobar sequestration lies within the visceral pleura of a normal lobe, most often the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe, and drains into pulmonary veins; it presents in older children and adults with recurrent infection, and histology shows chronically inflamed, fibrotic lung with cystic, dilated bronchial structures filled with mucus or pus, lymphoid follicles, cholesterol clefts and a thick-walled elastic systemic artery. Extralobar sequestration is invested by its own pleura, presents in infants, is often between the lower lobe and diaphragm or below the diaphragm, drains into systemic veins and is frequently associated with diaphragmatic hernia and other anomalies; histology shows lung with dilated bronchioles, alveolar ducts and subpleural lymphatics resembling CPAM type 2. Bronchopulmonary foregut malformations communicate with the oesophagus or stomach. Differentials include CPAM, bronchogenic cyst, chronic abscess, bronchiectasis and pulmonary infarct.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role; diagnosis is radiological (systemic arterial supply) and confirmed at resection. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed. Elastic stains confirm the elastic systemic-type feeding artery, and special stains for organisms may be used in infected intralobar sequestrations. Diagnosis requires the surgeon to document the anomalous artery.

entities.variants: Mediastinal (paratracheal, subcarinal; commonest); intrapulmonary; cervical, pericardial, subdiaphragmatic and cutaneous ectopic sites; infected or haemorrhagic cysts
entities.remarks: Foregut duplication cyst lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium with cartilage, smooth muscle and seromucous glands in the wall; usually unilocular; rarely complicated by malignancy.
entities.histo: A bronchogenic cyst is a congenital foregut duplication cyst derived from abnormal budding of the tracheobronchial tree. Most are in the middle mediastinum near the carina or trachea, and a minority are intrapulmonary, usually in the lower lobes. They are typically unilocular, thin-walled cysts containing clear mucoid, milky or haemorrhagic fluid, sometimes infected. Microscopically the lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium, which may become cuboidal, squamous or denuded in infected cysts, and the wall contains the diagnostic elements of bronchial wall: hyaline cartilage plates, bronchial-type seromucous glands, smooth muscle and elastic fibres. The cyst does not usually communicate with the airway unless infected. Rare complications include infection, haemorrhage, compression of airways or vessels and very rare malignant transformation. Differentials include oesophageal duplication cyst (two muscle layers, no cartilage), enteric cyst (gastric or intestinal mucosa), pericardial cyst (mesothelial lining), CPAM type 1, cystic teratoma and thymic cyst.
entities.cyto: EUS- or EBUS-guided aspiration of a bronchogenic cyst yields thick mucoid fluid containing ciliated columnar cells, macrophages and debris, which can mimic a mucinous neoplasm; aspiration also risks infection. Presence of benign ciliated cells without atypia supports a benign cyst. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed. Respiratory epithelium is CK7 and TTF-1 positive and CK20 negative, which can help in distinguishing it from enteric duplication cysts (CK20 and CDX2 positive). Elastic and trichrome stains highlight wall components, and Alcian blue shows cartilage.

entities.variants: Classic congenital lobar overinflation (left upper lobe, right middle lobe); bronchial cartilage deficiency or extrinsic compression; polyalveolar lobe (increased number of alveoli)
entities.remarks: Progressive hyperinflation of a lobe in infancy causing respiratory distress and mediastinal shift; alveoli are overdistended but not destroyed (not true emphysema).
entities.histo: Congenital lobar overinflation, previously called infantile lobar emphysema, is progressive hyperinflation of one lobe in neonates and infants, most often the left upper lobe followed by the right middle lobe, causing respiratory distress, compression of adjacent lung and mediastinal shift. It results from a check-valve bronchial obstruction due to deficient or dysplastic bronchial cartilage, redundant mucosa, mucus plugs or extrinsic compression by vessels or cysts, although no cause is found in about half. The resected lobe is large, pale and fails to collapse. Microscopically the alveoli are uniformly overdistended with thin, stretched septa, but alveolar walls are not destroyed, so this is overinflation rather than true emphysema. A variant, the polyalveolar lobe, shows a normal number of airways but an increased number of alveoli per acinus, measured by radial alveolar count. Differentials include CPAM type 4, pneumothorax, interstitial emphysema of ventilated infants and bronchial atresia.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in congenital lobar overinflation. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Diagnosis rests on gross and microscopic examination, with morphometry (radial alveolar count, mean linear intercept) and evaluation of bronchial cartilage.

entities.variants: Classic (old) BPD (pre-surfactant era; barotrauma and oxygen toxicity; fibrosis, airway injury); new BPD (extreme prematurity; arrested alveolarisation and dysmorphic microvasculature); BPD with pulmonary hypertension
entities.remarks: Chronic lung disease of prematurity; oxygen requirement at 36 weeks corrected age; new BPD shows alveolar simplification with fewer, larger alveoli.
entities.histo: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is chronic lung disease of preterm infants who receive oxygen and ventilation. Classic BPD, seen before surfactant therapy and antenatal steroids, followed hyaline membrane disease and showed alternating areas of overinflation and atelectasis, airway injury with necrotising bronchiolitis, squamous metaplasia and peribronchiolar fibrosis, interstitial fibrosis and pulmonary hypertensive vascular changes. New BPD affects extremely premature infants treated with gentler ventilation and is characterised by arrested lung development: alveolar simplification, with fewer and larger alveoli, reduced secondary septation, a decreased radial alveolar count, mild variable interstitial fibrosis and a dysmorphic, reduced capillary bed, with little airway injury. Pulmonary hypertension with medial hypertrophy of small arteries is an important complication. Differentials include pulmonary hypoplasia, alveolar capillary dysplasia, surfactant protein disorders and pulmonary interstitial glycogenosis, which can coexist in growth-abnormality lungs.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. CD31 or CD34 can demonstrate reduced and dysmorphic capillaries, and elastic stains show abnormal septation and vascular remodelling. Morphometry is the key method in research and autopsy.

entities.entity: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease)
entities.variants: Hyaline membrane disease of prematurity; surfactant deficiency in infants of diabetic mothers and after caesarean section; complicated by pulmonary interstitial emphysema, pneumothorax, intraventricular haemorrhage and BPD
entities.remarks: Surfactant deficiency in preterm infants causing atelectasis and hyaline membranes; prevented by antenatal steroids and treated with exogenous surfactant.
entities.histo: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, or hyaline membrane disease, results from deficiency of pulmonary surfactant, mainly in infants born before 34 weeks, and is aggravated by maternal diabetes, caesarean delivery and male sex. Without surfactant, alveoli collapse at end-expiration, leading to hypoxia, epithelial and endothelial damage and leakage of fibrin-rich plasma. Grossly the lungs are solid, airless, reddish purple and sink in water. Microscopically there is widespread atelectasis with poorly developed alveoli, dilated terminal bronchioles and alveolar ducts lined by eosinophilic hyaline membranes composed of fibrin and necrotic epithelial cells, with congestion and few inflammatory cells. Membranes appear within hours and organise after a few days. Complications include pulmonary interstitial emphysema, with air dissecting along bronchovascular sheaths, pneumothorax and later bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Differentials include neonatal pneumonia (group B streptococcus also causes hyaline membranes), meconium aspiration, surfactant protein gene mutations and alveolar capillary dysplasia.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in neonatal RDS. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Hyaline membranes are seen on H&E and stain with PAS and fibrin stains. Gram stain is useful to identify group B streptococcal infection, which mimics RDS with hyaline membranes containing cocci.

entities.variants: Meconium aspiration syndrome (post-term, fetal distress); amniotic fluid aspiration (squames, lanugo, vernix); persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn as complication
entities.remarks: Meconium (bile-stained debris, squames, mucin) in airways and alveoli with chemical pneumonitis, surfactant inactivation and pulmonary hypertension; amniotic content in alveoli is common in stillbirths.
entities.histo: Meconium aspiration syndrome occurs mainly in term and post-term infants subjected to intrauterine stress, which stimulates passage of meconium and gasping. Meconium obstructs airways, inactivates surfactant and causes chemical pneumonitis, leading to air trapping, atelectasis, pneumothorax and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. Microscopically the bronchi and alveoli contain yellow-green to brown meconium, anucleate squamous cells (squames), mucus, lanugo hairs and bile pigment, accompanied by acute inflammation, hyaline membranes and later macrophages. Amniotic fluid aspiration, with squames and vernix in alveoli, is common in stillborn and asphyxiated infants and indicates fetal gasping. Persistent pulmonary hypertension shows muscularisation of small arteries. Differentials include congenital pneumonia (neutrophils and organisms, often with chorioamnionitis), hyaline membrane disease and alveolar capillary dysplasia, which presents with persistent pulmonary hypertension but without aspirated material.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Tracheal aspirates may contain squames and meconium pigment, but the diagnosis is clinical. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed. Keratin staining (AE1/AE3) highlights squames in alveoli and vessels when they are subtle, and Alcian blue or PAS highlight mucin; bile pigment is identified with Fouchet or Hall stain if required.

entities.variants: Diffuse PIG; patchy PIG associated with lung growth abnormalities (BPD, congenital heart disease, alveolar simplification)
entities.remarks: Neonatal tachypnoea with interstitial infiltrates; alveolar septa widened by bland glycogen-rich mesenchymal cells; good prognosis with steroids or spontaneous resolution.
entities.histo: Pulmonary interstitial glycogenosis is a form of childhood interstitial lung disease presenting in the neonatal period with tachypnoea and hypoxaemia. It is considered a developmental disorder of interstitial mesenchymal cells. Histologically the alveolar septa are diffusely or patchily widened by an accumulation of bland, round to oval interstitial cells with pale, clear, vacuolated cytoplasm containing glycogen, without significant inflammation, fibrosis or epithelial abnormality. Patchy PIG is frequently seen together with lung growth abnormalities such as alveolar simplification, BPD and congenital heart disease, and outcome then depends on the associated condition. Isolated diffuse PIG generally has a favourable prognosis. Differentials include alveolar capillary dysplasia, surfactant dysfunction disorders (with alveolar proteinosis-like material and pneumocyte hyperplasia), NEHI (normal-appearing biopsy) and infection.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in pulmonary interstitial glycogenosis. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is of limited use. The interstitial cells are vimentin positive and negative for CD68 and keratin, and PAS on fresh or properly fixed tissue shows diastase-sensitive glycogen, although glycogen is often lost in routine processing. Electron microscopy demonstrates abundant monoparticulate cytoplasmic glycogen. CD31 helps assess capillaries in the differential with alveolar capillary dysplasia.

entities.variants: Persistent tachypnoea of infancy; familial NKX2-1 variants in some
entities.remarks: Infants with tachypnoea, crackles and hypoxaemia; characteristic CT ground glass in right middle lobe, lingula and central regions; near-normal biopsy with increased bombesin-positive neuroendocrine cells in bronchioles.
entities.histo: Neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia of infancy is a form of childhood interstitial lung disease presenting in the first year of life with tachypnoea, retractions, crackles and hypoxaemia, and a characteristic CT pattern of ground glass in the right middle lobe, lingula and perihilar regions with air trapping. Biopsies show remarkably normal or near-normal lung architecture with minimal airway inflammation or smooth muscle hyperplasia, and the diagnosis rests on demonstrating an increased number of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells within bronchioles and neuroepithelial bodies in the lobular parenchyma. Most children gradually improve over years. Differentials include other childhood ILDs (PIG, surfactant disorders), constrictive bronchiolitis, chronic aspiration and DIPNECH in adults, which is a different entity with tumorlets and constrictive bronchiolitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in NEHI. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is the key to diagnosis: bombesin (gastrin-releasing peptide) staining shows increased neuroendocrine cells, with published criteria of neuroendocrine cells forming more than 10 percent of airway epithelium in several bronchioles and prominent neuroepithelial bodies; synaptophysin and chromogranin also highlight them, but bombesin is most sensitive. Adequate sampling of at least several bronchioles is necessary.

entities.entity: Alveolar capillary dysplasia with misalignment of pulmonary veins (ACD/MPV)
entities.variants: Classic diffuse ACD/MPV; patchy or late-onset forms; FOXF1 deletions or mutations (16q24.1); associated gastrointestinal, cardiac and genitourinary anomalies
entities.remarks: Lethal neonatal persistent pulmonary hypertension; reduced alveolar capillaries away from epithelium, thickened septa, muscularised arterioles and veins accompanying arteries in bronchovascular bundles.
entities.histo: Alveolar capillary dysplasia with misalignment of pulmonary veins is a rare, usually lethal developmental disorder of the pulmonary vasculature caused in most cases by FOXF1 mutations or deletions. Infants present within hours to days of birth with severe hypoxaemia and persistent pulmonary hypertension refractory to treatment. Histologically there are reduced numbers of alveolar capillaries, which lie centrally within thickened alveolar septa rather than abutting the alveolar epithelium, lobular maldevelopment with simplification, marked medial hypertrophy and muscularisation of small pulmonary arteries and arterioles, and the characteristic misalignment of pulmonary veins, which lie within bronchovascular bundles adjacent to arteries instead of in interlobular septa. Lymphangiectasia may be present. Associated anomalies include intestinal malrotation and atresia, cardiac and genitourinary defects. Differentials include persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn due to other causes, pulmonary hypoplasia, pulmonary interstitial glycogenosis and pulmonary vein stenosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in ACD/MPV. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC with endothelial markers (CD31, CD34) demonstrates the reduced number and abnormal central position of alveolar capillaries, which supports the diagnosis. Elastic stains help identify veins within bronchovascular bundles and show arterial muscularisation. Genetic testing for FOXF1 deletions or mutations confirms the diagnosis and informs counselling.

entities.variants: SFTPB deficiency (neonatal lethal; congenital alveolar proteinosis); SFTPC mutations (chronic pneumonitis of infancy, NSIP, DIP, familial pulmonary fibrosis in adults); ABCA3 mutations (neonatal RDS or childhood ILD); NKX2-1 (brain-lung-thyroid syndrome); CSF2RA/CSF2RB mutations (hereditary PAP); patterns: congenital PAP, chronic pneumonitis of infancy, DIP, NSIP
entities.remarks: Genetic disorders of surfactant production causing neonatal respiratory failure or childhood and adult ILD; patterns include alveolar proteinosis, pneumocyte hyperplasia, interstitial thickening and foamy macrophages.
entities.histo: Surfactant dysfunction disorders are genetic diseases of surfactant protein or lipid production and handling, presenting as fatal neonatal respiratory failure, chronic interstitial lung disease of infancy or childhood, or adult-onset pulmonary fibrosis. SFTPB deficiency and many ABCA3 mutations present at birth like severe RDS and show congenital alveolar proteinosis with granular eosinophilic material in alveoli. SFTPC and milder ABCA3 mutations produce a chronic pneumonitis of infancy with marked type II pneumocyte hyperplasia, interstitial widening by mesenchymal cells and inflammation, intra-alveolar foamy macrophages with cholesterol clefts and variable proteinaceous material, or DIP and NSIP patterns; SFTPC mutations also cause familial pulmonary fibrosis in adults. NKX2-1 haploinsufficiency causes brain-lung-thyroid syndrome with neonatal respiratory distress, hypothyroidism and chorea. Hereditary PAP is caused by GM-CSF receptor mutations. Differentials include autoimmune or secondary PAP, PIG, DIP of smoking (adults), infection and NSIP of other causes.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. BAL in alveolar proteinosis patterns shows granular PAS-positive material and foamy macrophages. Not diagnostic for the specific genetic disorder. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC for surfactant proteins (pro-SP-B, pro-SP-C, mature SP-B) can show absence or abnormal processing in SFTPB or SFTPC deficiency, and PAS with diastase highlights proteinaceous material. Electron microscopy is valuable: ABCA3 deficiency shows small, dense lamellar bodies with eccentric inclusions (fried-egg appearance). Genetic testing (SFTPB, SFTPC, ABCA3, NKX2-1, CSF2RA, CSF2RB) is definitive.

entities.variants: Primary congenital pulmonary lymphangiectasia (isolated or with generalised lymphangiectasia, Noonan, Turner, Down syndromes); secondary lymphangiectasia (pulmonary venous obstruction, hypoplastic left heart, total anomalous venous return)
entities.remarks: Dilated lymphatics in pleura, interlobular septa and bronchovascular bundles; neonatal respiratory distress and chylothorax; distinct from diffuse lymphangiomatosis (increased number of lymphatics).
entities.histo: Pulmonary lymphangiectasia is dilatation of normally distributed pulmonary lymphatics in the pleura, interlobular septa and bronchovascular bundles, without an increase in their number. Primary congenital lymphangiectasia is a developmental abnormality that presents at birth with severe respiratory distress and chylous effusions and may be isolated or part of generalised lymphatic disease and syndromes such as Noonan, Turner and Down. Secondary lymphangiectasia results from obstruction to pulmonary venous outflow, as in hypoplastic left heart or total anomalous pulmonary venous return. Grossly the pleural surface shows a lattice of dilated, cystic lymphatic channels. Microscopically there are dilated, thin-walled, endothelial-lined spaces with little or no smooth muscle, sometimes containing proteinaceous fluid, in the normal lymphatic locations. Differentials include diffuse pulmonary lymphangiomatosis (proliferation of anastomosing lymphatic channels with spindle cells), interstitial emphysema of ventilated infants (air spaces without endothelial lining, giant cells) and lymphangioleiomyomatosis in adults.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. Pleural fluid shows chylous effusion with numerous small lymphocytes, which is nonspecific. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign; for pleural fluid, a non-malignant category in the relevant serous effusion reporting system.
entities.ihc: IHC with D2-40 (podoplanin), PROX1 or LYVE-1 confirms the lymphatic nature of the dilated channels, and CD31 stains both blood and lymphatic endothelium. Lack of a smooth muscle proliferation (SMA, desmin) and HMB45 negativity help exclude LAM, and absence of CD68-positive giant cells lining spaces separates it from interstitial emphysema.

entities.variants: Classic CF (CFTR mutations, e.g. F508del); mild or atypical CF; CF-related bronchiectasis, mucoid impaction, ABPA, NTM and Burkholderia infection, haemoptysis; post-transplant CF lungs
entities.remarks: Autosomal recessive CFTR channel defect causing thick airway mucus, chronic infection (S. aureus, Pseudomonas, Burkholderia cepacia complex) and bronchiectasis; leading indication for lung transplant in young adults.
entities.histo: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations of the CFTR chloride channel, leading to dehydrated, viscous airway secretions, impaired mucociliary clearance and chronic infection. The lungs show widespread bronchiectasis, most severe in the upper lobes, with bronchi and bronchioles filled by thick, purulent mucus plugs. Microscopically the airways show mucus plugging, marked hyperplasia and hypertrophy of submucosal glands and goblet cells, dense chronic and acute inflammation with lymphoid follicles, ulceration, squamous metaplasia and destruction of the wall, progressing to bronchiectasis with peribronchial fibrosis, obstructive pneumonia, abscesses and emphysema-like changes. Chronic infection by Staphylococcus aureus, mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa (biofilms), Burkholderia cepacia complex and non-tuberculous mycobacteria, as well as ABPA, complicate the course. Bronchial arteries enlarge and can bleed. Explanted lungs at transplant show end-stage suppurative bronchiectasis. Differentials include primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency-related bronchiectasis and ABPA without CF.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. Sputum and BAL show abundant thick mucus, neutrophils and bacteria, and are used for culture surveillance. Diagnosis rests on sweat chloride testing and CFTR genotyping. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Special stains on explants or biopsies identify organisms (Gram, GMS, Ziehl-Neelsen for NTM), and mucin stains highlight plugs. Diagnosis is by sweat chloride, nasal potential difference and CFTR mutation analysis, which also guides CFTR modulator therapy.

entities.variants: Kartagener syndrome (situs inversus, sinusitis, bronchiectasis); PCD with normal situs; heterotaxy-associated PCD; ultrastructural defects (outer dynein arm, inner dynein arm with microtubular disorganisation, central pair, radial spoke); normal ultrastructure forms (DNAH11)
entities.remarks: Inherited defect of motile cilia causing neonatal respiratory distress, chronic wet cough, sinusitis, otitis, bronchiectasis (middle and lower lobes) and infertility; about half have situs inversus.
entities.histo: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is a genetically heterogeneous, usually autosomal recessive disorder of motile cilia structure or function, causing impaired mucociliary clearance. Patients present with neonatal respiratory distress at term, chronic wet cough, rhinosinusitis, otitis media and progressive bronchiectasis, typically of the middle and lower lobes, and many have situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome) or other laterality defects, as well as male infertility. Histology of resected or explanted lung shows nonspecific bronchiectasis with mucus plugging, chronic inflammation, lymphoid follicles and fibrosis, like other causes of bronchiectasis. Diagnosis relies on nasal nitric oxide, high-speed video microscopy of ciliary beat, transmission electron microscopy of ciliary ultrastructure (absence of outer or inner dynein arms, central pair or radial spoke defects, microtubular disorganisation), immunofluorescence for ciliary proteins and genetic testing. Some genetic forms have normal ultrastructure. Differentials include cystic fibrosis, immunodeficiency, secondary ciliary dyskinesia from infection or smoking (compound cilia, random defects).
entities.cyto: Cytology contributes through nasal or bronchial brushings for ciliary beat analysis by high-speed video microscopy and for electron microscopy; routine stained cytology is not diagnostic. Secondary ciliary changes in infected samples are a pitfall. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: Immunofluorescence on ciliated brush samples for proteins such as DNAH5 (outer dynein arms), GAS8, RSPH4A and CCDC39 shows absent or mislocalised staining in many genetic forms and is a valuable diagnostic test. Transmission electron microscopy remains a reference test. Routine IHC on lung tissue is not useful.

entities.variants: Simple and complex PAVMs; hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (ENG, ACVRL1); post-surgical (Glenn shunt) and hepatopulmonary syndrome-related diffuse microscopic AVMs; acquired (trauma, infection, schistosomiasis, tumours)
entities.remarks: Abnormal direct communication between pulmonary artery and vein bypassing capillaries; right-to-left shunt with paradoxical emboli and brain abscess; about 80 percent associated with HHT.
entities.histo: A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation is an abnormal direct communication between a pulmonary artery and vein, bypassing the capillary bed and causing a right-to-left shunt. Most are associated with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and are often multiple, lower lobe and subpleural. Complications include hypoxaemia, paradoxical embolism with stroke and brain abscess, and haemoptysis or haemothorax. Grossly there is a lobulated vascular sac or tangle of dilated vessels with a feeding artery and draining vein. Microscopically the lesion consists of thin- and thick-walled vascular channels of varying calibre, with irregular muscular and elastic walls, fibrointimal thickening, thrombi and haemorrhage. Diffuse microscopic AVMs occur in hepatopulmonary syndrome and after cavopulmonary shunts lacking hepatic venous flow. Most are treated by embolisation, so pathology specimens are uncommon. Differentials include haemangioma, pulmonary varix, pulmonary artery aneurysm and vascular tumours.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role and FNA is contraindicated because of bleeding risk. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not required. Elastic stains (EVG) characterise the abnormal arterial and venous walls and their direct connections, and CD31 or ERG confirm endothelial lining if a vascular tumour is in question. Genetic testing for HHT genes is clinically indicated.

entities.variants: Pulmonary artery agenesis or interruption; pulmonary artery sling; partial and total anomalous pulmonary venous return; scimitar syndrome (hypogenetic lung with anomalous right pulmonary venous drainage to IVC); congenital pulmonary vein stenosis or atresia; pulmonary varix; congenital pulmonary artery stenosis
entities.remarks: Anomalies of arterial and venous connections; often with congenital heart disease; venous obstruction causes pulmonary hypertension, lymphangiectasia and haemorrhage.
entities.histo: Congenital anomalies of the pulmonary vessels include absent or interrupted pulmonary artery (with systemic collateral supply), pulmonary artery sling compressing the trachea, stenoses of pulmonary arteries, and anomalies of venous drainage. Anomalous pulmonary venous return, partial or total, drains pulmonary veins into the systemic venous circulation and when obstructed causes severe pulmonary venous hypertension. Scimitar syndrome combines right lung hypoplasia with an anomalous vein draining into the inferior vena cava and often systemic arterial supply. Congenital pulmonary vein stenosis is a progressive intimal myofibroblastic proliferation narrowing the veins, causing pulmonary hypertension, venous arterialisation, lymphangiectasia and haemosiderosis. Pulmonary varix is a localised dilatation of a pulmonary vein. Pathology specimens show intimal fibrosis and muscularisation of veins, medial hypertrophy of arteries, dilated lymphatics, and congestion with haemosiderin-laden macrophages. Differentials include acquired pulmonary venous obstruction (fibrosing mediastinitis, PVOD) and chronic thromboembolic disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in congenital pulmonary vascular anomalies. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. Elastic stains distinguish arteries from veins and show venous arterialisation, while SMA highlights myofibroblastic intimal proliferation in vein stenosis. Iron stain shows haemosiderosis from venous congestion.

entities.variants: Resorption (obstructive) atelectasis (mucus plug, tumour, foreign body); compression (passive) atelectasis (effusion, pneumothorax, mass); contraction (cicatrisation) atelectasis (fibrosis); patchy (microatelectasis, surfactant loss); rounded atelectasis (folded lung, asbestos-related pleural disease); middle lobe syndrome; neonatal atelectasis
entities.remarks: Incomplete expansion or collapse of lung; reversible except contraction type; rounded atelectasis mimics a mass; obstructive atelectasis in adults warrants exclusion of endobronchial tumour.
entities.histo: Atelectasis is loss of lung volume due to inadequate expansion of airspaces, producing shunting of blood through unventilated lung. Resorption atelectasis follows complete airway obstruction, by mucus plugs after surgery, aspirated foreign bodies or endobronchial tumours, with absorption of trapped air and shift of the mediastinum towards the affected side. Compression atelectasis results from fluid, air, blood or tumour in the pleural cavity, with mediastinal shift away. Contraction atelectasis is caused by local or generalised fibrosis and is irreversible. Microatelectasis is patchy collapse due to surfactant loss, as in ARDS and neonatal RDS. Rounded atelectasis is a peripheral mass-like area of folded, collapsed lung adjacent to thickened, fibrotic pleura, often asbestos related, with a characteristic comet-tail sign on CT. Histologically collapsed lung shows closely apposed alveolar walls with slit-like airspaces, congestion and, in chronic cases, fibrosis and obstructive (endogenous lipoid) pneumonia with foamy macrophages. The middle lobe syndrome is recurrent collapse of the right middle lobe from compression or inflammation. Differentials include consolidation, pneumonectomy changes, and in rounded atelectasis, carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in atelectasis itself, but in obstructive atelectasis bronchial washings and brushings are used to look for an underlying carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: not applicable to atelectasis; the category depends on any lesion found.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Elastic stains can demonstrate pleural infolding and collapsed alveoli in rounded atelectasis. When obstructive atelectasis is due to tumour, the tumour is worked up with standard panels.

entities.variants: Centriacinar (centrilobular; smokers, upper lobes); panacinar (panlobular; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, lower lobes; also intravenous methylphenidate or talc); distal acinar (paraseptal; subpleural, bullae, spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults); irregular (paracicatricial, around scars); bullous emphysema and giant bullae; blebs; interstitial emphysema (air in interstitium; ventilated neonates); compensatory hyperinflation; senile hyperinflation; combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema; congenital lobar overinflation (separate row)
entities.remarks: Permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles with destruction of walls and without obvious fibrosis; part of COPD; protease-antiprotease imbalance; smoking and biomass smoke exposure.
entities.histo: Emphysema is permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole accompanied by destruction of their walls, without obvious fibrosis, and is a principal component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It is classified by distribution within the acinus. Centriacinar emphysema, the commonest type in smokers, affects respiratory bronchioles in the central acinus with sparing of distal alveoli, is most severe in the apical segments of the upper lobes, and often contains black anthracotic pigment and inflammation around bronchioles. Panacinar emphysema involves the entire acinus uniformly from respiratory bronchiole to terminal alveoli, predominates in the lower lobes and is characteristic of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Distal acinar (paraseptal) emphysema affects the distal acinus beneath the pleura and along septa, often forming bullae that may rupture causing spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults. Irregular emphysema surrounds scars. Bullae are emphysematous spaces over 1 cm, blebs are subpleural collections of air within the pleura, and interstitial emphysema is air dissecting into the interstitium after alveolar rupture. Microscopically there are enlarged airspaces with free-floating fragments of alveolar walls, clubbed septal ends, loss of capillaries, and associated small airway inflammation and fibrosis. Differentials include overinflation without destruction (compensatory, senile), airspace enlargement with fibrosis, LAM and other cystic diseases, and honeycombing.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in emphysema itself. Sputum may show pigmented macrophages and inflammatory cells in smokers. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Diagnosis is primarily radiological and morphological, best assessed on inflation-fixed whole lung sections. PAS with diastase shows alpha-1 antitrypsin globules in hepatocytes rather than lung, and serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level and genotyping (PiZZ) are important in young or lower-lobe predominant emphysema. Elastic stains highlight destroyed alveolar walls.
