entities.variants: Cylindrical (tubular), varicose and saccular (cystic) types; post-infectious (TB, measles, pertussis, adenovirus, necrotising pneumonia; commonest in India); obstruction (tumour, foreign body); cystic fibrosis; primary ciliary dyskinesia; immunodeficiency (CVID, hypogammaglobulinaemia); ABPA (central); NTM; connective tissue disease and IBD; traction bronchiectasis in fibrosis; congenital (Williams-Campbell, Mounier-Kuhn); idiopathic; middle lobe syndrome
entities.remarks: Permanent dilatation of bronchi and bronchioles from destruction of muscle and elastic tissue due to infection and obstruction; chronic productive cough, haemoptysis; lower lobes commonly.
entities.histo: Bronchiectasis is a permanent dilatation of bronchi and bronchioles caused by destruction of the muscular and elastic supporting tissue, resulting from or associated with chronic necrotising infection, and the vicious cycle of impaired clearance, infection and inflammation. It usually affects the lower lobes bilaterally, especially vertical air passages, except in ABPA (central upper lobe) and post-tuberculous disease (upper lobes). Grossly the airways are dilated up to four times normal and can be followed to the pleura; they may be cylindrical, varicose (beaded) or saccular (cystic), and contain mucopurulent secretions. Microscopically there is intense acute and chronic inflammation of the bronchial wall with lymphoid follicles (follicular bronchiectasis), ulceration, squamous metaplasia, desquamation, destruction of smooth muscle, elastic tissue and cartilage, and peribronchial fibrosis that obliterates distal bronchioles. Abscesses, enlarged tortuous bronchial arteries (causing haemoptysis) and amyloidosis are complications. Traction bronchiectasis in fibrotic ILD is a different mechanism with less inflammation. Differentials include cystic lung diseases, honeycombing, CPAM and dilated airways in cystic fibrosis or PCD, which are underlying causes rather than alternative diagnoses.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. Sputum shows abundant mucopurulent material, neutrophils and bacteria, and is used for culture surveillance, including mycobacteria. Reactive and metaplastic cells may appear atypical. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. Elastic stains show loss of bronchial wall elastic tissue, Congo red identifies secondary AA amyloidosis, and special stains (Ziehl-Neelsen, GMS, Gram) identify infecting organisms. Investigation of the cause (immunoglobulins, sweat chloride, ciliary studies, Aspergillus serology) is clinical.

entities.entity: Pulmonary oedema and pulmonary venous congestion
entities.variants: Haemodynamic (cardiogenic) oedema (left heart failure, mitral stenosis, volume overload, hypoalbuminaemia, renal failure); chronic passive congestion with heart failure cells and brown induration; oedema due to microvascular or alveolar injury (infection, ARDS, toxins, drugs); neurogenic oedema; high-altitude pulmonary oedema; re-expansion and negative-pressure oedema; transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) and transfusion-associated circulatory overload
entities.remarks: Fluid accumulation in interstitium and alveoli; haemodynamic oedema is protein-poor, injury-related is protein-rich; chronic congestion gives haemosiderin-laden macrophages and septal fibrosis.
entities.histo: Pulmonary oedema is the accumulation of fluid in the lung interstitium and alveoli. Haemodynamic oedema results from raised pulmonary venous pressure, most often in left ventricular failure or mitral stenosis, and initially affects the dependent lower lobes. Grossly the lungs are heavy and wet and exude frothy, blood-tinged fluid on sectioning. Microscopically alveolar capillaries are engorged, and the alveoli contain pale, finely granular pink transudate, sometimes with air bubbles; interstitial oedema widens interlobular septa (Kerley B lines on imaging) and peribronchovascular sheaths. In chronic passive congestion, recurrent microhaemorrhages lead to haemosiderin-laden macrophages (heart failure cells), septal fibrosis and the gross brown induration of the lung, with pulmonary venous hypertensive changes in vessels. Oedema caused by alveolar or endothelial injury (ARDS, infections, toxins, TRALI) is protein-rich and often accompanied by hyaline membranes and inflammation. Neurogenic, high-altitude, re-expansion and negative-pressure oedema are additional mechanisms. Differentials include alveolar proteinosis (granular PAS-positive material), Pneumocystis pneumonia (foamy casts) and early DAD.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. BAL in chronic congestion shows numerous haemosiderin-laden macrophages, and in oedema a low-cellularity specimen with proteinaceous background may be seen. Haemosiderin-laden macrophages also occur in alveolar haemorrhage syndromes, so clinical correlation is essential. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Perls Prussian blue confirms haemosiderin in heart failure cells and quantifies chronic haemorrhage, and PAS helps separate oedema fluid (weakly positive) from alveolar proteinosis material (strongly positive, granular). GMS excludes Pneumocystis in foamy-appearing exudates.

entities.entity: Acute respiratory distress syndrome and diffuse alveolar damage
entities.variants: Exudative (acute) phase; organising (proliferative) phase; fibrotic phase; causes: sepsis, pneumonia (bacterial, viral including influenza and COVID-19), aspiration, trauma and shock, pancreatitis, transfusion (TRALI), drugs (chemotherapy, amiodarone), toxic inhalation, radiation, connective tissue disease, acute exacerbation of ILD, idiopathic (see AIP)
entities.remarks: ARDS is the clinical syndrome; DAD is its histological counterpart; hyaline membranes in the exudative phase; diffuse, uniform, temporally homogeneous injury; high mortality.
entities.histo: Acute respiratory distress syndrome is a clinical syndrome of acute bilateral lung infiltrates and severe hypoxaemia not explained by cardiac failure, and its pathological correlate is diffuse alveolar damage, caused by injury to alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium. Grossly the lungs are heavy, firm, red and boggy. In the exudative phase, during the first week, there is interstitial and intra-alveolar oedema, haemorrhage, fibrin and characteristic hyaline membranes lining alveolar ducts and alveoli, composed of fibrin, plasma proteins and necrotic epithelial debris, with sloughing of type I pneumocytes and microthrombi. The organising phase, from about the second week, shows type II pneumocyte hyperplasia (often with marked cytological atypia), interstitial myofibroblast proliferation, organising granulation tissue in airspaces and septa, squamous metaplasia of bronchiolar epithelium and organising thrombi. Some patients progress to a fibrotic phase with remodelling and honeycomb-like cysts. The pattern is uniform in age throughout. Causes include sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, drugs and many others, and an identifiable cause should be sought (viral inclusions, organisms, foreign material). Differentials include AFOP, organising pneumonia, acute exacerbation of UIP, eosinophilic pneumonia, diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and infection.
entities.cyto: Cytology contributes mainly by BAL to exclude infection. Reactive type II pneumocytes in organising DAD are enlarged with prominent nucleoli and can form three-dimensional clusters, closely mimicking adenocarcinoma; in the clinical context of ARDS, caution is needed. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical.
entities.ihc: IHC has no specific diagnostic role but helps identify causes: viral IHC (CMV, HSV, adenovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2), GMS and Ziehl-Neelsen for organisms. Fibrin stains highlight hyaline membranes. Keratin and TTF-1 do not separate reactive pneumocytes from adenocarcinoma; morphology, Ki-67 and context are more useful. CD61 highlights platelet thrombi.

entities.entity: Acute interstitial pneumonia (idiopathic diffuse alveolar damage)
entities.variants: Hamman-Rich syndrome; exudative and organising phases; distinct from acute exacerbation of IPF
entities.remarks: Rapidly progressive idiopathic interstitial pneumonia with DAD in previously healthy individuals; diagnosis of exclusion; mortality around 50 percent.
entities.histo: Acute interstitial pneumonia, historically known as Hamman-Rich syndrome, is a rapidly progressive idiopathic interstitial pneumonia presenting with a viral-like prodrome followed by respiratory failure in a previously healthy person, without any identifiable cause of ARDS. It is classified among the rare idiopathic interstitial pneumonias. Histologically it is diffuse alveolar damage identical to ARDS of known cause: an exudative phase with hyaline membranes, oedema and microthrombi, and an organising phase with diffuse interstitial myofibroblastic proliferation, type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and organising airspace tissue, uniform in age throughout the lung. The background lung shows no pre-existing fibrotic interstitial disease, which separates it from acute exacerbation of IPF or other fibrotic ILD. Survivors may recover or develop fibrosis, and recurrences occur. The diagnosis requires thorough exclusion of infection, drugs, connective tissue disease, inhalational injuries and sepsis. Differentials include DAD of known cause, AFOP, acute eosinophilic pneumonia and organising pneumonia.
entities.cyto: Cytology is used to exclude infection, with BAL showing nonspecific inflammatory cells and reactive pneumocytes, which may be highly atypical. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role; it serves to exclude infection (viral IHC, GMS, Ziehl-Neelsen) and to highlight fibrin. Diagnosis requires multidisciplinary correlation with exclusion of known causes of DAD.

entities.variants: Acute pulmonary embolism (saddle embolus, massive, submassive, small peripheral); pulmonary infarction (wedge-shaped haemorrhagic infarct, septic infarct); recurrent emboli and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) with organised thrombi, webs and bands; in situ thrombosis (sickle cell disease, COVID-19, vasculitis); pulmonary vein thrombosis (after lobectomy or lung transplantation, or with tumour)
entities.remarks: Deep vein thrombosis of legs is the source in most cases; infarction occurs in a minority because of dual blood supply; organised emboli form intravascular webs and recanalised channels.
entities.histo: Pulmonary thromboembolism is the lodgement of thrombi, usually from the deep veins of the legs, within the pulmonary arteries. Large emboli occlude the main pulmonary artery or straddle its bifurcation (saddle embolus) and cause sudden death from acute right heart failure, while smaller emboli travel peripherally. Because of the dual pulmonary and bronchial circulation, only about 10 percent of emboli cause infarction, usually when circulation is compromised by heart failure. Infarcts are wedge-shaped, haemorrhagic, red-blue, raised, subpleural lesions with the apex pointing to the occluded vessel and an overlying fibrinous pleuritis; with time they become brown and are replaced by fibrous scar. Microscopically there is ischaemic coagulative necrosis of alveolar walls with haemorrhage, a peripheral zone of acute inflammation and later granulation tissue and organisation. Emboli are distinguished from postmortem clots by lines of Zahn and attachment to the vessel wall. Organised emboli produce fibrous webs, bands and recanalised colanders within arteries, and recurrent emboli cause chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. Septic emboli produce cavitating abscesses. Differentials include infarct-like necrosis in angioinvasive fungal infection, GPA and carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in pulmonary embolism. FNA of an organising infarct may show necrotic debris, haemosiderin-laden macrophages and markedly atypical reactive pneumocytes and squamous metaplasia, which can mimic carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical when reactive atypia is marked.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Elastic stains show the thrombosed vessel and organised webs in CTEPH, Perls iron highlights haemosiderin, and GMS and Gram stain exclude septic or fungal infarcts. In infarcts with squamous metaplasia, p40 is positive in reactive cells, so morphology is crucial to avoid a misdiagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma.

entities.variants: Fat embolism (long bone fractures; fat embolism syndrome); bone marrow embolism (CPR, fractures, sickle cell acute chest syndrome); amniotic fluid embolism (squames, mucin, lanugo in maternal vessels); air embolism; tumour embolism and pulmonary tumour thrombotic microangiopathy (gastric, breast carcinoma); foreign body emboli (talc, cellulose, catheter fragments, cement after vertebroplasty, cotton, hydrophilic polymer coating, embolic agents); septic emboli; trophoblastic and hepatic tissue emboli; parasitic emboli (schistosoma eggs, Dirofilaria)
entities.remarks: Material other than thrombus obstructing pulmonary vessels; fat emboli need oil red O on frozen sections; amniotic fluid embolism is a catastrophic obstetric event; tumour thrombotic microangiopathy causes rapidly progressive pulmonary hypertension.
entities.histo: Non-thrombotic pulmonary embolism covers emboli of fat, marrow, amniotic fluid, air, tumour and foreign material. Fat embolism follows long bone fractures and soft tissue trauma, and the fat embolism syndrome combines respiratory failure, neurological signs and petechiae, with fat droplets occluding pulmonary capillaries. Bone marrow emboli, containing haematopoietic cells and fat, are frequent after CPR and in sickle cell acute chest syndrome. Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare, often fatal obstetric complication in which fetal squames, lanugo hair, vernix fat and mucin are found in maternal pulmonary arterioles and capillaries, with DIC and DAD. Air embolism results from venous access or barotrauma. Tumour emboli and pulmonary tumour thrombotic microangiopathy, most often from gastric adenocarcinoma, cause intimal fibrocellular proliferation of small arteries around tumour cell emboli, producing subacute pulmonary hypertension. Foreign material emboli include talc and excipients from intravenous drug use, polymer coating from catheters, cement after vertebroplasty and embolisation agents, typically with giant cell reactions. Septic emboli lead to abscesses. Differentials include thrombotic emboli and lymphangitic carcinomatosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a minor role. Pulmonary artery catheter blood cytology has been used to identify amniotic fluid elements or tumour cells, and BAL with fat-laden macrophages has been proposed for fat embolism, but both lack specificity. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Malignant when tumour emboli are identified.
entities.ihc: IHC and special stains are helpful. Oil red O or osmium on frozen or wet tissue demonstrates fat emboli, which are dissolved in paraffin sections. Keratin (AE1/AE3, CK13) highlights fetal squames and mucin stains (Alcian blue) show mucin in amniotic fluid embolism. Keratin and tumour-specific markers identify tumour emboli, and CD68 highlights giant cells around foreign material. Polarisation identifies birefringent foreign material.

entities.variants: Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic, heritable BMPR2, drug and toxin, CTD especially systemic sclerosis, HIV, portopulmonary, congenital heart disease with shunts and Eisenmenger, schistosomiasis); group 2 left heart disease (venous hypertension); group 3 lung disease and hypoxia (COPD, ILD, high altitude); group 4 CTEPH and other obstructions; group 5 unclear or multifactorial (sarcoidosis, haematological, tumour thrombotic microangiopathy); persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn; plexiform arteriopathy; Heath-Edwards grading
entities.remarks: Mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg at rest; medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis and plexiform lesions in PAH; venous changes in group 2; vascular remodelling secondary to lung disease in group 3.
entities.histo: Pulmonary hypertension is raised pressure in the pulmonary circulation, defined by a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg at rest, and is classified into five clinical groups. Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension, which includes idiopathic, heritable (BMPR2), drug-related, connective tissue disease, HIV, portopulmonary and congenital shunt-related forms, shows medial hypertrophy of muscular arteries, muscularisation of arterioles, concentric laminar (onion-skin) intimal fibrosis and characteristic plexiform lesions: glomeruloid tufts of capillary-like channels within a dilated arterial branch beyond a narrowed segment, often with dilatation lesions and fibrinoid necrotising arteritis in severe disease. Atherosclerosis of large pulmonary arteries and right ventricular hypertrophy accompany longstanding disease. Group 2 (left heart disease) shows venous and arterial medial thickening, venous arterialisation and haemosiderosis. Group 3 (lung disease and hypoxia) shows medial hypertrophy and intimal fibrosis without plexiform lesions. Group 4 shows organised thrombi and webs, and group 5 includes sarcoidosis and tumour thrombotic microangiopathy. The historical Heath-Edwards grading describes the progression of arterial lesions from medial hypertrophy to plexiform and necrotising lesions. Differentials include PVOD and PCH (venous and capillary involvement), CTEPH and vasculitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in pulmonary hypertension. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. Elastic stains (EVG, Movat) are essential to identify arteries and veins, assess medial thickness and intimal lesions, and recognise plexiform and dilatation lesions; trichrome highlights fibrosis. CD31 or CD34 outlines the endothelial channels within plexiform lesions. Iron stain shows haemosiderosis in venous hypertension and PVOD.

entities.entity: Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease and pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis
entities.variants: PVOD (idiopathic, heritable EIF2AK4 mutations, drug-induced: mitomycin C, alkylating agents; occupational: trichloroethylene; systemic sclerosis; post-HSCT); PCH (capillary proliferation pattern); combined PVOD/PCH spectrum (WHO group 1 prime)
entities.remarks: Pulmonary hypertension from fibrous occlusion of septal and preseptal veins and capillary proliferation; poor response and risk of pulmonary oedema with vasodilators; EIF2AK4 biallelic mutations in heritable forms.
entities.histo: Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease and pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis are now considered a single disease spectrum causing pulmonary hypertension, classified as group 1 prime. PVOD shows intimal fibrosis, loose or dense, that narrows and occludes small septal and preseptal pulmonary veins and venules, sometimes with recanalisation, together with arterialisation of veins, congestion of capillaries, interstitial oedema, haemosiderin-laden macrophages, lymphatic dilatation and variable medial hypertrophy and intimal fibrosis of arteries. PCH shows a patchy proliferation of capillaries that duplicate or triplicate the layers of alveolar septal capillaries, invade bronchiolar and vascular walls and pleura, and form nodular aggregates, typically with haemosiderin. Both patterns often coexist. Causes include heritable EIF2AK4 mutations, chemotherapy (mitomycin C), organic solvent exposure, systemic sclerosis and stem cell transplantation. Clinically these patients may develop severe pulmonary oedema with vasodilator therapy, which is why recognition matters; lung transplantation is the definitive treatment. Differentials include PAH without venous disease, pulmonary venous hypertension due to left heart disease, chronic haemorrhage syndromes and fibrosing mediastinitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role, although BAL may show occult alveolar haemorrhage with haemosiderin-laden macrophages, which supports PVOD in the clinical context. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is helpful only in specific respects. Elastic stains are essential to recognise venous involvement and arterialised veins. CD31 or CD34 highlights capillary duplication in PCH. Perls stain demonstrates haemosiderin. Genetic testing for EIF2AK4 is recommended in suspected heritable PVOD.

entities.variants: DAH with capillaritis (GPA, MPA, anti-GBM disease, SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, drugs); bland pulmonary haemorrhage (coagulopathy, anticoagulants, mitral stenosis, idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis, PVOD, leptospirosis); DAH with diffuse alveolar damage (HSCT, sepsis, drugs, cocaine); vaping or crack lung; haemorrhage due to infections
entities.remarks: Triad of haemoptysis, anaemia and diffuse infiltrates; BAL with increasingly bloody aliquots; histology classifies into capillaritis, bland haemorrhage or DAD with haemorrhage.
entities.histo: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage is bleeding into alveolar spaces from the microvasculature, causing haemoptysis, anaemia, diffuse infiltrates and respiratory failure. Histologically, acute haemorrhage shows fresh red cells filling alveoli, followed within two to three days by haemosiderin-laden macrophages and, with recurrence, interstitial haemosiderin, iron encrustation of elastic fibres (endogenous pneumoconiosis) and fibrosis. Three patterns help identify the cause. In capillaritis, alveolar septa are infiltrated by neutrophils with karyorrhexis, fibrinoid necrosis of capillary walls and fibrin thrombi, typical of ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-GBM disease, lupus and other immune disorders. In bland haemorrhage, red cells and siderophages fill alveoli without inflammation or vascular injury, due to coagulopathy, venous hypertension, idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis or PVOD. In DAD with haemorrhage, hyaline membranes and organising changes accompany the blood, as in HSCT, sepsis and drug toxicity. Surgical haemorrhage artefact contains fresh blood without siderophages and should not be overinterpreted. Differentials include infection and procedure-related bleeding.
entities.cyto: BAL is the principal diagnostic test: sequential aliquots become increasingly haemorrhagic, and haemosiderin-laden macrophages exceed about 20 percent of macrophages, confirming alveolar haemorrhage of more than 48 hours' duration. The cause cannot be determined cytologically, but infection can be excluded. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (haemorrhage with haemosiderin-laden macrophages).
entities.ihc: IHC has little role. Perls Prussian blue is used to grade haemosiderin in macrophages (Golde score) and interstitium. Elastic stains help identify vessels in capillaritis, and immunofluorescence on fresh tissue shows linear IgG in anti-GBM disease or granular immune complexes in lupus. ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA and antiphospholipid serology, coagulation studies and cultures are essential.

entities.variants: Childhood IPH (with or without coeliac disease, Lane-Hamilton syndrome); adult IPH; IPH with cow's milk hypersensitivity (Heiner syndrome)
entities.remarks: Recurrent bland diffuse alveolar haemorrhage without capillaritis or immune deposits; iron deficiency anaemia; diagnosis of exclusion; may progress to fibrosis.
entities.histo: Idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis is a rare disorder, mainly of children and young adults, characterised by recurrent episodes of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with haemoptysis, iron deficiency anaemia and diffuse infiltrates, without evidence of vasculitis, capillaritis, immune complex deposition or other known cause. Some patients have coeliac disease (Lane-Hamilton syndrome) or cow's milk hypersensitivity (Heiner syndrome). Histologically there is bland intra-alveolar haemorrhage with numerous haemosiderin-laden macrophages, type II pneumocyte hyperplasia, interstitial haemosiderin deposition and, with recurrent episodes, iron encrustation of elastic fibres and vessels and progressive interstitial fibrosis. Neutrophilic capillaritis and fibrinoid necrosis are absent, and immunofluorescence is negative. Differentials include capillaritis-associated DAH (ANCA vasculitis, SLE), anti-GBM disease, mitral stenosis and PVOD with chronic congestion, and other causes of bland haemorrhage such as coagulopathy.
entities.cyto: BAL shows abundant haemosiderin-laden macrophages and blood, supporting chronic alveolar haemorrhage; gastric aspirate in children may show siderophages from swallowed sputum. The cause cannot be determined cytologically. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. Perls stain demonstrates heavy haemosiderin deposition, including encrustation of elastic fibres, and elastic stains confirm absence of vasculitis. Immunofluorescence for IgG, IgA, IgM and complement is negative, separating it from anti-GBM disease and lupus. Coeliac serology should be checked.

entities.entity: Tracheal and bronchial stenosis (post-intubation, post-tracheostomy and idiopathic)
entities.variants: Post-intubation (cuff injury) and post-tracheostomy stenosis with granulation tissue; tracheostomy-associated atypia and pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia; idiopathic subglottic stenosis (women); anastomotic stenosis after lung transplant or sleeve resection; tracheomalacia acquired; post-tuberculous bronchial stenosis
entities.remarks: Iatrogenic airway injury healing with granulation tissue and fibrosis; idiopathic subglottic stenosis in women is a diagnosis of exclusion (rule out GPA, relapsing polychondritis, amyloid); reactive atypia should not be mistaken for carcinoma.
entities.histo: Acquired tracheal and bronchial stenosis is most often iatrogenic, following prolonged endotracheal intubation with cuff-related pressure necrosis or tracheostomy, and may also follow lung transplantation, sleeve resection, tuberculosis or inhalational injury. Histology shows ulcerated mucosa with granulation tissue, acute and chronic inflammation, dense submucosal fibrosis replacing the normal stroma and sometimes destroyed cartilage, with squamous metaplasia of the surface epithelium. Exuberant granulation tissue polyps and pseudoepitheliomatous squamous hyperplasia with reactive atypia, especially at tracheostomy sites, can mimic squamous cell carcinoma or a vascular tumour. Idiopathic subglottic stenosis occurs almost exclusively in women and shows dense keloidal fibrosis of the lamina propria with mild inflammation and sometimes oestrogen and progesterone receptor positivity of fibroblasts; it is a diagnosis of exclusion. Differentials include GPA, relapsing polychondritis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, tracheopathia osteochondroplastica and tumours (adenoid cystic carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma).
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. Brushings may show reactive squamous and bronchial cells with repair atypia, which is a pitfall for squamous carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical.
entities.ihc: IHC is limited. In pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia p40 is positive in both reactive and malignant squamous cells, so architecture and atypia decide. ANCA serology, Congo red and special stains for organisms help exclude GPA, amyloid and infection. ER and PR positivity of stromal fibroblasts has been described in idiopathic subglottic stenosis.

entities.variants: Diffuse submucosal osteocartilaginous nodules of trachea and main bronchi; association with amyloid in some cases; ozaena-like atrophic rhinitis associations
entities.remarks: Benign idiopathic condition with nodules of bone and cartilage arising from tracheal rings, sparing the posterior membranous wall; cobblestone appearance at bronchoscopy; usually incidental.
entities.histo: Tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica is a rare benign disorder characterised by multiple submucosal nodules of cartilage and bone projecting into the lumen of the lower two thirds of the trachea and the main bronchi, arising from or connected to the cartilaginous rings and sparing the posterior membranous wall. It is commoner in men over 50 years, is usually asymptomatic and found at bronchoscopy, where the nodules give a characteristic cobblestone or rock-garden appearance, or on CT as calcified nodules. Microscopically there are submucosal nodules of mature lamellar bone with fatty or haematopoietic marrow and hyaline cartilage, covered by intact or squamous metaplastic respiratory mucosa. Inflammation is minimal. Some cases show associated amyloid deposits, raising the possibility of a shared mechanism. Severe cases cause airway narrowing and recurrent infection. Differentials include tracheobronchial amyloidosis (amyloid with secondary ossification, involves posterior wall), relapsing polychondritis (inflamed cartilage, posterior wall spared), calcified tuberculous lesions, and chondroma or chondrosarcoma (solitary tumour).
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not required. Congo red with polarisation should be performed to exclude or document associated amyloid, and decalcification may be needed for histology. Diagnosis is mainly bronchoscopic and radiological.

entities.variants: Calcified hilar or peribronchial lymph nodes eroding into bronchi (healed histoplasmosis, tuberculosis); aspirated calcified foreign body; complications: haemoptysis, obstructive pneumonia, bronchiectasis, fistula
entities.remarks: Calcified material within or distorting a bronchus, usually derived from eroding calcified lymph nodes; lithoptysis (coughing up stones) is characteristic.
entities.histo: Broncholithiasis is the presence of calcified material within the bronchial lumen or distorting the bronchial wall, usually arising from erosion of calcified peribronchial or hilar lymph nodes into an adjacent bronchus. The nodes are typically calcified as a result of healed granulomatous infection, most often tuberculosis in India and histoplasmosis in North America. Patients present with cough, haemoptysis, recurrent pneumonia or expectoration of small stones (lithoptysis). Histologically resected specimens show a calcified or ossified mass of necrotic granulomatous tissue within or adjacent to the bronchus, surrounded by chronic inflammation, granulation tissue and fibrosis, with mucosal ulceration and squamous metaplasia. Distal lung shows obstructive pneumonia, bronchiectasis and atelectasis. Bronchoesophageal fistula is a rare complication. Differentials include carcinoid tumour with ossification, aspirated foreign body, tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica and calcified hamartoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role. Expectorated stones are examined grossly and chemically. Washings may show inflammatory debris and calcific material. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Ziehl-Neelsen and GMS stains on residual necrotic granulomatous material may identify the original infection, and von Kossa confirms calcium. Diagnosis is radiological and bronchoscopic.

entities.entity: Reactive bronchial and alveolar epithelial changes (squamous metaplasia, pneumocyte hyperplasia and atypia)
entities.variants: Squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium (smoking, injury, infection; with or without atypia); basal cell and goblet cell hyperplasia; reactive type II pneumocyte hyperplasia (DAD, OP, infection, infarct, radiation, chemotherapy); bronchiolar metaplasia (peribronchiolar metaplasia, lambertosis); Creola bodies; radiation and chemotherapy-induced atypia; post-tracheostomy atypia
entities.remarks: Common reactive epithelial responses to injury that frequently mimic carcinoma in small biopsies and cytology; recognition of the clinical context is essential.
entities.histo: The bronchial and alveolar epithelium responds to injury with several patterns that can mimic neoplasia. Squamous metaplasia replaces ciliated respiratory epithelium with stratified squamous epithelium in smokers, after infection or intubation and over infarcts, and may show reactive atypia without the full-thickness disorder and mitotic activity of dysplasia. Basal cell hyperplasia and goblet cell hyperplasia accompany chronic irritation. Reactive type II pneumocyte hyperplasia occurs in diffuse alveolar damage, organising pneumonia, infarcts, infection, radiation and chemotherapy; the cells become enlarged and cuboidal or hobnail, with large nuclei, prominent nucleoli and sometimes multinucleation, and line thickened septa in a continuous layer. Bronchiolar (peribronchiolar) metaplasia, or lambertosis, is extension of ciliated bronchiolar epithelium onto alveolar walls around scarred bronchioles. Features favouring reactive change include a heterogeneous population merging with normal cells, inflammation, fibrin or hyaline membranes, ciliated cells and absence of a discrete mass. Differentials include AAH, adenocarcinoma in situ, invasive adenocarcinoma, squamous dysplasia and squamous cell carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Reactive bronchial cells, Creola bodies, reparative squamous metaplasia and reactive pneumocytes are among the commonest causes of false-positive lung cytology. Reactive cells show cohesive flat or three-dimensional groups, terminal bars or cilia, smooth nuclear membranes, fine chromatin, a spectrum of changes and an inflammatory background. Marked atypia in the context of DAD, infarction, radiation or chemotherapy should be reported cautiously. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical; Suspicious or Malignant only when features are unequivocal.
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role because reactive and neoplastic cells share lineage markers: reactive pneumocytes are TTF-1 and napsin A positive and reactive squamous metaplasia is p40 and CK5/6 positive. Supporting features of a reactive process include low Ki-67, wild-type p53 pattern and preserved myoepithelial or basal layers in bronchial epithelium. Ciliated cells exclude malignancy. Morphology, distribution and clinical context remain decisive.

entities.variants: Reactive NE cell hyperplasia in chronic lung disease (bronchiectasis, fibrosis, smoking, chronic hypoxia, high altitude, BPD, cystic fibrosis); NE cell hyperplasia adjacent to carcinoid tumours; distinction from DIPNECH (preneoplastic) and NEHI (paediatric)
entities.remarks: Increased neuroendocrine cells in airway epithelium as a reaction to injury or hypoxia; usually incidental; distinguished from DIPNECH by context, distribution and absence of constrictive bronchiolitis and tumorlets.
entities.histo: Pulmonary neuroendocrine cells normally occur singly or as small neuroepithelial bodies in the bronchial and bronchiolar epithelium. Reactive neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia is an increase in these cells as individual cells, small clusters or linear proliferations within the basal epithelium, in response to chronic airway injury, inflammation, fibrosis and hypoxia, as in bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis, interstitial fibrosis, high-altitude residence, bronchopulmonary dysplasia and cystic fibrosis. Small nodular aggregates can occur in scars. It is usually an incidental histological finding without clinical significance. Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH) differs by occurring in otherwise normal lungs, often in middle-aged women with cough and mosaic attenuation, with widespread proliferations, tumorlets, carcinoids and constrictive bronchiolitis, and is regarded as a precursor of carcinoid tumours. Differentials include DIPNECH, tumorlets (nodules under 5 mm extending beyond the basement membrane), carcinoid tumour and NEHI in infants.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is used to demonstrate and quantify neuroendocrine cells: chromogranin A, synaptophysin, INSM1 and bombesin (gastrin-releasing peptide) highlight the cells within the epithelium. Ki-67 is very low. Quantification and the clinical setting distinguish reactive hyperplasia from DIPNECH.

entities.variants: Inflammatory (granulation tissue) polyp after foreign body, intubation, infection, burns or bronchiectasis; fibroepithelial polyp; polypoid granulation tissue after stent placement
entities.remarks: Benign polypoid lesion of granulation tissue or fibrovascular stroma covered by respiratory or squamous metaplastic epithelium; mimics endobronchial tumour at bronchoscopy.
entities.histo: Inflammatory endobronchial polyps are uncommon benign lesions composed of polypoid granulation tissue or oedematous fibrovascular stroma with chronic inflammation, covered by respiratory epithelium that may show squamous metaplasia or ulceration. They arise in response to chronic irritation from aspirated foreign bodies, intubation, smoke inhalation, infection (including tuberculosis), bronchiectasis and airway stents, and they can regress when the stimulus is removed. Bronchoscopically they resemble endobronchial tumours and may cause obstruction with distal atelectasis or pneumonia. Fibroepithelial polyps have more collagenous stroma and less inflammation. Granulation tissue may show reactive endothelial and stromal atypia. Differentials include squamous papilloma (papillary fronds lined by squamous epithelium), carcinoid tumour, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour, lobular capillary haemangioma, granular cell tumour and carcinoma with ulceration.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role; brushings show inflammatory cells, reactive bronchial cells and granulation tissue fragments, and are mainly used to exclude carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is usually unnecessary. When a neoplasm is in the differential, synaptophysin, chromogranin and INSM1 exclude carcinoid tumour, ALK excludes inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour, S100 excludes granular cell tumour and keratin excludes carcinoma, while CD31 and CD34 confirm a capillary-rich granulation tissue.

entities.entity: Usual interstitial pneumonia / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (UIP/IPF)
entities.variants: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (UIP pattern); familial pulmonary fibrosis (TERT, TERC, RTEL1, SFTPC, SFTPA2, MUC5B); secondary UIP pattern (rheumatoid arthritis and other CTD, chronic HP, asbestosis, drugs, Hermansky-Pudlak); acute exacerbation of IPF (DAD on UIP); combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema; ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT histological categories: UIP, probable UIP, indeterminate for UIP, alternative diagnosis
entities.remarks: Commonest IIP; older male smokers; patchy subpleural and paraseptal fibrosis with honeycombing and fibroblast foci (temporal and spatial heterogeneity); median survival 3 to 5 years untreated; antifibrotics; increased lung cancer risk.
entities.histo: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a chronic progressive fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown cause occurring in older adults, mostly male smokers, and is defined by the histological and radiological pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia. Grossly the lungs have a cobblestone pleural surface due to retraction along septa, and the cut surface shows fibrosis that predominates in the subpleural and basal regions, with honeycomb cysts in advanced disease. Microscopically, low-power examination shows a patchy, heterogeneous pattern in which dense, architecture-distorting collagenous fibrosis in subpleural and paraseptal regions alternates abruptly with relatively normal lung (spatial heterogeneity). Fibroblast foci, small dome-shaped aggregates of proliferating myofibroblasts in a pale myxoid matrix at the interface of scar and normal lung, represent active injury and repair (temporal heterogeneity). Honeycombing consists of cystic airspaces lined by bronchiolar epithelium and filled with mucus and inflammatory cells, with surrounding smooth muscle hyperplasia. Inflammation is mild. Features against UIP include prominent granulomas, marked inflammation, airway-centred fibrosis, organising pneumonia or hyaline membranes, suggesting an alternative diagnosis. Acute exacerbation shows DAD superimposed on UIP. Differentials include fibrotic HP, fibrotic NSIP, CTD-related UIP, asbestosis (asbestos bodies) and end-stage sarcoidosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. BAL in IPF shows nonspecific mild neutrophilia or eosinophilia, and its main value is excluding alternative diagnoses such as HP (marked lymphocytosis) and infection. Lung carcinoma arising in IPF may be diagnosed on cytology, but reactive atypical bronchiolar cells in honeycomb cysts are a pitfall. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role in UIP. Trichrome and elastic stains highlight the distribution of fibrosis, architectural distortion and fibroblast foci. Special stains exclude infection in acute exacerbation. Genetic testing (telomere length and telomerase genes) is recommended in familial or young-onset cases. Any carcinoma arising in fibrotic lung is classified with standard markers (TTF-1, p40).

entities.variants: Idiopathic PPFE (rare IIP); secondary PPFE (after HSCT, lung transplantation as RAS, chemotherapy such as alkylating agents, recurrent infections, familial with telomere mutations); coexisting UIP or HP in lower lobes
entities.remarks: Upper lobe predominant pleural and subpleural intra-alveolar fibrosis with marked elastosis; flat chest, pneumothorax; sharp transition to normal lung.
entities.histo: Pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis is a rare fibrosing lung disease with upper lobe predominance, classified as a rare idiopathic interstitial pneumonia but often secondary to stem cell or lung transplantation, chemotherapy, recurrent infections or telomere-related genetic disease. Patients are often slender with a flattened thorax and recurrent pneumothoraces. Histologically there is marked fibrous thickening of the visceral pleura and subpleural parenchyma by intra-alveolar fibrosis, in which alveolar spaces are filled with collagen, together with prominent elastosis of the alveolar septa, so the original alveolar architecture remains visible as elastic skeletons within the scar. There is a sharp transition to adjacent normal lung, with few fibroblast foci at the edge and mild patchy lymphoplasmacytic inflammation. Coexisting UIP or HP patterns in the lower lobes are common. Differentials include the pulmonary apical cap (small, localised, incidental), UIP (interstitial rather than intra-alveolar fibrosis, less elastosis), chronic organising pneumonia and post-tuberculous upper lobe fibrosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in PPFE. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Elastic stains (EVG) are essential and show dense elastosis of the alveolar septa within the fibrotic zone, which is the defining feature, while trichrome highlights collagen filling the alveoli. Quantitative criteria for elastosis have been proposed.

entities.variants: Incidental apical subpleural fibroelastotic scar; bilateral apical caps; possible relationship to ischaemia or prior infection
entities.remarks: Common incidental, localised, wedge-shaped apical subpleural fibroelastotic scar; may be mistaken for carcinoma radiologically; distinct from diffuse PPFE.
entities.histo: Pulmonary apical cap is a common incidental lesion at the lung apex, seen at imaging as pleural thickening or a nodular opacity, and in resections or autopsies as a localised, wedge-shaped subpleural scar, usually less than 2 cm thick. It is thought to result from chronic ischaemia of the poorly perfused apex or from healed inflammation. Histologically there is dense subpleural fibrosis with marked elastosis and collapse of alveoli, preserved elastic framework of alveolar walls within the scar (fibroelastotic scar), mild chronic inflammation and occasionally entrapped bronchiolar epithelium, metaplastic bone and anthracotic pigment, with a sharp interface with normal lung. Entrapped, reactive epithelium can mimic carcinoma on frozen section or small biopsy. Differentials include PPFE (more extensive, progressive), healed tuberculosis (granulomas, calcification), scar carcinoma and solitary fibrous tumour.
entities.cyto: Cytology has little role. FNA of an apical cap is usually paucicellular, containing fibrous fragments and occasional benign bronchial or mesothelial cells, and may be reported as non-diagnostic. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Non-diagnostic or Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not usually needed. Elastic stains show the characteristic elastosis. When entrapped epithelium mimics adenocarcinoma, the lack of an infiltrative mass, low Ki-67 and wild-type p53 support a benign process, but morphology is decisive.

entities.entity: Smoking-related interstitial fibrosis (airspace enlargement with fibrosis)
entities.variants: SRIF; airspace enlargement with fibrosis (AEF); respiratory bronchiolitis-ILD with fibrosis; combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema overlap
entities.remarks: Hyalinised, eosinophilic, paucicellular alveolar septal fibrosis associated with emphysema and respiratory bronchiolitis in smokers; often incidental in lobectomies; distinguished from UIP and fibrotic NSIP.
entities.histo: Smoking-related interstitial fibrosis is a pattern of alveolar septal fibrosis found in heavy smokers, often incidentally in lobectomy specimens for lung cancer. It shows thickening of alveolar septa by dense, hyalinised, eosinophilic, ropy collagen with little inflammation, typically in subpleural and centrilobular regions, accompanied by centrilobular emphysema, respiratory bronchiolitis with pigmented macrophages and smooth muscle hyperplasia. Fibroblast foci and honeycombing are absent or minimal, and the fibrosis does not destroy lung architecture in the way UIP does. Airspace enlargement with fibrosis is a related concept describing enlarged cystic airspaces with fibrotic walls in smokers' lungs that may mimic honeycombing radiologically. The clinical significance is generally limited, but recognition prevents misdiagnosis as UIP or fibrotic NSIP. Differentials include UIP (fibroblast foci, honeycombing, patchy heterogeneous fibrosis), fibrotic NSIP (diffuse, lower lobe), RB-ILD, Langerhans cell histiocytosis scars and asbestosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in smoking-related interstitial fibrosis. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Trichrome and elastic stains characterise the hyalinised septal collagen and emphysematous destruction, and iron stain highlights smoker's macrophages. CD1a can exclude coexisting Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

entities.variants: Asymptomatic anthracosis (urban dwellers, smokers); simple CWP (coal macules and nodules); complicated CWP with progressive massive fibrosis; Caplan syndrome (rheumatoid pneumoconiosis); anthracofibrosis of bronchi (biomass, also in India); mixed dust pneumoconiosis
entities.remarks: Coal dust (carbon with variable silica) deposits around respiratory bronchioles with focal dust emphysema; PMF forms large black fibrotic masses in upper lobes; also seen in Indian coal miners (Jharkhand, Odisha).
entities.histo: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis is lung disease caused by inhalation of coal mine dust, which contains carbon and variable amounts of silica and silicates. Anthracosis, the harmless accumulation of carbon pigment in macrophages along lymphatics, is common in urban dwellers and smokers. Simple CWP shows coal macules, 1 to 2 mm collections of carbon-laden macrophages with little collagen around respiratory bronchioles, associated with focal dust emphysema, and coal nodules, larger palpable lesions with more collagen. Complicated CWP, or progressive massive fibrosis, forms coalescent black scars over 1 cm, up to 10 cm, usually in the upper lobes, composed of dense collagen and pigment, sometimes with central necrosis or cavitation, that impair lung function and may cause pulmonary hypertension. Caplan syndrome is the development of rapidly enlarging necrobiotic rheumatoid nodules with concentric dust rings in miners with rheumatoid arthritis. Bronchial anthracofibrosis, with pigment and fibrosis narrowing bronchi, is related to biomass smoke and tuberculosis. Differentials include silicosis (whorled hyalinised nodules), tuberculosis and silicotuberculosis, carcinoma (PMF mimics a mass), and mixed dust pneumoconiosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. Sputum and BAL contain carbon-laden macrophages, which indicate exposure but not disease, and FNA of PMF masses yields black pigment, macrophages and fibrous fragments; the main role is excluding carcinoma or tuberculosis. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Polarisation detects birefringent silicate particles within lesions (pure carbon is not birefringent), and Ziehl-Neelsen excludes coexisting tuberculosis in necrotic PMF. Elastic and trichrome stains show fibrosis and dust emphysema. Mineralogical analysis (SEM-EDX) quantifies dust where needed for compensation.

entities.variants: Chronic simple nodular silicosis; accelerated silicosis; acute silicosis (silicoproteinosis, sandblasting, quartz grinding); complicated silicosis with progressive massive fibrosis; silicotuberculosis; Caplan syndrome; eggshell calcification of hilar nodes; artificial stone (engineered stone) silicosis; important in Indian stone quarry, slate pencil and agate workers
entities.remarks: Commonest occupational lung disease worldwide; crystalline silica (quartz) causes whorled hyalinised collagen nodules with weakly birefringent particles; strong association with tuberculosis; increased lung cancer risk.
entities.histo: Silicosis is a fibrotic lung disease caused by inhalation of crystalline silica, mainly quartz, in miners, sandblasters, stone cutters, quarry and foundry workers and artificial stone fabricators. Silica particles are ingested by macrophages, which are damaged and release inflammatory and fibrogenic mediators. Chronic simple silicosis, after decades of exposure, produces silicotic nodules in the upper lobes and hilar nodes; these are 2 to 5 mm, rounded, with a central zone of hyalinised, concentrically whorled (onion-skin) collagen, a peripheral zone of dust-laden macrophages and lymphocytes, and weakly birefringent silica particles visible under polarised light. Nodules coalesce into progressive massive fibrosis. Hilar nodes may show eggshell calcification. Accelerated silicosis follows heavier exposure over a shorter period. Acute silicosis (silicoproteinosis) after massive exposure resembles alveolar proteinosis with PAS-positive granular material, inflammation and fibrosis. Silica impairs macrophage function, causing a markedly increased risk of tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis), and silica is a lung carcinogen. Differentials include CWP, sarcoidosis, healed granulomas of infection, hyalinizing granuloma (no birefringent particles, central location) and mixed dust pneumoconiosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. BAL may contain macrophages with birefringent particles, and in acute silicosis granular PAS-positive proteinaceous material similar to alveolar proteinosis. EBUS-TBNA of nodes may show anthracotic pigment, fibrosis and histiocytes, and should be screened for tuberculosis and metastatic carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Polarisation microscopy shows weakly birefringent silica and more strongly birefringent silicates, Ziehl-Neelsen and culture exclude tuberculosis, and PAS demonstrates the proteinaceous material in acute silicosis. Mineralogical analysis can confirm silica. Carcinomas arising in silicotic lungs are worked up with standard panels.

entities.variants: Asbestosis (diffuse interstitial fibrosis; grades 1 to 4 CAP-NIOSH); asbestos bodies (ferruginous bodies); pleural plaques and diffuse pleural thickening; benign asbestos pleural effusion; rounded atelectasis; asbestos-related lung carcinoma and mesothelioma (pleura chapter); fibre types: amphiboles (crocidolite, amosite) and serpentine (chrysotile)
entities.remarks: Interstitial fibrosis plus asbestos bodies (2 or more per square cm of lung or specified counts); lower lobe subpleural predominance; synergistic lung cancer risk with smoking.
entities.histo: Asbestosis is diffuse interstitial fibrosis caused by inhalation of asbestos fibres, typically after heavy, prolonged exposure in mining, insulation, shipbuilding, construction and brake manufacture. Long, thin amphibole fibres are most fibrogenic. Fibrosis begins around respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts in the lower lobes and subpleural regions and progresses to diffuse interstitial fibrosis and honeycombing, resembling UIP, although fibroblast foci are fewer and peribronchiolar accentuation is common. The diagnosis requires demonstration of asbestos bodies: golden-brown, beaded or dumbbell-shaped rods with a thin translucent core, formed by deposition of iron-protein on the fibre. The CAP-NIOSH grading ranges from grade 1 (fibrosis of the walls of respiratory bronchioles) to grade 4 (honeycombing). Associated lesions include visceral and parietal pleural plaques (dense, acellular, basket-weave collagen, often calcified), diffuse pleural fibrosis, benign effusions and rounded atelectasis. Asbestos increases the risk of lung carcinoma, synergistically with smoking, and of mesothelioma. Differentials include IPF (no asbestos bodies or fewer than threshold), fibrotic HP, other pneumoconioses and pseudo-asbestos bodies (non-asbestos cores such as carbon, black core).
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. Asbestos bodies may be seen in sputum or BAL, where finding more than 1 per ml of BAL fluid suggests significant exposure but not disease. Cytology of pleural effusions in exposed patients is used to look for mesothelioma or metastatic carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used for asbestosis. Perls Prussian blue stains the iron coat of asbestos bodies and helps detect them in thick sections, and tissue digestion with light or electron microscopy quantifies asbestos bodies and fibres for medicolegal purposes. Trichrome shows fibrosis. When a tumour arises, calretinin, WT1, D2-40, BAP1 and MTAP (mesothelioma) versus TTF-1, napsin A and p40 (carcinoma) are used.

entities.variants: Acute beryllium pneumonitis (high exposure); chronic beryllium disease (beryllium sensitisation with granulomas); beryllium sensitisation without disease
entities.remarks: Delayed-type hypersensitivity to beryllium (aerospace, electronics, nuclear industries, dental alloys); non-necrotising granulomas identical to sarcoidosis; beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test is key.
entities.histo: Chronic beryllium disease is a granulomatous lung disease caused by a cell-mediated hypersensitivity to beryllium in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DPB1 Glu69) exposed in aerospace, electronics, nuclear, ceramics and dental alloy industries. Acute beryllium pneumonitis after heavy exposure causes DAD and is now rare. In chronic disease the lungs show non-necrotising, well-formed epithelioid granulomas with multinucleated giant cells, distributed along lymphatic routes in bronchovascular bundles, septa and pleura, together with interstitial lymphocytic infiltrates and, in later stages, interstitial fibrosis. Schaumann bodies and asteroid bodies may be present. Hilar nodes contain granulomas. The histology is indistinguishable from sarcoidosis, and the diagnosis requires a history of exposure and evidence of sensitisation by the beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test on blood or BAL, or demonstration of beryllium in tissue. Differentials include sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, mycobacterial and fungal infection, and other metal-induced granulomatous diseases (aluminium, titanium, zirconium).
entities.cyto: BAL shows lymphocytosis, and beryllium lymphocyte proliferation testing on BAL cells is highly specific. EBUS-TBNA of nodes may show non-necrotising granulomas identical to sarcoidosis. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (granulomatous inflammation).
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. Special stains exclude infection (Ziehl-Neelsen, GMS). Beryllium can be detected in tissue by laser ion mass analysis or SEM-EDX in reference laboratories. The beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test is the key laboratory tool.

entities.entity: Hard metal lung disease (giant cell interstitial pneumonia)
entities.variants: Giant cell interstitial pneumonia (GIP); hard metal asthma; hypersensitivity-type reactions to cobalt and tungsten carbide; diamond polishing exposure
entities.remarks: Bizarre multinucleated giant cells in alveoli and lining alveolar walls with centrilobular fibrosis; virtually pathognomonic of cobalt-containing hard metal exposure.
entities.histo: Hard metal lung disease is caused by inhalation of cobalt-containing hard metal, usually tungsten carbide cemented with cobalt, in tool sharpening, diamond polishing and hard metal manufacturing. Only a minority of exposed workers develop disease, which reflects individual susceptibility to cobalt. The characteristic histological pattern is giant cell interstitial pneumonia: centrilobular and peribronchiolar interstitial fibrosis and inflammation, with numerous large multinucleated giant cells, of macrophage and type II pneumocyte origin, lying in alveolar spaces and lining alveolar walls, sometimes engulfing other cells (cannibalism). Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and a DIP-like intra-alveolar macrophage accumulation are common, and dark metallic particles may be seen within macrophages. Disease may progress to diffuse fibrosis. Differentials include measles and RSV giant cell pneumonia (viral inclusions), DIP, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (granulomas, bronchiolitis) and foreign-body reactions.
entities.cyto: BAL may contain characteristic multinucleated giant cells and macrophages, which in the context of hard metal exposure strongly support the diagnosis. Giant cells may be mistaken for malignant giant cells or viral cytopathic effect. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. The giant cells are CD68 positive and may also be keratin positive if of pneumocyte origin. Mineralogical analysis (SEM-EDX) of tissue or BAL demonstrates tungsten, cobalt and other metals, confirming exposure. Viral IHC and history exclude viral giant cell pneumonia.

entities.entity: Other pneumoconioses and occupational lung diseases
entities.variants: Siderosis (iron; welders, haematite miners; siderosilicosis); silicatosis (talc, kaolin/china clay, mica, fuller's earth); mixed dust pneumoconiosis; aluminium lung (aluminosis); stannosis (tin); baritosis (barium); indium lung disease (PAP-like); flock worker's lung (lymphocytic bronchiolitis); byssinosis (cotton dust); diatomaceous earth (cristobalite); welding-related lung disease; nanoparticle exposure
entities.remarks: Diverse inorganic dust reactions; inert dusts (iron, tin, barium) cause dense radiological shadows with little fibrosis; silicates and mixed dusts cause fibrosis; occupational history essential.
entities.histo: Many inorganic dusts other than coal, silica, asbestos and beryllium cause lung disease. Siderosis in welders and iron workers shows macrophages laden with brown-black iron oxide particles around bronchioles and vessels with little fibrosis, unless silica is also present (siderosilicosis). Inert dusts such as tin (stannosis) and barium (baritosis) produce striking radiological opacities without significant fibrosis. Silicates, including talc, kaolin and mica, produce dust macules, nodules and interstitial fibrosis, with plate-like birefringent particles in macrophages and giant cells. Mixed dust pneumoconiosis, from silica combined with less fibrogenic dusts, shows irregular stellate (medusa-head) dust-laden fibrotic lesions with less than half silicotic nodules. Aluminium causes fibrosis or granulomatous disease, indium causes a PAP-like disease and fibrosis, and flock workers develop lymphocytic bronchiolitis and peribronchiolar lymphoid hyperplasia. Byssinosis in cotton textile workers is an asthma-like airway disease with little specific pathology. Differentials include silicosis, CWP, sarcoidosis, HP and haemosiderin deposition, separated by mineral properties and history.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. BAL or sputum may contain macrophages with characteristic particles (iron-laden macrophages in welders, birefringent silicates), which indicate exposure. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Polarisation microscopy distinguishes birefringent silicates (talc, mica) from weakly birefringent silica and non-birefringent metals. Perls stain highlights iron oxide (often weakly), and SEM-EDX mineralogical analysis identifies the specific dust. Trichrome assesses fibrosis.

entities.variants: Autoimmune PAP (anti-GM-CSF antibodies; about 90 percent of adults); secondary PAP (haematological malignancy especially myelodysplasia and CML, inhalation of silica or indium, infections, immunodeficiency, lysinuric protein intolerance); hereditary PAP (CSF2RA, CSF2RB mutations); congenital PAP (surfactant gene defects; see surfactant dysfunction row)
entities.remarks: Surfactant accumulation in alveoli due to impaired macrophage clearance; granular PAS-positive diastase-resistant material with cholesterol clefts and preserved septa; crazy-paving CT; whole lung lavage and inhaled GM-CSF; risk of Nocardia and other infections.
entities.histo: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is a rare disorder in which surfactant lipids and proteins accumulate in alveoli because alveolar macrophages fail to clear them, usually due to autoantibodies against GM-CSF (autoimmune PAP). Patients present with gradual dyspnoea, and CT shows ground glass with interlobular septal thickening in a crazy-paving pattern. Grossly the lungs are heavy, with yellow-white firm areas exuding turbid fluid. Microscopically alveoli and alveolar ducts are filled with a homogeneous to finely granular, pale eosinophilic material that is strongly PAS positive and diastase resistant, containing cholesterol clefts, dense eosinophilic globules and scattered foamy macrophages, with characteristic retraction artefact and preserved, thin alveolar septa showing minimal inflammation or fibrosis. Secondary PAP, related to haematological disorders, inhaled dusts and infections, may show more patchy changes and associated pathology. Opportunistic infections (Nocardia, mycobacteria, fungi) complicate the disease. Differentials include pulmonary oedema (pale, non-granular, weakly PAS positive), Pneumocystis pneumonia (foamy casts with organisms), acute silicoproteinosis, mucinous adenocarcinoma and amyloid.
entities.cyto: BAL is often diagnostic, producing a milky or turbid fluid containing abundant extracellular granular, lipoproteinaceous PAS-positive material, acellular globules and foamy macrophages, with few inflammatory cells. Pneumocystis must be excluded with GMS or immunofluorescence. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not usually needed, but the material stains positively for surfactant proteins (SP-A, SP-B) and is strongly PAS positive with diastase resistance. GMS excludes Pneumocystis and fungi, and modified acid-fast and Gram stains look for Nocardia and mycobacteria. Serum anti-GM-CSF antibody testing confirms autoimmune PAP, and haematological evaluation is indicated in secondary PAP.

entities.entity: Pulmonary amyloidosis - diffuse alveolar-septal and tracheobronchial
entities.variants: Diffuse alveolar-septal (interstitial) amyloidosis (usually systemic AL, also ATTR wild-type in elderly); tracheobronchial amyloidosis (localised AL; diffuse or nodular submucosal plaques, airway narrowing); light chain deposition disease and light and heavy chain deposition (non-amyloid, Congo red negative); AA amyloidosis secondary to chronic inflammation (bronchiectasis, TB, RA); amyloid-associated cystic lung disease (Sjogren)
entities.remarks: Amorphous eosinophilic material with apple-green birefringence on Congo red; diffuse septal form indicates systemic disease with poor prognosis; tracheobronchial form is localised; typing is essential.
entities.histo: Pulmonary amyloidosis comprises several forms. Diffuse alveolar-septal amyloidosis is usually a manifestation of systemic AL amyloidosis, or wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis in elderly men, and shows deposition of amorphous, pale eosinophilic, waxy material along alveolar septa and in vessel walls, thickening septa and narrowing capillaries; the lungs are firm and rubbery and the prognosis depends on systemic, especially cardiac, involvement. Tracheobronchial amyloidosis is a localised AL process with submucosal plaques or nodules of amyloid in the trachea and bronchi, often around glands and cartilage, with plasma cells and giant cells, sometimes calcification and ossification, causing stenosis, atelectasis and haemoptysis. AA amyloidosis secondary to chronic infections such as bronchiectasis and tuberculosis is mainly vascular and septal. Light chain deposition disease forms Congo red negative, non-fibrillar deposits that are monotypic for kappa. In Sjogren syndrome, amyloid nodules may accompany thin-walled cysts and MALT lymphoma. Differentials include hyalinised fibrosis, pulmonary hyalinizing granuloma, PAP and tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. FNA or BAL may yield amorphous, waxy, acellular material that is pale on Papanicolaou and blue-purple on Giemsa, which can be confirmed by Congo red on the smear or cell block. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: Congo red staining with apple-green birefringence under polarised light (or Texas red fluorescence) confirms amyloid, and thioflavin T is an alternative. Typing is mandatory: immunohistochemistry for kappa, lambda, transthyretin, serum amyloid A and others can be used, but mass spectrometry-based proteomics is the gold standard. Kappa and lambda in situ hybridisation and CD138 evaluate associated clonal plasma cells, and light chain deposition disease is Congo red negative but monotypic for light chains.

entities.variants: Solitary or multiple nodular AL amyloid; association with MALT lymphoma, Sjogren syndrome and plasmacytoma; calcified and ossified nodules
entities.remarks: Localised peripheral nodules of AL amyloid with plasma cells and giant cells; mimics carcinoma; always evaluate for underlying extranodal marginal zone lymphoma.
entities.histo: Nodular pulmonary amyloidosis presents as one or more peripheral, well-circumscribed nodules found incidentally or during evaluation for lung cancer, often in older patients, and some patients have Sjogren syndrome. Grossly the nodules are firm, waxy and grey-tan, sometimes calcified. Microscopically they consist of large masses of amorphous, eosinophilic, acellular amyloid that replace the lung parenchyma, with a peripheral infiltrate of plasma cells and lymphocytes, multinucleated foreign-body giant cells that engulf amyloid, and frequent calcification and metaplastic ossification. The amyloid is almost always AL type, produced locally by a clonal plasma cell or B-cell population, and a significant proportion of cases are associated with an extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation, so the surrounding infiltrate must be carefully evaluated. Systemic amyloidosis is uncommon in this form and prognosis is usually excellent after excision. Differentials include pulmonary hyalinizing granuloma (lamellar collagen, Congo red negative), light chain deposition disease, healed granulomas, carcinoma and MALT lymphoma with amyloid.
entities.cyto: FNA yields amorphous waxy material with occasional plasma cells and giant cells, which can be confirmed as amyloid by Congo red on cell block; the main role is to exclude carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical if a clonal lymphoplasmacytic population is suspected.
entities.ihc: Congo red with apple-green birefringence confirms amyloid, and typing (by IHC or mass spectrometry) usually shows AL lambda or kappa. Kappa and lambda in situ hybridisation, CD138, CD20 and B-cell clonality studies identify a monotypic plasma cell or B-cell population and associated MALT lymphoma. IgG4 staining may be considered when plasma cells are numerous.

entities.variants: Exogenous lipoid pneumonia (aspirated mineral oil laxatives, nasal drops, petroleum jelly, ghee or oil pulling and oil massage of infants in India, fire-eaters, vaping); endogenous (obstructive, golden) pneumonia distal to airway obstruction by tumour, foreign body or stricture; cholesterol pneumonitis; lipid storage diseases (separate row)
entities.remarks: Exogenous: large lipid vacuoles in macrophages and interstitium with giant cells and fibrosis, lower lobes; endogenous: fine foamy macrophages in alveoli distal to obstruction; always look for an obstructing carcinoma in endogenous cases.
entities.histo: Lipoid pneumonia is the accumulation of lipid within alveoli and the interstitium. Exogenous lipoid pneumonia results from aspiration or inhalation of oils, most commonly mineral oil laxatives, oily nose drops and petroleum jelly, and in India the instillation of oil into infants' nostrils or mouths and oil pulling. Mineral oils are not metabolised and are engulfed by macrophages that contain large, variable-sized empty vacuoles, which also lie free in alveoli and the interstitium, provoking foreign-body giant cells, chronic inflammation and progressive interstitial fibrosis; lesions may form mass-like paraffinomas mimicking carcinoma. Vegetable and animal oils cause more acute inflammation. Endogenous lipoid pneumonia, also called obstructive or golden pneumonia, develops distal to bronchial obstruction, when cell breakdown products and surfactant accumulate in alveolar macrophages, which have finely vacuolated foamy cytoplasm, accompanied by cholesterol clefts, chronic inflammation and fibrosis, and the gross lung is golden yellow. Differentials include amiodarone toxicity and other causes of foamy macrophages, PAP, storage disorders, infections such as MAC with foamy histiocytes, and mucinous adenocarcinoma.
entities.cyto: BAL and sputum show lipid-laden macrophages with large vacuoles in exogenous disease (positive with oil red O) and finely foamy macrophages in endogenous disease. FNA of a mass-like lesion shows lipid vacuoles, macrophages and giant cells, and in endogenous cases the cytology of the obstructing lesion may reveal carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. Oil red O or Sudan black on fresh or frozen material and on BAL highlights neutral lipid, which is dissolved during routine processing, leaving empty vacuoles. CD68 confirms macrophages, and keratin and TTF-1 help exclude carcinoma in mass-like lesions. Special stains (Ziehl-Neelsen) exclude mycobacterial infection, especially rapidly growing mycobacteria, which can complicate exogenous lipoid pneumonia.

entities.variants: Familial (SLC34A2 mutations, autosomal recessive); sporadic
entities.remarks: Innumerable calcium phosphate microliths (calcospherites) filling alveoli; sandstorm chest radiograph; clinical-radiological dissociation; slowly progressive fibrosis.
entities.histo: Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis is a rare autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations of SLC34A2, encoding a sodium-phosphate cotransporter in type II pneumocytes, leading to failure to clear phosphate from the alveolar space and precipitation of calcium phosphate. Patients are often asymptomatic for many years despite a dramatic sandstorm appearance of diffuse micronodular calcification on chest imaging, and later develop restrictive lung disease, respiratory failure and cor pulmonale. Grossly the lungs are heavy, hard and gritty on cutting. Microscopically innumerable round, concentrically laminated, basophilic calcified microliths (calcospherites) 50 to 1000 micrometres in diameter fill the alveolar spaces, with progressive interstitial fibrosis and occasional giant cells in later stages. Differentials include metastatic pulmonary calcification (calcium deposited in alveolar walls and vessels), dendriform pulmonary ossification (branching bone), corpora amylacea (non-calcified, few) and healed miliary infections (calcified granulomas).
entities.cyto: BAL may contain calcified microliths with concentric laminations, which supports the diagnosis in the appropriate radiological context. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Von Kossa and alizarin red stains confirm calcium phosphate in microliths, and PAS stains their laminated organic matrix. Genetic testing for SLC34A2 is confirmatory.

entities.entity: Metastatic pulmonary calcification and dendriform pulmonary ossification
entities.variants: Metastatic calcification (chronic kidney disease and dialysis, hyperparathyroidism, hypercalcaemia of malignancy, vitamin D toxicity, after liver transplant); dystrophic calcification (necrotic or scarred lung, healed granulomas); dendriform pulmonary ossification (branching bone; associated with UIP, chronic aspiration, heart failure, idiopathic); nodular pulmonary ossification (mitral stenosis)
entities.remarks: Calcium deposition in normal alveolar walls and vessels (metastatic) versus damaged tissue (dystrophic); dendriform ossification forms branching marrow-containing bone spicules in interstitium.
entities.histo: Pulmonary calcification and ossification occur in several settings. Metastatic pulmonary calcification is deposition of calcium salts in normal alveolar septa, bronchial walls and vessels in patients with hypercalcaemia or a raised calcium-phosphate product, especially chronic kidney disease on dialysis, hyperparathyroidism and malignancy, and favours the upper lobes because of their relatively alkaline environment; it may cause restrictive disease and respiratory failure. Histology shows fine basophilic granular calcium encrusting alveolar walls and elastic fibres, with fibrosis and giant cells in advanced cases. Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissue, such as healed granulomas, infarcts and tumours. Dendriform pulmonary ossification forms branching spicules of mature lamellar bone, sometimes with marrow, along the interstitium and alveolar septa, often associated with UIP, chronic aspiration or heart failure, while nodular ossification forms rounded bone nodules within alveoli in chronic venous congestion such as mitral stenosis. Differentials include alveolar microlithiasis (intra-alveolar microliths), tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica and calcified hamartoma or carcinoid.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Von Kossa and alizarin red confirm calcium deposits, and elastic stains show encrustation of elastic fibres. Bone is recognised on H&E.

entities.variants: Solitary or multiple nodules; association with mediastinal or retroperitoneal fibrosis, histoplasmosis or tuberculosis exposure, autoimmune disease and IgG4-related disease in some
entities.remarks: Benign nodules of whorled lamellar hyalinised collagen with peripheral lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate; mimic metastases; Congo red negative.
entities.histo: Pulmonary hyalinizing granuloma is a rare benign fibrosing lesion presenting as one or, more often, multiple well-circumscribed nodules that radiologically mimic metastatic disease. It is thought to represent an exaggerated immune response to infection (especially histoplasmosis or tuberculosis) or autoimmune processes, and some cases are associated with sclerosing mediastinitis or retroperitoneal fibrosis and with IgG4-related disease. Microscopically the nodules consist of dense, central, whorled to lamellar bands of hyalinised collagen arranged in a concentric or storiform pattern, with a sparse population of fibroblasts and a peripheral rim of lymphocytes, plasma cells and occasional histiocytes. Necrosis and calcification may occur, but granulomas with epithelioid cells are typically absent despite the name. Differentials include nodular amyloid (amorphous, Congo red positive), healed infectious granulomas, silicotic nodules (birefringent particles), IgG4-related disease, solitary fibrous tumour and metastatic sarcoma.
entities.cyto: FNA is usually paucicellular, with fragments of acellular hyalinised collagen and occasional inflammatory cells, and is often reported as non-diagnostic or benign; malignancy must be excluded. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Non-diagnostic or Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is mainly used to exclude mimics. Congo red is negative, distinguishing it from amyloid. IgG4 and IgG stains assess an IgG4-related component, STAT6 and CD34 exclude solitary fibrous tumour, and special stains (GMS, Ziehl-Neelsen) look for residual organisms. Polarisation excludes silicotic nodules.

entities.entity: Pulmonary involvement in storage and metabolic diseases
entities.variants: Gaucher disease (Gaucher cells in alveolar capillaries and interstitium, pulmonary hypertension); Niemann-Pick disease types A, B and C (foamy macrophages); Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HPS1, HPS4; pulmonary fibrosis with foamy type II pneumocytes); Fabry disease; mucopolysaccharidoses; glycogen storage disease; lysinuric protein intolerance (PAP); Erdheim-Chester and other histiocytoses (neoplastic, see separate rows)
entities.remarks: Rare genetic disorders depositing storage material in macrophages or pneumocytes; patterns include interstitial infiltration, foamy macrophages, PAP-like disease and fibrosis.
entities.histo: Several inherited metabolic diseases affect the lungs. Gaucher disease, due to glucocerebrosidase deficiency, causes infiltration of the alveolar capillaries, interstitium and alveoli by Gaucher cells with abundant fibrillary, crumpled tissue-paper cytoplasm, and can lead to pulmonary hypertension and hepatopulmonary syndrome. Niemann-Pick disease, especially types B and C, shows numerous foamy macrophages (sea-blue histiocytes) in alveoli, interstitium and lymphatics, producing interstitial lung disease. Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, with albinism and platelet dysfunction, causes progressive pulmonary fibrosis resembling UIP, with characteristic foamy, vacuolated type II pneumocytes (giant lamellar bodies) and ceroid-laden macrophages. Lysinuric protein intolerance causes PAP. Fabry disease and mucopolysaccharidoses cause airway disease and vacuolated cells. Diagnosis rests on enzyme assays and genetic testing.
