Differentials include amiodarone toxicity, endogenous lipoid pneumonia, MAC infection with foamy histiocytes, DIP and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
entities.cyto: BAL may show characteristic storage cells such as Gaucher cells or foamy Niemann-Pick cells, which suggest the diagnosis and prompt enzyme testing. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is of limited value. CD68 and CD163 confirm the histiocytic nature of storage cells, and PAS (Gaucher cells strongly positive), Sudan black and Perls stains help characterise the material. Electron microscopy shows tubular inclusions in Gaucher cells and giant lamellar bodies in Hermansky-Pudlak pneumocytes. Enzyme assays and genetic testing are definitive.

entities.variants: Tuberous sclerosis complex associated (often with LAM); rarely sporadic
entities.remarks: Multiple small nodules of bland hyperplastic type II pneumocytes along thickened alveolar septa in TSC; distinguish from AAH and adenocarcinoma.
entities.histo: Multifocal micronodular pneumocyte hyperplasia is a benign proliferation of type II pneumocytes that occurs almost exclusively in patients with tuberous sclerosis complex, often in association with lymphangioleiomyomatosis, and affects both men and women. CT shows multiple small nodules and ground glass opacities. Microscopically there are multiple well-demarcated nodules, usually a few millimetres in size, in which alveolar septa are mildly thickened by collagen and elastic fibres and lined by plump, cuboidal type II pneumocytes without significant atypia, often with intra-alveolar macrophages. The lesions are thought to be hamartomatous and have no malignant potential. Differentials include atypical adenomatous hyperplasia (more atypia, sharp demarcation, not associated with TSC), adenocarcinoma in situ, LAM nodules (spindle cells, HMB45 positive), minute meningothelial-like nodules (whorled meningothelial cells in septa) and reactive pneumocyte hyperplasia.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC confirms the pneumocyte phenotype: keratin, TTF-1 and surfactant proteins positive, with low Ki-67. Unlike LAM, the cells are negative for HMB45, melan-A and smooth muscle markers, and EMA and PR negativity distinguish them from meningothelial-like nodules. TSC1 or TSC2 alterations are present in the setting of tuberous sclerosis.

entities.variants: Single (incidental) MPMN; diffuse pulmonary meningotheliomatosis (multiple, bilateral, miliary ground-glass nodules); association with thromboembolic disease and other lung diseases
entities.remarks: Tiny interstitial perivenular nests of whorled meningothelial-like cells; incidental in resections; diffuse form mimics metastases or miliary disease; EMA, PR and CD56 positive, keratin negative.
entities.histo: Minute pulmonary meningothelial-like nodules are small, usually incidental interstitial proliferations of meningothelial-like cells, found in a few percent of lung resections and autopsies, more often in women. They are typically less than 3 mm, located in the interstitium around small veins, and composed of nests and whorls of bland ovoid to spindle cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and oval nuclei with intranuclear pseudoinclusions, similar to meningothelial cells, expanding alveolar septa in a zellballen-like or zigzag pattern. Diffuse pulmonary meningotheliomatosis refers to multiple bilateral nodules producing miliary or ground-glass patterns on CT that may be mistaken for metastases. They were once considered chemodectomas but are not neuroendocrine. Their relationship to pulmonary meningioma is uncertain. Differentials include carcinoid tumorlets (neuroendocrine markers), metastatic carcinoma, micronodular pneumocyte hyperplasia, LAM and primary pulmonary meningioma (larger lesion).
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role; lesions are too small for sampling. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC shows a meningothelial phenotype: EMA, progesterone receptor, CD56 and vimentin positive, with SSTR2A often positive; keratin, synaptophysin, chromogranin, S100 and HMB45 are negative, distinguishing them from carcinoid tumorlets, LAM and carcinoma.

entities.entity: Genetic and other diffuse cystic lung diseases (Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome)
entities.variants: Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome (FLCN; basal subpleural cysts, pneumothorax, renal tumours, fibrofolliculomas); other cystic lung diseases summary (LAM, PLCH, LIP, amyloid and light chain deposition, Sjogren syndrome, Pneumocystis, metastatic cystic tumours; see own rows); Proteus syndrome; Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes
entities.remarks: Diffuse cystic lung disease differential: BHD causes irregular, basal, paramediastinal cysts with recurrent pneumothorax; histologically cysts have bland walls without the smooth muscle proliferation of LAM.
entities.histo: Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations of FLCN, encoding folliculin, characterised by skin fibrofolliculomas, renal tumours (often hybrid oncocytic tumours and chromophobe carcinoma) and multiple pulmonary cysts with recurrent pneumothorax. Lung cysts are typically irregular, variable in size, and predominate in the lower lobes, subpleural and paramediastinal regions, often abutting vessels and septa. Histologically the cysts are lined by alveolar or bronchiolar epithelium, with thin walls lacking inflammation, fibrosis or the spindle cell proliferation of LAM, and some cysts incorporate septa or vessels into the wall (intraparenchymal septal cysts). This row also serves as an overview of the diffuse cystic lung disease differential diagnosis, which includes lymphangioleiomyomatosis, pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis, LIP and Sjogren syndrome, amyloid and light chain deposition disease, Pneumocystis infection, metastases (such as sarcomas) and connective tissue disorders such as Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes. Differentials for BHD include LAM (HMB45-positive spindle cells), emphysema (centrilobular, no walls), PLCH (stellate nodules) and LIP.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome or most cystic lung diseases, apart from serum VEGF-D testing in LAM and BAL in PLCH (more than 5 percent CD1a-positive cells). Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is mainly used to exclude LAM: HMB45, melan-A, SMA, desmin, ER and PR are negative in BHD cyst walls but positive in LAM cells. CD1a and langerin exclude PLCH, Congo red and light chain studies exclude amyloid and light chain deposition. FLCN germline testing confirms BHD.

entities.variants: Pleural endometriosis (catamenial pneumothorax, haemothorax); pulmonary parenchymal endometriosis (catamenial haemoptysis); diaphragmatic endometriosis
entities.remarks: Endometrial glands and stroma in lung or pleura, usually right sided; symptoms cyclical with menses; most common form of extrapelvic endometriosis in the chest.
entities.histo: Thoracic endometriosis syndrome comprises catamenial pneumothorax, haemothorax, haemoptysis and lung nodules associated with endometrial tissue in the thorax, typically in women in their thirties, often with pelvic endometriosis. Pleural and diaphragmatic involvement, usually on the right, is more common than parenchymal disease, and diaphragmatic fenestrations are often found at surgery. Histologically there are endometrial-type glands lined by columnar cells, surrounded by cellular endometrial stroma with small spiral-like vessels, together with fresh and old haemorrhage and haemosiderin-laden macrophages; stroma alone (stromal endometriosis) or decidualised stroma in pregnancy may be the only finding. Parenchymal nodules can mimic metastases. Differentials include metastatic endometrial stromal sarcoma or adenocarcinoma, benign metastasising leiomyoma, mesothelial hyperplasia and haemosiderosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology of pleural fluid or bronchial washings may show haemosiderin-laden macrophages and rarely endometrial glandular and stromal cells, which are hard to identify; cyclical haemoptysis is a clinical clue. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC confirms endometrial differentiation: glands are PAX8, ER and PR positive and CK7 positive, and stroma is CD10, ER and PR positive. These markers help separate endometriosis from mesothelial proliferations (calretinin, WT1) and lung adenocarcinoma (TTF-1). In metastatic endometrial stromal sarcoma, CD10 and ER are positive but the clinical history and molecular fusions (JAZF1-SUZ12) help.

entities.entity: Other heterotopias and ectopic tissues in the lung
entities.variants: Extramedullary haematopoiesis (thalassaemia, myelofibrosis); glial heterotopia (anencephaly, trisomies); thyroid, adrenal, liver, pancreatic and skeletal muscle (rhabdomyomatosis, striated muscle heterotopia) heterotopia; decidual reaction; splenosis (traumatic); pulmonary placental transmogrification (see separate row)
entities.remarks: Rare incidental findings; extramedullary haematopoiesis can form masses in thalassaemia (common in India); recognition prevents misdiagnosis of tumour.
entities.histo: Various ectopic tissues can be found in the lung. Extramedullary haematopoiesis occurs in chronic haemolytic anaemias such as thalassaemia, myelofibrosis and other marrow disorders, as interstitial foci of erythroid, myeloid and megakaryocytic precursors or as paravertebral and intrapulmonary masses, sometimes causing pulmonary hypertension; megakaryocytes in alveolar capillaries are a normal finding. Glial heterotopia, with nodules of mature glial tissue, occurs in fetuses with anencephaly or after trauma. Thyroid, adrenal cortical, liver, pancreatic and striated muscle heterotopias are rare, the last associated with congenital malformations (rhabdomyomatous dysplasia). Thoracic splenosis follows splenic and diaphragmatic trauma. Decidual reaction may affect the pleura in pregnancy. These lesions are incidental but can mimic neoplasms, such as myeloid sarcoma, metastatic thyroid carcinoma or rhabdomyosarcoma. Differentials depend on the tissue type and include true neoplasms and metastases.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. FNA of extramedullary haematopoiesis shows a trilineage haematopoietic population with megakaryocytes, which can be mistaken for malignant giant cells. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC helps identify tissue type: glycophorin, MPO and CD61 for haematopoiesis (and CD34, CD117 to exclude myeloid sarcoma with blasts), GFAP and S100 for glial tissue, thyroglobulin and TTF-1/PAX8 for thyroid, desmin and myogenin for skeletal muscle, and keratin with hepatocyte or adrenal markers for other heterotopias.

entities.variants: Unilateral bullous lesion in young adults; associated with lipomatous change and fibrolipomatous stroma; possibly related to emphysema or hamartoma
entities.remarks: Rare benign cystic or bullous lesion with papillary villous structures resembling chorionic villi; usually unilateral upper lobe; excision is curative.
entities.histo: Pulmonary placental transmogrification, or placentoid bullous lesion, is a rare benign lesion, mostly in young to middle-aged men, presenting as a unilateral bullous or cystic lesion that may cause pneumothorax. Its nature is uncertain, with theories including a hamartomatous process, a variant of emphysema with stromal proliferation, or a lipomatous lesion. Grossly the lung contains cystic and bullous spaces with spongy or grape-like tissue. Microscopically there are papillary, villous-like structures projecting into cystic spaces, resembling placental chorionic villi, with cores of loose, oedematous stroma containing clear interstitial cells, mature adipose tissue, lymphoid aggregates and capillaries, covered by flattened or cuboidal pneumocytes. There is no trophoblast. Excision is curative. Differentials include CPAM, emphysematous bullae, lipoma or lipomatous hamartoma, lymphangioleiomyomatosis and pulmonary hamartoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not usually required. The surface cells are keratin and TTF-1 positive pneumocytes, while the stromal clear cells are CD10 positive and negative for HMB45 and melan-A, helping exclude PEComa and LAM. Absence of hCG and trophoblastic markers excludes true placental tissue.

entities.entity: Primary graft dysfunction and other non-rejection post-lung-transplant pathology
entities.variants: Primary graft dysfunction (DAD within 72 hours; ischaemia-reperfusion injury); anastomotic complications (dehiscence, stenosis, malacia, infection, ischaemic necrosis); infections (bacterial, CMV, respiratory viruses, Aspergillus, Pneumocystis, NTM); recurrence of native disease (sarcoidosis, LAM, PLCH, PAP); aspiration; drug toxicity (sirolimus, everolimus); donor-derived malignancy; PTLD (see haematolymphoid rows)
entities.remarks: Early graft failure from ischaemia-reperfusion injury shows DAD; the allograft is also a site for many infections and recurrence of original disease.
entities.histo: Lung transplant recipients develop many non-rejection complications. Primary graft dysfunction is acute lung injury within 72 hours of transplantation due to ischaemia-reperfusion injury, and shows diffuse alveolar damage with oedema, hyaline membranes and neutrophilic infiltrates; it is the main cause of early mortality. Bronchial anastomotic complications include ischaemic necrosis, dehiscence, infection (often fungal), stenosis and malacia. Infections are frequent throughout, including bacterial pneumonia, CMV, community respiratory viruses, Aspergillus tracheobronchitis and invasive aspergillosis, Pneumocystis and non-tuberculous mycobacteria. Native diseases such as sarcoidosis, LAM, PLCH and PAP can recur in the allograft. Aspiration related to gastro-oesophageal reflux contributes to graft injury, and mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus cause pneumonitis. Donor-derived malignancy and PTLD are rare. Differentials always include acute cellular and antibody-mediated rejection, and multiple processes often coexist.
entities.cyto: BAL is essential for surveillance and diagnosis of infection in transplant recipients, detecting viral cytopathic effects, fungi, Pneumocystis and bacteria. Reactive atypia is common. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical.
entities.ihc: IHC is used to identify infections (CMV, adenovirus and other viral antigens, GMS, Ziehl-Neelsen) and to assess AMR (C4d). EBER and CD20 are used when PTLD is suspected, and markers of the native disease (HMB45 for LAM, CD1a for PLCH) help recognise recurrence.

entities.variants: Necrotizing sialometaplasia of trachea and bronchi (after intubation, tracheostomy, surgery, radiation or infarction); post-tracheostomy squamous metaplasia and atypia
entities.remarks: Rare reactive ischaemic necrosis of bronchial submucosal glands with lobular squamous metaplasia, mimicking squamous or mucoepidermoid carcinoma; preserved lobular architecture and lack of atypia are key.
entities.histo: Necrotizing sialometaplasia is a benign, self-limited, reactive lesion of seromucinous glands, best known in the palate but also described in the tracheobronchial submucosal glands, usually after ischaemic injury from intubation, tracheostomy, surgery, radiation, trauma or infarction. It may present as a mucosal nodule or ulcer and, in biopsy material, can closely mimic squamous cell carcinoma or mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Microscopically there is coagulative necrosis of gland acini (acinar infarction) with mucin extravasation and inflammation, and the residual ducts and acini undergo squamous metaplasia, forming rounded nests and islands of bland squamous cells that preserve the lobular configuration of the glands, often with residual mucous cells, a smooth outline, reactive nuclear changes, granulation tissue and fibrosis. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of the overlying epithelium may be present. Squamous metaplasia and atypia after tracheostomy show similar reactive changes. Differentials include invasive squamous cell carcinoma (irregular infiltrative nests, marked atypia, desmoplasia), mucoepidermoid carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and granular cell tumour with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role and may be misleading, as brushings can contain reactive or atypical squamous cells. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical (reactive squamous atypia) or Benign; correlation with history of instrumentation and histology is required.
entities.ihc: IHC is mainly used to show the preserved lobular structure: p63 and p40 highlight the metaplastic squamous nests and myoepithelial cells around residual acini, SMA and calponin outline intact myoepithelial layers, and Ki-67 is only moderately raised and basally located. Mucicarmine and PAS-D show residual mucous cells and extravasated mucin. Absence of MAML2 rearrangement helps exclude mucoepidermoid carcinoma when doubt remains.

entities.entity: Plastic bronchitis and mucoid bronchial casts
entities.variants: Type I inflammatory casts (fibrin, neutrophils, eosinophils; asthma, ABPA, infection); type II acellular casts (mucin; after Fontan procedure and congenital heart disease, lymphatic disorders); lymphatic plastic bronchitis; sickle cell acute chest syndrome
entities.remarks: Formation of large branching, rubbery casts of the airways that are coughed up or removed at bronchoscopy; composition guides underlying cause (inflammatory versus lymphatic or cardiac).
entities.histo: Plastic bronchitis is an uncommon condition in which large, branching, gelatinous or rubbery casts form within the tracheobronchial tree, causing airway obstruction, cough, wheeze and respiratory failure, and sometimes being expectorated in the shape of the bronchial tree. Inflammatory (type I) casts occur in asthma, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, cystic fibrosis, influenza and other infections, and are composed of fibrin, mucin and abundant inflammatory cells including eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals and neutrophils. Acellular (type II) casts, composed mainly of mucin with few cells, occur in children with congenital heart disease after the Fontan procedure, and in disorders of central lymphatic flow with lymphobronchial leakage of chyle, where the casts may be lipid-rich. Sickle cell disease with acute chest syndrome can also produce casts. Microscopically the casts show laminated fibrin and mucin, variable inflammatory cells, and sometimes fungal hyphae. Differentials include allergic mucin of ABPA, mucoid impaction from obstruction, aspirated material, and blood clots.
entities.cyto: Cytology of expectorated or bronchoscopically removed casts shows mucus, fibrin and inflammatory cells, and a cellular or acellular pattern helps separate inflammatory from lymphatic or cardiac causes. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (inflammatory or mucinous material).
entities.ihc: IHC has no role. Special stains help characterise the cast: PAS and Alcian blue for mucin, phosphotungstic acid haematoxylin or Martius scarlet blue for fibrin, Oil Red O on fresh material for lipid (lymphatic casts), Congo red and Luna stain if eosinophils are prominent, and GMS for fungi. Imaging of lymphatics (dynamic contrast lymphangiography) and cardiac evaluation are used to find the cause.

entities.variants: Low-grade and high-grade AAH (descriptive only; not formally graded by WHO); multifocal AAH in lungs resected for adenocarcinoma
entities.remarks: Small (usually 5 mm or less) localised proliferation of mildly atypical type II pneumocytes or club cells lining alveolar walls; pure ground-glass nodule on CT; precursor of non-mucinous adenocarcinoma; frequent KRAS and EGFR mutations.
entities.histo: Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia is a small, localised proliferation of mildly to moderately atypical type II pneumocytes and/or club cells lining alveolar walls and sometimes respiratory bronchioles, typically 5 mm or less, and is regarded as the earliest recognisable precursor of non-mucinous adenocarcinoma. It is usually an incidental finding in lungs resected for carcinoma and appears as a faint pure ground-glass nodule on CT. Microscopically the lesion is a discrete area in which alveolar septa, often mildly thickened by collagen and lymphocytes, are lined by a discontinuous, single layer of round, cuboidal, low columnar or peg-shaped cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, occasional nucleoli and intranuclear inclusions, with gaps between cells. The transition to surrounding lung is gradual rather than abrupt. There is no invasion, papillary or micropapillary growth, or mucin production. Distinguishing AAH from adenocarcinoma in situ relies on size (AIS is usually over 5 mm), more crowded and continuous cell lining, greater atypia and sharper demarcation in AIS. Differentials include reactive pneumocyte hyperplasia (inflammatory or fibrotic background), micronodular pneumocyte hyperplasia in tuberous sclerosis, peribronchiolar metaplasia and AIS.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no practical role, since AAH is too small to be targeted and cannot be distinguished from reactive pneumocytes or AIS on cytology. If sampled, cells would be indistinguishable from mildly atypical pneumocytes. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical; AAH is not diagnosed on cytology.
entities.ihc: IHC has a limited role. AAH cells are TTF-1, napsin A and CK7 positive, like normal pneumocytes and adenocarcinoma, so these markers do not separate AAH from AIS or invasive carcinoma. Ki-67 is low. Molecular studies show KRAS and EGFR mutations and loss of heterozygosity in some lesions, supporting their neoplastic nature, but are not used clinically. Diagnosis is morphological on resection specimens.

entities.variants: Non-mucinous AIS (type II pneumocyte and/or club cell); rare mixed mucinous and non-mucinous AIS; pure ground-glass nodule; multifocal AIS
entities.remarks: Localised adenocarcinoma 3 cm or less with pure lepidic growth, no invasion, no STAS; 100 percent disease-specific survival after complete resection; cannot be diagnosed on small biopsy or cytology; pTis.
entities.histo: Non-mucinous adenocarcinoma in situ is a small (3 cm or less), localised adenocarcinoma composed purely of neoplastic cells growing along pre-existing alveolar structures (lepidic growth), without stromal, vascular, pleural or airspace invasion, papillary or micropapillary patterns, intra-alveolar tumour cells or spread through air spaces. It usually presents as a pure ground-glass nodule. The neoplastic cells are type II pneumocyte-like or club cell-like, cuboidal to low columnar or hobnail, forming a continuous crowded lining with mild to moderate nuclear atypia, often with nuclear inclusions. Alveolar septa may be widened by sclerosis and elastosis, particularly in collapse, but this does not represent invasion. The whole lesion must be examined histologically to exclude invasion, so the diagnosis cannot be made on small biopsies or cytology. Completely resected AIS has a disease-specific survival close to 100 percent and is staged pTis. Differentials include AAH (smaller, less atypical, discontinuous), minimally invasive adenocarcinoma (invasion 5 mm or less), lepidic adenocarcinoma (invasion over 5 mm or tumour over 3 cm), reactive pneumocyte hyperplasia and alveolar adenoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology cannot diagnose AIS, because invasion cannot be excluded. Lepidic-type tumour cells may appear as cohesive flat sheets or small clusters of mildly atypical cuboidal cells with nuclear grooves and inclusions, which may be reported as atypical or suspicious, or as adenocarcinoma with a comment that the lepidic component may represent AIS. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical, Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant (adenocarcinoma) depending on atypia; the term AIS is not used in cytology.
entities.ihc: IHC shows a pneumocyte phenotype: TTF-1, napsin A and CK7 positive, CK20 negative. IHC does not distinguish AIS from invasive adenocarcinoma; however, elastic stains can help to demonstrate preserved alveolar architecture and to identify true invasion where elastic framework is destroyed, while myofibroblastic stroma (SMA) suggests invasion. EGFR mutations are frequent but molecular testing is not usually needed for AIS.

entities.variants: Mucinous AIS (tall columnar goblet-like cells); mixed mucinous and non-mucinous AIS
entities.remarks: Very rare; tall columnar mucinous cells with basal nuclei growing lepidically, 3 cm or less, no invasion; often solid or part-solid nodule rather than ground glass; KRAS mutations.
entities.histo: Mucinous adenocarcinoma in situ is a rare localised adenocarcinoma 3 cm or less composed of tall columnar cells with abundant apical mucin and small basally located nuclei, resembling goblet or gastric foveolar cells, growing purely along alveolar walls without invasion, airspace spread or STAS. Unlike non-mucinous AIS, it frequently appears as a solid or part-solid nodule because the alveoli are filled with mucin. Nuclear atypia is minimal and mitoses are rare. Intra-alveolar mucin and mucin-laden macrophages are often present. KRAS mutations are common. The diagnosis requires complete examination of the lesion; any invasive focus over 5 mm makes it invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma, and invasion 5 mm or less makes it mucinous MIA. Differentials include mucinous MIA and invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma, mucinous cell clusters in CPAM type 1, bronchiolar adenoma (bilayered with basal cells), mucinous metaplasia in fibrotic lung and metastatic mucinous adenocarcinoma from pancreas or gastrointestinal tract.
entities.cyto: Cytology cannot diagnose mucinous AIS. Specimens show bland columnar mucinous cells in flat honeycomb sheets with abundant mucin, which are easily under-called as benign bronchial or goblet cells or contaminants. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical or Suspicious for malignancy; mucinous adenocarcinoma when unequivocal; the term AIS is not used on cytology.
entities.ihc: IHC shows CK7 positivity, frequent CK20 and HNF4-alpha positivity, MUC5AC expression and usually absent or weak TTF-1 and napsin A, a profile shared with invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma that overlaps with metastatic pancreatobiliary and gastric adenocarcinoma, so clinical correlation is needed. CDX2 is usually negative or focal. The absence of a p40- or CK5/6-positive basal layer distinguishes it from bronchiolar adenoma.

entities.variants: Mild, moderate and severe squamous dysplasia; angiogenic squamous dysplasia; basal cell hyperplasia and squamous metaplasia (reactive precursors, see reactive changes row)
entities.remarks: Graded by thickness of atypical cell proliferation and maturation; arises in smokers' central airways; detected by autofluorescence bronchoscopy; high-grade lesions may progress to squamous cell carcinoma.
entities.histo: Squamous dysplasia is a preinvasive lesion of the bronchial epithelium that develops in smokers through basal cell hyperplasia and squamous metaplasia and may progress to carcinoma in situ and invasive squamous cell carcinoma. It is usually found in central airways at bifurcations and can be detected by autofluorescence or narrow-band imaging bronchoscopy. Grading reflects the extent of the atypical basal zone and the degree of cellular atypia. Mild dysplasia shows minimal architectural and cytological disturbance, with expansion of the basal zone into the lower third, mild anisocytosis and pleomorphism, and mitoses confined to the basal layer. Moderate dysplasia extends into the middle third with more nuclear atypia and vertically oriented nuclei. Severe dysplasia shows marked atypia, little maturation and expansion of the basal zone into the upper third, with mitoses in the lower two thirds. Angiogenic squamous dysplasia shows capillary loops projecting into the dysplastic epithelium. The intact basement membrane separates dysplasia from invasion. Differentials include reactive squamous metaplasia (maturation preserved, inflammation), carcinoma in situ, tangentially cut epithelium and regenerative atypia after intubation or infection.
entities.cyto: Sputum and bronchial brushings may contain atypical squamous metaplastic cells with mild to marked atypia, and the degree of atypia roughly correlates with the grade of dysplasia, but cytology cannot reliably grade lesions or exclude invasion. Keratinised atypical cells in sputum should prompt bronchoscopy. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical (low-grade atypia) or Suspicious for malignancy (marked atypia).
entities.ihc: IHC is not required for diagnosis but can help. p40 and CK5/6 confirm squamous differentiation, and Ki-67 shows proliferation extending above the basal layer in proportion to the grade of dysplasia; p53 overexpression or null pattern supports a neoplastic process. These markers do not separate reactive atypia reliably on their own, so morphology remains decisive.

entities.variants: Carcinoma in situ with or without extension into bronchial glands; field cancerisation in smokers; radiographically occult carcinoma
entities.remarks: Full-thickness atypia without maturation and with intact basement membrane; high risk of progression to invasive squamous cell carcinoma; extension into glands is not invasion.
entities.histo: Squamous cell carcinoma in situ is the most advanced preinvasive squamous lesion of the bronchial epithelium, typically found in heavy smokers at airway bifurcations and often in a field of dysplasia, and may coexist with invasive squamous cell carcinoma elsewhere. Microscopically the full thickness of the epithelium is replaced by markedly atypical cells with no or minimal maturation, pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei, coarse chromatin, prominent nucleoli and mitoses at all levels, including atypical forms. The surface may be keratinised or non-keratinised. The basement membrane remains intact, and extension of the in situ lesion into bronchial glands and ducts can mimic invasion but has smooth, rounded contours without a stromal reaction. Carcinoma in situ has a high risk of progression and is treated by endobronchial therapy or resection. Differentials include severe dysplasia (some maturation in upper layers), invasive squamous cell carcinoma (irregular nests in stroma, desmoplasia), reactive atypia with regenerative changes, and tangential sectioning.
entities.cyto: Sputum or brushings show malignant squamous cells, including keratinised pleomorphic forms, that cannot be distinguished from invasive squamous cell carcinoma, because invasion cannot be assessed on cytology; the background usually lacks tumour diathesis. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (squamous cell carcinoma, with a comment that invasion cannot be assessed) or Suspicious for malignancy.
entities.ihc: IHC confirms squamous lineage with p40, p63 and CK5/6, and Ki-67 shows full-thickness proliferation; p53 is frequently overexpressed or null. IHC does not distinguish carcinoma in situ from invasive carcinoma; collagen IV or laminin can outline an intact basement membrane but are rarely used. Assessment of invasion is morphological. Autofluorescence and narrow-band imaging bronchoscopy are used to find these lesions, and biopsies should be oriented so that the full epithelial thickness and the basement membrane can be assessed. Molecular changes such as 3p loss, TP53 mutation and SOX2 amplification are shared with invasive carcinoma and are not used diagnostically.

entities.entity: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH)
entities.variants: DIPNECH with tumorlets; DIPNECH with carcinoid tumours (multiple typical or atypical carcinoids); DIPNECH with constrictive bronchiolitis
entities.remarks: Generalised proliferation of neuroendocrine cells in airway epithelium with tumorlets and constrictive bronchiolitis; middle-aged women with chronic cough and mosaic attenuation; WHO precursor of carcinoid tumours.
entities.histo: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia is a generalised proliferation of scattered single cells, small nodules (neuroendocrine bodies) or linear proliferations of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells within the bronchial and bronchiolar epithelium, without an underlying cause such as chronic lung disease, and is recognised by WHO as a precursor of carcinoid tumours. It typically affects middle-aged and older non-smoking women, who present with chronic cough and dyspnoea with an obstructive or mixed pattern, or it is found incidentally in lungs resected for carcinoid. CT shows mosaic attenuation with air trapping and multiple small nodules. Microscopically the neuroendocrine cells proliferate within the epithelium, sometimes extending beyond the basement membrane to form tumorlets (less than 5 mm) and carcinoid tumours (5 mm or more). Affected airways frequently show constrictive bronchiolitis with submucosal fibrosis, explaining the obstructive physiology. Differentials include reactive neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia secondary to chronic lung disease, NEHI in infants, isolated tumorlets and minute meningothelial-like nodules.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in DIPNECH itself. Associated carcinoid tumours may be sampled and show monotonous neuroendocrine cells. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: not applicable to DIPNECH; Malignant (carcinoid tumour) or Suspicious for associated tumours. Transbronchial or cryobiopsy samples rarely capture the lesion, and the diagnosis is usually made on wedge resections or lobectomies, often removed for a carcinoid tumour, in correlation with CT mosaic attenuation and obstructive physiology.
entities.ihc: IHC is essential: chromogranin A, synaptophysin, INSM1 and CD56 highlight neuroendocrine cells, demonstrating their number and distribution; bombesin (GRP) is also useful. Ki-67 is very low in hyperplasia and tumorlets. Elastic stain highlights associated constrictive bronchiolitis. Quantitative criteria (for example multiple foci of neuroendocrine cell proliferation and at least three tumorlets in a resection) have been proposed but are not uniformly applied.

entities.variants: Isolated tumorlets in scarred or bronchiectatic lungs; multiple tumorlets in DIPNECH
entities.remarks: Nodular neuroendocrine proliferation under 5 mm extending beyond the basement membrane; often incidental and associated with scarring; 5 mm or more defines carcinoid tumour.
entities.histo: A carcinoid tumorlet is a small nodular proliferation of neuroendocrine cells that extends beyond the bronchiolar basement membrane into the surrounding tissue but measures less than 5 mm; lesions 5 mm or larger are classified as carcinoid tumours. Tumorlets are often incidental findings in lungs with bronchiectasis, chronic inflammation or scarring, where they are considered reactive, and they also occur in multiples as part of DIPNECH. Microscopically they consist of nests and cords of bland, uniform, round to spindle cells with moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm and finely granular salt-and-pepper chromatin, embedded in fibrous stroma, often adjacent to a bronchiole. Mitoses and necrosis are absent. Tumorlets can involve peribronchial lymphatics and, very rarely, lymph nodes, without implying aggressive behaviour. Differentials include minute meningothelial-like nodules (EMA and PR positive, neuroendocrine negative), typical carcinoid, small cell carcinoma in crushed biopsies (high Ki-67), and metastatic carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role because tumorlets are too small to sample. Not applicable to the WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology. If a nodule thought to be a tumorlet is aspirated, the cells resemble those of carcinoid tumour (monotonous, salt-and-pepper chromatin, plasmacytoid or spindled), and the size criterion can only be applied on radiology or histology, so such a sample is reported as a neuroendocrine neoplasm with a comment. Crushed tumorlets in transbronchial biopsies are a recognised pitfall for small cell carcinoma.
entities.ihc: IHC shows neuroendocrine markers (chromogranin A, synaptophysin, INSM1, CD56) and keratin positivity, often with TTF-1 negative or weak staining, and a very low Ki-67, which distinguishes tumorlets from small cell carcinoma. EMA and PR negativity and neuroendocrine marker positivity separate them from meningothelial-like nodules. Measurement of size is the critical criterion against carcinoid tumour.

entities.variants: Exophytic squamous papilloma; inverted squamous papilloma; solitary (adult, HPV 6/11 or HPV-negative) vs recurrent respiratory papillomatosis with tracheobronchial and parenchymal spread (juvenile and adult onset, HPV 6/11); papilloma with dysplasia or malignant transformation (HPV 16/18 or 11)
entities.remarks: Benign papillary tumour of central airways with fibrovascular cores lined by squamous epithelium; koilocytes in HPV-related lesions; recurrent respiratory papillomatosis may spread to lung and rarely transform to SCC.
entities.histo: Squamous cell papilloma is a benign papillary tumour of the bronchial and tracheal mucosa composed of delicate fibrovascular cores covered by stratified squamous epithelium. It is usually a solitary endobronchial lesion in adults, causing obstruction, haemoptysis or post-obstructive pneumonia, or part of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, which begins in the larynx in children or adults and can extend to the trachea, bronchi and lung parenchyma, where it forms cystic, cavitating nodules lined by papillomatous squamous epithelium. Exophytic papillomas show papillary fronds lined by mature squamous epithelium that may be keratinising or non-keratinising, often with koilocytes, binucleation and dyskeratosis in HPV 6 or 11-associated cases. Inverted papillomas grow endophytically into the bronchial wall and glands but with smooth borders. Dysplasia can occur, and malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma, particularly with HPV 11, 16 or 18 or after radiation, is a rare but important complication. Differentials include papillary squamous cell carcinoma (atypia, invasion), inflammatory polyp (granulation tissue core), glandular and mixed papillomas, and bronchial squamous metaplasia.
entities.cyto: Brushings may show benign mature squamous cells, sometimes with koilocytic atypia (perinuclear halos, nuclear enlargement, binucleation), which can be mistaken for dysplasia or squamous carcinoma. The papillary architecture is not appreciable in cytology. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical (koilocytic or dysplastic squamous cells).
entities.ihc: IHC shows p40, p63 and CK5/6 positivity in the squamous epithelium, with Ki-67 restricted to basal layers in non-dysplastic lesions. p16 is usually negative or patchy in low-risk HPV papillomas, and HPV in situ hybridisation or PCR can identify HPV 6 or 11; diffuse p16 with high-risk HPV raises concern for malignant transformation. p53 abnormalities and extended Ki-67 support dysplasia or carcinoma.

entities.variants: Endobronchial glandular papilloma; peripheral glandular papilloma (rare)
entities.remarks: Rare benign papillary tumour lined by ciliated and non-ciliated columnar cells with goblet cells; central or peripheral; no atypia; middle-aged adults.
entities.histo: Glandular papilloma is a rare benign papillary tumour of the bronchi composed of fibrovascular cores lined by ciliated or non-ciliated columnar cells, cuboidal cells and variable numbers of goblet cells, without squamous epithelium. It usually presents as an endobronchial polyp in middle-aged adults, causing obstruction or haemoptysis, and less often as a peripheral nodule. The epithelial cells have uniform, basally located nuclei, without significant atypia, mitoses or necrosis, and a basal cell layer may be present. The stroma may be oedematous or hyalinised and contain inflammatory cells. Recurrence after incomplete excision is possible but malignant transformation is not established. Differentials include mixed squamous and glandular papilloma, bronchiolar adenoma (bilayered, peripheral), papillary adenoma (peripheral, pneumocyte-lined), mucous gland adenoma (submucosal glands, not papillary), and papillary adenocarcinoma, which shows atypia, invasion and lack of cilia.
entities.cyto: Brushings show benign columnar and ciliated cells with goblet cells, which are indistinguishable from normal bronchial epithelium, so cytology is non-specific. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign. Brushings may show benign ciliated and mucinous columnar cells in papillary groups, which are indistinguishable from normal bronchial epithelium or reactive hyperplasia, and the key differential of papillary adenocarcinoma cannot be excluded on cytology alone.
entities.ihc: IHC shows CK7 positivity and variable TTF-1 in the luminal cells, with a p40 or CK5/6-positive basal layer in some cases and low Ki-67. The presence of ciliated cells and basal cells supports a benign tumour over papillary adenocarcinoma. BRAF V600E mutations have been described in some glandular and mixed papillomas, and BRAF VE1 IHC can be positive. Ki-67 is low and p16 and HPV studies are usually negative. Absence of TTF-1-positive pneumocyte-type atypical cells and of invasion helps separate it from papillary adenocarcinoma, and BRAF V600E testing has been reported positive in some cases.

entities.entity: Mixed squamous cell and glandular papilloma
entities.variants: Endobronchial mixed papilloma (rarest papilloma type)
entities.remarks: Rare benign papilloma with both squamous and glandular epithelium, the glandular component forming at least one third of the lining; middle-aged men, smokers; BRAF V600E in some.
entities.histo: Mixed squamous cell and glandular papilloma is the rarest bronchial papilloma, composed of fibrovascular cores lined by a mixture of squamous epithelium and glandular epithelium (ciliated and non-ciliated columnar cells and goblet cells), with the glandular component accounting for at least one third of the epithelium. It usually presents as an endobronchial polyp in middle-aged men, often smokers. The squamous areas may show mild atypia, but significant dysplasia is unusual, and there is no invasion. Some lesions harbour BRAF V600E mutations, linking them to glandular papillomas. Complete excision is curative. Differentials include squamous papilloma with entrapped glands, glandular papilloma, mucoepidermoid carcinoma (submucosal, mucin, intermediate cells, MAML2 fusion) and adenosquamous carcinoma or papillary carcinomas with atypia and invasion.
entities.cyto: Brushings or washings may contain a mixture of benign squamous and glandular cells, which cannot be distinguished from metaplastic bronchial epithelium; atypical squamous cells should prompt evaluation for carcinoma rather than a papilloma diagnosis. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, or Atypical if the squamous component is atypical.
entities.ihc: IHC highlights the two components: squamous areas are p40, p63 and CK5/6 positive and glandular areas CK7 positive with variable TTF-1. BRAF VE1 IHC may be positive. Ki-67 is low. MAML2 rearrangement testing can be used to exclude mucoepidermoid carcinoma if needed. Ki-67 confined to the basal layer, absence of p53 aberrancy and negative HPV in most cases support a benign lesion, while BRAF V600E has been described in some mixed papillomas. p40 in the basal and squamous cells helps show that the lesion is not a mucoepidermoid carcinoma, whose intermediate cells form solid nests rather than papillae.

entities.variants: Mixed patterns: papillary, sclerotic, solid and haemorrhagic (angiomatoid); rare lymph node metastasis (does not alter benign behaviour); multiple or bilateral lesions rare
entities.remarks: Benign tumour (formerly sclerosing haemangioma) of primitive respiratory epithelium with two cell types (surface cuboidal cells and round stromal cells), both TTF-1 positive; middle-aged Asian women; well-circumscribed peripheral nodule.
entities.histo: Sclerosing pneumocytoma, formerly called sclerosing haemangioma, is a benign lung tumour derived from primitive respiratory epithelium, occurring most often in middle-aged women, particularly in East Asia. It presents as a solitary, well-circumscribed, peripheral nodule, often incidental. Grossly it is a firm, tan-yellow to haemorrhagic circumscribed mass. Microscopically it shows a mixture of four patterns, typically in combination: papillary structures, sclerotic areas with dense hyalinised collagen, solid sheets, and haemorrhagic areas with blood-filled spaces, cholesterol clefts and haemosiderin-laden macrophages. Two cell types are characteristic: cuboidal surface cells resembling type II pneumocytes that line papillae and spaces, and round stromal cells with pale eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm, bland round nuclei and well-defined borders that form the solid areas and papillary cores. Mitoses are rare. Lymph node metastases occur rarely and do not seem to affect prognosis. Differentials include carcinoid tumour (round stromal cells mimic carcinoid; neuroendocrine positive), papillary adenocarcinoma, papillary adenoma, metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma and PEComa.
entities.cyto: FNA shows a dual cell population: cuboidal surface cells in papillary groups and sheets of bland round stromal cells, often with haemosiderin-laden macrophages and foamy cells. Intranuclear inclusions and papillae can mimic adenocarcinoma or papillary thyroid carcinoma, and monotonous round cells can mimic carcinoid, a frequent pitfall. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign if confidently recognised, otherwise Atypical or Suspicious for malignancy (a known cause of false positives).
entities.ihc: IHC is diagnostic: both surface and round cells are TTF-1 and EMA positive, which is the key feature. The surface cells are also pancytokeratin, CK7 and napsin A positive and express surfactant proteins, whereas the round cells are negative or only focally positive for pancytokeratin and napsin A but positive for TTF-1, EMA and often progesterone receptor. Neuroendocrine markers are negative (versus carcinoid), and Ki-67 is low. AKT1 alterations are frequent.

entities.variants: Solitary multicystic peripheral alveolar adenoma
entities.remarks: Rare benign peripheral multicystic nodule composed of alveolar-like spaces lined by type II pneumocytes with a septal stromal component; well-circumscribed, incidental.
entities.histo: Alveolar adenoma is a rare benign tumour that usually presents as a solitary, well-circumscribed, peripheral subpleural nodule in middle-aged and older adults, often incidentally. Grossly it is a soft, multicystic spongy lesion containing clear fluid, sharply demarcated from surrounding lung. Microscopically it consists of a network of variably sized cystic spaces resembling alveoli, larger at the centre, lined by flattened to cuboidal type II pneumocytes, with the spaces often containing eosinophilic proteinaceous or granular PAS-positive material and occasional macrophages. The septa between cysts are thickened by a stromal component of bland spindle or stellate cells within a myxoid or collagenous matrix. There is no atypia, papillary growth or invasion. Differentials include lymphangioma (endothelial-lined spaces, D2-40 positive), sclerosing pneumocytoma (papillary and solid areas, round cells), papillary adenoma, adenocarcinoma in situ (no stromal component, more atypia) and CPAM.
entities.cyto: Cytology is rarely performed. Aspirates would yield few bland cuboidal pneumocytes, macrophages and proteinaceous material and are usually non-diagnostic. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Non-diagnostic or Benign. FNA of the peripheral nodule may yield scant bland cuboidal cells, macrophages and proteinaceous fluid, which can be mistaken for a cyst or a lepidic adenocarcinoma; awareness of the radiological appearance of a well-circumscribed, cystic peripheral nodule avoids overdiagnosis.
entities.ihc: IHC shows that the lining cells are pneumocytes, positive for pancytokeratin, TTF-1, napsin A and surfactant proteins, and the stromal cells are vimentin positive and may be SMA positive, with keratin and TTF-1 negativity. D2-40 and CD31 are negative in the lining, excluding lymphangioma. Ki-67 is low. The stromal cells are not myofibroblastic and lack keratin, which helps separate it from sclerosing pneumocytoma, whose round stromal cells are TTF-1 and EMA positive. Lymphatic endothelial markers (D2-40) help exclude lymphangioma, and Ki-67 is very low.

entities.variants: Peripheral papillary adenoma (benign; rare reports of local recurrence)
entities.remarks: Rare benign well-circumscribed peripheral tumour with fibrovascular papillae lined by uniform cuboidal to columnar type II pneumocyte or club cells; no invasion.
entities.histo: Papillary adenoma is a rare benign tumour that presents as a well-circumscribed, peripheral nodule, often incidental, in adults and occasionally children. Grossly it is soft, granular and tan, sharply demarcated or encapsulated. Microscopically it consists of branching papillae with fibrovascular cores lined by a single layer of uniform cuboidal to columnar cells resembling type II pneumocytes or club cells, with mild nuclear atypia, occasional intranuclear inclusions and no or very rare mitoses. Necrosis, vascular, pleural or stromal invasion, and lepidic spread at the periphery are absent. Some cases harbour BRAF mutations. The distinction from papillary adenocarcinoma rests on circumscription, lack of invasion and minimal atypia, and the lesion should be completely excised and examined. Differentials include papillary adenocarcinoma, sclerosing pneumocytoma (two cell types, solid and sclerotic areas), glandular papilloma (central, ciliated cells), bronchiolar adenoma and metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show cohesive papillary groups of bland cuboidal to columnar cells without nuclear atypia, which overlap with papillary adenocarcinoma and sclerosing pneumocytoma, so the diagnosis is not made on cytology. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical or Benign (low-grade epithelial lesion, histology recommended).
entities.ihc: IHC shows TTF-1, napsin A, CK7 and surfactant protein positivity of the lining cells, with low Ki-67. Thyroglobulin and PAX8 are negative, excluding metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma. EMA and TTF-1 positivity in round stromal cells would favour sclerosing pneumocytoma instead. Ki-67 is low and p53 is wild-type. The fibrovascular cores lack the round TTF-1- and EMA-positive stromal cells of sclerosing pneumocytoma, and the absence of invasion and of significant atypia separates it from papillary adenocarcinoma, which is frequently EGFR or KRAS mutant; BRAF mutations have been reported in some papillary adenomas.

entities.entity: Bronchiolar adenoma / ciliated muconodular papillary tumour
entities.variants: Proximal-type bronchiolar adenoma (classic CMPT; papillary, mucinous and ciliated cells); distal-type bronchiolar adenoma (flat, non-mucinous, alveolar-like cuboidal cells with basal layer); driver mutations BRAF V600E, EGFR, KRAS, HRAS, AKT1, ALK fusions
entities.remarks: WHO 5th new entity; small peripheral nodule with bilayered bronchiolar-type epithelium (luminal ciliated or mucinous cells and continuous basal cell layer, p40/CK5/6 positive); benign; frozen section pitfall for mucinous adenocarcinoma.
entities.histo: Bronchiolar adenoma, a newly recognised entity in the WHO 5th edition that includes the ciliated muconodular papillary tumour, is a benign peripheral lung tumour composed of a bilayered proliferation of bronchiolar-type epithelium with a continuous layer of basal cells. It usually presents in middle-aged and older adults as a small (often under 2 cm) peripheral nodule. Two subtypes are recognised. The proximal type, which includes classic CMPT, shows papillary and glandular structures lined by mucinous, ciliated and club cells, often with abundant intra-alveolar mucin, resembling bronchial epithelium. The distal type shows flat, lepidic-like or glandular growth of cuboidal non-mucinous cells resembling club cells or type II pneumocytes, with an underlying basal cell layer. Both types lack significant atypia, mitoses and necrosis, and spread along alveolar walls may occur at the edge. Driver mutations (BRAF V600E most common, also EGFR, KRAS, HRAS, AKT1 and ALK fusions) indicate a neoplastic nature. The main differentials are invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma and lepidic adenocarcinoma, particularly on frozen section, which lack the basal cell layer, and also mucous gland adenoma and peribronchiolar metaplasia.
entities.cyto: Cytology is rarely diagnostic. Aspirates may show ciliated cells, mucinous cells and basal cells in a mucinous background, which can be mistaken for benign bronchial contamination or mucinous adenocarcinoma. The presence of cilia and basal cells argues against carcinoma but is not reliable. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign, Atypical or Suspicious for malignancy depending on findings.
entities.ihc: IHC is key to demonstrate the continuous basal cell layer: p40, p63 and CK5/6 highlight basal cells beneath the luminal cells, which is absent in adenocarcinoma. Luminal cells are TTF-1 positive (variable in mucinous cells), CK7 positive and napsin A variable. BRAF VE1 IHC may detect BRAF V600E mutations. Ki-67 is low. The continuous p40 or CK5/6-positive basal cell layer is the most useful feature separating bronchiolar adenoma from invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma and lepidic non-mucinous adenocarcinoma, which lack this layer. Driver alterations (BRAF V600E, EGFR exon 19 or 20, KRAS, ALK fusions) are common, supporting a neoplastic nature, and should not by themselves prompt a diagnosis of carcinoma.

entities.variants: Pulmonary mucinous cystadenoma (benign); distinction from mucinous cystic tumour of low malignant potential and colloid adenocarcinoma
entities.remarks: Very rare unilocular cyst filled with mucin, lined by bland columnar mucinous epithelium with fibrous wall; smokers; benign.
entities.histo: Mucinous cystadenoma of the lung is a very rare benign tumour, usually in middle-aged or older smokers, presenting as a well-circumscribed peripheral cystic nodule. Grossly it is a unilocular cyst filled with mucin, with a thin fibrous wall. Microscopically the cyst is lined by a single layer of bland, columnar to cuboidal mucinous epithelium with basal nuclei, sometimes discontinuous or replaced by inflammatory and granulation tissue, and the fibrous wall may contain chronic inflammation and mucin-laden macrophages. There is no significant atypia, papillary proliferation, invasion or floating tumour cells within the mucin. The distinction from colloid adenocarcinoma, which shows abundant extracellular mucin dissecting through the lung with floating or lining atypical cells, and from mucinous cystic tumours with borderline atypia, requires thorough sampling. Differentials include bronchogenic cyst (cartilage, ciliated cells), mucous gland adenoma (central), CPAM type 1 with mucinous cells, colloid adenocarcinoma and metastatic mucinous tumours from ovary, pancreas or appendix.
entities.cyto: Cytology would show abundant mucin with sparse bland columnar mucinous cells and macrophages, which cannot exclude a mucinous adenocarcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical, or Non-diagnostic if only mucin is present. Aspirates are dominated by mucin with few bland columnar cells and macrophages, and the main concern is a low-grade mucinous adenocarcinoma or colloid adenocarcinoma, which cannot be excluded on cytology; the lesion should be reported as a mucinous lesion with a recommendation for complete excision.
entities.ihc: IHC shows CK7 positivity, with variable CK20 and CDX2; TTF-1 is often weak or negative. These findings overlap with mucinous adenocarcinomas and metastases, so morphology and clinical exclusion of extrapulmonary primary tumours are essential. Low Ki-67 and wild-type p53 support benignity. Ki-67 is very low and p53 is wild-type. Absence of invasive growth and of CDX2- and CK20-positive intestinal differentiation helps distinguish it from colloid adenocarcinoma and metastatic appendiceal or ovarian mucinous neoplasms; PAX8 and SATB2 negativity also support a pulmonary lesion.

entities.variants: Endobronchial mucous gland adenoma (bronchial gland adenoma)
entities.remarks: Rare benign exophytic endobronchial tumour of bronchial submucosal gland origin, with mucin-filled cysts and acini lined by bland mucinous, oncocytic and myoepithelial cells.
entities.histo: Mucous gland adenoma is a rare benign tumour arising from the submucosal seromucinous glands of the bronchi, presenting as an exophytic, well-circumscribed, polypoid endobronchial mass, typically in the main or lobar bronchi, causing obstruction, cough, haemoptysis or post-obstructive pneumonia. Grossly it is a soft, gelatinous, mucoid nodule above the cartilage plates. Microscopically it consists of numerous mucin-filled cysts, glands, tubules and papillae lined by bland columnar, cuboidal or flattened mucinous cells, with oncocytic and clear cells and an outer myoepithelial layer in some areas, set in fibrous stroma with inflammation. There is no atypia, necrosis, invasion or significant mitotic activity. Differentials include low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma (squamoid and intermediate cells, MAML2 rearrangement), adenoid cystic carcinoma, mucinous cystadenoma (peripheral), glandular papilloma and bronchial gland hyperplasia.
entities.cyto: Cytology is rarely diagnostic. Brushings may show mucin and bland mucinous columnar cells, which cannot be distinguished from normal bronchial glands or low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical. Brushings of the polypoid lesion may show benign mucous cells and mucin, which are indistinguishable from normal bronchial glands, and low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma remains the key differential that cytology cannot exclude.
entities.ihc: IHC shows CK7 positivity of luminal cells with variable myoepithelial markers (p63, SMA, calponin) in an outer layer and low Ki-67. The absence of intermediate and squamoid cells and of MAML2 rearrangement (by FISH or RT-PCR) helps exclude low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma. TTF-1 is usually negative. The absence of squamoid and intermediate cells (p40-positive solid nests) and of MAML2 rearrangement distinguishes it from low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Ki-67 is low, and mucicarmine and PAS-diastase show abundant intracellular and luminal mucin in the acini.

entities.variants: Endobronchial pleomorphic adenoma; peripheral intrapulmonary pleomorphic adenoma; carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma (rare, see other salivary carcinomas row)
entities.remarks: Rare benign biphasic tumour of bronchial glands with epithelial and myoepithelial cells in chondromyxoid stroma; PLAG1 or HMGA2 rearrangements; recurrence after incomplete excision.
entities.histo: Pleomorphic adenoma of the lung is a rare benign salivary gland-type tumour arising from bronchial submucosal glands, presenting as a polypoid endobronchial mass in the trachea or main bronchi or, less often, as a peripheral parenchymal nodule. Grossly it is a well-circumscribed, lobulated, grey-white to myxoid mass. Microscopically it is a biphasic tumour composed of ducts and glands lined by luminal epithelial cells surrounded by myoepithelial cells, which are plasmacytoid, spindled, clear or epithelioid and merge into a myxoid, chondroid or hyalinised stroma. Pulmonary examples often have less chondromyxoid stroma than salivary tumours and may be more cellular. Mitoses are rare and there is no necrosis. Recurrence occurs after incomplete excision, and malignant transformation (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma) is rare. Differentials include pulmonary hamartoma (cartilage, fat, entrapped respiratory epithelium), adenoid cystic carcinoma (cribriform, infiltrative), mucoepidermoid carcinoma, myoepithelioma, metastatic pleomorphic adenoma from salivary glands and chondroid tumours.
entities.cyto: FNA would show cohesive clusters of bland epithelial and myoepithelial cells embedded in a fibrillary metachromatic chondromyxoid matrix on Giemsa stains, which is characteristic; scant matrix may lead to confusion with other salivary-type tumours. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign if typical, otherwise Atypical.
entities.ihc: IHC confirms the biphasic nature: luminal cells are CK7 positive and myoepithelial cells are positive for p63, p40, SOX10, S100, calponin, SMA and GFAP. PLAG1 nuclear IHC is positive in tumours with PLAG1 fusions, and HMGA2 alterations occur in others. MYB is negative (versus adenoid cystic carcinoma), MAML2 rearrangements are absent, and Ki-67 is low. Ki-67 is low in benign tumours, and a raised Ki-67, p53 aberrancy, HER2 overexpression or AR positivity in the epithelial component should raise concern for carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma. MYB and MAML2 testing helps exclude adenoid cystic and mucoepidermoid carcinomas in limited samples.

entities.variants: Spindle cell, epithelioid, plasmacytoid and clear cell myoepithelioma; EWSR1-rearranged soft tissue-type myoepithelial tumours also reported in lung
entities.remarks: Rare benign tumour composed entirely of myoepithelial cells without ductal component; endobronchial or peripheral; distinguish from myoepithelial carcinoma by circumscription, low mitoses and absence of necrosis.
entities.histo: Myoepithelioma of the lung is a rare benign tumour composed exclusively or almost exclusively of myoepithelial cells, without significant ductal elements, presenting either as an endobronchial mass or as a peripheral parenchymal nodule. Grossly it is well circumscribed, firm and grey-white. Microscopically the cells may be spindled, epithelioid, plasmacytoid or clear, arranged in sheets, nests, trabeculae or fascicles within a myxoid, hyalinised or collagenous stroma. Nuclei are bland with little pleomorphism, and mitoses and necrosis are absent or minimal. Some intrapulmonary myoepithelial tumours resemble their soft tissue counterparts and harbour EWSR1 rearrangements. Myoepithelial carcinoma differs by infiltrative growth, nuclear atypia, high mitotic activity and necrosis. Differentials include pleomorphic adenoma (ductal component, chondromyxoid matrix), myoepithelial carcinoma, solitary fibrous tumour, schwannoma, smooth muscle tumours, PEComa, and spindle cell carcinoid.
entities.cyto: FNA would show bland spindle, epithelioid or plasmacytoid cells with myxoid or hyaline matrix, often indistinguishable from other spindle cell lesions on cytology alone. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical or Suspicious for malignancy pending histology. Aspirates show bland spindle, epithelioid or plasmacytoid cells singly and in clusters with a variable myxoid or chondromyxoid matrix that stains magenta with Giemsa, and the main differentials are pleomorphic adenoma, low-grade sarcomas and myoepithelial carcinoma, which cannot be separated without histology.
entities.ihc: IHC confirms myoepithelial differentiation: keratins (AE1/AE3, CK5/6) and myoepithelial markers (p63, p40, SMA, calponin, S100, SOX10, GFAP) are expressed in various combinations. STAT6 is negative (versus SFT), HMB45 negative (versus PEComa) and neuroendocrine markers negative (versus spindle cell carcinoid). EWSR1 FISH may be positive. Ki-67 is low, which with morphology helps to exclude myoepithelial carcinoma.

entities.entity: Other benign salivary gland-type and bronchial gland tumours
entities.variants: Oncocytoma (oncocytic adenoma) of bronchus; bronchial cystadenoma; sialadenoma papilliferum-like tumour (rare); bronchial gland hyperplasia and oncocytic metaplasia (non-neoplastic mimics)
entities.remarks: Very rare benign tumours of bronchial submucosal glands; oncocytoma composed of mitochondria-rich eosinophilic granular cells; differential with oncocytic carcinoid is important.
entities.histo: Benign salivary gland-type tumours other than pleomorphic adenoma and myoepithelioma are exceedingly rare in the lung. Bronchial oncocytoma presents as an endobronchial polypoid mass composed of sheets, nests and acini of large polygonal cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm due to numerous mitochondria, round central nuclei and small nucleoli, without atypia, necrosis or significant mitoses. Its main differential is oncocytic carcinoid tumour, which is far more common and expresses neuroendocrine markers. Bronchial cystadenomas and papillary cystic gland tumours are lined by bland columnar or oncocytic epithelium. Oncocytic metaplasia of bronchial glands is common with ageing and should not be mistaken for a tumour. Differentials include oncocytic carcinoid, granular cell tumour (S100 and SOX10 positive), mucoepidermoid carcinoma with oncocytic change, acinic cell carcinoma and metastatic oncocytic renal or thyroid tumours.
entities.cyto: Cytology would show cohesive clusters of large oncocytic cells with granular cytoplasm and bland round nuclei, which overlap with oncocytic carcinoid cells, so neuroendocrine markers on cell block are essential. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical pending histology and IHC.
entities.ihc: IHC is crucial to exclude oncocytic carcinoid: chromogranin A, synaptophysin and INSM1 are negative in oncocytoma but positive in carcinoid. Oncocytomas are keratin positive and show granular staining with antimitochondrial antibody, and PTAH highlights mitochondria. S100 and SOX10 exclude granular cell tumour, and PAX8, thyroglobulin and TTF-1 help exclude metastatic renal and thyroid oncocytic tumours. MAML2 testing excludes oncocytic mucoepidermoid carcinoma.

entities.variants: Peripheral (intraparenchymal, chondroid) hamartoma; endobronchial hamartoma (lipomatous predominance); multiple hamartomas (Cowden syndrome); fibroleiomyomatous hamartoma (see benign metastasizing leiomyoma row)
entities.remarks: Commonest benign lung tumour; coin lesion with popcorn calcification and fat on CT; lobules of cartilage, fat, smooth muscle and myxoid tissue with entrapped respiratory epithelial clefts; HMGA2 rearrangements (true neoplasm).
entities.histo: Pulmonary hamartoma is the commonest benign tumour of the lung and despite its name is a true mesenchymal neoplasm, with HMGA2 rearrangements in many cases. It usually occurs in adults in the sixth decade as a solitary, well-circumscribed, peripheral coin lesion, often with popcorn calcification and fat density on CT, and about 10 percent are endobronchial. Grossly it is lobulated, firm, white-grey, cartilaginous and easily shelled out. Microscopically it consists of variable proportions of mature hyaline cartilage (often dominant), fat, smooth muscle, fibromyxoid connective tissue and occasionally bone, arranged in lobules separated by cleft-like spaces lined by entrapped respiratory epithelium (ciliated or cuboidal cells), which is not part of the neoplasm. Endobronchial lesions contain more fat and less cartilage. Malignant transformation is exceptional. Differentials include chondroma (pure cartilage without epithelial clefts, Carney triad), chondrosarcoma, lipoma, pleomorphic adenoma, mesenchymal cystic hamartoma, and metastatic chondroid tumours.
entities.cyto: FNA is often diagnostic, showing fragments of fibromyxoid stroma or chondromyxoid matrix that stains bright magenta on Giemsa, scattered bland spindle cells, mature fat, and sheets of benign bronchial epithelial cells. Pitfalls include mistaking the reactive epithelial cells for adenocarcinoma or the matrix for pleomorphic adenoma or mucinous carcinoma, and samples may be scant because the lesion is hard. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign.
entities.ihc: IHC is rarely needed. The chondroid cells are S100 positive, smooth muscle elements SMA and desmin positive, and the entrapped epithelium TTF-1 and keratin positive. HMGA2 rearrangement (by FISH) or HMGA2 IHC can support the diagnosis. Keratin negativity of the mesenchymal component excludes carcinoma, and MDM2 and SOX10 help in uncommon differentials. The entrapped epithelium is TTF-1 and CK7 positive and should not be interpreted as an adenocarcinoma, especially when the cleft-like spaces are prominent. HMGA2 rearrangements, detectable by FISH, support the diagnosis in difficult cases, and Ki-67 is very low in all components.

entities.variants: Pulmonary chondroma in Carney triad (gastric GIST, paraganglioma, pulmonary chondroma; young women, SDH deficiency-related); sporadic chondroma (rare)
entities.remarks: Benign cartilaginous tumour without entrapped epithelium, often within bronchial wall or peripheral; frequently multiple and calcified in Carney triad.
entities.histo: Pulmonary chondroma is a rare benign cartilaginous tumour that most often occurs in young women as part of Carney triad, together with gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumour and paraganglioma, and may be multiple and bilateral. Sporadic chondromas also occur. Grossly the tumour is well circumscribed, lobulated, firm, white-grey and often calcified or ossified. Microscopically it consists of lobules of mature hyaline cartilage, sometimes with myxoid change, calcification and bone formation, often surrounded by a thin fibrous pseudocapsule. Unlike pulmonary hamartoma, it lacks entrapped respiratory epithelium, fat and smooth muscle, and is often related to the bronchial wall cartilage. Chondrocytes are bland, with occasional binucleation, without atypia or mitoses. Differentials include pulmonary hamartoma (mixed mesenchymal elements and epithelial clefts), low-grade chondrosarcoma (atypia, permeation, larger size), metastatic chondrosarcoma, tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica and calcified granulomas.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show chondroid matrix fragments that stain magenta on Giemsa with scattered bland chondrocytes in lacunae, which are indistinguishable from the cartilage of a hamartoma or a well-differentiated chondrosarcoma, so radiological correlation, especially multiplicity of lesions in Carney triad, is important. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical (chondroid lesion).
entities.ihc: IHC is rarely needed; chondrocytes are S100 and SOX9 positive. In suspected Carney triad, the associated GIST and paraganglioma show SDHB loss on IHC, while chondromas themselves are not routinely tested. Lack of IDH1 or IDH2 mutations and absence of atypia favour chondroma over chondrosarcoma. Testing for SDH deficiency (SDHB IHC loss) in gastric stromal tumour and paraganglioma, together with a family and clinical evaluation, helps confirm Carney triad when a pulmonary chondroma is found in a young woman. IDH1 and IDH2 mutations are absent, which helps distinguish it from chondrosarcoma, and Ki-67 is very low.

entities.variants: Endobronchial lipoma (commonest); peripheral or subpleural lipoma; angiolipoma; lipomatous hamartoma (see hamartoma)
entities.remarks: Rare benign tumour of mature fat, usually endobronchial in main or lobar bronchi causing obstruction; fat density on CT.
entities.histo: Lipoma of the lung is uncommon and usually endobronchial, arising from submucosal fat in the main or lobar bronchi of middle-aged and older men and causing obstruction with atelectasis or recurrent pneumonia; peripheral parenchymal and subpleural lipomas are rarer. Grossly the tumour is a soft, yellow, polypoid, smooth-surfaced mass covered by bronchial mucosa, sometimes with a dumb-bell shape extending through the bronchial wall. Microscopically it is composed of lobules of mature adipocytes with uniform small eccentric nuclei, separated by thin fibrous septa, covered by intact or squamous metaplastic respiratory mucosa. Bronchial glands may be entrapped. Atypia, lipoblasts and atypical stromal cells are absent. Differentials include lipomatous endobronchial hamartoma (contains cartilage and epithelial clefts), atypical lipomatous tumour or well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical hyperchromatic stromal cells, MDM2 amplification), and fat-containing tumours such as angiomyolipoma-like PEComa.
entities.cyto: Brushings or washings of an endobronchial lipoma usually show only benign bronchial cells, and FNA yields fragments of mature adipose tissue that may be dismissed as contamination; correlation with the fat density on CT is diagnostic. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Non-diagnostic.
entities.ihc: IHC is not usually needed. Adipocytes are S100 positive. MDM2 and CDK4 IHC, or MDM2 FISH, exclude atypical lipomatous tumour in large or atypical lesions, and HMB45 or melan-A exclude fat-rich PEComa. MDM2 and CDK4 IHC and MDM2 FISH are negative, which excludes atypical lipomatous tumour or well-differentiated liposarcoma in large or atypical lesions. Ki-67 is negligible, and S100 highlights mature adipocytes. HMGA2 rearrangements may be found but are not used diagnostically.

entities.variants: Endobronchial or tracheal leiomyoma; peripheral parenchymal leiomyoma; distinction from benign metastasizing leiomyoma (see Neoplastic - Others) and leiomyomatous hamartoma
entities.remarks: Rare benign smooth muscle tumour, endobronchial or parenchymal; in women with prior hysterectomy, multiple lung smooth muscle nodules suggest benign metastasizing leiomyoma.
entities.histo: Primary leiomyoma of the lung is a rare benign smooth muscle tumour that may arise in the trachea or bronchi, where it forms a polypoid endobronchial mass causing obstruction, or in the lung parenchyma as a circumscribed nodule, probably originating from bronchial or vascular smooth muscle. Grossly it is firm, whorled and grey-white. Microscopically it shows intersecting fascicles of spindle cells with eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasm and blunt-ended cigar-shaped nuclei, without significant atypia, necrosis or mitotic activity, often with hyalinisation. In women, especially with a history of uterine leiomyomas or hysterectomy, multiple pulmonary smooth muscle nodules should prompt consideration of benign metastasizing leiomyoma. Differentials include leiomyosarcoma (atypia, mitoses, necrosis), benign metastasizing leiomyoma, LAM, PEComa, solitary fibrous tumour, schwannoma, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour and spindle cell carcinoid.
entities.cyto: FNA of a parenchymal lesion yields cohesive fascicles of bland spindle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei and fibrillary cytoplasm, which cannot be separated from benign metastasizing leiomyoma, LAM or low-grade leiomyosarcoma; clinical history of uterine leiomyoma is important. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical (bland spindle cell lesion).
entities.ihc: IHC confirms smooth muscle differentiation with SMA, desmin, h-caldesmon and calponin positivity. ER and PR are often positive in benign metastasizing leiomyoma and can also be positive in some primary leiomyomas in women. HMB45 and melan-A are negative (versus LAM and PEComa), STAT6 negative (versus SFT), S100 and SOX10 negative (versus schwannoma) and ALK negative (versus IMT). Ki-67 is low.

entities.entity: PEComa, benign (clear cell tumour of the lung)
entities.variants: Clear cell 'sugar' tumour; angiomyolipoma-like PEComa (rare in lung); TSC-associated and sporadic; malignant PEComa (see malignant row); LAM (see Neoplastic - Others)
entities.remarks: Benign perivascular epithelioid cell tumour of large clear to eosinophilic glycogen-rich cells around thin-walled vessels; HMB45 and melan-A positive, keratin negative; distinguish from metastatic clear cell renal carcinoma.
entities.histo: Benign PEComa of the lung, historically called clear cell tumour or sugar tumour because of its glycogen-rich cytoplasm, is a rare, usually solitary, well-circumscribed peripheral nodule in adults, found incidentally. Grossly it is a red-tan, circumscribed mass under 3 cm. Microscopically it consists of sheets of round to polygonal epithelioid cells with abundant clear or lightly eosinophilic, finely granular cytoplasm and distinct cell borders, arranged around numerous thin-walled sinusoidal vessels, often with a radial perivascular orientation. Nuclei are uniform and small with inconspicuous nucleoli, and mitoses and necrosis are absent. Glycogen is abundant (PAS positive, diastase sensitive). It belongs to the family of perivascular epithelioid cell neoplasms with LAM and angiomyolipoma, and some cases are associated with tuberous sclerosis. Malignant PEComa shows size over 5 cm, infiltration, marked atypia, necrosis and mitoses. Differentials include metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (keratin, PAX8, CAIX positive), clear cell variants of lung carcinoma, clear cell carcinoid, hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma, granular cell tumour and sclerosing pneumocytoma.
entities.cyto: FNA shows loosely cohesive or single epithelioid cells with abundant clear or granular cytoplasm and bland nuclei, often associated with vessels, which may be mistaken for clear cell carcinoma or carcinoid; cell block IHC is essential. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical or Suspicious for malignancy pending IHC; Benign only with confirmatory IHC.
entities.ihc: IHC shows a melanocytic and smooth muscle phenotype: HMB45, melan-A, cathepsin K and MITF positive, with variable SMA and desmin, and negative keratin, EMA, PAX8 and TTF-1, which excludes metastatic renal cell carcinoma and lung carcinoma. S100 is usually negative or weak and SOX10 negative, separating it from melanoma. TFE3 IHC and FISH identify TFE3-rearranged PEComas. PAS with diastase confirms glycogen.

entities.variants: Endobronchial or tracheal granular cell tumour (solitary or multiple); parenchymal (rare); malignant granular cell tumour (exceptional)
entities.remarks: Benign Schwann cell tumour of large cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, S100 and SOX10 positive; endobronchial lesion causing obstruction; overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia can mimic SCC.
entities.histo: Granular cell tumour of the respiratory tract is a benign tumour of Schwann cell origin that most often involves the main or lobar bronchi and trachea of middle-aged adults, presenting as a small endobronchial nodule causing obstruction, cough or haemoptysis, and multiple lesions occur in some patients. Grossly it is a firm, grey-yellow submucosal nodule. Microscopically it consists of nests and sheets of large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm (due to lysosomes), small central bland nuclei and indistinct cell borders, infiltrating the submucosa and sometimes the bronchial wall, cartilage and adjacent lung, which can make complete excision difficult. Pustulo-ovoid bodies of Milian may be present. The overlying epithelium often shows pseudoepitheliomatous squamous hyperplasia, which in a superficial biopsy may be mistaken for squamous cell carcinoma. Malignant granular cell tumour, with necrosis, mitoses and pleomorphism, is exceptional.
