Fragments of malignant cartilage or osteoid matrix and rhabdomyoblasts, if seen with carcinoma cells, support the diagnosis, and the differential includes pulmonary blastoma, pleomorphic carcinoma, synovial sarcoma and metastatic carcinosarcoma from uterus or other sites.
entities.ihc: IHC confirms the carcinoma component (keratins, p40 or TTF-1) and heterologous sarcoma (desmin, myogenin and MyoD1 for rhabdomyosarcoma; S100 and SOX9 for cartilage; SATB2 for osteoid). Keratin is negative in the true sarcomatous component. PAX8 and WT1 help exclude metastatic Mullerian carcinosarcoma, and TLE1 or SS18 fusion testing exclude synovial sarcoma.

entities.variants: NUTM1-rearranged carcinoma (BRD4::NUTM1 commonest; BRD3, NSD3 and other partners); thoracic (lung, mediastinum) and head and neck sites
entities.remarks: Highly aggressive poorly differentiated carcinoma with abrupt keratinisation; monotonous intermediate-sized cells; speckled nuclear NUT IHC (over 50 percent of cells) is diagnostic; young adults but any age; median survival under 1 year.
entities.histo: NUT carcinoma is an aggressive, poorly differentiated carcinoma defined by rearrangement of the NUTM1 gene, most commonly BRD4::NUTM1, and arises in midline structures including the lung, mediastinum and head and neck. It affects adolescents and young adults but occurs at any age, often presenting with a large mass, extensive local invasion and metastases, and has a median survival of less than a year. Microscopically it consists of sheets and nests of monotonous, undifferentiated, small to intermediate-sized round cells with scant to moderate cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei with fine to vesicular chromatin and distinct nucleoli, frequently with abrupt foci of keratinisation without intermediate maturation, which is a helpful clue. Necrosis and neutrophilic infiltrates are common. Differentials include poorly differentiated or basaloid squamous cell carcinoma, small cell carcinoma, thoracic SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated tumour, Ewing sarcoma and other round cell sarcomas, lymphoma, germ cell tumours and thymic carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows monotonous, discohesive to loosely cohesive small to intermediate-sized cells with high N:C ratio, fine chromatin and small nucleoli, sometimes with abrupt squamous differentiation, crush artefact and necrosis; it is often misinterpreted as small cell carcinoma, lymphoma or poorly differentiated carcinoma, and NUT IHC on cell block is diagnostic. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (with recommendation for NUT IHC).
entities.ihc: NUT IHC (clone C52B1) shows diffuse speckled nuclear staining in more than 50 percent of tumour cells and is diagnostic, with FISH or NGS confirming NUTM1 rearrangement and identifying the partner. The tumour is usually keratin positive and p63 or p40 positive, with variable CD34, and may be focally positive for TTF-1, synaptophysin or chromogranin, which can mislead. Testing should be performed in any poorly differentiated midline carcinoma lacking glandular differentiation, especially in young patients.

entities.variants: Thoracic SMARCA4-UT; distinction from SMARCA4-deficient NSCLC (adenocarcinoma with BRG1 loss, separate entity); SMARCA2 (BRM) co-loss; rhabdoid features
entities.remarks: WHO 5th new entity; heavy smokers, young to middle-aged men; large mediastinal-pulmonary mass; discohesive sheets of epithelioid cells with prominent nucleoli; BRG1 loss, keratin weak or negative, CD34, SOX2, SALL4 positive; very poor prognosis.
entities.histo: Thoracic SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated tumour is a highly aggressive malignant neoplasm of the thorax, newly recognised in the WHO 5th edition, characterised by an undifferentiated phenotype and inactivation of the SMARCA4 gene encoding BRG1, a subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complex. It predominantly affects young to middle-aged male heavy smokers, often with emphysema, and presents as a large compressive mass involving the mediastinum, lung or pleura, with nodal and distant metastases. Microscopically it consists of diffuse sheets of discohesive, relatively monotonous, large round to epithelioid cells with vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli, often with rhabdoid cells, abundant necrosis and occasionally myxoid stroma, without glandular or squamous differentiation. Median survival is a few months. It is distinguished from SMARCA4-deficient non-small cell carcinoma, which retains epithelial differentiation (strong keratin, claudin-4, glands) despite BRG1 loss. Differentials include large cell carcinoma, SMARCA4-deficient NSCLC, NUT carcinoma, lymphoma, melanoma, germ cell tumours, epithelioid sarcoma, malignant rhabdoid tumour and SMARCA4-deficient sarcomas.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows discohesive large epithelioid or rhabdoid cells with vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli, often in a necrotic background, resembling large cell lymphoma, melanoma or poorly differentiated carcinoma. Cell block IHC for BRG1 is diagnostic. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (malignant neoplasm, with recommendation for BRG1 IHC).
entities.ihc: IHC shows complete loss (or marked reduction) of SMARCA4 (BRG1) with frequent concurrent SMARCA2 (BRM) loss, keratin negative or only focally and weakly positive, claudin-4 negative, and frequent positivity for CD34, SOX2, SALL4 and synaptophysin (focal), with variable p53. TTF-1 and p40 are generally negative. INI1 (SMARCB1) is retained. These features, together with negative CD45, SOX10, OCT4 and NUT, distinguish it from lymphoma, melanoma, germ cell tumour and NUT carcinoma. PD-L1 and molecular profiling (often STK11, KEAP1, KRAS co-mutations) are relevant.

entities.variants: Cribriform, tubular and solid patterns (solid over 30 percent worse prognosis); tracheal (commonest malignant salivary-type tumour of trachea) and bronchial sites; MYB::NFIB or MYBL1 fusions
entities.remarks: Second commonest primary tracheal malignancy after SCC; slow-growing, extensive submucosal and perineural spread; positive margins and late recurrences common; myoepithelial and ductal cells.
entities.histo: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a malignant salivary gland-type tumour arising from submucosal glands of the trachea and major bronchi, where it is the second most common primary malignant tumour after squamous cell carcinoma. It affects middle-aged adults without a strong smoking association and presents with airway obstruction, wheeze or haemoptysis, often mistaken for asthma. Grossly it forms a polypoid or annular submucosal mass that infiltrates the airway wall and extends longitudinally beyond its visible edges. Microscopically it is composed of two cell types, luminal ductal cells and abluminal myoepithelial cells, arranged in cribriform nests with punched-out pseudocysts containing basophilic glycosaminoglycan matrix or hyaline basement membrane material, tubules with true ducts, and solid nests. Cells are small and basaloid with angulated hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm. Perineural invasion and extensive submucosal and perichondrial spread are characteristic, so positive margins are common. The course is indolent but with late local recurrences and distant metastases, and a solid pattern over 30 percent indicates worse prognosis. Differentials include basaloid squamous cell carcinoma, pleomorphic adenoma, epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma, small cell carcinoma, cribriform adenocarcinoma and metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma from the head and neck.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows cohesive clusters of small basaloid cells with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei surrounding or wrapping around characteristic acellular hyaline globules and cylinders of matrix, which stain magenta on Giemsa. Solid variants may mimic small cell carcinoma or basaloid SCC. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (or Suspicious for malignancy, salivary gland-type neoplasm).
entities.ihc: IHC demonstrates the dual population: luminal cells are CK7 and CD117 positive, and myoepithelial or basal cells are p63, p40, SOX10, SMA, calponin and S100 positive. MYB protein is strongly expressed in most cases, and MYB::NFIB or MYBL1 rearrangements can be confirmed by FISH or RNA sequencing. TTF-1 is negative and neuroendocrine markers are negative, excluding adenocarcinoma and small cell carcinoma. Basaloid SCC shows diffuse p40 without a dual pattern and lacks MYB rearrangement.

entities.variants: Low-grade MEC (cystic, mucin-rich, often children and young adults); intermediate-grade; high-grade MEC (solid, atypical, overlaps adenosquamous); oncocytic and clear cell variants; CRTC1::MAML2 or CRTC3::MAML2 fusions
entities.remarks: Commonest salivary-type tumour of the lung; central endobronchial polypoid mass; mucous, intermediate and epidermoid cells without keratinisation; MAML2 fusion distinguishes from adenosquamous carcinoma.
entities.histo: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the commonest salivary gland-type tumour of the lung, arising from bronchial submucosal glands, typically as an exophytic, polypoid endobronchial mass in the main, lobar or segmental bronchi, and is one of the commonest lung cancers in children and young adults. It is composed of three cell types: mucus-secreting columnar or goblet cells, squamoid (epidermoid) cells without keratinisation, and intermediate cells, which are small to medium-sized polygonal cells with eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm. Low-grade tumours are predominantly cystic and glandular, with abundant mucin, mucinous cells lining cysts, bland intermediate cells and few mitoses, and have an excellent prognosis after resection. High-grade tumours are solid, with predominant squamoid and intermediate cells, marked atypia, mitoses and necrosis, and overlap with adenosquamous carcinoma. CRTC1::MAML2 or CRTC3::MAML2 fusions are present in most tumours, especially low-grade ones. Surface keratinisation, in situ squamous carcinoma and extensive keratin pearls argue against MEC. Differentials include adenosquamous carcinoma, mucous gland adenoma, squamous cell carcinoma, hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma (clear cell variant) and metastatic mucoepidermoid carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows a mixture of mucinous cells, intermediate cells and squamoid cells in a mucoid background; low-grade tumours may be paucicellular with mucin and bland cells, leading to under-diagnosis, while high-grade tumours resemble squamous or adenosquamous carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical, Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant depending on cellularity and atypia.
entities.ihc: IHC shows p63, p40 and CK5/6 positivity in squamoid and intermediate cells and CK7 positivity in mucinous and intermediate cells, with TTF-1 and napsin A negative, which helps separate MEC from adenosquamous carcinoma (TTF-1 positive glandular component). Mucicarmine and PAS-diastase highlight intracellular mucin. MAML2 rearrangement by FISH or RT-PCR is diagnostic and particularly useful in high-grade tumours. SOX10 is usually negative. EGFR mutations are generally absent, unlike some adenosquamous carcinomas.

entities.variants: Classic biphasic EMC; myoepithelial-predominant (clear cell) EMC; HRAS mutations
entities.remarks: Low-grade biphasic tumour of inner ductal cells and outer clear myoepithelial cells; endobronchial in adults; favourable prognosis.
entities.histo: Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma is a rare, low-grade salivary gland-type malignancy of the bronchial glands, usually presenting as an endobronchial polypoid mass in middle-aged adults. It is characterised by a biphasic tubular or ductal arrangement of an inner layer of cuboidal, eosinophilic ductal epithelial cells and an outer layer of myoepithelial cells with clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm, set in a hyalinised or myxoid stroma. Solid sheets of clear myoepithelial cells may predominate in some tumours. Nuclear atypia is mild, mitoses are scarce and necrosis is unusual. HRAS mutations are frequent. Local recurrence can occur, but metastasis is uncommon and prognosis is generally favourable. Differentials include pleomorphic adenoma (chondromyxoid stroma, PLAG1), adenoid cystic carcinoma (cribriform pattern, MYB), myoepithelioma or myoepithelial carcinoma (no ductal component), hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma (EWSR1::ATF1), PEComa and metastatic clear cell renal carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology may show a dual population of cohesive ductal cells and clear or naked myoepithelial nuclei, sometimes with hyaline globules, which overlaps with other salivary-type tumours. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant (salivary gland-type neoplasm).
entities.ihc: IHC highlights the two layers: inner ductal cells are CK7 and EMA positive, and outer myoepithelial cells are p63, p40, SMA, calponin, S100 and SOX10 positive. PAS with diastase shows glycogen in clear cells. HRAS mutation testing supports the diagnosis. TTF-1, HMB45 and PAX8 are negative, excluding adenocarcinoma, PEComa and metastatic renal carcinoma, and MYB and PLAG1 help exclude adenoid cystic carcinoma and pleomorphic adenoma.

entities.variants: Hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma of bronchus (EWSR1::ATF1 fusion); called clear cell carcinoma in head and neck WHO
entities.remarks: WHO 5th addition; low-grade tumour of clear to eosinophilic cells in cords and nests within hyalinised stroma; p63 positive, myoepithelial markers negative; EWSR1::ATF1.
entities.histo: Hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma is a rare low-grade salivary gland-type carcinoma arising from bronchial submucosal glands and added to the WHO 5th edition thoracic classification. It presents as an endobronchial mass in adults. Microscopically it consists of cords, trabeculae, nests and sheets of polygonal cells with clear to pale eosinophilic, glycogen-rich cytoplasm and mildly atypical round nuclei, embedded in a characteristic hyalinised, sclerotic or fibrocellular stroma. Squamoid features may be seen, but true ductal or myoepithelial differentiation is absent, and mucin is focal or absent. EWSR1::ATF1 fusion is characteristic. The behaviour is indolent, with occasional local recurrence or nodal metastasis. Differentials include mucoepidermoid carcinoma with clear cells (MAML2), epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma (biphasic), myoepithelial carcinoma (myoepithelial markers), clear cell PEComa, clear cell variants of lung carcinoma and metastatic clear cell renal carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology would show cohesive clusters of clear to eosinophilic cells with bland nuclei, sometimes with fragments of hyalinised stroma, which are non-specific. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant (salivary gland-type neoplasm). The differential diagnosis on cytology includes metastatic clear cell renal carcinoma, PEComa, clear cell squamous carcinoma, mucoepidermoid carcinoma with clear cells and epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma, so cell blocks and EWSR1 FISH are recommended when a bronchial clear cell tumour is sampled.
entities.ihc: IHC shows keratin (AE1/AE3, CK7) and p63 or p40 positivity with negative myoepithelial markers (SMA, calponin, S100 often negative), supporting non-myoepithelial squamoid differentiation. PAS with diastase confirms glycogen. EWSR1 rearrangement by FISH, or EWSR1::ATF1 fusion by RNA sequencing, is diagnostic. TTF-1, HMB45 and PAX8 are negative, and MAML2 rearrangement is absent.

entities.variants: Myoepithelial carcinoma (malignant myoepithelioma) of bronchus or lung; spindle, epithelioid, plasmacytoid and clear cell types; EWSR1 rearrangements in some
entities.remarks: Rare malignant counterpart of myoepithelioma with infiltrative growth, atypia, high mitotic activity and necrosis; myoepithelial markers positive.
entities.histo: Myoepithelial carcinoma is a rare malignant salivary gland-type tumour of the lung composed predominantly of myoepithelial cells with malignant features, arising endobronchially or in the lung parenchyma, sometimes from a pre-existing pleomorphic adenoma or myoepithelioma. Microscopically it forms multinodular, infiltrative growth of spindle, epithelioid, plasmacytoid or clear cells in sheets, nests and cords within myxoid or hyalinised stroma, often with zonal arrangement of cells at the periphery of nodules and central necrosis. Nuclear pleomorphism, increased mitoses and necrosis distinguish it from myoepithelioma. Some tumours harbour EWSR1 rearrangements similar to soft tissue myoepithelial carcinomas. It can metastasise and recur. Differentials include myoepithelioma, epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma, pleomorphic carcinoma and spindle cell carcinoma, synovial sarcoma, MPNST, melanoma and metastatic myoepithelial tumours.
entities.cyto: Cytology would show malignant spindle, epithelioid or plasmacytoid cells with myxoid matrix, which cannot be classified without IHC. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (malignant neoplasm, salivary-type suspected). Atypical plasmacytoid, epithelioid or clear myoepithelial cells with chondromyxoid matrix fragments can be seen, and the differential includes pleomorphic adenoma, myoepithelioma, chondrosarcoma, chordoma, myxoid sarcomas and melanoma, which require IHC and molecular testing on cell blocks.
entities.ihc: IHC shows co-expression of keratins (AE1/AE3, CK5/6) and myoepithelial markers (p63, p40, SMA, calponin, S100, SOX10, GFAP) in various combinations. Ki-67 is raised. EWSR1 FISH may be positive. SOX10 and S100 positivity with keratin negativity would favour melanoma, so keratin and myoepithelial markers must be assessed together; TTF-1 negativity and BRG1 and INI1 retention help exclude other mimics.

entities.entity: Other salivary gland-type carcinomas of lung (rare)
entities.variants: Acinic cell carcinoma; secretory carcinoma (ETV6::NTRK3); carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma; salivary duct carcinoma; polymorphous adenocarcinoma; oncocytic carcinoma; basal cell adenocarcinoma; sebaceous carcinoma (exceptional)
entities.remarks: Exceptionally rare primary pulmonary tumours of bronchial gland origin; diagnosis requires exclusion of metastasis from head and neck salivary primaries; some have targetable fusions (NTRK).
entities.histo: Several other salivary gland-type carcinomas have been described as rare primary tumours of the lung and airways, arising from bronchial submucosal glands. Acinic cell carcinoma consists of serous acinar-type cells with basophilic zymogen granules (PAS positive, diastase resistant) in solid, microcystic and papillary patterns. Secretory carcinoma forms microcystic and tubular structures with eosinophilic secretions, lined by bland vacuolated cells, and harbours ETV6::NTRK3 fusions, a target for TRK inhibitors. Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma arises within a pre-existing pleomorphic adenoma. Salivary duct carcinoma resembles high-grade ductal breast carcinoma with comedonecrosis and apocrine cells. Polymorphous adenocarcinoma, oncocytic carcinoma and basal cell adenocarcinoma are exceedingly rare. In every case, a metastasis from a head and neck salivary gland primary must be excluded clinically. Differentials include adenocarcinoma with acinar or secretory features, metastatic breast carcinoma, oncocytic carcinoid and other salivary-type tumours.
entities.cyto: Cytology varies by type: acinic cells with granular vacuolated cytoplasm, secretory carcinoma with vacuolated cells and secretions, salivary duct carcinoma with high-grade apocrine cells. Specific classification usually requires histology and molecular testing. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant.
entities.ihc: IHC is type specific: acinic cell carcinoma is DOG1 and SOX10 positive with NR4A3 nuclear staining; secretory carcinoma is S100, mammaglobin and SOX10 positive with pan-TRK nuclear staining, and ETV6::NTRK3 can be confirmed by FISH or RNA NGS; salivary duct carcinoma is AR and GATA3 positive with frequent HER2 overexpression; carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma may retain PLAG1 or HMGA2. TTF-1 and napsin A are negative, which helps separate them from conventional lung adenocarcinoma.

entities.variants: Central (endobronchial) and peripheral carcinoid; spindle cell, oncocytic, clear cell, melanocytic (pigmented), papillary, mucinous stroma, sclerosing and paraganglioma-like patterns; ectopic ACTH syndrome and carcinoid syndrome (rare); carcinoid with elevated mitotic or Ki-67 index (rare, behaves like atypical); MEN1 association
entities.remarks: Fewer than 2 mitoses per 2 square mm and no necrosis, size at least 5 mm; low-grade malignant; excellent prognosis but nodal metastases possible; Ki-67 not a defining criterion in lung but useful in small biopsies to avoid SCLC misdiagnosis; MEN1 mutations.
entities.histo: Typical carcinoid is a low-grade neuroendocrine tumour of the lung, 5 mm or more in size, with fewer than 2 mitoses per 2 square mm and no necrosis. It occurs at any age, including young adults and children, without strong smoking association, and most arise centrally in main or lobar bronchi as polypoid, well-vascularised endobronchial masses that cause obstruction, haemoptysis or recurrent pneumonia, while peripheral tumours are often subpleural and spindle cell. Grossly the tumour is well circumscribed, tan-yellow and may extend through the bronchial wall (iceberg lesion). Microscopically it shows an organoid architecture of nests, trabeculae, rosettes, ribbons and palisades of uniform polygonal cells with moderate eosinophilic, finely granular cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei with finely granular salt-and-pepper chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli, in a richly vascular stroma that may be hyalinised, amyloid-rich or ossified. Morphological variants include spindle cell, oncocytic, clear cell, melanocytic, papillary, mucinous and sclerosing patterns. Nodal metastases occur in about 10 to 15 percent but prognosis is excellent after resection. DIPNECH may coexist in peripheral cases. Differentials include atypical carcinoid, small cell carcinoma and LCNEC in crushed biopsies, paraganglioma, glomus tumour, sclerosing pneumocytoma, salivary gland tumours, metastatic neuroendocrine tumours and metastatic breast or prostate carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows a monotonous population of loosely cohesive and single round to plasmacytoid or spindle cells with moderate granular cytoplasm, round nuclei with salt-and-pepper chromatin and small or inconspicuous nucleoli, often with naked nuclei, capillaries and rosettes, without necrosis or significant mitoses. Spindle cell carcinoids may mimic mesenchymal tumours, and crushed samples may be mistaken for small cell carcinoma. Cytology cannot reliably separate typical from atypical carcinoid. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (carcinoid tumour or neuroendocrine tumour, grade cannot be determined on cytology).
entities.ihc: IHC confirms neuroendocrine differentiation with diffuse chromogranin A, synaptophysin, INSM1 and CD56 positivity, and keratin positivity (often weaker or dot-like than in carcinomas); TTF-1 is positive in many peripheral carcinoids but often negative in central ones, and OTP and CD44 positivity are favourable prognostic markers. Ki-67 is usually below 5 percent and is especially useful in small, crushed biopsies to distinguish carcinoid from small cell carcinoma (over 50 percent). Rb is retained and p53 is wild-type, unlike high-grade NECs. SSTR2 IHC supports somatostatin analogue therapy, and ACTH IHC is used in ectopic Cushing syndrome. GATA3, CDX2 and ISL1 help exclude metastatic neuroendocrine tumours.

entities.variants: Atypical carcinoid with 2 to 10 mitoses per 2 square mm and/or punctate necrosis; carcinoid with elevated proliferation (over 10 mitoses per 2 square mm but carcinoid morphology, classified as LCNEC with a comment); central and peripheral
entities.remarks: Intermediate-grade NET; 2 to 10 mitoses per 2 square mm or punctate necrosis; nodal metastases in 40 to 50 percent; worse prognosis than typical carcinoid; MEN1 mutations.
entities.histo: Atypical carcinoid is an intermediate-grade neuroendocrine tumour of the lung with carcinoid morphology and either 2 to 10 mitoses per 2 square mm or foci of necrosis, which is usually punctate (comedo-like) within nests rather than extensive. Atypical carcinoids are less common than typical carcinoids, occur in older patients and are more often associated with smoking and peripheral location. Microscopically they show the same organoid architecture as typical carcinoid, with nests, trabeculae and rosettes of uniform cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin, but with more nuclear pleomorphism, occasional nucleoli and the defining mitotic activity or necrosis. Mitoses should be counted in the most active areas. Regional nodal metastases are present in 40 to 50 percent of cases, and five-year survival is lower than for typical carcinoid. Rare carcinoids with carcinoid morphology but more than 10 mitoses per 2 square mm are, by current WHO recommendation, classified as LCNEC with a note on carcinoid morphology, though they resemble carcinoids molecularly. Differentials include typical carcinoid, LCNEC (higher mitoses, extensive necrosis, large cells with nucleoli), small cell carcinoma and metastatic NET.
entities.cyto: Cytology is similar to typical carcinoid, with monotonous neuroendocrine cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin, but may show more atypia, occasional mitoses or necrosis; grading requires histology. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (carcinoid tumour or neuroendocrine tumour, grade cannot be determined on cytology).
entities.ihc: IHC shows diffuse chromogranin, synaptophysin and INSM1 positivity with keratin positivity and variable TTF-1. Ki-67 is typically between about 5 and 20 to 30 percent, and although not a WHO criterion for lung carcinoid, it helps separate carcinoids from high-grade NEC in small biopsies. Retained Rb and wild-type p53 favour carcinoid over LCNEC or SCLC. OTP and CD44 loss is associated with worse outcome. SSTR2 status is relevant for therapy and imaging.

entities.variants: Pure small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC); molecular subtypes by transcription factors (SCLC-A ASCL1, SCLC-N NEUROD1, SCLC-P POU2F3, SCLC-I inflamed); transformed SCLC from EGFR-mutant adenocarcinoma after TKI; paraneoplastic syndromes (SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis)
entities.remarks: Aggressive high-grade NEC strongly linked to smoking; central mass with bulky mediastinal nodes; small cells with scant cytoplasm, finely granular chromatin, absent nucleoli, nuclear moulding, crush artefact and very high mitoses (over 10 per 2 square mm; usually over 60); TP53 and RB1 inactivation; limited vs extensive stage.
entities.histo: Small cell lung carcinoma is a high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma accounting for about 15 percent of lung cancers, almost exclusively in heavy smokers. It usually arises centrally, with a perihilar mass, bulky mediastinal lymphadenopathy and early haematogenous metastases to brain, liver, bone and adrenals, and is frequently associated with paraneoplastic syndromes such as SIADH, ectopic ACTH secretion and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Grossly it is a soft, white-tan, necrotic mass spreading along bronchi and lymphatics. Microscopically there are sheets, nests, trabeculae and ribbons of small round, oval or spindle cells, usually less than the diameter of three resting lymphocytes, with scant cytoplasm, finely granular salt-and-pepper chromatin, absent or inconspicuous nucleoli, nuclear moulding, frequent apoptotic bodies, extensive necrosis and a very high mitotic rate (more than 10 per 2 square mm, often over 60). Crush artefact and the Azzopardi effect (basophilic DNA encrustation of vessel walls) are common. Rosettes and peripheral palisading may be seen. Nearly all tumours have biallelic TP53 and RB1 inactivation. Tumours are subtyped by transcription factor expression for research and emerging therapy. Differentials include LCNEC, basaloid SCC, NUT carcinoma, carcinoid with crush artefact, lymphoma, Ewing sarcoma and other small round cell tumours, Merkel cell carcinoma metastasis and chronic inflammation with crush.
entities.cyto: Cytology is highly characteristic and often diagnostic: loosely cohesive clusters, chains and single small cells with scant cytoplasm, high N:C ratio, finely granular chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, nuclear moulding, smearing (crush) artefact with nuclear streaks, apoptotic bodies, mitoses and necrotic background. Pitfalls include lymphocytes and lymphoma (single cells, lymphoglandular bodies), reserve cell hyperplasia, basaloid SCC, carcinoid and Merkel cell carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (small cell carcinoma).
entities.ihc: IHC confirms the diagnosis: pancytokeratin (dot-like perinuclear or weak), at least one neuroendocrine marker (synaptophysin, chromogranin A, INSM1, CD56; some SCLC are marker negative or POU2F3-type), TTF-1 positive in about 85 to 90 percent, Ki-67 very high (usually over 70 to 80 percent), Rb loss and aberrant p53 in most. CD45, CD99/NKX2.2, CK20 with neurofilament (Merkel cell), p40, NUT and SOX10 help exclude lymphoma, Ewing sarcoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, basaloid SCC, NUT carcinoma and melanoma. ASCL1, NEUROD1 and POU2F3 IHC define molecular subtypes, and DLL3 expression is a therapeutic target (tarlatamab). PD-L1 is not required for immunotherapy selection.

entities.variants: SCLC combined with adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma, LCNEC (at least 10 percent large cell component) or spindle/giant cell carcinoma; transformed SCLC after EGFR TKI in EGFR-mutant adenocarcinoma
entities.remarks: SCLC with any amount of non-small cell component (at least 10 percent if the component is LCNEC or large cell carcinoma); managed as SCLC; transformation from EGFR-mutant adenocarcinoma is a resistance mechanism.
entities.histo: Combined small cell carcinoma is small cell carcinoma admixed with a component of non-small cell carcinoma, which may be adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma, LCNEC or sarcomatoid carcinoma. Any proportion of adenocarcinoma, squamous or sarcomatoid carcinoma qualifies, whereas a large cell or LCNEC component must constitute at least 10 percent because of the morphological continuum between small and large neuroendocrine cells. The components may be intermixed or form separate areas. Clinically the tumour behaves and is treated like SCLC. A distinct scenario is histological transformation of EGFR-mutant (or ALK-rearranged) adenocarcinoma to SCLC or combined SCLC after targeted therapy, in which both components retain the original EGFR mutation and acquire RB1 and TP53 loss; recognising this in rebiopsies is crucial for treatment. Differentials include pure SCLC with crush artefact, LCNEC, collision tumours and NSCC with focal neuroendocrine differentiation.
entities.cyto: Cytology may show both small cell carcinoma cells and non-small cell cells (glandular or squamous), but proportions cannot be determined; such cases are reported as small cell carcinoma with a comment on a possible non-small cell component. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant.
entities.ihc: IHC demonstrates the components: neuroendocrine markers, high Ki-67 and Rb loss in the SCLC component, and TTF-1, napsin A or p40 in the non-small cell component. In patients with treated EGFR-mutant adenocarcinoma, EGFR mutation testing on the transformed tumour confirms its origin. PD-L1 and molecular testing of the NSCLC component may be considered. The combined diagnosis requires at least 10 percent large cell (LCNEC or large cell carcinoma) component, but any amount of adenocarcinoma, squamous carcinoma or sarcomatoid carcinoma suffices. RB1 and TP53 co-alteration is typical, and in EGFR- or ALK-driven transformation, the original driver is retained in both components.

entities.variants: LCNEC (resection diagnosis; on small biopsies NSCC with neuroendocrine morphology and markers, possible LCNEC); molecular subsets: SCLC-like (TP53 and RB1 inactivated) and NSCLC-like (TP53 with STK11, KEAP1, KRAS; RB1 retained); carcinoid-like LCNEC (carcinoid morphology with over 10 mitoses); LCNEC with non-neuroendocrine features
entities.remarks: High-grade NEC with neuroendocrine morphology (organoid nests, rosettes, palisading), large cells with nucleoli, over 10 mitoses per 2 square mm (median about 70), extensive necrosis and at least one neuroendocrine marker; prognosis similar to SCLC.
entities.histo: Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma is a high-grade non-small cell carcinoma with neuroendocrine morphology, defined by an organoid nesting, trabecular, rosette-like or peripheral palisading architecture, large cells with moderate to abundant cytoplasm, vesicular or coarse chromatin and frequently prominent nucleoli, a mitotic rate over 10 per 2 square mm (typically 60 to 80), extensive geographic necrosis, and immunohistochemical expression of at least one neuroendocrine marker. It occurs mainly in older heavy smokers, often as a peripheral mass, and has a prognosis similar to small cell carcinoma. The diagnosis is best made on resections; on small biopsies, NSCC with neuroendocrine morphology and positive markers is reported as possible LCNEC. Molecular studies show at least two subsets, SCLC-like with TP53 and RB1 inactivation and NSCLC-like with STK11, KEAP1 and KRAS mutations and retained Rb, which may respond differently to chemotherapy. Carcinoid-like tumours with high mitotic counts are classified as LCNEC with a comment. Differentials include atypical carcinoid (fewer mitoses), small cell carcinoma (scant cytoplasm, no nucleoli), solid adenocarcinoma and SCC with neuroendocrine marker expression without neuroendocrine morphology (NSCC with neuroendocrine differentiation, classified as NSCC), basaloid SCC and metastatic NEC.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows large malignant cells, singly and in loose clusters with rosettes or palisading, granular to coarse chromatin and frequent nucleoli, with necrosis and mitoses; it overlaps with poorly differentiated NSCC and with SCLC, and a definitive diagnosis usually requires histology; cytology reports NSCC with neuroendocrine features. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (NSCC, possible LCNEC, or neuroendocrine carcinoma).
entities.ihc: IHC requires at least one neuroendocrine marker (synaptophysin, chromogranin A, INSM1 or CD56, in at least 10 percent of cells for CD56 to count), with keratin positivity, TTF-1 positivity in about half, and Ki-67 usually 40 to 80 percent or more. Rb loss and p53 aberrancy identify the SCLC-like subset. p40 is negative or focal, and napsin A usually negative. Neuroendocrine markers should be applied only when neuroendocrine morphology is present, to avoid labelling NSCC with focal marker expression as LCNEC. PD-L1, DLL3 and NGS (STK11, KEAP1, KRAS) may be considered.

entities.variants: LCNEC combined with adenocarcinoma (commonest), squamous cell carcinoma, spindle or giant cell carcinoma
entities.remarks: LCNEC with a component of adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma or sarcomatoid carcinoma; combined LCNEC with SCLC is classified as combined SCLC.
entities.histo: Combined large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma is LCNEC admixed with a non-neuroendocrine non-small cell carcinoma component, most often adenocarcinoma, less frequently squamous cell carcinoma, spindle cell or giant cell carcinoma. When LCNEC is combined with small cell carcinoma, the tumour is classified as combined small cell carcinoma instead. The neuroendocrine component shows organoid nests, rosettes and palisading with high mitotic activity and necrosis and expresses neuroendocrine markers, while the non-neuroendocrine component shows conventional glandular or squamous differentiation. Clinical behaviour is similar to pure LCNEC. Molecular profiles of the two components are usually shared, indicating clonal relationship. Differentials include pure LCNEC, adenocarcinoma with focal neuroendocrine marker expression, combined SCLC and collision tumours.
entities.cyto: Cytology may show both neuroendocrine-type large cells and glandular or squamous malignant cells, but specific classification requires histology. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (NSCC with neuroendocrine features). Cytology may show large neuroendocrine-type cells forming rosettes and palisades together with gland-forming or keratinised cells, and the differential includes adenocarcinoma with neuroendocrine marker expression, combined SCLC and basaloid SCC, which require histology to resolve.
entities.ihc: IHC highlights the neuroendocrine component with synaptophysin, chromogranin A and INSM1 and high Ki-67, and the non-neuroendocrine component with TTF-1 and napsin A (adenocarcinoma) or p40 (squamous). Rb and p53 IHC may support molecular subsetting. Predictive testing (PD-L1, NGS) should include the adenocarcinoma component where present. Molecular profiling shows that combined LCNEC often has an NSCLC-like genotype (KRAS, STK11, KEAP1) when an adenocarcinoma component is present, which may influence chemotherapy choice. ALK and EGFR alterations are rare but should be tested in never-smokers.

entities.variants: Type I (purely cystic); type Ir (regressed cystic, no primitive cells); type II (cystic and solid); type III (purely solid); DICER1 tumour predisposition syndrome (cystic nephroma, ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour, multinodular goitre)
entities.remarks: Commonest primary lung malignancy of childhood (usually under 6 years); embryonal sarcoma with cambium layer and rhabdomyoblasts in type I, solid blastemal and anaplastic sarcoma in II and III; germline DICER1 mutation in most; type I may mimic CPAM type 4.
entities.histo: Pleuropulmonary blastoma is the most common primary malignant lung tumour of childhood, a dysontogenetic embryonal sarcoma that arises in the lung periphery or pleura, usually before the age of six years, and is strongly associated with germline DICER1 mutations as part of the DICER1 tumour predisposition syndrome. It progresses through three types. Type I is a purely cystic, multiloculated lesion in infants with thin septa lined by benign respiratory epithelium, beneath which lies a subepithelial cambium layer of small primitive mesenchymal cells, often with rhabdomyoblasts and nodules of immature cartilage; it can be mistaken for CPAM type 4. Type Ir is a regressed cystic lesion without primitive cells. Type II is mixed cystic and solid, and type III is entirely solid, composed of blastemal small round cells, embryonal rhabdomyosarcomatous areas, fascicles of spindle cell sarcoma, malignant cartilage nodules and anaplastic cells with large hyperchromatic nuclei and atypical mitoses. Types II and III have a much poorer prognosis than type I. Differentials include CPAM type 4, fetal lung interstitial tumour, congenital peribronchial myofibroblastic tumour, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, synovial sarcoma and pulmonary blastoma of adults (malignant epithelium).
entities.cyto: Cytology has a minimal role. Pleural fluid or FNA of solid types may show small round blue cells and pleomorphic anaplastic cells, which cannot be classified without histology. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (malignant small round cell or spindle cell neoplasm), or Non-diagnostic for cystic lesions.
entities.ihc: IHC is supportive: primitive and rhabdomyoblastic cells are desmin, myogenin and MyoD1 positive, cartilage is S100 positive, and anaplastic cells may show p53 overexpression; the lining epithelium is keratin and TTF-1 positive but non-neoplastic. Keratin negativity of the mesenchymal component excludes carcinoma and pulmonary blastoma. DICER1 testing (germline and tumour) is essential, and families should be offered genetic counselling and surveillance. TLE1 and SS18 fusion testing helps exclude synovial sarcoma.

entities.variants: Pulmonary artery intimal sarcoma (undifferentiated pleomorphic, myxoid, with osteosarcomatous, chondrosarcomatous, rhabdomyosarcomatous or angiosarcomatous differentiation); MDM2 amplification
entities.remarks: Malignant mesenchymal tumour arising in the intima of large pulmonary arteries, growing intraluminally and mimicking pulmonary thromboembolism; MDM2 amplified; poor prognosis.
entities.histo: Intimal sarcoma of the pulmonary artery is a rare malignant mesenchymal tumour arising from the intima of large elastic arteries, most commonly the pulmonary trunk and main pulmonary arteries. It grows predominantly intraluminally as a polypoid, gelatinous or firm mass along the vessel lumen, causing progressive obstruction that is frequently misdiagnosed clinically and radiologically as chronic pulmonary thromboembolism, and may extend into the right ventricle, lung parenchyma and distal arteries, metastasising to lung and distant sites. Microscopically it is usually a poorly differentiated or undifferentiated spindle and pleomorphic sarcoma with variable myxoid areas, mitoses and necrosis, often admixed with thrombus, and may show heterologous osteosarcomatous, chondrosarcomatous, rhabdomyosarcomatous or angiosarcomatous differentiation. MDM2 amplification is present in most cases. Prognosis is poor. Differentials include organised thrombus with reactive myofibroblasts, leiomyosarcoma of pulmonary artery, metastatic sarcoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma, and dedifferentiated liposarcoma involving vessels.
entities.cyto: Cytology has little role; endovascular biopsy or aspirate may yield atypical spindle and pleomorphic cells admixed with blood and fibrin, which require IHC. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant or Suspicious for malignancy (malignant spindle cell neoplasm). Endovascular aspiration or EBUS-guided sampling of the intraluminal mass can yield atypical spindle and pleomorphic cells mixed with blood and fibrin, and cell blocks should be prepared for MDM2 IHC and FISH, which can establish the diagnosis without surgery.
entities.ihc: IHC shows nuclear MDM2 positivity, often with CDK4, and MDM2 amplification by FISH confirms the diagnosis and distinguishes it from organised thrombus and most other sarcomas. Vimentin is positive and SMA variably positive, desmin is usually negative or focal, and keratins are negative or focal. Heterologous elements express relevant markers (SATB2, myogenin, ERG or CD31). PDGFRA amplification may also occur.

entities.entity: Pulmonary myxoid sarcoma with EWSR1::CREB1 fusion
entities.variants: Primary pulmonary myxoid sarcoma (endobronchial, usually low-grade)
entities.remarks: Rare, well-circumscribed often endobronchial tumour of reticular cords of spindle to stellate cells in myxoid stroma with lymphoplasmacytic rim; EWSR1::CREB1 fusion; usually indolent.
entities.histo: Pulmonary myxoid sarcoma with EWSR1::CREB1 fusion is a rare sarcoma of the lung, usually arising in young to middle-aged women as a well-circumscribed, lobulated mass often closely related to or within a bronchus. Grossly it is gelatinous and myxoid. Microscopically it shows lobules of a myxoid matrix containing reticular cords, strands and nests of mildly atypical spindle, stellate and polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, sometimes with more pleomorphic cells, surrounded by a fibrous pseudocapsule and a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate at the periphery. Mitoses are usually low and necrosis is uncommon. The tumour shares its EWSR1::CREB1 fusion with angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma, and some consider it closely related. Most behave indolently, though a minority metastasise. Differentials include extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma (NR4A3 rearrangement), angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma, myoepithelial tumours (myoepithelial markers, EWSR1 with other partners), myxoid liposarcoma, low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma and mucinous adenocarcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology would show stellate and spindle cells in abundant myxoid matrix with scattered lymphocytes, which is non-specific and may be mistaken for a mucinous carcinoma or myxoid sarcoma of other types. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant (myxoid spindle cell neoplasm).
entities.ihc: IHC is non-specific: vimentin positive, with EMA positive in some cases, and negative or focal keratin, S100, SMA, desmin and myogenin. Diagnosis is confirmed by EWSR1 rearrangement on FISH and EWSR1::CREB1 fusion by RNA sequencing. NR4A3 and MUC4 negativity help exclude extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma and low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma, and myoepithelial marker negativity helps exclude myoepithelial tumours.

entities.variants: Monophasic (spindle cell), biphasic and poorly differentiated (round cell) types; SS18::SSX1, SS18::SSX2 or SS18::SSX4 fusions
entities.remarks: Commonest primary sarcoma of lung in young adults; spindle cell fascicles with staghorn vessels; TLE1 and SS18::SSX-specific IHC; must exclude metastasis from soft tissue primary.
entities.histo: Primary synovial sarcoma of the lung and pleura is a rare high-grade sarcoma occurring in adolescents and young to middle-aged adults, presenting as a large, well-circumscribed mass, sometimes cystic or haemorrhagic, and requiring exclusion of a metastasis from an extrathoracic primary. Microscopically the monophasic type, which is commonest in the lung, consists of densely cellular fascicles of uniform, plump spindle cells with scant cytoplasm and overlapping ovoid hyperchromatic nuclei, with a haemangiopericytoma-like staghorn vascular pattern, wiry collagen, calcifications and mast cells. The biphasic type contains glandular or solid epithelial areas in addition, and the poorly differentiated type is composed of small round cells with high mitotic activity and necrosis. It is defined by the SS18::SSX fusion resulting from t(X;18). Differentials include solitary fibrous tumour (STAT6), MPNST (S100 patchy, H3K27me3 loss), spindle cell carcinoma and sarcomatoid mesothelioma, spindle cell carcinoid, pleuropulmonary blastoma, Ewing sarcoma (round cell variant) and leiomyosarcoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows cellular smears of uniform spindle to ovoid cells in tight clusters and singly, sometimes with branching capillaries and a few epithelial-like clusters in biphasic tumours, which require ancillary testing. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (malignant spindle cell neoplasm, ancillary testing recommended).
entities.ihc: IHC shows focal keratin and EMA positivity (even in monophasic tumours), strong diffuse nuclear TLE1, frequent CD99 and BCL2 positivity, with CD34 negativity, which helps distinguish it from SFT. SS18::SSX fusion-specific antibodies and SSX C-terminus IHC are highly sensitive and specific. Confirmation by FISH (SS18 break-apart) or RT-PCR or RNA NGS is recommended. STAT6, S100, SOX10, desmin and calretinin help exclude mimics.

entities.variants: Classic WWTR1::CAMTA1 fused EHE; YAP1::TFE3 fused EHE (vasoformative, more cytoplasm); multifocal bilateral nodules; pleural and hepatic involvement
entities.remarks: Low to intermediate-grade malignant vascular tumour; multiple bilateral small nodules in young women; cords of epithelioid cells with intracytoplasmic vacuoles (blister cells) in myxohyaline stroma, filling alveoli with a micropolypoid pattern; CAMTA1 nuclear IHC.
entities.histo: Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma is a malignant vascular tumour of low to intermediate grade that in the lung usually presents as multiple, bilateral, small, well-defined nodules, often in young to middle-aged women, sometimes with concurrent liver or pleural involvement. Grossly the nodules are firm, grey-white and cartilage-like. Microscopically they show a characteristic micropolypoid growth in which the tumour fills alveolar spaces and small airways and vessels, with a central sclerotic, hypocellular, myxohyaline or chondroid stroma and a more cellular periphery. Tumour cells are epithelioid, arranged in cords, nests and single cells, with eosinophilic cytoplasm and intracytoplasmic vacuoles (blister cells) representing primitive vascular lumens, sometimes containing red cells. Atypia is mild and mitoses are few; marked atypia, necrosis and high mitoses indicate aggressive behaviour. WWTR1::CAMTA1 fusion occurs in most cases, and YAP1::TFE3 fusion in a subset with more vasoformative architecture and abundant cytoplasm. Pleural involvement and haemorrhagic symptoms worsen prognosis. Differentials include metastatic carcinoma (signet-ring cells mimicking vacuoles), mucinous adenocarcinoma, epithelioid angiosarcoma, chondroid tumours, amyloid nodules and hyalinizing granuloma.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows epithelioid cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and intracytoplasmic vacuoles in a myxoid or hyaline background, which may resemble adenocarcinoma with signet-ring features. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant (with recommendation for vascular markers).
entities.ihc: IHC confirms endothelial differentiation with CD31, ERG, FLI1 and CD34 positivity; keratin (AE1/AE3, CAM5.2) is positive in up to a third of cases and can mislead towards carcinoma. Nuclear CAMTA1 IHC is a sensitive and specific surrogate for WWTR1::CAMTA1 fusion, and TFE3 nuclear staining identifies the YAP1::TFE3 subtype. TTF-1 and napsin A are negative. FISH or RNA sequencing confirms the fusion.

entities.variants: Primary pulmonary angiosarcoma (rare); metastatic angiosarcoma (heart, breast, skin, soft tissue; much commoner); epithelioid angiosarcoma; post-radiation angiosarcoma; pulmonary artery angiosarcoma
entities.remarks: Most lung angiosarcomas are metastatic, often presenting with haemoptysis and multiple haemorrhagic nodules; anastomosing atypical vascular channels or epithelioid sheets; ERG, CD31 positive.
entities.histo: Angiosarcoma in the lung is usually metastatic, from primaries in the heart, skin of the scalp, breast or soft tissues, and presents with multiple haemorrhagic nodules, haemoptysis, pneumothorax or diffuse alveolar haemorrhage; primary pulmonary angiosarcoma is very rare. Microscopically it shows irregular, anastomosing vascular channels dissecting through alveolar septa and lined by atypical, hyperchromatic, multilayered endothelial cells with papillary tufts, together with solid areas of spindle or epithelioid cells, extensive haemorrhage, haemosiderin and necrosis. Epithelioid angiosarcoma, composed of sheets of large epithelioid cells with prominent nucleoli and abundant cytoplasm, often mimics carcinoma. Haemorrhage can obscure the tumour, so biopsies are often non-diagnostic. Differentials include epithelioid haemangioendothelioma (lower grade, myxohyaline stroma), Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8), poorly differentiated carcinoma, melanoma, diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, organising haemorrhage with reactive granulation tissue and pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology is usually bloody, with scattered atypical spindle or epithelioid cells, sometimes forming vasoformative structures or containing intracytoplasmic red cells, and is frequently non-diagnostic or misinterpreted as carcinoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant; Non-diagnostic when only blood is present.
entities.ihc: IHC shows endothelial markers: ERG (nuclear, most specific), CD31, FLI1, with variable CD34 and D2-40. Keratin is often positive in epithelioid angiosarcoma, a major pitfall for carcinoma, so ERG and CD31 should be included in panels for poorly differentiated tumours with haemorrhage. MYC amplification (IHC or FISH) characterises post-radiation angiosarcoma. HHV-8 is negative (versus Kaposi sarcoma), and TTF-1 and p40 are negative.

entities.variants: AIDS-associated (epidemic) Kaposi sarcoma; iatrogenic (transplant-associated); classic and endemic forms rarely involve lung; patch, plaque and nodular stages
entities.remarks: HHV-8 driven vascular tumour; pulmonary involvement in AIDS with bronchovascular and pleural distribution, endobronchial violaceous plaques; spindle cells with slit-like vessels and extravasated red cells; LANA-1 positive.
entities.histo: Kaposi sarcoma is a locally aggressive, HHV-8 driven vascular neoplasm that involves the lungs mainly in patients with AIDS and, less often, in iatrogenically immunosuppressed transplant recipients, usually with concurrent skin or mucosal disease. Bronchoscopically it forms red-violet endobronchial plaques, and CT shows peribronchovascular and interlobular septal thickening, flame-shaped nodules and pleural effusions. Microscopically the lesions follow lymphatic routes along bronchovascular bundles, interlobular septa and pleura, and consist of fascicles of mildly atypical spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing extravasated red blood cells, with haemosiderin, hyaline globules (PAS-positive, diastase-resistant), plasma cells and lymphocytes. Early patch lesions show subtle proliferations of thin-walled vessels around pre-existing vessels. Biopsies are often small and haemorrhagic, and bronchoscopic biopsy can cause bleeding. Differentials include granulation tissue, organising pneumonia, angiosarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella), inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour and other spindle cell tumours.
entities.cyto: Cytology is rarely diagnostic; BAL and FNA may contain blood and a few bland spindle cells, and the diagnosis rests on bronchoscopic appearance and biopsy with HHV-8 IHC. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Non-diagnostic, Atypical or Suspicious for malignancy. BAL is mainly used to exclude coexisting opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis, CMV and mycobacteria, which frequently accompany pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma in AIDS.
entities.ihc: IHC is diagnostic: nuclear HHV-8 latency-associated nuclear antigen (LANA-1) is positive in the spindle cells, together with CD31, CD34, ERG, FLI1 and D2-40. Warthin-Starry stain helps exclude bacillary angiomatosis. Keratin is negative. HIV status should be confirmed. CD34 and D2-40 are positive in most cases, and the proliferation index is low to moderate. Additional markers of lymphatic differentiation (PROX1) support the lymphatic endothelial phenotype, while SMA highlights the pericytic layer. LANA-1 positivity separates it from angiosarcoma and from granulation tissue in biopsies of patients with AIDS.

entities.variants: Malignant PEComa of lung (primary or metastatic from uterus, retroperitoneum, kidney); TFE3-rearranged PEComa; TSC2-altered PEComa
entities.remarks: Rare; PEComa with size over 5 cm, infiltration, high nuclear grade, necrosis and mitoses over 1 per 50 HPF; HMB45, melan-A, cathepsin K positive; often responds to mTOR inhibitors.
entities.histo: Malignant PEComa is a rare malignant perivascular epithelioid cell tumour. Primary malignant PEComa of the lung is exceptional, and lung nodules more often represent metastases from uterine, retroperitoneal or renal primaries. Features associated with malignant behaviour include size over 5 cm, infiltrative growth, high nuclear grade and cellularity, necrosis, vascular invasion and a mitotic rate over 1 per 50 high-power fields. Microscopically the tumour shows sheets and nests of epithelioid and spindle cells with clear to granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, pleomorphic nuclei with prominent nucleoli, multinucleated cells, mitoses and necrosis, arranged around vessels. TSC2 alterations and TFE3 rearrangements are the two main molecular groups. Malignant PEComas may respond to mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus or nab-sirolimus. Differentials include benign PEComa, metastatic melanoma, metastatic clear cell renal carcinoma, epithelioid leiomyosarcoma, alveolar soft part sarcoma (TFE3) and clear cell sarcoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows atypical epithelioid cells with clear to granular cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli, sometimes with intranuclear inclusions, which mimic melanoma or carcinoma and require cell block IHC. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (malignant neoplasm, ancillary testing recommended).
entities.ihc: IHC shows a melanocytic and myoid phenotype: HMB45, melan-A, MITF and cathepsin K positivity, with variable SMA, desmin and caldesmon, and negative keratins and PAX8 (versus renal carcinoma) and SOX10 and S100 (largely, versus melanoma). TFE3 nuclear IHC and FISH identify TFE3-rearranged tumours, which also need to be separated from alveolar soft part sarcoma (TFE3 positive, myogenic markers negative, ASPSCR1::TFE3). Ki-67 is raised.

entities.entity: Other primary sarcomas of lung and airway
entities.variants: Leiomyosarcoma (bronchial, parenchymal, pulmonary artery or vein); rhabdomyosarcoma (embryonal in children, trachea; pleomorphic in adults); chondrosarcoma (bronchial or tracheal); osteosarcoma (extraskeletal); malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour; fibrosarcoma and myxofibrosarcoma; undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma; Ewing sarcoma and round cell sarcomas (CIC- and BCOR-rearranged); desmoplastic small round cell tumour (rare); liposarcoma (rare); malignant solitary fibrous tumour (see SFT row); malignant glomus tumour; alveolar soft part sarcoma (usually metastatic); follicular dendritic cell sarcoma (rare)
entities.remarks: Primary pulmonary sarcomas are rare and diagnosis requires exclusion of metastatic sarcoma and sarcomatoid carcinoma or mesothelioma; classify per WHO Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours.
entities.histo: Primary sarcomas of the lung and airways are rare, accounting for well under 1 percent of lung malignancies, and the diagnosis requires exclusion of metastasis from a soft tissue or bone primary and of sarcomatoid carcinoma or mesothelioma. Leiomyosarcoma, the commonest, arises from bronchial walls, parenchyma or pulmonary vessels and shows fascicles of atypical spindle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, blunt nuclei, mitoses and necrosis. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma occurs in the trachea and bronchi of children and must be distinguished from pleuropulmonary blastoma, while pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma occurs in adults. Chondrosarcoma may arise from bronchial or tracheal cartilage. Osteosarcoma, MPNST, fibrosarcoma, myxofibrosarcoma and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma are very rare. Ewing sarcoma and CIC- or BCOR-rearranged round cell sarcomas can present as chest wall or lung masses in young patients. These tumours are classified according to the WHO Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours volume. Differentials include sarcomatoid carcinoma, sarcomatoid mesothelioma, synovial sarcoma, intimal sarcoma, metastatic sarcomas and melanoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows malignant spindle, pleomorphic or round cells depending on type, and classification requires cell block IHC and molecular tests; round cell sarcomas may mimic small cell carcinoma or lymphoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (malignant mesenchymal neoplasm suspected).
entities.ihc: IHC is type specific: leiomyosarcoma (SMA, desmin, h-caldesmon), rhabdomyosarcoma (desmin, myogenin, MyoD1), chondrosarcoma (S100, SOX9; IDH1/2 mutations), osteosarcoma (SATB2), MPNST (patchy S100 and SOX10, H3K27me3 loss), Ewing sarcoma (CD99 membranous, NKX2.2; EWSR1 FISH), CIC-rearranged sarcoma (WT1, ETV4, DUX4) and BCOR sarcoma (BCOR, SATB2). Keratin, p40, TTF-1, calretinin and WT1 help exclude sarcomatoid carcinoma and mesothelioma. Molecular testing (FISH, RNA NGS) is often required.

entities.variants: Primary melanoma of bronchus or lung (requires exclusion of metastasis; junctional activity in bronchial mucosa); BRAF, NRAS, KIT mutations
entities.remarks: Very rare; most pulmonary melanomas are metastatic; criteria for primary include solitary central lesion, junctional or in situ component in bronchial epithelium and no other primary after thorough search.
entities.histo: Primary melanoma of the lung is exceedingly rare and listed in the WHO classification under tumours of ectopic tissues, whereas metastatic melanoma to the lung is common. Proposed criteria for a primary tumour include a solitary, usually endobronchial or central lesion, demonstration of junctional change or an in situ component in the overlying bronchial epithelium, absence of a previous or current cutaneous, mucosal or ocular melanoma after thorough clinical examination, and consistent morphology. Microscopically the tumour consists of sheets and nests of epithelioid or spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, large vesicular nuclei with prominent macronucleoli, intranuclear pseudoinclusions and variable brown melanin pigment, with frequent mitoses and necrosis. Prognosis is poor. Differentials include metastatic melanoma (the most important), melanocytic carcinoid, PEComa, clear cell sarcoma, poorly differentiated carcinoma, epithelioid angiosarcoma and pigmented schwannoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows discohesive epithelioid or spindle cells with macronucleoli, intranuclear inclusions, binucleation and fine dusty melanin pigment, which can be confirmed by cell block IHC; amelanotic tumours mimic carcinoma or lymphoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (melanoma).
entities.ihc: IHC shows SOX10 and S100 positivity (most sensitive), with HMB45, melan-A, PRAME and MITF variably positive, and negative keratins, TTF-1 and CD45. Melanocytic carcinoids are neuroendocrine marker positive with variable melanocytic markers, so chromogranin and synaptophysin should be included. BRAF V600E (VE1 IHC or molecular testing), NRAS and KIT status guide therapy, and PD-L1 is not required for immunotherapy in melanoma.

entities.entity: Intrapulmonary thymoma and ectopic thymic tumours
entities.variants: Intrapulmonary thymoma (types A, AB, B1, B2, B3 per WHO thymic classification); pleural thymoma; ectopic thymic carcinoma (rare)
entities.remarks: Rare thymoma arising within lung parenchyma or hilum, without mediastinal thymic tumour; may have myasthenia gravis; morphology and IHC identical to mediastinal thymoma.
entities.histo: Intrapulmonary thymoma is a rare tumour arising from ectopic thymic tissue within the lung or visceral pleura, without a mediastinal thymic mass, and is classified using the WHO thymic epithelial tumour classification. It presents as a peripheral or hilar well-circumscribed nodule, sometimes with myasthenia gravis or other paraneoplastic autoimmune disorders. Microscopically it has the same histological types as mediastinal thymoma: type A (bland spindle epithelial cells, few lymphocytes), type AB (mixed lymphocyte-poor spindle areas and lymphocyte-rich areas), and types B1, B2 and B3 with increasing epithelial cell content and atypia, in a lobulated architecture with fibrous septa, perivascular spaces and medullary islands. All thymomas are regarded as malignant with variable potential for recurrence. Differentials include spindle cell carcinoid, solitary fibrous tumour, synovial sarcoma, lymphoma (lymphocyte-rich types), sclerosing pneumocytoma, metastatic thymoma and lymphoepithelial carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows a dual population of epithelial cells (spindle or polygonal) and immature T lymphocytes in variable proportion, which can be mistaken for lymphoma (lymphocyte-rich types) or a spindle cell tumour (type A). WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant (thymic epithelial tumour suspected), with flow cytometry and IHC.
entities.ihc: IHC shows epithelial cells positive for pancytokeratin, p63, p40 and PAX8 (often), with CD5 and CD117 usually negative in thymoma (positive in thymic carcinoma). Lymphocytes are immature T cells positive for TdT, CD1a, CD99 and CD3, distinguishing them from lymphoma. Type A thymoma is CD20 positive in epithelial cells in some cases. TTF-1 is negative, and neuroendocrine markers, STAT6 and SS18::SSX testing exclude carcinoid, SFT and synovial sarcoma.

entities.entity: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of MALT (pulmonary MALT lymphoma)
entities.variants: Bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (BALT) lymphoma; with plasmacytic differentiation; with amyloid deposition; tracheal MALT lymphoma; association with Sjogren syndrome and other autoimmune diseases
entities.remarks: Commonest primary pulmonary lymphoma; indolent; lymphangitic spread along bronchovascular bundles and septa, lymphoepithelial lesions, monocytoid and plasmacytoid cells, may have amyloid; light chain restriction; MALT1 translocations.
entities.histo: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue is the most common primary lymphoma of the lung, arising from acquired bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue, often in older adults and in patients with Sjogren syndrome, other autoimmune diseases or chronic antigenic stimulation. It presents as single or multiple nodules, consolidation with air bronchograms, or ground-glass opacities, and is usually indolent. Microscopically there is a dense, monotonous infiltrate of small B cells, including centrocyte-like cells, monocytoid cells with pale cytoplasm and plasmacytoid cells, which spreads in a lymphangitic pattern along bronchovascular bundles, interlobular septa and pleura and then expands to obliterate alveoli. Lymphoepithelial lesions in bronchiolar epithelium, reactive follicles colonised by neoplastic cells, Dutcher bodies, prominent plasmacytic differentiation, amyloid deposits and giant-cell granulomas may be present. Large cell transformation is diagnosed when sheets of large cells occur. Differentials include lymphoid interstitial pneumonia, follicular bronchiolitis, nodular lymphoid hyperplasia, IgG4-related disease, lymphomatoid granulomatosis, small lymphocytic lymphoma, mantle cell and follicular lymphoma, and amyloidoma or light chain deposition disease.
entities.cyto: BAL or FNA shows a monotonous population of small lymphoid cells with some monocytoid and plasmacytoid forms, which on morphology alone is difficult to separate from reactive lymphoid proliferations; flow cytometry of BAL or aspirate showing light chain restricted B cells strongly supports the diagnosis. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical or Suspicious for malignancy, or Malignant when flow cytometry or clonality supports lymphoma.
entities.ihc: IHC shows neoplastic cells positive for CD20, CD79a, PAX5 and BCL2, and negative for CD5, CD10, BCL6, cyclin D1, SOX11 and CD23 (which also highlights disrupted follicular dendritic cell meshworks). Keratin staining highlights lymphoepithelial lesions. Plasmacytic cells show light chain restriction by kappa and lambda IHC or ISH, and IgG4 should be checked to exclude IgG4-related disease. Ki-67 is low. Clonal IGH rearrangement by PCR and MALT1 translocations, especially t(11;18) BIRC3::MALT1, by FISH support the diagnosis. Congo red is used if amyloid is suspected.

entities.variants: Primary pulmonary DLBCL; DLBCL transformed from MALT lymphoma; secondary lung involvement by systemic DLBCL; germinal centre and activated B-cell types; EBV-positive DLBCL; fibrin-associated or pyothorax-associated forms (pleural)
entities.remarks: Second commonest primary pulmonary lymphoma; sheets of large atypical B cells with necrosis and vascular invasion; may arise from MALT lymphoma; more aggressive.
entities.histo: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the lung may be primary, may arise by transformation of MALT lymphoma, or more commonly represents secondary involvement by systemic disease. Primary pulmonary DLBCL presents as a solitary or multiple masses, often with symptoms, and can be bilateral. Microscopically there are diffuse sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells, two or more times the size of a normal lymphocyte, with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, centroblastic or immunoblastic features and frequent mitoses, effacing lung architecture and invading vessel walls, bronchi and pleura, with necrosis. A residual MALT lymphoma component may be seen at the periphery. EBV-positive cases and those in immunosuppressed patients must be distinguished from lymphomatoid granulomatosis and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder. Differentials include poorly differentiated carcinoma, small cell carcinoma (crush artefact), LCNEC, melanoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma, lymphomatoid granulomatosis grade 3 and myeloid sarcoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows dispersed large atypical lymphoid cells with scant basophilic cytoplasm, vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli, numerous lymphoglandular bodies and apoptotic debris, which can be confirmed by flow cytometry and cell block IHC. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (large B-cell lymphoma, ancillary studies recommended).
entities.ihc: IHC shows CD45, CD20, PAX5 and CD79a positivity, with cell-of-origin subtyping using the Hans algorithm (CD10, BCL6, MUM1), and BCL2 and MYC expression to identify double-expressor lymphomas. Ki-67 is high. EBER ISH identifies EBV-positive cases. CD30 and CD15 help exclude Hodgkin lymphoma and ALCL, keratin and neuroendocrine markers exclude carcinoma, and SOX10 excludes melanoma. FISH for MYC, BCL2 and BCL6 rearrangements identifies high-grade B-cell lymphomas.

entities.variants: Grade 1 (few EBV+ large B cells, under 5 per HPF); grade 2 (5 to 50 EBV+ cells per HPF); grade 3 (over 50 EBV+ cells per HPF or sheets; managed as DLBCL); skin, CNS and kidney involvement
entities.remarks: EBV-driven angiocentric and angiodestructive B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder with T-cell-rich background; multiple bilateral lung nodules with necrosis; graded by number of EBV+ large B cells.
entities.histo: Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is an EBV-driven, angiocentric and angiodestructive lymphoproliferative disorder composed of EBV-positive large B cells in a prominent background of reactive T cells, typically in adults with underlying immune dysfunction. The lungs are involved in nearly all cases, with multiple bilateral nodules, often cavitating, and the skin, central nervous system, kidneys and liver may also be affected, while lymph nodes and spleen are usually spared. Microscopically the nodules show a polymorphous infiltrate of small lymphocytes, plasma cells, histiocytes and scattered large atypical B cells, which infiltrates and destroys vessel walls (angiocentric and angiodestructive), with geographic infarct-like necrosis. Despite the name, true well-formed granulomas are absent. Grading depends on the number of EBV-positive large B cells per high-power field: grade 1 under 5, grade 2 between 5 and 50, and grade 3 more than 50 or forming sheets, which behaves as a large B-cell lymphoma. Differentials include granulomatosis with polyangiitis (necrotising granulomatous inflammation, vasculitis, neutrophils), extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, DLBCL, Hodgkin lymphoma, PTLD, infection and other EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorders.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role; aspirates show a mixed population of small lymphocytes, histiocytes and occasional atypical large cells with necrosis, which cannot be distinguished from reactive or granulomatous inflammation. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical or Non-diagnostic; surgical or core biopsy is needed.
entities.ihc: IHC shows the large atypical cells positive for CD20, CD79a and PAX5, with variable CD30, and negative CD15, in a background of CD3-positive T cells (CD4 more than CD8). EBER in situ hybridisation is essential for grading by counting EBV-positive cells per high-power field. Elastic stains highlight vascular destruction, and special stains for fungi and mycobacteria exclude infection. ANCA serology helps exclude GPA. Clonal IG rearrangement is often found in grades 2 and 3. CD56 and EBER in T or NK cells point to extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma instead.

entities.variants: Classic (Western) form; haemophagocytic syndrome-associated (Asian) variant; cutaneous variant; lung-limited presentations
entities.remarks: Rare aggressive lymphoma with large B cells confined to lumina of small vessels including alveolar capillaries; presents with hypoxaemia, fever, unexplained pulmonary hypertension; random transbronchial or skin biopsy may be diagnostic.
entities.histo: Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma is a rare, aggressive extranodal large B-cell lymphoma in which neoplastic cells grow almost exclusively within the lumina of small blood vessels, particularly capillaries, without forming a mass. Pulmonary involvement may cause hypoxaemia, dyspnoea, fever, interstitial or ground-glass opacities, or unexplained pulmonary hypertension, while radiology can be nearly normal, and diagnosis is often delayed or made at autopsy. Microscopically alveolar septal capillaries and small arteries and veins are filled and distended by large atypical lymphoid cells with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli and frequent mitoses, which may be subtle at low magnification and mistaken for leucocytes in septal capillaries or interstitial pneumonia. Some cases show fibrin thrombi and haemorrhage. Random transbronchial lung biopsy and random skin biopsy have been used for diagnosis. Differentials include intravascular spread of other lymphomas, leukaemic infiltration, intravascular carcinomatosis or tumour thrombotic microangiopathy, interstitial pneumonia, and intravascular NK/T-cell lymphoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has essentially no role because tumour cells remain intravascular and rarely enter BAL fluid; diagnosis depends on tissue biopsy with IHC. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Non-diagnostic or Benign (reactive) in most samples. Bone marrow aspirate and peripheral blood occasionally show tumour cells, and bone marrow biopsy, random skin biopsies and transbronchial biopsy are preferred over cytology for diagnosis; high LDH and soluble IL-2 receptor levels support the clinical suspicion.
entities.ihc: IHC is central to recognition: CD20 and PAX5 highlight intravascular large B cells, with CD31 or CD34 outlining the vessel walls around them, and most cases are non-germinal centre type with MUM1 positivity, frequent CD5 expression and negative CD10. Ki-67 is high. CD3 and CD56 identify the rare NK/T-cell intravascular lymphoma, and keratins exclude intravascular carcinoma.

entities.variants: Secondary pulmonary involvement by nodal classic Hodgkin lymphoma (most cases, usually nodular sclerosis); primary pulmonary Hodgkin lymphoma (rare); nodular lymphocyte predominant B-cell lymphoma (rare)
entities.remarks: Lung usually involved by contiguous spread from mediastinal or hilar nodes; nodules with Reed-Sternberg cells in a mixed inflammatory background, sclerosis and necrosis; primary pulmonary Hodgkin very rare.
entities.histo: Hodgkin lymphoma involves the lung most often as secondary spread from mediastinal or hilar lymph nodes, usually in nodular sclerosis classic Hodgkin lymphoma, either by direct extension or as separate nodules, and primary pulmonary Hodgkin lymphoma without nodal disease is very rare. Radiology shows nodules, masses, consolidations or cavitating lesions. Microscopically the lesions contain scattered large Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells, which are binucleate or multinucleate with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, and mononuclear and lacunar variants, in a polymorphous background of small lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells, histiocytes and neutrophils, with fibrosis, granuloma-like histiocytic aggregates and necrosis. Infiltration along bronchovascular bundles and destruction of bronchial walls can occur. Differentials include granulomatous infections, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, lymphomatoid granulomatosis, DLBCL, T-cell lymphomas, anaplastic large cell lymphoma, IgG4-related disease and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour.
entities.cyto: Cytology may show scattered large binucleate or multinucleate cells with macronucleoli in a mixed inflammatory background of lymphocytes and eosinophils, which can suggest the diagnosis, but tissue is needed for classification. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant (Hodgkin lymphoma suspected).
entities.ihc: IHC of the Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells shows CD30 and CD15 positivity, weak PAX5 (dim nuclear staining compared with background B cells), MUM1 positivity, and negative CD45, CD20 (or weak and variable), CD3 and ALK. EBER ISH is positive in a subset. Nodular lymphocyte predominant tumours are CD20, OCT2, BOB1 and CD45 positive with negative CD30 and CD15. ALK and T-cell markers help exclude anaplastic large cell lymphoma, and special stains for fungi and mycobacteria exclude infection.

entities.variants: Non-destructive PTLD (plasmacytic hyperplasia, infectious mononucleosis-like, florid follicular hyperplasia); polymorphic PTLD; monomorphic PTLD (DLBCL, Burkitt, plasma cell neoplasms, T/NK-cell types); classic Hodgkin lymphoma-type PTLD; lung allograft and other organ recipients
entities.remarks: EBV-driven lymphoid proliferation after solid organ or stem cell transplantation; the lung allograft is a frequent site in lung transplant recipients; must be distinguished from acute rejection.
entities.histo: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders are lymphoid or plasmacytic proliferations arising in the setting of immunosuppression after solid organ or haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, most of which are EBV-driven, especially those occurring early after transplantation. In lung transplant recipients the allograft is a common site, presenting as single or multiple nodules, frequently in the first year. The spectrum includes non-destructive lesions (plasmacytic hyperplasia, infectious mononucleosis-like and florid follicular hyperplasia) that preserve architecture; polymorphic PTLD, a destructive mixed infiltrate of small and large lymphocytes, immunoblasts and plasma cells with necrosis that does not meet criteria for lymphoma; monomorphic PTLD, which fulfils criteria for a specific lymphoma (most commonly DLBCL, also Burkitt, plasma cell neoplasm or T/NK-cell lymphoma); and classic Hodgkin lymphoma-type PTLD. Reduction in immunosuppression may cause regression of early lesions. Differentials include acute cellular rejection (perivascular and interstitial T-cell infiltrates without destructive B-cell masses), infection (CMV, fungal), organising pneumonia and recurrent primary disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology from FNA or BAL may show a mixed or monotonous population of atypical lymphoid cells and plasma cells, which with flow cytometry may suggest a lymphoproliferative disorder, but tissue biopsy is required to classify it. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical, Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant depending on cellular composition and ancillary studies.
entities.ihc: IHC uses CD20, PAX5, CD79a, CD3, CD138 and kappa and lambda light chains to characterise the infiltrate, together with CD30 and CD15 in Hodgkin-like lesions, and Ki-67. EBER ISH is essential, being positive in most early cases. Clonality testing (IG and TR gene rearrangement), MYC FISH in Burkitt-like lesions, and correlation with peripheral blood EBV viral load help classification. C4d, CMV and fungal stains assist in excluding rejection and infection.

entities.entity: Plasma cell neoplasms of lung and airway
