entities.variants: Extramedullary (extraosseous) plasmacytoma of lung, trachea or bronchus; pulmonary involvement by plasma cell myeloma; plasmacytoma with amyloid; light chain deposition disease (non-amyloid, see deposits)
entities.remarks: Rare; sheets of monoclonal plasma cells, sometimes with amyloid; exclude MALT lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation and systemic myeloma.
entities.histo: Plasma cell neoplasms of the lung and airway are rare and include solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma arising in the lung parenchyma, trachea or bronchi, and secondary pulmonary involvement by plasma cell myeloma, which may present as nodules, consolidation or pleural effusion. Microscopically there are diffuse sheets of mature to immature plasma cells with eccentric nuclei, clock-face chromatin, perinuclear hofs and abundant amphophilic cytoplasm, sometimes with binucleation, Dutcher and Russell bodies, plasmablastic forms and associated amyloid deposits. The diagnosis of solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma requires exclusion of systemic myeloma by bone marrow examination, imaging and serum and urine studies. Differentials include MALT lymphoma with extensive plasmacytic differentiation (presence of a B-cell component and lymphoepithelial lesions), plasma cell granuloma or inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour, IgG4-related disease, Castleman disease, plasmablastic lymphoma, nodular amyloid and mucous membrane plasmacytosis of the trachea.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows numerous discohesive plasma cells, often with atypical, immature or binucleate forms, which with flow cytometry or cell block light chain studies can confirm monotypia. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (plasma cell neoplasm) when monoclonality is confirmed; otherwise Atypical.
entities.ihc: IHC shows CD138, CD38 and MUM1 positivity, with frequent CD56 and cyclin D1 expression and negative or weak CD19, CD20 and PAX5. Kappa and lambda IHC or ISH demonstrates light chain restriction. CD20 and PAX5 identify a B-cell component that points to MALT lymphoma. IgG4 staining excludes IgG4-related disease, and EBER and CD20-negative plasmablastic morphology suggest plasmablastic lymphoma. Congo red stain detects associated amyloid.

entities.entity: Leukaemic infiltration and myeloid sarcoma of lung
entities.variants: Pulmonary leukaemic infiltrates (AML, ALL, CLL, hairy cell leukaemia, adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma); myeloid sarcoma (granulocytic sarcoma; chloroma); pulmonary leukostasis; blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (rare); mast cell infiltrates (systemic mastocytosis, rare)
entities.remarks: Lung involvement in leukaemia is common at autopsy, often in bronchovascular and septal distribution; myeloid sarcoma forms a mass of myeloid blasts; leukostasis occurs in hyperleucocytosis.
entities.histo: Leukaemic infiltration of the lung is frequent in patients with acute and chronic leukaemias, particularly at autopsy, but is often overshadowed clinically by infection, haemorrhage and drug toxicity. Infiltrates characteristically follow lymphatic routes along bronchovascular bundles, interlobular septa and pleura, and may extend into alveolar septa and spaces. In hyperleucocytic AML, pulmonary leukostasis shows small vessels packed with blasts, with associated haemorrhage and hypoxaemia. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia gives monotonous small lymphocytic infiltrates in a lymphangitic pattern. Myeloid sarcoma is a tumour mass of myeloid blasts, with or without maturation, that occurs extramedullarily, sometimes preceding or heralding relapse of AML, and appears as sheets of immature cells with fine chromatin, small nucleoli and scant cytoplasm, sometimes with eosinophilic myelocytes as a clue. Differentials include lymphoma (DLBCL, lymphoblastic lymphoma), small cell carcinoma, poorly differentiated carcinoma, extramedullary haematopoiesis and infection with inflammatory infiltrates.
entities.cyto: BAL or FNA may contain blasts or atypical lymphoid cells, confirmed by flow cytometry, and peripheral blood correlation is essential. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant when blasts or a clonal population are confirmed; Atypical otherwise. Pleural fluid and BAL samples can show blasts, which should be quantified and characterised by flow cytometry; infections and drug reactions should be excluded in parallel, since these are more common than leukaemic infiltrates as causes of pulmonary infiltrates in leukaemia.
entities.ihc: IHC for myeloid sarcoma includes myeloperoxidase, lysozyme, CD33, CD117, CD34, CD68 (KP1) and CD43, with CD45 positivity and negative CD20 and CD3; CD14, CD163 and CD4 indicate monocytic differentiation, and CD123, CD4, CD56 and TCF4 identify blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm. Lymphoid leukaemias are characterised with CD20, CD5, CD23, LEF1 (CLL), TdT and CD10 (lymphoblastic), annexin A1 and CD103 (hairy cell), and CD3, CD4, CD25 (ATLL). CD117 and tryptase identify mast cells. Molecular and cytogenetic studies should be correlated with marrow findings. Chloroacetate esterase stain highlights myeloid cells.

entities.variants: Follicular lymphoma; mantle cell lymphoma; small lymphocytic lymphoma; lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma; Burkitt lymphoma; lymphoblastic lymphoma; peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS; anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALK+ and ALK-); extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (nasal type); angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma; adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma; primary effusion lymphoma and extracavitary PEL (pleural); mycosis fungoides involving lung
entities.remarks: Lung is involved secondarily by many systemic lymphomas, usually in a lymphangitic pattern; primary forms are rare; classification follows WHO haematolymphoid tumour criteria.
entities.histo: Many systemic non-Hodgkin lymphomas involve the lung secondarily, while primary pulmonary forms other than MALT lymphoma, DLBCL and lymphomatoid granulomatosis are rare. Low-grade B-cell lymphomas such as follicular, mantle cell, small lymphocytic and lymphoplasmacytic lymphomas produce monotonous small cell infiltrates distributed along bronchovascular bundles, septa and pleura and forming nodules, with morphology similar to nodal disease. Aggressive B-cell lymphomas such as Burkitt and lymphoblastic lymphoma give sheets of medium-sized blasts with high mitotic and apoptotic activity. T-cell lymphomas, including peripheral T-cell lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma (large hallmark cells with horseshoe nuclei), extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (angiocentric, angiodestructive with necrosis) and adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma, may produce nodules, interstitial infiltrates or angiodestructive lesions. Primary effusion lymphoma, related to HHV-8, typically involves pleural effusions without a mass. Differentials include reactive lymphoid hyperplasias, MALT lymphoma, lymphomatoid granulomatosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, small cell carcinoma and poorly differentiated carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology of BAL, pleural fluid or FNA with flow cytometry and cell block IHC can establish the diagnosis of lymphoma in many cases, particularly in effusions and in patients with known systemic disease. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (lymphoma, with subtype from ancillary tests) or Suspicious for malignancy.
entities.ihc: IHC panels are subtype specific: follicular lymphoma (CD10, BCL6, BCL2), mantle cell lymphoma (CD5, cyclin D1, SOX11), small lymphocytic lymphoma (CD5, CD23, LEF1), lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (MYD88 L265P), Burkitt lymphoma (CD10, BCL6, MYC, Ki-67 near 100 percent, BCL2 negative), lymphoblastic lymphoma (TdT, CD34, CD99), ALCL (CD30 uniform, ALK, EMA), NK/T-cell lymphoma (CD56, cytoplasmic CD3, TIA1, granzyme B, EBER), angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (PD1, CXCL13, ICOS, CD10), ATLL (CD4, CD25, HTLV-1 serology) and primary effusion lymphoma (HHV-8, CD138, CD30, with loss of B-cell markers). Clonality testing and FISH (BCL2, CCND1, MYC) support diagnosis.

entities.variants: Sporadic LAM (women of reproductive age, somatic TSC2 mutations); tuberous sclerosis complex-associated LAM (TSC-LAM); with angiomyolipoma; chylous effusions; multifocal micronodular pneumocyte hyperplasia in TSC (separate entity)
entities.remarks: Low-grade, destructive, metastasizing PEComatous neoplasm of women; diffuse thin-walled cysts; nodules of spindle and epithelioid LAM cells along cyst walls, lymphatics and vessels; HMB45 and cathepsin K positive, ER/PR positive; serum VEGF-D raised; sirolimus therapy.
entities.histo: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis is a low-grade, slowly progressive, metastasizing PEComatous neoplasm that occurs almost exclusively in women, either sporadically (with somatic TSC2 mutations) or in association with tuberous sclerosis complex, and is driven by mTOR pathway activation. It presents with progressive dyspnoea, recurrent pneumothorax, chylothorax or chylous ascites, and renal angiomyolipomas may coexist. CT shows numerous diffuse thin-walled round cysts throughout both lungs. Microscopically the cysts are lined by or have walls containing small nodules and bundles of LAM cells, which are plump spindle cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm resembling immature smooth muscle, together with epithelioid cells with clear to granular cytoplasm, arranged around lymphatic channels, bronchioles and small vessels. The proliferation obstructs airways and lymphatics, causes cyst formation and haemosiderin deposition from haemorrhage, and may involve axial lymph nodes, with lymphangioleiomyomas in the retroperitoneum. Elevated serum VEGF-D supports the diagnosis and sirolimus slows progression. Differentials include emphysema, pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis, Birt-Hogg-Dube cysts, benign metastasizing leiomyoma, lymphoid interstitial pneumonia cysts, light chain deposition disease and diffuse pulmonary lymphangiomatosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a very limited role; chylous pleural fluid may rarely contain clusters of LAM cells (LAM cell clusters covered by lymphatic endothelium), which can be confirmed by HMB45 on cell block. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Non-diagnostic or Atypical for most samples; diagnosis relies on CT, VEGF-D and biopsy.
entities.ihc: IHC shows LAM cells positive for SMA, desmin and caldesmon (myoid), and for HMB45 (often focal, mainly in epithelioid cells), melan-A, MITF and cathepsin K (sensitive), with oestrogen and progesterone receptor positivity. D2-40 highlights lymphatic channels around LAM cell clusters. Keratin and S100 are negative. These features separate LAM from benign metastasizing leiomyoma (HMB45 negative) and from Langerhans cell histiocytosis (CD1a, langerin).

entities.variants: Diffuse lymphangiomatosis of lung, mediastinum and pleura; generalised lymphatic anomaly; kaposiform lymphangiomatosis (KLA, with NRAS mutations); Gorham-Stout disease association
entities.remarks: Rare proliferation of anastomosing lymphatic channels along lymphatic routes (bronchovascular bundles, septa, pleura) in children and young adults; chylothorax; D2-40 positive; may be kaposiform.
entities.histo: Diffuse pulmonary lymphangiomatosis is a rare disorder of the lymphatic system, usually presenting in children and young adults with progressive dyspnoea, wheeze, chylothorax, chylopericardium and lytic bone lesions, and forming part of the spectrum of complex lymphatic anomalies such as generalised lymphatic anomaly and kaposiform lymphangiomatosis. Radiologically there is diffuse thickening of interlobular septa, bronchovascular bundles and pleura with mediastinal soft tissue infiltration. Microscopically there is an increase in the number of complex, anastomosing, thin-walled lymphatic channels lined by bland endothelium, distributed along the normal lymphatic routes of the lung (bronchovascular bundles, interlobular septa and pleura), accompanied by collagen, spindle-shaped smooth muscle-like cells and haemosiderin. Kaposiform lymphangiomatosis additionally shows clusters of spindled lymphatic endothelial cells, haemorrhage and coagulopathy and carries a worse prognosis. Unlike lymphangiectasia, there is a true increase in the number of channels rather than only dilatation. Differentials include pulmonary lymphangiectasia, LAM, Kaposi sarcoma, lymphangioma, interstitial oedema and lymphangitic carcinomatosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role, though chylous effusion fluid with lymphocytes and fat may be the presenting sample. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign (chylous effusion) or Non-diagnostic. BAL is usually non-specific, with lymphocytes and macrophages, and lymphangiography or MR lymphangiography is used to demonstrate abnormal lymphatic flow.
entities.ihc: IHC shows the proliferating channels to be positive for D2-40 (podoplanin), PROX1, LYVE1 and CD31, with variable CD34, while the accompanying spindle cells are SMA and desmin positive but HMB45 and cathepsin K negative, distinguishing it from LAM. HHV-8 is negative (versus Kaposi sarcoma). Keratin helps exclude lymphangitic carcinomatosis. NRAS and PIK3CA testing may be informative in complex lymphatic anomalies.

entities.variants: Fibrohistiocytic, organising pneumonia-like, lymphoplasmacytic and fibrous (sclerosing) patterns; ALK-rearranged; ROS1-, NTRK-, RET- or PDGFRB-rearranged; epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma (RANBP2::ALK, nuclear membrane ALK, aggressive); old term inflammatory pseudotumour or plasma cell granuloma
entities.remarks: Intermediate (rarely metastasizing) neoplasm of children and young adults; myofibroblastic spindle cells in a fascicular or storiform pattern with prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate; ALK or other kinase fusions in most; responds to ALK inhibitors.
entities.histo: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour is a distinctive neoplasm of intermediate biological potential, the most common primary lung tumour of childhood after the age of one year, also seen in young adults, presenting as a solitary well-circumscribed peripheral or endobronchial mass. Microscopically it is composed of myofibroblastic and fibroblastic spindle cells with vesicular nuclei and small nucleoli arranged in fascicles or a storiform pattern, accompanied by a prominent inflammatory infiltrate of plasma cells, lymphocytes and sometimes eosinophils, histiocytes and foamy macrophages. Three patterns can coexist: a myxoid, vascular, organising pneumonia-like pattern; a compact spindle cell pattern; and a hypocellular fibrous pattern resembling scar. Endobronchial growth, vascular invasion and calcification may occur. Epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma is an aggressive variant with round epithelioid cells, myxoid stroma and neutrophils, usually with RANBP2::ALK fusion. Most tumours harbour ALK rearrangements, with others having ROS1, NTRK, RET or PDGFRB fusions, which can be targeted with kinase inhibitors. Differentials include organising pneumonia, IgG4-related disease, sclerosing pneumocytoma, solitary fibrous tumour, sarcomatoid carcinoma (especially in adults), follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, inflammatory leiomyosarcoma and nodular lymphoid hyperplasia.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows bland spindle cells singly and in loose fascicles mixed with lymphocytes, plasma cells and histiocytes, which is non-specific and easily mistaken for reactive inflammation or a low-grade spindle cell neoplasm; cell block ALK IHC can help. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical or Suspicious for malignancy (spindle cell lesion), with ancillary testing.
entities.ihc: IHC shows spindle cells positive for SMA, often desmin and calponin, and focal keratin, with ALK expression (cytoplasmic, or nuclear membrane in epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma) in most cases. ROS1, pan-TRK and other fusion-specific IHC or RNA NGS identify ALK-negative cases. Plasma cells are polyclonal, and the IgG4 count is usually below the threshold for IgG4-related disease. STAT6, CD21 and CD35, and p40 and TTF-1 exclude SFT, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma and carcinoma. ALK FISH or NGS confirms the fusion for treatment.

entities.variants: Congenital peribronchial myofibroblastic tumour (congenital or neonatal pulmonary myofibroblastic tumour; some with ETV6::NTRK3 or other kinase fusions)
entities.remarks: Rare large mass in fetus or neonate composed of fascicles of uniform spindle cells surrounding bronchovascular structures, resembling infantile fibrosarcoma; may cause hydrops; good prognosis after resection.
entities.histo: Congenital peribronchial myofibroblastic tumour is a rare neoplasm that presents prenatally or in the neonatal period as a large, solid, intrapulmonary mass, sometimes causing polyhydramnios, fetal hydrops or respiratory distress, and is considered closely related to infantile fibrosarcoma or congenital mesoblastic nephroma. Grossly it is a large, solid, white to tan mass that may replace much of a lobe. Microscopically it consists of interlacing fascicles of uniform, spindle-shaped cells with oval nuclei and moderate cytoplasm, which characteristically surround and grow along bronchovascular bundles and around airway cartilage, extending into interlobular septa and pleura, with mitoses that may be frequent, areas of haemorrhage, and sometimes immature cartilage. Despite the cellularity and mitotic activity, the behaviour is usually benign after complete resection. Some cases have ETV6::NTRK3 fusion, supporting the relationship with infantile fibrosarcoma. Differentials include pleuropulmonary blastoma (cystic, cambium layer, DICER1), fetal lung interstitial tumour, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour, CPAM, synovial sarcoma and infantile fibrosarcoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role; diagnosis is made on resection specimens following prenatal or neonatal imaging. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: not applicable; short note only.
entities.ihc: IHC is largely supportive: the spindle cells are positive for vimentin and SMA (variable), with negative desmin, myogenin, keratin, CD34, S100 and ALK. Pan-TRK IHC and NTRK FISH or RNA NGS identify fusion-positive cases, which may be eligible for TRK inhibitor therapy. DICER1 testing helps exclude pleuropulmonary blastoma. Ki-67 can be high despite the benign course, so proliferation markers should not be over-interpreted in this setting. Desmin and myogenin negativity excludes embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, and the lack of a cystic cambium layer and DICER1 mutation separates it from pleuropulmonary blastoma.

entities.variants: Intrapulmonary SFT; pleural-based SFT extending into lung (see pleura); malignant SFT (high cellularity, atypia, mitoses 4 or more per 10 HPF, necrosis); fat-forming and giant cell-rich variants; NAB2::STAT6 fusion; hypoglycaemia (Doege-Potter syndrome)
entities.remarks: Fibroblastic neoplasm with patternless spindle cells, alternating cellular and hypocellular areas, staghorn vessels and ropey collagen; NAB2::STAT6 fusion with nuclear STAT6; risk stratification by age, size, mitoses and necrosis.
entities.histo: Solitary fibrous tumour is a fibroblastic neoplasm characterised by NAB2::STAT6 fusion, most often arising from the visceral pleura but occasionally located entirely within the lung parenchyma, where it forms a well-circumscribed, often large mass in middle-aged adults, sometimes with paraneoplastic hypoglycaemia due to IGF-2 secretion. Grossly it is firm, white and whorled. Microscopically it shows a patternless architecture of bland ovoid to spindle cells with scant cytoplasm in alternating hypercellular and hypocellular sclerotic areas, separated by thick ropey or keloidal collagen and a prominent network of branching, dilated, thin-walled staghorn (haemangiopericytoma-like) vessels, sometimes with entrapped alveolar epithelium at the edges. Malignant SFTs show high cellularity, nuclear atypia, at least 4 mitoses per 10 high-power fields and necrosis, and risk models incorporate age, size, mitoses and necrosis. Differentials include synovial sarcoma, sarcomatoid mesothelioma, spindle cell carcinoma, MPNST, desmoid fibromatosis, spindle cell carcinoid, monophasic synovial sarcoma and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows bland spindle cells singly and in loose clusters with fragments of collagen, which is non-specific; cell block STAT6 IHC can establish the diagnosis. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical or Suspicious for malignancy (spindle cell neoplasm), with ancillary testing.
entities.ihc: IHC shows strong diffuse nuclear STAT6 positivity, which is highly sensitive and specific, together with CD34 (frequent, may be lost in malignant tumours), BCL2 and CD99, and negative keratins, S100, desmin and calretinin, separating SFT from mesothelioma, carcinoma, MPNST and synovial sarcoma (TLE1, SS18::SSX). GRIA2 and ALDH1 are additional supportive markers. NAB2::STAT6 fusion can be confirmed by RNA sequencing. TERT promoter mutations correlate with aggressive behaviour.

entities.variants: Pulmonary benign metastasizing leiomyoma (women with history of uterine leiomyoma or hysterectomy); multiple leiomyomatous hamartomas; intravenous leiomyomatosis with lung involvement
entities.remarks: Multiple well-circumscribed bland smooth muscle nodules in lungs of women with uterine leiomyomas; ER and PR positive, HMB45 negative; usually indolent; considered metastasis of a uterine leiomyoma.
entities.histo: Benign metastasizing leiomyoma is a condition in which histologically benign smooth muscle tumours occur in the lungs, typically as multiple, bilateral, well-circumscribed nodules, in women of reproductive or perimenopausal age who have a history of uterine leiomyoma, often after hysterectomy or myomectomy, sometimes years earlier. Molecular studies show clonal relationship with the uterine tumours, supporting haematogenous spread of a low-grade uterine smooth muscle tumour. Microscopically the nodules consist of interlacing fascicles of bland spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells with eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasm and cigar-shaped nuclei, with little or no atypia, mitoses under 5 per 10 high-power fields and no necrosis, often entrapping alveolar epithelium at the periphery to form gland-like or cleft-like spaces. The course is usually indolent, and lesions may respond to hormonal manipulation. Differentials include metastatic leiomyosarcoma (atypia, mitoses, necrosis), LAM (HMB45 positive), primary pulmonary leiomyoma, hamartoma, PEComa, and solitary fibrous tumour.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a minor role; FNA yields cohesive fascicles of bland spindle cells without atypia, which with clinical history may suggest the diagnosis but cannot exclude low-grade leiomyosarcoma. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical or Benign (bland spindle cell lesion), with recommendation for histological confirmation.
entities.ihc: IHC shows SMA, desmin and h-caldesmon positivity, with strong nuclear oestrogen and progesterone receptor positivity supporting a uterine origin, and negative HMB45, melan-A and cathepsin K (versus LAM). Ki-67 is low. Keratin, TTF-1 highlight entrapped epithelium. STAT6 and CD34 exclude solitary fibrous tumour. Comparison with the uterine tumour (if available) and molecular studies (for example clonal X-chromosome inactivation patterns or shared copy number changes) can demonstrate the relationship. A 1p and 19q deletion pattern has been reported in some cases, and the lack of TP53 or RB1 alterations supports a benign tumour.

entities.variants: Primary pulmonary paraganglioma (rare); tracheal paraganglioma; metastatic paraganglioma; SDH-deficient forms; distinguish from carcinoid
entities.remarks: Very rare in lung and trachea; nests (zellballen) of chief cells surrounded by S100/SOX10 positive sustentacular cells; keratin negative, GATA3 positive; distinguishes from carcinoid; check SDH status.
entities.histo: Paraganglioma is a neuroendocrine neoplasm of non-epithelial paraganglionic origin that rarely arises primarily in the lung or trachea, and many reported pulmonary paragangliomas were in fact carcinoids; metastasis from another site should also be excluded. It presents as a well-circumscribed, often vascular peripheral or endobronchial nodule. Microscopically it consists of nests (zellballen) of polygonal chief cells with granular eosinophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm and round nuclei with salt-and-pepper chromatin, sometimes with marked nuclear pleomorphism, surrounded by a delicate fibrovascular network and inconspicuous sustentacular cells. Mitoses and necrosis are uncommon. All paragangliomas are considered to have metastatic potential, and a significant proportion are associated with germline mutations, especially in SDH genes, so genetic testing is recommended. Differentials include typical carcinoid (keratin positive), metastatic paraganglioma, alveolar soft part sarcoma, granular cell tumour, PEComa, and minute meningothelial nodules.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows loosely cohesive polygonal cells with granular cytoplasm and anisonucleosis in a bloody background, which resembles carcinoid and needs cell block IHC with keratin. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Suspicious for malignancy or Malignant (neuroendocrine neoplasm), with ancillary testing.
entities.ihc: IHC shows chief cells positive for chromogranin, synaptophysin, INSM1, GATA3 and tyrosine hydroxylase, and negative or only focally positive for keratins (AE1/AE3, CAM5.2), which distinguishes paraganglioma from carcinoid. S100 and SOX10 highlight sustentacular cells. SDHB IHC loss indicates SDH deficiency and should prompt germline testing. TTF-1 is negative.

entities.variants: Adult pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (smokers; isolated lung); multisystem LCH with lung involvement (children); cellular nodular, fibrotic stellate and cystic stages; BRAF V600E and MAP2K1 mutations
entities.remarks: Clonal myeloid neoplasm of Langerhans cells; adult PLCH strongly linked to smoking, with upper-zone nodules and bizarre cysts; stellate bronchiolocentric nodules with Langerhans cells and eosinophils; CD1a and langerin positive.
entities.histo: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a clonal myeloid neoplasm of Langerhans-type dendritic cells driven by MAPK pathway mutations, most frequently BRAF V600E or MAP2K1. In adults pulmonary LCH occurs almost exclusively in cigarette smokers, often as isolated lung disease, and CT shows centrilobular nodules and bizarre-shaped cysts predominantly in the upper and middle zones, sparing the costophrenic angles. In children the lung may be involved as part of multisystem disease. Microscopically early lesions are cellular, bronchiolocentric, stellate (star-shaped) nodules composed of Langerhans cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and grooved, folded or coffee-bean nuclei, mixed with eosinophils, lymphocytes, macrophages and pigmented smoker macrophages, often with eosinophilic abscesses. Older lesions become fibrotic stellate scars with few Langerhans cells and may cavitate to form cysts, with surrounding respiratory bronchiolitis and emphysema. Smoking cessation may lead to stabilisation or regression. Differentials include respiratory bronchiolitis, desmoplastic interstitial pneumonia, eosinophilic pneumonia, LAM and Birt-Hogg-Dube cysts, Erdheim-Chester disease, and reactive Langerhans cell hyperplasia around other lesions (small numbers of Langerhans cells are not diagnostic).
entities.cyto: BAL may show an increased proportion of CD1a-positive cells (above 5 percent supports the diagnosis), together with pigmented macrophages, but the finding is neither sensitive nor specific in smokers. FNA is rarely used. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Atypical or Benign, with diagnosis relying on CT and biopsy.
entities.ihc: IHC shows Langerhans cells positive for CD1a, langerin (CD207) and S100, with cyclin D1 frequently positive; they are negative for keratins and usually weak or negative for CD163, which mainly highlights admixed macrophages. BRAF V600E (VE1) IHC or molecular testing identifies the most common mutation, and MAP2K1 testing can be performed in BRAF-negative cases for targeted therapy. CD68 also stains admixed macrophages, and electron microscopy (Birbeck granules) is seldom needed now.

entities.variants: Lung involvement in Erdheim-Chester disease (interstitial, pleural and septal); mixed LCH and ECD; BRAF V600E and other MAPK mutations
entities.remarks: Clonal histiocytic neoplasm of foamy CD68/CD163-positive, CD1a-negative histiocytes with Touton cells and fibrosis in a lymphangitic distribution (pleura, septa, bronchovascular bundles); systemic involvement of bones, retroperitoneum (hairy kidney) and aorta.
entities.histo: Erdheim-Chester disease is a rare clonal histiocytic neoplasm driven by MAPK pathway alterations, especially BRAF V600E, that predominantly affects middle-aged and older adults and involves long bones (symmetrical sclerosis), retroperitoneum (perirenal hairy kidney appearance), aorta (coated aorta), heart, orbit and central nervous system, with the lung involved in a substantial minority. Pulmonary disease produces interlobular septal thickening, pleural thickening and effusions, centrilobular nodules and ground-glass opacities. Microscopically there is a lymphangitic distribution of the infiltrate along the visceral pleura, interlobular septa and bronchovascular bundles, consisting of foamy or eosinophilic histiocytes, Touton giant cells, scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells, within a background of fibrosis. Some patients have mixed LCH and ECD. Targeted therapies such as BRAF and MEK inhibitors are effective. Differentials include LCH, Rosai-Dorfman disease, xanthogranulomatous inflammation, IgG4-related disease, pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis, UIP and other fibrosing interstitial lung diseases.
entities.cyto: Cytology has little role; pleural fluid or BAL may contain foamy histiocytes, which are non-specific. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Non-diagnostic, with diagnosis by biopsy and clinico-radiological correlation. BAL may show increased lymphocytes and foamy macrophages, which are not diagnostic, and the diagnosis rests on biopsy of an accessible site (often bone or perirenal tissue) together with imaging.
entities.ihc: IHC shows histiocytes positive for CD68, CD163, factor XIIIa and fascin, and negative for CD1a and langerin (unlike LCH), with S100 negative or weak (unlike Rosai-Dorfman disease, which is strongly S100 positive with emperipolesis). BRAF V600E (VE1) IHC or molecular testing is positive in many cases, and testing for MAP2K1, KRAS, NRAS and ARAF alterations is used in negative cases. IgG4 staining excludes IgG4-related disease.

entities.variants: Rosai-Dorfman disease (pulmonary or tracheobronchial; S100 positive with emperipolesis); ALK-positive histiocytosis; juvenile xanthogranuloma; histiocytic sarcoma (rare); follicular dendritic cell sarcoma (rare); interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma (rare)
entities.remarks: Rare histiocytic and dendritic cell proliferations involving lung or airway; Rosai-Dorfman shows large S100-positive histiocytes with emperipolesis; others defined by IHC and molecular features.
entities.histo: Other histiocytic and dendritic cell lesions occasionally involve the lung or airways. Rosai-Dorfman disease, which is now regarded as a clonal histiocytic disorder in some cases (with MAPK pathway mutations), may involve the trachea, bronchi or lung parenchyma, usually in association with nodal or other extranodal disease, and shows sheets of large pale histiocytes with abundant cytoplasm and round vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli, containing intact lymphocytes and plasma cells (emperipolesis), in a background of plasma cells and lymphocytes with fibrosis. ALK-positive histiocytosis, often in infants with systemic disease, shows sheets of histiocytes with KIF5B::ALK fusion. Juvenile xanthogranuloma rarely involves lung in systemic forms and shows foamy histiocytes with Touton cells. Histiocytic sarcoma consists of sheets of large, pleomorphic histiocytic cells with malignant features, and follicular dendritic cell sarcoma and interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma are rare tumours of the dendritic cell lineage. Differentials include LCH, Erdheim-Chester disease, IgG4-related disease, infections with histiocytic response, lymphoma, melanoma and carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology may show large histiocytes with emperipolesis in Rosai-Dorfman disease, which can suggest the diagnosis, and malignant pleomorphic cells in histiocytic sarcoma, which need IHC. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Atypical for Rosai-Dorfman disease and Malignant for histiocytic sarcoma.
entities.ihc: IHC is key: Rosai-Dorfman cells are positive for S100 (highlighting emperipolesis), CD68, CD163, OCT2 and cyclin D1, and negative for CD1a and langerin. ALK-positive histiocytosis is CD68, CD163 and ALK positive. Histiocytic sarcoma expresses CD163, CD68, lysozyme and CD4 and lacks CD1a, langerin, follicular dendritic markers and B and T cell markers. Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma expresses CD21, CD23, CD35 and clusterin, and interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma is S100 positive and CD1a negative. IgG4 staining helps exclude IgG4-related disease.

entities.variants: Intrapulmonary mature teratoma; immature teratoma; malignant germ cell tumours (seminoma, choriocarcinoma, yolk sac tumour; primary rare, mostly metastatic from testis or mediastinum); exclude choriocarcinomatous differentiation in lung carcinoma
entities.remarks: Primary pulmonary germ cell tumours are very rare and mostly mature teratomas, which may communicate with bronchi (trichoptysis); malignant forms are usually metastatic; mediastinal and gonadal primaries must be excluded.
entities.histo: Germ cell tumours arising primarily in the lung are exceedingly rare and are considered tumours of ectopic tissue, most commonly intrapulmonary mature teratoma, which typically occurs in the upper lobes in young adults and may cause haemoptysis, recurrent infection or the expectoration of hair (trichoptysis) when it communicates with a bronchus. Microscopically mature teratoma contains well-differentiated tissues from two or three germ layers, such as skin with adnexa, respiratory and gastrointestinal epithelium, cartilage, bone, fat, neural tissue and pancreatic tissue, often within a cystic lesion. Immature teratoma contains immature neuroectodermal tissue. Malignant germ cell tumours such as seminoma, choriocarcinoma and yolk sac tumour in the lung are almost always metastatic from the testis, ovary or mediastinum, and primary pulmonary forms are diagnosed only after thorough exclusion. Choriocarcinoma-like or hepatoid differentiation can also occur in lung carcinomas, which must be distinguished. Differentials include pulmonary hamartoma, bronchogenic cyst, mediastinal teratoma extending into lung, metastatic germ cell tumours, and lung carcinoma with germ cell-like differentiation.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a minimal role for teratoma, showing squamous cells, keratin debris and mixed elements; malignant germ cell tumours yield malignant cells that can be typed by cell block IHC. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Benign or Non-diagnostic for teratoma; Malignant for malignant germ cell tumours.
entities.ihc: IHC is used for malignant germ cell tumours: SALL4 (all germ cell tumours), OCT3/4, CD117 and D2-40 for seminoma, OCT3/4, SOX2 and CD30 for embryonal carcinoma, glypican-3, AFP and SALL4 for yolk sac tumour, and beta-hCG and GATA3 for choriocarcinoma, with serum tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) and testicular imaging. Teratomas show the expected lineage markers for each tissue. Keratin, TTF-1, p40 and SALL4 help separate lung carcinoma with germ cell-like features from true germ cell tumours.

entities.variants: Haematogenous nodular metastases (cannonball pattern); lymphangitic carcinomatosis; endobronchial metastases (kidney, breast, colon, melanoma); lepidic-pattern metastases (pancreas, colorectal mucinous); cavitating metastases (squamous cell carcinoma); calcified metastases (osteosarcoma); pulmonary tumour thrombotic microangiopathy; intravascular tumour emboli; miliary metastases (thyroid); common primaries - breast, colorectal, kidney, head and neck, melanoma, sarcomas, germ cell tumours, thyroid, uterus, prostate, choriocarcinoma
entities.remarks: The lung is the commonest site of metastasis; usually multiple peripheral nodules; morphology resembling primary and organ-specific IHC are needed to separate metastasis from primary lung carcinoma, particularly for adenocarcinomas and squamous carcinomas.
entities.histo: The lung is the most frequent site of metastatic disease because it receives the entire venous return and lymphatic drainage, and metastases are much more common than primary lung neoplasms in many series of pulmonary nodules. They typically appear as multiple, well-circumscribed, round peripheral nodules of varying sizes in the lower zones (cannonball pattern), but may also present as solitary nodules, miliary nodules (thyroid carcinoma, melanoma), cavitating nodules (squamous cell carcinoma, sarcomas), calcified nodules (osteosarcoma, mucinous carcinomas), endobronchial lesions (kidney, breast, colon, melanoma), or lymphangitic carcinomatosis, in which tumour spreads through lymphatics of the bronchovascular bundles, interlobular septa and pleura (breast, stomach, lung, pancreas, prostate). Some metastases grow along alveolar walls in a lepidic pattern and mimic primary adenocarcinoma, especially from pancreas and colorectal mucinous tumours. Pulmonary tumour thrombotic microangiopathy, associated most often with gastric adenocarcinoma, causes subacute pulmonary hypertension due to tumour emboli with fibrocellular intimal proliferation in small arteries. Morphology is generally that of the primary tumour, such as the dirty necrosis and tall columnar cells of colorectal carcinoma, or the clear cells of renal cell carcinoma. Distinguishing metastasis from primary lung cancer relies on clinical history, comparison with previous tumour, a precursor lesion (AIS or squamous dysplasia) favouring primary, and IHC.
entities.cyto: Cytology from FNA, EBUS-TBNA, BAL, bronchial brushings and pleural fluid is commonly used to diagnose metastatic disease, and comparison with the morphology of the previous primary and IHC on cell blocks usually allows the site of origin to be determined; molecular studies can also be performed. WHO Reporting System for Lung Cytopathology category: Malignant (metastatic carcinoma, melanoma or sarcoma consistent with known primary), or Suspicious for malignancy.
entities.ihc: IHC panels depend on morphology and history. For adenocarcinoma, TTF-1 and napsin A favour lung (noting TTF-1 positivity in thyroid and some other tumours), CDX2, CK20 and SATB2 favour colorectal origin, GATA3, ER, PR, mammaglobin and TRPS1 favour breast, PAX8 and CA-IX favour kidney and Mullerian origin, NKX3.1 and PSA favour prostate, thyroglobulin and PAX8 favour thyroid, and HepPar-1 and arginase-1 favour liver. Squamous cell carcinoma of head and neck origin may be shown by p16 and HPV testing or by comparison with the primary. SOX10, S100, melan-A and HMB45 identify melanoma, and sarcomas require lineage-specific markers. CK7 and CK20 patterns guide initial triage. Molecular profiling of the tumour may help clarify the origin and guide therapy.

entities.entity: Acute viral hepatitis (acute hepatitic pattern of injury)
entities.variants: Classic acute (lobular) hepatitis; acute hepatitis with confluent (zone 3) necrosis; bridging necrosis; submassive and massive (panacinar) necrosis; cholestatic acute hepatitis; periportal-predominant pattern (HAV)
entities.remarks: Common end pattern of hepatotropic viruses A-E, systemic viruses, drugs and autoimmune hepatitis; lobular disarray, ballooning, acidophil bodies, lobular inflammation exceeding portal inflammation; aetiology needs serology, PCR and drug history.
entities.histo: Acute hepatitis is a pattern of injury rather than a single disease, and the biopsy is used to confirm the pattern, judge its severity and look for clues to the cause. The lobule shows disarray, with swollen (ballooned) hepatocytes, acidophil (Councilman) bodies, spotty necrosis and a mixed lymphocyte-macrophage infiltrate in the sinusoids, often with Kupffer cell hypertrophy and ceroid-laden macrophages after the necrotic cells have been cleared. Portal tracts carry a lymphocytic infiltrate with mild interface activity, but lobular change usually outweighs portal change, which helps separate acute from chronic hepatitis. Canalicular cholestasis, hepatocyte rosettes and regenerative binucleated cells are common. Severe cases show confluent necrosis around central veins, bridging necrosis linking vascular structures, or submassive to massive necrosis with collapse of the reticulin framework and ductular reaction. A reticulin stain separates true collapse from intact framework, Masson trichrome helps tell fresh collapse (pale, loose) from established fibrosis (dense, mature), and orcein or Victoria blue stain elastic fibres that are absent in recent collapse. PAS after diastase highlights ceroid-laden macrophages that mark recent injury. Differentials include drug-induced liver injury, acute presentation of autoimmune hepatitis (plasma cell rich, zone 3 necrosis), Wilson disease, ischaemic hepatitis (zone 3 coagulative necrosis with little inflammation) and an acute flare of chronic hepatitis B, where portal fibrosis and ground-glass cells may be found.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role in acute hepatitis, and FNA is not used to evaluate diffuse parenchymal injury; a core or transjugular biopsy is the standard. If a liver aspirate is taken incidentally it may show reactive hepatocytes with nuclear enlargement and binucleation, scattered lymphocytes and macrophages, which should not be overcalled as dysplasia. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: Immunohistochemistry plays only a supporting role in acute hepatitis. HBsAg and HBcAg stains are usually negative in acute hepatitis B, because viral antigen expression is low during brisk immune clearance, so serology is far more useful. CMV, HSV-1/2 and adenovirus immunostains are applied when inclusions, punched-out necrosis or an immunosuppressed host suggest these viruses, and EBER in situ hybridisation confirms EBV hepatitis. CK7 shows ductular reaction and periportal hepatocyte metaplasia in cholestatic or severe cases, and CD138 or MUM1 can quantify plasma cells when autoimmune hepatitis is in the differential. CK19 and CK7 also highlight residual ductules in collapsed areas, which helps judge the extent of necrosis.

entities.variants: Acute icteric and anicteric hepatitis; cholestatic HAV hepatitis; relapsing HAV hepatitis; fulminant HAV hepatitis; HAV-triggered autoimmune hepatitis (rare)
entities.remarks: Faeco-oral picornavirus, endemic in India; never chronic; periportal (zone 1) predominant plasma-cell-rich hepatitis with cholestasis; IgM anti-HAV is diagnostic.
entities.histo: Hepatitis A is an acute, self-limited infection that never becomes chronic, so biopsy is rarely needed and is taken mainly when the clinical picture is atypical or prolonged. The characteristic pattern is a periportal (zone 1) predominant hepatitis, with dense portal and interface infiltrates rich in plasma cells, which can mimic autoimmune hepatitis. The lobules show hepatocyte swelling, acidophil bodies and spotty necrosis that are often less striking around the central vein than in hepatitis B or E. Cholestasis in zone 3 is common and may dominate in the cholestatic form, which can last for weeks. Fulminant cases show submassive or massive necrosis with reticulin collapse and ductular reaction. Fibrin-ring granulomas and relapsing disease are uncommon findings. The differential includes autoimmune hepatitis (also plasma cell rich, but usually with interface activity in a background of fibrosis and autoantibodies), drug-induced liver injury, and other acute viral hepatitides, so the diagnosis depends on IgM anti-HAV serology rather than morphology.
entities.cyto: FNA cytology has no role in hepatitis A; the diagnosis is serological. Incidental aspirates show only reactive hepatocytes, lymphocytes and plasma cells.
entities.ihc: There is no routinely used immunostain for HAV in diagnostic practice, and the diagnosis rests on IgM anti-HAV serology. IHC is used mainly to exclude other causes: HBsAg and HBcAg are negative, CMV, HSV and adenovirus stains are negative, and CD138 or MUM1 highlights the abundant portal plasma cells, which on their own cannot separate HAV from autoimmune hepatitis. CK7 shows ductular reaction in severe or cholestatic cases.

entities.variants: Acute hepatitis B; chronic hepatitis B (immune-tolerant, HBeAg-positive immune-active, inactive carrier, HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis, occult HBV infection); HBV reactivation; fulminant hepatitis B; fibrosing cholestatic hepatitis B (post-transplant/immunosuppression); HBV-related cirrhosis
entities.remarks: Hepadnavirus, DNA integration drives HCC even without cirrhosis; ground-glass hepatocytes (HBsAg), sanded nuclei (HBcAg); grade and stage chronic disease (Ishak, METAVIR, Batts-Ludwig); HDV coinfection can worsen course.
entities.histo: Hepatitis B shows the acute hepatitic pattern in acute infection, with lobular disarray, ballooning, acidophil bodies and lobular-predominant inflammation, and may progress to submassive or massive necrosis in fulminant cases. Chronic hepatitis B shows portal lymphoid infiltrates, sometimes with lymphoid aggregates, variable interface hepatitis and lobular activity, together with portal and periportal fibrosis that can progress to bridging fibrosis and macronodular cirrhosis. The best clue is the ground-glass hepatocyte, whose cytoplasm is filled with finely granular, pale eosinophilic material (endoplasmic reticulum stuffed with HBsAg) separated from the cell membrane by a clear halo; it is seen in chronic rather than acute infection. Sanded nuclei with pale eosinophilic nucleoplasm reflect HBcAg. Ground-glass change can be confirmed by orcein, Victoria blue or Shikata stain, which colour HBsAg brown to purple. Fibrosing cholestatic hepatitis, seen in transplant recipients and other immunosuppressed patients, is a severe pattern with hepatocyte ballooning, marked cholestasis, ductular reaction and periportal sinusoidal fibrosis but scanty inflammation. Biopsies are graded for necroinflammatory activity and staged for fibrosis using Ishak, METAVIR or Batts-Ludwig systems, with Masson trichrome and reticulin for fibrosis. Differentials of ground-glass change include drug-induced (polypharmacy) ground-glass inclusions, glycogen pseudoground glass in transplant or immunosuppressed patients, Lafora-like and type IV glycogen storage disease inclusions, and cyanamide toxicity, all of which are HBsAg negative. Dysplastic foci (large and small cell change) and HCC should be looked for in chronic disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology is not used to diagnose hepatitis B. Its main role is in chronic HBV carriers who develop a mass, where FNA may be used to diagnose hepatocellular carcinoma. Background hepatocytes in such aspirates may show ground-glass cytoplasm and large cell change, which should not be mistaken for malignancy; the separation of well-differentiated HCC from regenerative or dysplastic nodules is unreliable on cytology alone and needs cell block reticulin and immunostains. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: HBsAg immunostaining shows cytoplasmic (ground-glass, diffuse) or membranous staining in hepatocytes; membranous staining is linked to active viral replication. HBcAg shows nuclear and cytoplasmic staining, and cytoplasmic or extensive nuclear positivity points to high replication, while the antigens are often negative in acute hepatitis B and in inactive carriers with low viral load. These stains are useful to confirm HBV as the cause, to show HBV in a transplant graft (recurrent disease, fibrosing cholestatic hepatitis), and to identify HBV in tumour-bearing livers. HDAg (delta antigen) nuclear staining confirms HDV co-infection where available. CK7 and CK19 highlight ductular reaction, and glypican-3, HSP70 and glutamine synthetase are used when a nodule in an HBV liver must be separated from HCC.

entities.variants: HBV-HDV coinfection (acute); HDV superinfection of chronic HBV carrier; chronic hepatitis D; fulminant delta hepatitis
entities.remarks: Defective RNA virus needing HBsAg envelope; most severe chronic viral hepatitis with rapid progression to cirrhosis; superinfection can cause fulminant hepatitis; HDAg nuclear stain or anti-HDV/HDV RNA.
entities.histo: Hepatitis D can only occur alongside hepatitis B, either as simultaneous coinfection or as superinfection of a chronic HBsAg carrier, and superinfection carries the highest risk of severe and chronic disease. The histology is that of hepatitis B with greater necroinflammatory activity: prominent lobular inflammation, many acidophil bodies, confluent or bridging necrosis and brisk interface hepatitis, and a faster rate of fibrosis progression to cirrhosis. In some outbreaks a microvesicular steatosis pattern with eosinophilic swollen hepatocytes (morula-like cells) has been described, especially in South American populations. Ground-glass hepatocytes may be fewer because HDV suppresses HBV replication. Chronic HDV is graded and staged with the same systems used for HBV and HCV. The differential is mainly with an HBV flare, drug injury or autoimmune hepatitis, and confirmation requires anti-HDV antibody and HDV RNA testing.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the diagnosis of HDV hepatitis. FNA is relevant only for mass lesions such as HCC arising in HBV-HDV cirrhosis.
entities.ihc: HDAg immunostaining, where available, shows granular nuclear staining of hepatocytes and is the tissue confirmation of HDV infection. HBsAg and HBcAg stains are often weaker than in HBV mono-infection because HDV suppresses HBV replication. Otherwise IHC is supportive only: CK7 for ductular reaction and stains used to separate dysplastic nodules from HCC in cirrhotic livers.

entities.variants: Acute hepatitis C; chronic hepatitis C; HCV-related cirrhosis; recurrent hepatitis C after transplant; fibrosing cholestatic hepatitis C; HCV after sustained virological response (residual changes); genotype 3-related steatosis
entities.remarks: RNA flavivirus; usually chronic; triad of portal lymphoid aggregates/follicles, bile duct damage (Poulsen-Christoffersen lesion) and macrovesicular steatosis; mild lobular activity with acidophil bodies; DAAs now cure most infections.
entities.histo: Chronic hepatitis C is the usual biopsy picture, and its classic features are dense portal lymphoid aggregates or follicles with germinal centres, mild lymphocytic bile duct injury, and macrovesicular steatosis, which is especially marked with genotype 3. Interface hepatitis is usually mild to moderate, and lobular activity is modest, with scattered acidophil bodies and sinusoidal lymphocytes in an "Indian file" pattern. Fibrosis develops slowly from portal and periportal areas through bridging fibrosis to cirrhosis, which is the main risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma. Acute hepatitis C shows a non-specific acute hepatitic pattern and is rarely biopsied. After transplantation, recurrent HCV shows lobular disarray and acidophil bodies early, then portal-based chronic hepatitis; fibrosing cholestatic hepatitis C shows ballooning, cholestasis, ductular reaction and pericellular fibrosis. After cure with direct-acting antivirals, inflammation subsides and fibrosis can regress, with thin, perforated septa. Grading and staging use Ishak, METAVIR or Batts-Ludwig systems, with Masson trichrome and reticulin. Differentials include autoimmune hepatitis (more plasma cells and interface activity), MASH (zone 3 steatosis and ballooning with pericellular fibrosis), drug injury, PBC (florid duct lesions, granulomas, ductopenia) and low-grade lymphoma when lymphoid aggregates are very large.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the diagnosis of chronic hepatitis C. FNA is used in HCV cirrhosis mainly for mass lesions, especially HCC, where the background may show steatosis and reactive changes. Lymphoid-rich aspirates from large portal aggregates should not be mistaken for lymphoma.
entities.ihc: There is no routine diagnostic immunostain for HCV in tissue; the diagnosis rests on anti-HCV antibody and HCV RNA. IHC is used to exclude coexisting hepatitis B (HBsAg, HBcAg), to characterise lymphoid aggregates (mixed CD20 B cells and CD3 T cells with intact follicular dendritic meshworks, no light chain restriction) when lymphoma is a concern, and to evaluate nodules in cirrhotic livers with glypican-3, HSP70, glutamine synthetase and CD34. CK7 and CK19 show ductular reaction and bile duct injury.

entities.variants: Acute hepatitis E (genotypes 1 and 2, waterborne, endemic in India); HEV in pregnancy with acute liver failure; chronic hepatitis E in immunosuppressed (genotype 3, transplant recipients); acute-on-chronic liver failure; cholestatic HEV hepatitis
entities.remarks: Faeco-oral RNA virus; major cause of epidemic and sporadic acute hepatitis in India; high mortality in pregnancy (third trimester); genotype 3 can become chronic in transplant recipients; cholestatic hepatitis with pseudoglandular (rosette) change.
entities.histo: Acute hepatitis E shows an acute hepatitic pattern that is often strikingly cholestatic, with canalicular and hepatocellular bile, gland-like (pseudoglandular or rosette) transformation of hepatocytes around bile plugs, lobular disarray, acidophil bodies and a mixed portal infiltrate that may contain neutrophils. Ductular reaction with cholangiolitis can mimic large duct obstruction. In pregnant women and in patients with pre-existing chronic liver disease, HEV can cause submassive or massive necrosis with acute liver failure or acute-on-chronic liver failure. Chronic hepatitis E, mainly genotype 3 in transplant recipients and other immunosuppressed patients, shows portal lymphocytic inflammation, interface activity and progressive fibrosis that can reach cirrhosis within a few years. The main differentials are drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis, large duct obstruction, other acute viral hepatitides and, after transplant, acute or late T-cell-mediated rejection, so HEV IgM and HEV RNA testing is needed to confirm the diagnosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the diagnosis of hepatitis E, which is serological and molecular (anti-HEV IgM, HEV RNA). Aspirates are not used for diffuse acute hepatitis.
entities.ihc: An HEV ORF2 capsid protein immunostain has been described and can show cytoplasmic staining of hepatocytes in acute and chronic infection, but it is not widely available; tissue HEV RNA by PCR or in situ hybridisation is an alternative. IHC otherwise helps to exclude other causes: HBsAg and HBcAg negative, CMV, HSV and adenovirus negative. CK7 highlights ductular reaction and periportal hepatocyte CK7 metaplasia in the cholestatic form.

entities.variants: Ishak (modified HAI) grading and staging; METAVIR activity and fibrosis stage; Batts-Ludwig grade and stage; Scheuer system; Knodell HAI; Laennec cirrhosis substaging (4A-4C); fibrosis regression features (Beijing classification - predominantly progressive, indeterminate, predominantly regressive)
entities.remarks: Chronic hepatitis = hepatitis lasting more than 6 months; grade = necroinflammatory activity (interface, lobular, confluent necrosis), stage = fibrosis; essential for HBV, HCV, AIH reporting; use trichrome and reticulin; report adequacy (at least 11 to 15 portal tracts, 2 cm length).
entities.histo: Chronic hepatitis is defined clinically by inflammation lasting more than six months, and histologically by a portal-based lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with variable interface hepatitis, lobular inflammation and fibrosis. Biopsy reporting has two parts: the grade, which scores necroinflammatory activity, and the stage, which scores fibrosis and architectural change. Interface hepatitis (piecemeal necrosis) is the destruction of the limiting plate by lymphocytes and plasma cells; lobular activity includes spotty necrosis, acidophil bodies and confluent or bridging necrosis. Staging runs from portal fibrous expansion through periportal fibrosis and bridging septa to cirrhosis with regenerative nodules. The Ishak system scores interface hepatitis, confluent necrosis, spotty lobular necrosis and portal inflammation (maximum 18) and stages fibrosis from 0 to 6; METAVIR scores activity A0 to A3 and fibrosis F0 to F4; Batts-Ludwig grades and stages from 0 to 4. The Laennec system subdivides cirrhosis by septal thickness and nodule size, and the Beijing classification describes whether fibrosis looks progressive or regressive after antiviral treatment. A biopsy at least 2 cm long with 11 or more complete portal tracts is regarded as adequate, and small or fragmented samples underestimate stage. Masson trichrome, reticulin, and orcein or Victoria blue (for elastic fibres in older septa) are the key stains. The pathologist should also report the likely cause, steatosis, iron, and any dysplasia.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in grading or staging chronic hepatitis, which requires a histological core showing architecture and fibrosis. Non-invasive tests (transient elastography, serum fibrosis panels) are the clinical alternatives to biopsy.
entities.ihc: Grading and staging are performed on H&E and special stains rather than on immunostains. IHC adds aetiological information (HBsAg, HBcAg, HDAg), plasma cell quantification (CD138, MUM1) when autoimmune hepatitis is suspected, and CK7 for ductular reaction and periportal metaplasia, which can mark chronic cholestatic components. CK19 or CK7 can also confirm bile duct loss when a biliary overlap is considered.

entities.variants: HSV-1 and HSV-2 hepatitis; neonatal disseminated HSV; HSV hepatitis in pregnancy (third trimester); HSV hepatitis in immunosuppressed and transplant patients
entities.remarks: Rare but often fatal; anicteric hepatitis with very high transaminases; non-zonal, punched-out geographic coagulative necrosis with little inflammation and Cowdry A / ground-glass nuclear inclusions at the edges; urgent acyclovir.
entities.histo: HSV hepatitis is rare but important because it is treatable and usually fatal if missed. It affects neonates, pregnant women in the third trimester, transplant recipients and other immunosuppressed patients, and occasionally healthy adults. The liver shows randomly distributed, non-zonal areas of coagulative (punched-out) necrosis, which may merge into large geographic zones, with surprisingly little inflammation apart from neutrophils and nuclear debris. At the edges of the necrotic areas, infected hepatocytes show ground-glass (smudged) nuclei with margination of chromatin, Cowdry type A eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions with a halo, and occasional multinucleation with nuclear moulding. Haemorrhage may be present. The differentials include adenovirus hepatitis (similar non-zonal necrosis with smudgy nuclei but no multinucleation), VZV hepatitis (identical pattern, needs immunostain or PCR), ischaemic necrosis (zonal, zone 3, without inclusions), and paracetamol toxicity (zone 3).
entities.cyto: FNA cytology is not used for diagnosis, although aspirates or touch preparations of necrotic areas can show multinucleated cells with nuclear moulding, chromatin margination and ground-glass nuclei (the three Ms), with necrotic debris. These changes are not specific between HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV, and confirmation requires immunostaining or PCR.
entities.ihc: HSV-1 and HSV-2 immunostains show strong nuclear and cytoplasmic staining in hepatocytes at the edge of necrotic areas and confirm the diagnosis; antibodies often cross-react between the two types, so typing relies on PCR. Adenovirus and VZV immunostains are part of the panel for non-zonal necrosis with nuclear inclusions, and CMV is usually negative. PCR on blood or tissue is complementary.

entities.variants: CMV hepatitis in transplant recipients (graft infection); CMV in HIV/AIDS and other immunosuppression; congenital CMV (neonatal giant cell hepatitis pattern); CMV mononucleosis-like hepatitis in immunocompetent adults (granulomatous / lymphocytic sinusoidal)
entities.remarks: Immunosuppressed host: owl-eye intranuclear and granular cytoplasmic inclusions in hepatocytes, bile duct and endothelial cells, with neutrophilic microabscesses; immunocompetent host: mononucleosis-like sinusoidal lymphocytosis, occasional fibrin-ring granulomas.
entities.histo: CMV hepatitis has two patterns. In transplant recipients and other immunosuppressed patients, infected hepatocytes, cholangiocytes, endothelial cells and Kupffer cells are enlarged (cytomegaly), with large, deeply eosinophilic or amphophilic intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a halo (owl-eye), and smaller granular basophilic cytoplasmic inclusions. Small clusters of neutrophils around infected or necrotic hepatocytes (microabscesses) are a valuable clue, and lipogranulomas or microgranulomas may be present. In a liver graft this must be distinguished from acute rejection, which shows portal mixed inflammation, bile duct damage and endotheliitis, and the two may coexist. Congenital CMV infection may produce neonatal giant cell hepatitis with cholestasis and extramedullary haematopoiesis. In immunocompetent adults, CMV causes a mononucleosis-like hepatitis with lymphocytes lined up in sinusoids, mild portal inflammation and sometimes granulomas, and inclusions are usually absent. The differentials include EBV hepatitis, HSV and adenovirus (nuclear smudging without owl-eye change or cytoplasmic granules) and, in transplants, rejection and recurrent viral hepatitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no routine role, although cytomegalic cells with owl-eye intranuclear inclusions may occasionally be seen in aspirates or touch preparations from immunosuppressed patients; confirmation needs immunostaining or PCR.
entities.ihc: CMV immunostaining (early and immediate-early antigen) is far more sensitive than H&E and shows nuclear, and sometimes cytoplasmic, staining in infected cells, including those without visible inclusions. It is used routinely in transplant biopsies with neutrophilic microabscesses or unexplained hepatitis. HSV and adenovirus immunostains are negative, and EBER in situ hybridisation is negative, which helps in the mononucleosis-like pattern. CMV PCR on blood or tissue is complementary.

entities.variants: Infectious mononucleosis hepatitis; cholestatic EBV hepatitis; chronic active EBV infection; EBV-related acute liver failure (rare); EBV-associated haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
entities.remarks: Usually mild transaminitis in infectious mononucleosis; sinusoidal 'Indian file' lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, mild hepatocyte injury, portal lymphoid infiltrate; may mimic lymphoma or PTLD; EBER-ISH positive scattered cells.
entities.histo: EBV hepatitis usually accompanies infectious mononucleosis and causes only mild transaminase rise, so biopsy is uncommon. The characteristic finding is a striking sinusoidal infiltrate of small and activated lymphocytes arranged in single file ("Indian file" or beads on a string) with relatively little hepatocyte damage. Portal tracts contain a mixed infiltrate of lymphocytes, immunoblasts and plasma cells, sometimes with mild bile duct injury and endotheliitis. Acidophil bodies, mild steatosis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, small epithelioid granulomas or fibrin-ring granulomas and cholestasis may occur. Rare cases progress to submassive necrosis or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. The atypical lymphoid infiltrate can resemble lymphoma, hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma, leukaemic infiltration or post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder, and in transplant patients it must be separated from acute rejection. CMV hepatitis can produce a similar sinusoidal lymphocytosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role in EBV hepatitis. In aspirates, polymorphous lymphoid cells with immunoblasts may raise concern for lymphoma; a polymorphous population and clinical and serological context (heterophile antibody, EBV VCA IgM) favour a reactive process.
entities.ihc: EBER in situ hybridisation shows scattered positive lymphocytes in sinusoids and portal tracts and is the most useful tissue test. The infiltrate is mostly CD3-positive and CD8-positive T cells, with scattered CD20-positive and CD30-positive immunoblasts, and it lacks the CD56 and TCR gamma-delta phenotype of hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma. CMV, HSV and adenovirus immunostains are negative. Clonality studies (TCR, IGH) and a polymorphous phenotype help separate EBV hepatitis from lymphoma or PTLD.

entities.variants: Adenovirus hepatitis in solid organ and haematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients; in children with immunodeficiency; acute severe hepatitis of unknown aetiology in children (adenovirus 41 association, 2022)
entities.remarks: Immunosuppressed host; non-zonal (random) coagulative necrosis with smudgy basophilic intranuclear inclusions at edges, no multinucleation; high mortality; adenovirus IHC confirms.
entities.histo: Adenovirus hepatitis occurs mainly in transplant recipients, children with immunodeficiency and patients on chemotherapy, and can cause fulminant hepatic failure. The histology closely resembles HSV hepatitis: randomly distributed, non-zonal areas of coagulative necrosis with nuclear debris and little inflammation, which may enlarge into geographic zones. At the edges, infected hepatocytes have enlarged nuclei filled with amphophilic to basophilic, smudged, ground-glass inclusions that obscure the chromatin, but multinucleation and nuclear moulding are absent, unlike HSV. Granulomas are not a feature. The differential includes HSV and VZV hepatitis, ischaemic or drug-induced necrosis (zonal, without inclusions), and CMV (owl-eye nuclei, cytoplasmic granules, neutrophilic microabscesses). The 2022 cluster of severe paediatric hepatitis associated with adenovirus 41 showed non-specific hepatitis with few or no inclusions, so testing was mainly molecular.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no routine diagnostic role; smudged intranuclear inclusions may be noted in touch preparations of necrotic tissue, but immunostaining or PCR is needed.
entities.ihc: Adenovirus immunostaining shows strong nuclear staining of the smudgy inclusion-bearing hepatocytes and is the key confirmation; HSV, VZV and CMV stains are negative. PCR on blood or tissue supports the diagnosis and is needed when inclusions are scarce.

entities.entity: Other viral hepatitides (VZV, HHV-6, parvovirus B19, measles, enteroviruses)
entities.variants: Varicella-zoster virus hepatitis (disseminated, immunosuppressed); human herpesvirus 6 hepatitis (transplant, DRESS association); parvovirus B19 hepatitis (with aplastic crisis); measles hepatitis; enteroviral (coxsackie, echovirus) neonatal hepatitis; rubella (congenital)
entities.remarks: Rare systemic viral causes of hepatitis; VZV mimics HSV (non-zonal necrosis with inclusions); others give non-specific hepatitis, sometimes giant cells; molecular confirmation (PCR) usually needed.
entities.histo: Several systemic viruses can cause hepatitis, usually with non-specific histology. Disseminated varicella-zoster infection in immunosuppressed adults and children produces random, non-zonal coagulative necrosis with Cowdry A intranuclear inclusions and multinucleated cells at the edges, identical to HSV hepatitis. HHV-6 can cause hepatitis or graft dysfunction after transplantation and is linked to drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, with lobular and portal lymphocytic inflammation. Parvovirus B19 may cause acute hepatitis, sometimes with aplastic crisis and erythroid precursors showing intranuclear inclusions in sinusoids. Measles and enteroviruses (coxsackievirus, echovirus) can cause neonatal hepatitis with giant cells, necrosis and haemorrhage, and congenital rubella causes neonatal giant cell hepatitis with cholestasis and extramedullary haematopoiesis. Because the morphology is rarely specific, these diagnoses rely on clinical context and PCR or serology.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role for these infections. Rarely, multinucleated cells with nuclear inclusions (VZV) or erythroid precursors with inclusions (parvovirus) may be seen in aspirates or smears, but confirmation is molecular.
entities.ihc: VZV immunostaining shows nuclear and cytoplasmic staining of inclusion-bearing cells and separates VZV from HSV, which can cross-react only weakly. Parvovirus B19 immunostaining (VP1/VP2 capsid) highlights infected erythroid precursors, and HHV-6 immunostains exist but are used mainly in research. For the other viruses, tissue or blood PCR is the practical test. A negative HSV, CMV and adenovirus panel narrows the differential.

entities.entity: Viral haemorrhagic fever and arboviral hepatitis (yellow fever, dengue, Ebola, Lassa, Crimean-Congo)
entities.variants: Yellow fever hepatitis (midzonal necrosis, Councilman bodies); dengue hepatitis and dengue-associated acute liver failure; Ebola and Marburg virus disease; Lassa fever; Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever; Kyasanur Forest disease (India)
entities.remarks: Dengue hepatitis common in India (transaminitis, occasionally liver failure); yellow fever gives classic zone 2 (midzonal) necrosis with many acidophil (Councilman) bodies and microvesicular steatosis; biosafety precautions for tissue from suspected viral haemorrhagic fevers.
entities.histo: Viral haemorrhagic fevers damage the liver through direct infection of hepatocytes and Kupffer cells and through shock and coagulopathy. Yellow fever shows the classic pattern of midzonal (zone 2) coagulative necrosis with numerous eosinophilic apoptotic hepatocytes (Councilman bodies, first described here), microvesicular steatosis and strikingly little inflammation, with relative sparing of periportal and centrilobular hepatocytes. Dengue hepatitis, very common in India, usually causes only a transaminase rise, but severe cases show midzonal and centrilobular necrosis, Councilman bodies, microvesicular steatosis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia and haemorrhage, and can lead to acute liver failure. Ebola, Marburg, Lassa and Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fevers produce multifocal or diffuse necrosis with acidophil bodies and sometimes viral inclusions, little inflammation, and haemorrhage. Kyasanur Forest disease, a tick-borne flavivirus infection of Karnataka, also causes hepatocellular necrosis. The differential includes ischaemic hepatitis (zone 3), drug toxicity, leptospirosis and severe malaria. Tissue from suspected haemorrhagic fever must be handled under biosafety precautions, and diagnosis is serological and molecular.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in these infections, and aspiration of tissue from patients with suspected haemorrhagic fever is avoided because of bleeding risk and biosafety concerns.
entities.ihc: Viral antigen immunostains (for yellow fever, dengue, Ebola and others) exist mainly in reference and public health laboratories and show staining of hepatocytes and Kupffer cells. In routine practice, diagnosis relies on serology, NS1 antigen (dengue) and RT-PCR. Routine IHC is otherwise limited to excluding HSV, adenovirus and CMV.

entities.variants: Acute hepatitis with mild lobular inflammation; ischaemic (shock) injury; sinusoidal microthrombi and vascular injury; post-COVID cholangiopathy (secondary sclerosing cholangitis in critically ill patients); drug-related injury during treatment
entities.remarks: Usually mild transaminitis; autopsy livers show steatosis, mild lobular hepatitis, sinusoidal microthrombi, portal vein endothelial changes and ischaemic necrosis; severe cases may develop post-COVID secondary sclerosing cholangitis.
entities.histo: Liver injury in COVID-19 is common but usually mild, and most histological data come from autopsy series. The changes are largely non-specific and include macrovesicular steatosis (often reflecting pre-existing metabolic disease), mild lobular and portal inflammation, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, scattered acidophil bodies and congestion. Vascular changes are characteristic of severe disease: sinusoidal microthrombi and fibrin, portal vein branch thrombosis or endotheliitis, sinusoidal dilatation and patchy zone 3 ischaemic necrosis. A subset of critically ill patients develop post-COVID cholangiopathy, a form of secondary sclerosing cholangitis in critically ill patients, with bile duct injury, ductopenia, biliary casts, ductular reaction and rapid progression to biliary fibrosis. Drug toxicity from treatments such as tocilizumab, remdesivir and antimicrobials must also be considered. The differential includes ischaemic hepatitis from shock, drug-induced liver injury, sepsis-associated cholestasis and pre-existing MASLD.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role in COVID-19 liver injury, which is a diffuse process assessed on biopsy or autopsy tissue. If a focal lesion is aspirated in a patient with COVID-19, the findings reflect that lesion, and SARS-CoV-2 testing is done on respiratory samples.
entities.ihc: SARS-CoV-2 spike or nucleocapsid immunostaining and in situ hybridisation have been used in research and autopsy settings, with sparse and inconsistent positivity in hepatocytes and endothelium, so they are not diagnostic tools. CD61 or fibrin stains can highlight sinusoidal microthrombi, and CK7 and CK19 show ductular reaction and bile duct loss in post-COVID cholangiopathy.

entities.variants: Biliary (ascending cholangitis-related) abscess; portal (pylephlebitic) abscess from appendicitis or diverticulitis; haematogenous (arterial) abscess; contiguous spread; cryptogenic abscess; Klebsiella pneumoniae invasive liver abscess syndrome (hypervirulent K1/K2); post-procedural (post-TACE, post-ablation) abscess; infected tumour or cyst
entities.remarks: Commonest causes Klebsiella pneumoniae, E. coli, Streptococcus anginosus group, anaerobes; right lobe; diabetes is a risk factor; exclude underlying malignancy (colorectal, cholangiocarcinoma) in older patients; drainage plus antibiotics.
entities.histo: A pyogenic abscess is a localised collection of pus within the liver, formed by bacteria arriving through the biliary tree, the portal vein, the hepatic artery or by direct spread. Grossly it is single or multiple, often in the right lobe, with a cavity containing creamy or foul-smelling pus and a shaggy, haemorrhagic wall. Microscopically the centre is composed of necrotic debris and dense neutrophils, surrounded by a zone of granulation tissue with macrophages, plasma cells and, in older lesions, a fibrous capsule. The adjacent liver shows compressed hepatocytes, sinusoidal dilatation, ductular reaction and sometimes acute cholangitis or portal pylephlebitis indicating the route of infection. Gram stain may reveal clusters of bacteria, and actinomycotic sulphur granules or fungal hyphae should be specifically looked for. The differential includes amoebic abscess (anchovy-paste, few neutrophils, trophozoites at the edge), infected hydatid cyst (laminated membrane), necrotic or infected tumours such as metastatic colorectal carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma or HCC, and infected biliary cysts. In older patients a careful search for an underlying tumour in the abscess wall is essential.
entities.cyto: Image-guided aspiration is diagnostic and therapeutic. Aspirates yield thick purulent material with abundant degenerated neutrophils, necrotic debris and macrophages, sometimes with bacteria visible on Gram stain, and the material should be sent for culture and sensitivity. Atypical reactive hepatocytes and reactive cholangiocytes at the abscess edge can mimic carcinoma, and conversely, a necrotic tumour may yield only inflammatory debris, so any atypical epithelial cells require a cell block and correlation with imaging. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: Immunohistochemistry is not needed for diagnosis, which relies on morphology, Gram stain and culture. When atypical epithelium is present in the abscess wall, a keratin panel (CK7, CK20, CDX2, SATB2) and hepatocellular markers (HepPar1, arginase-1) help detect an underlying metastatic carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma or HCC. Special stains such as Gram, GMS and Ziehl-Neelsen exclude actinomyces, fungi and mycobacteria.

entities.variants: Acute suppurative cholangitis; cholangitic abscesses; acute cholangitis complicating choledocholithiasis, malignant stricture, stent or post-ERCP; cholangitis in biliary atresia after Kasai portoenterostomy
entities.remarks: Bacterial infection of an obstructed biliary tree (Charcot triad: fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain); neutrophils within duct epithelium and lumen on a background of large duct obstruction; can lead to cholangitic abscesses and sepsis.
entities.histo: Acute ascending cholangitis results from bacterial infection of an obstructed biliary tree, usually caused by stones, strictures, tumours or indwelling stents. Biopsy is uncommon, but the histology shows the features of large duct obstruction, including portal oedema, ductular reaction with periductular neutrophils and bile in ductules, together with neutrophils infiltrating the epithelium of interlobular bile ducts and filling their lumens. Severe cases develop cholangitic abscesses, in which a bile duct is destroyed and replaced by a collection of neutrophils and bile-stained debris. Zone 3 canalicular cholestasis and bile infarcts may also be present. Ductular neutrophils alone (pericholangiolitis) are non-specific and also occur in alcoholic hepatitis, sepsis and drug injury, so true intraluminal and intraepithelial neutrophils in interlobular ducts are needed for the diagnosis. The differential includes sepsis-associated cholestasis (cholangitis lenta, with inspissated bile in dilated ductules), primary sclerosing cholangitis with superimposed infection, recurrent pyogenic cholangitis and drug-induced cholestasis.
entities.cyto: Cytology is not used for diagnosis. Bile aspirated at ERCP or percutaneous drainage contains neutrophils and bacteria and is sent for culture; biliary brushing in this setting may show reactive atypia that must not be overcalled as malignancy.
entities.ihc: IHC has no diagnostic role. CK7 or CK19 can highlight bile duct destruction and ductular reaction, and Gram stain may show bacteria within ducts.

entities.variants: Hepatolithiasis with recurrent cholangitis; left lateral segment predominant disease; biliary strictures with proximal dilatation; parasite-associated (Clonorchis, Ascaris) forms
entities.remarks: Common in East and South-East Asia; brown pigment (calcium bilirubinate) stones in intrahepatic ducts, recurrent cholangitis, strictures, abscesses, segmental atrophy; increased risk of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and BilIN/IPNB.
entities.histo: Recurrent pyogenic cholangitis is a chronic disease of the large intrahepatic bile ducts characterised by intrahepatic pigment stones, recurrent bacterial infection and stricturing.
