Grossly, segments, especially the left lateral segment, contain dilated ducts packed with soft, brown, muddy calcium bilirubinate stones, with alternating strictures, abscesses and atrophic, fibrotic parenchyma. Microscopically, the large ducts show chronic and acute inflammation of the wall, ulceration, dense periductal fibrosis and proliferation of peribiliary glands (proliferative cholangitis), with mucinous metaplasia, and the epithelium may show reactive atypia, biliary intraepithelial neoplasia or intraductal papillary neoplasm. The portal tracts in the affected segments show changes of large duct obstruction and may progress to biliary fibrosis. Parasites such as Clonorchis or Ascaris remnants may occasionally be found within stones. The disease carries a significant risk of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, so resection specimens should be sampled widely. The differential includes primary sclerosing cholangitis, IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, secondary sclerosing cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma infiltrating the duct wall.
entities.cyto: Cytology is used mainly on bile or brushings to screen for cholangiocarcinoma. Smears show inflammatory cells, bile pigment, stone debris and reactive biliary epithelium with nuclear enlargement and prominent nucleoli, which can mimic malignancy; overcalling in this inflammatory setting is a known pitfall, so only cells with marked nuclear irregularity, crowding and loss of polarity should be called suspicious or malignant.
entities.ihc: IHC does not establish the diagnosis. In biopsies of stricture walls, p53 overexpression or complete loss, loss of SMAD4 and a high Ki-67 favour dysplasia or carcinoma over reactive epithelium, and S100P and IMP3 positivity also support malignancy. Mucin stains highlight mucinous metaplasia of peribiliary glands.

entities.variants: Miliary (disseminated) hepatic tuberculosis; granulomatous hepatitis in pulmonary TB; tuberculoma (local nodular form); tuberculous liver abscess; hepatobiliary (tubular) TB with bile duct involvement; TB in HIV-positive and transplant patients; drug-induced injury from antitubercular therapy (separate DILI)
entities.remarks: Very relevant in India; caseating epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells, most often portal or lobular; ZN or auramine for AFB, GeneXpert (CBNAAT) and culture; tuberculoma and abscess can mimic tumour on imaging.
entities.histo: The liver is involved in most cases of disseminated tuberculosis, and less commonly in a localised form. Miliary tuberculosis shows numerous small, discrete epithelioid granulomas throughout portal tracts and lobules, often with central caseous necrosis and Langhans-type giant cells, with a rim of lymphocytes. Tuberculomas are larger confluent caseating nodules that may calcify or soften into tuberculous abscesses with abundant caseous debris. Hepatobiliary tuberculosis involves bile ducts and causes strictures and obstructive jaundice. Granulomas in HIV-positive or immunosuppressed patients may be poorly formed, with sheets of macrophages and many bacilli. Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine-rhodamine staining often shows few acid-fast bacilli, so molecular testing (GeneXpert MTB/RIF, PCR) and culture on fresh tissue are important. The differentials include sarcoidosis (non-caseating, often portal, with fibrosis), atypical mycobacteria (MAC with foamy macrophages), fungal infections (GMS stain), brucellosis, Q fever (fibrin-ring granulomas), drug-induced granulomas, PBC (granulomas near damaged ducts) and lymphoma with granulomatous reaction. Hepatotoxicity from isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide is a separate drug-induced injury that may appear in the same patient.
entities.cyto: Image-guided FNA of a focal lesion can show epithelioid histiocyte clusters (granulomas), Langhans giant cells and granular caseous necrosis, with lymphocytes. Smears should be stained with Ziehl-Neelsen and material sent for GeneXpert and culture, which improves the yield. Pitfalls include confusing epithelioid cell clusters with spindle cell tumours or poorly cohesive carcinoma cells, and the necrotic debris of tumour with caseation; a mixture of granulomas with atypical epithelial cells should prompt a search for carcinoma. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: Immunohistochemistry is not needed for the diagnosis in most cases. CD68 highlights epithelioid macrophages, and mycobacterial antigen (MPT64) immunostaining or polyclonal anti-BCG antibodies, where available, can show mycobacterial antigens in granulomas with improved sensitivity over ZN. PCR on paraffin tissue is a useful adjunct. Stains for fungi (GMS, PAS) are performed to exclude fungal granulomas.

entities.variants: Acute Q fever with granulomatous hepatitis; chronic Q fever (endocarditis-associated) liver involvement
entities.remarks: Zoonosis from cattle, sheep and goats; classic fibrin-ring (doughnut) granuloma with central fat vacuole; serology or PCR for diagnosis; fibrin-ring granulomas also occur with EBV, CMV, hepatitis A, allopurinol, leishmaniasis and lymphoma.
entities.histo: Q fever is a zoonotic rickettsial-like infection acquired by inhaling aerosols from infected livestock, and acute infection often involves the liver. The most characteristic finding is the fibrin-ring granuloma, a small epithelioid granuloma with a central clear fat vacuole surrounded by a ring of eosinophilic fibrin and a cuff of histiocytes, lymphocytes and occasional neutrophils, giving a doughnut appearance. These granulomas lie in portal tracts and lobules, accompanied by mild lobular hepatitis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, steatosis and portal inflammation. A phosphotungstic acid-haematoxylin (PTAH) or Masson trichrome stain highlights the fibrin ring. Fibrin-ring granulomas are not specific; they also occur in EBV, CMV and hepatitis A infections, leishmaniasis, toxoplasmosis, typhoid fever, Hodgkin lymphoma and allopurinol hypersensitivity, so serology or PCR is needed to confirm Q fever. Chronic Q fever, usually with endocarditis, may give non-specific granulomas or none at all.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role. Diagnosis relies on Coxiella serology (phase I and II antibodies) and PCR.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used routinely. Immunostaining for Coxiella burnetii has been described in reference laboratories, and CD68 highlights histiocytes in the fibrin-ring granulomas. Fibrin can be highlighted with PTAH or anti-fibrinogen immunostain.

entities.variants: Acute brucellosis with granulomatous hepatitis; chronic brucellosis with suppurative hepatic abscess (brucelloma, B. suis); hepatosplenic brucellosis
entities.remarks: Zoonosis (unpasteurised milk, livestock contact); small non-caseating granulomas or non-specific hepatitis in acute disease; calcified suppurative 'brucelloma' in chronic disease; serology and blood culture for diagnosis.
entities.histo: Brucellosis is a systemic zoonotic infection acquired from unpasteurised dairy products or contact with livestock, and the liver is involved in most patients. In acute infection, especially due to Brucella abortus, the liver shows small, loose, non-caseating epithelioid granulomas in lobules and portal tracts, often accompanied by mild lobular hepatitis with Kupffer cell hyperplasia and portal lymphocytic infiltrates. Brucella melitensis tends to produce non-specific hepatitis with scattered necrosis rather than well-formed granulomas. Chronic infection, typically with Brucella suis, can form suppurative abscesses with central necrosis, a fibrous capsule and calcification (hepatic brucelloma). The differential includes tuberculosis (caseating granulomas, positive AFB or molecular tests), sarcoidosis, Q fever and typhoid fever, so diagnosis relies on serology (standard agglutination test) and blood or tissue culture.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no routine role. Aspirates of a brucelloma may show necrotic debris, histiocytes and neutrophils, and should be cultured with warning to the laboratory because of biosafety risk.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used in routine diagnosis; CD68 highlights granulomas, and stains for AFB and fungi help exclude other granulomatous infections.

entities.variants: Typhoid hepatitis (Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi); typhoid nodules; Salmonella liver abscess (rare); acute acalculous cholecystitis association
entities.remarks: Common in India; mild transaminitis; Kupffer cell hyperplasia and lobular 'typhoid nodules' (aggregates of macrophages with phagocytosed debris); blood culture and Widal test; may form fibrin-ring granulomas.
entities.histo: Liver involvement is frequent in enteric fever and usually causes mild hepatomegaly and a transaminase rise; occasionally it mimics acute viral hepatitis. The characteristic lesion is the typhoid nodule, a small cluster of macrophages (some containing phagocytosed red cells, lymphocytes and nuclear debris) replacing necrotic hepatocytes in the lobule. There is also Kupffer cell hyperplasia, mild portal inflammation, focal hepatocyte necrosis, steatosis and sometimes fibrin-ring granulomas. Bile stasis may be present. Rare complications include Salmonella liver abscess, especially in patients with pre-existing liver lesions or haemoglobinopathies. The differential includes viral hepatitis, other bacterial infections such as brucellosis and leptospirosis, malaria and drug-induced injury, and diagnosis rests on blood, bone marrow or stool culture.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role in typhoid hepatitis. The diagnosis rests on blood, bone marrow or stool culture and serology, and FNA is used only if a complicating abscess needs aspiration for culture.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used in diagnosis; CD68 highlights macrophage aggregates (typhoid nodules), and culture is required to identify the organism.

entities.variants: Congenital syphilis (neonatal hepatitis, diffuse pericellular fibrosis, hepar lobatum in late form); secondary syphilitic hepatitis; tertiary syphilis with gummas (hepar lobatum)
entities.remarks: Secondary syphilis gives cholestatic hepatitis with disproportionately raised ALP, pericholangitis and portal neutrophils with granulomas; congenital syphilis gives diffuse pericellular fibrosis; gummas create coarse scarring (hepar lobatum); Treponema IHC.
entities.histo: Syphilis affects the liver in three settings. Congenital syphilis presents as neonatal hepatitis with giant cell transformation, cholestasis, extramedullary haematopoiesis and a characteristic diffuse pericellular (sinusoidal) fibrosis that isolates single hepatocytes or small groups, with many spirochaetes in the tissue. Secondary syphilis causes a cholestatic hepatitis with a disproportionately high alkaline phosphatase; the biopsy shows portal inflammation rich in lymphocytes, plasma cells and neutrophils, pericholangitis or bile duct injury, scattered lobular necroinflammatory foci, occasional non-caseating granulomas and perivascular plasma cells with endothelial swelling. Tertiary syphilis produces gummas, areas of rubbery necrosis surrounded by histiocytes, plasma cells and fibrosis, which heal with deep scars that divide the liver into irregular lobes (hepar lobatum). The differentials include drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis, PBC, granulomatous hepatitis of other causes, and, for gummas, tuberculosis or necrotic tumour. Warthin-Starry silver stain can show spirochaetes but is insensitive in acquired disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no routine role. Aspirates of a gumma may show necrotic material, histiocytes and plasma cells, which is non-specific.
entities.ihc: Treponema pallidum immunostaining is more sensitive and specific than silver stains and shows spirochaetes in portal tracts, sinusoids and around vessels, especially in congenital and secondary syphilis. CD138 highlights the plasma cell-rich infiltrate. Serology (VDRL/RPR with treponemal tests) confirms the diagnosis.

entities.variants: Anicteric leptospirosis; icterohaemorrhagic leptospirosis (Weil disease) with hepatorenal involvement and haemorrhage; pulmonary haemorrhagic form
entities.remarks: Common in coastal India (Kerala) after monsoon flooding; deep jaundice with only modest transaminase rise; liver shows hepatocyte dissociation (loss of cohesion), cholestasis, Kupffer cell hyperplasia and little necrosis.
entities.histo: Leptospirosis is a spirochaetal zoonosis spread by water contaminated with rodent urine, common in Kerala and other monsoon-affected regions of India. In Weil disease, patients have deep jaundice, renal failure and bleeding, yet the transaminases are only moderately raised, and the liver histology mirrors this, showing relatively little necrosis. The characteristic finding is dissociation of liver cell plates, with hepatocytes losing their cohesion and lying singly in the sinusoids, together with canalicular cholestasis, prominent mitoses and binucleation, Kupffer cell hyperplasia with erythrophagocytosis, and a mild portal infiltrate of lymphocytes and neutrophils. Haemorrhages and focal necrosis may be present. Silver stains such as Warthin-Starry may show spirochaetes but are often negative. The differentials include viral hepatitis (more necrosis and inflammation), sepsis-associated cholestasis, malaria, typhoid and dengue, and diagnosis relies on serology (IgM ELISA, MAT) and PCR.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the diagnosis of leptospirosis, which is confirmed by serology (microscopic agglutination test) or PCR on blood and urine. Liver tissue is rarely sampled during the acute illness.
entities.ihc: Leptospiral immunostaining (polyclonal anti-Leptospira) can demonstrate intact organisms or granular antigen in the liver, kidney and lung in reference laboratories, mostly on autopsy tissue. Routine diagnosis relies on serology and PCR rather than IHC.

entities.entity: Rickettsial infections of liver (scrub typhus, spotted fevers)
entities.variants: Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi); Indian tick typhus and Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia spp.); murine typhus; ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis
entities.remarks: Scrub typhus is a major cause of acute febrile illness with hepatitis in India (eschar, transaminitis); liver shows portal and lobular mononuclear infiltrate, small granulomas, Kupffer cell hyperplasia and portal vasculitis; doxycycline-responsive.
entities.histo: Rickettsial infections infect endothelial cells and cause a systemic vasculitis, and the liver is commonly involved. Scrub typhus, caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and very common in India, typically causes fever, an eschar and elevated transaminases. The liver shows portal tract inflammation with lymphocytes, macrophages and some neutrophils, portal vasculitis with endothelial swelling, Kupffer cell hyperplasia and erythrophagocytosis, mild lobular hepatitis and scattered microgranulomas or small granulomas, sometimes with fibrin-ring appearance. Cholestasis and focal necrosis can occur in severe disease. Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other spotted fevers show similar portal vasculitis with thrombi, and ehrlichiosis may produce granulomas and haemophagocytosis. The differential includes typhoid, leptospirosis, dengue, viral hepatitis and drug injury, and diagnosis is by serology (IgM ELISA, Weil-Felix historically) and PCR.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the diagnosis of rickettsial liver disease. Diagnosis depends on the clinical picture (eschar, rash), serology and PCR on blood, and liver involvement is usually inferred from liver function tests.
entities.ihc: Rickettsial immunostains, available mainly in reference laboratories, can demonstrate organisms within endothelial cells and macrophages. In routine practice, diagnosis is serological or molecular, and IHC has no routine role.

entities.variants: Primary hepatic actinomycosis; secondary (abdominal, from appendix, colon or IUD-related pelvic disease); actinomycotic liver abscess
entities.remarks: Actinomyces israelii; chronic suppurative mass that mimics tumour; abscesses with sulphur granules (filamentous Gram-positive bacteria with Splendore-Hoeppli material), dense fibrosis, sinus tracts.
entities.histo: Hepatic actinomycosis is an uncommon chronic suppurative infection, usually spreading from an abdominal source through the portal vein, and it often presents as a mass suspected to be malignant. The lesion consists of multiple interconnecting abscesses separated by dense fibrous tissue and granulation tissue rich in foamy macrophages and plasma cells. Within the abscesses are sulphur granules, rounded basophilic colonies of radiating filamentous bacteria with a club-like eosinophilic periphery (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon). Gram stain shows branching Gram-positive filaments, and GMS also stains them, while modified acid-fast stains are negative, which separates Actinomyces from Nocardia. The differentials include pyogenic abscess from other bacteria, botryomycosis (granules made of non-filamentous bacteria), nocardiosis, fungal infection, inflammatory pseudotumour and an infiltrating carcinoma with desmoplasia.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show neutrophils, macrophages and, if sampled, sulphur granules composed of tangled filamentous organisms, which can be seen on Papanicolaou or Giemsa stains and confirmed with Gram stain; culture requires anaerobic conditions.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed. Gram, GMS and modified Ziehl-Neelsen stains characterise the organism, and keratin stains may be used to exclude an underlying carcinoma in a fibrotic mass.

entities.entity: Bartonella infections of liver (bacillary peliosis, cat-scratch disease)
entities.variants: Bacillary peliosis hepatis and bacillary angiomatosis (B. henselae, B. quintana, immunosuppressed and HIV patients); hepatosplenic cat-scratch disease (necrotising granulomas, immunocompetent children)
entities.remarks: Immunosuppressed hosts: blood-filled peliotic spaces surrounded by myxoid stroma with granular purple clumps of bacteria (Warthin-Starry positive); immunocompetent: stellate necrotising granulomas with central neutrophils.
entities.histo: Bartonella henselae and Bartonella quintana cause two distinct hepatic patterns depending on immune status. In HIV-infected and other immunosuppressed patients, bacillary peliosis hepatis consists of multiple blood-filled cystic spaces in the parenchyma, surrounded by a myxoid or fibromyxoid stroma containing granular purplish clumps that are masses of bacteria, with mixed inflammatory cells and neutrophils. Bacillary angiomatosis-type lobular capillary proliferations with plump epithelioid endothelial cells may also be seen. In immunocompetent children and adults, hepatosplenic cat-scratch disease produces multiple small hypodense lesions which are necrotising granulomas with stellate microabscesses containing neutrophils, surrounded by palisading epithelioid histiocytes. The differentials include ordinary (non-infectious) peliosis hepatis, angiosarcoma or Kaposi sarcoma for the vascular pattern, and tuberculosis, fungal infection, tularaemia and lymphogranuloma-type infections for the granulomatous pattern. Warthin-Starry or Steiner silver stain demonstrates clusters of bacilli.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role. Aspirates of granulomatous lesions show epithelioid histiocytes, neutrophils and necrotic debris; the organisms are not usually seen on routine stains, and PCR or serology is needed.
entities.ihc: Bartonella henselae immunostaining highlights the bacterial clusters in peliotic lesions and granulomas and is more specific than silver stains. In vascular lesions, CD31 and ERG outline the endothelium, while HHV-8 (LANA-1) is negative, which separates bacillary angiomatosis from Kaposi sarcoma. PCR on tissue confirms the species.

entities.variants: Acute septicaemic melioidosis with multiple liver abscesses; chronic localised hepatic and splenic abscesses
entities.remarks: Burkholderia pseudomallei; endemic in South and South-East Asia including India; diabetes is the major risk factor; multiple small 'honeycomb' or 'necklace' abscesses in liver and spleen; culture is essential.
entities.histo: Melioidosis is an infection by Burkholderia pseudomallei, a soil and water bacterium endemic in parts of India and South-East Asia, and diabetes is the commonest predisposing condition. In the liver it produces multiple small abscesses that may coalesce into multiloculated lesions with a honeycomb pattern on imaging, often with similar lesions in the spleen. Histologically, early lesions are microabscesses with neutrophils and necrosis, while older lesions become granulomatous with central necrosis, epithelioid histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells and a fibrous capsule, resembling tuberculosis. Gram stain may show small Gram-negative bacilli with bipolar (safety pin) staining within macrophages. The differentials include pyogenic abscess due to other organisms, tuberculosis, fungal infection and amoebic abscess, so culture of pus or blood is essential for diagnosis and correct antibiotic choice.
entities.cyto: Aspirated pus shows neutrophils, macrophages and necrotic debris; Gram stain may show bipolar-staining Gram-negative bacilli, and the specimen must be cultured with a request to look for Burkholderia because the laboratory needs to apply biosafety precautions.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used in routine diagnosis; diagnosis rests on culture and, where available, antigen detection or PCR. Stains for AFB and fungi help exclude other granulomatous causes.

entities.variants: Chronic disseminated candidiasis after neutropenia (haematological malignancy); acute disseminated candidiasis with microabscesses; Candida liver abscess
entities.remarks: Appears after neutrophil recovery in leukaemia patients; multiple small target lesions in liver and spleen; necrotising granulomas or microabscesses with yeasts and pseudohyphae (PAS, GMS); cultures often negative.
entities.histo: Hepatosplenic candidiasis is typically seen in patients with haematological malignancy who develop persistent fever after recovery from chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, with multiple small hypoechoic or target lesions in the liver and spleen. Biopsies show necrotising granulomas or microabscesses with central necrosis and neutrophils, surrounded by epithelioid histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells and fibrosis in older lesions. Budding yeasts (3 to 5 micrometres) and pseudohyphae can be identified in the necrotic centres, but they may be sparse and are best seen with PAS-diastase and GMS stains. In acute disseminated candidiasis during neutropenia, there are microabscesses or necrotic foci with abundant fungi and little inflammation. The differential includes aspergillosis (septate hyphae with acute-angle branching), mucormycosis (broad pauciseptate hyphae), mycobacterial infection and leukaemic or lymphomatous infiltrates.
entities.cyto: Aspirates of lesions may show necrotic debris, neutrophils, histiocytes and fungal elements; budding yeast and pseudohyphae are visible on Papanicolaou, PAS or GMS stains, and material should be sent for culture and fungal PCR.
entities.ihc: Candida-specific immunostains and in situ hybridisation exist but are not widely used; PAS and GMS special stains are the main tools. Immunostaining for leukaemic markers (CD34, MPO, CD117) helps exclude recurrent leukaemia in the same patient population.

entities.variants: Disseminated histoplasmosis (HIV/AIDS, immunosuppressed); granulomatous hepatitis with Histoplasma; African histoplasmosis (H. duboisii, rare)
entities.remarks: Histoplasma capsulatum; endemic pockets in India (Gangetic plain); diffuse Kupffer cell and portal macrophage parasitisation by small (2-4 micrometre) intracellular yeasts with halo, or epithelioid granulomas; GMS stain positive.
entities.histo: Liver involvement by Histoplasma capsulatum is common in disseminated disease, especially in people with HIV or other immunosuppression, and the condition is endemic in parts of India. In severely immunosuppressed patients, there is diffuse parasitisation of Kupffer cells and portal macrophages by numerous small, oval, intracellular yeasts with a surrounding clear halo, often with little granulomatous response, and hepatocyte necrosis may be present. In patients with better immunity, the liver shows small epithelioid granulomas in portal tracts and lobules containing fewer organisms, sometimes with necrosis and later calcification. GMS and PAS stains highlight the yeasts with narrow-based budding. The differential includes visceral leishmaniasis (amastigotes with kinetoplast, Giemsa-positive, GMS-negative), Talaromyces marneffei (septate, sausage-shaped yeasts dividing by fission), Pneumocystis, Cryptococcus (larger, variable sized yeasts with mucicarmine-positive capsule), Candida glabrata and toxoplasma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role, although aspirates or bone marrow smears may show macrophages containing numerous small yeasts with halos on Giemsa stain; GMS stain separates them from Leishmania, which is GMS negative.
entities.ihc: Immunostains for Histoplasma are available in some reference laboratories, but GMS and PAS special stains are the routine tools. CD68 highlights the parasitised macrophages; the yeasts are negative with Leishmania-specific stains. Urine antigen testing and culture confirm the diagnosis.

entities.entity: Other fungal infections of liver (aspergillosis, mucormycosis, cryptococcosis, Pneumocystis, talaromycosis, coccidioidomycosis)
entities.variants: Invasive aspergillosis (angioinvasive, infarct-like); mucormycosis (angioinvasive, infarcts); cryptococcosis (granulomatous or mucoid); Pneumocystis jirovecii hepatic infection (foamy exudate); Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffei (HIV, North-East India); coccidioidomycosis and blastomycosis (granulomas)
entities.remarks: Rare, almost always in immunosuppressed patients; pattern ranges from angioinvasive necrosis (Aspergillus, Mucorales) to granulomas or macrophage parasitisation; identify by morphology on GMS/PAS and confirm by culture or PCR.
entities.histo: Several fungi other than Candida and Histoplasma may involve the liver, usually in immunosuppressed patients or as part of disseminated infection. Invasive aspergillosis produces haemorrhagic infarct-like areas of necrosis with angioinvasion by narrow (3 to 6 micrometre), septate hyphae with regular acute-angle (dichotomous) branching. Mucormycosis shows broader (6 to 15 micrometre), ribbon-like, pauciseptate hyphae with irregular right-angle branching, also invading vessels and causing infarcts. Cryptococcosis forms granulomas or mucoid lesions containing round yeasts of variable size with a thick capsule that stains with mucicarmine and Alcian blue; Fontana-Masson staining of the cell wall helps in capsule-deficient forms. Pneumocystis jirovecii causes foamy, frothy eosinophilic exudate in sinusoids and vessels, with cup-shaped cysts on GMS. Talaromyces marneffei, endemic in North-East India and South-East Asia, fills macrophages with small yeasts that divide by central transverse septation. Coccidioidomycosis and blastomycosis produce granulomas with large spherules or broad-based budding yeasts respectively. The differentials include each other and bacterial or mycobacterial infections, so culture or molecular identification is important for management.
entities.cyto: Cytology may occasionally identify fungi in aspirates from focal lesions, for example cryptococcal yeasts with capsules on Giemsa or mucicarmine, or hyphae in necrotic material, but culture and PCR are required for species identification.
entities.ihc: Organism-specific immunostains (Aspergillus, Mucorales, Cryptococcus) and in situ hybridisation are available in some reference laboratories and can help separate morphologically similar hyphae. GMS, PAS, mucicarmine and Fontana-Masson special stains are the main routine tools. Serum galactomannan and cryptococcal antigen tests support the diagnosis.

entities.variants: Acute amoebic liver abscess (usually single, right lobe); multiple amoebic abscesses; complicated abscess (rupture into pleura, pericardium or peritoneum); secondarily infected amoebic abscess
entities.remarks: Entamoeba histolytica; common in India; 'anchovy paste' necrotic contents with few neutrophils; trophozoites found at the abscess wall, not the centre; serology (anti-amoebic antibodies) and imaging; responds to metronidazole.
entities.histo: An amoebic liver abscess develops when Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites from the colon reach the liver through the portal vein. It is usually single and located in the right lobe, and grossly contains thick, odourless, reddish-brown necrotic material often compared to anchovy paste. The centre consists of liquefied, granular, eosinophilic necrotic debris with remarkably few neutrophils, because the trophozoites lyse them. The wall contains a narrow rim of necrotic hepatocytes, fibrin and inflammatory cells, and this is where trophozoites are best found. Trophozoites are 15 to 50 micrometres, with foamy cytoplasm, a small eccentric nucleus with a central karyosome, and often ingested red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis), which is the most specific feature. They are highlighted by PAS (strongly positive cytoplasm) and trichrome stains. Older abscesses develop a fibrous capsule. The differential includes pyogenic abscess (neutrophil-rich pus, bacteria), necrotic tumour, infected hydatid cyst and hepatic tuberculosis. Macrophages can mimic trophozoites, but they have larger nuclei, lack erythrophagocytosis, and are CD68 positive.
entities.cyto: Aspiration yields thick, chocolate-brown or anchovy-paste material composed of granular necrotic debris with few inflammatory cells; trophozoites are often absent because they lie in the wall, so the last portion of the aspirate (from the wall) has the best yield. When present, trophozoites show foamy cytoplasm, a round nucleus with central karyosome and ingested red cells, and they stain magenta with PAS. Histiocytes and degenerated hepatocytes are the main mimics. Serology and antigen tests are more sensitive than cytology. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: IHC is not usually required. Entamoeba histolytica-specific immunostains are available in some laboratories, and CD68 is negative in trophozoites but positive in macrophage mimics. PAS staining is the most useful practical stain.

entities.variants: Unilocular hydatid cyst; cyst with daughter cysts (multivesicular); calcified/dead cyst; infected cyst; ruptured cyst (into biliary tree, peritoneum or thorax); WHO-IWGE ultrasound stages CE1 to CE5
entities.remarks: Echinococcus granulosus (dog tapeworm), endemic in India; three-layered cyst: outer host fibrous pericyst, acellular laminated (PAS-positive) membrane, inner germinal layer with brood capsules, protoscolices and hooklets; risk of anaphylaxis on rupture.
entities.histo: Cystic echinococcosis is caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus granulosus, and the liver, especially the right lobe, is the commonest site. Grossly the cyst is filled with clear fluid (hydatid sand) and often contains daughter cysts, and it is surrounded by a thick fibrous host capsule. Microscopically there are three layers. The outer pericyst is host-derived fibrous tissue with chronic inflammation, eosinophils, foreign-body giant cells and sometimes calcification. The middle laminated membrane is a thick, acellular, eosinophilic layer with characteristic parallel laminations, strongly PAS positive and GMS positive. The inner germinal layer is thin and nucleated, producing brood capsules which contain protoscolices bearing refractile hooklets; free hooklets persist in old or degenerated cysts and are acid-fast and birefringent. Infected cysts show neutrophils and necrotic debris, and ruptured cysts may cause biliary obstruction or eosinophilic peritonitis. The differentials include alveolar echinococcosis (infiltrative small vesicles), simple and other cysts (epithelial lining, no laminated membrane), mucinous cystic neoplasm (ovarian-type stroma) and abscesses.
entities.cyto: Diagnostic aspiration of a suspected hydatid cyst is avoided because of the risk of anaphylaxis and dissemination, but percutaneous treatment (PAIR) or accidental aspiration yields clear fluid with protoscolices, refractile hooklets and fragments of laminated membrane, which are diagnostic. Hooklets are well seen on Papanicolaou and with polarised light, and laminated membrane fragments are PAS positive.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed for the diagnosis, which rests on morphology, serology and imaging. PAS and GMS highlight the laminated membrane, and modified Ziehl-Neelsen stains hooklets. Echinococcus-specific immunostains (for example Em2G11 for E. multilocularis) are used in reference laboratories to separate the two main species.

entities.variants: Hepatic alveolar echinococcosis (Echinococcus multilocularis); polycystic echinococcosis (E. vogeli, E. oligarthrus; South America)
entities.remarks: Behaves like a slowly growing malignant tumour: infiltrative, multivesicular, with central necrosis and calcification, invades vessels and bile ducts and may metastasise; thin PAS-positive laminated membranes without fibrous pericyst; rare in India.
entities.histo: Alveolar echinococcosis is caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus multilocularis, mainly in the Northern Hemisphere, and it behaves like a slowly growing infiltrative tumour. Grossly the lesion is a firm, ill-defined, pale mass with numerous small vesicles giving a sponge-like or alveolar appearance, often with central necrosis and calcification. Microscopically, many small irregular vesicles bounded by thin PAS-positive laminated membranes infiltrate the parenchyma, surrounded by granulomatous inflammation, epithelioid histiocytes, giant cells and dense fibrosis, without a well-formed host capsule. Protoscolices are rare in human infection. The lesion may invade hepatic veins, bile ducts and the diaphragm, and can spread to the lungs and brain. The differentials include cholangiocarcinoma and metastatic carcinoma (on imaging and gross examination), cystic echinococcosis (large cyst with thick laminated membrane and pericyst) and tuberculosis.
entities.cyto: Aspiration may yield fragments of thin, PAS-positive laminated membrane, necrotic debris and histiocytes; protoscolices are rarely seen. Cytology can raise the possibility but histology, serology and imaging confirm it.
entities.ihc: Em2G11 monoclonal antibody immunostaining highlights E. multilocularis antigen in the laminated layer and in small particles within macrophages, and separates alveolar from cystic echinococcosis. PAS and GMS stain the membranes.

entities.variants: Schistosoma mansoni and S. japonicum hepatic schistosomiasis; acute (Katayama) schistosomiasis; chronic hepatosplenic schistosomiasis with Symmers pipe-stem fibrosis; schistosomiasis coexisting with HBV/HCV
entities.remarks: Eggs lodge in portal venules, induce granulomas with eosinophils, and heal with dense portal 'pipe-stem' fibrosis; causes presinusoidal portal hypertension with preserved liver function; S. mansoni egg has a lateral spine; S. japonicum egg small, no prominent spine.
entities.histo: Hepatic schistosomiasis results from eggs of Schistosoma mansoni or Schistosoma japonicum carried by the portal blood from mesenteric veins, where adult worms live. Eggs lodge in small portal vein branches and provoke a granulomatous reaction with epithelioid histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells and many eosinophils, sometimes with Splendore-Hoeppli material around the egg. Over time the granulomas heal with dense portal fibrosis, and in heavy infection large portal tracts become encircled by thick fibrous collars, giving the gross appearance of white pipe-stem (Symmers) fibrosis without true cirrhosis. Portal vein branches are obliterated, causing presinusoidal portal hypertension with splenomegaly and varices, while hepatocellular function is preserved. Eggs may be intact, degenerated or calcified; S. mansoni eggs are oval with a lateral spine, whereas S. japonicum eggs are smaller and round with a minute spine. Black schistosomal pigment (haemozoin-like) is seen in Kupffer cells and portal macrophages. Modified Ziehl-Neelsen stains the egg shell of S. mansoni and S. japonicum (but not S. haematobium). The differentials include other causes of portal fibrosis and non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (porto-sinusoidal vascular disease, congenital hepatic fibrosis), other parasitic granulomas, tuberculosis and malarial pigment.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no routine role; eggs may occasionally be seen in aspirates of granulomatous lesions. Diagnosis relies on stool or rectal biopsy egg detection, serology and imaging.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used in diagnosis. Special stains such as modified Ziehl-Neelsen highlight eggs, and CD68 shows granulomas. Trichrome shows the extent of portal fibrosis.

entities.variants: Clonorchis sinensis (East Asia); Opisthorchis viverrini (South-East Asia); Opisthorchis felineus (Eastern Europe, Russia); acute and chronic infection; fluke-associated cholangiocarcinoma
entities.remarks: Acquired by eating raw freshwater fish; flukes live in intrahepatic bile ducts; chronic cholangitis with periductal fibrosis, adenomatous hyperplasia of duct epithelium and goblet cell metaplasia; Group 1 carcinogens for cholangiocarcinoma.
entities.histo: The liver flukes Clonorchis sinensis and Opisthorchis species are acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish containing metacercariae, and the adult flukes live for years in medium and large intrahepatic bile ducts. The infected ducts become dilated, with thickened walls showing chronic inflammation with eosinophils, dense periductal fibrosis, epithelial hyperplasia with adenomatous proliferation of peribiliary glands, and goblet cell and mucinous metaplasia. Adult flukes, flat and leaf-shaped, 1 to 2.5 cm long, may be found within the lumen with a tegument, suckers and internal organs, and their eggs are small (about 30 micrometres) and operculated. Chronic infection predisposes to stones, recurrent pyogenic cholangitis, biliary intraepithelial neoplasia and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, particularly the large duct type, which is endemic in north-east Thailand and parts of China and Korea. The differentials include recurrent pyogenic cholangitis without flukes, fascioliasis, primary sclerosing cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma in other settings.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role; eggs may occasionally be found in bile aspirates or duodenal fluid. Biliary brushing cytology is used to detect cholangiocarcinoma in endemic areas, where reactive changes induced by flukes can mimic dysplasia.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed for diagnosis of the infection. In associated dysplasia or carcinoma, p53, SMAD4 and Ki-67 help separate neoplastic from reactive epithelium, and CK7, CK19 and S100P support biliary carcinoma.

entities.variants: Acute (hepatic migratory) phase with necrotic tracks and eosinophilic abscesses; chronic biliary phase with flukes in large bile ducts; ectopic fascioliasis
entities.remarks: Fasciola hepatica and F. gigantica (sheep and cattle; watercress ingestion); acute phase shows serpiginous tracks of necrosis with eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals; chronic phase mimics choledocholithiasis; marked eosinophilia.
entities.histo: Fascioliasis is caused by the sheep liver fluke Fasciola hepatica or the larger Fasciola gigantica, acquired by eating watercress or other water plants contaminated by metacercariae. In the acute hepatic phase, immature flukes penetrate the liver capsule and migrate through the parenchyma, leaving serpiginous tracks of necrosis surrounded by eosinophil-rich inflammation, eosinophilic microabscesses, Charcot-Leyden crystals, granulomas and haemorrhage; subcapsular lesions may appear as multiple clustered nodules on imaging. In the chronic biliary phase, adult flukes, up to 3 cm long, reside in large bile ducts and the gallbladder, causing duct dilatation, hyperplasia, periductal fibrosis, cholangitis and obstruction. Eggs are large (130 to 150 micrometres) and operculated. The differentials include visceral larva migrans, other parasitic and eosinophilic abscesses, hypereosinophilic syndrome, metastatic tumour on imaging, and clonorchiasis or opisthorchiasis in the biliary phase.
entities.cyto: Cytology has little role. Aspirates of acute lesions show necrotic debris with numerous eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals, which suggests a parasitic process; eggs may be found in bile or duodenal aspirates in the chronic phase.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Diagnosis rests on serology (Fasciola antibodies), stool egg detection in the chronic phase, imaging and peripheral eosinophilia.

entities.variants: Visceral leishmaniasis (L. donovani, Indian kala-azar of Bihar and eastern India); L. infantum; leishmaniasis in HIV co-infection; post kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (skin, not liver)
entities.remarks: Endemic in Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal; massive hepatosplenomegaly, fever, pancytopenia; Kupffer cells and portal macrophages stuffed with amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies with kinetoplast); fibrin-ring granulomas; may cause portal fibrosis (Rogers cirrhosis).
entities.histo: Visceral leishmaniasis, known in India as kala-azar, is caused by Leishmania donovani transmitted by sandflies, and is endemic in Bihar and neighbouring states. The liver is enlarged and shows marked Kupffer cell hyperplasia, with Kupffer cells and portal macrophages distended by numerous small (2 to 4 micrometres) oval amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies), each with a nucleus and a rod-shaped kinetoplast, best seen on Giemsa staining. There may be small epithelioid granulomas or fibrin-ring granulomas, portal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates and sinusoidal congestion. Long-standing infection can cause perisinusoidal and portal fibrosis (Rogers cirrhosis), and severe disease can be complicated by haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. The differentials include histoplasmosis (GMS-positive yeasts without kinetoplast), Talaromyces marneffei (transverse septum), toxoplasmosis, Pneumocystis, and other storage or macrophage disorders. Confirmation is by splenic or bone marrow aspiration, rK39 antigen test and PCR.
entities.cyto: The diagnosis is usually made on splenic or bone marrow aspirates rather than liver aspirates; Giemsa-stained smears show macrophages and free extracellular forms containing amastigotes with a nucleus and kinetoplast. Splenic aspirate has the highest sensitivity. Liver aspirates, if taken, show the same organisms in Kupffer cells.
entities.ihc: Leishmania-specific immunostaining (for example antibodies to Leishmania antigens, or CD1a, which cross-reacts with amastigotes in some studies) can help when organisms are sparse. GMS is negative in Leishmania and positive in Histoplasma, which is a useful special-stain distinction. PCR on tissue or blood confirms the species.

entities.variants: Falciparum malaria hepatopathy (malarial hepatitis); Plasmodium vivax liver dysfunction; chronic malaria with haemozoin deposition; hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly with hepatic sinusoidal lymphocytosis
entities.remarks: Common in India; jaundice from haemolysis and hepatocyte injury; Kupffer cells laden with black-brown malarial pigment (haemozoin, birefringent, Perls negative); sinusoidal congestion with parasitised red cells; liver-stage (exoerythrocytic) forms not seen in biopsies.
entities.histo: The liver is affected in malaria through haemolysis, sequestration of parasitised red cells, Kupffer cell activation and, in severe falciparum malaria, reduced hepatic blood flow. Biopsy or autopsy liver shows sinusoidal congestion, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, and abundant black-brown, granular malarial pigment (haemozoin) within Kupffer cells and portal macrophages, which is birefringent under polarised light and Perls negative, unlike haemosiderin. Parasitised red cells may be seen in sinusoids in Plasmodium falciparum infection. Hepatocytes may show focal necrosis, cholestasis and mild steatosis, and portal tracts contain lymphocytes and pigment-laden macrophages. In hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly, there is marked sinusoidal lymphocytosis. The pre-erythrocytic liver stage is not seen in diagnostic biopsies. The differentials include schistosomal pigment (also black, Perls negative, but with eggs and portal fibrosis), formalin pigment (artefact, extracellular, removed by picric acid), haemosiderin (Perls positive), and lipofuscin (zone 3 hepatocytes, fine, golden).
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role in hepatic malaria; peripheral blood smear and antigen tests are diagnostic.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Haemozoin is identified by its morphology, birefringence and Perls negativity; Perls stain distinguishes it from haemosiderin. Peripheral blood smear, rapid antigen tests and PCR establish the diagnosis.

entities.variants: Biliary ascariasis (worm in common bile duct or intrahepatic ducts); Ascaris-related liver abscess; Ascaris-associated hepatolithiasis and recurrent pyogenic cholangitis; egg granulomas in liver
entities.remarks: Ascaris lumbricoides, common in India; migrating adult worms cause biliary colic, cholangitis, pancreatitis and abscess; dead worms and eggs form granulomas and nidus for stones.
entities.histo: Ascaris lumbricoides adult worms can migrate from the duodenum into the ampulla and bile ducts, especially in children and in regions with heavy infection, including parts of India. Live worms in the common bile duct or intrahepatic ducts cause biliary colic, obstructive jaundice, acute cholangitis and pancreatitis. Dead or trapped worms provoke suppurative cholangitis and liver abscesses, and fragments of cuticle, worm remnants and eggs become surrounded by granulomas with eosinophils, foreign body giant cells and fibrosis, sometimes serving as a nidus for intrahepatic stones. Ascaris eggs are oval, about 45 to 75 micrometres, with a thick mammillated (bumpy) outer shell; decorticated eggs lack the mammillated layer. The differentials include other parasitic causes of cholangitis (Clonorchis, Fasciola), recurrent pyogenic cholangitis, pyogenic abscess and eosinophilic granulomas due to visceral larva migrans.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role; eggs may be seen in bile or abscess aspirates, recognised by their mammillated shell, and worm fragments may occasionally be recovered.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used; diagnosis rests on imaging (ultrasound and ERCP showing worms), stool microscopy and morphology of worms and eggs.

entities.variants: Toxocara canis and T. cati visceral larva migrans; eosinophilic liver abscess; ocular larva migrans (not liver)
entities.remarks: Children with pica and dog contact; multiple small eosinophilic granulomas and abscesses with Charcot-Leyden crystals; larvae rarely found; marked eosinophilia; serology (Toxocara ELISA).
entities.histo: Visceral larva migrans results from ingestion of eggs of the dog or cat roundworm, Toxocara canis or Toxocara cati, typically by young children with pica, and the larvae migrate through the liver without maturing. On imaging there are multiple small, ill-defined, hypodense lesions, which can mimic metastases. Histologically these are eosinophilic granulomas and microabscesses with central necrosis containing abundant eosinophils, eosinophilic debris and Charcot-Leyden crystals, surrounded by palisading epithelioid histiocytes, giant cells and fibrosis. Larvae (about 18 to 21 micrometres in diameter) are rarely identified, and step sections may be needed. Portal tracts can contain eosinophils, and the surrounding liver may show mild hepatitis. The differentials include fascioliasis (serpiginous tracts), capillariasis (eggs with bipolar plugs), strongyloidiasis (larvae in hyperinfection), hypereosinophilic syndrome, drug reaction, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and eosinophilic infiltration around tumours.
entities.cyto: Aspirates may show necrotic debris, numerous eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals, suggesting a parasitic or eosinophilic process; larvae are rarely aspirated.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Diagnosis relies on Toxocara serology (ELISA, Western blot), peripheral eosinophilia and imaging, with biopsy reserved for atypical cases.

entities.entity: Other parasitic infections of liver (Capillaria hepatica, strongyloidiasis, toxoplasmosis, cysticercosis, pentastomiasis)
entities.variants: Hepatic capillariasis (Capillaria hepatica, eggs with bipolar plugs); Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection with larvae in portal tracts; congenital and disseminated toxoplasmosis; hepatic cysticercosis; pentastomiasis (Armillifer nymphs, calcified C-shaped nodules); trichinosis (rare); Dicrocoelium (false fascioliasis)
entities.remarks: Rare parasites, often found incidentally or in immunosuppressed patients; recognise the organism (egg, larva, cyst or nymph) and the eosinophil-rich granulomatous reaction; stool, serology and molecular confirmation.
entities.histo: A range of uncommon parasites may involve the liver. Capillaria hepatica, a rodent nematode, produces granulomas containing adult worms and characteristic barrel-shaped eggs with bipolar plugs and a striated shell, surrounded by eosinophils and fibrosis. Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection, seen in patients on steroids or with HTLV-1 infection, causes filariform larvae in portal tracts, sinusoids and vessels, with granulomas or little inflammation, and often bacterial sepsis. Toxoplasma gondii causes congenital hepatitis with giant cells, necrosis and extramedullary haematopoiesis, and in immunosuppressed adults may produce necrotising hepatitis with tachyzoites and tissue cysts. Hepatic cysticercosis (Taenia solium larvae) and pentastomiasis (Armillifer nymphs, forming C-shaped calcified subcapsular nodules) are found as incidental nodules at surgery or autopsy. The differentials include other parasitic granulomas, tuberculosis, fungal infection and calcified healed granulomas, and the key to diagnosis is identifying the organism, often on deeper levels.
entities.cyto: Cytology has little role; occasionally eggs, larvae or parasite fragments are seen in aspirates from nodules or necrotic lesions, accompanied by eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals.
entities.ihc: IHC is rarely used; Toxoplasma immunostaining is the main exception and highlights tachyzoites and cysts in congenital or disseminated disease. Other parasites are identified by morphology, with serology and PCR as needed.

entities.variants: Type 1 AIH (ANA, ASMA); type 2 AIH (anti-LKM1, anti-LC1; children); acute presentation and acute severe (fulminant) AIH with zone 3 (centrilobular) necrosis; chronic AIH; AIH-related cirrhosis; AIH in pregnancy and post-partum; de novo AIH after transplant (see plasma cell-rich rejection); seronegative AIH
entities.remarks: Female predominance; raised IgG and autoantibodies; interface hepatitis rich in plasma cells, emperipolesis, hepatocyte rosettes; simplified IAIHG score and 2022 IAIHG histology criteria; excellent response to steroids and azathioprine.
entities.histo: Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic immune-mediated hepatitis that typically affects women, with raised IgG and autoantibodies, and the biopsy is essential for diagnosis. The classic pattern is moderate to severe interface hepatitis, with a dense portal and periportal infiltrate of lymphocytes and many plasma cells, often in clusters at the interface and in the lobule. Hepatocyte rosettes (small gland-like groups of regenerating hepatocytes) and emperipolesis (lymphocytes within hepatocyte cytoplasm) are supportive. Lobular hepatitis can be prominent, and bridging or confluent necrosis is common. Acute presentations, including acute severe AIH, often show centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis with plasma cells and minimal fibrosis, and may be the only finding early in disease. Giant cell transformation of hepatocytes may occur. The 2022 International AIH Group criteria regard a predominantly portal lymphoplasmacytic hepatitis with more than mild interface activity, or a more than mild lobular hepatitis, as likely AIH in the absence of features of another disease. Bile duct injury may be present mildly, but marked duct damage, ductopenia or copper deposition raises the question of a variant (overlap) syndrome. Fibrosis is staged with trichrome and reticulin, and cirrhosis may be present at diagnosis. The differentials include drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (nitrofurantoin, minocycline, statins, biologics), viral hepatitis A, B, C and E, Wilson disease, PBC and PSC, IgG4-related disease and MASH with autoantibodies.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis, which needs a histological core with serology. Aspirates are only relevant for focal lesions, such as HCC in AIH-related cirrhosis.
entities.ihc: CD138 or MUM1 immunostaining quantifies plasma cells, which are characteristically numerous at the interface and in clusters, and their IgG subclass can be tested (IgG4 when IgG4-related hepatitis is suspected, as most AIH plasma cells are IgG4 negative). CK7 shows ductular reaction and highlights bile ducts in suspected overlap. HBsAg, HBcAg, CMV and other viral stains help exclude infection. There is no IHC test that proves AIH; the diagnosis integrates histology, IgG, autoantibodies and exclusion of other causes.

entities.variants: AIH-PBC variant (Paris criteria); AIH-PSC variant (autoimmune sclerosing cholangitis, paediatric); sequential (consecutive) variants; PBC with interface hepatitis
entities.remarks: Features of AIH plus a cholestatic disease; 'overlap' is a descriptive term rather than a separate disease; histology should report both interface hepatitis and bile duct injury/ductopenia/copper; therapy combines ursodeoxycholic acid and immunosuppression.
entities.histo: Variant or overlap syndromes describe patients who show features of autoimmune hepatitis together with a cholestatic autoimmune liver disease, either simultaneously or sequentially. In the AIH-PBC variant, the biopsy shows the lymphocytic cholangitis, florid duct lesions, granulomas or ductopenia of PBC, together with moderate to severe interface hepatitis rich in plasma cells, beyond the mild interface activity often seen in PBC alone. The Paris criteria require at least two features of each disease, and moderate or severe lymphocytic piecemeal necrosis is mandatory on the AIH side. In the AIH-PSC variant, more common in children and young adults with inflammatory bowel disease (autoimmune sclerosing cholangitis), there is interface hepatitis plus fibro-obliterative duct lesions, periductal concentric fibrosis, ductopenia and cholate stasis, with cholangiographic duct strictures. Copper-associated protein deposition (orcein, rhodanine) and CK7-positive periportal hepatocytes indicate chronic cholestasis. The differentials include each disease alone, drug-induced injury and IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role in overlap syndromes, which require a core biopsy to assess interface hepatitis, plasma cells and bile duct injury together. Serology (ANA, ASMA, AMA, IgG) and cholangiography complete the assessment.
entities.ihc: CK7 is the key stain, showing ductopenia, ductular reaction and aberrant CK7 expression in periportal hepatocytes as a marker of chronic cholestasis, while CK19 confirms loss of interlobular ducts. CD138 or MUM1 helps quantify plasma cells, and IgG4 immunostaining helps exclude IgG4-related disease in the AIH-PSC setting.

entities.variants: Classic AMA-positive PBC; AMA-negative PBC (formerly autoimmune cholangitis, often ANA sp100/gp210 positive); premature ductopenic variant; PBC with interface hepatitis (AIH-PBC variant); stages per Ludwig/Scheuer (1 to 4) and Nakanuma system
entities.remarks: Middle-aged women, raised ALP and anti-mitochondrial antibody; non-suppurative destructive cholangitis of small interlobular ducts (florid duct lesion) with granulomas, ductopenia, copper deposition and progression to biliary cirrhosis; treated with UDCA.
entities.histo: Primary biliary cholangitis is a chronic autoimmune disease that destroys small intrahepatic (interlobular and septal) bile ducts, mainly in middle-aged women with anti-mitochondrial antibodies. The diagnostic lesion is the florid duct lesion, a non-suppurative destructive cholangitis in which a damaged interlobular duct is surrounded and infiltrated by lymphocytes and plasma cells, sometimes with an epithelioid granuloma close to the duct. The disease is patchy, so biopsies may sample only a few diagnostic portal tracts. Later stages show ductular reaction, loss of interlobular ducts (ductopenia, defined as loss in more than half of portal tracts), periportal cholate stasis with feathery degeneration of hepatocytes, Mallory-Denk bodies and copper-associated protein deposition (orcein, Victoria blue or rhodanine for copper), and biliary-type fibrosis with a halo of oedematous periportal hepatocytes around jigsaw-shaped nodules in cirrhosis. Mild interface hepatitis is common. The Ludwig and Scheuer systems stage the disease from 1 (portal) to 4 (cirrhosis), and the Nakanuma system scores fibrosis, bile duct loss and orcein-positive granules with separate activity grades. The differentials include PSC (periductal onion-skin fibrosis, larger ducts), drug-induced cholangitis and vanishing bile duct syndrome, sarcoidosis (larger, more numerous granulomas), chronic hepatitis C (duct lesions with lymphoid aggregates), AIH and chronic ductopenic rejection.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the diagnosis of PBC, which relies on biochemistry, AMA serology and biopsy when needed.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 are the most useful immunostains; they confirm the absence of interlobular ducts (ductopenia), highlight ductular reaction, and CK7 shows aberrant staining of periportal hepatocytes in chronic cholestasis, often appearing before ductopenia is obvious. CD138 or MUM1 highlights plasma cells, and IgM-positive plasma cells are characteristically increased in PBC. IgG4 staining helps exclude IgG4-related cholangitis.

entities.variants: Classic large duct PSC; small duct PSC (normal cholangiogram, biopsy features); PSC with inflammatory bowel disease (mostly ulcerative colitis); paediatric PSC and autoimmune sclerosing cholangitis; PSC with high-grade dysplasia or cholangiocarcinoma; Nakanuma or Ludwig staging
entities.remarks: Young men, usually with ulcerative colitis; beaded strictures on MRCP/ERCP; concentric periductal onion-skin fibrosis and fibro-obliterative scars replacing ducts; risk of cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder carcinoma and colorectal cancer; exclude IgG4-related and secondary sclerosing cholangitis.
entities.histo: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a chronic fibro-inflammatory disease of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis. The diagnosis is usually made by cholangiography, and biopsy is used in small duct disease, to stage the disease, or to exclude overlap features. The characteristic lesion is concentric, laminated periductal fibrosis (onion-skin fibrosis) around interlobular and septal ducts, which progressively narrows the lumen and replaces the duct by a round fibrous scar (fibro-obliterative cholangitis). These diagnostic lesions are uncommon in needle biopsies, which more often show non-specific portal oedema, mild mixed inflammation, ductular reaction, ductopenia, periportal cholate stasis and copper deposition. Large duct specimens (resections, explants) show strictures, dilated ducts with bile sludge, ulceration, xanthogranulomatous inflammation, peribiliary gland hyperplasia, and the precursors of cholangiocarcinoma, such as biliary intraepithelial neoplasia. Fibrosis progresses to biliary cirrhosis. The differentials include IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis (storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, many IgG4 plasma cells), secondary sclerosing cholangitis from ischaemia, stones, surgery or infection, PBC (florid duct lesions, granulomas), sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and drug-induced cholangiopathy.
entities.cyto: Cytology plays an important role in surveillance: ERCP brushing of dominant strictures is used to detect cholangiocarcinoma. Smears often show reactive atypia due to inflammation and stents, so specificity depends on conservative interpretation, with diagnoses reported as atypical, suspicious or positive for malignancy and supplemented by FISH for polysomy (UroVysion-type probes) where available. Biliary brushings are reported using the Papanicolaou Society categories in many centres, and no IAC-IARC-WHO system specific to liver or bile duct cytology is presumed here.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 show ductopenia and ductular reaction, and CK7 marks periportal hepatocyte metaplasia in chronic cholestasis. IgG4 immunostaining, with counts per high-power field and the IgG4/IgG ratio, helps separate IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, although modest numbers of IgG4 plasma cells can occur in PSC. In biliary biopsies and brushings with atypia, p53 aberrant staining, SMAD4 loss, high Ki-67, S100P and IMP3 favour dysplasia or carcinoma over reactive change.

entities.entity: IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis and IgG4-related hepatopathy
entities.variants: IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis (hilar, intrahepatic and distal types, Nakazawa cholangiographic types 1 to 4); IgG4-related hepatopathy (portal inflammation, lobular hepatitis, AIH-like); IgG4-related inflammatory pseudotumour (sclerosing pseudotumour) of liver; association with type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis
entities.remarks: Older men; raised serum IgG4; storiform fibrosis, dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, obliterative phlebitis and many IgG4-positive plasma cells (over 50 per HPF in resections, over 10 per HPF in biopsies, ratio over 40%); responds to steroids; mimics PSC and hilar cholangiocarcinoma.
entities.histo: IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis is the biliary manifestation of IgG4-related disease, often associated with type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis, and it typically presents in older men with obstructive jaundice and strictures that mimic PSC or hilar cholangiocarcinoma. The bile duct wall is diffusely thickened by a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and storiform fibrosis, which involve the full thickness of the wall, while the epithelium is usually preserved, in contrast to PSC. Obliterative phlebitis is characteristic, and eosinophils are common, while neutrophils and granulomas are rare. Large intrahepatic and hilar ducts are involved most often, so needle biopsies may show only portal inflammation with plasma cells, portal-based fibroinflammatory nodules or features of large duct obstruction. IgG4-related hepatopathy includes portal inflammation, lobular hepatitis and an AIH-like pattern with IgG4-positive plasma cells. A mass-forming lesion (IgG4-related inflammatory pseudotumour) consists of storiform fibrosis and plasma cells with phlebitis. The differentials include PSC (onion-skin fibrosis, epithelial ulceration, fewer IgG4 cells), cholangiocarcinoma with a lymphoplasmacytic reaction (malignant glands must be searched for), inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma and autoimmune hepatitis.
entities.cyto: Biliary brushings show reactive epithelium, lymphocytes and plasma cells, and the main role of cytology is to exclude cholangiocarcinoma; IgG4-related disease cannot be diagnosed on cytology, and reactive atypia must not be overinterpreted.
entities.ihc: IgG4 and IgG immunostaining is central: more than 10 IgG4-positive plasma cells per high-power field in biopsies (over 50 in resections) with an IgG4 to IgG ratio above 40% supports the diagnosis in the right histological and clinical context. IgG4 positivity alone is not specific, because it can be seen in PSC, cholangiocarcinoma and other inflammatory conditions. CD138 shows the plasma cell density, and keratin stains help exclude infiltrating carcinoma. ALK is negative, which separates the pseudotumour form from inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour.

entities.variants: Epithelioid (non-caseating) granulomas; caseating granulomas; fibrin-ring granulomas; lipogranulomas (mineral oil, fat); microgranulomas (Kupffer cell aggregates); foreign-body granulomas (talc, starch in drug users, suture); drug-induced granulomatous hepatitis (allopurinol, sulfonamides, carbamazepine, BCG); granulomas in PBC; idiopathic granulomatous hepatitis
entities.remarks: Granulomas found in 2 to 15% of liver biopsies; causes include sarcoidosis, TB, PBC, drugs, infections, lipogranulomas and lymphoma; classify by type and location; special stains (ZN, GMS, PAS) and culture; many remain idiopathic.
entities.histo: Granulomas are found in a small but significant proportion of liver biopsies, and the pathologist's task is to describe their type and location and to narrow the list of causes. Epithelioid granulomas are compact aggregates of activated macrophages with variable giant cells and a lymphocytic rim; they are caseating in tuberculosis and some fungal infections, and non-caseating in sarcoidosis, PBC, drug reactions and many infections. Fibrin-ring granulomas suggest Q fever, EBV, CMV, hepatitis A, leishmaniasis, allopurinol or Hodgkin lymphoma. Lipogranulomas, small clusters of macrophages around fat vacuoles in portal tracts and near central veins, are very common and usually reflect mineral oil ingestion or steatosis, with no clinical significance. Microgranulomas are tiny clusters of Kupffer cells that mark recent hepatocyte necrosis. Foreign-body granulomas containing talc or starch occur in intravenous drug users, and BCG granulomas occur after intravesical therapy. Granulomas near damaged bile ducts suggest PBC, and portal granulomas with fibrosis favour sarcoidosis. Special stains for acid-fast bacilli and fungi, polarisation for foreign material, and culture or PCR for mycobacteria are important. Lymphoma, especially Hodgkin lymphoma, can cause granulomas without hepatic infiltration. When no cause is found, the term idiopathic granulomatous hepatitis is used.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role, though aspirates of focal granulomatous lesions can show epithelioid histiocyte clusters, giant cells and necrosis; special stains and microbiological testing of aspirated material improve the yield.
entities.ihc: CD68 highlights macrophages and small microgranulomas, and CK7 or CK19 helps assess bile ducts near granulomas when PBC is suspected. Immunostains for Mycobacterium, Treponema, Toxoplasma or CMV may be applied depending on the context, and CD30 and CD15 with PAX5 help identify Hodgkin cells if lymphoma is suspected.

entities.variants: Asymptomatic granulomatous involvement; cholestatic sarcoidosis (chronic intrahepatic cholestasis, ductopenia); sarcoid-related portal hypertension; hepatic sarcoid nodules (mass-forming); sarcoid cirrhosis
entities.remarks: Liver involved in most patients with systemic sarcoidosis; numerous non-caseating, well-formed epithelioid granulomas, mainly portal and periportal, with hyaline fibrosis, giant cells with asteroid and Schaumann bodies; exclude infection and drugs; may cause ductopenia and portal hypertension.
entities.histo: The liver is involved in most patients with systemic sarcoidosis, often without symptoms. The biopsy shows numerous, discrete, well-formed, non-caseating epithelioid granulomas, mainly in portal and periportal regions, which may become confluent. Multinucleated giant cells may contain asteroid bodies or concentrically laminated, calcified Schaumann bodies, and older granulomas are replaced by hyaline fibrous scars. Granulomas can damage bile ducts, causing chronic intrahepatic cholestasis, ductopenia and copper accumulation, a pattern that may mimic PBC. Granulomas around portal and hepatic veins can cause portal hypertension and Budd-Chiari-like changes, and extensive fibrosis may lead to cirrhosis. The diagnosis requires exclusion of mycobacterial and fungal infection with special stains and culture, of drug-induced granulomas and of PBC. PBC differs by florid duct lesions centred on the duct, less numerous and less well-formed granulomas, and AMA positivity.
entities.cyto: Cytology has limited use; aspirates of nodules show cohesive clusters of epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells without necrosis, which are non-specific and require microbiological exclusion of infection.
entities.ihc: CD68 confirms histiocytic granulomas. CK7 and CK19 show bile duct loss and ductular reaction in cholestatic disease, and AFB and fungal stains (ZN, GMS) are performed to exclude infection. There is no IHC marker specific for sarcoidosis.

entities.variants: Idiopathic neonatal hepatitis; neonatal giant cell hepatitis of known cause (infection: CMV, rubella, HSV, syphilis, toxoplasma; metabolic: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, galactosaemia, tyrosinaemia, bile acid synthesis defects, PFIC; Alagille syndrome; hypopituitarism; GALD); transient neonatal cholestasis
entities.remarks: Pattern of neonatal cholestasis rather than one disease; diffuse giant cell transformation of hepatocytes, cholestasis, extramedullary haematopoiesis and lobular inflammation; key differential is biliary atresia (portal ductular reaction, bile plugs, portal oedema) - early biopsy decides surgery.
entities.histo: Neonatal hepatitis describes a pattern of injury in infants with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, in which hepatocytes fuse into large multinucleated syncytial giant cells containing up to dozens of nuclei. The lobules show disarray, canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis, acidophil bodies, mild lobular and portal inflammation and prominent extramedullary haematopoiesis. Portal tracts are relatively normal or mildly inflamed, with little ductular reaction. The pattern has many causes, including congenital infections, metabolic and genetic disorders such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, galactosaemia, tyrosinaemia, bile acid synthesis defects and PFIC, endocrine disorders and Alagille syndrome, and remains idiopathic in a proportion of cases. The critical differential is biliary atresia, in which portal tracts show oedema, marked ductular reaction with bile plugs in ductules and portal fibrosis; giant cells may occur in both, and an accurate early distinction is crucial because Kasai portoenterostomy must be done within the first two months. PAS after diastase (for alpha-1 antitrypsin globules, which may be inconspicuous in infancy), iron stains (for GALD), CK7 (for bile duct paucity) and electron microscopy can aid in identifying specific causes.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in neonatal cholestasis, which is evaluated by a combination of imaging, HIDA scan, laboratory tests, genetic panels and liver biopsy.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 assess bile duct numbers (to identify paucity in Alagille syndrome) and ductular reaction (prominent in biliary atresia). BSEP and MDR3 immunostains help identify PFIC2 (loss of canalicular BSEP) and PFIC3 (loss of MDR3), and CD10 or polyclonal CEA show canalicular patterns. CMV immunostaining excludes congenital CMV, and C5b-9 staining of hepatocytes supports gestational alloimmune liver disease.

entities.entity: Postinfantile (adult) giant cell hepatitis (syncytial giant cell hepatitis)
entities.variants: Adult giant cell hepatitis associated with autoimmune hepatitis; with viral infection (HCV, HEV, paramyxovirus, HIV); drug-induced; post-transplant; giant cell hepatitis with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (infants and young children)
entities.remarks: Rare; extensive giant cell (syncytial) transformation of hepatocytes in children or adults beyond infancy, usually with severe hepatitis; most cases linked to AIH; Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia variant in young children is aggressive.
entities.histo: Postinfantile giant cell hepatitis is an uncommon pattern in which extensive syncytial giant cell transformation of hepatocytes occurs beyond the neonatal period, typically with a severe hepatitis and sometimes acute liver failure. The giant cells are large, contain many nuclei, and are diffusely distributed through the lobules, accompanied by lobular disarray, lymphocytic and plasma cell inflammation, interface hepatitis, cholestasis and confluent or bridging necrosis. It most often occurs in the setting of autoimmune hepatitis, and less often with viral infections (hepatitis C or E, HIV, paramyxovirus), drugs or after transplantation. In young children, the combination with Coombs-positive autoimmune haemolytic anaemia forms a distinct, aggressive syndrome that may need intense immunosuppression and anti-CD20 therapy. Differentials include neonatal hepatitis (age), focal giant cells in other chronic hepatitides and multinucleated hepatocytes in regenerating liver.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role. Multinucleated hepatocytes may occasionally be seen in aspirates, but they are non-specific, and the diffuse lobular pattern can only be assessed on biopsy.
entities.ihc: IHC is supportive only: CD138 or MUM1 quantifies plasma cells in the autoimmune setting, and viral immunostains (HBsAg, HBcAg, CMV, HSV) help exclude specific infections. The multinucleated cells are hepatocytes, positive with HepPar1 and arginase-1.

entities.variants: Polyarteritis nodosa (HBV-associated or idiopathic); giant cell (temporal) arteritis with hepatic involvement; granulomatosis with polyangiitis; systemic lupus erythematosus; Behcet disease (veins, Budd-Chiari); isolated hepatic arteritis; drug-induced vasculitis
entities.remarks: Rare; medium-sized portal artery fibrinoid necrosis and inflammation (PAN), granulomatous arteritis (GCA); may cause infarcts, aneurysm, haemorrhage, NRH; PAN classically linked to HBV.
entities.histo: Vasculitis involving the liver is rare and usually part of a systemic process. Polyarteritis nodosa, which is classically associated with chronic hepatitis B, affects medium-sized hepatic arteries, which show segmental fibrinoid necrosis of the wall with a mixed infiltrate of neutrophils, eosinophils and lymphocytes; healing lesions show fibrosis and aneurysm formation. The consequences include infarcts, subcapsular haemorrhage, rupture of aneurysms and nodular regenerative hyperplasia. Giant cell arteritis may involve hepatic arteries with granulomatous inflammation and giant cells, and patients may have raised alkaline phosphatase and small granulomas in the lobules. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, lupus and drug-induced vasculitis cause small vessel involvement, and Behcet disease affects veins and can cause Budd-Chiari syndrome. Isolated vasculitis may be found incidentally in surgical specimens such as cholecystectomies. Elastic stains (Verhoeff-van Gieson or orcein) are useful to evaluate arterial wall damage. The differentials include arterial changes in portal hypertension, post-transplant arteriopathy, amyloid angiopathy and hepatic artery injury after chemoembolisation.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no diagnostic role in hepatic vasculitis, as vessel wall inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis can only be assessed in tissue sections. The diagnosis is made on biopsy or resection specimens together with systemic serology such as ANCA.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used for diagnosis; elastic stains define vessel wall damage. Serological ANCA testing, HBV markers and clinical correlation are essential, and HBsAg immunostaining may support HBV-associated PAN.

entities.variants: Fibrohistiocytic (xanthogranulomatous) type; lymphoplasmacytic (IgG4-related) type; infection-associated (bacterial, mycobacterial, Bartonella); post-cholangitis or post-abscess organising inflammatory nodule; sclerosed lesions
entities.remarks: Tumour-like mass of inflammatory cells and fibroblasts; mostly reactive to infection or IgG4-related disease; must exclude IMT (ALK, ROS1), inflammatory pseudotumour-like FDC sarcoma (EBV), lymphoma and carcinoma with inflammation.
entities.histo: Inflammatory pseudotumour of the liver is a heterogeneous, non-neoplastic mass composed of inflammatory cells and fibroblastic stroma, which radiologically mimics a neoplasm. Two main patterns are described. The fibrohistiocytic or xanthogranulomatous type shows foamy macrophages, neutrophils, multinucleated giant cells, fibroblasts and sometimes abscess formation, and is often a reaction to bacterial infection, ascending cholangitis or an organising abscess. The lymphoplasmacytic type consists of a dense infiltrate of plasma cells and lymphocytes with storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis, and most cases belong to IgG4-related disease. Lesions frequently arise near the hilum and large bile ducts. The term should be applied only after exclusion of true neoplasms with an inflammatory component: inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour (fascicles of atypical myofibroblasts with ALK or ROS1 rearrangement), EBV-positive inflammatory follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, inflammatory HCC variants, lymphoma (Hodgkin, marginal zone), cholangiocarcinoma with dense desmoplasia and inflammation, and infections such as mycobacteria or Bartonella. Special stains for organisms (Gram, ZN, GMS, Warthin-Starry) are part of the work-up.
entities.cyto: FNA shows a mixed population of lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, neutrophils and bland spindle cells, which is non-diagnostic and does not exclude a neoplasm; atypical spindle or epithelial cells should prompt core biopsy.
entities.ihc: The panel is aimed at excluding mimics: ALK and ROS1 (negative, excluding IMT), EBER in situ hybridisation with CD21, CD23 and CD35 (negative, excluding inflammatory FDC sarcoma), keratins (to exclude carcinoma), CD30 and CD15 (Hodgkin cells) and light chain studies (lymphoma). IgG4 and IgG counts identify the IgG4-related subtype, and SMA highlights reactive myofibroblasts.

entities.variants: Nodular lymphoid lesion with germinal centres (single or multiple); association with autoimmune disease (PBC, Hashimoto, Sjogren), HCV, malignancy elsewhere
entities.remarks: Rare, mostly middle-aged women; small nodule (usually under 2 cm) of polyclonal lymphoid follicles with germinal centres and mixed interfollicular cells, often perisinusoidal pattern at the edge; must be separated from MALT lymphoma by IHC and clonality.
entities.histo: Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia, also called pseudolymphoma or nodular lymphoid lesion, is an uncommon benign lymphoproliferation that forms a discrete nodule in the liver, usually small and solitary, most often in middle-aged women with autoimmune disease or chronic viral hepatitis. It consists of reactive lymphoid follicles with well-formed polarised germinal centres and mantle zones, set among interfollicular small lymphocytes, plasma cells and histiocytes, with variable fibrous stroma and hyalinised vessels. At the periphery, lymphocytes may extend along sinusoids (perisinusoidal pattern), and portal tracts may be involved. Bile duct epithelium is not destroyed by lymphoepithelial lesions. The main differential is extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, which shows sheets of monocytoid or centrocyte-like B cells colonising follicles, lymphoepithelial lesions of bile ducts, light chain restriction and clonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangement. Other differentials include follicular lymphoma, inflammatory pseudotumour, IgG4-related disease and lymphoid aggregates in hepatitis C.
