entities.cyto: Aspirates show a polymorphous lymphoid population with small lymphocytes, centroblasts, tingible body macrophages and plasma cells. Cytology alone cannot reliably exclude low-grade lymphoma, so flow cytometry on aspirated material or core biopsy is recommended.
entities.ihc: Immunohistochemistry shows a reactive architecture: CD20-positive follicles with BCL2-negative germinal centres, CD10 and BCL6 restricted to germinal centres, intact CD21 or CD23 follicular dendritic meshworks and abundant CD3 and CD5 interfollicular T cells. Kappa and lambda light chains (IHC or ISH) are polytypic in plasma cells, and Ki-67 shows the normal polarised high proliferation in germinal centres. Clonality testing (IGH rearrangement) is negative, which is the key separation from MALT lymphoma.

entities.variants: Banff grading: indeterminate, mild, moderate and severe acute TCMR; Rejection Activity Index (RAI, portal inflammation, bile duct inflammation/damage, venous endothelial inflammation; 0-9); central perivenulitis-predominant TCMR
entities.remarks: Usually within 4 to 6 weeks of transplant; Banff triad of mixed portal inflammation (lymphocytes, eosinophils, blast cells), bile duct inflammation/damage and venous endotheliitis; graded by Banff global assessment and RAI; severe cases show central perivenulitis with zone 3 necrosis.
entities.histo: Acute T-cell-mediated rejection is the commonest form of liver allograft rejection, usually occurring in the first weeks to months after transplantation. The Banff diagnostic triad consists of mixed portal inflammation with activated lymphocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils and macrophages, bile duct inflammation and damage in which lymphocytes infiltrate the duct epithelium causing vacuolation, nuclear crowding and apoptosis, and subendothelial inflammation of portal and terminal hepatic venules (endotheliitis), with lymphocytes lifting the endothelium. At least two of these features are required, and the severity is graded by the Banff global assessment (indeterminate, mild, moderate, severe) and by the Rejection Activity Index, which scores portal inflammation, bile duct damage and venous endothelial inflammation from 0 to 3 each. Severe rejection shows inflammation spilling into periportal parenchyma and central perivenulitis with zone 3 hepatocyte dropout, haemorrhage and necrosis. The differentials include recurrent viral hepatitis (C, B, E) with less duct damage and endotheliitis, CMV and EBV infection, preservation injury, biliary obstruction, antibody-mediated rejection, drug toxicity and recurrent autoimmune disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the diagnosis of rejection; fine-needle aspiration biopsy has been used historically in some centres for monitoring, but core biopsy is the standard.
entities.ihc: IHC is supportive. C4d staining of portal capillaries and venules is assessed to look for an antibody-mediated component, and CMV, EBER (EBV) and HBsAg/HBcAg stains exclude infection or recurrent viral disease. CD3 and CD8 highlight the T-cell infiltrate, and CK7 or CK19 helps evaluate bile duct damage and ductopenia.

entities.variants: Hyperacute rejection (preformed antibodies, ABO-incompatible graft); acute antibody-mediated rejection (DSA-positive, C4d-positive; Banff 2016 criteria, suspicious/indeterminate); ABO-incompatible graft injury
entities.remarks: Rare in liver; DSA plus microvascular injury (portal capillaritis, endothelial hypertrophy, portal oedema, ductular reaction, cholestasis) and diffuse C4d deposition in portal microvasculature; hyperacute form causes haemorrhagic necrosis within hours to days.
entities.histo: Antibody-mediated rejection is much less common in liver transplants than in kidney transplants because the liver resists antibody injury, but it is increasingly recognised. Hyperacute rejection, caused by preformed antibodies, especially in ABO-incompatible grafts, develops within hours to days, with neutrophil margination and fibrin thrombi in vessels, widespread haemorrhagic necrosis and graft failure. Acute antibody-mediated rejection develops later and shows microvascular injury: portal capillary dilatation, endothelial cell hypertrophy, portal capillaritis with monocytes, eosinophils and neutrophils, portal oedema, ductular reaction, hepatocyte swelling and cholestasis, sometimes with centrilobular hepatocyte dropout. Banff 2016 criteria require histological evidence of acute injury, positive serum donor-specific antibody, diffuse microvascular C4d deposition, and reasonable exclusion of other causes, with a suspicious category when some criteria are missing. The differentials include acute TCMR (which may coexist), preservation injury, biliary obstruction, hepatic artery thrombosis and sepsis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in diagnosing antibody-mediated rejection. Diagnosis needs a graft biopsy with C4d staining, combined with donor-specific antibody testing in serum.
entities.ihc: C4d immunostaining is central: diffuse (over 50% of portal tracts) linear staining of portal capillaries and veins supports antibody-mediated injury, scored on a 0 to 3 scale per Banff. C4d must be interpreted with serum DSA and histology, as focal or stromal staining is less specific. CD68 highlights portal capillary monocytes, and CMV and other viral stains exclude infection.

entities.variants: Early chronic rejection (duct atrophy, senescence changes, perivenular fibrosis); late chronic rejection (ductopenia in at least 50% of portal tracts, bridging perivenular fibrosis, foam cell arteriopathy); Banff staging of chronic rejection
entities.remarks: Irreversible injury to bile ducts and arteries; ductopenia over 50% of portal tracts and obliterative (foam cell) arteriopathy of large and medium arteries; zone 3 cholestasis and perivenular fibrosis; may follow repeated or unresolved TCMR.
entities.histo: Chronic rejection is a progressive immune injury that targets bile ducts and arteries and may follow repeated or unresolved episodes of acute rejection or inadequate immunosuppression. In early chronic rejection, many interlobular ducts show senescence-related changes: eosinophilic cytoplasm, uneven nuclear spacing, nuclear enlargement and hyperchromasia, and ducts lined by only some epithelial cells, together with loss of small portal arteries, and zone 3 perivenular inflammation, hepatocyte dropout and mild fibrosis. Late chronic rejection shows loss of bile ducts in at least half of portal tracts (ductopenia), loss of hepatic arterioles, centrilobular cholestasis, bridging perivenular (central-to-central) fibrosis and, in large and medium-sized arteries of explants, obliterative (foam cell) arteriopathy with intimal foamy macrophages narrowing the lumen. Ductular reaction is characteristically weak or absent, in contrast to biliary obstruction. The differentials include biliary strictures, hepatic artery stenosis or thrombosis, drug-induced ductopenia, recurrent PBC or PSC, and chronic antibody-mediated rejection.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in chronic rejection, as ductopenia and obliterative arteriopathy can only be judged on an adequate core biopsy with enough portal tracts. Biliary brushings are taken only to exclude strictures or malignancy.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 are essential to count the remaining interlobular ducts and confirm ductopenia, and CK7 often shows aberrant periportal hepatocyte expression in chronic cholestasis. C4d may show staining when chronic antibody-mediated injury coexists, and CD68 highlights intimal foam cells in obliterative arteriopathy.

entities.variants: Chronic active antibody-mediated rejection (Banff 2016): low-grade portal and perivenular inflammation, interface and perivenular activity, with unusual portal, periportal, sinusoidal and perivenular fibrosis; DSA-positive; C4d positive
entities.remarks: Late graft injury with persistent class II DSA; histology often mild and nonspecific with unexplained portal/periportal/perisinusoidal fibrosis; C4d in at least 10% of portal tract microvasculature supports; leads to graft fibrosis.
entities.histo: Chronic antibody-mediated rejection is a late form of graft injury associated with persistent donor-specific antibodies, often class II and high titre, and it contributes to graft fibrosis and loss. The histology is subtle and non-specific: mild portal and perivenular mononuclear inflammation, mild interface or perivenular necroinflammatory activity, and, most characteristically, an unusual pattern of fibrosis involving portal, periportal, sinusoidal and perivenular areas without another explanation such as viral hepatitis, steatohepatitis or biliary obstruction. Portal capillary dilatation, endothelial swelling and mild ductular reaction may be present. The Banff criteria require compatible histology, serum DSA, at least focal C4d positivity of the portal microvasculature, and exclusion of other causes, and a probable category is used when C4d is negative. The differentials include late TCMR and plasma cell-rich rejection, recurrent disease, chronic ductopenic rejection and idiopathic post-transplant hepatitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Chronic antibody-mediated rejection is diagnosed on graft biopsy (portal and perivenular fibrosis, C4d staining) together with persistent donor-specific antibodies.
entities.ihc: C4d immunostaining is the key marker, with at least focal positivity in portal microvascular endothelium, interpreted alongside DSA and histology; trichrome and reticulin show the pattern of fibrosis. CK7 and CK19 help exclude ductopenic chronic rejection.

entities.entity: Late T-cell-mediated rejection and plasma cell-rich rejection
entities.variants: Late acute TCMR (portal-based with less endotheliitis); central perivenulitis pattern of late TCMR; plasma cell-rich rejection (formerly de novo autoimmune hepatitis); chronic hepatitis-like rejection
entities.remarks: Occurs more than 6 months after transplant, often with low immunosuppression; resembles chronic hepatitis or AIH more than early TCMR; plasma cell-rich rejection shows interface hepatitis and perivenulitis with plasma cells over 30%; responds to more immunosuppression.
entities.histo: Late T-cell-mediated rejection, arising more than six months after transplantation, often during reduced immunosuppression, looks different from early rejection. The portal infiltrate is mainly mononuclear, bile duct damage and venous endotheliitis are less prominent, and interface hepatitis, lobular inflammation and central perivenulitis (inflammation around terminal hepatic venules with zone 3 hepatocyte dropout) are often the dominant findings, so it can resemble chronic viral or autoimmune hepatitis. Plasma cell-rich rejection, formerly called de novo autoimmune hepatitis when it occurred in patients transplanted for non-autoimmune disease, shows portal and periportal plasma cell-rich inflammation (plasma cells usually over 30% of the infiltrate), interface hepatitis and perivenular plasma cell-rich necroinflammation, often with lymphocytic cholangitis; it is associated with donor-specific antibodies and anti-GSTT1 antibodies and can lead to graft fibrosis. The differentials include recurrent viral hepatitis, recurrent AIH, idiopathic post-transplant hepatitis, drug-induced injury and chronic antibody-mediated rejection.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in late rejection. Interface and perivenular inflammation, plasma cell density and duct damage need a core biopsy, and serum donor-specific antibodies and autoantibodies support the diagnosis.
entities.ihc: CD138 or MUM1 quantifies the plasma cell fraction, IgG4 helps exclude IgG4-rich infiltrates, and C4d is assessed for antibody-mediated injury, which commonly accompanies plasma cell-rich rejection. HBsAg, HBcAg and other viral stains, and HEV testing, help exclude recurrent viral disease.

entities.variants: Idiopathic post-transplant chronic hepatitis (paediatric and adult); progression to graft fibrosis
entities.remarks: Chronic hepatitis pattern in long-term grafts without a definable cause (viral, autoimmune, drug or rejection excluded); common in protocol biopsies of children; may represent a form of low-grade rejection; can progress to fibrosis.
entities.histo: Idiopathic post-transplant hepatitis is a diagnosis of exclusion describing a chronic hepatitis pattern in liver allografts, typically identified in long-term protocol biopsies, especially in children. The biopsy shows portal mononuclear inflammation with variable interface hepatitis and lobular inflammation, sometimes with central perivenulitis, but without the duct damage and endotheliitis typical of rejection, and without evidence of viral, autoimmune, drug-induced or biliary disease. Some cases show progressive portal and periportal fibrosis, and many experts regard the condition as a form of chronic low-grade T-cell or antibody-mediated rejection. The differentials include late TCMR, plasma cell-rich rejection, chronic AMR, recurrent hepatitis C, B or E, de novo viral infection, and recurrent autoimmune disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in idiopathic post-transplant hepatitis, which is a diagnosis of exclusion on graft biopsy after viral, drug-related, rejection-related and recurrent autoimmune causes have been ruled out.
entities.ihc: IHC is used to exclude other causes: viral stains (HBsAg, HBcAg, CMV, EBER), C4d for antibody-mediated injury, CD138 for plasma cell-rich rejection and CK7 for biliary injury.

entities.variants: Acute hepatic GVHD after haematopoietic stem cell transplant; chronic hepatic GVHD (ductopenic, cholestatic); hepatitic variant of GVHD (lobular hepatitis pattern); GVHD after liver or other solid organ transplant (donor lymphocytes, often fatal)
entities.remarks: Occurs after allogeneic HSCT; targets small bile ducts: epithelial dysmorphism (nuclear irregularity, vacuolation, apoptosis) with relatively sparse inflammation, cholestasis; chronic form causes ductopenia; differentials SOS, drug toxicity, viral infection.
entities.histo: Hepatic graft-versus-host disease follows allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, when donor T cells attack recipient bile ducts and hepatocytes. The key finding is injury to small interlobular bile ducts out of proportion to the inflammation: duct epithelium shows nuclear irregularity, pleomorphism, overlap and loss of polarity, cytoplasmic eosinophilia or vacuolation, apoptotic bodies and segmental loss of lining cells, often with only a mild lymphocytic infiltrate. Canalicular cholestasis, mainly in zone 3, and endotheliitis may be seen. Chronic GVHD shows progressive ductopenia, portal fibrosis and cholestasis, which can progress to biliary cirrhosis. A hepatitic variant, typically following tapering of immunosuppression or donor lymphocyte infusion, shows lobular hepatitis with acidophil bodies and portal inflammation resembling viral or autoimmune hepatitis. GVHD after liver transplantation is rare and caused by donor lymphocytes attacking recipient tissues, usually skin, gut and marrow, not the graft. The differentials include drug-induced cholestasis, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, sepsis, iron overload, viral infections (CMV, adenovirus, HSV, HBV reactivation) and recurrence of leukaemia.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in hepatic GVHD. Bile duct injury and endotheliitis can only be assessed on biopsy, often taken by the transjugular route because of thrombocytopenia, and skin or gut biopsies may be easier to obtain.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 show bile duct dysmorphism and confirm ductopenia in chronic disease. Viral immunostains (CMV, adenovirus, HSV, HBsAg, HBcAg) and EBER are essential to exclude opportunistic infections in this immunosuppressed setting, and leukaemic markers (CD34, CD117, MPO, TdT) exclude relapse.

entities.variants: Micronodular (nodules under 3 mm; alcohol, MASH, haemochromatosis, biliary); macronodular (viral, Wilson, AAT); mixed; biliary cirrhosis (jigsaw pattern); cardiac cirrhosis; incomplete septal cirrhosis; Laennec substages 4A, 4B, 4C; regressing (perforated septa) cirrhosis; compensated vs decompensated
entities.remarks: Diffuse process of fibrous septa surrounding regenerative nodules with vascular distortion; end stage of most chronic liver diseases; complications are portal hypertension, liver failure and HCC; reticulin and trichrome essential on biopsy.
entities.histo: Cirrhosis is a diffuse process in which the whole liver is converted into regenerative parenchymal nodules surrounded by fibrous septa, with distortion of the vascular architecture and intrahepatic shunting. Grossly the liver is firm and nodular, and may be shrunken or enlarged. Nodules smaller than about 3 mm define micronodular cirrhosis, typical of alcohol, MASH, haemochromatosis and biliary obstruction, while larger nodules define macronodular cirrhosis, typical of viral hepatitis, Wilson disease and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, with mixed patterns common. Microscopically, septa contain ductular reaction, inflammatory cells and abnormal vessels, and nodules lack normal portal tract and central vein relationships. Biliary cirrhosis has irregular jigsaw-shaped nodules with a pale halo of cholestatic hepatocytes at the edges, whereas cardiac cirrhosis has fibrosis linking central veins with relatively spared portal tracts. In needle biopsies, signs of cirrhosis include fragmentation, rounded fragments with a rim of fibrous tissue, and nodules lacking normal landmarks, best appreciated with reticulin and trichrome stains, and orcein shows elastic fibres in established septa. The Laennec system subdivides stage 4 by septal width and nodule size, and regressing cirrhosis shows thin, perforated, delicate septa. The pathologist should try to identify the cause (steatohepatitis, viral features, cholestatic features, iron, copper, AAT globules) and look for dysplastic foci and nodules. The differentials include nodular regenerative hyperplasia (nodules without fibrosis), porto-sinusoidal vascular disease with incomplete septal cirrhosis, congenital hepatic fibrosis, and large regenerative or dysplastic nodules mistaken for normal liver.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in diagnosing cirrhosis. However, most liver FNAs are performed in cirrhotic patients for nodules, and aspirates of cirrhotic liver show reactive hepatocytes with anisonucleosis, large cell change, binucleation and bile ductular cells and fibrous fragments, which can be mistaken for well-differentiated HCC; conversely, well-differentiated HCC may resemble benign hepatocytes. Features favouring HCC include thickened trabeculae wrapped by endothelium, transgressing vessels, naked atypical nuclei and absence of bile duct cells. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed to diagnose cirrhosis. CK7 and CK19 highlight ductular reaction in septa and help identify aetiology (biliary pattern), and CD34 may show patchy sinusoidal capillarisation in cirrhotic nodules, which is a pitfall for HCC. In nodules, a panel of glypican-3, HSP70 and glutamine synthetase (two of three positive supports HCC) with CD34 and reticulin helps separate high-grade dysplastic nodules and early HCC from regenerative nodules. Aetiological stains include HBsAg, HBcAg and PAS-D for AAT globules.

entities.entity: Acute liver failure and massive or submassive hepatic necrosis
entities.variants: Hyperacute, acute and subacute liver failure; massive (panlobular) necrosis; submassive (multilobular) necrosis; acute-on-chronic liver failure; causes: paracetamol, idiosyncratic DILI, viral (HAV, HBV, HEV), AIH, Wilson, ischaemia, AFLP, HSV, mushroom poisoning
entities.remarks: Coagulopathy and encephalopathy within 26 weeks without pre-existing liver disease; histology shows extensive confluent necrosis with collapse, ductular reaction and regenerating islands; pattern (zonal vs non-zonal) points to cause; important for transplant decision.
entities.histo: Acute liver failure is defined clinically by coagulopathy and encephalopathy developing within weeks in a patient without pre-existing cirrhosis, and the explant or biopsy usually shows massive or submassive hepatic necrosis. Grossly the liver is shrunken, soft and wrinkled, with a red or yellow mottled cut surface and capsular wrinkling. Microscopically there is loss of hepatocytes over whole lobules (massive) or multiple adjacent lobules (submassive), with collapse of the reticulin framework so that portal tracts approximate one another, residual macrophages with ceroid pigment, and a striking ductular reaction from progenitor cell activation, sometimes forming duct-like hepatocyte islands. Residual islands of regenerating hepatocytes may form nodules that mimic cirrhosis. The distribution of necrosis provides clues: zone 3 coagulative necrosis with little inflammation suggests paracetamol toxicity or ischaemia, non-zonal punched-out necrosis suggests HSV or adenovirus, plasma cell-rich panlobular necrosis suggests AIH, microvesicular steatosis suggests AFLP or drug toxicity, and copper and Mallory-Denk bodies with background cirrhosis suggest Wilson disease. A biopsy can underestimate necrosis because of sampling. Reticulin, trichrome and orcein stains separate recent collapse from established fibrosis, which is important when distinguishing acute liver failure from acute-on-chronic liver failure.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in acute liver failure. Transjugular biopsy, when done, assesses the extent of necrosis and possible causes such as viral, autoimmune or drug-induced injury, Wilson disease or malignant infiltration.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 highlight the extensive ductular reaction and show that residual epithelial islands are progenitor-derived. Viral immunostains (HSV, adenovirus, CMV, HBsAg, HBcAg) are part of the work-up. Ki-67 shows regenerative activity in surviving hepatocytes and may have prognostic value, and CD68 highlights macrophages clearing debris.

entities.variants: Prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis, EHPVO, splenic vein thrombosis); intrahepatic presinusoidal (schistosomiasis, porto-sinusoidal vascular disease, congenital hepatic fibrosis, PBC, sarcoidosis), sinusoidal (cirrhosis, SOS, amyloid) and postsinusoidal; posthepatic (Budd-Chiari, cardiac); non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis (India)
entities.remarks: Portal pressure gradient over 5 mmHg, clinically significant over 10 mmHg; complications varices, ascites, splenomegaly, encephalopathy; biopsy mainly to find the cause when cirrhosis is absent.
entities.histo: Portal hypertension is a haemodynamic syndrome, and liver pathology is used to identify its cause, particularly when cirrhosis is not obvious. Causes are classified by the site of increased resistance: prehepatic causes include portal vein thrombosis and extrahepatic portal vein obstruction, which is a common cause in Indian children; intrahepatic presinusoidal causes include schistosomiasis, porto-sinusoidal vascular disease (non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis or idiopathic portal hypertension), congenital hepatic fibrosis, sarcoidosis and early PBC; sinusoidal causes include cirrhosis, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, amyloidosis and infiltrative diseases; and postsinusoidal or posthepatic causes include hepatic vein obstruction (Budd-Chiari syndrome) and right heart failure. Histological signs that support portal hypertension in a non-cirrhotic biopsy include dilated or herniated portal veins into the parenchyma, multiple aberrant vessels in portal tracts, portal vein obliteration, sinusoidal dilatation and nodular regenerative hyperplasia. The complications, such as congestive splenomegaly with Gamna-Gandy bodies, varices and portal hypertensive gastropathy, are seen in other specimens. Trichrome and reticulin stains are essential to exclude cirrhosis and NRH.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in evaluating portal hypertension. Its cause, whether cirrhosis, porto-sinusoidal vascular disease, schistosomiasis or outflow obstruction, is established on core or wedge biopsy with reticulin and trichrome stains.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used for the diagnosis of portal hypertension. CD34 and smooth muscle markers may highlight abnormal portal vessels, and CK7 helps assess biliary changes in conditions like PBC or congenital hepatic fibrosis.

entities.entity: Cholestasis - histological patterns of cholestatic injury
entities.variants: Bland (canalicular, pure) cholestasis; cholestatic hepatitis; acute cholangitic pattern; chronic cholestasis with cholate stasis (pseudoxanthomatous change, feathery degeneration, Mallory-Denk bodies, copper deposition); ductular reaction (types 1-3); bile infarcts and bile lakes; ductopenia; ductular (cholangiolar) cholestasis
entities.remarks: Morphological framework for the work-up of jaundice: bland cholestasis (drugs, sepsis, benign recurrent cholestasis), cholestatic hepatitis (drugs, viruses), obstructive pattern (large duct), chronic cholestatic pattern (PBC, PSC, ductopenia); CK7 and copper stains define chronicity.
entities.histo: Cholestasis means failure of bile flow, and liver biopsies reveal several patterns that guide the work-up. Bland or canalicular cholestasis shows bile plugs in dilated canaliculi and bile pigment in hepatocytes and Kupffer cells, mainly in zone 3, with little inflammation, and is typical of drugs such as anabolic steroids and oestrogens, sepsis, benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Cholestatic hepatitis combines cholestasis with hepatocellular injury and lobular inflammation, as in drug injury and viral hepatitis. The obstructive pattern shows portal oedema, ductular reaction with periductular neutrophils, bile plugs in interlobular ducts and ductules, and bile infarcts or extravasated bile lakes in severe cases. Ductular cholestasis, with inspissated bile in dilated ductules at the edge of portal tracts, is characteristic of sepsis (cholangitis lenta). Chronic cholestasis shows periportal cholate stasis with swollen, pale, feathery hepatocytes, Mallory-Denk bodies, copper and copper-binding protein deposition (rhodanine and orcein), and CK7 positivity in periportal hepatocytes, together with portal-to-portal biliary fibrosis. Ductular reaction (proliferation of ductules at the portal-parenchymal interface) accompanies many forms of injury and must be separated from true ducts when assessing ductopenia, which is defined as loss of interlobular ducts in more than half of portal tracts. Cholestasis should not be confused with lipofuscin, iron or Dubin-Johnson pigment, and Hall (Fouchet) stain confirms bile.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the work-up of cholestasis except for biliary brushing of strictures, where reactive changes must be separated from cholangiocarcinoma.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 distinguish native interlobular ducts from ductular reaction and confirm ductopenia, and CK7 periportal hepatocyte staining is a sensitive marker of chronic cholestasis. BSEP, MDR3 and CD10 (canalicular) immunostains help in suspected PFIC. Rhodanine and orcein stains (copper and copper-binding protein) are useful special stains in chronic cholestasis.

entities.variants: Type I (common bile duct), type II (common hepatic duct) and type III (porta hepatis, commonest) extrahepatic biliary atresia; isolated (perinatal) BA; syndromic BA with splenic malformation (BASM: polysplenia, situs inversus); cystic biliary atresia; CMV IgM-positive BA
entities.remarks: Progressive fibro-obliterative cholangiopathy of the extrahepatic ducts in infants, the commonest indication for paediatric liver transplant; liver biopsy shows portal oedema, marked ductular reaction with bile plugs and portal fibrosis; Kasai portoenterostomy best before 60 days.
entities.histo: Biliary atresia is a progressive, inflammatory and fibro-obliterative disease of the extrahepatic bile ducts in infancy, which secondarily damages intrahepatic ducts and causes rapid biliary cirrhosis if untreated. Infants present in the first weeks with conjugated jaundice, pale stools and dark urine. A liver biopsy shows the pattern of large duct obstruction: portal tract expansion by oedema and fibrosis, marked ductular reaction with ductules arranged around the edge of portal tracts, bile plugs in ductules and interlobular ducts, and canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis in the lobule. Giant cell transformation and extramedullary haematopoiesis can occur, but are less prominent than in neonatal hepatitis. Ductal plate malformation-like configuration of ducts is seen in some cases and suggests early onset. The excised remnant of the extrahepatic ducts at the porta hepatis shows fibrous obliteration, residual small ducts with inflammation, and occasional larger lumens, and the size of residual ductules may relate to prognosis after Kasai portoenterostomy. Cirrhosis develops within months if biliary drainage fails. The differentials include idiopathic neonatal hepatitis, Alagille syndrome (bile duct paucity), PFIC, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, choledochal cyst and total parenteral nutrition-associated cholestasis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the diagnosis of biliary atresia. Diagnosis relies on an urgent core biopsy and intraoperative cholangiography, and the excised biliary remnant from the Kasai procedure is examined histologically.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 highlight the striking ductular reaction and the configuration of ducts, which helps separate biliary atresia from neonatal hepatitis and Alagille syndrome (paucity). CD56 expression in ductular cells and CK7 positivity of periportal hepatocytes have been reported to support biliary atresia. MMP-7 is a serum biomarker and not used in tissue.

entities.entity: Non-syndromic paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts (intrahepatic biliary hypoplasia)
entities.variants: Non-syndromic bile duct paucity of infancy (associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, infections such as CMV and rubella, hypopituitarism, Down syndrome, cystic fibrosis, PFIC, chromosomal abnormalities); idiopathic; intrahepatic biliary atresia (historical term)
entities.remarks: Reduced bile duct to portal tract ratio (under 0.5 to 0.9 depending on age) without Alagille features; many secondary causes; requires adequate number of portal tracts (at least 10) and CK7/CK19 to count ducts.
entities.histo: Bile duct paucity means a reduced ratio of interlobular bile ducts to portal tracts, usually below 0.5 in term infants and older children (normal ratio 0.9 to 1.8), and it can be syndromic (Alagille syndrome) or non-syndromic. Non-syndromic paucity is associated with many conditions, including alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, congenital infections, hypopituitarism, Down syndrome and other chromosomal abnormalities, cystic fibrosis, some forms of PFIC and drug injury, and some cases remain idiopathic. The term intrahepatic biliary atresia has been used historically. Biopsies show portal tracts lacking interlobular ducts despite the presence of the accompanying hepatic artery branches, with little or no ductular reaction, together with canalicular cholestasis and sometimes giant cell transformation. In premature infants, ducts may not yet be fully developed and paucity must be interpreted with caution. Adequate sampling with at least ten portal tracts is required. The differentials include Alagille syndrome (cardiac, vertebral, ocular and facial features with JAG1 or NOTCH2 mutations), biliary atresia (ductular reaction), and neonatal hepatitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Duct paucity can only be assessed by counting bile ducts in at least 10 portal tracts on a core biopsy, supported by CK7 and CK19 immunostaining.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 are essential to count interlobular ducts accurately and to distinguish them from ductular reaction; arteries without accompanying CK19-positive ducts confirm paucity.

entities.entity: Alagille syndrome (syndromic paucity of interlobular bile ducts)
entities.variants: JAG1-related (type 1, most); NOTCH2-related (type 2); Alagille-associated HCC (rare)
entities.remarks: Autosomal dominant; bile duct paucity with chronic cholestasis plus characteristic facies, butterfly vertebrae, posterior embryotoxon, peripheral pulmonary stenosis and renal anomalies; paucity may not be apparent in early infancy; risk of HCC.
entities.histo: Alagille syndrome is an autosomal dominant multisystem disorder caused mainly by mutations in JAG1 and less often NOTCH2, both in the Notch signalling pathway. Its hepatic hallmark is paucity of interlobular bile ducts with chronic cholestasis, combined with characteristic triangular facies, butterfly vertebrae, posterior embryotoxon of the eye, cardiac defects such as peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis and renal anomalies. In the first months of life, biopsies may show a nearly normal number of ducts with ductular reaction and giant cell transformation, which can mimic biliary atresia or neonatal hepatitis, and paucity often becomes evident only with time. Later biopsies show portal tracts with arteries but no accompanying ducts, little ductular reaction, canalicular cholestasis and copper accumulation, but fibrosis usually progresses slowly, and cirrhosis is uncommon. Some patients develop hepatocellular carcinoma. The differentials include non-syndromic paucity, biliary atresia and PFIC, and genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in Alagille syndrome. Diagnosis rests on biopsy evidence of duct paucity, the clinical criteria (cardiac, vertebral, ocular and facial features) and JAG1 or NOTCH2 genetic testing.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 confirm the absence of interlobular ducts and the lack of ductular reaction, and CK7 may stain periportal hepatocytes as a marker of chronic cholestasis. Glypican-3 and glutamine synthetase are used if a nodule raises concern for HCC.

entities.variants: PFIC1 (ATP8B1, FIC1 disease; low GGT); PFIC2 (ABCB11, BSEP deficiency; low GGT, giant cell hepatitis, HCC risk); PFIC3 (ABCB4, MDR3 deficiency; high GGT, ductular reaction, biliary fibrosis); PFIC4 (TJP2); PFIC5 (NR1H4, FXR); PFIC6 (MYO5B); other newer forms (USP53, KIF12, ZFYVE19)
entities.remarks: Autosomal recessive defects of canalicular transport; low-GGT forms (1, 2, 4, 5, 6) have bland canalicular cholestasis, high-GGT PFIC3 shows ductular reaction and portal fibrosis; BSEP and MDR3 IHC help; PFIC2 risk of HCC and cholangiocarcinoma in childhood.
entities.histo: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis is a group of autosomal recessive disorders of bile formation at the canalicular membrane, presenting in infancy or childhood with cholestasis, pruritus and progressive liver disease. PFIC1 (ATP8B1) shows bland canalicular cholestasis with little hepatocyte injury, coarse granular Byler bile on electron microscopy, and extrahepatic features such as diarrhoea and pancreatitis. PFIC2 (ABCB11, BSEP deficiency) is more severe, with neonatal giant cell hepatitis, lobular inflammation, hepatocyte necrosis and progressive fibrosis, and it carries a risk of HCC and cholangiocarcinoma in early childhood. Both PFIC1 and PFIC2 have low serum GGT. PFIC3 (ABCB4, MDR3 deficiency) causes high GGT cholestasis with ductular reaction, portal inflammation and biliary-type fibrosis leading to cirrhosis, and adults with milder mutations develop low phospholipid-associated cholelithiasis or drug-induced cholestasis. PFIC4 (TJP2), PFIC5 (NR1H4) and PFIC6 (MYO5B) show low GGT cholestasis with giant cells, and FXR deficiency causes early severe liver failure. The differentials include biliary atresia, Alagille syndrome, bile acid synthesis defects, neonatal hepatitis, and benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis (milder episodic disease from the same genes).
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in PFIC. Diagnosis needs a core biopsy with BSEP, MDR3 and other transporter immunostains, together with serum GGT levels and genetic testing.
entities.ihc: BSEP immunostaining shows absent or markedly reduced canalicular staining in many PFIC2 cases, and MDR3 immunostaining shows absent canalicular staining in many PFIC3 cases, although normal staining does not rule out a missense mutation. CD10 and polyclonal CEA outline canaliculi and can show abnormal patterns in FIC1 and MYO5B disease, and claudin-1 or ZO-2 staining is lost in TJP2 disease. CK7 helps assess ductular reaction, and glypican-3 or AFP is used to screen tumour nodules in PFIC2.

entities.variants: BRIC1 (ATP8B1); BRIC2 (ABCB11); BRIC triggered by infection, drugs or pregnancy
entities.remarks: Episodes of severe cholestasis with pruritus lasting weeks to months, separated by symptom-free intervals with normal liver; low GGT; biopsy during attack shows bland zone 3 canalicular cholestasis without fibrosis; milder allelic form of PFIC1 and PFIC2.
entities.histo: Benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis is a rare inherited disorder caused by milder mutations in ATP8B1 (BRIC1) or ABCB11 (BRIC2), and it is allelic with PFIC1 and PFIC2. Patients have recurrent episodes of severe pruritus and jaundice, sometimes triggered by infections, pregnancy or medications, separated by symptom-free intervals of months to years. During an episode, the liver biopsy shows bland canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis, predominantly in zone 3, with minimal inflammation, scattered Kupffer cells laden with bile and no significant hepatocyte necrosis or ductular reaction. Between episodes, the liver is histologically normal, and fibrosis does not usually develop, although some patients progress to a persistent PFIC-like phenotype. Serum GGT remains low. The differentials include drug-induced bland cholestasis, intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, sepsis and the other low-GGT cholestatic disorders, and genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in BRIC. Biopsy during an attack shows bland canalicular cholestasis, and the diagnosis rests on the recurrent clinical course and ATP8B1 or ABCB11 genetic testing.
entities.ihc: IHC is not usually necessary; BSEP staining may be preserved or reduced in BRIC2. CK7 helps exclude chronic biliary disease.

entities.entity: Inborn errors of bile acid synthesis
entities.variants: 3-beta-hydroxy-delta5-C27-steroid dehydrogenase (HSD3B7) deficiency; delta4-3-oxosteroid 5-beta-reductase (AKR1D1) deficiency; oxysterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP7B1) deficiency; amidation (BAAT, SLC27A5) defects; Zellweger spectrum (peroxisomal) disorders
entities.remarks: Rare, treatable (oral cholic acid) causes of neonatal and childhood cholestasis with low or normal GGT and low serum bile acids; giant cell hepatitis pattern; diagnosis by urinary bile acid mass spectrometry.
entities.histo: Inborn errors of bile acid synthesis are rare autosomal recessive disorders in which defective enzymes prevent synthesis of normal primary bile acids, leading to accumulation of toxic intermediates. They present in infancy with cholestasis and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption, and paradoxically normal or low serum bile acids and low GGT. Liver biopsy shows giant cell hepatitis with canalicular cholestasis, hepatocyte necrosis, lobular inflammation and extramedullary haematopoiesis, and later portal fibrosis, which may progress to cirrhosis. The histology is not specific and overlaps with idiopathic neonatal hepatitis and PFIC2, so diagnosis rests on urinary bile acid analysis by mass spectrometry and genetic testing. Zellweger spectrum peroxisomal disorders show similar hepatic changes with cholestasis, fibrosis and iron deposition, with distinctive neurological and facial features. Identification matters because oral primary bile acid therapy can reverse the liver disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Diagnosis rests on urine or serum bile acid analysis by mass spectrometry and genetic testing, while biopsy shows non-specific giant cell hepatitis or cholestasis.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic; BSEP and MDR3 staining are normal, which helps exclude PFIC2 and PFIC3. CK7 assesses ductular changes.

entities.variants: ABCC2 (MRP2) deficiency; neonatal presentation; pregnancy- or contraceptive-unmasked hyperbilirubinaemia
entities.remarks: Benign autosomal recessive conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; grossly black liver; coarse dark brown lysosomal pigment in zone 3 hepatocytes (PAS-D positive, Fontana-Masson positive, Perls negative); otherwise normal architecture; MRP2 canalicular staining absent.
entities.histo: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a benign autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in ABCC2, which encodes the canalicular transporter MRP2 responsible for excreting conjugated bilirubin and other organic anions. Patients have chronic or intermittent conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, often unmasked by pregnancy or oral contraceptives, with otherwise normal liver tests. The liver is strikingly black or green-black on gross examination. Microscopically the architecture is normal, but hepatocytes, predominantly in zone 3, contain coarse, dark brown to black lysosomal pigment granules, which resemble lipofuscin but are larger and darker. The pigment is PAS positive after diastase, stains with Fontana-Masson, and is Perls negative, and it is thought to be a melanin-like polymer of epinephrine metabolites. There is no cholestasis, inflammation or fibrosis. The differentials include lipofuscin (finer, lighter, zone 3), haemosiderin (Perls positive), bile (Hall stain positive, canalicular), malarial and schistosomal pigment (Kupffer cells), and Rotor syndrome, which shows no pigment.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role, although aspirates may incidentally show hepatocytes with coarse dark brown cytoplasmic pigment that must not be mistaken for melanin in metastatic melanoma.
entities.ihc: MRP2 immunostaining shows absent canalicular staining, confirming the diagnosis, whereas canalicular MRP2 staining is retained in Rotor syndrome and other conditions. Melanoma markers (SOX10, S100, Melan-A) are negative, which helps if the pigment raises concern for melanoma.

entities.entity: Other hereditary hyperbilirubinaemias (Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar, Rotor syndromes)
entities.variants: Gilbert syndrome (UGT1A1 promoter polymorphism, mild unconjugated); Crigler-Najjar type 1 (absent UGT1A1, kernicterus) and type 2 (Arias, partial, phenobarbital-responsive); Rotor syndrome (SLCO1B1/SLCO1B3, conjugated, no pigment)
entities.remarks: Clinical and biochemical diagnoses; liver histology essentially normal (Gilbert may show slight zone 3 lipofuscin); Crigler-Najjar may show canalicular bile plugs; biopsy mainly to exclude other diseases.
entities.histo: These inherited disorders of bilirubin metabolism produce isolated hyperbilirubinaemia with essentially normal liver histology, and biopsy is usually done only to exclude other disease. Gilbert syndrome, caused by reduced UGT1A1 activity due to a promoter polymorphism, is common, benign and causes mild fluctuating unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, often with fasting or illness; the liver is normal apart from occasional increased lipofuscin in zone 3. Crigler-Najjar syndrome type 1 is caused by complete absence of UGT1A1 activity and leads to severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and kernicterus, requiring phototherapy and often liver transplantation; the liver shows only occasional canalicular bile plugs and pigment. Type 2 (Arias syndrome) is milder and responds to phenobarbital. Rotor syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia due to combined deficiency of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3, and, unlike Dubin-Johnson syndrome, there is no hepatocellular pigment. The differentials include haemolysis, drug-induced hyperbilirubinaemia, Dubin-Johnson syndrome and early cholestatic disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. These are diagnosed by bilirubin fractionation and genetic testing, and liver tissue, when available, is usually histologically normal apart from cholestasis in Crigler-Najjar type 1.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed. In Rotor syndrome, OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 immunostaining is absent in hepatocytes, while MRP2 is retained, helping separate it from Dubin-Johnson syndrome.

entities.variants: Isolated congenital hepatic fibrosis; with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (PKHD1, fibrocystin); with Caroli disease (Caroli syndrome); with ciliopathy syndromes (Meckel-Gruber, Joubert, Bardet-Biedl, nephronophthisis, Jeune); portal hypertensive, cholangitic and mixed forms
entities.remarks: Ciliopathy-related ductal plate malformation; broad portal fibrous bands containing numerous irregular, ectatic bile duct profiles at the edge, hypoplastic portal veins, preserved lobules (not cirrhosis); presents with portal hypertension in children and young adults; risk of cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma.
entities.histo: Congenital hepatic fibrosis is a developmental disorder caused by failure of remodelling of the embryonic ductal plate, usually as part of a ciliopathy, and most commonly associated with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease due to PKHD1 mutations. It typically presents in childhood or young adulthood with portal hypertension and variceal bleeding, with preserved liver function. The liver is enlarged and firm, and microscopically portal tracts are linked by broad bands of dense fibrous tissue containing numerous irregularly shaped, interconnected and sometimes ectatic bile duct profiles, often lying at the periphery of the bands in a ductal plate-like arrangement, and bile plugs may be present in them. Portal vein branches are small or hypoplastic, which explains presinusoidal portal hypertension, and hepatic artery branches may be increased. The intervening hepatic lobules are normal without regenerative nodules, which separates this condition from cirrhosis. Cholangitis may complicate cases associated with Caroli disease, and cholangiocarcinoma can rarely arise. The differentials include biliary cirrhosis (nodules, cholestasis, inflammation), von Meyenburg complexes (focal), and schistosomiasis or porto-sinusoidal vascular disease (no ductal plate malformation).
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in congenital hepatic fibrosis. The ductal plate malformation and portal fibrosis can only be assessed on core or wedge biopsy, and renal imaging looks for associated polycystic kidney disease.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 highlight the abundant ductal plate malformation-type bile duct structures within the fibrous bands, demonstrating their continuity, and the lack of ductular reaction typical of biliary cirrhosis. IHC is otherwise not needed.

entities.variants: Caroli disease (pure segmental or diffuse saccular dilatation of large intrahepatic ducts); Caroli syndrome (with congenital hepatic fibrosis, often ARPKD); monolobar (left lobe) form; complicated by cholangitis, intrahepatic stones, abscess and cholangiocarcinoma
entities.remarks: Congenital multifocal saccular dilatation of large intrahepatic bile ducts communicating with the biliary tree (central dot sign on imaging); recurrent cholangitis and hepatolithiasis; cholangiocarcinoma risk; treated by resection or transplant.
entities.histo: Caroli disease is a congenital malformation of the large intrahepatic bile ducts caused by abnormal ductal plate remodelling at the level of the large ducts, resulting in multifocal saccular or fusiform dilatations that communicate with the biliary tree. When combined with congenital hepatic fibrosis, the condition is called Caroli syndrome, and both are often associated with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. The dilated ducts appear as cysts containing bile, sludge or stones, with portal radicles bulging into their lumen (the central dot sign on imaging). Microscopically, the cyst walls are lined by biliary epithelium that may be ulcerated, hyperplastic or show mucinous metaplasia, with fibrous walls containing chronic and acute inflammation and peribiliary glands. Bridging fibrous septa with ductal plate malformation are present in Caroli syndrome. Complications include recurrent cholangitis, intrahepatic stones, abscesses, secondary biliary cirrhosis and cholangiocarcinoma, so resected specimens should be widely sampled for dysplasia. The differentials include choledochal cyst type V (often synonymous), polycystic liver disease (cysts that do not communicate with the biliary tree), recurrent pyogenic cholangitis and secondary dilatation from obstruction.
entities.cyto: Cytology is limited to bile or brushing samples to exclude cholangiocarcinoma, where inflammation and stones may cause reactive atypia.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed for diagnosis; CK7 and CK19 confirm biliary lining. In dysplasia or carcinoma, p53, SMAD4 and Ki-67 help separate neoplastic from reactive epithelium.

entities.variants: Solitary von Meyenburg complex; multiple biliary hamartomas (diffuse, in polycystic liver disease or congenital hepatic fibrosis); cystic variant
entities.remarks: Common incidental small (under 5 mm) grey-white nodules near portal tracts; irregular, dilated bile duct-like structures with inspissated bile in fibrous stroma; frozen section mimic of metastatic adenocarcinoma and bile duct adenoma.
entities.histo: Von Meyenburg complexes, also called biliary microhamartomas, are small ductal plate malformations of the interlobular ducts and are common incidental findings at surgery, autopsy and on imaging. They appear as single or multiple grey-white nodules a few millimetres across, often near the capsule, and multiple lesions occur in polycystic liver disease and congenital hepatic fibrosis. Microscopically, they consist of irregularly shaped, angulated or dilated duct-like structures lined by a single layer of bland cuboidal or flattened biliary cells, often containing inspissated bile or eosinophilic secretions, embedded in a fibrous or hyalinised stroma, usually adjacent to a portal tract. They are important at frozen section because they can mimic metastatic adenocarcinoma, particularly in patients with known primary tumours. The differentials include bile duct adenoma (small, tightly packed tubules without dilatation or bile, often with inflammation), metastatic adenocarcinoma (cytological atypia, mitoses, necrosis), cholangiocarcinoma and ductular reaction. Rarely, cholangiocarcinoma has been reported to arise in von Meyenburg complexes.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role; if aspirated, they yield small sheets of bland biliary cells, which can be mistaken for well-differentiated adenocarcinoma, especially in patients with a known primary tumour.
entities.ihc: The duct cells are CK7 and CK19 positive with a low Ki-67 and wild-type p53 staining. Unlike metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma, they are CK20 and CDX2 negative, and SMAD4 is retained. Bile duct adenoma differs by often expressing MUC6 and BRAF V600E in some cases.

entities.variants: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKD1, PKD2) with liver cysts; isolated autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease (PRKCSH, SEC63, ALG8, LRP5, GANAB); Gigot types I to III (by cyst number and size)
entities.remarks: Multiple biliary-type cysts that do not communicate with the bile ducts, plus von Meyenburg complexes; liver function preserved; massive hepatomegaly may require fenestration, resection or transplantation; women and oestrogen exposure worsen it.
entities.histo: Polycystic liver disease is characterised by numerous cysts throughout the liver, either as part of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKD1 or PKD2) or as isolated autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease caused by mutations in genes such as PRKCSH and SEC63. Cysts increase with age, female sex and oestrogen exposure, and massive hepatomegaly can cause pain, early satiety and compression of nearby structures, while liver function remains intact. Grossly the liver is replaced by many thin-walled cysts of varying size filled with clear, watery fluid. Microscopically the cysts are lined by a single layer of cuboidal to flattened biliary epithelium, sometimes attenuated, with a thin fibrous wall, and they do not communicate with the biliary tree. Numerous von Meyenburg complexes are present in the intervening parenchyma, reflecting the shared ductal plate origin. Complications include cyst haemorrhage, infection and rupture. The differentials include simple cysts (solitary or few), Caroli disease (communicating saccular ductal dilatation), mucinous cystic neoplasm (ovarian-type stroma, mucinous lining) and ciliated foregut cyst.
entities.cyto: Cyst fluid aspiration yields clear fluid with few cells, mostly macrophages and occasional bland cuboidal biliary cells; cytology is mainly used to exclude infection or neoplasia in a complex cyst.
entities.ihc: The lining is CK7 and CK19 positive, and the cyst wall lacks the ER-positive, PR-positive ovarian-type stroma of mucinous cystic neoplasm, which is a useful negative finding. IHC is otherwise not needed.

entities.variants: Todani type I (cystic or fusiform dilatation of extrahepatic duct; Ia, Ib, Ic), type II (diverticulum), type III (choledochocele), type IVa (intra- and extrahepatic), IVb (multiple extrahepatic), type V (intrahepatic, Caroli disease); forme fruste; associated pancreaticobiliary maljunction
entities.remarks: Congenital dilatation of the biliary tree, common in Asian populations and females; associated with anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction and reflux of pancreatic enzymes; risk of cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma; complete excision with hepaticojejunostomy.
entities.histo: Choledochal cysts are congenital dilatations of the bile ducts, more common in East Asian populations and in females, often associated with an anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction that allows reflux of pancreatic juice into the bile ducts. The Todani classification defines types by location: type I (dilatation of the extrahepatic duct, the commonest), type II (diverticulum), type III (choledochocele at the ampulla), type IV (multiple cysts, IVa intra- and extrahepatic, IVb extrahepatic), and type V (intrahepatic, equivalent to Caroli disease). Intrahepatic involvement is relevant to the liver chapter in types IVa and V. Resected cysts have a thick fibrous wall with chronic inflammation, smooth muscle bundles, and a lining of biliary epithelium that is often denuded or ulcerated, with metaplasia (pyloric, intestinal, squamous) and reactive atypia. Bile stasis leads to stones and cholangitis, and the risk of biliary dysplasia and carcinoma (cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma) increases with age, so specimens should be thoroughly sampled. The differentials include secondary duct dilatation from obstruction, Caroli disease and intraductal papillary neoplasms with cystic change.
entities.cyto: Bile aspirates or brushings are used to detect dysplasia or carcinoma in adults; reactive changes from inflammation and stones are common and must be interpreted conservatively.
entities.ihc: IHC is not required for the diagnosis. In atypical epithelium, p53, SMAD4 and Ki-67 help separate dysplasia from reactive atypia, and CK7 or CK20 may highlight metaplastic changes.

entities.variants: Solitary simple cyst; multiple simple cysts (fewer than in polycystic liver disease); haemorrhagic or infected cyst; giant simple cyst
entities.remarks: Common, usually asymptomatic, incidental; unilocular thin-walled cyst with clear serous fluid, lined by single layer of cuboidal biliary epithelium without ovarian-type stroma; does not communicate with bile ducts.
entities.histo: Simple hepatic cysts are common, benign, non-communicating cysts of biliary type, thought to arise from aberrant bile ducts that lost their connection with the biliary tree. They are usually discovered incidentally on imaging, more often in women and older adults, and large cysts may cause pain or compression. Grossly they are unilocular, thin-walled and filled with clear, watery serous fluid. Microscopically, the lining is a single layer of cuboidal or flattened biliary epithelium resting on a thin fibrous wall, without mucinous epithelium or ovarian-type stroma. Haemorrhage or infection may denude the lining and produce a fibrous wall with haemosiderin, cholesterol clefts and inflammation, which can mimic a neoplasm on imaging. The differentials include mucinous cystic neoplasm (multilocular, mucinous lining, ovarian-type stroma), ciliated hepatic foregut cyst (ciliated pseudostratified epithelium, smooth muscle layer), hydatid cyst (laminated membrane), polycystic liver disease and cystic metastases or cystic HCC.
entities.cyto: Aspirated fluid is clear and paucicellular, containing a few macrophages and occasional cuboidal cells. Cytology is used only to exclude malignancy or infection in a complex cyst, and low cyst fluid CEA and CA19-9 are not entirely reliable in separating it from mucinous cystic neoplasm.
entities.ihc: The lining is CK7 and CK19 positive. The absence of ER-positive, PR-positive and inhibin-positive ovarian-type stroma separates it from mucinous cystic neoplasm, and IHC is otherwise unnecessary.

entities.variants: Classical subcapsular segment IV cyst; cyst with squamous metaplasia; carcinoma arising in ciliated foregut cyst (rare, squamous cell carcinoma)
entities.remarks: Rare solitary cyst of foregut origin, usually segment IV, subcapsular, under 4 cm; four layers: ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells, subepithelial connective tissue, smooth muscle layer, outer fibrous capsule; rare squamous cell carcinoma.
entities.histo: The ciliated hepatic foregut cyst is a rare congenital cyst thought to arise from embryonic foregut remnants, homologous to bronchogenic and oesophageal duplication cysts. It is usually a solitary, unilocular, subcapsular lesion in segment IV of the left lobe, typically less than 4 cm, discovered incidentally on imaging. The cyst contains clear or mucoid fluid. Microscopically the wall has four characteristic layers: a lining of ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells, a subepithelial loose connective tissue layer, a well-defined smooth muscle layer and an outer fibrous capsule. Squamous metaplasia may occur, and rare cases of squamous cell carcinoma arising in the cyst have been reported, particularly in large cysts. The differentials include simple biliary cyst (cuboidal lining, no smooth muscle), mucinous cystic neoplasm (ovarian-type stroma), intrahepatic bronchogenic-like cysts and cystic metastases.
entities.cyto: Aspirated fluid may show ciliated columnar cells, goblet cells and mucoid material, and identification of ciliated cells in an aspirate from a segment IV cyst strongly suggests the diagnosis; cilia exclude malignancy in most contexts.
entities.ihc: The ciliated epithelium is CK7 positive and often positive for TTF-1 in some reports, with CK20 negative, and the smooth muscle layer is SMA and desmin positive. ER and PR negative stroma excludes mucinous cystic neoplasm.

entities.variants: Multiple peribiliary cysts in cirrhosis and portal hypertension; in polycystic disease; post-ischaemic
entities.remarks: Small cysts arising from peribiliary glands along large intrahepatic ducts at the hilum, mainly in cirrhosis and portal hypertension; may cause biliary obstruction and mimic cholangiocarcinoma or dilated ducts on imaging.
entities.histo: Peribiliary cysts arise from cystic dilatation of the extramural peribiliary glands that surround large intrahepatic and hilar bile ducts. They are found mainly in cirrhosis and portal hypertension, but also in polycystic liver disease, infection and after ischaemic injury. They form multiple small cysts, usually 0.2 to 2 cm, clustered along the hilar ducts and portal tracts, which on imaging may resemble dilated bile ducts or a cystic tumour. Microscopically the cysts are lined by a single layer of cuboidal or columnar biliary epithelium, sometimes with mucinous features, set in the connective tissue around large ducts, and they do not communicate with the duct lumen. Large cysts may compress bile ducts and cause obstructive jaundice. The differentials include dilated bile ducts, choledochal cyst, Caroli disease, intraductal papillary neoplasm with cystic change and mucinous cystic neoplasm.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no routine role. If aspirated, the cyst fluid is clear and contains a few bland cuboidal biliary cells, without atypia or mucin, which helps exclude mucinous cystic neoplasm.
entities.ihc: The lining is CK7 and CK19 positive, sometimes MUC6 positive reflecting peribiliary gland origin; IHC is otherwise not needed.

entities.entity: Other hepatic cysts and pseudocysts (endometriotic, mesothelial, traumatic, pancreatic, intrahepatic pseudocyst)
entities.variants: Endometriotic cyst of liver; mesothelial cyst (subcapsular); post-traumatic or post-haematoma pseudocyst; pancreatic pseudocyst extending into the liver; biloma (extravasated bile); cystic degeneration of tumours (cystic HCC, metastases, cystic NET)
entities.remarks: Heterogeneous group of rare cysts; identify the lining (endometrial glands and stroma, mesothelium, none in pseudocysts) and exclude cystic neoplasms by thorough sampling.
entities.histo: Several uncommon cystic lesions may occur in the liver. Endometriotic cysts contain endometrial glands and stroma with haemosiderin-laden macrophages and are seen in women with pelvic endometriosis. Mesothelial cysts are thin-walled, subcapsular cysts lined by flattened mesothelial cells. Pseudocysts lack an epithelial lining and include post-traumatic cysts formed from organised haematomas, bilomas (extravasated bile walled off by fibrosis and inflammation), and pancreatic pseudocysts extending into the liver. Cystic degeneration of neoplasms, including cystic hepatocellular carcinoma, cystic metastases (neuroendocrine tumours, GIST, sarcomas, squamous carcinoma), and cystic cholangiocarcinoma, must always be excluded by careful gross examination and sampling of solid areas or nodules in the wall. The differentials also include simple cysts, mucinous cystic neoplasm, hydatid cyst and abscess.
entities.cyto: Aspirated fluid from pseudocysts contains blood, haemosiderin-laden macrophages, bile or amylase-rich fluid, and endometriotic cysts may yield haemosiderin-laden macrophages with scant endometrial-type cells. Atypical cells should prompt evaluation for a cystic neoplasm.
entities.ihc: CD10 (endometrial stroma), ER and PR identify endometriosis, and calretinin, WT1 and D2-40 identify mesothelial lining. In cystic tumours, appropriate markers such as HepPar1, CK7 and CK19 or synaptophysin and chromogranin define the neoplasm.

entities.entity: Anatomical anomalies and heterotopias (Riedel lobe, accessory and ectopic liver, adrenal, pancreatic and splenic heterotopia)
entities.variants: Riedel lobe (tongue-like inferior projection of right lobe); accessory liver lobe; ectopic liver tissue (gallbladder wall, umbilical, thoracic); agenesis or hypoplasia of a lobe; heterotopic pancreas or adrenal (adrenal rest) in liver; hepatic splenosis (after splenic trauma)
entities.remarks: Usually incidental; ectopic liver tissue can develop the same diseases as orthotopic liver (including HCC); intrahepatic adrenal rests and splenosis mimic tumours on imaging.
entities.histo: Several developmental and acquired anatomical variants can be encountered in the liver. Riedel lobe is a tongue-like downward extension of the right lobe that may be palpated as a mass. Accessory lobes are connected to the main liver by a pedicle, while ectopic liver tissue, without a connection, may be found in the gallbladder wall, umbilical region, thorax or elsewhere. Ectopic liver has normal hepatic histology but may lack complete portal tracts or venous drainage, and it can develop steatosis, cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma. Heterotopic tissues within the liver include pancreatic tissue (acini and ducts, rarely islets), adrenal cortical rests (nests of clear or eosinophilic adrenal cortical cells beneath the capsule, which can give rise to adrenal rest tumours), and hepatic splenosis (implantation of splenic tissue after splenic rupture), which can mimic a hypervascular tumour on imaging. Agenesis or hypoplasia of a lobe causes compensatory hypertrophy of the remainder. The differentials for adrenal rests include clear cell HCC and metastatic renal cell carcinoma, and for splenosis, haemangioma or HCC.
entities.cyto: FNA of a heterotopic nodule may yield adrenal cortical cells (foamy or granular cytoplasm, naked nuclei), pancreatic acinar cells or splenic lymphoid tissue with endothelium-lined sinus cells, each of which can be mistaken for neoplasia.
entities.ihc: Adrenal cortical rests are SF-1, inhibin, melan-A and calretinin positive and HepPar1 negative, separating them from clear cell HCC, and they are PAX8 negative unlike renal cell carcinoma. Splenic tissue shows CD8-positive littoral (sinus lining) cells, and pancreatic heterotopia shows trypsin and BCL10 positive acini. Ectopic liver shows normal hepatocyte markers.

entities.variants: Type 1 extrahepatic shunt (complete absence of intrahepatic portal flow; 1a and 1b); type 2 extrahepatic (partial shunt); intrahepatic portosystemic shunts; patent ductus venosus
entities.remarks: Rare congenital diversion of portal blood into systemic veins; liver shows absent or hypoplastic portal veins, arterialisation, and nodular lesions (FNH-like nodules, hepatocellular adenoma, NRH, HCC); hepatopulmonary syndrome and encephalopathy.
entities.histo: Congenital portosystemic shunts are rare vascular malformations in which portal venous blood bypasses the liver, either completely (type 1, absent intrahepatic portal flow) or partially (type 2). Lack of portal venous inflow leads to compensatory arterialisation and abnormal hepatocyte growth. Biopsies of the background liver show small portal tracts with absent or hypoplastic portal vein branches, increased numbers of hepatic artery branches (arterial hypertrophy), mild sinusoidal dilatation and sometimes nodular regenerative hyperplasia. Patients frequently develop liver nodules, including FNH and FNH-like nodules, hepatocellular adenomas (often inflammatory or beta-catenin-activated) and occasionally hepatoblastoma or hepatocellular carcinoma. Systemic complications include hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension and hepatic encephalopathy. The differentials include porto-sinusoidal vascular disease, portal vein thrombosis and Budd-Chiari syndrome, which may produce similar regenerative nodules.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the diagnosis of the shunt itself; FNA of nodules in this setting faces the same challenges as for FNH and adenoma, where benign hepatocytes cannot be reliably classified on cytology.
entities.ihc: IHC is used mainly to characterise nodules: map-like glutamine synthetase staining identifies FNH, while CRP or SAA, LFABP and beta-catenin or diffuse glutamine synthetase help subtype hepatocellular adenomas. CD34 highlights arterialised sinusoids, and smooth muscle markers can show abnormal portal vessels.

entities.variants: Type 1 (HFE C282Y homozygous, commonest in Northern Europeans); type 2A (HJV, juvenile) and 2B (HAMP, juvenile); type 3 (TFR2); type 4 ferroportin disease (SLC40A1; 4A macrophage-type, 4B classic); haemochromatosis-related cirrhosis and HCC
entities.remarks: Inherited hepcidin deficiency causing increased intestinal iron absorption; periportal (zone 1) hepatocellular iron in a decreasing gradient towards zone 3, later pigment cirrhosis; Perls stain graded 0-4; type 4A shows Kupffer cell iron; HCC risk in cirrhosis; venesection therapy.
entities.histo: Hereditary haemochromatosis is a group of inherited disorders causing inappropriately low hepcidin activity, increased intestinal iron absorption and progressive iron deposition in the liver, pancreas, heart and other organs. HFE-related type 1, mainly due to C282Y homozygosity, is the commonest form in people of Northern European descent and is uncommon in India, whereas juvenile forms (HJV, HAMP) cause severe early disease. The liver shows granular golden-brown haemosiderin in hepatocytes, predominantly in periportal (zone 1) hepatocytes with a decreasing gradient towards the central vein, accumulating at the biliary pole of the cell. With increasing iron, deposits involve all zones, biliary epithelium and Kupffer cells, and portal fibrosis leads to micronodular pigment cirrhosis, in which iron-laden septa and nodules are seen. Perls Prussian blue stain is essential, and iron can be graded semiquantitatively (0 to 4, Scheuer or Deugnier systems) and measured biochemically as hepatic iron concentration. Ferroportin disease type 4A shows predominantly Kupffer cell (macrophage) iron with normal transferrin saturation. Hepatocellular carcinoma develops mainly in cirrhosis, and iron-free foci within an iron-laden liver may indicate dysplasia. The differentials include secondary iron overload (transfusion, ineffective erythropoiesis; Kupffer cell iron), iron in alcoholic liver disease, MASLD-associated dysmetabolic iron overload, porphyria cutanea tarda and chronic hepatitis C, and other pigments such as lipofuscin, bile and Dubin-Johnson pigment.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in diagnosis; however, aspirates of hepatocytes in iron overload may contain coarse golden-brown granular pigment that stains blue with Perls stain, and iron-free tumour cells may be seen in HCC.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed; Perls Prussian blue is the key special stain, and the pattern (hepatocellular versus Kupffer cell, zonal gradient) helps separate hereditary from secondary iron overload. In nodules, glypican-3, HSP70 and glutamine synthetase help identify HCC.

entities.variants: Transfusional iron overload (thalassaemia major, sickle cell disease, myelodysplasia); iron-loading anaemias with ineffective erythropoiesis (thalassaemia intermedia, sideroblastic anaemia); dysmetabolic iron overload syndrome (MASLD); iron in alcoholic liver disease and chronic hepatitis C; porphyria cutanea tarda; dietary (African) iron overload; iron in end-stage cirrhosis
entities.remarks: Very relevant in India (thalassaemia); early Kupffer cell and portal macrophage iron, later hepatocellular iron with fibrosis and cirrhosis in heavy transfusional overload; Perls grade and pattern guide chelation; liver iron also measured by MRI (T2*).
entities.histo: Secondary iron overload results from repeated blood transfusions, ineffective erythropoiesis or chronic liver disease, and in India is most often seen in thalassaemia major. In transfusional overload, iron initially accumulates in Kupffer cells and portal macrophages as coarse clumps of haemosiderin, and as the load increases it spreads to hepatocytes in all zones and to biliary epithelium, leading to portal fibrosis and eventually micronodular cirrhosis, often also aggravated by hepatitis C from transfusions. In ineffective erythropoiesis without transfusion, iron is absorbed excessively and deposited mainly in hepatocytes in a periportal pattern similar to hereditary haemochromatosis. Dysmetabolic iron overload, associated with MASLD, shows mild mixed hepatocellular and Kupffer cell iron. Alcoholic liver disease, chronic hepatitis C and porphyria cutanea tarda cause mild to moderate mixed iron deposition. Perls stain shows the amount and distribution of iron, and semiquantitative grading together with MRI T2* measurements guide chelation therapy. The differentials include hereditary haemochromatosis (hepatocellular, periportal, high transferrin saturation, genetic tests), ferroportin disease (Kupffer cell iron) and other pigments.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role, though Perls-positive pigment may be seen in hepatocytes and macrophages in aspirates from iron-loaded livers.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role; Perls Prussian blue stain is the key tool. HCV status should be assessed serologically in multiply transfused patients.

entities.entity: Gestational alloimmune liver disease (GALD, neonatal haemochromatosis)
entities.variants: GALD with neonatal haemochromatosis phenotype (extrahepatic siderosis); GALD causing fetal death; recurrence in subsequent pregnancies (preventable with maternal IVIG)
entities.remarks: Commonest cause of neonatal haemochromatosis; maternal IgG against fetal hepatocytes activates complement (C5b-9) causing fetal liver injury and secondary siderosis; liver shows severe fibrosis, giant cells, hepatocyte loss and iron; extrahepatic iron in salivary glands (lip biopsy) and pancreas.
entities.histo: Gestational alloimmune liver disease is caused by maternal IgG alloantibodies directed against an antigen on fetal hepatocytes, which activate complement and destroy fetal liver cells, beginning in utero. It is the commonest cause of the neonatal haemochromatosis phenotype, in which severe fetal liver injury is accompanied by iron deposition in extrahepatic tissues such as the pancreas, heart, thyroid and minor salivary glands, but not in reticuloendothelial cells. Newborns present with liver failure, hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy, or the disease may cause late fetal death. The liver is small and firm, and microscopy shows extensive hepatocyte loss, collapse and fibrosis, giant cell transformation, pseudoacinar (rosette) transformation of residual hepatocytes, cholestasis and regenerative nodules, with heavy hepatocellular iron. Diagnosis is supported by demonstration of extrahepatic siderosis on MRI or a lip biopsy containing minor salivary glands with iron in acinar cells. Identification matters because maternal intravenous immunoglobulin prevents recurrence in later pregnancies. The differentials include other causes of neonatal liver failure, such as mitochondrial disease, tyrosinaemia, perinatal infections and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in GALD. Diagnosis relies on liver biopsy or autopsy with C5b-9 immunostaining, and extrahepatic iron is shown by buccal (minor salivary gland) biopsy or MRI.
entities.ihc: C5b-9 (membrane attack complex) immunostaining shows strong staining of residual hepatocytes, which is the key tissue test for GALD. Perls stain shows iron in hepatocytes and in extrahepatic tissues such as salivary glands. Viral stains help exclude congenital infection.

entities.variants: Hepatic presentation (asymptomatic transaminitis, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis); fulminant Wilson disease (with Coombs-negative haemolysis); neuropsychiatric presentation; Wilson disease in children
entities.remarks: Autosomal recessive ATP7B mutations impair biliary copper excretion; histology variable: steatosis, glycogenated nuclei, Mallory-Denk bodies, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis; rhodanine copper stain often patchy and unreliable early; quantitative hepatic copper over 250 micrograms per gram dry weight; Kayser-Fleischer rings, low ceruloplasmin.
entities.histo: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in ATP7B, which impair copper excretion into bile and lead to copper accumulation in the liver, brain and cornea. It presents from childhood to young adulthood with hepatic, neuropsychiatric or combined disease, and is an important cause of acute liver failure and cirrhosis in young patients in India. The liver histology is variable and non-specific. Early disease shows macrovesicular and microvesicular steatosis, glycogenated nuclei in periportal hepatocytes, mild portal inflammation and sometimes lipofuscin. Later, the pattern may resemble chronic hepatitis with interface activity, plasma cells and Mallory-Denk bodies, progressing to macronodular cirrhosis. Fulminant Wilson disease shows massive or submassive necrosis superimposed on an often cirrhotic liver, accompanied by Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia, with abundant copper and Mallory-Denk bodies. Rhodanine stain for copper and orcein or Victoria blue for copper-associated protein may be positive in periportal hepatocytes, but the staining is patchy and can be negative early in disease, so quantitative hepatic copper measurement (above 250 micrograms per gram dry weight) is more reliable. The differentials include autoimmune hepatitis, MASH, chronic viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury and copper accumulation due to chronic cholestasis (PBC, PSC), which is periportal and accompanied by biliary features.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the diagnosis of Wilson disease. It is diagnosed using serum caeruloplasmin, 24-hour urine copper, Kayser-Fleischer rings, quantitative hepatic copper on a dedicated biopsy core and ATP7B genetic testing.
entities.ihc: IHC does not establish the diagnosis; rhodanine (copper), orcein or Victoria blue (copper-binding protein) are the key special stains, interpreted with ceruloplasmin, urinary copper, Kayser-Fleischer rings and genetic testing. CK7 can help separate cholestasis-related copper from Wilson disease, since periportal CK7 metaplasia is typical of chronic cholestasis.

entities.entity: Indian childhood cirrhosis and idiopathic copper toxicosis
entities.variants: Indian childhood cirrhosis (ICC); endemic Tyrolean infantile cirrhosis; idiopathic copper toxicosis (non-Indian childhood cirrhosis)
entities.remarks: Historically common in India in children aged 1 to 3 years, linked to ingestion of milk boiled or stored in brass/copper vessels (with probable genetic predisposition); massive copper deposition, Mallory-Denk bodies, ballooning, pericellular fibrosis and micronodular cirrhosis; now rare after change in feeding practices.
entities.histo: Indian childhood cirrhosis was once a leading cause of childhood liver disease in India, typically affecting children between one and three years of age, and is associated with high dietary copper from milk boiled or stored in brass or copper vessels, possibly combined with an inherited susceptibility. Its incidence has fallen dramatically following education about feeding practices. Similar diseases, such as endemic Tyrolean infantile cirrhosis and idiopathic copper toxicosis, have been reported elsewhere. The liver histology is distinctive: hepatocytes show marked ballooning, numerous Mallory-Denk bodies, necrosis and inflammation with neutrophils, together with fine pericellular (chicken-wire) fibrosis that isolates individual hepatocytes, progressing to micronodular cirrhosis. Massive deposits of copper and copper-associated protein are seen throughout the lobules on rhodanine and orcein staining, more diffusely than in Wilson disease. Steatosis is usually minimal. The differentials include Wilson disease (older children, ATP7B mutations, low ceruloplasmin), alcoholic-like steatohepatitis patterns, cholestatic copper accumulation and other childhood cirrhoses.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Diagnosis needs a core biopsy showing Mallory-Denk bodies, pericellular fibrosis and heavy copper deposition (orcein or rhodanine stain), supported by quantitative copper estimation.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used; rhodanine and orcein stains demonstrate the diffuse heavy copper and copper-associated protein, and ubiquitin or p62 immunostaining highlights the numerous Mallory-Denk bodies.

entities.variants: PiZZ homozygous deficiency (neonatal cholestasis, childhood and adult cirrhosis, HCC); PiMZ heterozygote (modifier of other liver diseases); PiSZ; null variants (lung disease without liver globules)
entities.remarks: SERPINA1 mutation causes misfolded Z protein retained in hepatocyte ER; round PAS-positive diastase-resistant eosinophilic globules in periportal hepatocytes; neonatal hepatitis, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and HCC; lung emphysema.
