entities.histo: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an autosomal codominant disorder in which mutant AAT protein, most commonly the Z variant, misfolds and polymerises in the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes instead of being secreted. The retained protein is toxic and causes liver disease, while low serum AAT predisposes to emphysema. Liver disease ranges from neonatal cholestasis and giant cell hepatitis in infants to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in children and adults. The characteristic histological feature is the presence of round to oval, eosinophilic, hyaline globules of variable size within the cytoplasm of periportal (zone 1) hepatocytes, which are strongly PAS positive and resistant to diastase digestion. In neonates the globules may be small or absent, so immunostaining and serum phenotyping are important. Heterozygotes (PiMZ) may show fewer globules and act as disease modifiers in MASLD and alcoholic liver disease. In cirrhosis, globules are prominent at the edges of nodules. HCC can arise even without cirrhosis. The differentials include other PAS-D positive inclusions such as fibrinogen storage disease, megamitochondria (PAS negative), Mallory-Denk bodies (irregular, PAS negative), and globules in congestive hepatopathy (PAS-D positive in zone 3 but AAT negative).
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role; occasionally hepatocytes in aspirates contain round magenta PAS-positive cytoplasmic globules, which should not be mistaken for tumour inclusions.
entities.ihc: Alpha-1 antitrypsin immunostaining confirms the nature of the PAS-D positive globules and is particularly helpful in infants, where globules are small, and in the separation from other inclusions. Serum AAT levels and phenotyping or genotyping confirm the diagnosis. In nodules, HCC markers (glypican-3, HSP70, glutamine synthetase) are used.

entities.variants: Type Ia (von Gierke, G6Pase) and Ib (G6P translocase, neutropenia); type III (Cori, debrancher, fibrosis); type IV (Andersen, brancher, amylopectin-like inclusions, cirrhosis); type VI (Hers) and type IX (phosphorylase kinase); type 0 (glycogen synthase, no storage); Fanconi-Bickel (GLUT2); type II Pompe (lysosomal, mainly muscle)
entities.remarks: Inherited enzyme defects; swollen pale hepatocytes with mosaic (plant-cell) pattern, compressed sinusoids, glycogenated nuclei; PAS positive, diastase sensitive; GSD Ia/III at risk of hepatocellular adenomas (and HCC); GSD IV shows PAS-D resistant ground-glass inclusions and cirrhosis.
entities.histo: Hepatic glycogen storage diseases are inherited defects in glycogen synthesis or breakdown that present in childhood with hepatomegaly, hypoglycaemia and growth failure. In types I, III, VI and IX, hepatocytes are swollen and pale, with clear or finely granular cytoplasm and distinct cell membranes, giving a mosaic or plant cell appearance, with compressed sinusoids, glycogenated nuclei and variable macrovesicular steatosis, especially in type I. The stored glycogen is PAS positive and digested by diastase. Type I causes little fibrosis but predisposes to multiple hepatocellular adenomas, which can undergo malignant transformation to HCC, particularly beta-catenin-activated adenomas. Type III often shows portal and septal fibrosis that can progress to cirrhosis. Type IV (Andersen disease) stores an abnormal, amylopectin-like glycogen forming pale ground-glass cytoplasmic inclusions that are PAS positive and partially diastase resistant, and leads to cirrhosis early in childhood. Electron microscopy and enzyme or genetic testing confirm the subtype. The differentials include glycogenic hepatopathy in poorly controlled diabetes, MASLD, Lafora disease and drug-induced ground-glass changes.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in diagnosis; FNA in GSD is used for liver nodules, mainly adenomas and HCC, where benign-appearing hepatocytes cannot be reliably classified without histology.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used to diagnose the GSD itself, which relies on PAS with and without diastase, electron microscopy and genetic testing. In GSD-related nodules, a hepatocellular adenoma panel (LFABP, CRP or SAA, glutamine synthetase, beta-catenin) and HCC markers (glypican-3, HSP70) are applied; LFABP is often retained in GSD adenomas, and many are inflammatory or beta-catenin-activated.

entities.variants: Glycogenic hepatopathy in poorly controlled type 1 diabetes (Mauriac syndrome in children); glycogenic hepatopathy in type 2 diabetes or steroid treatment
entities.remarks: Reversible hepatomegaly and transaminitis with marked hepatocellular glycogen accumulation (pale swollen hepatocytes, PAS positive diastase sensitive), minimal steatosis or inflammation; improves with glycaemic control; differentiate from MASLD and GSD.
entities.histo: Glycogenic hepatopathy is a reversible condition seen mainly in adolescents and young adults with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes, in which repeated hyperglycaemia and insulin therapy cause excessive glycogen accumulation in hepatocytes. In children it may form part of Mauriac syndrome with growth retardation and Cushingoid features. Patients have hepatomegaly and elevated transaminases. The biopsy shows diffusely swollen, pale hepatocytes with clear or rarefied cytoplasm and prominent cell membranes, compressed sinusoids, glycogenated nuclei and occasional megamitochondria, with little or no steatosis, inflammation or fibrosis. PAS stain is strongly positive and diastase digestion removes the material. The differentials include glycogen storage diseases (childhood onset, enzyme defects), MASLD and MASH (fat, ballooning, fibrosis) and hepatic oedema or hydropic change. Recognition is important because the condition resolves with improved glycaemic control.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Aspirates, if done, would show pale, swollen hepatocytes with glycogen, but the diagnosis is made on core biopsy in a patient with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. PAS with and without diastase confirms abundant hepatocyte glycogen, trichrome shows the absence of significant fibrosis, and the main differential, steatohepatitis or glycogen storage disease, is excluded by the clinical setting and the lack of fat, ballooning and Mallory-Denk bodies.

entities.variants: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP; FECH) with protoporphyrin hepatopathy and cirrhosis; X-linked protoporphyria; porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT; UROD; with iron, HCV, alcohol); acute hepatic porphyrias (acute intermittent porphyria; HCC risk)
entities.remarks: EPP: dark brown protoporphyrin deposits in canaliculi, hepatocytes and Kupffer cells with red-orange birefringence and Maltese cross under polarised light, may progress to cirrhosis; PCT: needle-like uroporphyrin crystals (birefringent, best in unstained sections), iron overload, steatosis; acute porphyrias carry HCC risk.
entities.histo: Porphyrias are inherited or acquired disorders of haem biosynthesis, and several have important liver pathology. Erythropoietic protoporphyria causes accumulation of protoporphyrin that is excreted through bile; in a minority, deposits of dark brown pigment form in canaliculi, bile ducts, hepatocytes and Kupffer cells, causing cholestasis, portal fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis and liver failure. Under polarised light the deposits show red-orange birefringence, often with a Maltese cross pattern. Porphyria cutanea tarda, the commonest porphyria, is caused by reduced uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity, frequently triggered by iron overload, alcohol, oestrogens or hepatitis C. The liver shows siderosis, steatosis, chronic hepatitis features and needle-shaped uroporphyrin crystals in hepatocytes, which are best seen in unstained or lightly stained sections, and fluoresce red under ultraviolet light. Acute hepatic porphyrias, such as acute intermittent porphyria, usually show non-specific histology but carry an increased risk of HCC. The differentials include other pigments (bile, lipofuscin, Dubin-Johnson pigment, haemosiderin) and other causes of iron overload.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in porphyrias. Diagnosis is biochemical (urine, stool and blood porphyrins) and genetic, and liver tissue shows the features described under histology, including red fluorescence of fresh tissue in some types.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role; diagnosis relies on biochemical porphyrin profiles, polarisation microscopy and fluorescence of unstained sections, Perls stain for iron in PCT, and genetic testing.

entities.variants: Type 1 (non-neuronopathic, commonest); type 2 (acute neuronopathic); type 3 (chronic neuronopathic, including Norrbottnian); perinatal lethal form
entities.remarks: GBA1 deficiency of glucocerebrosidase; Kupffer cells and portal macrophages stuffed with glucocerebroside: Gaucher cells with abundant 'crumpled tissue paper' or wrinkled silk cytoplasm (PAS positive, diastase resistant); sinusoidal and portal fibrosis; enzyme replacement therapy.
entities.histo: Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of glucocerebrosidase, leading to accumulation of glucosylceramide in macrophages throughout the reticuloendothelial system. The liver is enlarged, and Kupffer cells and portal macrophages are replaced by large Gaucher cells, measuring up to 100 micrometres, with small eccentric nuclei and abundant pale, striated cytoplasm with a characteristic wrinkled tissue paper or crumpled silk appearance. Gaucher cells form clusters in sinusoids and expand portal tracts, and they are PAS positive and diastase resistant, weakly iron positive, and stain blue with trichrome. Pericellular and portal fibrosis can develop, occasionally progressing to cirrhosis and portal hypertension, and there is an increased risk of HCC and haematological malignancies. Hepatocytes themselves are not involved. The differentials include pseudo-Gaucher cells in chronic myeloid leukaemia, myeloma and mycobacterial infection (particularly Mycobacterium avium complex in AIDS, which are acid-fast positive), Niemann-Pick disease (foamy, vacuolated macrophages), and other storage disorders.
entities.cyto: Gaucher cells may occasionally be seen in aspirates as large histiocytes with abundant striated cytoplasm; bone marrow aspirates are more commonly used. Enzyme assays and genetic testing confirm the diagnosis.
entities.ihc: Gaucher cells are CD68 and CD163 positive histiocytes, and they are acid-fast negative, which separates them from mycobacteria-laden pseudo-Gaucher cells. IHC is not diagnostic in itself; enzyme assay and GBA1 sequencing are definitive.

entities.variants: Acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (ASMD; Niemann-Pick types A and B, SMPD1); Niemann-Pick type C (NPC1, NPC2; neonatal cholestasis, neurological disease)
entities.remarks: Foamy (vacuolated) Kupffer cells and hepatocytes containing sphingomyelin or cholesterol; sea-blue histiocytes; type C a cause of neonatal cholestasis with giant cell hepatitis and foam cells; cirrhosis in some.
entities.histo: Niemann-Pick disease comprises two groups of autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorders. Acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (types A and B) causes accumulation of sphingomyelin in macrophages and hepatocytes, while type C results from defects in intracellular cholesterol trafficking (NPC1, NPC2). The liver shows enlarged, pale foamy Kupffer cells and portal macrophages, with finely vacuolated cytoplasm (foam cells), and similarly vacuolated hepatocytes, particularly in type A and B disease. Lipid in the foam cells is PAS weakly positive, Sudan black positive and may appear blue-green on Giemsa as sea-blue histiocytes. Type B can progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis in adults. Type C presents in infancy with neonatal cholestasis, giant cell hepatitis and foamy macrophages, and in later childhood with progressive neurological disease; liver failure occurs in some neonates. The differentials include Gaucher disease (striated, not foamy cytoplasm), lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (cholesterol ester crystals), Wolman disease, mucopolysaccharidoses, and foamy macrophages from drugs such as amiodarone.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in liver diagnosis; bone marrow aspirates may show foam cells and sea-blue histiocytes.
entities.ihc: Foam cells are CD68 and CD163 positive histiocytes. Filipin staining of fibroblasts (type C), enzyme assays, oxysterol and lysosphingolipid biomarkers and genetic testing establish the diagnosis; IHC is not diagnostic.

entities.entity: Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (Wolman disease and cholesteryl ester storage disease)
entities.variants: Infantile-onset Wolman disease (rapidly fatal, adrenal calcification); later-onset cholesteryl ester storage disease (CESD; hepatomegaly, dyslipidaemia, fibrosis, cirrhosis)
entities.remarks: LIPA mutation; diffuse microvesicular steatosis of hepatocytes and foamy Kupffer cells containing birefringent cholesteryl ester crystals; frequently misdiagnosed as MASLD or cryptogenic cirrhosis; enzyme replacement (sebelipase alfa).
entities.histo: Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by LIPA mutations, leading to accumulation of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides in lysosomes. Infantile Wolman disease presents with vomiting, diarrhoea, hepatosplenomegaly and adrenal calcification, and is fatal in early infancy without treatment. Cholesteryl ester storage disease presents later in childhood or adulthood with hepatomegaly, raised transaminases and dyslipidaemia. The liver is enlarged and bright yellow-orange. Microscopically, hepatocytes are diffusely filled with fine microvesicular fat, often accompanied by enlarged foamy Kupffer cells and portal macrophages, which contain birefringent cholesterol ester crystals visible under polarised light in frozen or unstained sections. Fibrosis can progress to micronodular cirrhosis. The condition is often misdiagnosed as MASLD or cryptogenic cirrhosis, and the clue is diffuse microvesicular steatosis with foamy macrophages in a young patient with dyslipidaemia. The diagnosis is confirmed by enzyme assay in dried blood spots and genetic testing, which matters because enzyme replacement therapy is available.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Diagnosis is confirmed by dried blood spot lysosomal acid lipase enzyme assay and LIPA genetic testing, while biopsy shows microvesicular steatosis with cholesterol ester crystals.
entities.ihc: Lysosomal markers such as LAMP-2 or cathepsin D highlight lysosomes rimming lipid vacuoles, a pattern that is suggestive in some studies. Foamy macrophages are CD68 positive. Enzyme assay and genetic testing are definitive.

entities.entity: Other lysosomal storage disorders with liver involvement (mucopolysaccharidoses, GM1 gangliosidosis, Fabry, cystinosis, Farber, oligosaccharidoses)
entities.variants: Mucopolysaccharidoses (Hurler, Hunter, Sanfilippo, Morquio, Sly); GM1 and GM2 gangliosidosis; Fabry disease; cystinosis; Farber disease; alpha-mannosidosis and fucosidosis; sialidosis; Wolman (see LAL deficiency)
entities.remarks: Rare; vacuolated (clear, foamy or ballooned) hepatocytes and Kupffer cells; storage material identification by special stains, electron microscopy (zebra bodies, membranous inclusions), enzyme assays and genetic testing; cystinosis shows birefringent cystine crystals in Kupffer cells.
entities.histo: Several other lysosomal storage disorders involve the liver, usually as part of a multisystem disease presenting in childhood. In the mucopolysaccharidoses, hepatocytes and Kupffer cells are enlarged with pale, clear or finely vacuolated cytoplasm due to stored glycosaminoglycans, which may be washed out in routine processing, and portal fibrosis may develop. GM1 gangliosidosis and related disorders show foamy Kupffer cells and hepatocytes containing membranous cytoplasmic bodies on electron microscopy. Fabry disease shows vacuolated endothelial and smooth muscle cells, and lamellated zebra bodies are seen ultrastructurally. Cystinosis deposits rectangular or hexagonal birefringent cystine crystals in Kupffer cells and portal macrophages, best seen in alcohol-fixed tissue under polarised light. Farber disease and oligosaccharidoses (alpha-mannosidosis, fucosidosis, sialidosis) show vacuolated macrophages and hepatocytes. The differentials include Niemann-Pick, Gaucher and LAL deficiency, drug-induced phospholipidosis (amiodarone), and glycogen storage disease. Electron microscopy, enzyme assays and genetic testing are the key to definitive diagnosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the liver; vacuolated lymphocytes on peripheral blood smears and bone marrow foam cells can provide clues.
entities.ihc: IHC has a minor role; CD68 highlights storage macrophages and LAMP-1 or LAMP-2 highlights lysosomes. Diagnosis relies on biochemical and genetic testing.

entities.variants: Acute infantile form (liver failure); chronic form (cirrhosis, renal Fanconi syndrome, rickets); treated tyrosinaemia (nitisinone)
entities.remarks: FAH deficiency with toxic fumarylacetoacetate and succinylacetone; neonatal hepatitis-like pattern with steatosis, giant cells, iron, pseudoacinar transformation, progressing to macronodular or mixed cirrhosis with dysplastic nodules; very high HCC risk (reduced by nitisinone).
entities.histo: Hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1 is an autosomal recessive defect of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, the last enzyme of tyrosine breakdown, which leads to accumulation of toxic metabolites in the liver and kidney. The acute form presents in infancy with liver failure and coagulopathy, and the chronic form with cirrhosis, renal Fanconi syndrome and rickets in later infancy or childhood. Liver biopsy in infancy shows a neonatal hepatitis-like pattern with steatosis, cholestasis, giant cell transformation, pseudoacinar transformation of hepatocytes, iron deposition and progressive fibrosis. Later there is a mixed micronodular and macronodular cirrhosis, often with nodules of varying appearance including large cell change and dysplastic nodules. The risk of hepatocellular carcinoma is extremely high in untreated patients, even in childhood, and treatment with nitisinone and dietary restriction lowers but does not eliminate it, so surveillance with alpha-fetoprotein and imaging is essential. The differentials include other metabolic and infectious causes of neonatal liver failure, GALD and galactosaemia, and the diagnosis is made by succinylacetone in urine or blood.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in diagnosis; FNA may be used for nodules in surveillance, where well-differentiated HCC is difficult to separate from dysplastic nodules on cytology.
entities.ihc: IHC is used for nodules: glypican-3, HSP70 and glutamine synthetase identify HCC, CD34 shows sinusoidal capillarisation, and AFP may be positive. FAH immunostaining can show absent enzyme in hepatocytes and, interestingly, revertant FAH-positive nodules in some livers.

entities.entity: Galactosaemia, hereditary fructose intolerance and urea cycle disorders
entities.variants: Classic galactosaemia (GALT); hereditary fructose intolerance (ALDOB); urea cycle disorders (OTC deficiency, citrullinaemia type II/citrin deficiency with neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis, argininosuccinic aciduria); organic acidaemias
entities.remarks: Neonatal or infantile liver disease with steatosis, cholestasis, pseudoacinar transformation and fibrosis (galactosaemia, HFI); citrin deficiency causes neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis with marked steatosis; diagnosis is biochemical and genetic; dietary treatment.
entities.histo: Several inherited metabolic disorders produce liver disease in infancy that is usually diagnosed biochemically, but biopsy may be performed in unexplained neonatal cholestasis or liver failure. Classic galactosaemia, due to galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency, presents after starting milk feeds with jaundice, vomiting, cataracts and E. coli sepsis; the liver shows macrovesicular and microvesicular steatosis, cholestasis, pseudoacinar (rosette) transformation of hepatocytes around bile plugs, giant cells and progressive fibrosis leading to cirrhosis. Hereditary fructose intolerance, due to aldolase B deficiency, produces a similar pattern when fructose or sucrose is introduced. Citrin deficiency (citrullinaemia type II), particularly common in East Asia, causes neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis with prominent steatosis and fibrosis, and other urea cycle disorders and organic acidaemias may show only mild steatosis or glycogen change, with hyperammonaemia dominating the clinical picture. The histological changes are not specific, and the differentials include other causes of neonatal hepatitis, tyrosinaemia and mitochondrial disorders.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. These disorders are diagnosed by newborn screening, enzyme assays, metabolite analysis and genetic testing, and liver biopsy is rarely needed.
entities.ihc: IHC has no role in diagnosis; biochemical assays (enzyme activity, plasma amino acids, urine organic acids) and genetic testing are definitive.

entities.variants: Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes (DGUOK, MPV17 including Navajo neurohepatopathy, POLG including Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome, TWINKLE); respiratory chain defects; fatty acid oxidation defects (LCHAD, MCAD, CPT deficiencies); valproate-triggered POLG liver failure
entities.remarks: Infantile or childhood liver failure with microvesicular steatosis, cholestasis, oncocytic hepatocytes and fibrosis; Navajo neurohepatopathy (MPV17) in Navajo children with neuropathy and liver disease; POLG patients risk fatal valproate hepatotoxicity; diagnosis by genetics and respiratory chain studies.
entities.histo: Mitochondrial hepatopathies are inherited disorders of mitochondrial DNA maintenance, respiratory chain function or fatty acid oxidation that cause liver disease, often with neurological and muscle involvement. Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes due to DGUOK, MPV17, POLG and other genes present in infancy or childhood with liver failure, lactic acidosis and hypoglycaemia. Navajo neurohepatopathy, caused by an MPV17 mutation in Navajo children, combines sensorimotor neuropathy, corneal ulceration and progressive liver disease. Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome (POLG) causes refractory seizures and liver failure, which can be precipitated by sodium valproate. Liver biopsies show microvesicular and macrovesicular steatosis, canalicular cholestasis, hepatocyte oncocytic change (granular eosinophilic cytoplasm packed with mitochondria), ductular reaction, iron deposition and progressive fibrosis or micronodular cirrhosis; electron microscopy shows abnormal, swollen or pleomorphic mitochondria. Fatty acid oxidation defects show microvesicular steatosis with episodic decompensation. The differentials include Reye syndrome, drug-induced microvesicular steatosis, tyrosinaemia, GALD and other causes of neonatal liver failure.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Diagnosis relies on metabolic studies, respiratory chain enzyme analysis on frozen liver or muscle tissue, mitochondrial DNA depletion studies and genetic testing.
entities.ihc: IHC for respiratory chain complexes (for example COX, complex I and complex IV subunits) can show deficient staining in hepatocytes, and enzyme histochemistry (COX, SDH) on frozen tissue is used in specialist centres. Genetic testing and mitochondrial DNA quantification establish the diagnosis.

entities.variants: Focal biliary cirrhosis (inspissated eosinophilic secretions in ductules); multilobular biliary cirrhosis; steatosis; neonatal cholestasis; microgallbladder and gallstones; non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (obliterative portal venopathy)
entities.remarks: CFTR dysfunction in cholangiocytes causes thick bile; pathognomonic focal biliary cirrhosis with ductules plugged by PAS-positive eosinophilic concretions; steatosis common; portal hypertension may occur without cirrhosis.
entities.histo: Liver disease is a frequent complication of cystic fibrosis, resulting from defective CFTR chloride channel function in cholangiocytes, which produces thick, viscous bile that obstructs small ducts. The pathognomonic lesion is focal biliary cirrhosis, in which scattered portal areas show ductular reaction with ductules plugged by inspissated, eosinophilic, PAS-positive concretions, with chronic inflammation and focal portal fibrosis. These foci may coalesce into multilobular biliary cirrhosis with irregular nodules and portal hypertension. Macrovesicular steatosis is common and probably related to malnutrition and other factors. Neonates may present with prolonged cholestasis and meconium ileus. A subset of patients develops non-cirrhotic portal hypertension with obliterative portal venopathy and nodular regenerative hyperplasia. The differentials include other causes of biliary obstruction, PSC (also seen in CF patients), biliary atresia in infants and MASLD.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in cystic fibrosis liver disease, which is assessed by imaging, elastography and occasionally biopsy, and the patchy focal biliary cirrhosis can be missed by sampling.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 highlight the ductular reaction, and PAS-D shows the eosinophilic ductular concretions. IHC is otherwise not diagnostic.

entities.variants: Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (AGXT; most common, severe); type 2 (GRHPR); type 3 (HOGA1); systemic oxalosis
entities.remarks: Liver enzyme defect; the liver is histologically normal or near normal but is the source of oxalate; systemic oxalosis deposits birefringent calcium oxalate crystals in kidney, vessels and bone; combined liver-kidney transplant is curative for type 1; explanted livers serve as donor livers in domino transplants.
entities.histo: Primary hyperoxaluria is a group of autosomal recessive disorders of glyoxylate metabolism in which a hepatic enzyme defect causes excessive oxalate production, leading to nephrocalcinosis, recurrent stones and renal failure, followed by systemic oxalosis. Type 1, due to deficiency of the peroxisomal enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGXT), is the commonest and most severe. Although the defect lies in the liver, the hepatic histology is usually normal or shows only mild non-specific changes; calcium oxalate crystals are rarely seen in the liver, apart from deposits in portal vessel walls in advanced systemic oxalosis. Pathologists most often encounter the condition in explanted livers removed during combined liver-kidney transplantation, and in kidney biopsies showing abundant birefringent, fan-shaped or rhomboid calcium oxalate crystals. The differentials for oxalate deposition include secondary hyperoxaluria (enteric, ethylene glycol poisoning). Diagnosis relies on urinary oxalate measurement and genetic testing.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Diagnosis rests on urine oxalate and glycolate measurement and AGXT, GRHPR or HOGA1 genetic testing, while the liver itself is histologically normal.
entities.ihc: AGXT immunostaining can show absent or mislocalised enzyme in hepatocytes in some type 1 cases, but genetic testing is the standard diagnostic method. Polarised light microscopy identifies calcium oxalate crystals in tissues.

entities.entity: Hepatic amyloidosis (and light chain deposition disease)
entities.variants: AL (light chain) amyloidosis; AA (secondary) amyloidosis; ATTR (hereditary and wild-type) amyloidosis; ALECT2 amyloidosis (common hepatic finding in some ethnic groups); sinusoidal (perisinusoidal) pattern; vascular pattern; globular amyloid; light chain deposition disease (non-amyloid, Congo red negative)
entities.remarks: Amorphous eosinophilic extracellular deposits in the space of Disse (sinusoidal pattern) or vessel walls; Congo red apple-green birefringence; marked hepatomegaly with raised ALP; typing by mass spectrometry or IHC; risk of rupture and bleeding after biopsy.
entities.histo: Hepatic amyloidosis is the deposition of misfolded proteins as extracellular fibrils in the liver, usually as part of systemic AL (light chain) or AA (inflammation-related) amyloidosis, and less commonly ATTR or ALECT2 types. The liver is enlarged, firm and waxy, and patients typically have hepatomegaly with a disproportionate rise in alkaline phosphatase. Microscopically, amorphous, pale eosinophilic, glassy deposits fill the space of Disse in a sinusoidal pattern, compressing hepatocyte plates, which become atrophic, or are restricted to the walls of portal vessels in a vascular pattern, which is more typical of AA and ATTR amyloid. A globular pattern, with round globules in sinusoids, is associated with AL amyloid, and ALECT2 amyloid is often globular or perisinusoidal. Congo red stain shows salmon pink deposits with apple-green birefringence under polarised light, and Thioflavin T fluorescence is an alternative. Light chain deposition disease shows similar perisinusoidal deposits that are Congo red negative and composed of non-fibrillary light chains, usually kappa. The differentials include perisinusoidal collagen fibrosis (trichrome blue), hyaline change, fibrinogen deposits and light chain cast-like deposits. Biopsy carries an increased risk of bleeding, and typing by laser microdissection mass spectrometry is the gold standard.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in hepatic amyloidosis; abdominal fat pad aspiration with Congo red staining is a useful minimally invasive diagnostic test for systemic amyloidosis.
entities.ihc: Immunohistochemistry or immunofluorescence for kappa and lambda light chains, serum amyloid A, transthyretin and LECT2 can type the amyloid, though light chain staining may be unreliable because of background serum proteins; mass spectrometry is preferred. SAA positivity indicates AA amyloid, and kappa light chain staining with Congo red negativity supports light chain deposition disease.

entities.entity: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) - steatosis (MASL)
entities.variants: Simple steatosis (MASL; formerly NAFL/NAFLD); macrovesicular (large and small droplet) steatosis; zone 3, zone 1 (paediatric, azonal) patterns; MetALD (MASLD with moderate alcohol intake); lean MASLD; steatosis grade 1-3 (5-33%, 34-66%, over 66%)
entities.remarks: Commonest chronic liver disease worldwide and in India; 2023 nomenclature (MASLD/MASH replaces NAFLD/NASH, requires cardiometabolic risk factor); steatosis over 5% of hepatocytes without ballooning; report grade and fibrosis; MASL has low progression risk.
entities.histo: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease is the umbrella term, introduced in 2023, for hepatic steatosis in a patient with at least one cardiometabolic risk factor such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia or hypertension, replacing the earlier term non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver (MASL), previously called simple steatosis or NAFL, is the non-progressive or slowly progressive end of the spectrum. Histologically it shows macrovesicular steatosis, with single large fat droplets displacing the nucleus or small droplets of varying size, affecting more than 5% of hepatocytes, often in zone 3 in adults and in zone 1 or azonal patterns in children. There may be mild lobular inflammation, lipogranulomas and glycogenated nuclei, but ballooning, which defines steatohepatitis, is absent. Steatosis is graded as mild (5 to 33%), moderate (34 to 66%) or severe (over 66%) and fibrosis is staged (Kleiner/NASH CRN stages 0 to 4) using Masson trichrome. MetALD describes patients with MASLD who also drink moderate amounts of alcohol. The differentials include alcohol-associated liver disease, drug-induced steatosis (steroids, methotrexate, tamoxifen, amiodarone), hepatitis C genotype 3, Wilson disease, nutritional causes (malnutrition, rapid weight loss, TPN), lipodystrophies and inherited metabolic diseases such as LAL deficiency.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in diagnosing steatosis. FNA of focal lesions in steatotic livers may yield hepatocytes with clear lipid vacuoles, and steatotic tumour cells in steatohepatitic HCC or adenoma should not be confused with benign fatty liver.
entities.ihc: IHC is not required for diagnosis. Keratin 8/18 loss and ubiquitin or p62 staining can highlight ballooned cells when separating MASL from MASH in research and difficult cases, and CK7 shows ductular reaction associated with fibrosis.

entities.variants: Adult (zone 3, type 1) steatohepatitis; paediatric (zone 1, type 2, portal-predominant) pattern; borderline steatohepatitis; MASH with fibrosis (stages 1a-c, 2, 3, 4); burnt-out MASH cirrhosis (cryptogenic cirrhosis); chemotherapy-associated steatohepatitis (irinotecan, CASH); MASH-related HCC
entities.remarks: Steatosis plus lobular inflammation plus hepatocyte ballooning (with or without Mallory-Denk bodies) and characteristic zone 3 pericellular/perisinusoidal (chicken-wire) fibrosis; scored with NAS (NAFLD activity score, 0-8) and SAF score; fibrosis stage is the main prognostic factor; HCC can arise without cirrhosis.
entities.histo: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, previously non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, is the progressive form of MASLD. The diagnosis requires a combination of macrovesicular steatosis, lobular inflammation and hepatocyte ballooning, typically centred on zone 3 in adults. Ballooned hepatocytes are enlarged and rounded with rarefied, wispy cytoplasm and often contain Mallory-Denk bodies, ropy eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions of aggregated keratin. Other features include acidophil bodies, glycogenated nuclei, megamitochondria, lipogranulomas and mild portal inflammation. The characteristic fibrosis begins as delicate perisinusoidal and pericellular collagen around zone 3 hepatocytes (chicken-wire pattern), then extends to periportal fibrosis, bridging fibrosis and cirrhosis, best shown with Masson trichrome. In children, a type 2 pattern is common, with zone 1 steatosis, portal inflammation and portal fibrosis, often without ballooning. In established cirrhosis, steatosis and ballooning may disappear (burnt-out MASH), which is a common cause of cryptogenic cirrhosis. The NASH CRN activity score (steatosis 0 to 3, lobular inflammation 0 to 3, ballooning 0 to 2) and fibrosis stage (0 to 4, with subdivided stage 1), and the European SAF score, are used in clinical trials and practice. Chemotherapy-associated steatohepatitis (mainly irinotecan) has a similar appearance. HCC can arise in MASH even without cirrhosis. The differentials include alcohol-associated steatohepatitis (more neutrophils, Mallory-Denk bodies, sclerosing hyaline necrosis, cholestasis), drug-induced steatohepatitis (amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen), Wilson disease and MASH with overlapping autoimmune hepatitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in diagnosing MASH. In FNA of nodules in MASH livers, background steatotic hepatocytes and Mallory-Denk bodies should not be confused with steatohepatitic HCC, which shows atypia, trabecular thickening and naked atypical nuclei.
entities.ihc: Keratin 8/18 immunostaining shows loss of staining in ballooned hepatocytes, and ubiquitin or p62 highlights Mallory-Denk bodies, which can help identify subtle ballooning. CK7 shows ductular reaction, which correlates with fibrosis, and CD34 may show sinusoidal capillarisation in advanced fibrosis. In nodules, glypican-3, HSP70 and glutamine synthetase help separate steatohepatitic HCC from regenerative nodules.

entities.variants: Alcoholic steatosis (fatty liver); alcoholic steatohepatitis and severe alcoholic hepatitis (clinical syndrome); alcoholic foamy degeneration (microvesicular); sclerosing hyaline necrosis; acute cholestasis of alcoholic hepatitis; alcohol-related cirrhosis (micronodular, Laennec); MetALD; Zieve syndrome
entities.remarks: Spectrum from steatosis to steatohepatitis to cirrhosis; alcoholic hepatitis: ballooning, numerous Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophil satellitosis, cholestasis, zone 3 pericellular fibrosis, perivenular fibrosis and phlebosclerosis; histological prognostic scores (AHHS); HCC risk in cirrhosis.
entities.histo: Alcohol-associated liver disease covers a spectrum of injury caused by heavy alcohol use, including steatosis, steatohepatitis and cirrhosis, which may coexist. Alcoholic steatosis is macrovesicular, mainly zone 3, and resolves with abstinence. Alcoholic foamy degeneration is a rarer form with extensive microvesicular steatosis in zone 3 and cholestasis, presenting with jaundice. Alcoholic steatohepatitis shows hepatocyte ballooning, abundant Mallory-Denk bodies, lobular inflammation with neutrophils that surround hepatocytes containing Mallory-Denk bodies (satellitosis), apoptotic bodies, megamitochondria and canalicular or ductular cholestasis, with zone 3 pericellular fibrosis. Sclerosing hyaline necrosis is a severe form with extensive zone 3 fibrosis obliterating central veins (phlebosclerosis), causing portal hypertension even without cirrhosis. Cirrhosis is classically micronodular but becomes mixed with abstinence. Clinically severe alcoholic hepatitis is associated with marked ductular reaction, cholestasis (especially ductular bilirubinostasis), neutrophilic infiltration and fibrosis, and these features form the Alcoholic Hepatitis Histological Score (AHHS), which predicts survival. Iron deposition may be present. The differentials include MASH (milder, fewer neutrophils, less cholestasis), drug-induced steatohepatitis (amiodarone), Wilson disease, Indian childhood cirrhosis, and MetALD where both alcohol and metabolic factors contribute.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in diagnosing alcohol-associated liver disease. FNA of nodules in alcohol-related cirrhosis may show reactive hepatocytes, Mallory-Denk bodies and large cell change, which should not be overinterpreted as HCC.
entities.ihc: Ubiquitin and p62 immunostaining highlight Mallory-Denk bodies, and keratin 8/18 loss marks ballooned hepatocytes. CK7 shows the ductular reaction, which correlates with clinical severity, and CD34 may demonstrate sinusoidal capillarisation in advanced disease. HCC markers (glypican-3, HSP70, glutamine synthetase) are used in nodules.

entities.variants: Classic Reye syndrome (aspirin with viral infection in children); Reye-like syndromes (fatty acid oxidation and urea cycle defects); drug-induced microvesicular steatosis (valproate, tetracycline, salicylates, nucleoside analogues, amiodarone); alcoholic foamy degeneration; acute fatty liver of pregnancy (see pregnancy); Jamaican vomiting sickness (ackee fruit)
entities.remarks: Acute encephalopathy with liver dysfunction after viral infection and aspirin; panlobular microvesicular steatosis (foamy hepatocytes with central nuclei) without inflammation or necrosis; mitochondrial injury; oil red O on frozen tissue.
entities.histo: Reye syndrome is an acute, often fatal illness of children characterised by encephalopathy and liver dysfunction following a viral infection, strongly associated with aspirin use, and it has become very rare since aspirin was avoided in children. It is the prototype of the microvesicular steatosis pattern, a form of injury reflecting mitochondrial dysfunction. Hepatocytes throughout the lobule are swollen and filled with innumerable tiny fat droplets that give a foamy appearance while the nucleus remains central, and there is little or no inflammation or necrosis. The fat may be inconspicuous on H&E and is best shown by oil red O or Sudan black on frozen sections, while electron microscopy reveals swollen, pleomorphic mitochondria with loss of cristae. The same pattern occurs in inherited fatty acid oxidation and urea cycle defects (Reye-like syndromes), drug toxicity (valproate, tetracycline, salicylates, nucleoside analogues, amiodarone), alcoholic foamy degeneration, acute fatty liver of pregnancy, and toxins such as hypoglycin from unripe ackee fruit. The differentials include glycogen accumulation (PAS positive, no fat stain), hydropic swelling and small droplet macrovesicular steatosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Microvesicular fat is best shown on frozen sections stained with oil red O, and electron microscopy demonstrates the mitochondrial changes.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used; oil red O on frozen tissue confirms microvesicular fat, and metabolic testing and electron microscopy help identify the cause.

entities.entity: Focal fatty change and focal fatty sparing
entities.variants: Focal fatty change (focal steatosis, pseudotumour); multifocal nodular steatosis; perivascular and subcapsular steatosis (insulin-dialysis related); focal fatty sparing in a diffusely fatty liver (gallbladder fossa, segment IV, near hilum)
entities.remarks: Imaging pseudotumours caused by altered regional blood supply (aberrant venous drainage); geographic area of macrovesicular steatosis with preserved architecture; biopsy needed only when imaging is atypical; must be separated from steatotic tumours (adenoma, steatohepatitic HCC, angiomyolipoma).
entities.histo: Focal fatty change is a localised area of hepatic steatosis that can resemble a mass on imaging, while focal fatty sparing is a localised area of normal liver within a diffusely fatty liver, which can also simulate a lesion. Both are often caused by altered regional blood flow, such as aberrant gastric venous drainage, and typically occur near the falciform ligament, gallbladder fossa or porta hepatis. Subcapsular steatosis may follow intraperitoneal insulin administration in diabetic patients on peritoneal dialysis. Biopsy is required only when imaging is atypical, and it shows a geographic area of macrovesicular steatosis with preserved lobular architecture, normal portal tracts and central veins, and no atypia, or alternatively a non-fatty area in a steatotic background. There is no capsule, pseudocapsule, unpaired arteries or loss of reticulin. The differentials include steatotic hepatocellular adenoma (especially HNF1A-inactivated, which lacks portal tracts), steatohepatitic HCC (atypia, reticulin loss, glypican-3), angiomyolipoma (fat with epithelioid myoid cells and thick vessels, HMB45 positive), lipoma and liposarcoma, and metastases on imaging.
entities.cyto: FNA yields benign hepatocytes with macrovesicular fat and bile duct cells; this is not specific, so correlation with imaging and, if doubtful, core biopsy with reticulin and immunostains is needed to exclude a steatotic neoplasm.
entities.ihc: IHC confirms benign hepatocytes: LFABP retained (unlike HNF1A-inactivated adenoma), glutamine synthetase in a normal perivenular pattern, glypican-3 negative, CD34 limited to periportal sinusoids, and HMB45 and Melan-A negative (excluding angiomyolipoma). Reticulin shows intact plates.

entities.entity: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) - general and patterns
entities.variants: Acute hepatitic pattern; chronic hepatitic pattern; cholestatic (bland) pattern; cholestatic hepatitis (mixed); granulomatous hepatitis; zonal (centrilobular) necrosis; massive necrosis; macrovesicular steatosis; microvesicular steatosis; steatohepatitis; vanishing bile duct syndrome; vascular injury (SOS, NRH, peliosis, Budd-Chiari); neoplasms (adenoma, angiosarcoma); intrinsic (dose-dependent) and idiosyncratic DILI; DRESS-associated hepatitis
entities.remarks: Common cause of acute liver injury; anti-tubercular drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide) the leading cause in India; also antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate), anticonvulsants, NSAIDs, herbals; RUCAM causality scoring and R ratio; pathologist describes the pattern and severity, and supports causality; eosinophils and granulomas favour drug cause.
entities.histo: Drug-induced liver injury can mimic almost any primary liver disease, so the pathologist's main contributions are to define the pattern of injury, assess its severity and chronicity, and indicate whether the findings fit the suspected drug. Intrinsic (dose-dependent) injury, such as paracetamol toxicity, typically produces zonal necrosis, whereas idiosyncratic injury produces hepatitic, cholestatic or mixed patterns. The acute hepatitic pattern shows lobular disarray, acidophil bodies, spotty or confluent necrosis and portal inflammation, often with eosinophils, and is caused for example by isoniazid, the commonest cause of DILI in India in combination with rifampicin and pyrazinamide. Bland cholestasis, typical of anabolic steroids and oral contraceptives, shows zone 3 canalicular bile plugs without inflammation. Cholestatic hepatitis, seen with amoxicillin-clavulanate, macrolides and chlorpromazine, combines cholestasis with hepatitis and bile duct injury. Other patterns include granulomatous hepatitis (allopurinol, sulfonamides, carbamazepine), macrovesicular steatosis (steroids, methotrexate), microvesicular steatosis (valproate, tetracycline), steatohepatitis (amiodarone, tamoxifen), vanishing bile duct syndrome, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (oxaliplatin, pyrrolizidine alkaloids), nodular regenerative hyperplasia (azathioprine, oxaliplatin), peliosis hepatis (anabolic steroids) and neoplasms. Features favouring a drug cause include eosinophils, granulomas, zone 3 necrosis, bile duct injury disproportionate to the hepatitis, and a mixed hepatitic-cholestatic picture. A careful drug and herbal history, causality scoring and the course after withdrawal of the drug are essential, as histology alone cannot prove causation. LiverTox and similar databases describe expected patterns for individual agents.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in DILI. The pattern of injury needs a core biopsy, and the diagnosis rests on clinicopathological correlation, timing of drug exposure and causality scoring such as RUCAM.
entities.ihc: IHC is supportive only: CD138 or MUM1 for plasma cells when autoimmune-like DILI is suspected, CK7 and CK19 to evaluate bile duct injury and loss, and viral stains (HBsAg, HBcAg, CMV, HSV, adenovirus) to exclude infection. Ubiquitin or p62 highlights Mallory-Denk bodies in drug-induced steatohepatitis.

entities.variants: Intentional overdose; therapeutic misadventure (staggered overdose, alcohol, fasting, CYP2E1 inducers); acute liver failure; recovery phase
entities.remarks: Commonest cause of acute liver failure in the West; NAPQI-mediated, dose-dependent zone 3 (centrilobular) coagulative necrosis with minimal inflammation, sharp demarcation, microvesicular steatosis at the edge; very high transaminases; N-acetylcysteine antidote; liver regenerates without fibrosis if the patient survives.
entities.histo: Paracetamol is a dose-dependent hepatotoxin, and overdose, either intentional or through unintentional excess use, is the commonest cause of acute liver failure in many Western countries. The drug is metabolised by CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which is detoxified by glutathione; when glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds to cellular proteins and causes necrosis of zone 3 hepatocytes, where CYP2E1 is concentrated. The liver shows sharply demarcated centrilobular coagulative necrosis, with hypereosinophilic hepatocytes or loss of hepatocytes, haemorrhage, and minimal inflammation, extending to zone 2 or causing massive necrosis in severe cases. Hepatocytes at the edge of the necrotic zone may show microvesicular steatosis. Portal tracts are usually spared. The risk is increased by chronic alcohol use, fasting and enzyme-inducing drugs. If the patient survives, the liver regenerates completely without fibrosis. The differentials include ischaemic (hypoxic) hepatitis, which shows a similar zone 3 necrosis, other toxins (CCl4, halothane), HSV hepatitis (non-zonal) and acute autoimmune hepatitis with centrilobular necrosis (plasma cells).
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Diagnosis rests on the history of ingestion and serum paracetamol levels, and biopsy, when done, shows zone 3 coagulative necrosis.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed; protein adducts of paracetamol can be detected in serum in research settings. Viral stains help exclude HSV or adenovirus when necrosis is extensive.

entities.variants: Asymptomatic transaminase elevation; amiodarone steatohepatitis (pseudoalcoholic); phospholipidosis; cirrhosis; acute hepatitis with intravenous amiodarone
entities.remarks: Lysosomal phospholipidosis (foamy Kupffer cells and hepatocytes; lamellar inclusions on EM) and alcohol-like steatohepatitis with Mallory-Denk bodies and neutrophils; liver appears dense on CT due to iodine; long half-life.
entities.histo: Amiodarone, an iodinated antiarrhythmic drug, causes a range of liver injury, from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to steatohepatitis and cirrhosis. Its hallmark is drug-induced phospholipidosis, in which amiodarone binds to phospholipids and accumulates within lysosomes, giving Kupffer cells, portal macrophages and hepatocytes a foamy, finely vacuolated cytoplasm. On electron microscopy, the lysosomes contain concentric lamellar (myelin-like) bodies. Prolonged use can cause a steatohepatitis that closely resembles alcoholic hepatitis, with ballooning, numerous Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophilic infiltrates, pericellular fibrosis and occasionally cirrhosis; unlike MASH, macrovesicular steatosis may be minimal. Intravenous amiodarone can cause acute hepatitis or zone 3 necrosis. The liver may appear dense on CT due to its iodine content. The differentials include alcoholic hepatitis, MASH, other causes of phospholipidosis (for example certain antidepressants and antipsychotics), and lysosomal storage disorders.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Biopsy shows phospholipidosis and pseudoalcoholic changes, and CT shows increased liver density due to the iodine content of the drug.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic; ubiquitin or p62 highlight Mallory-Denk bodies, and LAMP-2 can highlight lysosomal accumulation. Electron microscopy confirms lamellar lysosomal inclusions.

entities.variants: Steatosis; steatohepatitis; portal and pericellular fibrosis; cirrhosis; Roenigk grades I, II, IIIA, IIIB, IV
entities.remarks: Chronic low-dose therapy (psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis) causes steatosis, nuclear pleomorphism, portal inflammation and fibrosis; Roenigk classification used to guide therapy; risk higher with alcohol, obesity, diabetes; now largely monitored by non-invasive tests.
entities.histo: Methotrexate, used for psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis and other diseases, can cause chronic liver injury, particularly with long-term use and additional risk factors such as alcohol, obesity and diabetes. The histology includes macrovesicular steatosis, hepatocyte nuclear pleomorphism and enlargement (anisonucleosis), glycogenated nuclei, mild portal inflammation, and progressive portal and pericellular fibrosis, which can lead to cirrhosis, sometimes with little inflammation. Stellate cell hyperplasia may be present. The Roenigk classification grades biopsies from I (normal or mild steatosis) to IV (cirrhosis), with grade IIIB (moderate to severe fibrosis) and IV prompting discontinuation of the drug. The changes overlap considerably with MASLD, which is common in the same patients, and attribution to the drug may be difficult. Biopsy monitoring has largely been replaced by non-invasive fibrosis assessment. The differentials include MASH, alcohol-associated liver disease, and other drug toxicity.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Fibrosis assessment uses elastography and, when needed, core biopsy graded by the Roenigk classification.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. Trichrome and reticulin stains assess fibrosis for Roenigk grading, and CK7 may help to show the ductular reaction that accompanies progressive fibrosis.

entities.variants: Lobular (acute hepatitic) pattern with granulomas (CTLA-4 inhibitors, ipilimumab); hepatitic pattern with CD8 T cells (PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors: nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab); cholangitic pattern (ICI-associated cholangiopathy, sclerosing); mixed pattern
entities.remarks: Immune-related adverse event of cancer immunotherapy; panlobular hepatitis with CD8-dominant lymphocytes and histiocytes, fibrin-ring granulomas (ipilimumab), central vein endotheliitis; fewer plasma cells than AIH; usually steroid-responsive; cholangitic forms less responsive.
entities.histo: Immune checkpoint inhibitors, including anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) and anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 antibodies (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab), can trigger immune-related hepatitis, usually within weeks to months of starting therapy and more often with combination treatment. The commonest pattern is an acute lobular hepatitis with lymphocytes and histiocytes, spotty or confluent necrosis, acidophil bodies and sometimes central vein endotheliitis, with relatively mild portal inflammation. Ipilimumab-associated hepatitis often shows granulomatous hepatitis, including fibrin-ring granulomas and microgranulomas, with zone 3 necrosis. A cholangitic pattern, with bile duct injury, cholangitis and sometimes sclerosing cholangitis-like changes on imaging, is seen more often with PD-1 inhibitors and tends to respond less well to steroids. Compared with autoimmune hepatitis, plasma cells are less prominent and the infiltrate is dominated by CD8 T cells and histiocytes. The differentials include autoimmune hepatitis, other drug injury, viral hepatitis (including HBV reactivation), metastatic tumour and tumour-related biliary obstruction.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Diagnosis relies on the treatment history, exclusion of other causes and core biopsy, which shows lobular hepatitis, granulomas or cholangitis.
entities.ihc: The infiltrate is predominantly CD3-positive and CD8-positive T cells with CD68-positive histiocytes and relatively few CD20-positive B cells and CD138-positive plasma cells, which helps separate it from autoimmune hepatitis. CK7 and CK19 assess bile duct injury in the cholangitic pattern, and viral stains (HBsAg, HBcAg, CMV) exclude infection. Tumour markers may be needed to exclude metastatic infiltration.

entities.variants: Nitrofurantoin; minocycline; statins; methyldopa; hydralazine; anti-TNF agents (infliximab, adalimumab); diclofenac; herbal products; immune checkpoint inhibitors (separate)
entities.remarks: Drug-triggered hepatitis with autoantibodies, raised IgG and plasma cell-rich interface hepatitis indistinguishable from AIH; usually resolves after drug withdrawal and steroids without relapse when steroids are stopped.
entities.histo: Drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis is a form of idiosyncratic drug injury that closely mimics autoimmune hepatitis clinically, serologically and histologically. Patients develop raised transaminases, positive antinuclear or smooth muscle antibodies and elevated IgG after exposure to drugs such as nitrofurantoin, minocycline, statins, methyldopa, hydralazine and anti-TNF biologic agents. The biopsy shows interface hepatitis with plasma cells, lobular inflammation, rosettes and sometimes confluent or bridging necrosis, which may be indistinguishable from autoimmune hepatitis; eosinophils, granulomas, cholestasis or a lack of advanced fibrosis may favour a drug cause. Distinguishing DI-ALH from idiopathic autoimmune hepatitis often depends on the clinical course: most cases resolve after the drug is stopped, sometimes with a short course of corticosteroids, and do not relapse when steroids are withdrawn. The differentials include idiopathic autoimmune hepatitis, viral hepatitis, other DILI patterns and immune checkpoint inhibitor hepatitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Distinguishing DI-ALH from idiopathic AIH depends on drug history, response to stopping the drug and steroid withdrawal, with biopsy showing an AIH-like pattern.
entities.ihc: CD138 or MUM1 highlights plasma cells, but IHC cannot separate DI-ALH from autoimmune hepatitis; viral stains exclude infection. The diagnosis depends on the drug history and outcome.

entities.entity: Herbal and dietary supplement-induced liver injury (including pyrrolizidine alkaloids and anabolic steroids)
entities.variants: Ayurvedic and traditional medicine-associated injury (including heavy metals); green tea extract; Garcinia cambogia; kava; germander; Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera); turmeric/curcumin; pyrrolizidine alkaloid-induced SOS (Gynura, Crotalaria, comfrey, 'bush teas'); anabolic-androgenic steroids (bland cholestasis, peliosis, adenoma, HCC); bodybuilding supplements
entities.remarks: Rising cause of DILI in India and worldwide; patterns are hepatitic, cholestatic, or vascular (SOS from pyrrolizidine alkaloids); anabolic steroids cause bland cholestasis, peliosis, adenoma and HCC; products are often contaminated or adulterated.
entities.histo: Herbal and dietary supplements are an important and increasing cause of liver injury, and in India traditional and complementary medicines contribute substantially to drug-induced liver injury and acute-on-chronic liver failure. The patterns are diverse. Many products, such as green tea extract, Garcinia cambogia, kava, germander, Ashwagandha and turmeric, cause an acute hepatitic pattern with lobular inflammation, necrosis and sometimes autoimmune-like features. Some Ayurvedic preparations contain heavy metals such as arsenic, mercury or lead, which may add their own toxicity. Pyrrolizidine alkaloids from plants such as Gynura segetum, Crotalaria and comfrey cause sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, with zone 3 sinusoidal congestion, haemorrhage and hepatocyte loss, and fibrous obliteration of central veins. Anabolic-androgenic steroids used in bodybuilding cause bland canalicular cholestasis, peliosis hepatis, hepatocellular adenomas (often beta-catenin-activated) and, rarely, hepatocellular carcinoma. Multi-ingredient bodybuilding and weight-loss supplements are frequently adulterated. The pathologist should describe the pattern and suggest that a careful history of herbal and supplement intake be taken, as patients often do not volunteer this information. The differentials include idiosyncratic DILI from conventional drugs, autoimmune hepatitis, viral hepatitis and other vascular disorders.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in herbal and supplement injury. FNA may, however, be performed on anabolic steroid-associated hepatocellular adenomas or carcinomas, where it shows the features of those tumours.
entities.ihc: IHC is supportive only, as for DILI in general: CD138 for plasma cells, CK7 for bile duct injury, CD34 and smooth muscle actin to evaluate sinusoidal and venous changes in SOS. In adenomas related to anabolic steroids, beta-catenin and glutamine synthetase are used to identify beta-catenin activation.

entities.entity: Toxin-induced liver injury (Amanita mushroom, arsenic, vinyl chloride, carbon tetrachloride, yellow phosphorus, aflatoxin)
entities.variants: Amanita phalloides (amatoxin) poisoning - zone 3 necrosis and microvesicular steatosis; chronic arsenic exposure (contaminated groundwater in West Bengal, Bangladesh) - non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis, angiosarcoma, HCC; vinyl chloride - perisinusoidal fibrosis and angiosarcoma; carbon tetrachloride - zone 3 necrosis with steatosis; yellow phosphorus (rat poison, common in India) - zone 1 necrosis with steatosis; aflatoxin B1 - HCC with TP53 R249S; Thorotrast (historical) - angiosarcoma, cholangiocarcinoma
entities.remarks: Toxins are dose-dependent and usually zonal; yellow phosphorus (rodenticide) poisoning is an important cause of acute liver failure in India with periportal (zone 1) necrosis; chronic arsenic causes non-cirrhotic portal hypertension and angiosarcoma.
entities.histo: Many chemical toxins cause predictable, dose-dependent liver injury with zonal patterns that provide clues to the cause. Amanita phalloides and related mushrooms contain amatoxins, which inhibit RNA polymerase II and cause zone 3 necrosis with microvesicular steatosis, progressing to massive necrosis and liver failure after a latent period of gastrointestinal symptoms. Carbon tetrachloride causes zone 3 necrosis with steatosis. Yellow phosphorus, found in rodenticide pastes and an important cause of poisoning and acute liver failure in India, characteristically causes periportal (zone 1) necrosis with microvesicular and macrovesicular steatosis. Chronic arsenic exposure from contaminated groundwater in West Bengal and Bangladesh, or from some traditional medicines, causes portal fibrosis and non-cirrhotic portal hypertension and is associated with angiosarcoma and HCC. Vinyl chloride exposure in industry causes subcapsular and perisinusoidal fibrosis, sinusoidal dilatation and angiosarcoma. Aflatoxin B1 from contaminated grains and nuts is a major cofactor of hepatocellular carcinoma in Africa and parts of Asia, causing the characteristic TP53 R249S mutation. Thorotrast, a historical radiocontrast agent, deposited radioactive granules in macrophages and caused angiosarcoma and cholangiocarcinoma decades later. The differentials include ischaemic necrosis, paracetamol toxicity, viral hepatitis and other DILI.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in acute toxic injury. In vinyl chloride, arsenic or aflatoxin exposure, FNA may be used for resulting angiosarcoma or hepatocellular carcinoma, with the cytological features of those tumours.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used to identify toxins. Vascular tumours associated with arsenic or vinyl chloride are confirmed with CD31, ERG and CD34, and p53 immunostaining may be strong in aflatoxin-related HCC with TP53 mutation.

entities.variants: Chronic vitamin A excess (supplements, retinoids, liver ingestion); acute toxicity; non-cirrhotic portal hypertension; perisinusoidal fibrosis and cirrhosis
entities.remarks: Hepatic stellate (Ito) cell hyperplasia and hypertrophy, with lipid-laden stellate cells containing multiple small fat vacuoles indenting the nucleus; perisinusoidal fibrosis, non-cirrhotic portal hypertension, eventually cirrhosis; vitamin A shows green autofluorescence.
entities.histo: Hypervitaminosis A results from chronic excessive intake of vitamin A from supplements, retinoid drugs or foods rich in vitamin A. Vitamin A is stored in hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells), which lie in the space of Disse, and excessive intake causes their marked hyperplasia and hypertrophy. On H&E, stellate cells appear as conspicuous perisinusoidal cells with pale, clear cytoplasm containing multiple small lipid vacuoles that indent the nucleus, forming a scalloped or ruffled outline. The activated stellate cells produce collagen, leading to perisinusoidal fibrosis, sinusoidal narrowing, non-cirrhotic portal hypertension and, eventually, cirrhosis. Vitamin A shows a characteristic, rapidly fading green autofluorescence under ultraviolet light in frozen sections. Other causes of stellate cell hyperplasia, such as methotrexate, chronic alcohol use and other drugs, should be considered. The differentials include microvesicular steatosis of hepatocytes, lipogranulomas and other causes of perisinusoidal fibrosis such as MASH and diabetic hepatosclerosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Hypertrophic, lipid-laden stellate (Ito) cells are best seen on biopsy with H&E and confirmed by their autofluorescence or electron microscopy.
entities.ihc: Stellate cells are highlighted by SMA when activated and by CRBP-1, and desmin and synaptophysin have been used to identify them. IHC is not essential for diagnosis.

entities.entity: Total parenteral nutrition (intestinal failure)-associated liver disease
entities.variants: Neonatal and infantile TPN cholestasis (preterm infants, short bowel syndrome); adult TPN-associated steatosis and steatohepatitis; intestinal failure-associated liver disease with biliary fibrosis and cirrhosis; gallbladder sludge and gallstones; protein-energy malnutrition (kwashiorkor) steatosis
entities.remarks: Infants: cholestasis, ductular reaction and portal fibrosis progressing to biliary cirrhosis; adults: macrovesicular steatosis and steatohepatitis; related to lipid emulsions (phytosterols), lack of enteral feeding and sepsis; fish-oil lipid emulsions reduce risk.
entities.histo: Liver disease associated with parenteral nutrition, now often called intestinal failure-associated liver disease, develops in patients receiving long-term TPN, particularly preterm infants and those with short bowel syndrome. Contributing factors include lack of enteral feeding, soybean-based lipid emulsions rich in phytosterols, recurrent sepsis and bacterial overgrowth. In infants, the dominant pattern is cholestasis, with canalicular and hepatocellular bile, ductular reaction with bile plugs and portal inflammation, which can resemble biliary atresia, followed by portal and bridging fibrosis and biliary cirrhosis. Giant cell transformation and extramedullary haematopoiesis may be present. In adults, macrovesicular steatosis predominates, sometimes with steatohepatitis and progressive fibrosis, and cholestasis develops later. Gallbladder sludge and stones are common. The condition improves with enteral feeding and with fish oil-based lipid emulsions. Protein-energy malnutrition (kwashiorkor) also causes marked macrovesicular steatosis without inflammation. The differentials include biliary atresia and other causes of neonatal cholestasis, sepsis-related cholestasis, MASLD and drug injury.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Diagnosis relies on the clinical setting of long-term parenteral nutrition, and biopsy assesses steatosis, cholestasis and fibrosis.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic. CK7 and CK19 assess ductular reaction and biliary injury, and trichrome stains assess portal and pericellular fibrosis, which can progress to biliary-type cirrhosis in infants.

entities.entity: Large bile duct obstruction (extrahepatic biliary obstruction)
entities.variants: Acute obstruction (choledocholithiasis, tumour, stricture); chronic obstruction; with ascending cholangitis; bile infarcts and bile lakes; obstruction by pancreatic head carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary tumours, chronic pancreatitis, IgG4-related disease, PSC
entities.remarks: Portal oedema, ductular reaction with periductular neutrophils, bile plugs in ductules and zone 3 canalicular cholestasis; chronic obstruction leads to cholate stasis, copper deposition, bile infarcts and secondary biliary cirrhosis; needs imaging (US, MRCP) correlation.
entities.histo: Obstruction of the large extrahepatic or hilar bile ducts produces a characteristic pattern in the liver. Early changes include portal tract oedema, ductular reaction at the edge of portal tracts with periductular neutrophils (acute pericholangitis), and bile plugs in interlobular ducts and ductules, together with zone 3 canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis. Bile infarcts, which are foci of hepatocyte necrosis impregnated with bile, and bile lakes from ruptured ducts in portal tracts are highly characteristic of obstruction. Neutrophils within duct epithelium and lumen indicate superimposed acute cholangitis. With persistent obstruction, periportal hepatocytes show cholate stasis with feathery degeneration, Mallory-Denk bodies, copper and copper-associated protein deposits, and portal fibrosis progresses to biliary-type bridging fibrosis and secondary biliary cirrhosis. The common causes are stones, benign strictures, pancreatic and biliary malignancies, chronic pancreatitis and PSC. The differentials include drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis, sepsis-related cholestasis, PBC (florid duct lesions, no ductular bile plugs), PSC (onion-skin fibrosis), and ductular reaction in alcoholic hepatitis. Imaging with ultrasound and MRCP is essential to confirm obstruction.
entities.cyto: Cytology plays a role in identifying the cause, not in assessing the liver: ERCP brushing, bile cytology and EUS-guided FNA of pancreatic or ampullary masses are used to detect malignancy, and reactive atypia from stones and stents is a common pitfall.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 highlight ductular reaction and periportal CK7-positive hepatocytes in chronic obstruction, and orcein and rhodanine show copper-associated protein. In brushings and biopsies of the obstructing lesion, p53, SMAD4, Ki-67, S100P and IMP3 support malignancy.

entities.variants: Due to chronic large duct obstruction (stones, strictures, chronic pancreatitis); after biliary atresia; in cystic fibrosis; after surgical biliary injury or ischaemic cholangiopathy
entities.remarks: End stage of prolonged biliary obstruction; jigsaw-pattern nodules with periportal halo of cholate stasis, ductular reaction, bile infarcts and copper deposition; may regress partially after relief of obstruction.
entities.histo: Secondary biliary cirrhosis is the end result of long-standing obstruction of large bile ducts, caused by stones, benign strictures (including post-surgical and ischaemic), chronic pancreatitis, choledochal cysts, biliary atresia or cystic fibrosis. Grossly the liver is green, finely nodular and enlarged in early stages. Microscopically, portal tracts are linked by broad fibrous septa containing marked ductular reaction, so that nodules have an irregular, jigsaw-puzzle outline. A pale halo of oedematous periportal hepatocytes with cholate stasis, feathery degeneration, Mallory-Denk bodies and copper deposition surrounds the nodules, and canalicular cholestasis, bile infarcts and bile plugs within ductules are common. Interlobular ducts may be dilated, inflamed or contain inspissated bile. The differentials include primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis in their cirrhotic stage, chronic ductopenic rejection and other forms of cirrhosis. The cause is often evident from imaging or clinical history.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in the cirrhosis itself, but brushing cytology of the causative stricture is important to exclude cholangiocarcinoma or pancreatic carcinoma.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 highlight the ductular reaction and periportal CK7-positive hepatocytes, and orcein and rhodanine show copper deposition; IHC is not otherwise diagnostic.

entities.variants: Ductular cholestasis (cholangitis lenta) in severe sepsis and septic shock; canalicular cholestasis of systemic infection; cholestasis of critical illness
entities.remarks: Inspissated bile casts in dilated ductules (ductular bilirubinostasis) at the edge of portal tracts with minimal inflammation; marker of severe sepsis and poor prognosis; often with zone 3 canalicular cholestasis and Kupffer cell hyperplasia.
entities.histo: Sepsis and systemic infection commonly cause cholestasis, and biopsies or autopsy livers show two main patterns. The milder pattern is bland canalicular cholestasis in zone 3, with bile plugs, Kupffer cell hyperplasia and minimal hepatocyte injury, which often accompanies severe infection with or without bacteraemia. The more severe and characteristic pattern, called ductular cholestasis or cholangitis lenta, shows dilated cholangioles (canals of Hering and ductules) at the edge of portal tracts, filled with dense, dark, inspissated bile concretions, often with flattened lining epithelium and only mild periductular inflammation. This pattern is associated with septic shock, endotoxaemia and a poor prognosis. Portal tracts may also show oedema and mild neutrophilic infiltration, but true acute cholangitis with neutrophils in interlobular ducts is not typical. The differentials include large duct obstruction and ascending cholangitis (bile plugs in interlobular ducts, portal oedema, neutrophilic cholangitis), drug-induced cholestasis, alcoholic hepatitis with ductular bilirubinostasis, cystic fibrosis and TPN-associated cholestasis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. The ductular bile plugs are a histological and usually autopsy finding, and blood cultures identify the underlying sepsis.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 confirm that the bile-filled structures are ductules, and IHC is otherwise not diagnostic; blood cultures and clinical correlation identify the infection.

entities.entity: Vanishing bile duct syndrome (ductopenia) including idiopathic adulthood ductopenia
entities.variants: Drug-induced vanishing bile duct syndrome (amoxicillin-clavulanate, carbamazepine, chlorpromazine, sulfonamides, azathioprine, checkpoint inhibitors); idiopathic adulthood ductopenia; ductopenia in PBC, PSC, sarcoidosis, chronic rejection, GVHD, Hodgkin lymphoma (paraneoplastic), cystic fibrosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis
entities.remarks: Loss of interlobular ducts in more than 50% of portal tracts, causing chronic cholestasis; many causes; idiopathic adulthood ductopenia is a diagnosis of exclusion in young adults; Hodgkin lymphoma-associated VBDS can precede the lymphoma diagnosis.
entities.histo: Vanishing bile duct syndrome refers to the acquired loss of intrahepatic bile ducts, defined as loss of interlobular ducts in more than half of the portal tracts in an adequate biopsy (at least ten portal tracts), leading to chronic cholestasis that may progress to biliary cirrhosis. Many conditions cause ductopenia, including PBC, PSC, sarcoidosis, chronic rejection, GVHD, cystic fibrosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and drug-induced injury. Drug-induced VBDS typically follows an episode of cholestatic hepatitis caused by drugs such as amoxicillin-clavulanate, carbamazepine, chlorpromazine and sulfonamides, and can be part of severe cutaneous reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Hodgkin lymphoma can cause paraneoplastic VBDS, sometimes before the lymphoma is diagnosed. Idiopathic adulthood ductopenia is a diagnosis of exclusion in young adults with chronic cholestasis without another cause, and some cases are linked to mild ABCB4 mutations. The biopsy shows portal tracts containing hepatic artery branches without accompanying bile ducts, variable ductular reaction, periportal cholate stasis, copper deposition and progressive biliary fibrosis. Residual ducts may show lymphocytic or degenerative injury. The differentials include early stages of the specific diseases that cause ductopenia, as well as sampling error in small biopsies.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Ductopenia requires counting bile ducts in at least 10 portal tracts on a core biopsy, with CK7 and CK19 staining.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 are essential to confirm the absence of interlobular ducts and to separate native ducts from ductular reaction, and CK7 shows periportal hepatocyte metaplasia in chronic cholestasis. CD30, CD15 and PAX5 identify Hodgkin cells when lymphoma is suspected, and CD1a and langerin identify Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

entities.variants: Ischaemic cholangiopathy (post-transplant hepatic artery thrombosis, intra-arterial chemotherapy, TACE); secondary sclerosing cholangitis in critically ill patients (SSC-CIP, including post-COVID cholangiopathy); recurrent pyogenic cholangitis; post-surgical biliary injury; chronic biliary obstruction; HIV (AIDS) cholangiopathy (Cryptosporidium, CMV, microsporidia); toxic (intra-arterial floxuridine, formaldehyde in hydatid surgery); ketamine cholangiopathy; eosinophilic cholangitis; Langerhans cell histiocytosis; IgG4-related (separate)
entities.remarks: Sclerosing cholangitis with an identifiable cause; mimics PSC on cholangiography; histology shows large duct obstruction, biliary casts, ductopenia and biliary fibrosis; SSC-CIP progresses rapidly to cirrhosis.
entities.histo: Secondary sclerosing cholangitis is a chronic cholestatic disease with multifocal biliary strictures and dilatation, similar to PSC on imaging, but with an identifiable cause. Ischaemic cholangiopathy, after hepatic artery thrombosis in liver transplants, intra-arterial chemotherapy or chemoembolisation, damages the peribiliary vascular plexus, leading to necrosis of the bile duct wall, bile leakage, bilomas and strictures. Secondary sclerosing cholangitis in critically ill patients, including those with severe COVID-19, follows prolonged intensive care with shock, high-dose vasopressors and mechanical ventilation, and is marked by biliary casts in the ducts, rapid ductopenia and progression to biliary cirrhosis within months. AIDS cholangiopathy is related to opportunistic infections such as Cryptosporidium, CMV and microsporidia. Other causes include recurrent pyogenic cholangitis, surgical injury, chronic obstruction, toxic chemicals, ketamine abuse, eosinophilic cholangitis and Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Histologically, liver biopsies show features of large duct obstruction, including portal oedema, ductular reaction, cholestasis, bile infarcts, ductopenia and biliary-type fibrosis, sometimes with periductal fibrosis similar to PSC. Large duct specimens may show necrotic duct walls, biliary casts and inflammation. The differentials include PSC, IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology is limited to bile or brushing samples, mainly to exclude malignancy or detect organisms such as Cryptosporidium or CMV in AIDS cholangiopathy; reactive atypia is common.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 show ductopenia and ductular reaction; CMV immunostaining and special stains identify infections in AIDS cholangiopathy, and CD1a or langerin identifies Langerhans cell histiocytosis. IgG4 immunostaining helps exclude IgG4-related disease.

entities.variants: Primary Budd-Chiari syndrome (thrombosis of hepatic veins; myeloproliferative neoplasm with JAK2 V617F, antiphospholipid syndrome, PNH, factor V Leiden, OCP, pregnancy); membranous obstruction of the IVC (hepatic vena cava syndrome; common in India and Nepal); secondary Budd-Chiari (tumour invasion or compression: HCC, RCC, adrenal carcinoma, leiomyosarcoma); acute, subacute and chronic forms
entities.remarks: Obstruction at the hepatic veins or suprahepatic IVC; zone 3 sinusoidal dilatation, congestion, haemorrhage with hepatocyte atrophy and loss, later veno-centric fibrosis and reversed-lobulation cirrhosis; large regenerative and FNH-like nodules; caudate lobe hypertrophy; look for myeloproliferative neoplasm.
entities.histo: Budd-Chiari syndrome is obstruction of hepatic venous outflow at any level from the small hepatic veins to the junction of the inferior vena cava with the right atrium, excluding cardiac causes and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome. Primary Budd-Chiari syndrome is caused by thrombosis, frequently due to a myeloproliferative neoplasm (often with JAK2 V617F), antiphospholipid syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, inherited thrombophilia, pregnancy or oral contraceptives, while membranous obstruction of the IVC is particularly common in India and Nepal. Secondary Budd-Chiari syndrome results from invasion or compression by tumours. In acute disease the liver is enlarged, purple and congested, and biopsy shows marked zone 3 sinusoidal dilatation and congestion, red cells extravasated into the space of Disse and liver cell plates, and atrophy, dropout and necrosis of centrilobular hepatocytes. Thrombi may be seen in small hepatic veins. In chronic disease, fibrosis develops around central veins and links them (veno-centric bridging fibrosis), producing a reversed lobulation pattern and eventually cirrhosis with portal tracts at the centre of the nodules. Large regenerative nodules, FNH-like nodules and occasionally HCC develop, and the caudate lobe, which drains directly into the IVC, hypertrophies. The differentials include congestive hepatopathy from cardiac failure (identical histology, requiring clinical and imaging correlation), sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (sinusoidal endothelial injury, patent hepatic veins), and sinusoidal dilatation from other causes.
