entities.cyto: Cytology has no role in diagnosing Budd-Chiari syndrome; FNA of regenerative nodules that arise in this setting may be misinterpreted as well-differentiated HCC because the hepatocytes may be reactive.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used to diagnose Budd-Chiari syndrome. Glutamine synthetase shows map-like staining in FNA-like nodules and a strong perivenular pattern in regenerating areas, and glypican-3, HSP70 and CD34 help evaluate nodules for HCC. JAK2 mutation analysis (bone marrow or blood) is part of the aetiological work-up.

entities.variants: SOS after haematopoietic stem cell transplant conditioning (busulfan, cyclophosphamide, total body irradiation); chemotherapy-associated (oxaliplatin, 'blue liver'); pyrrolizidine alkaloid (herbal, bush tea, Gynura) SOS; radiation-induced liver disease; gemtuzumab and inotuzumab ozogamicin; azathioprine and 6-thioguanine
entities.remarks: Toxic injury to sinusoidal endothelial cells and terminal hepatic venules; zone 3 sinusoidal congestion and haemorrhage, hepatocyte loss, subendothelial oedema and fibrous obliteration of central veins; oxaliplatin causes SOS, peliosis and NRH in resected livers with colorectal metastases.
entities.histo: Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, formerly veno-occlusive disease, is caused by toxic injury to sinusoidal endothelial cells, which detach and embolise downstream, obstructing sinusoids and terminal hepatic venules. It occurs after myeloablative conditioning for haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with chemotherapy agents such as oxaliplatin, with antibody-drug conjugates, after radiation and after ingestion of pyrrolizidine alkaloids in herbal preparations. Clinically there is painful hepatomegaly, jaundice, weight gain and ascites. Histologically, the acute phase shows marked zone 3 sinusoidal dilatation and congestion with red cells penetrating the space of Disse and liver cell plates, hepatocyte atrophy and necrosis, and subendothelial oedema, fibrin and red cells narrowing the lumen of central veins. Later, central veins are obliterated by loose then dense collagen, and perisinusoidal fibrosis develops in zone 3. In livers resected for colorectal metastases after oxaliplatin, the background shows SOS, peliosis and nodular regenerative hyperplasia, which grossly gives a blue-grey or red mottled appearance (blue liver) and increases postoperative complications. Masson trichrome is essential to show venous obliteration. The differentials include Budd-Chiari syndrome (larger vein thrombosis), congestive hepatopathy, GVHD and drug-induced hepatitis, and nodular regenerative hyperplasia may be a sequel.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Diagnosis rests on the clinical criteria (Baltimore or EBMT) after stem cell transplantation or chemotherapy, and transjugular biopsy with hepatic venous pressure measurement when needed.
entities.ihc: IHC is not necessary; CD34 may highlight sinusoidal endothelial injury and capillarisation, and smooth muscle actin highlights activated stellate cells. Masson trichrome and reticulin are the key stains for venous obliteration and NRH.

entities.entity: Passive congestion, congestive (cardiac) hepatopathy and Fontan-associated liver disease
entities.variants: Acute passive congestion; chronic passive congestion ('nutmeg liver'); cardiac sclerosis and cardiac cirrhosis; Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD) with sinusoidal dilatation, sinusoidal fibrosis, FNH-like nodules and HCC risk; constrictive pericarditis
entities.remarks: Right heart failure, tricuspid regurgitation, constrictive pericarditis or Fontan circulation; zone 3 sinusoidal dilatation, congestion and hepatocyte atrophy; sinusoidal and perivenular fibrosis leads to cardiac cirrhosis; Fontan patients develop fibrosis, FNH-like nodules and HCC.
entities.histo: Congestive hepatopathy results from elevated venous pressure transmitted from the right heart to the hepatic veins and sinusoids, and is seen in right heart failure, tricuspid regurgitation, constrictive pericarditis, cardiomyopathy and after the Fontan operation for single-ventricle congenital heart disease. Grossly, chronic passive congestion produces a nutmeg liver, with dark red congested centrilobular areas contrasting with paler periportal parenchyma. Microscopically there is zone 3 sinusoidal dilatation and congestion, atrophy and loss of centrilobular hepatocytes, red cells in the space of Disse, mild canalicular cholestasis, and PAS-D-positive globules in zone 3 hepatocytes in some cases. Prolonged congestion produces perisinusoidal fibrosis and fibrosis linking central veins (cardiac sclerosis), and eventually cardiac cirrhosis with reversed lobulation. Superimposed acute ischaemia from low cardiac output may cause zone 3 coagulative necrosis. Fontan-associated liver disease develops in almost all patients years after the procedure, showing sinusoidal dilatation, sinusoidal fibrosis, bridging fibrosis, cirrhosis, FNH-like regenerative nodules and an increased risk of HCC. The differentials include Budd-Chiari syndrome (identical histology, requiring imaging), SOS, and sinusoidal dilatation from other causes.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role; FNA of FNH-like nodules in Fontan livers may be confused with HCC.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed to diagnose congestion. In Fontan livers, glutamine synthetase map-like staining helps identify FNH-like nodules, and glypican-3, HSP70 and CD34 help evaluate nodules suspicious for HCC.

entities.variants: Shock liver (cardiogenic, septic, hypovolaemic shock); hypoxic hepatitis in respiratory failure; heat stroke; cocaine and MDMA toxicity; perioperative ischaemia; centrilobular necrosis of other causes
entities.remarks: Massive rapid rise in transaminases followed by fall; zone 3 coagulative necrosis with eosinophilic dead hepatocytes, minimal inflammation and haemorrhage; often superimposed on congestive hepatopathy; liver recovers without fibrosis if perfusion is restored.
entities.histo: Ischaemic hepatitis, or hypoxic hepatitis, occurs when liver perfusion or oxygenation falls abruptly, typically in cardiogenic, septic or hypovolaemic shock, respiratory failure, heat stroke or after recreational drugs such as cocaine and MDMA. It is most common in patients with underlying congestive heart failure, as passive congestion increases susceptibility. Serum transaminases rise to very high levels within one to three days and fall rapidly as perfusion is restored. Histologically, there is zone 3 (centrilobular) coagulative necrosis, in which hepatocytes are hypereosinophilic with pyknotic or absent nuclei, accompanied by sinusoidal congestion and haemorrhage and little or no inflammation, and the necrosis may extend to zone 2 in severe cases. Neutrophils may appear at the edge of the necrotic zone during resolution. Underlying passive congestion and atrophy of zone 3 are often present. If the patient survives, the liver regenerates without significant fibrosis. The differentials include paracetamol toxicity and other zone 3 toxins (similar morphology, requiring history and drug levels), acute autoimmune hepatitis with centrilobular necrosis (plasma cells), and viral hepatitis (inflammation and acidophil bodies).
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Ischaemic hepatitis is diagnosed clinically by the rapid rise and fall of transaminases after a hypotensive event, and biopsy is rarely needed.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used; viral immunostains may be applied to exclude HSV or adenovirus hepatitis if the necrosis is not clearly zonal.

entities.variants: True hepatic infarct (hepatic artery thrombosis or embolism, transplant, vasculitis, sickle cell disease, pregnancy-related HELLP, post-TACE or post-surgery); infarct of Zahn (pseudoinfarct from portal vein branch obstruction with congestion and atrophy, no necrosis); infarcted tumours (post-ablation)
entities.remarks: Infarction is uncommon due to dual blood supply; true infarcts are pale, wedge-shaped areas of coagulative necrosis; Zahn infarcts are red, congested, atrophic areas without necrosis from intrahepatic portal vein obstruction.
entities.histo: Because the liver has a dual blood supply from the hepatic artery and portal vein, true infarction is uncommon and usually requires hepatic artery occlusion in the setting of reduced portal flow or shock. Causes include hepatic artery thrombosis after transplantation, embolism, vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa, sickle cell crises, HELLP syndrome, surgery and procedures such as transarterial chemoembolisation. True infarcts are pale, sharply demarcated, often wedge-shaped areas of coagulative necrosis with ghosts of hepatocytes and portal tracts, surrounded by a haemorrhagic and inflammatory rim, and they heal with fibrosis. Biliary necrosis and bilomas may accompany infarcts in transplanted livers. The so-called infarct of Zahn is not a true infarct but a well-demarcated red-blue area of sinusoidal congestion and hepatocyte atrophy without necrosis, caused by obstruction of an intrahepatic portal vein branch, often by thrombus or tumour. The differentials include ischaemic hepatitis (diffuse zone 3 necrosis), necrotic tumours and abscesses, and post-ablation necrosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role; aspirates of infarcts yield necrotic debris that may be mistaken for necrotic tumour.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used; reticulin stain shows the preserved framework of infarcted parenchyma, and keratin and hepatocyte markers in ghost cells help identify necrotic tumour versus infarcted liver.

entities.entity: Portal vein thrombosis and extrahepatic portal vein obstruction (EHPVO)
entities.variants: Acute portal vein thrombosis; chronic portal vein thrombosis with cavernous transformation (portal cavernoma); EHPVO in children (umbilical sepsis, catheterisation) - common in India; portal vein thrombosis in cirrhosis; tumour thrombus (HCC); pylephlebitis (septic)
entities.remarks: Prehepatic portal hypertension with preserved liver function; liver biopsy shows sparse or absent portal veins, sinusoidal dilatation, atrophy and NRH; HCC tumour thrombus must be separated from bland thrombus; portal biliopathy may follow.
entities.histo: Portal vein thrombosis may occur in cirrhosis, myeloproliferative neoplasms and other prothrombotic states, abdominal infection or inflammation (pylephlebitis), pancreatitis, surgery and malignancy. In India, extrahepatic portal vein obstruction is a common cause of portal hypertension in children and young adults, often related to neonatal umbilical sepsis or catheterisation, and presents with variceal bleeding and splenomegaly with normal liver function. Chronic thrombosis results in cavernous transformation of the portal vein, with numerous collateral vessels at the hilum, which may compress bile ducts and cause portal biliopathy. Liver biopsy shows small, inconspicuous or absent portal veins in portal tracts, sometimes with thickened walls, together with periportal sinusoidal dilatation, hepatocyte atrophy and nodular regenerative hyperplasia, but no cirrhosis. Intrahepatic portal vein branches may contain organising thrombi. Tumour thrombus in HCC contains viable tumour cells and should be distinguished from bland thrombus on imaging and histology, as it affects staging. Septic pylephlebitis shows inflamed thrombi with bacteria. The differentials include porto-sinusoidal vascular disease (intrahepatic portal vein obliteration without main vein thrombosis), schistosomiasis and congenital hepatic fibrosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a role mainly in tumour thrombi: FNA of a portal vein thrombus can confirm tumour thrombus in HCC by showing malignant hepatocytes, which changes staging and treatment.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used for bland thrombosis; in suspected tumour thrombus, HepPar1, arginase-1 and glypican-3 confirm HCC cells. CD34 and smooth muscle markers can outline obliterated vessels.

entities.entity: Porto-sinusoidal vascular disease (idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal hypertension, non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis, hepatoportal sclerosis)
entities.variants: Obliterative portal venopathy; hepatoportal sclerosis; non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis (India); idiopathic portal hypertension (Japan); incomplete septal cirrhosis; PSVD with or without portal hypertension; associations: HIV (didanosine), azathioprine, oxaliplatin, arsenic, immunodeficiency (CVID), Turner syndrome, Adams-Oliver syndrome, telomere disorders
entities.remarks: VALDIG 2019 definition: absence of cirrhosis with specific histological signs (obliterative portal venopathy, NRH, incomplete septal fibrosis/cirrhosis) or portal hypertension; non-specific signs include portal tract abnormalities (herniated, multiple or periportal abnormal vessels), sinusoidal dilatation and mild perisinusoidal fibrosis; adequate biopsy (at least 20 mm) needed.
entities.histo: Porto-sinusoidal vascular disease is the 2019 umbrella term for a group of conditions previously called idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal hypertension, non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis (the term common in India), hepatoportal sclerosis, obliterative portal venopathy and incomplete septal cirrhosis. It is defined by the absence of cirrhosis together with either specific histological lesions or signs of portal hypertension, after excluding other causes such as Budd-Chiari syndrome and schistosomiasis. Specific histological signs are obliterative portal venopathy (portal tracts with absent or narrowed, thick-walled portal veins and dense portal fibrosis), nodular regenerative hyperplasia and incomplete septal fibrosis or cirrhosis (thin, incomplete septa ending blindly without well-formed nodules). Non-specific signs include portal tract abnormalities such as multiple dilated vessels, herniated portal veins protruding into the adjacent parenchyma and periportal abnormal vessels (shunt vessels), as well as sinusoidal dilatation and mild perisinusoidal fibrosis. Associations include chronic arsenic exposure, drugs such as azathioprine, didanosine and oxaliplatin, HIV infection, immunodeficiencies, autoimmune diseases, thrombophilia and genetic syndromes. A biopsy of at least 20 mm is needed, and reticulin and trichrome stains are essential. The differentials include cirrhosis (complete septa and nodules), schistosomiasis (eggs), congenital hepatic fibrosis (ductal plate malformation) and chronic portal vein thrombosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Diagnosis requires an adequate core biopsy (at least 20 mm) to show obliterative portal venopathy and exclude cirrhosis, using reticulin and trichrome stains.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic; CD34 may show the abnormal vessels and patchy sinusoidal capillarisation, smooth muscle actin or desmin outline thickened portal veins, and CK7 helps exclude biliary diseases. Reticulin and trichrome are essential for NRH and septal fibrosis.

entities.variants: NRH associated with autoimmune and rheumatological diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, Felty syndrome, scleroderma), myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders, drugs (azathioprine, 6-thioguanine, oxaliplatin, didanosine), CVID and other immunodeficiencies, post-transplant; part of porto-sinusoidal vascular disease
entities.remarks: Diffuse micronodular transformation without fibrous septa; nodules of hypertrophic hepatocytes with compressed atrophic plates between them, best seen on reticulin stain; cause of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension; easily missed on H&E.
entities.histo: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia is a diffuse transformation of the liver into small regenerative nodules without fibrous septa, believed to result from heterogeneous blood flow caused by obliteration of small portal veins, with hypertrophy of well-perfused areas and atrophy of poorly perfused areas. It is associated with autoimmune diseases, haematological disorders, immunodeficiencies, drugs such as azathioprine, 6-thioguanine and oxaliplatin, and organ transplantation, and is one of the specific lesions of porto-sinusoidal vascular disease. Grossly the liver may appear normal or finely nodular. On H&E the changes are subtle, but nodules of hypertrophic hepatocytes with thickened plates (two cells thick) alternate with zones of atrophic, compressed plates with dilated sinusoids, often around central veins. A reticulin stain is essential, as it shows the alternating pattern of thickened plates in nodules and condensed reticulin fibres at their periphery, without fibrous septa on trichrome. Portal veins may be small or absent. Clinically it can cause portal hypertension with preserved liver function. The differentials include cirrhosis (septa on trichrome), normal liver (in small biopsies), partial nodular transformation (larger perihilar nodules), large regenerative nodules and well-differentiated hepatocellular neoplasms.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role; aspirates yield benign hepatocytes indistinguishable from normal liver.
entities.ihc: IHC is not needed; reticulin and trichrome are the key stains. Glutamine synthetase may show irregular perivenular staining patterns, and CD34 is not significantly increased in sinusoids.

entities.variants: Parenchymal (phlebectatic) type; phlebectatic type with endothelial lining; associated with anabolic steroids, oral contraceptives, azathioprine, vitamin A, tamoxifen, tuberculosis, HIV, malignancies (HCC, adenoma), haematological diseases; bacillary peliosis (Bartonella, separate)
entities.remarks: Blood-filled cystic spaces in the parenchyma, with or without endothelial lining, without fibrous walls; may rupture causing haemoperitoneum; also seen within hepatocellular adenomas (inflammatory HCA) and HCC; exclude Bartonella in immunosuppressed patients.
entities.histo: Peliosis hepatis is characterised by multiple blood-filled cystic spaces in the liver parenchyma, ranging from microscopic to several centimetres, which may be scattered or diffuse. It is associated with drugs, particularly anabolic-androgenic steroids, oral contraceptives, azathioprine and tamoxifen, chronic infections such as tuberculosis and HIV, malignancies and haematological diseases, and it can occur focally within inflammatory hepatocellular adenomas and HCC. Bartonella infection causes bacillary peliosis in immunosuppressed patients. Microscopically, the parenchymal type shows irregular blood lakes without an endothelial lining, bordered directly by hepatocytes, while the phlebectatic type shows spaces lined by endothelium, sometimes communicating with dilated sinusoids and central veins. There is no fibrous wall, and organising thrombi or fibrosis may be present in older lesions. Rupture causes haemoperitoneum. The differentials include sinusoidal dilatation (less severe, no cystic spaces), haemangioma (fibrous septa and endothelial lining), angiosarcoma (atypical endothelial cells), bacillary peliosis (myxoid stroma and bacterial clumps), and haemorrhagic tumours.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role; aspirates yield blood only.
entities.ihc: CD31, ERG and CD34 outline endothelial-lined spaces in the phlebectatic type and are absent in the parenchymal type; Bartonella immunostaining or Warthin-Starry staining excludes bacillary peliosis, and the endothelium lacks the atypia and high Ki-67 of angiosarcoma.

entities.variants: Periportal (zone 1) sinusoidal dilatation (oral contraceptives, pregnancy); zone 3 sinusoidal dilatation (outflow obstruction, see Budd-Chiari and congestion); panlobular dilatation in systemic inflammatory disease (Crohn disease, rheumatoid arthritis), Hodgkin lymphoma, Castleman disease, renal cell carcinoma (paraneoplastic), POEMS syndrome; adjacent to mass lesions
entities.remarks: Non-specific finding; zone 1 dilatation suggests drugs (OCP) or systemic inflammation, often with raised ALP; zone 3 suggests outflow obstruction; associated with IL-6-driven conditions.
entities.histo: Sinusoidal dilatation is a non-specific but common finding in liver biopsies, and its distribution helps narrow the possible causes. Zone 3 (centrilobular) dilatation suggests impaired venous outflow, as in Budd-Chiari syndrome, congestive hepatopathy and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, and is accompanied by congestion and atrophy of hepatocyte plates. Periportal (zone 1) or panlobular dilatation without congestion is associated with oral contraceptive use, pregnancy, systemic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases such as Crohn disease and rheumatoid arthritis, and malignancies, especially Hodgkin lymphoma and renal cell carcinoma (as part of a paraneoplastic syndrome with raised alkaline phosphatase, sometimes called Stauffer syndrome), as well as Castleman disease and POEMS syndrome, in which interleukin-6 is thought to play a role. Sinusoidal dilatation is also common next to space-occupying lesions and in the setting of portal vein obstruction or porto-sinusoidal vascular disease. The differentials include peliosis hepatis (cystic blood spaces), sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (endothelial injury and venous obliteration) and NRH (reticulin shows nodules).
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Sinusoidal dilatation is a histological pattern recognised on biopsy, and its cause, such as oral contraceptives, inflammation or adjacent mass lesions, is sought clinically.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used; CD34 may show endothelial capillarisation in some causes, and reticulin helps exclude NRH. Correlation with clinical findings is essential.

entities.variants: HHT type 1 (ENG) and type 2 (ACVRL1, more liver involvement); SMAD4-related juvenile polyposis-HHT; hepatic arteriovenous malformations (arteriovenous, arterioportal and portovenous shunts); high-output cardiac failure; ischaemic biliary necrosis; FNH-like nodules and NRH
entities.remarks: Autosomal dominant; liver involved in most patients (ACVRL1 especially); dilated tortuous vessels in portal tracts and parenchyma forming AV shunts; complications are high-output heart failure, portal hypertension and biliary ischaemia; liver biopsy risky due to bleeding.
entities.histo: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal dominant vascular disorder, most often due to ENG or ACVRL1 mutations, characterised by mucocutaneous telangiectasias, epistaxis and visceral arteriovenous malformations. The liver is involved in many patients, particularly those with ACVRL1 mutations, but most remain asymptomatic. Hepatic vascular malformations form arteriovenous, arterioportal and portovenous shunts, leading to high-output cardiac failure, portal hypertension, biliary ischaemia (due to steal from the peribiliary plexus) and encephalopathy. Histologically, portal tracts and the parenchyma contain numerous dilated, thin-walled vascular channels of varying size, with abnormal arteries and veins, sometimes with fibrosis. The altered blood flow leads to nodular regenerative hyperplasia and FNH-like nodules, which can mimic tumours on imaging, and is sometimes called pseudocirrhosis. Liver biopsy carries a high risk of bleeding and is generally avoided, so the diagnosis is usually made clinically and radiologically. The differentials include cirrhosis, haemangiomas, other vascular malformations and porto-sinusoidal vascular disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role, and FNA is generally avoided due to bleeding risk.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic; CD31 and CD34 outline the abnormal vessels, and glutamine synthetase shows map-like staining in FNH-like nodules.

entities.variants: Hepatic artery aneurysm and pseudoaneurysm (atherosclerosis, trauma, vasculitis, infection, post-procedure); hepatic artery thrombosis (post-transplant, after TACE); fibromuscular dysplasia; segmental arterial mediolysis; arteriopathy in portal hypertension; arterial changes in chronic rejection (see rejection)
entities.remarks: Uncommon; aneurysms can rupture and cause haemobilia or haemoperitoneum; arterial thrombosis causes ischaemic cholangiopathy and infarcts, especially in transplants; biopsy findings indirect (biliary ischaemia, infarcts).
entities.histo: Disorders of the hepatic artery are uncommon but can have serious consequences. Hepatic artery aneurysms and pseudoaneurysms result from atherosclerosis, trauma, iatrogenic injury during biliary procedures, vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa, infection (mycotic aneurysm) or segmental arterial mediolysis, and rupture may cause haemobilia or haemoperitoneum. Hepatic artery thrombosis is mainly a complication of liver transplantation, where it causes ischaemic cholangiopathy, bile duct necrosis, bilomas, infarcts and graft failure, because the bile ducts depend on arterial blood supply; it can also follow chemoembolisation and surgery. Histologically, specimens show arterial wall disruption, thrombus, inflammation or medial lysis depending on the cause, and liver biopsies show indirect evidence such as ischaemic biliary injury, cholestasis and infarcts. Fibromuscular dysplasia and segmental arterial mediolysis show characteristic medial changes. Portal hypertension may cause hypertrophy of hepatic artery branches. The differentials include vasculitis, rejection-related arteriopathy and tumour-related vessel changes.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. These disorders are diagnosed by Doppler ultrasound, CT or angiography, and FNA of a suspected aneurysm is dangerous and must be avoided.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used; elastic stains (Verhoeff-van Gieson) and trichrome assess arterial wall structure, and CK7 and CK19 evaluate ischaemic bile duct injury.

entities.variants: AFLP with fetal LCHAD (HADHA) deficiency; AFLP without known fetal defect; AFLP overlapping with HELLP; Swansea criteria diagnosis
entities.remarks: Third trimester; microvesicular steatosis predominantly in zone 3 (foamy hepatocytes with central nuclei), minimal inflammation or necrosis; associated with fetal long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects; obstetric emergency, delivery is curative; oil red O on frozen section; test infant for LCHAD.
entities.histo: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare, life-threatening disorder of the third trimester, presenting with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy and sometimes encephalopathy and renal failure. It is associated in some cases with fetal deficiency of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD), which leads to accumulation of toxic fatty acid metabolites in the maternal circulation. Liver biopsy is rarely performed because of coagulopathy, and diagnosis usually rests on the Swansea criteria. Histologically, hepatocytes, predominantly in zone 3 and zone 2, are swollen with finely vacuolated foamy cytoplasm due to microvesicular steatosis, with central nuclei, while periportal hepatocytes are relatively spared. Inflammation and necrosis are minimal, though canalicular cholestasis, scattered acidophil bodies and extramedullary haematopoiesis may be present. The fat may be subtle on paraffin sections and is better shown by oil red O on frozen tissue. Prompt delivery is curative, and the liver recovers without fibrosis. The differentials include HELLP syndrome and pre-eclampsia (periportal fibrin and haemorrhage), acute viral hepatitis, including hepatitis E with its high mortality in pregnancy, drug toxicity and Reye-like syndromes.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. AFLP is a clinical diagnosis using the Swansea criteria, and biopsy is rarely done because of coagulopathy.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used; oil red O on frozen sections confirms microvesicular fat, and the infant should be tested for LCHAD deficiency.

entities.entity: HELLP syndrome and pre-eclampsia-associated liver injury
entities.variants: Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia liver involvement; HELLP (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets); subcapsular haematoma and hepatic rupture; hepatic infarction
entities.remarks: Third trimester or postpartum; periportal (zone 1) fibrin deposition in sinusoids with haemorrhage and periportal hepatocyte necrosis; may cause subcapsular haematoma and rupture; delivery is the treatment.
entities.histo: Pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome are pregnancy-specific disorders with endothelial dysfunction and microangiopathy, typically in the third trimester or shortly after delivery. Liver involvement causes right upper quadrant pain, raised transaminases and, in HELLP, haemolysis and thrombocytopenia. The characteristic histology is periportal (zone 1) deposition of fibrin in sinusoids, with sinusoidal haemorrhage and periportal hepatocyte coagulative necrosis, which may become confluent and extend to infarcts. Severe cases develop subcapsular haematomas and hepatic rupture, an obstetric and surgical emergency. Inflammation is minimal, and microvesicular steatosis may coexist when there is overlap with acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Biopsy is rarely performed because of bleeding risk, and the diagnosis is clinical. Delivery is the definitive treatment. The differentials include acute fatty liver of pregnancy (zone 3 microvesicular steatosis), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, viral hepatitis and ischaemic injury.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. HELLP is diagnosed by laboratory criteria (haemolysis, raised liver enzymes, low platelets), and imaging assesses haematoma or rupture.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used. PTAH or fibrin immunostaining can highlight periportal sinusoidal fibrin deposits, and viral immunostains may help exclude HSV hepatitis, which can also present with liver failure in pregnancy.

entities.variants: ICP associated with ABCB4, ABCB11 or ATP8B1 variants; recurrent ICP; ICP with hepatitis C
entities.remarks: Commonest pregnancy-specific liver disease; second or third trimester pruritus with raised serum bile acids; bland zone 3 canalicular cholestasis without inflammation; resolves after delivery; risk to fetus (preterm birth, stillbirth); biopsy rarely needed.
entities.histo: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is the most common liver disorder specific to pregnancy, typically presenting in the second or third trimester with pruritus, especially of the palms and soles, and elevated serum bile acids, with or without jaundice. It results from the effects of pregnancy hormones on hepatocyte bile transport in genetically predisposed women, some of whom carry variants in ABCB4, ABCB11 or ATP8B1. Maternal outcome is good, as symptoms resolve after delivery, but the fetus is at risk of preterm delivery, meconium staining and stillbirth, particularly with very high bile acid levels. Liver biopsy is rarely needed and shows bland canalicular cholestasis with bile plugs, predominantly in zone 3, without significant inflammation, hepatocyte necrosis or ductular reaction. The condition often recurs in subsequent pregnancies or with oral contraceptive use. The differentials include drug-induced cholestasis, benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis, hepatitis C, PBC and gallstone disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. ICP is diagnosed by pruritus and raised serum bile acids in pregnancy, and biopsy is not needed.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used; BSEP and MDR3 staining is normal in most cases, and genetic testing may identify predisposing variants in recurrent disease.

entities.variants: Mild, moderate and severe preservation injury; primary non-function; early allograft dysfunction; donor-related changes (steatosis, donation after circulatory death); small-for-size syndrome (living donor grafts)
entities.remarks: First days to weeks after transplant; zone 3 hepatocyte ballooning, cholestasis, apoptosis and neutrophil clusters, with coagulative necrosis in severe cases; worse with donor steatosis and prolonged cold ischaemia; DCD grafts prone to ischaemic cholangiopathy.
entities.histo: Preservation or ischaemia-reperfusion injury results from cold storage of the donor liver followed by warm reperfusion in the recipient, and it is the commonest cause of early graft dysfunction. Risk factors include prolonged cold or warm ischaemia, older donor age, significant macrovesicular steatosis in the donor liver and donation after circulatory death. Biopsies in the first days show zone 3 hepatocyte ballooning (hydropic swelling), canalicular cholestasis, scattered apoptotic hepatocytes and small clusters of neutrophils in sinusoids (surgical hepatitis), with mild ductular reaction. Severe injury shows confluent coagulative necrosis in zone 3 or panlobular necrosis, and primary non-function results in graft failure requiring retransplantation. Cholestatic changes may persist for weeks during recovery. Small-for-size syndrome in partial grafts shows similar features with portal hyperperfusion injury and cholestasis. Donation after circulatory death grafts are prone to ischaemic cholangiopathy. Donor liver evaluation by frozen section before transplantation assesses macrovesicular steatosis, necrosis, fibrosis and incidental lesions. The differentials include acute rejection (portal inflammation, duct damage, endotheliitis), hepatic artery thrombosis, biliary obstruction, sepsis and drug toxicity.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Preservation injury is assessed on post-reperfusion or early graft biopsies, which show centrilobular hepatocyte swelling, cholestasis and necrosis.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used for preservation injury; C4d helps exclude antibody-mediated rejection, and viral stains exclude infection. Oil red O on frozen sections may be used to quantify donor steatosis.

entities.entity: Surgical and vascular complications of liver transplantation
entities.variants: Hepatic artery thrombosis and stenosis; portal vein thrombosis or stenosis; hepatic vein or IVC outflow obstruction; biliary anastomotic strictures and leaks; non-anastomotic (ischaemic-type) biliary strictures; bilomas; infarcts and abscesses; small-for-size syndrome
entities.remarks: Major causes of graft dysfunction and loss; biopsies show indirect signs: ischaemic necrosis and cholangiopathy (arterial), atrophy and NRH (portal), zone 3 congestion (outflow), obstructive features (biliary); confirm with imaging.
entities.histo: Surgical and vascular complications are important causes of graft dysfunction after liver transplantation, and the pathologist's role is to recognise their indirect effects in biopsies and to evaluate failed grafts. Hepatic artery thrombosis or stenosis, the most serious, causes ischaemic necrosis of bile ducts and hepatocytes, bilomas, abscesses, infarcts and non-anastomotic biliary strictures, because the biliary tree depends on the arterial supply. Portal vein thrombosis or stenosis leads to portal hypertension and parenchymal atrophy or nodular regenerative hyperplasia. Hepatic vein or IVC outflow obstruction causes zone 3 sinusoidal dilatation and congestion similar to Budd-Chiari syndrome. Biliary anastomotic strictures and leaks produce the pattern of large duct obstruction, with portal oedema, ductular reaction with neutrophils and cholestasis, sometimes with cholangitis. Small-for-size syndrome in partial grafts causes cholestasis and portal hyperperfusion changes. Explanted failed grafts may show infarcts, necrotic ducts and organising thrombi. The differentials include rejection, recurrent disease, preservation injury and infection, and correlation with Doppler ultrasound and cholangiography is essential.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role, except bile cytology for infection or biliary brushing in strictures.
entities.ihc: IHC is not diagnostic; CK7 and CK19 evaluate biliary injury, C4d helps exclude antibody-mediated rejection, and CMV and other viral stains exclude infection.

entities.variants: Recurrent hepatitis B, C and E; recurrent autoimmune hepatitis; recurrent PBC; recurrent PSC; recurrent MASLD/MASH; recurrent alcohol-associated liver disease; recurrent HCC and cholangiocarcinoma; recurrent metabolic disease (rare)
entities.remarks: Original disease may recur in the graft; HCV recurrence was near universal before DAAs; recurrent PSC must be separated from ischaemic biliary strictures; recurrent AIH and PBC may need to be separated from plasma cell-rich rejection and chronic rejection.
entities.histo: Many diseases that lead to liver transplantation can recur in the graft, with consequences for graft function and survival. Recurrent hepatitis C was almost universal before direct-acting antivirals, showing acute lobular hepatitis and then chronic portal hepatitis with progressive fibrosis, and a severe fibrosing cholestatic form, while hepatitis B recurrence has been largely prevented by antiviral prophylaxis. Hepatitis E can cause chronic hepatitis in grafts. Recurrent autoimmune hepatitis shows plasma cell-rich interface hepatitis similar to the original disease and must be distinguished from plasma cell-rich rejection. Recurrent PBC shows florid duct lesions, granulomas and ductopenia, and recurrent PSC shows biliary strictures and fibro-obliterative duct lesions, which must be separated from ischaemic-type biliary strictures due to arterial insufficiency or donation after circulatory death. Recurrent MASLD and alcohol-related liver disease are common and show the same features as in native livers. Recurrent HCC and cholangiocarcinoma occur in the graft or elsewhere and are related to tumour burden before transplant. The differentials in each case include rejection, drug toxicity, biliary and vascular complications and de novo disease.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a role mainly for recurrent tumours, where FNA of new nodules may confirm recurrent HCC or cholangiocarcinoma.
entities.ihc: Viral immunostains (HBsAg, HBcAg), CD138 for plasma cells, CK7 and CK19 for biliary injury, C4d for antibody-mediated injury, and tumour markers (HepPar1, arginase-1, glypican-3; CK7, CK19) for recurrent neoplasms are used according to the clinical question.

entities.variants: Acute sickle hepatic crisis; sickle cell intrahepatic cholestasis (severe, life-threatening); hepatic sequestration crisis; transfusional iron overload; pigment gallstones and choledocholithiasis; HCV infection from transfusions
entities.remarks: Sickled red cells occluding sinusoids, with sinusoidal dilatation, Kupffer cell erythrophagocytosis and hepatocyte ischaemia; intrahepatic cholestasis variant has marked canalicular cholestasis; iron overload from transfusion; relevant in tribal populations of central and eastern India.
entities.histo: The liver in sickle cell disease is affected by vaso-occlusion, haemolysis, transfusions and their complications. Sickle cell disease is prevalent in tribal populations of central and eastern India, including Odisha. During acute crises, sinusoids are distended by aggregates of sickled red cells, with Kupffer cell hypertrophy and erythrophagocytosis, haemosiderin deposition, and ischaemic necrosis of hepatocytes, particularly in zone 3. Sickle cell intrahepatic cholestasis is a rare, severe complication with marked canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis, sinusoidal sickling and hepatocyte ballooning, and it can lead to liver failure. Hepatic sequestration crisis causes rapid liver enlargement with trapped red cells. Chronic changes include transfusional iron overload (initially in Kupffer cells, later in hepatocytes) with fibrosis, pigment gallstones from chronic haemolysis, and viral hepatitis from transfusions. Sickled cells can also be seen as an artefact in liver tissue from patients with sickle trait, especially if fixation is delayed. The differentials include other causes of cholestasis and ischaemia, iron overload of other causes and viral hepatitis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role. Sickled red cells in sinusoids are seen on biopsy, and peripheral blood smear and haemoglobin electrophoresis confirm the disease.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used; Perls stain assesses iron, and viral serology excludes transfusion-related hepatitis.

entities.variants: Physiological fetal and neonatal haematopoiesis; extramedullary haematopoiesis in myelofibrosis and other myeloproliferative neoplasms; in haemolytic anaemias and thalassaemia; in hepatoblastoma, hepatocellular adenoma, angiomyolipoma and other tumours; after G-CSF; tumour-forming EMH (rare)
entities.remarks: Clusters of erythroid precursors, myeloid precursors and megakaryocytes in sinusoids and portal tracts; normal in neonates; in adults suggests myelofibrosis or severe anaemia; megakaryocytes may mimic malignant cells.
entities.histo: The liver is the main site of haematopoiesis in the fetus, and small foci persist in neonates. In older children and adults, extramedullary haematopoiesis occurs when the bone marrow is replaced or under stress, as in primary myelofibrosis and other myeloproliferative neoplasms, thalassaemia and severe haemolytic anaemias, and after growth factor treatment. It is also commonly found within certain tumours, including hepatoblastoma, hepatocellular adenomas and angiomyolipomas. Microscopically, clusters of erythroid precursors with round dark nuclei, myeloid precursors including eosinophilic myelocytes, and large megakaryocytes with lobated nuclei are seen within sinusoids and in portal tracts. In myelofibrosis, the sinusoids may be markedly infiltrated, with atypical megakaryocytes and sinusoidal fibrosis, causing hepatomegaly and portal hypertension. Rarely, extramedullary haematopoiesis forms a mass. The differentials include leukaemic infiltration, metastatic small round cell tumours, lymphomas and, for megakaryocytes, pleomorphic carcinoma or sarcoma cells.
entities.cyto: Aspirates may contain erythroid and myeloid precursors and megakaryocytes, which can be mistaken for malignant cells (particularly large atypical megakaryocytes mimicking carcinoma or sarcoma); recognising the trilineage mixture prevents misdiagnosis.
entities.ihc: Glycophorin A or CD71 highlights erythroid precursors, myeloperoxidase marks myeloid cells, and CD61 or CD42b identifies megakaryocytes. CD34 and CD117 help exclude a leukaemic infiltrate, and keratin negativity excludes carcinoma.

entities.variants: Primary (familial) HLH (PRF1, UNC13D, STX11 and others); secondary HLH triggered by infection (EBV, CMV, leishmaniasis, TB), malignancy (lymphoma, especially T and NK cell types) and autoimmune disease (macrophage activation syndrome)
entities.remarks: Hyperinflammatory syndrome with fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, very high ferritin; liver shows sinusoidal and portal infiltration by activated histiocytes with haemophagocytosis, lymphocytic infiltrates and hepatitis; HLH-2004 criteria; look for trigger including lymphoma.
entities.histo: Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is a life-threatening syndrome of excessive immune activation, either inherited or secondary to infections, malignancies or autoimmune diseases, and the liver is commonly involved. Patients have fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, very high ferritin, hypertriglyceridaemia, hypofibrinogenaemia and liver dysfunction. The liver shows sinusoidal and portal infiltration by activated lymphocytes and enlarged histiocytes, many of which contain phagocytosed red cells, platelets, lymphocytes and neutrophils (haemophagocytosis), along with Kupffer cell hyperplasia, a chronic hepatitis-like portal infiltrate, lobular inflammation, cholestasis and sometimes endotheliitis and necrosis. Haemophagocytosis in the liver is supportive but not required for diagnosis, which follows the HLH-2004 criteria. Identifying the trigger is essential, so the biopsy should be examined for viral inclusions, Leishmania amastigotes and a lymphomatous infiltrate. The differentials include viral hepatitis, sepsis, Kupffer cell erythrophagocytosis in other conditions, hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma and other lymphomas.
entities.cyto: Cytology is relevant mainly in bone marrow aspirates, which show histiocytes engulfing red cells, platelets and other cells; liver aspirates are not used.
entities.ihc: CD68 and CD163 highlight the activated histiocytes, making haemophagocytosis easier to see. EBER in situ hybridisation identifies EBV-driven HLH, CMV immunostain excludes CMV infection, and T-cell markers (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD56, TIA-1, granzyme B) and clonality studies help identify an underlying T or NK cell lymphoma.

entities.variants: Large regenerative nodule in cirrhosis (macroregenerative nodule, over 1 cm); large regenerative nodules in non-cirrhotic livers (Budd-Chiari syndrome, portal vein obstruction, Fontan, PSVD); partial nodular transformation (perihilar); FNH-like nodules (overlap)
entities.remarks: Well-circumscribed regenerative nodule distinctly larger than the background cirrhotic nodules, without atypia; contains portal tracts; normal reticulin; separated from dysplastic nodules and early HCC by lack of cytological and architectural atypia and lack of glypican-3/HSP70.
entities.histo: Large regenerative nodules are distinct nodules of regenerating hepatocytes that are larger than surrounding nodules, typically over 1 cm, arising in cirrhosis (where they are also called macroregenerative nodules) or in non-cirrhotic livers with vascular disorders such as Budd-Chiari syndrome, portal vein obstruction, porto-sinusoidal vascular disease and Fontan circulation. Partial nodular transformation is a related condition with large perihilar regenerative nodules in non-cirrhotic livers. Microscopically, a large regenerative nodule consists of hepatocytes arranged in plates one to two cells thick, with intact reticulin framework, portal tracts within the nodule, and no cytological atypia or increased nuclear density. Unpaired arteries are absent or few. In non-cirrhotic vascular disorders, nodules may show features overlapping with FNH, including fibrous scars, ductular reaction and map-like glutamine synthetase staining, and are called FNH-like nodules. The differentials include low-grade and high-grade dysplastic nodules (increased cell density, clonal small or large cell change, unpaired arteries), well-differentiated HCC, hepatocellular adenoma and FNH.
entities.cyto: Aspirates of a large regenerative nodule contain benign hepatocytes and bile duct cells, which are indistinguishable from background cirrhosis and do not exclude well-differentiated HCC in a missed sample; cell block with reticulin and immunostains is preferable. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: Glypican-3 and HSP70 are negative, glutamine synthetase shows patchy or perivenular or map-like (in FNH-like nodules) rather than diffuse staining, and CD34 shows only patchy periportal sinusoidal capillarisation. The intact reticulin network and CK7-positive portal tracts and ductules support a regenerative lesion over HCC.

entities.variants: Early (collapse with hepatocyte loss) phase; nodular elastosis phase (elastic fibre-rich nodule); late fibrotic phase; associated with vascular injury
entities.remarks: Pseudotumour, usually subcapsular in segment IV or VIII, mimicking metastasis or cholangiocarcinoma; loss of hepatocytes with crowded portal tracts and ductular reaction, then dense elastic-rich nodular scar; elastic stain (orcein, EVG) helpful.
entities.histo: Segmental atrophy is a non-neoplastic lesion thought to result from vascular injury in a localised region of the liver, producing a subcapsular pseudotumour that is frequently mistaken for a metastasis or cholangiocarcinoma on imaging. It evolves through stages. In the early phase there is loss of hepatocytes with parenchymal collapse, closely crowded portal tracts and marked ductular reaction in a fibrotic background, often with chronic inflammation. In the nodular elastosis phase, the lesion contains nodules of dense elastic tissue, highlighted by elastic stains such as orcein or Verhoeff-van Gieson, admixed with collagen and residual ducts and vessels. Late lesions are densely fibrotic scars with few remaining structures. Thick-walled, sometimes thrombosed vessels are frequently seen. The differentials include cholangiocarcinoma (atypical infiltrating glands), metastatic adenocarcinoma, sclerosed haemangioma (residual vascular channels), solitary necrotic nodule (necrotic core and fibrous capsule) and inflammatory pseudotumour. Recognition prevents unnecessary radical surgery.
entities.cyto: Aspirates are often paucicellular, yielding fragments of fibrous tissue and a few bland bile duct cells, which must not be misinterpreted as adenocarcinoma.
entities.ihc: CK7 and CK19 highlight bland ductules within the lesion, which lack p53 aberrant staining, SMAD4 loss and high Ki-67, helping to exclude cholangiocarcinoma. Elastic stains are more useful than IHC.

entities.entity: Solitary necrotic nodule of the liver
entities.variants: Solitary necrotic nodule; multiple necrotic nodules; with parasitic remnants; sclerosed haemangioma-related; post-traumatic
entities.remarks: Rare benign nodule with central necrosis surrounded by a hyalinised fibrous capsule with elastic fibres; many probably represent end-stage sclerosed haemangioma or healed parasitic infection; mimics metastasis on imaging.
entities.histo: The solitary necrotic nodule is an uncommon benign lesion, usually found incidentally or during evaluation for suspected metastases, typically subcapsular in the right lobe. It consists of a central area of amorphous coagulative necrosis, which may contain ghost outlines of vessels or parasites, surrounded by a dense hyalinised fibrous capsule containing elastic fibres and a rim of chronic inflammatory cells. Calcification may occur. Its origin is thought to be heterogeneous, with many cases representing end-stage sclerosed haemangiomas, healed parasitic infections such as toxocariasis or larva migrans, or old trauma. The differentials include necrotic metastasis (viable tumour cells at the periphery), tuberculoma (caseating granulomas, AFB), healed abscess, sclerosed haemangioma and segmental atrophy. Careful examination of the periphery and use of special stains for organisms help exclude infection and tumour.
entities.cyto: FNA yields necrotic debris and fibrous fragments, which cannot distinguish a necrotic nodule from a necrotic tumour; core biopsy or excision is required.
entities.ihc: IHC is used to exclude residual tumour: keratins (AE1/AE3, CK7, CK20) and hepatocellular markers are negative in the necrotic nodule, and residual vascular channels may be highlighted with CD34 or CD31 in sclerosed haemangioma.

entities.variants: Encapsulated fat necrosis nodule on the liver surface; calcified pseudolipoma
entities.remarks: Incidental small encapsulated nodule of mature, often necrotic fat attached to the liver capsule, probably detached appendix epiploica; benign; mimics a tumour at surgery or imaging.
entities.histo: The pseudolipoma of Glisson capsule is a small, well-circumscribed, encapsulated nodule of mature adipose tissue, usually less than 2 cm, located on the surface of the liver within a depression of the capsule. It is believed to originate from a detached colonic appendix epiploica that became trapped between the liver and the diaphragm. Microscopically, it consists of mature fat, often with fat necrosis, saponification, calcification and hyalinisation, enclosed in a fibrous capsule. It is benign and found incidentally at surgery or on imaging. The differentials include lipoma, angiomyolipoma (epithelioid myoid cells and thick-walled vessels), myelolipoma, liposarcoma and fat-containing hepatocellular tumours.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no role; if aspirated, mature adipocytes and necrotic fat would be seen.
entities.ihc: IHC is rarely necessary; HMB45 and Melan-A are negative, excluding angiomyolipoma, and MDM2 is negative, excluding well-differentiated liposarcoma.

entities.variants: Large cell change in chronic hepatitis B and C; in cirrhosis of any cause; in cholestatic liver disease; focal and diffuse
entities.remarks: Enlarged hepatocytes with proportionately enlarged, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic, often multinucleated nuclei, preserved nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio; reflects senescence and DNA damage; independent risk marker for HCC (especially HBV), not a direct precursor in most cases.
entities.histo: Large cell change, formerly called large cell dysplasia, describes hepatocytes that are enlarged together with their nuclei, so that the nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio is preserved, and the nuclei are pleomorphic, hyperchromatic and often multiple, with prominent nucleoli. It occurs in clusters or diffusely in chronic liver disease, most often in cirrhosis due to hepatitis B and in chronic cholestasis. Large cell change is thought to reflect hepatocyte senescence and DNA damage rather than a direct clonal precursor, but its presence in a biopsy is an independent marker of increased HCC risk, particularly in hepatitis B. It does not form a nodule by itself. The differentials include small cell change (increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio and cell crowding), dysplastic foci and nodules, well-differentiated HCC (architectural changes, reticulin loss, unpaired arteries) and reactive changes in regeneration, drugs (methotrexate) or after chemotherapy.
entities.cyto: In FNA, large cell change in cirrhosis produces enlarged hepatocytes with large, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant cytoplasm, which can be alarming; the preserved nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, cohesive flat sheets, admixed bile duct cells and lack of trabecular or endothelial wrapping favour a non-malignant process. Overcalling large cell change as HCC is a recognised pitfall. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: Large cell change is negative for glypican-3 and HSP70 in most cases, has a low Ki-67, and lacks the diffuse glutamine synthetase staining and CD34 sinusoidal capillarisation of HCC. p21 and other senescence markers may be expressed. IHC is used mainly when large cell change must be separated from HCC in a small biopsy.

entities.variants: Small cell change in cirrhosis; small cell change forming dysplastic foci; small cell change within dysplastic nodules
entities.remarks: Hepatocytes with decreased cell volume and increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, crowded, slightly hyperchromatic nuclei; true premalignant (clonal) lesion; can form dysplastic foci and nodules; cell density about 1.3 to 2 times normal.
entities.histo: Small cell change, formerly small cell dysplasia, is a precursor lesion in which hepatocytes have a smaller cell volume but normal or slightly enlarged nuclei, so that the nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio is increased and the cells appear crowded with increased nuclear density. The nuclei may be mildly hyperchromatic and irregular, and the cytoplasm is often more basophilic. Small cell change typically appears as foci in cirrhotic livers, may expand into dysplastic foci or nodules, and is considered a clonal premalignant lesion with genetic alterations similar to HCC, such as TERT promoter mutations in later stages. It is found adjacent to small HCCs and within high-grade dysplastic nodules. The differentials include large cell change, regenerating hepatocytes (normal nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio), well-differentiated HCC (stromal invasion, reticulin loss, thickened plates, pseudoglands, unpaired arteries) and ductular reaction or hepatic progenitor cell proliferation.
entities.cyto: On FNA, small cell change may produce crowded groups of small hepatocytes with high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, which overlaps with well-differentiated HCC; cytology alone cannot reliably separate these lesions, and cell block immunostains and histology are needed.
entities.ihc: Small cell change is usually negative or only focally positive for glypican-3, may show patchy HSP70 or glutamine synthetase staining, and has a modestly increased Ki-67. CD34 sinusoidal staining is limited. When two or more of glypican-3, HSP70 and glutamine synthetase are diffusely positive, well-differentiated HCC is favoured.

entities.variants: Dysplastic focus of small cell change; dysplastic focus of large cell change; iron-free focus in haemochromatosis; glycogen-storing (clear cell) foci; Mallory body-rich foci
entities.remarks: Cluster of dysplastic hepatocytes under 1 mm, found incidentally in chronic liver disease; usually small cell change; iron-free and glycogen-storing foci in iron-laden or other livers are also regarded as potential precursors.
entities.histo: A dysplastic focus is a microscopic cluster of hepatocytes with dysplastic features, by definition less than 1 mm across, found incidentally in chronic liver disease, usually in cirrhosis. Most are composed of small cell change, with increased cell density and nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, while some show large cell change. Iron-free foci in livers with haemochromatosis, which lack iron because of altered metabolism, and foci of glycogen-storing or clear cells in other conditions are also regarded as possible precursors of HCC. Dysplastic foci are not visible on imaging or gross examination and have no specific management, but they are markers of increased cancer risk and may evolve into dysplastic nodules or HCC. The differentials include regenerating hepatocytes, focal steatosis or glycogenosis, and small HCC.
entities.cyto: Dysplastic foci are not targeted by FNA, as they are microscopic and not visible on imaging.
entities.ihc: IHC is not used routinely; dysplastic foci may show patchy glypican-3 or glutamine synthetase positivity, and iron-free foci are recognised on Perls stain.

entities.variants: Low-grade dysplastic nodule in cirrhosis (HBV, HCV, alcohol, MASH); with large cell change; with clonal steatosis or clear cell change
entities.remarks: Nodule usually 1 to 1.5 cm, distinct from surrounding cirrhosis, with mild increase in cell density, no or minimal atypia, plates up to 2 cells thick, portal tracts present, few unpaired arteries; difficult to separate from large regenerative nodule.
entities.histo: A low-grade dysplastic nodule is a nodular lesion in cirrhosis, usually 1 to 1.5 cm, that is distinct from the background nodules by colour, size or texture, and contains hepatocytes with a mild increase in cell density and often large cell change but without significant architectural atypia. The plates are mostly one to two cells thick, the reticulin framework is preserved, portal tracts are present within the nodule, and unpaired arteries are absent or few. Clonal steatosis or clear cell change may distinguish the nodule from its surroundings. Low-grade dysplastic nodules have a low rate of progression to HCC and are difficult to distinguish from large regenerative nodules both histologically and radiologically, so they are often managed by surveillance. The differentials include large regenerative nodule (no clonal features, normal cell density), high-grade dysplastic nodule (marked atypia, small cell change, pseudoglands, more unpaired arteries) and well-differentiated HCC.
entities.cyto: FNA of a low-grade dysplastic nodule yields benign-appearing hepatocytes, sometimes with large cell change, which are indistinguishable from regenerative nodules or background cirrhosis. Cytology cannot classify these nodules, and core biopsy is preferred.
entities.ihc: Low-grade dysplastic nodules are generally negative for glypican-3 and HSP70, with glutamine synthetase in a patchy or perivenular pattern, CD34 sinusoidal staining limited to the periphery of the nodule, and low Ki-67. Positive staining for two or three of glypican-3, HSP70 and glutamine synthetase would favour HCC.

entities.variants: High-grade dysplastic nodule in cirrhosis; with nodule-in-nodule pattern (focus of HCC within HGDN, 'early HCC' transition); with small cell change; with steatosis or clear cells
entities.remarks: Nodule usually under 2 cm with moderate atypia but insufficient for HCC: increased cell density over twice normal, small cell change, focal pseudoglands, plates up to 3 cells, scattered unpaired arteries, no stromal invasion; high risk of progression to HCC; treat like early HCC in many centres.
entities.histo: A high-grade dysplastic nodule is a nodular lesion in cirrhosis that shows architectural and cytological atypia exceeding that of a low-grade dysplastic nodule, but insufficient for a diagnosis of HCC. It is usually less than 2 cm and may appear vaguely nodular. Microscopically, there is increased cell density, often more than twice that of the surrounding liver, frequent small cell change, focal pseudoglandular formation, plates up to three cells thick, focal reticulin loss and scattered unpaired arteries, while portal tracts may still be present within the nodule. The absence of stromal invasion, defined as invasion of tumour cells into portal tracts or fibrous septa, separates it from early HCC. A focus of HCC may develop within the nodule, producing a nodule-in-nodule appearance. High-grade dysplastic nodules carry a significant risk of progression to HCC, and many centres treat them similarly to early HCC. The differentials include early HCC (stromal invasion, more reticulin loss, more unpaired arteries, two of three HCC markers positive), low-grade dysplastic nodule, large regenerative nodule and hepatocellular adenoma in rare cirrhotic cases.
entities.cyto: On FNA, high-grade dysplastic nodules yield crowded groups of small hepatocytes with high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio and mild atypia, which overlap substantially with well-differentiated HCC. The distinction is not possible on cytology alone, and cell block reticulin and immunostains or core biopsy are needed.
entities.ihc: The International Consensus Group panel of glypican-3, HSP70 and glutamine synthetase is helpful: positivity for two or three markers favours early or well-differentiated HCC over a high-grade dysplastic nodule, though some HGDNs show one positive marker. CD34 shows increased but incomplete sinusoidal capillarisation, and CK7 or CK19 can show ductular reaction at the nodule periphery, which is preserved in dysplastic nodules and lost where stromal invasion occurs in early HCC.

entities.variants: Low-grade BilIN (formerly BilIN-1 and BilIN-2); high-grade BilIN (formerly BilIN-3, carcinoma in situ); flat, micropapillary and pseudopapillary patterns; intestinal-type BilIN; in large intrahepatic and hilar ducts, peribiliary glands, PSC, hepatolithiasis, liver fluke infection and choledochal cyst
entities.remarks: Microscopic (usually not visible on imaging or gross), flat or micropapillary dysplasia of large bile duct epithelium; two-tier grading (low and high grade); precursor of large duct intrahepatic and perihilar cholangiocarcinoma; frequent at resection margins.
entities.histo: Biliary intraepithelial neoplasia is a microscopic precursor lesion of cholangiocarcinoma that involves the large intrahepatic, hilar and extrahepatic bile ducts and their peribiliary glands. It arises in conditions such as hepatolithiasis, PSC, liver fluke infection and choledochal cysts, and is commonly found next to large duct cholangiocarcinoma and at resection margins. BilIN is flat or forms low micropapillary or pseudopapillary projections, without the tall papillae of intraductal papillary neoplasm, and it is not visible macroscopically or radiologically. It is graded in a two-tier system: low-grade BilIN shows mild to moderate atypia, with pseudostratified, elongated nuclei but preserved polarity, while high-grade BilIN shows marked atypia with loss of polarity, nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli and frequent mitoses, equivalent to carcinoma in situ. The differentials include reactive biliary atypia in inflammation or stents (gradual transition, inflammation, preserved polarity), intraductal papillary neoplasm (grossly visible, papillae on fibrovascular cores) and cancerisation of ducts by invasive carcinoma.
entities.cyto: In biliary brushings and bile cytology, high-grade BilIN cannot be distinguished from invasive carcinoma, and both are reported as suspicious or positive for malignancy, while low-grade BilIN is usually reported as atypical or negative. Reactive atypia in stented or inflamed ducts is a major pitfall.
entities.ihc: High-grade BilIN often shows aberrant p53 staining (strong diffuse or null), high Ki-67, loss of p16 and occasionally SMAD4 loss, and S100P and IMP3 are expressed more often in high-grade lesions and carcinoma than in reactive epithelium. MUC5AC is expressed in most BilIN, and MUC2 and CDX2 in intestinal-type lesions. These markers help, but none is absolutely specific.

entities.entity: Intraductal papillary neoplasm of the bile duct (IPNB)
entities.variants: Type 1 IPNB (intrahepatic, resembles pancreatic IPMN, mucin-rich, mostly low grade) and type 2 IPNB (extrahepatic, complex, often high grade with invasion); histological types: gastric, intestinal, pancreatobiliary and oncocytic (see IOPN); low-grade and high-grade dysplasia; IPNB with associated invasive carcinoma (tubular or colloid); cystic (formerly biliary cystadenoma without ovarian stroma) variant
entities.remarks: Grossly visible intraductal papillary or villous neoplasm with fibrovascular cores in dilated bile ducts, sometimes mucin-producing; counterpart of pancreatic IPMN; frequent in East Asia, hepatolithiasis and clonorchiasis; associated invasive carcinoma in a significant proportion; better prognosis than conventional cholangiocarcinoma.
entities.histo: Intraductal papillary neoplasm of the bile duct is a grossly visible premalignant neoplasm that grows within the lumen of intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile ducts as papillary or villous fronds supported by fibrovascular cores, causing ductal dilatation, often with mucin hypersecretion, and may be cystic. It is more common in East Asia and associated with hepatolithiasis and Clonorchis infection. Histologically it is classified by the predominant epithelium: pancreatobiliary type (cuboidal cells with complex papillae, often high grade), intestinal type (tall columnar cells with elongated nuclei and goblet cells), gastric type (gastric foveolar-like cells, often low grade) and oncocytic type, now considered a separate entity. Dysplasia is graded as low or high grade. Type 1 IPNB, usually intrahepatic, resembles pancreatic IPMN with regular papillae and frequent low-grade dysplasia, while type 2 IPNB, often extrahepatic, shows complex, irregular papillae, high-grade dysplasia and frequent invasion. Associated invasive carcinoma is tubular (pancreatobiliary type) or colloid (mucinous) and must be measured and staged separately. Thorough sampling is required. The differentials include BilIN (flat or micropapillary, microscopic), mucinous cystic neoplasm (no duct communication, ovarian-type stroma), intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm (tubular, little mucin), intraductal growth of cholangiocarcinoma or metastatic colorectal carcinoma, and reactive papillary hyperplasia.
entities.cyto: Bile and brushing cytology shows papillary clusters of columnar cells, sometimes with mucin; distinguishing low-grade from high-grade or invasive lesions is difficult, and the presence of mucin and papillary fragments is suggestive. Cytology is mainly used to detect high-grade or malignant cells.
entities.ihc: The epithelial type is defined by mucin markers: gastric type MUC5AC positive and MUC2 negative; intestinal type MUC2 and CDX2 positive; pancreatobiliary type MUC1 positive and MUC5AC positive; oncocytic type HepPar1 and MUC6 positive. CK7 is positive in most, and CK20 is positive in intestinal type. Aberrant p53, SMAD4 loss and high Ki-67 support high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. KRAS, GNAS and RNF43 alterations are found in subsets.

entities.entity: Intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasm (IOPN) of the bile ducts
entities.variants: IOPN with high-grade dysplasia (usual); IOPN with associated invasive carcinoma (usually minimal)
entities.remarks: Rare intraductal papillary neoplasm with complex arborising papillae lined by oncocytic cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli and intraepithelial lumens; usually high-grade; lacks KRAS/GNAS mutations, often PRKACA/PRKACB fusions; excellent prognosis even with invasion.
entities.histo: Intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasm of the bile ducts is a rare intraductal neoplasm, analogous to the pancreatic counterpart, now regarded as a distinct entity separate from other IPNB types. It forms a mass within dilated intrahepatic or extrahepatic ducts, composed of complex, arborising papillae lined by multiple layers of cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular (mitochondria-rich) cytoplasm and round nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Intraepithelial lumens creating a cribriform appearance are characteristic, and goblet cells may be scattered. Almost all cases show high-grade dysplasia, but associated invasive carcinoma is uncommon and usually minimal, and the prognosis is excellent after complete resection. Molecularly, IOPN lacks the KRAS and GNAS mutations of other IPNBs and often harbours PRKACA or PRKACB fusions. The differentials include other IPNB types, hepatocellular carcinoma with intraductal growth (HepPar1 can be positive in IOPN, which is a pitfall), oncocytic metastases and intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm.
entities.cyto: Cytology may show papillary clusters of oncocytic cells with abundant granular cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli, which can resemble hepatocytes or HCC; immunostains on cell block help.
entities.ihc: IOPN expresses CK7, CK19, MUC6 and MUC1, and often HepPar1, which can cause confusion with HCC; arginase-1 and glypican-3 are negative. Hep Par 1 positivity with negative arginase-1 is a clue. Mitochondrial antigen stains highlight the oncocytic cytoplasm. Ki-67 is variable. PRKACA rearrangements can be confirmed by FISH or sequencing.

entities.entity: Intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm (ITPN) of the bile ducts
entities.variants: ITPN with high-grade dysplasia; ITPN with associated invasive carcinoma
entities.remarks: Rare, mostly intrahepatic or hilar; intraductal solid nodules of back-to-back tubules with little mucin and frequent comedo-like necrosis; uniformly high-grade; lacks KRAS/GNAS mutations; may harbour FGFR2 fusions or PIK3CA alterations; better outcome than conventional cholangiocarcinoma.
entities.histo: Intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm of the bile ducts is a rare intraductal neoplasm, analogous to the pancreatic counterpart, that forms polypoid or solid nodules filling dilated ducts, mostly in the intrahepatic and hilar ducts. Microscopically, it consists of densely packed, back-to-back tubular glands and occasional papillae, lined by cuboidal cells with scant cytoplasm, little or no intracellular mucin and uniformly high-grade atypia, often with foci of comedo-like necrosis. Associated invasive carcinoma occurs in a proportion of cases but is often limited. Molecularly, ITPN lacks the KRAS and GNAS mutations of IPNB and may have FGFR2 fusions, PIK3CA or other alterations. The prognosis is generally better than for conventional cholangiocarcinoma. The differentials include IPNB (papillary fronds, mucin), intraductal spread of invasive cholangiocarcinoma, intraductal growth of metastatic carcinoma (colorectal, CDX2 and CK20 positive), and acinar cell carcinoma or neuroendocrine tumours with intraductal growth.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows crowded, three-dimensional tubular clusters of high-grade cuboidal cells with little mucin, which are usually reported as suspicious or positive for malignancy; distinction from invasive carcinoma is not possible on cytology.
entities.ihc: ITPN is positive for CK7, CK19 and MUC1, often MUC6 positive, and negative for MUC5AC and MUC2, unlike IPNB; trypsin and BCL10 are negative (excluding acinar cell carcinoma), and synaptophysin and chromogranin are negative (excluding NET). CDX2 and CK20 are negative, helping to exclude metastatic colorectal carcinoma.

entities.entity: Mucinous cystic neoplasm (MCN) of the liver
entities.variants: MCN with low-grade dysplasia; MCN with high-grade dysplasia; MCN with associated invasive carcinoma (formerly biliary cystadenocarcinoma); WHO older term hepatobiliary cystadenoma
entities.remarks: Almost exclusively women; multilocular cyst, usually left lobe (segment IV), without communication to bile ducts; columnar mucinous epithelium over ovarian-type stroma (ER, PR, inhibin positive) is mandatory; complete excision; invasive carcinoma in a minority.
entities.histo: Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver is a cyst-forming epithelial neoplasm, previously called hepatobiliary cystadenoma or cystadenocarcinoma, that arises almost exclusively in middle-aged women, typically in the left lobe, especially segment IV. It forms a large, multilocular cyst with smooth or trabeculated internal septa, containing mucinous or clear fluid, and characteristically does not communicate with the bile ducts. Microscopically, the cysts are lined by cuboidal to columnar mucinous epithelium, sometimes with gastric, intestinal or biliary differentiation, resting on a dense cellular ovarian-type stroma, which is required for the diagnosis. Dysplasia is graded as low or high grade, and a minority of cases harbour an associated invasive carcinoma, usually tubular adenocarcinoma, which should be searched for in solid areas and mural nodules. Complete surgical excision is curative for non-invasive lesions, whereas fenestration or aspiration leads to recurrence. The differentials include simple biliary cyst (no ovarian-type stroma), intraductal papillary neoplasm with cystic change (communicates with bile ducts, no ovarian stroma), ciliated hepatic foregut cyst, hydatid cyst, cystic metastases and endometriotic cysts.
entities.cyto: Cyst fluid aspiration yields mucinous material with scant columnar or cuboidal mucinous cells and macrophages; cytology has low sensitivity and is not specific, and the stroma is not sampled. Elevated cyst fluid CEA and CA19-9 support a mucinous lesion but are not definitive. Atypical cells suggest high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma.
entities.ihc: The ovarian-type stroma is positive for ER, PR and often inhibin, calretinin and SMA, which confirms the diagnosis and separates MCN from IPNB and simple cysts. The epithelium is CK7 and CK19 positive, with variable MUC5AC and CK20 expression. Aberrant p53 and high Ki-67 support high-grade dysplasia or invasion.

entities.entity: Hepatocellular adenoma - overview (including adenomatosis and special settings)
entities.variants: Solitary hepatocellular adenoma; multiple adenomas and liver adenomatosis (10 or more); HCA in men, GSD I and III, MODY3, anabolic steroid use, congenital portosystemic shunt, obesity and metabolic syndrome; pigmented HCA; HCA with haemorrhage or rupture; HCA with malignant transformation; molecular subtypes (see separate rows)
entities.remarks: Benign clonal hepatocellular neoplasm, mostly young women on oral contraceptives, in non-cirrhotic liver; sheets of benign hepatocytes in thin plates without portal tracts, with unpaired arteries; risks are bleeding (over 5 cm) and malignant transformation (mainly beta-catenin exon 3, men); subtype by IHC.
entities.histo: Hepatocellular adenoma is a benign neoplasm of hepatocytes that usually occurs in non-cirrhotic livers of young women, strongly associated with oral contraceptive use, and increasingly with obesity and metabolic syndrome. It also arises in men, in glycogen storage diseases, with anabolic steroids, in congenital portosystemic shunts and in MODY3 (germline HNF1A mutation). Adenomas may be single or multiple, and liver adenomatosis is defined as ten or more. Grossly they are well-circumscribed, unencapsulated, soft, tan to yellow nodules, often with haemorrhage or necrosis. Microscopically they are composed of sheets and plates of benign hepatocytes, one to two cells thick, without portal tracts, with scattered thin-walled unpaired arteries and a preserved reticulin framework. Cytoplasm may be normal, clear, steatotic or contain pigment (pigmented adenoma with lipofuscin). Haemorrhage and peliosis are common. Complications are rupture with haemoperitoneum, particularly in tumours over 5 cm, and malignant transformation into HCC, most often in beta-catenin exon 3-mutated adenomas and in men. The molecular classification divides adenomas into HNF1A-inactivated, inflammatory, beta-catenin-activated (exon 3 and exon 7/8), mixed beta-catenin-activated inflammatory, sonic hedgehog-activated and unclassified subtypes, which are identified by immunohistochemistry and have different risks. The differentials include FNH (central scar, ductular reaction, map-like glutamine synthetase), well-differentiated HCC (reticulin loss, thick plates, atypia, glypican-3), large regenerative and dysplastic nodules, and angiomyolipoma with epithelioid morphology.
entities.cyto: FNA of a hepatocellular adenoma yields sheets of benign-appearing hepatocytes with abundant cytoplasm, sometimes with fat or glycogen, and characteristically lacks bile duct cells; however, cytology cannot reliably separate adenoma from FNH, normal liver or well-differentiated HCC, and core biopsy with immunostains is preferred. Haemorrhagic aspirates are common. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: Subtyping requires a panel: LFABP (loss in HNF1A-inactivated adenoma), CRP and SAA (positive in inflammatory adenoma), glutamine synthetase and beta-catenin (diffuse strong GS and nuclear beta-catenin in exon 3 mutation; faint or patchy GS in exon 7/8), and argininosuccinate synthase or prostaglandin D2 synthase (positive in sonic hedgehog adenoma). Glypican-3 is negative and HSP70 negative; CD34 shows diffuse sinusoidal staining, which is not helpful for HCC distinction. Ki-67 is low. Reticulin preservation and lack of glypican-3 help separate adenoma from well-differentiated HCC, and molecular testing for CTNNB1 and TERT promoter mutations is used in borderline lesions.

entities.variants: Sporadic (somatic biallelic HNF1A inactivation); germline HNF1A mutation (MODY3) with adenomatosis; steatotic and non-steatotic forms
entities.remarks: About 30 to 35% of HCAs; women, OCP-related; frequently multiple; marked diffuse steatosis, no inflammatory infiltrate, no atypia; diagnostic LFABP loss; very low risk of malignant transformation.
entities.histo: HNF1A-inactivated hepatocellular adenoma accounts for about a third of adenomas and is caused by biallelic inactivation of the HNF1A gene, which is somatic in most cases and germline in patients with MODY3, who often have adenomatosis. It occurs almost exclusively in women, often in association with oral contraceptive use, and is frequently multiple. Grossly the tumours are yellow and soft. Microscopically they show marked diffuse macrovesicular steatosis, often more than in the surrounding liver, in sheets of benign hepatocytes without portal tracts and without the inflammatory infiltrate, sinusoidal dilatation or ductular reaction seen in inflammatory adenomas. Cytological atypia is absent, and the reticulin framework is preserved. The risk of malignant transformation is very low, and the risk of bleeding is lower than for inflammatory adenomas. Microadenomas may be present in the background liver. The differentials include focal fatty change (portal tracts preserved, LFABP retained), steatohepatitic HCC (atypia, reticulin loss), angiomyolipoma with fat (epithelioid myoid cells, HMB45 positive) and FNH.
entities.cyto: FNA yields benign hepatocytes with prominent macrovesicular fat, lacking bile duct cells; it cannot distinguish this subtype from steatotic background liver or focal fatty change without immunostaining of a cell block.
