entities.ihc: The diagnostic finding is complete loss of LFABP (liver fatty acid binding protein) expression in tumour hepatocytes, with retained expression in adjacent non-tumoural liver as an internal control. CRP and SAA are negative, glutamine synthetase shows a normal or patchy pattern, and beta-catenin is membranous only. Glypican-3 and HSP70 are negative.

entities.variants: Inflammatory HCA with IL6ST, STAT3, GNAS, JAK1, FRK or ROS1 alterations; telangiectatic adenoma (formerly telangiectatic FNH); inflammatory HCA in obesity and alcohol use; with steatosis
entities.remarks: Commonest subtype (about 40 to 50%); obesity, metabolic syndrome, alcohol; inflammatory infiltrate, sinusoidal dilatation, peliosis, thick-walled arteries in pseudoportal tracts with ductular reaction; CRP and SAA strongly positive; highest bleeding risk; malignant transformation mainly when beta-catenin also activated.
entities.histo: Inflammatory hepatocellular adenoma is the commonest subtype, caused by activation of the IL-6/JAK/STAT3 pathway through mutations in genes such as IL6ST, STAT3, GNAS, JAK1 and FRK. It occurs mainly in women using oral contraceptives, and in patients with obesity, metabolic syndrome or alcohol use. It is the subtype formerly known as telangiectatic FNH. Grossly, the tumour is often haemorrhagic. Microscopically, it shows sheets of benign hepatocytes with prominent sinusoidal dilatation, congestion and peliosis, thick-walled unpaired arteries, and pseudoportal tracts consisting of arteries surrounded by inflammatory cells and a ductular reaction, which can mimic FNH. The inflammatory infiltrate is lymphocytic and may be patchy. Steatosis may be present. Inflammatory adenomas have the highest risk of bleeding among the subtypes, and about 10% also harbour a beta-catenin activating mutation (beta-catenin-activated inflammatory adenoma), which increases the risk of malignant transformation. Patients may have systemic inflammatory symptoms such as fever, anaemia and raised CRP. The differentials include FNH (central scar, nodular architecture, map-like glutamine synthetase, CRP negative or only patchy), well-differentiated HCC, and peliosis hepatis.
entities.cyto: Aspirates are often bloody and contain benign hepatocytes with occasional inflammatory cells and ductular cells from pseudoportal tracts, which can be mistaken for FNH; cytology cannot subtype adenomas without immunostaining.
entities.ihc: CRP and SAA show strong, diffuse cytoplasmic staining in tumour hepatocytes, with a sharp contrast to the background liver (although background CRP staining can be positive in inflamed livers). LFABP is retained. Glutamine synthetase is normal or patchy, unless beta-catenin is also activated, in which case GS is diffuse and beta-catenin may be nuclear. Glypican-3 is negative.

entities.variants: Exon 3 non-S45 mutations (deletions, strong activation); exon 3 S45 mutations (moderate activation, weaker GS staining); HCA with atypical features in men and with anabolic steroids or GSD
entities.remarks: About 10% of HCAs; more common in men, anabolic steroid users and GSD; often mild cytological atypia and pseudoglands; highest risk of malignant transformation to HCC; diffuse strong glutamine synthetase and nuclear beta-catenin; resection recommended regardless of size.
entities.histo: Beta-catenin-activated hepatocellular adenoma with CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation accounts for about one in ten adenomas and is clinically important because it carries the highest risk of malignant transformation into hepatocellular carcinoma. It is relatively more common in men, in patients using anabolic-androgenic steroids, and in glycogen storage disease. Microscopically the tumour consists of hepatocytes that often show mild cytological atypia, increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, pseudoglandular formations and cholestasis, without the inflammatory features of inflammatory adenomas, and the boundaries with well-differentiated HCC may be difficult to define. Areas with focal reticulin loss, increased atypia or TERT promoter mutation indicate malignant transformation, and such lesions are sometimes called atypical hepatocellular neoplasm or HCA with focal atypia. Exon 3 S45 mutations cause weaker pathway activation and may show only heterogeneous GS staining. Because of the malignancy risk, resection is recommended regardless of size, and in men all adenomas are usually resected. The differentials include well-differentiated HCC, high-grade dysplastic nodules, FNH and other adenoma subtypes.
entities.cyto: FNA cannot reliably separate this subtype from well-differentiated HCC; aspirates show hepatocytes with mild atypia and occasional acinar arrangements, and cell block immunostains (GS, beta-catenin) plus histology are required.
entities.ihc: Glutamine synthetase shows strong, diffuse (homogeneous) cytoplasmic staining throughout the tumour, and beta-catenin shows nuclear staining in a proportion of tumour cells, which can be focal, so GS is the more sensitive marker. LFABP is retained, and CRP and SAA are negative unless mixed inflammatory type. Glypican-3 is negative or focal; diffuse glypican-3, HSP70 positivity and reticulin loss suggest transformation to HCC. Molecular testing for CTNNB1 exon 3 and TERT promoter mutations aids risk assessment.

entities.variants: CTNNB1 exon 7 or exon 8 mutations (weak activation)
entities.remarks: About 5% of HCAs; weak beta-catenin activation; GS staining faint or patchy (often perivascular or rim), nuclear beta-catenin absent; no clear increase in malignancy risk; easily misclassified as unclassified HCA without molecular testing.
entities.histo: Hepatocellular adenomas with CTNNB1 exon 7 or exon 8 mutations represent a small group, around 5% of adenomas, in which beta-catenin pathway activation is weak. They usually lack distinctive histological features and resemble unclassified adenomas, consisting of sheets of benign hepatocytes without portal tracts, with scattered unpaired arteries and preserved reticulin. Atypia and pseudoglands are generally absent. Unlike exon 3-mutated adenomas, they do not appear to have a substantially increased risk of malignant transformation. The diagnosis relies on immunohistochemistry patterns and confirmation by molecular testing. The differentials include unclassified adenoma, exon 3 S45-mutated adenoma (which may also show heterogeneous GS) and FNH.
entities.cyto: Cytology cannot identify this subtype; aspirates show benign hepatocytes without bile duct cells.
entities.ihc: Glutamine synthetase staining is faint and patchy or heterogeneous, sometimes accentuated around vessels or at the periphery, and nuclear beta-catenin is not seen. LFABP is retained, and CRP and SAA are negative (unless mixed). Molecular testing of CTNNB1 confirms exon 7/8 mutations.

entities.variants: Inflammatory HCA with CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation; inflammatory HCA with exon 7/8 mutation
entities.remarks: About 10% of HCAs; combines inflammatory features (sinusoidal dilatation, inflammation, CRP/SAA positive) with beta-catenin activation (diffuse GS, nuclear beta-catenin); carries risk of malignant transformation like beta-catenin-activated HCA.
entities.histo: Beta-catenin-activated inflammatory hepatocellular adenoma combines the features of inflammatory adenoma, caused by IL-6/JAK/STAT3 activation, with an additional CTNNB1 mutation, and accounts for around one in ten adenomas. Histologically it shows the sinusoidal dilatation, peliosis, inflammatory infiltrates, thick-walled arteries and pseudoportal tracts with ductular reaction of inflammatory adenoma, together, in exon 3-mutated cases, with features of beta-catenin activation such as mild atypia and pseudoglands. The importance of recognising this subtype lies in its risk of malignant transformation, which depends on the beta-catenin mutation type and is greatest for exon 3 mutations. The differentials include pure inflammatory adenoma, beta-catenin-activated adenoma, FNH and well-differentiated HCC.
entities.cyto: Cytology cannot subtype the lesion; aspirates show benign hepatocytes with occasional inflammatory cells and ductular cells.
entities.ihc: CRP and SAA show diffuse strong staining, and glutamine synthetase shows diffuse strong (exon 3) or patchy (exon 7/8) staining, with nuclear beta-catenin in a proportion of exon 3 cases. LFABP is retained. Glypican-3 and HSP70 are negative unless transformation to HCC is present. CTNNB1 mutation testing confirms the type.

entities.variants: INHBE::GLI1 fusion-driven adenoma; shHCA with haemorrhage
entities.remarks: About 4% of HCAs; obesity-associated; frequently symptomatic bleeding; activation of sonic hedgehog pathway through INHBE::GLI1 fusion; argininosuccinate synthase (ASS1) and prostaglandin D2 synthase (PTGDS) positive.
entities.histo: Sonic hedgehog-activated hepatocellular adenoma is a recently described subtype, accounting for a small proportion of adenomas, defined by focal deletions that fuse INHBE and GLI1, activating the sonic hedgehog pathway. It is associated with obesity and is particularly prone to symptomatic haemorrhage. Histologically it lacks specific features, but haemorrhage, necrosis and peliosis are common, and it lacks the inflammatory infiltrates and pseudoportal tracts of inflammatory adenoma. Most of these tumours were previously classified as unclassified adenomas. The risk of malignant transformation appears low, but haemorrhage is a significant clinical risk. The differentials include unclassified adenoma, inflammatory adenoma and haemorrhagic HCC.
entities.cyto: Cytology cannot identify this subtype; aspirates show benign hepatocytes without bile duct cells, sometimes with blood and haemosiderin from the haemorrhage that is typical of this adenoma. Subtyping requires tissue with argininosuccinate synthase 1 (ASS1) and prostaglandin D2 synthase immunostains or molecular testing.
entities.ihc: Argininosuccinate synthase 1 (ASS1) and prostaglandin D2 synthase (PTGDS) immunostaining are positive in shHCA and help identify it, although ASS1 can also be expressed in some inflammatory adenomas. LFABP is retained, CRP and SAA are negative, and glutamine synthetase is not diffusely positive. Molecular testing for INHBE::GLI1 fusion confirms the diagnosis.

entities.variants: Adenoma without HNF1A, inflammatory, beta-catenin or sonic hedgehog features on IHC and molecular testing
entities.remarks: Under 10% of HCAs after full IHC and molecular work-up; no specific morphology; diagnosis of exclusion; management according to size and sex.
entities.histo: Unclassified hepatocellular adenoma is the term for adenomas that do not show the immunohistochemical or molecular features of the defined subtypes. The proportion of such tumours has fallen with the identification of sonic hedgehog-activated and exon 7/8-mutated adenomas, and it is now under one in ten adenomas. Histologically they show the general features of adenoma: sheets of benign hepatocytes without portal tracts, with unpaired arteries, preserved reticulin and no significant atypia. Management depends on clinical factors such as tumour size, sex and growth. The differentials include FNH, well-differentiated HCC and the defined adenoma subtypes, which should be excluded with a complete IHC panel and molecular testing where available.
entities.cyto: Cytology shows benign hepatocytes and cannot subtype the adenoma.
entities.ihc: The panel shows retained LFABP, negative CRP and SAA, normal or patchy glutamine synthetase without nuclear beta-catenin, and negative ASS1 or PTGDS, by definition. Glypican-3 is negative. Molecular testing is used where available to exclude subtle subtypes.

entities.variants: Classic FNH (central stellate scar); non-classic FNH (no visible scar, small, multiple); multiple FNH syndrome (with haemangiomas, vascular malformations, CNS tumours); FNH-like nodules in vascular disorders (Budd-Chiari, Fontan, portosystemic shunts, HHT, after chemotherapy); former 'telangiectatic FNH' is now inflammatory HCA
entities.remarks: Polyclonal hyperplastic response to arterial malformation, mainly young women; well-circumscribed lobulated nodule with central stellate scar containing dystrophic thick-walled arteries, fibrous septa with ductular reaction, no normal portal tracts; map-like glutamine synthetase is diagnostic; no malignant potential.
entities.histo: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a benign, polyclonal hepatocellular lesion that represents a hyperplastic response of hepatocytes to a localised arterial malformation with increased blood flow. It is the second most common benign liver lesion after haemangioma, mostly found in young to middle-aged women, and is usually asymptomatic and solitary. Grossly it is a well-circumscribed but unencapsulated, lobulated, tan nodule, often with a central stellate fibrous scar from which septa radiate, dividing the lesion into nodules. Microscopically, the central scar contains large, dystrophic, thick-walled arteries with intimal hyperplasia and medial thickening, and fibrous septa with chronic inflammation and ductular reaction at their interface with hepatocytes, but no true bile ducts or normal portal tracts. The hepatocyte nodules show normal or slightly thickened plates, and may contain cholate stasis, copper-associated protein, Mallory-Denk bodies and steatosis near the septa. Non-classic forms lack a visible scar, and small needle biopsies may be difficult to interpret. FNH has no malignant potential and rarely bleeds, so it is usually managed conservatively. The differentials include hepatocellular adenoma (especially inflammatory type with pseudoportal tracts and ductular reaction), well-differentiated HCC and fibrolamellar carcinoma (both of which can have central scars), cirrhosis (in small biopsies), and FNH-like nodules in vascular disorders.
entities.cyto: Aspirates of FNH yield benign hepatocytes, bile ductular cells and occasional fragments of fibrous stroma with vessels; the presence of ductular cells is a clue, but the distinction from cirrhosis, adenoma and well-differentiated HCC is not reliable on cytology alone, and core biopsy with glutamine synthetase staining is preferred.
entities.ihc: Glutamine synthetase shows a characteristic map-like pattern of anastomosing groups of positive hepatocytes, often surrounding hepatic veins and sparing areas near septa, which is diagnostic and distinguishes FNH from adenoma (normal, absent or diffuse GS). CK7 and CK19 highlight ductular reaction in the septa. CRP and SAA can be patchily positive, which can cause confusion with inflammatory adenoma. LFABP is retained, beta-catenin is membranous, and glypican-3 is negative. CD34 shows patchy sinusoidal staining near septa.

entities.variants: Conventional bile duct adenoma; clear cell bile duct adenoma; bile duct adenoma with alpha-1 antitrypsin globules; oncocytic variant; BRAF V600E-mutated adenoma
entities.remarks: Common incidental small (usually under 1 cm) subcapsular firm white nodule; small, tightly packed, uniform tubules without bile, in fibrous stroma with chronic inflammation; thought to derive from peribiliary glands; key mimic of metastatic adenocarcinoma at frozen section.
entities.histo: Bile duct adenoma is a small benign lesion, often found incidentally during surgery for other conditions, usually as a single, firm, well-circumscribed, white subcapsular nodule smaller than 1 cm. It is thought to arise from peribiliary glands, and some regard it as a reactive lesion or hamartoma, although BRAF V600E mutations in a subset suggest a neoplastic nature. Microscopically, it consists of numerous small, uniform, round to oval tubules or acini lined by cuboidal cells with bland nuclei and no mitoses, closely packed in a fibrous stroma that often contains lymphocytes and plasma cells, especially at the periphery. The tubules lack lumen bile and do not show the dilated irregular shape of von Meyenburg complexes. Clear cell, oncocytic and alpha-1 antitrypsin globule-containing variants exist. Portal tracts may be entrapped at the periphery. The main importance of bile duct adenoma is at frozen section, where it can mimic metastatic adenocarcinoma or well-differentiated cholangiocarcinoma. Features favouring adenoma include small size, circumscription, uniform bland tubules, lack of mitoses or necrosis, and inflammation in the stroma. The differentials also include von Meyenburg complex, biliary adenofibroma, ductular reaction and neuroendocrine tumour.
entities.cyto: Aspirates are rarely obtained; if sampled, they yield small cohesive clusters of bland cuboidal cells, which can be mistaken for well-differentiated adenocarcinoma.
entities.ihc: The tubules are CK7 and CK19 positive, and they often express MUC6 and CD56, reflecting peribiliary gland differentiation. Ki-67 is very low, p53 shows wild-type staining, and SMAD4 is retained, unlike many adenocarcinomas. CDX2 and CK20 are negative, excluding colorectal metastasis. BRAF V600E immunostaining may be positive in a subset.

entities.variants: Biliary adenofibroma; with dysplasia; with malignant transformation (adenofibroma with associated cholangiocarcinoma)
entities.remarks: Rare benign tumour of microcystic and tubular biliary glands in abundant fibrous stroma, often large (up to 20 cm); can show atypia and malignant transformation; complete resection.
entities.histo: Biliary adenofibroma is a rare benign biliary neoplasm that presents as a solitary, well-circumscribed, solid and microcystic mass, sometimes very large. Microscopically, it consists of tubules, acini and microcysts lined by cuboidal to low columnar biliary epithelium with bland nuclei, sometimes with apocrine-like snouts, embedded in abundant fibrous stroma that may resemble fibroblastic or cellular stroma. Bile may be present in some lumens. The lesion is considered a counterpart of the pancreatic microcystic adenoma or a neoplastic von Meyenburg complex. Cases with epithelial dysplasia or malignant transformation into cholangiocarcinoma have been reported, so complete resection and thorough sampling are recommended. The differentials include bile duct adenoma (small, no microcysts), von Meyenburg complexes, mucinous cystic neoplasm (ovarian-type stroma), cholangiocarcinoma (atypia, infiltration) and mesenchymal hamartoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology is rarely performed; aspirates would show small clusters of bland biliary cells and stromal fragments, which are non-specific.
entities.ihc: The epithelium is CK7 and CK19 positive, and the stroma is vimentin and SMA positive and lacks ER and PR, unlike mucinous cystic neoplasm. Ki-67 is low, p53 shows wild-type staining in benign areas, and aberrant p53 or high Ki-67 suggests dysplasia or malignant transformation.

entities.variants: Cavernous haemangioma (commonest); giant haemangioma (over 5 to 10 cm); sclerosing (sclerosed, hyalinised) haemangioma; capillary haemangioma; anastomosing haemangioma; multiple haemangiomas; Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon (giant haemangioma with consumptive coagulopathy)
entities.remarks: Commonest benign liver tumour; dilated vascular spaces lined by flat endothelium and separated by fibrous septa; sclerosed forms with hyalinised fibrosis mimic metastasis; peripheral nodular enhancement on imaging; FNA risk of bleeding is low but often non-diagnostic.
entities.histo: Cavernous haemangioma is the most common benign tumour of the liver, found in a significant proportion of the population and more common in women. Most are small, solitary and asymptomatic, but giant haemangiomas can cause pain, compression, consumptive coagulopathy (Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon) or rarely rupture. Grossly, it is a well-circumscribed, red-blue, spongy lesion that collapses on sectioning, often with central fibrosis or thrombosis. Microscopically, it consists of large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces lined by a single layer of flat, bland endothelial cells and separated by fibrous septa of varying thickness. Thrombosis, organisation, calcification and hyalinisation are common, and in sclerosing haemangioma the vascular channels are largely replaced by dense hyalinised fibrous tissue with residual compressed vessels, which can mimic metastatic carcinoma or cholangiocarcinoma on imaging. Anastomosing haemangioma shows anastomosing sinusoidal capillary-sized vessels lined by hobnail endothelium, often with extramedullary haematopoiesis, and must be separated from angiosarcoma. Capillary haemangioma has small, capillary-sized channels. The differentials include angiosarcoma (infiltrative, atypical multilayered endothelium, high Ki-67), peliosis hepatis (no fibrous septa), hepatic small vessel neoplasm, epithelioid haemangioendothelioma and solitary necrotic nodule.
entities.cyto: FNA of a haemangioma typically yields blood only, sometimes with a few spindle endothelial cells or fragments of fibrous stroma with capillaries; the procedure is considered relatively safe with fine needles but is rarely diagnostic, and the diagnosis is usually made on imaging.
entities.ihc: The endothelium is positive for CD31, CD34, ERG and FLI1, with a very low Ki-67 and negative GLUT1, which distinguishes it from infantile haemangioma. Angiosarcoma shows nuclear atypia, multilayering, high Ki-67 and often MYC amplification in secondary cases. D2-40 is negative or focal. In sclerosing haemangioma, CD34 and CD31 identify the residual compressed vessels among the hyalinised stroma.

entities.variants: Focal, multifocal and diffuse hepatic infantile haemangioma; associated with cutaneous infantile haemangiomas; diffuse form with hypothyroidism (type 3 iodothyronine deiodinase) and high-output cardiac failure; historical term infantile haemangioendothelioma (type 1)
entities.remarks: Commonest benign hepatic vascular tumour of infancy; proliferating small capillary-sized vessels lined by plump endothelium with pericytes, involuting with fibrosis; GLUT1 positive (unlike congenital haemangioma); multifocal and diffuse forms carry risk of heart failure and hypothyroidism; treated with propranolol.
entities.histo: Hepatic infantile haemangioma is a benign vascular tumour of infancy that typically appears in the first months of life, proliferates and then involutes, analogous to cutaneous infantile haemangioma, which often coexists in multifocal disease. It may be focal, multifocal or diffuse. Multifocal and diffuse forms can cause hepatomegaly, high-output cardiac failure due to shunting, abdominal compartment syndrome and consumptive hypothyroidism caused by tumour production of type 3 iodothyronine deiodinase. Microscopically, it consists of numerous small, capillary-sized vascular channels lined by plump endothelial cells with a surrounding pericyte layer, sometimes forming lobules, with entrapped bile ducts and hepatocytes at the periphery. During involution, the vessels become dilated and are replaced by fibrous tissue, with calcification and thrombosis. The term infantile haemangioendothelioma type 1 was used historically, while lesions formerly called type 2, with atypical endothelial cells and solid areas, are now regarded as angiosarcoma. Propranolol is the first-line treatment. The differentials include congenital haemangioma (GLUT1 negative, present at birth), angiosarcoma in childhood (atypia, solid areas, high Ki-67), mesenchymal hamartoma, hepatoblastoma, and arteriovenous malformation.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role; aspirates are usually bloody and contain small clusters of endothelial cells, which can raise concern for a small round cell tumour such as hepatoblastoma, and core biopsy or imaging diagnosis is preferred.
entities.ihc: Endothelial cells are positive for CD31, CD34, ERG and, characteristically, GLUT1 (also merosin, Lewis Y antigen), which distinguishes infantile haemangioma from congenital haemangioma, vascular malformations and other vascular tumours. SMA highlights the pericyte layer. Ki-67 is high during proliferation, which should not be misinterpreted as angiosarcoma in the absence of atypia.

entities.variants: Rapidly involuting congenital haemangioma (RICH); partially involuting (PICH); non-involuting (NICH); focal solitary hepatic haemangioma detected prenatally
entities.remarks: Fully formed at birth (often seen on prenatal imaging), solitary, focal; involutes rapidly in the first year (RICH); GLUT1 negative; lobules of capillaries with central draining vessels, thrombosis, calcification; GNAQ/GNA11 mutations.
entities.histo: Congenital haemangioma of the liver is a vascular tumour that is fully developed at birth, often detected on prenatal ultrasound, and typically presents as a solitary focal lesion. Most hepatic congenital haemangiomas are of the rapidly involuting type, regressing during the first year of life, while partially involuting and non-involuting forms are less common in the liver. They may cause transient anaemia, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy or high-output heart failure from shunting. Microscopically, the tumour shows lobules of small capillaries lined by plump endothelium with pericytes, separated by fibrous tissue, with central large draining vessels, and frequent thrombosis, haemorrhage, calcification and haemosiderin, reflecting involution. Somatic GNAQ or GNA11 mutations are present. Unlike infantile haemangioma, it does not respond to propranolol and is GLUT1 negative. The differentials include hepatic infantile haemangioma, arteriovenous malformation, mesenchymal hamartoma, angiosarcoma and hepatoblastoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role; aspirates are usually bloody and non-diagnostic.
entities.ihc: Endothelial cells are CD31, CD34 and ERG positive and GLUT1 negative, which separates congenital from infantile haemangioma. Ki-67 is low in involuting lesions, and SMA highlights pericytes.

entities.variants: Solitary hepatic lymphangioma (cystic lymphatic malformation); diffuse hepatic lymphangiomatosis (with splenic, bone and soft tissue involvement, generalised lymphatic anomaly, Gorham-Stout disease)
entities.remarks: Rare; multicystic spaces lined by flat endothelium containing proteinaceous lymph, with lymphoid aggregates and smooth muscle in walls; diffuse forms part of systemic lymphatic anomalies; D2-40 and PROX1 positive.
entities.histo: Lymphangioma of the liver is a rare lymphatic malformation that may be solitary or part of diffuse lymphangiomatosis involving the spleen, bones, soft tissue and other organs, as in generalised lymphatic anomaly and Gorham-Stout disease. It forms a multicystic or spongy lesion containing clear or milky fluid. Microscopically, it consists of irregular, dilated, thin-walled channels lined by flat endothelial cells, containing pale eosinophilic proteinaceous lymph with few red cells, often with lymphoid aggregates and smooth muscle bundles in the walls. Diffuse lymphangiomatosis infiltrates the liver between portal tracts and lobules. The differentials include cavernous haemangioma (blood-filled spaces), simple and polycystic cysts (biliary epithelial lining), mesenchymal hamartoma (myxoid stroma with ducts) and angiosarcoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates yield clear or chylous fluid rich in lymphocytes, which is non-specific.
entities.ihc: The endothelial lining is positive for D2-40 (podoplanin), PROX1 and LYVE1, as well as CD31 and ERG, while CD34 is often weak or negative, which separates lymphatic from blood vascular lesions. Keratins are negative, excluding biliary cysts.

entities.variants: Classic triphasic angiomyolipoma; epithelioid angiomyolipoma; lipoma-like (fat-predominant), myomatous (myoid-predominant), angiomatous and trabecular variants; inflammatory angiomyolipoma; tuberous sclerosis complex-associated angiomyolipoma; malignant PEComa (separate)
entities.remarks: Second commonest site after kidney; mostly sporadic in adults, women; mixture of thick-walled vessels, adipose tissue and epithelioid or spindle myoid perivascular epithelioid cells with extramedullary haematopoiesis; melanocytic (HMB45, Melan-A) and myoid (SMA, desmin) markers; can mimic HCC on imaging and histology.
entities.histo: Angiomyolipoma is a tumour of perivascular epithelioid cells (PEComa family), and the liver is the second most common site after the kidney. Most hepatic angiomyolipomas are sporadic and occur in adults, more often women, and only a minority are associated with tuberous sclerosis complex. Grossly the tumour is well-circumscribed, yellow to tan, and may be haemorrhagic. Microscopically, it classically contains three components in varying proportions: thick-walled, hyalinised blood vessels, mature adipose tissue, and smooth muscle-like perivascular epithelioid cells that may be spindle-shaped or epithelioid, with abundant clear to eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, sometimes with large nuclei and nucleoli. Extramedullary haematopoiesis is common, and melanin pigment may be seen. Variants include fat-predominant (lipomatous), myoid-predominant (myomatous), angiomatous, trabecular and inflammatory forms, and epithelioid angiomyolipoma, which consists predominantly of epithelioid cells and can closely mimic hepatocellular carcinoma. Most behave benignly, but epithelioid tumours with atypia, necrosis, mitoses and large size may behave aggressively (malignant PEComa). The differentials include HCC (especially clear cell and steatohepatitic types), hepatocellular adenoma with steatosis, lipoma or liposarcoma, focal fatty change, GIST or leiomyosarcoma metastases, melanoma and inflammatory pseudotumour.
entities.cyto: FNA may show clusters of epithelioid or spindle cells with abundant granular or vacuolated cytoplasm, mature fat and naked nuclei, which can be mistaken for hepatocytes or HCC; atypical epithelioid cells with prominent nucleoli are a pitfall. Cell block immunostains for HMB45 and Melan-A are essential.
entities.ihc: The perivascular epithelioid cells are positive for melanocytic markers HMB45, Melan-A and cathepsin K, and myoid markers SMA and often desmin, while they are negative for keratins, HepPar1, arginase-1 and glypican-3, which excludes HCC. TFE3 may be positive in a subset with TFE3 rearrangement. S100 and SOX10 are typically negative, which helps separate it from melanoma. Ki-67 is low in benign lesions.

entities.variants: Classic mesenchymal hamartoma of infancy and childhood; cystic and solid forms; mesenchymal hamartoma in adults (rare); association with undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma (shared chromosome 19q13.4 rearrangement)
entities.remarks: Usually under 2 years; large multicystic mass, mostly right lobe; loose myxoid mesenchyme with fluid-filled cysts, branching bile ducts and islands of hepatocytes, ductal plate-like; rare transformation to undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma; excision.
entities.histo: Mesenchymal hamartoma is a benign, developmental, tumour-like lesion of the liver that occurs predominantly in children under two years of age and presents as a large abdominal mass, often in the right lobe. Grossly it is a large, well-circumscribed, multicystic and solid mass, with cysts containing clear or gelatinous fluid. Microscopically, it consists of loose, oedematous to myxoid mesenchymal tissue with stellate cells, containing branching, irregularly shaped bile ducts, sometimes in a ductal plate-like arrangement, scattered islands of hepatocytes and blood vessels, together with cystic spaces formed by degeneration of the mesenchyme or dilatation of ducts and lymphatics. Extramedullary haematopoiesis is common. It is associated with rearrangements of chromosome 19q13.4, and some cases of undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma arise in or alongside mesenchymal hamartoma, suggesting a link. Complete excision is the treatment. The differentials include undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma (atypical, pleomorphic, mitotically active cells with PAS-positive globules), hepatoblastoma with mesenchymal components, infantile haemangioma, choledochal cyst, simple cysts and lymphangioma.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role; aspirates yield myxoid stroma with bland spindle and stellate cells and occasional hepatocytes and ductal cells, which may be confused with other myxoid lesions, and excision is required.
entities.ihc: The mesenchymal cells are positive for vimentin and SMA and negative for desmin, myogenin, keratins and CD34, while the bile ducts are CK7 and CK19 positive. Ki-67 is low. Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma differs by marked atypia, high Ki-67 and often glypican-3 and keratin positivity.

entities.entity: Benign lipomatous tumours of liver (lipoma, myelolipoma, angiolipoma)
entities.variants: Hepatic lipoma; myelolipoma (fat with haematopoietic elements); angiolipoma; hibernoma (rare); pseudolipoma of Glisson capsule (separate)
entities.remarks: Rare; mature adipose tissue tumours; must exclude angiomyolipoma (HMB45), focal fatty change, steatotic adenoma and HCC with fatty change; myelolipoma contains trilineage haematopoiesis.
entities.histo: True lipomatous tumours of the liver are rare, and most fat-containing liver lesions are angiomyolipomas, focal fatty change or steatotic hepatocellular tumours. Hepatic lipoma is composed of mature adipocytes without atypia, myoid cells or thick-walled vessels, and is well-circumscribed. Myelolipoma consists of mature fat admixed with trilineage haematopoietic tissue including erythroid and myeloid precursors and megakaryocytes, similar to adrenal myelolipoma, and some may arise from adrenal rest tissue. Angiolipoma contains mature fat with small vessels containing fibrin thrombi. The diagnosis requires exclusion of angiomyolipoma, which contains perivascular epithelioid cells that are HMB45 positive, and well-differentiated liposarcoma, which has atypical stromal cells and MDM2 amplification. The differentials also include focal fatty change (hepatocytes with fat, preserved portal tracts), steatotic hepatocellular adenoma, extramedullary haematopoiesis and pseudolipoma of Glisson capsule.
entities.cyto: Aspirates yield mature adipocytes, and, in myelolipoma, haematopoietic precursors and megakaryocytes; the findings are non-specific and must be correlated with imaging.
entities.ihc: Adipocytes are S100 positive. HMB45, Melan-A and SMA are negative in the lipoma itself, excluding angiomyolipoma, and MDM2 and CDK4 are negative, excluding well-differentiated liposarcoma. Haematopoietic markers (CD61, MPO, glycophorin) identify the marrow elements in myelolipoma.

entities.variants: Primary hepatic leiomyoma (sporadic); leiomyoma in immunosuppressed patients (most are EBV-associated smooth muscle tumours, separate row); benign metastasising leiomyoma (uterine origin)
entities.remarks: Very rare primary benign smooth muscle tumour; fascicles of bland spindle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei; exclude metastatic uterine or GI leiomyosarcoma, GIST, angiomyolipoma, and EBV-associated smooth muscle tumour (EBER) in immunosuppressed patients.
entities.histo: Primary leiomyoma of the liver is very rare and usually arises from the smooth muscle of vessels or bile ducts. It forms a well-circumscribed, firm, whorled, white mass, composed of intersecting fascicles of bland spindle cells with eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasm and blunt-ended, cigar-shaped nuclei, without significant atypia, necrosis or mitotic activity. Hyalinisation may be present. In immunosuppressed patients, particularly those with HIV or after transplantation, smooth muscle tumours of the liver are usually EBV-associated and are categorised separately. Benign metastasising leiomyoma from the uterus can also involve the liver. The diagnosis of primary hepatic leiomyoma requires exclusion of metastasis, particularly from the uterus or gastrointestinal tract, and of other spindle cell tumours. The differentials include leiomyosarcoma (atypia, necrosis, mitoses), GIST (CD117, DOG1), angiomyolipoma with myoid predominance (HMB45), solitary fibrous tumour (STAT6), schwannoma (S100) and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show cohesive fascicles of bland spindle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei and fibrillary cytoplasm, which is non-specific; cell block immunostaining is needed to exclude GIST and other spindle cell neoplasms.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for SMA, desmin, h-caldesmon and calponin, and negative for CD117, DOG1, S100, HMB45, STAT6 and keratins. EBER in situ hybridisation is negative, which excludes EBV-associated smooth muscle tumour. ER and PR positivity suggests a uterine origin. Ki-67 is very low.

entities.entity: Benign peripheral nerve sheath and neural tumours of liver (schwannoma, neurofibroma, granular cell tumour)
entities.variants: Schwannoma (conventional, cellular); neurofibroma (solitary, plexiform in NF1); granular cell tumour (biliary tree and liver); ganglioneuroma (rare); paraganglioma (rare, mainly hilar)
entities.remarks: Rare; usually arise from nerves in portal tracts or hilum; plexiform neurofibromas of the hilum in NF1 can cause biliary obstruction; granular cell tumour of bile ducts can mimic cholangiocarcinoma by causing strictures.
entities.histo: Benign nerve sheath and neural tumours of the liver are rare and usually arise from autonomic nerves in the hilum or portal tracts. Schwannomas are encapsulated tumours with cellular Antoni A areas showing Verocay bodies and hypocellular Antoni B areas, with thick-walled hyalinised vessels. Neurofibromas consist of bland spindle cells with wavy nuclei in a collagenous or myxoid stroma, and plexiform neurofibromas, typically in neurofibromatosis type 1, can involve the hilum and portal tracts diffusely, causing biliary obstruction or portal hypertension. Granular cell tumour, more frequent in the extrahepatic bile ducts, consists of sheets of cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and small nuclei, and can cause biliary strictures that mimic cholangiocarcinoma. Ganglioneuromas and paragangliomas are exceptional. The differentials include leiomyoma, GIST, solitary fibrous tumour, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour, MPNST and metastatic melanoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show cohesive clusters of spindle cells with wavy nuclei (schwannoma, neurofibroma) or cells with abundant granular cytoplasm and small nuclei (granular cell tumour), which can mimic histiocytes; cell block S100 staining is helpful.
entities.ihc: Schwannoma is diffusely and strongly positive for S100 and SOX10, with a collagen IV-positive basement membrane, while neurofibroma shows patchy S100 and SOX10 staining with CD34-positive fibroblasts and neurofilament-positive axons. Granular cell tumour is positive for S100, SOX10, CD68 and inhibin, and negative for keratins. HMB45 and Melan-A are negative, excluding melanoma and PEComa, and CD117 and DOG1 are negative.

entities.variants: Mature cystic teratoma; immature teratoma (malignant potential, see germ cell tumours); teratoma in infants and children; teratoid elements in hepatoblastoma (separate)
entities.remarks: Very rare primary hepatic germ cell tumour, mostly in infants and young children, often left lobe; tissues from two or three germ layers; must exclude hepatoblastoma with teratoid features (has fetal or embryonal epithelium) and immature elements.
entities.histo: Primary teratoma of the liver is a very rare germ cell tumour, occurring mainly in infants and young children, and only exceptionally in adults. It forms a cystic or solid mass, often in the left lobe, which may contain hair, sebaceous material, bone or teeth, and calcification is commonly seen on imaging. Microscopically, mature teratoma contains well-differentiated tissues derived from two or three germ layers, such as skin and adnexa, glial tissue, respiratory and intestinal epithelium, cartilage, bone and fat. The presence of immature neuroectodermal tissue indicates immature teratoma, which should be graded and treated as having malignant potential, and other germ cell components such as yolk sac tumour should be searched for. The main differential is hepatoblastoma with teratoid features, which contains fetal or embryonal hepatoblastomatous epithelium in addition to heterologous elements and typically elevated serum AFP. Other differentials include mesenchymal hamartoma, metastatic teratoma from the gonads and other cystic lesions.
entities.cyto: Cytology has a limited role; aspirates may show squamous cells, keratin debris and mixed epithelial and mesenchymal elements, and histological examination is required.
entities.ihc: IHC confirms the lineage of the different components (for example keratins in epithelium, GFAP in glia, S100 in cartilage). SALL4, glypican-3 and AFP are negative in mature elements and positive in yolk sac tumour or hepatoblastoma components. Beta-catenin nuclear staining and glypican-3 positivity in epithelial elements suggest hepatoblastoma rather than teratoma.

entities.variants: Growth patterns: trabecular (microtrabecular), pseudoglandular (acinar), compact (solid); cytological variants: clear cell change, fatty change, pleomorphic or giant cells, Mallory-Denk bodies, hyaline and pale bodies, bile production, oncocytic; grades: well, moderately, poorly differentiated (WHO three-tier); HCC with progenitor (stem) cell features (CK19-positive); HCC in cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic liver; HCC arising in adenoma; gross types: nodular, massive, diffuse (cirrhotomimetic), pedunculated, infiltrative
entities.remarks: Commonest primary liver malignancy; risk factors HBV, HCV, alcohol, MASLD, aflatoxin, haemochromatosis; diagnosis often by LI-RADS imaging without biopsy; thick trabeculae (over 3 cells) lined by endothelium, loss of reticulin, unpaired arteries, sinusoidal capillarisation; grade, size, vascular invasion and margins drive prognosis.
entities.histo: Hepatocellular carcinoma is the commonest primary malignancy of the liver and usually arises in cirrhosis due to chronic viral hepatitis, alcohol or MASLD, although a substantial proportion, particularly in hepatitis B and MASLD, develop in non-cirrhotic livers. Grossly, tumours are nodular, often with a fibrous capsule, multinodular, massive, or diffusely infiltrative (cirrhotomimetic), and the cut surface is soft, tan to yellow-green, often with haemorrhage and necrosis; portal vein invasion is common. Microscopically, tumour cells resemble hepatocytes to varying degrees, with polygonal shape, eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, central nuclei and prominent nucleoli, and they grow in trabeculae thicker than three cells, lined by endothelial cells, with absence of normal portal tracts, presence of unpaired arteries and capillarisation of sinusoids. Common architectural patterns are trabecular, pseudoglandular (acinar, often containing bile or proteinaceous material) and compact (solid), and cytological features include bile production, Mallory-Denk bodies, hyaline globules, pale bodies, clear cell change, fatty change and pleomorphic giant cells. A reticulin stain shows loss or marked reduction of the reticulin framework, which is one of the most useful features in separating well-differentiated HCC from adenoma, dysplastic nodules and benign liver. WHO grading is well, moderately or poorly differentiated, based on the resemblance to hepatocytes and nuclear features. Vascular invasion (microvascular and macrovascular), satellite nodules, tumour size and number, margins and pT stage are key prognostic factors to report, together with the background liver disease. HCC with CK19 expression in more than 5% of cells (progenitor features) has worse outcome. The differentials include hepatocellular adenoma, high-grade dysplastic nodule, metastatic carcinoma (especially from adrenal, kidney, neuroendocrine, and hepatoid adenocarcinomas of stomach, lung or ovary), intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and combined HCC-cholangiocarcinoma, angiomyolipoma, and melanoma.
entities.cyto: FNA of HCC typically yields cellular smears of polygonal tumour cells in thickened trabeculae and clusters wrapped by endothelial cells (peripheral endothelial wrapping) and traversed by capillaries (transgressing vessels), with high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, prominent nucleoli, intranuclear inclusions, numerous naked atypical nuclei and absence of bile duct cells. Bile pigment, Mallory-Denk bodies and hyaline globules may be present. Well-differentiated HCC is hard to separate from benign hepatocytes, regenerative nodules, dysplastic nodules and adenoma, and poorly differentiated HCC must be separated from metastatic carcinoma, so a cell block with reticulin and IHC is strongly recommended. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: Hepatocellular differentiation is confirmed with HepPar1 (cytoplasmic granular), arginase-1 (cytoplasmic and nuclear; the most sensitive, including in poorly differentiated tumours), albumin in situ hybridisation (very sensitive and specific), and polyclonal CEA or CD10 in a canalicular pattern. Glypican-3 is positive in most HCC, especially moderately and poorly differentiated tumours, but negative in benign liver and adenoma (it can be positive in hepatitis and regenerative cells). For well-differentiated HCC versus dysplastic nodule, the panel of glypican-3, HSP70 and glutamine synthetase (two or three positive favours HCC) and diffuse CD34 sinusoidal capillarisation are used. AFP is positive in a minority. CK7 and CK19 are usually negative, and CK19 positivity marks progenitor features and worse prognosis. Keratin profile (CK7, CK20), TTF-1 (cytoplasmic staining in HCC is common with some clones, a pitfall), PAX8, CDX2, SATB2, synaptophysin and SALL4 help exclude metastases and hepatoid carcinoma. Immune checkpoint markers are not used for patient selection in HCC.

entities.entity: Early hepatocellular carcinoma (vaguely nodular small HCC)
entities.variants: Small HCC of vaguely nodular type (early HCC); small HCC of distinctly nodular type (progressed); nodule-in-nodule HCC within dysplastic nodule
entities.remarks: Usually under 2 cm, vaguely nodular, indistinct margins, well differentiated; stromal invasion (into portal tracts or septa) is the key diagnostic feature; contains residual portal tracts; often hypovascular on imaging; excellent prognosis after resection or ablation.
entities.histo: Early hepatocellular carcinoma, as defined by the International Consensus Group for Hepatocellular Neoplasia, is a small (usually under 2 cm), vaguely nodular, well-differentiated HCC with indistinct margins that replaces the background liver rather than compressing it, in contrast to progressed HCC, which is distinctly nodular, often encapsulated and moderately differentiated. Microscopically, early HCC shows increased cell density, more than twice that of surrounding liver, thin trabeculae, frequent pseudoglands, fatty change in some cases, varying numbers of unpaired arteries and residual portal tracts within the nodule. The most important diagnostic feature is stromal invasion, meaning invasion of tumour cells into portal tracts or fibrous septa within the nodule, which separates early HCC from high-grade dysplastic nodule. Vascular invasion is rare. Early HCC is often hypovascular or isovascular on imaging, and progressed HCC may arise within it as a nodule-in-nodule. The prognosis after treatment is excellent. The differentials include high-grade dysplastic nodule, low-grade dysplastic nodule, large regenerative nodule and progressed HCC.
entities.cyto: FNA of early HCC yields well-differentiated hepatocytes with mild atypia and increased nuclear density, which are very difficult to distinguish from dysplastic nodules on cytology; core biopsy with the three-marker panel is preferred.
entities.ihc: The three-marker panel of glypican-3, HSP70 and glutamine synthetase is particularly useful, as positivity for any two markers supports early HCC over dysplastic nodule. Loss of CK7 or CK19-positive ductular reaction around invaded portal tracts helps identify stromal invasion, since ductular reaction is preserved at the edge of pseudo-invasion in dysplastic nodules. CD34 shows increased but sometimes incomplete sinusoidal capillarisation.

entities.variants: Steatohepatitic HCC in MASLD/MASH or alcohol; steatohepatitic features in conventional HCC (less than 50%); steatohepatitic HCC in non-cirrhotic livers
entities.remarks: WHO subtype; over 50% of tumour shows steatohepatitis-like features (steatosis, ballooning, Mallory-Denk bodies, inflammation, pericellular fibrosis); linked to metabolic syndrome and MASH background; IL-6/JAK/STAT activation; prognosis similar to conventional HCC.
entities.histo: Steatohepatitic hepatocellular carcinoma is a subtype in which the tumour itself shows the features of steatohepatitis: macrovesicular steatosis, ballooned tumour cells, Mallory-Denk bodies, inflammation and pericellular fibrosis, in more than half of the tumour. It is strongly associated with metabolic syndrome and with MASH or alcohol-related liver disease in the background, and it accounts for a notable proportion of HCCs in these settings. The tumour is often well to moderately differentiated, and reticulin loss is present, although the pericellular fibrosis may make it harder to evaluate. The differentials include steatotic HNF1A-inactivated hepatocellular adenoma (no atypia, preserved reticulin, LFABP loss), focal fatty change, angiomyolipoma (HMB45), clear cell HCC (clear rather than fatty cytoplasm), and regenerative nodules in MASH cirrhosis. The prognosis is similar to conventional HCC in most studies.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show atypical hepatocytes with fat vacuoles, Mallory-Denk bodies and inflammatory cells, which can be mistaken for background steatohepatitis; trabecular thickening, endothelial wrapping and naked atypical nuclei favour HCC.
entities.ihc: The tumour is positive for HepPar1, arginase-1 and often glypican-3, and CRP and SAA are frequently positive, reflecting inflammatory signalling. Ubiquitin or p62 highlights Mallory-Denk bodies. Reticulin loss and the HCC marker panel help separate it from steatotic adenoma and regenerative nodules, and HMB45 is negative, excluding angiomyolipoma.

entities.variants: Clear cell HCC (over 80% clear cells); HCC with focal clear cell change; clear cell HCC with steatosis
entities.remarks: WHO subtype; tumour cells with clear cytoplasm from glycogen (PAS positive, diastase sensitive) in more than 80% of the tumour; better prognosis than conventional HCC; mimics metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma and adrenal cortical carcinoma.
entities.histo: Clear cell hepatocellular carcinoma is a subtype in which more than 80% of the tumour cells have clear cytoplasm, caused mainly by accumulation of glycogen, with variable fat. Glycogen is PAS positive and removed by diastase. The tumour cells retain the trabecular or solid architecture and the nuclear features of HCC. Clear cell HCC tends to have a somewhat better prognosis than conventional HCC. The main differential is metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma, which shows a rich delicate capillary network, PAX8 and CA9 positivity and lacks hepatocellular markers; other differentials include adrenal cortical carcinoma, clear cell cholangiocarcinoma, PEComa or angiomyolipoma, and metastatic clear cell carcinomas from ovary or lung.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show tumour cells with abundant clear or vacuolated cytoplasm and atypical nuclei, which can be mistaken for renal cell carcinoma or adrenal cortical carcinoma; cell block immunostains are required.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for HepPar1, arginase-1 and glypican-3, and negative for PAX8, PAX2, CA9 and CD10 membranous staining (which suggest renal cell carcinoma), and for SF-1, inhibin and melan-A (which suggest adrenal cortical carcinoma). HMB45 is negative, excluding PEComa.

entities.variants: Macrotrabecular-massive HCC (MTM-HCC); HCC with focal macrotrabecular pattern (less than 50%)
entities.remarks: WHO subtype; macrotrabeculae (more than 6 cells thick) in more than 50% of the tumour; associated with HBV, high serum AFP, vascular invasion, TP53 mutations, FGF19 amplification and angiogenesis activation; poor prognosis.
entities.histo: Macrotrabecular-massive hepatocellular carcinoma is an aggressive subtype in which more than half of the tumour grows as thick macrotrabeculae, more than six cells thick, often resembling large solid nests surrounded by endothelium. It is associated with hepatitis B infection, high serum AFP, large tumour size, microvascular and macrovascular invasion, satellite nodules and early recurrence. Molecularly, it is enriched for TP53 mutations, FGF19 amplification and activation of angiogenesis pathways. Tumour cells are often moderately to poorly differentiated, and necrosis is frequent. The prognosis is poor, and recognition is important for risk stratification and possibly for selecting anti-angiogenic therapy. The differentials include conventional trabecular HCC with focal macrotrabeculae, hepatoblastoma with macrotrabecular pattern in children and adolescents, and metastatic neuroendocrine tumours with trabecular growth.
entities.cyto: Aspirates are highly cellular with large, thick, three-dimensional trabecular fragments wrapped by endothelium and atypical hepatocytes, which strongly suggests HCC; the subtype itself is defined histologically.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for HepPar1, arginase-1 and glypican-3, often strongly positive for AFP, and may show CAIX and ESM1 positivity reflecting angiogenesis; ESM1 endothelial staining has been suggested as a surrogate marker. p53 overexpression may indicate TP53 mutation. Synaptophysin and chromogranin are negative, excluding NET.

entities.variants: Scirrhous HCC (diffuse intratumoral fibrosis over 50%); HCC with fibrosis after treatment (not scirrhous)
entities.remarks: WHO subtype; dense intratumoral fibrosis in more than 50% of tumour, with thin cords of tumour cells; often expresses CK7, CK19 and EpCAM, mimicking cholangiocarcinoma; TSC1/TSC2 mutations; may lack capsule; exclude post-treatment fibrosis and fibrolamellar carcinoma.
entities.histo: Scirrhous hepatocellular carcinoma is a subtype characterised by marked, diffuse intratumoral fibrosis involving more than half of the tumour, with tumour cells arranged in thin trabeculae, cords and small nests compressed by dense collagenous stroma. The tumours are often subcapsular, lack a fibrous capsule, and may cause capsular retraction, so they can mimic cholangiocarcinoma or metastatic adenocarcinoma on imaging. The tumour cells resemble those of conventional HCC, with eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm, and pseudoglands may be present. Post-treatment fibrosis after ablation or chemoembolisation should not be called scirrhous HCC. Molecularly, TSC1 and TSC2 mutations and TGF-beta pathway activation have been reported. The prognosis is similar to or slightly worse than conventional HCC in different studies. The differentials include intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (mucin, CK7 and CK19 positive glands, HepPar1 and arginase-1 negative), combined HCC-cholangiocarcinoma, fibrolamellar carcinoma (young patients, lamellar fibrosis, large oncocytic cells, CK7 and CD68 positive), and metastatic carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates are often hypocellular due to fibrosis, containing small groups of atypical hepatocytes and stromal fragments; definitive diagnosis requires histology and immunostains.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for HepPar1 and arginase-1 and often glypican-3, while CK7 and CK19 are frequently positive, which can lead to misinterpretation as cholangiocarcinoma or combined tumour; the morphology and absence of mucin-producing glands help. Albumin ISH is positive in HCC and in some cholangiocarcinomas. CD68 is negative, unlike fibrolamellar carcinoma.

entities.variants: Chromophobe HCC with abrupt anaplasia
entities.remarks: WHO subtype; tumour cells with pale to clear (chromophobe) cytoplasm and bland, small nuclei, with scattered abrupt foci of marked nuclear anaplasia (clustered pleomorphic nuclei); strongly associated with alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT); prognosis similar to conventional HCC.
entities.histo: Chromophobe hepatocellular carcinoma is a rare subtype defined by tumour cells with lightly eosinophilic to pale, clear or chromophobic cytoplasm and mostly bland, small nuclei, in which there are scattered, abrupt, small foci of marked nuclear anaplasia, with clusters of large, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei, sometimes with multinucleation. These anaplastic foci appear suddenly within the otherwise bland tumour. The tumour usually arises in older adults, often in non-cirrhotic livers, and grows in trabecular or solid patterns. Molecularly, it is strongly associated with the alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) phenotype, frequently with ATRX loss, rather than TERT promoter mutation. The prognosis is similar to conventional HCC. The differentials include clear cell HCC (diffusely clear cells without abrupt anaplasia), chromophobe renal cell carcinoma metastasis (CK7 positive, CD117 positive, hepatocellular markers negative), well-differentiated HCC and hepatocellular adenoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show bland tumour cells with pale cytoplasm and scattered groups of highly pleomorphic nuclei; the abrupt anaplasia can raise concern for other high-grade tumours, and cell block IHC is needed.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for HepPar1, arginase-1 and glypican-3, and negative for CK7, CD117 and PAX8, which excludes chromophobe renal cell carcinoma. ATRX loss by IHC and ALT detection by telomere-specific FISH support the diagnosis.

entities.variants: Classic fibrolamellar carcinoma (DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion); PRKAR1A-inactivated fibrolamellar carcinoma (Carney complex associated or sporadic); mixed fibrolamellar-conventional HCC; fibrolamellar carcinoma with pseudoglands and mucin
entities.remarks: Adolescents and young adults without cirrhosis or viral hepatitis; large, well-circumscribed mass with central scar; large polygonal oncocytic cells with prominent nucleoli, pale bodies and hyaline bodies, separated by parallel lamellar collagen bands; DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion is diagnostic; CK7 and CD68 positive.
entities.histo: Fibrolamellar carcinoma is a distinct primary liver carcinoma that arises in adolescents and young adults, typically in a non-cirrhotic liver without viral hepatitis or metabolic disease, and accounts for a small fraction of all liver cancers. Grossly, it is a large, solitary, well-circumscribed, firm, lobulated, tan to brown mass, often with a central stellate fibrous scar and calcification, which can mimic FNH on imaging. Microscopically, it is composed of large polygonal tumour cells with abundant, deeply eosinophilic, granular (oncocytic) cytoplasm due to numerous mitochondria, large vesicular nuclei and very prominent nucleoli. The cells grow in sheets, cords and nests separated by characteristic parallel bands of dense, lamellar collagen. Pale bodies (pale, ground-glass cytoplasmic inclusions of fibrinogen) and hyaline bodies are common, and pseudoglands with mucin may be present. Lymph node metastases are frequent. The tumour is defined molecularly by a DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion in almost all cases, while a small number, including those in Carney complex, have PRKAR1A inactivation. The prognosis is similar to HCC in non-cirrhotic livers, and resection is the mainstay of treatment. The differentials include FNH (central scar but benign hepatocytes), scirrhous HCC, conventional HCC with oncocytic features, BAP1-inactivated HCC (fibrolamellar-like but lacks PRKACA fusion), cholangiocarcinoma and metastatic neuroendocrine tumours.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show large, discohesive polygonal cells with abundant granular oncocytic cytoplasm, very large nucleoli, intracytoplasmic pale bodies and fragments of lamellar collagen; these features in a young patient without cirrhosis strongly suggest the diagnosis, and the fusion can be confirmed on cell block material.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for HepPar1, arginase-1 and polyclonal CEA in a canalicular pattern, and characteristically positive for CK7 and CD68 (KP1), a combination that is useful for diagnosis; glypican-3 is variably positive and AFP is usually negative. Molecular confirmation by FISH or RT-PCR for DNAJB1::PRKACA, or PKA-C (PRKACA) immunostaining, which shows strong granular cytoplasmic staining, supports the diagnosis. PRKAR1A loss by IHC identifies the Carney-associated form.

entities.variants: Neutrophil-rich HCC (G-CSF producing); HCC with sarcomatoid features and neutrophils
entities.remarks: WHO subtype; diffuse infiltration of neutrophils within the tumour, usually due to tumour production of G-CSF, with peripheral leucocytosis and raised CRP; often poorly differentiated or sarcomatoid; aggressive with poor prognosis.
entities.histo: Neutrophil-rich hepatocellular carcinoma is a rare subtype in which the tumour is diffusely infiltrated by numerous neutrophils, generally as a result of tumour cell production of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF). Patients typically have marked peripheral blood leucocytosis and raised CRP and IL-6, sometimes with fever, which can lead to an initial clinical impression of a liver abscess. The tumour cells are usually poorly differentiated and may have sarcomatoid features, and necrosis is frequent. The prognosis is poor. The differentials include liver abscess with reactive hepatocyte atypia, sarcomatoid HCC or carcinoma, inflammatory HCC variants, undifferentiated carcinoma and metastatic carcinoma with neutrophils.
entities.cyto: Aspirates may contain abundant neutrophils that obscure tumour cells and lead to a misdiagnosis of abscess; careful search for atypical epithelial cells and a cell block are essential.
entities.ihc: Tumour cells are positive for hepatocellular markers to a variable extent, with arginase-1 more sensitive than HepPar1 in poorly differentiated areas, and keratins (CAM5.2, AE1/AE3) are positive; G-CSF immunostaining may show cytoplasmic staining in tumour cells. CD68 and myeloperoxidase highlight the infiltrate.

entities.variants: Lymphocyte-rich HCC (formerly lymphoepithelioma-like HCC); EBV-negative (most) and rare EBV-positive cases
entities.remarks: WHO subtype; lymphocytes outnumber tumour cells in most fields; usually EBV negative; better prognosis than conventional HCC; immune-hot phenotype; distinguish from lymphoma, lymphoepithelioma-like cholangiocarcinoma (EBV-positive) and inflammatory pseudotumour.
entities.histo: Lymphocyte-rich hepatocellular carcinoma, previously called lymphoepithelioma-like HCC, is a rare subtype in which a dense lymphocytic infiltrate outnumbers tumour cells in most microscopic fields. The tumour cells are poorly cohesive or arranged in small nests and trabeculae among the lymphocytes, which are mainly CD8-positive T cells, and lymphoid follicles may be present. Most cases are EBV negative, in contrast to lymphoepithelioma-like cholangiocarcinoma, which is usually EBV positive. The tumour usually has a better prognosis than conventional HCC, which may reflect a strong anti-tumour immune response. The differentials include lymphoma, inflammatory pseudotumour, reactive lymphoid hyperplasia, lymphoepithelioma-like cholangiocarcinoma, metastatic undifferentiated nasopharyngeal-type carcinoma, and conventional HCC with focal lymphocytic infiltrates.
entities.cyto: Aspirates are dominated by lymphocytes, with scattered atypical epithelial cells that may be overlooked, leading to a misdiagnosis of lymphoma or reactive process; keratin staining on cell block highlights the tumour cells.
entities.ihc: Keratins and hepatocellular markers (HepPar1, arginase-1, glypican-3) highlight the scattered tumour cells among CD3-positive and CD8-positive T lymphocytes. EBER in situ hybridisation is usually negative, which separates it from lymphoepithelioma-like cholangiocarcinoma (CK19 positive, EBER positive). PD-L1 expression may be high, though it is not used for treatment selection.

entities.variants: Sarcomatoid HCC (spindle cell, pleomorphic); HCC with heterologous elements (carcinosarcoma, see undifferentiated carcinoma); sarcomatoid change after TACE or ablation
entities.remarks: Rare; spindle cell or pleomorphic sarcoma-like areas in an HCC, often after locoregional treatment; may lose hepatocellular markers; keratin often retained; poor prognosis.
entities.histo: Sarcomatoid hepatocellular carcinoma is a rare form of HCC in which part or most of the tumour is composed of spindle-shaped or pleomorphic cells resembling a sarcoma, usually in continuity with areas of conventional HCC. It occurs more often in tumours that have been treated by transarterial chemoembolisation, radiofrequency ablation or chemotherapy, suggesting treatment-related dedifferentiation. The spindle cell component forms fascicles or storiform patterns, and may include giant cells, and true heterologous elements such as osteoid or cartilage define carcinosarcoma. Sampling is critical to find the conventional HCC component. The prognosis is poor, with frequent recurrence and metastasis. The differentials include sarcomatoid cholangiocarcinoma, carcinosarcoma, primary sarcomas of the liver (angiosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma), metastatic sarcomatoid carcinomas (renal, lung) and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour.
entities.cyto: Aspirates may show atypical spindle cells and pleomorphic cells with occasional hepatocyte-like cells, and the sarcomatoid component alone cannot be identified as hepatocellular on cytology.
entities.ihc: The spindle cell component often loses HepPar1 and arginase-1 but retains keratin (AE1/AE3, CAM5.2) expression in at least focal areas, and glypican-3 may persist; vimentin is positive. Vascular markers (CD31, ERG), myogenic markers (desmin, myogenin) and STAT6, ALK and S100 help exclude primary sarcomas and other spindle cell tumours.

entities.variants: BAP1-inactivated HCC with fibrolamellar-like morphology; HCC in BAP1 tumour predisposition syndrome
entities.remarks: Emerging entity; young adults, non-cirrhotic liver; oncocytic cells with lamellar fibrosis resembling fibrolamellar carcinoma, but with pseudoglands, and lacking DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion; loss of BAP1 nuclear staining; may be associated with germline BAP1 mutations.
entities.histo: BAP1-inactivated hepatocellular carcinoma is a recently described tumour that occurs in young to middle-aged adults, usually in non-cirrhotic livers, and shows morphological features resembling fibrolamellar carcinoma: large oncocytic tumour cells with prominent nucleoli and fibrous stroma, often with pseudoglandular formations. It lacks the DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion and instead shows biallelic inactivation of BAP1, a tumour suppressor gene, which may be somatic or germline in BAP1 tumour predisposition syndrome. Its biological behaviour is still being defined. Recognition matters because a germline BAP1 mutation predisposes patients and relatives to mesothelioma, uveal and cutaneous melanoma, renal cell carcinoma and other tumours. The differentials include fibrolamellar carcinoma, scirrhous HCC, conventional HCC with oncocytic features and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, which may also show BAP1 loss.
entities.cyto: Cytology resembles fibrolamellar carcinoma, with large oncocytic cells and prominent nucleoli; the distinction requires molecular or IHC testing.
entities.ihc: There is loss of nuclear BAP1 staining in tumour cells with retained staining in background cells. The tumours express hepatocellular markers (HepPar1, arginase-1) and often CK7 and CD68, like fibrolamellar carcinoma, but PRKACA fusion testing is negative. Genetic counselling for germline BAP1 testing is advised.

entities.entity: Other rare morphological types of hepatocellular carcinoma
entities.variants: HCC with osteoclast-like giant cells; HCC with syncytial giant cells; myxoid HCC; HCC with prominent pale bodies; HCC with lymphoid stroma (see lymphocyte-rich); HCC with hepatoid adenocarcinoma-like morphology; cirrhotomimetic (diffuse) HCC; pedunculated HCC
entities.remarks: Uncommon morphological appearances described in the literature but not established as distinct WHO subtypes; recognising them avoids misdiagnosis; behaviour generally that of conventional HCC.
entities.histo: Several uncommon morphological patterns of hepatocellular carcinoma have been described that are not established as separate subtypes but can cause diagnostic difficulty. HCC with osteoclast-like giant cells contains numerous benign multinucleated giant cells of histiocytic origin among malignant tumour cells, similar to giant cell tumours elsewhere. HCC with syncytial giant cells shows multinucleated malignant tumour giant cells. Myxoid HCC contains pools of extracellular myxoid material within pseudoglands, mimicking adenocarcinoma. Some tumours have prominent pale bodies outside the fibrolamellar setting. The cirrhotomimetic or diffuse type consists of numerous small nodules throughout a cirrhotic liver, closely resembling cirrhotic nodules on imaging and gross examination, and is associated with portal vein thrombosis and poor prognosis. Pedunculated HCC projects from the liver surface. The differentials depend on the pattern and include undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclast-like giant cells, cholangiocarcinoma, metastatic adenocarcinoma and cirrhosis.
entities.cyto: Aspirates may show giant cells or myxoid material that can mislead; recognising atypical hepatocyte-like tumour cells with endothelial wrapping supports HCC.
entities.ihc: Tumour cells retain hepatocellular markers (HepPar1, arginase-1, glypican-3), while osteoclast-like giant cells are CD68 positive and keratin negative. Mucin stains are negative in myxoid HCC pseudoglands, and keratin profiles help exclude adenocarcinoma.

entities.entity: Hepatoblastoma, well-differentiated fetal subtype (pure fetal with low mitotic activity)
entities.variants: Well-differentiated (pure) fetal hepatoblastoma with low mitotic activity (2 or fewer per 10 HPF); fetal hepatoblastoma with clear (glycogen) and dark (lipid-poor) areas ('light and dark' pattern)
entities.remarks: Commonest primary liver malignancy of childhood (usually under 3 years), associated with prematurity/low birth weight, FAP, Beckwith-Wiedemann, trisomy 18; high AFP; CTNNB1 mutation; fetal cells resemble fetal hepatocytes in thin trabeculae with light/dark pattern and extramedullary haematopoiesis; pure fetal with low mitoses in a resected tumour has excellent prognosis (may avoid chemotherapy).
entities.histo: Hepatoblastoma is the commonest primary liver malignancy of childhood, usually presenting before three years of age with an abdominal mass and markedly raised serum AFP. Risk factors include prematurity and very low birth weight, familial adenomatous polyposis, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and trisomy 18, and almost all tumours have Wnt pathway activation, mostly through CTNNB1 mutations. Under the international paediatric liver tumour consensus classification, hepatoblastoma is divided into epithelial and mixed epithelial-mesenchymal types, and the epithelial components include fetal, embryonal, small cell undifferentiated, cholangioblastic, macrotrabecular and pleomorphic patterns. The well-differentiated fetal subtype consists of uniform cells resembling fetal hepatocytes, smaller than normal hepatocytes, with round nuclei and clear (glycogen-rich) or eosinophilic (lipid-poor) cytoplasm, arranged in thin trabeculae two cells thick, producing a characteristic light and dark pattern at low power. Extramedullary haematopoiesis is common. Mitotic activity is very low, two or fewer per ten high-power fields. A tumour that is entirely well-differentiated fetal with low mitotic activity, completely resected, has an excellent prognosis and may be treated with surgery alone in some protocols, so extensive sampling is needed. The differentials include hepatocellular adenoma, hepatocellular carcinoma in older children, and normal or regenerating liver in small biopsies.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show cohesive clusters and trabeculae of small, uniform hepatocyte-like cells with round nuclei and granular or vacuolated cytoplasm, sometimes with extramedullary haematopoiesis; separating fetal hepatoblastoma from normal liver or HCC is difficult, so cell block immunostains and correlation with AFP are essential.
entities.ihc: Fetal cells show cytoplasmic and membranous beta-catenin with only focal nuclear staining, and glypican-3 shows a granular cytoplasmic pattern; glutamine synthetase is diffusely positive, and HepPar1 and arginase-1 are positive. Ki-67 is low in the well-differentiated fetal subtype. AFP is variably positive. These features separate fetal hepatoblastoma from normal liver (glypican-3 negative, perivenular GS).

entities.entity: Hepatoblastoma, fetal subtype with mitotic activity (crowded fetal)
entities.variants: Crowded fetal (mitotically active fetal) hepatoblastoma; pleomorphic fetal (pleomorphic epithelial) pattern; fetal hepatoblastoma with clear cell change
entities.remarks: Fetal-type cells with increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, more crowding and more than 2 mitoses per 10 HPF; intermediate between well-differentiated fetal and embryonal; standard chemotherapy needed; pleomorphic pattern (marked atypia) may follow chemotherapy and must be distinguished from HCC.
entities.histo: The crowded fetal or mitotically active fetal subtype of hepatoblastoma consists of fetal-type cells that are more crowded, with less cytoplasm, a higher nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio and more than two mitoses per ten high-power fields, often accompanied by less prominent light and dark pattern. This subtype is more common than pure well-differentiated fetal hepatoblastoma and is often mixed with embryonal areas. Patients receive standard chemotherapy. The pleomorphic epithelial pattern, which may appear after chemotherapy or in metastases, shows tumour cells with marked nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia and prominent nucleoli, and must be distinguished from hepatocellular carcinoma or the hepatocellular neoplasm NOS category. The differentials include embryonal hepatoblastoma, HCC in children and adolescents, and hepatocellular neoplasm NOS.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show crowded small hepatocyte-like cells with higher nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio and mitoses; distinction from embryonal hepatoblastoma or HCC requires histology.
entities.ihc: Tumour cells show beta-catenin cytoplasmic and focal nuclear staining, glypican-3 positivity, and diffuse glutamine synthetase, with a higher Ki-67 than in well-differentiated fetal subtype. HepPar1 and arginase-1 are positive.

entities.variants: Embryonal hepatoblastoma (pure or mixed with fetal); embryonal with pseudorosettes, glandular or acinar structures
entities.remarks: Small, primitive cells with scant cytoplasm and high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio forming sheets, acini, pseudorosettes and glands, resembling embryonic liver (6-8 weeks); higher mitotic activity; strong nuclear beta-catenin and diffuse glypican-3.
entities.histo: The embryonal subtype of hepatoblastoma consists of small, primitive epithelial cells resembling the liver of the six- to eight-week embryo, with scant, dark cytoplasm, angulated hyperchromatic nuclei, a high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio and frequent mitoses. The cells form solid sheets, ribbons, acini, pseudorosettes and gland-like structures, without the light and dark pattern or extramedullary haematopoiesis of fetal areas. Embryonal areas are commonly mixed with fetal components (mixed fetal and embryonal epithelial hepatoblastoma), and mesenchymal components may be present. The prognosis is related more to clinical stage (PRETEXT), AFP levels and metastasis than to the embryonal pattern itself. The differentials include small cell undifferentiated hepatoblastoma, malignant rhabdoid tumour, neuroblastoma metastasis, Wilms tumour and other small round blue cell tumours, and cholangioblastic or ductal components.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show cellular smears of small, primitive cells with high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, forming acini, rosette-like and pseudopapillary groups, which resemble other small round blue cell tumours; correlation with AFP and cell block immunostains is essential.
entities.ihc: Embryonal cells show strong nuclear and cytoplasmic beta-catenin, diffuse strong glypican-3, and they are less frequently positive for HepPar1 and arginase-1 than fetal cells, with variable glutamine synthetase. SALL4 and AFP are often positive. INI1 (SMARCB1) is retained, which excludes rhabdoid tumour, and neuroblastoma markers (PHOX2B, synaptophysin, chromogranin) and WT1 are negative.

entities.variants: Pure small cell undifferentiated hepatoblastoma (rare); SCU component within fetal or embryonal hepatoblastoma; INI1-retained SCU (true hepatoblastoma) vs INI1-lost tumours (reclassified as malignant rhabdoid tumour)
entities.remarks: Sheets of small, round, non-cohesive cells with scant cytoplasm and no hepatocytic differentiation; often low AFP and poor prognosis when pure; INI1 must be tested, as most pure SCU tumours with INI1 loss are rhabdoid tumours.
entities.histo: Small cell undifferentiated hepatoblastoma consists of sheets of small, round to oval, poorly cohesive cells with scant cytoplasm, fine chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli, without hepatocytic or ductal differentiation, closely resembling neuroblastoma, Ewing sarcoma or lymphoma. It may appear as a pure tumour, which is rare and has a poor prognosis, often with normal or low serum AFP, or as a focal component within otherwise typical hepatoblastoma, where its prognostic significance is less clear. It is now recognised that many pure SCU tumours with loss of INI1 (SMARCB1) are in fact malignant rhabdoid tumours of the liver, which should be classified separately. True SCU hepatoblastoma retains INI1 expression. The differentials include malignant rhabdoid tumour, neuroblastoma, Ewing sarcoma, desmoplastic small round cell tumour, rhabdomyosarcoma, lymphoma and leukaemia, and embryonal hepatoblastoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show discohesive small round blue cells, which cannot be distinguished from other small round cell tumours without immunostains; INI1 status on cell block is essential.
entities.ihc: SCU cells are positive for keratins (focally), often show nuclear beta-catenin, and are negative for HepPar1 and glypican-3 or show weak staining; INI1 (SMARCB1) nuclear staining is retained, whereas it is lost in rhabdoid tumour. SALL4 may be positive. CD99, FLI1, NKX2.2, PHOX2B, desmin, myogenin, CD45 and TdT help exclude Ewing sarcoma, neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma and lymphoma.

entities.entity: Mixed epithelial and mesenchymal hepatoblastoma (with stromal derivatives)
entities.variants: Mixed hepatoblastoma without teratoid features: with osteoid-like material (osteoid), cartilage, immature spindle mesenchyme (blastemal), and fibrous septa; mixed fetal and embryonal epithelium with mesenchyme
entities.remarks: Epithelial (fetal and/or embryonal) components admixed with mesenchymal tissues such as immature spindle cells, osteoid-like material and cartilage; osteoid is often more prominent after chemotherapy; prognosis depends on stage.
entities.histo: Mixed epithelial and mesenchymal hepatoblastoma contains fetal and/or embryonal epithelial components admixed with mesenchymal elements, which most commonly include immature spindle cell mesenchyme (blastemal-like), fibrous septa, osteoid-like material, and less often cartilage or skeletal muscle.
