The osteoid-like material is eosinophilic, hyaline and often contains lacunar cells, and it may represent metaplastic epithelial cells, as the cells within it can express keratin. Mesenchymal components often become more prominent after chemotherapy, as epithelial elements regress. The prognosis is related to stage and response to chemotherapy rather than to the mesenchymal component. The differentials include hepatoblastoma with teratoid features (which contains neural, squamous, or other heterologous tissues), teratoma, undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma and mesenchymal hamartoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates may contain both small hepatocyte-like epithelial cells and spindle mesenchymal cells or osteoid material, which supports the diagnosis in the right clinical context.
entities.ihc: The epithelial cells show beta-catenin nuclear staining and glypican-3 positivity, while osteoid-like material and spindle cells may also express beta-catenin and focal keratin, supporting their neoplastic nature; mesenchymal cells are vimentin positive and may be SMA positive.

entities.variants: Mixed hepatoblastoma with teratoid features: neuroectodermal tissue, melanin pigment, squamous epithelium, intestinal-type glands, skeletal muscle, other heterologous elements
entities.remarks: Mixed hepatoblastoma containing heterologous tissues such as neuroepithelium, melanin-containing cells, squamous epithelium with keratinisation and striated muscle; distinguish from teratoma (no fetal or embryonal hepatoblastoma epithelium).
entities.histo: Mixed hepatoblastoma with teratoid features contains, in addition to fetal or embryonal epithelium and common mesenchymal elements, heterologous tissues such as primitive neuroepithelium forming rosettes, melanin-containing cells, keratinising squamous epithelium, intestinal-type glandular epithelium, striated muscle and other tissues. These elements reflect the pluripotent nature of the tumour cells. The prognosis is related to stage and treatment response. The main differential is teratoma of the liver, which lacks hepatoblastoma epithelium and does not usually have high AFP, as well as germ cell tumours, in particular yolk sac tumour, and metastatic tumours with divergent differentiation.
entities.cyto: Aspirates may contain an unusual mixture of epithelial, squamous and neural-like cells along with hepatoblastoma cells; histology is required.
entities.ihc: Hepatoblastoma epithelium shows nuclear beta-catenin and glypican-3 positivity, whereas heterologous components express lineage-specific markers (for example GFAP or synaptophysin in neural tissue, p40 in squamous epithelium, desmin and myogenin in muscle, HMB45 or Melan-A in melanin-producing cells). SALL4 and AFP are positive in hepatoblastoma and in yolk sac tumour.

entities.entity: Hepatoblastoma with other epithelial patterns (cholangioblastic, macrotrabecular, pleomorphic)
entities.variants: Cholangioblastic pattern (bile duct-like structures at edges of epithelial islands); macrotrabecular pattern (trabeculae more than 5 cells thick, fetal or embryonal cells); pleomorphic pattern (marked atypia, often post-chemotherapy)
entities.remarks: Additional epithelial patterns in the international consensus classification; macrotrabecular pattern must be separated from HCC in older children; cholangioblastic cells mimic ductular structures; pleomorphic pattern suggests possible HCN-NOS.
entities.histo: Several additional epithelial patterns can be found in hepatoblastoma, usually in combination with fetal or embryonal components. The cholangioblastic pattern consists of small duct-like structures, often at the periphery of epithelial islands, lined by cells with biliary differentiation, which can resemble ductular reaction. The macrotrabecular pattern shows fetal or embryonal cells in trabeculae more than five cells thick, and when it is extensive in older children it raises the possibility of HCC or hepatocellular neoplasm NOS, so careful assessment of cytology is required. The pleomorphic epithelial pattern, seen especially after chemotherapy or in metastases, shows tumour cells with marked nuclear pleomorphism and prominent nucleoli, overlapping with HCC. These patterns do not have clear independent prognostic significance apart from their role in the differential with HCC. The differentials include HCC, hepatocellular neoplasm NOS and combined tumours.
entities.cyto: Aspirates may show thick trabecular fragments or pleomorphic cells that resemble HCC; integration with age, AFP and histology is essential.
entities.ihc: Cholangioblastic cells are CK7 and CK19 positive and often show nuclear beta-catenin, which separates them from reactive ductules (membranous beta-catenin). Macrotrabecular and pleomorphic areas show glypican-3 positivity and variable beta-catenin nuclear staining, and molecular testing (TERT promoter mutation, CTNNB1) may help separate hepatoblastoma from HCC.

entities.entity: Hepatocellular neoplasm, NOS (hepatoblastoma with HCC features)
entities.variants: Hepatocellular neoplasm NOS (provisional category, older children and adolescents); formerly transitional liver cell tumour
entities.remarks: Provisional category for paediatric tumours with features of both hepatoblastoma and HCC (or features intermediate between them), usually in older children (over 5 years); often high AFP, aggressive; CTNNB1 and TERT promoter mutations frequent.
entities.histo: Hepatocellular neoplasm, not otherwise specified, is a provisional diagnostic category introduced by the international paediatric liver tumour consensus for tumours in children, usually older than five years, that show histological features of both hepatoblastoma and hepatocellular carcinoma, or features intermediate between the two. It was previously referred to as transitional liver cell tumour. The tumours may show fetal or embryonal hepatoblastoma areas alongside areas with HCC-like pleomorphism, macrotrabecular growth or cytological atypia, or a uniform pattern that cannot be confidently assigned to either category. They often present with very high AFP, have frequent CTNNB1 and TERT promoter mutations, and behave aggressively. Treatment is usually with hepatoblastoma-based regimens combined with surgery, but outcomes are worse than for typical hepatoblastoma. The differentials include hepatoblastoma (especially pleomorphic or macrotrabecular patterns), conventional HCC in children (sometimes arising in PFIC2, tyrosinaemia or other diseases), and fibrolamellar carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show atypical hepatocyte-like cells, which cannot be categorised on cytology alone.
entities.ihc: Tumour cells often show nuclear beta-catenin and diffuse glypican-3 positivity, with expression of HepPar1 and arginase-1, and may express CK19 focally. SALL4 may be positive. IHC cannot reliably separate HCN-NOS from hepatoblastoma or HCC, so molecular testing (CTNNB1, TERT promoter) and morphology are integrated.

entities.variants: Primary hepatic malignant rhabdoid tumour (SMARCB1/INI1-deficient); rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome (germline SMARCB1)
entities.remarks: Highly aggressive tumour of infants and young children; sheets of discohesive cells with eccentric vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli and hyaline (rhabdoid) cytoplasmic inclusions; loss of INI1 (SMARCB1) nuclear expression; normal AFP; many previously called SCU hepatoblastoma.
entities.histo: Malignant rhabdoid tumour of the liver is a rare, highly aggressive tumour of infants and young children, defined by biallelic inactivation of SMARCB1, which may be germline in rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome. Patients usually present with a large liver mass, often with metastases, and serum AFP is normal or only mildly raised. Microscopically, the tumour shows sheets of discohesive cells with eccentric vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm containing hyaline, globular paranuclear inclusions composed of intermediate filaments, giving a rhabdoid appearance. Small cell areas without rhabdoid features are common, which explains why many cases were previously classified as small cell undifferentiated hepatoblastoma. The prognosis is very poor despite aggressive therapy. The differentials include SCU hepatoblastoma (INI1 retained), embryonal hepatoblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma, neuroblastoma, desmoplastic small round cell tumour and other tumours with rhabdoid features.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show discohesive cells with eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli and paranuclear hyaline inclusions, along with small round cells; INI1 immunostaining on cell block is essential.
entities.ihc: Loss of nuclear INI1 (SMARCB1) staining in tumour cells with retained staining in background cells is diagnostic. The tumour cells are positive for vimentin and often keratin and EMA, and may show focal SMA or CD99, while they are negative for HepPar1, arginase-1, glypican-3 (usually), desmin and myogenin.

entities.variants: Large duct iCCA (perihilar-like, mucin-producing); periductal-infiltrating, mass-forming and intraductal growth patterns; iCCA arising from BilIN, IPNB, MCN; associated with PSC, hepatolithiasis, liver flukes, choledochal cysts; with KRAS, TP53, SMAD4 alterations
entities.remarks: Arises in large intrahepatic ducts near the hilum; resembles perihilar/extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma: tall columnar mucin-producing cells forming large irregular glands in dense desmoplastic stroma, perineural invasion common; precursors BilIN and IPNB; KRAS/TP53/SMAD4; worse prognosis than small duct type.
entities.histo: Large duct intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises from the large intrahepatic bile ducts or peribiliary glands, usually close to the hilum, and shares many features with perihilar and distal extrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas. It is associated with chronic biliary diseases such as primary sclerosing cholangitis, hepatolithiasis, recurrent pyogenic cholangitis, liver fluke infection and choledochal cysts, and often develops through biliary intraepithelial neoplasia or intraductal papillary neoplasm. Grossly, it grows along the duct (periductal-infiltrating), forms a mass, or both, and may cause duct stricture with upstream dilatation. Microscopically, the tumour forms large, irregular glands and papillary structures lined by tall columnar cells, often with abundant intracellular and luminal mucin, in a dense desmoplastic stroma, with frequent perineural and lymphovascular invasion and lymph node metastasis. Precursor lesions are often found in adjacent ducts. Molecularly, KRAS, TP53 and SMAD4 alterations are common, while IDH1/2 mutations and FGFR2 fusions are rare. The prognosis is worse than for the small duct type. Reporting should include size, number, growth pattern, vascular and perineural invasion, margins, nodes and the pTNM stage. The differentials include small duct iCCA, metastatic adenocarcinoma from the pancreas, stomach, colon, lung or breast, which often requires clinical and imaging correlation, IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis and PSC with reactive atypia, and combined HCC-cholangiocarcinoma.
entities.cyto: FNA and biliary brushing cytology show crowded, overlapping, three-dimensional clusters of columnar cells with nuclear enlargement, irregular contours, chromatin clearing, prominent nucleoli and loss of honeycomb arrangement, sometimes with mucin; the 'drunken honeycomb' appearance and single atypical cells support malignancy. Reactive atypia from stents, stones and PSC is the main pitfall. Cytology cannot reliably separate cholangiocarcinoma from metastatic pancreatobiliary or upper GI adenocarcinoma. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: Tumour cells are positive for CK7 and CK19, often for CK20 focally, MUC5AC, MUC1, S100P and CEA, and negative for HepPar1 and arginase-1. Loss of SMAD4 and aberrant p53 staining are frequent. The IHC profile overlaps heavily with metastatic pancreatic and upper GI adenocarcinoma, so the diagnosis depends on clinical and imaging exclusion of another primary. CDX2, SATB2, TTF-1, napsin A, GATA3, ER, PAX8 and others help exclude metastases from colon, lung, breast and other sites. Albumin ISH can be positive in cholangiocarcinoma, especially the small duct type, and is negative in most metastatic adenocarcinomas, which is helpful. HER2 overexpression is found in a subset and can be tested for targeted therapy.

entities.variants: Small duct iCCA (mass-forming, peripheral); cholangiolocarcinoma subtype (see separate row); iCCA with ductal plate malformation pattern; IDH1/IDH2-mutated, FGFR2-fused, BAP1-mutated, BRAF-mutated and NTRK-fused iCCAs; iCCA in viral hepatitis and cirrhosis
entities.remarks: Peripheral mass-forming tumour of small ducts in background of chronic liver disease (HBV, HCV, MASLD); small tubular glands with cuboidal cells and little mucin, replacing parenchyma with compressive borders; C-reactive protein and N-cadherin positive, often loses S100P; actionable IDH1/2 mutations and FGFR2 fusions; better prognosis than large duct type.
entities.histo: Small duct intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises in the peripheral liver from small interlobular bile ducts or hepatic progenitor cells, and typically forms a mass-forming, well-circumscribed lesion. It is associated with chronic liver diseases such as hepatitis B and C, alcohol and MASLD, but also occurs in normal livers. Microscopically, it consists of small to medium-sized tubular glands, cords and anastomosing structures lined by cuboidal to low columnar cells with scant cytoplasm and little or no mucin, set in a fibrous stroma that is often denser centrally and more cellular at the periphery, where the tumour may replace hepatic plates with preservation of portal tracts. Perineural invasion and lymph node metastasis are less common than in the large duct type. Cholangiolocarcinoma and the ductal plate malformation pattern are regarded as variants of the small duct type. Molecularly, small duct iCCA frequently harbours IDH1 or IDH2 mutations, FGFR2 fusions, BAP1 mutations and occasionally BRAF V600E mutations or NTRK fusions, several of which are therapeutic targets, so molecular profiling is recommended in advanced disease. The prognosis is better than for the large duct type. The differentials include large duct iCCA, combined HCC-cholangiocarcinoma, scirrhous HCC, metastatic adenocarcinoma, bile duct adenoma and von Meyenburg complex (small, bland), and epithelioid haemangioendothelioma, which can grow in cords in a fibrous stroma.
entities.cyto: FNA shows cohesive, flat or three-dimensional clusters of cuboidal cells with moderate nuclear atypia, scant cytoplasm and little mucin, and the cytology overlaps with metastatic adenocarcinoma and occasionally with poorly differentiated HCC; cell block immunostains help, while the separation from metastatic adenocarcinoma usually requires imaging correlation.
entities.ihc: The tumour is positive for CK7 and CK19, and frequently expresses N-cadherin, CD56 (in some cases) and CRP, while it is often negative for S100P, MUC5AC and MUC6, which are more typical of the large duct type. HepPar1 and arginase-1 are negative. Albumin ISH is frequently positive and helps separate iCCA from metastatic adenocarcinoma. IDH1 R132H-specific antibodies detect a subset of IDH1 mutations, and BAP1 loss can be shown by IHC. FGFR2 fusions are detected by FISH or sequencing. HER2, PD-L1 and mismatch repair proteins (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6) are tested in advanced disease.

entities.variants: Pure cholangiolocarcinoma; cholangiolocarcinoma component in small duct iCCA; cholangiolocellular component in combined HCC-cholangiocarcinoma (WHO 5th: no longer a distinct cHCC-CCA subtype)
entities.remarks: Small duct iCCA subtype mimicking ductular reaction: small, uniform, anastomosing cord-like and antler-like ductules (canals of Hering-like) in a hyalinised or oedematous stroma, with tumour cells replacing hepatic plates at the edge; IDH1/2 mutations common; may have better prognosis.
entities.histo: Cholangiolocarcinoma, also called ductular cholangiocarcinoma, is a variant of small duct intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma composed of small, uniform, cuboidal cells arranged in anastomosing cords, antler-like branching ductules and small tubules, closely resembling ductular reaction or canals of Hering. The tumour cells have scant eosinophilic cytoplasm and bland, round nuclei, with no mucin. The stroma is often hyalinised or oedematous, and the tumour may infiltrate the adjacent parenchyma by replacing hepatocyte plates, sometimes with entrapped portal tracts. Historically it was considered to arise from hepatic progenitor cells and was classed as a subtype of combined HCC-cholangiocarcinoma with stem cell features, but WHO 5th edition places it within small duct iCCA, and when it occurs together with HCC the tumour is classified as combined HCC-cholangiocarcinoma. IDH1/2 mutations are frequent. The prognosis may be somewhat better than for conventional iCCA. The differentials include ductular reaction (lacks a mass, no atypia), bile duct adenoma (small, circumscribed), combined HCC-cholangiocarcinoma, and metastatic adenocarcinoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show small, uniform cohesive clusters and cords of bland cuboidal cells, which are easily mistaken for reactive ductular cells or bile duct adenoma; atypia may be mild, so imaging correlation and core biopsy are needed.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for CK7, CK19 and often CD56 and EpCAM, and frequently show luminal EMA staining; they are negative for HepPar1, arginase-1 and mucin. Albumin ISH may be positive. Aberrant p53 and higher Ki-67 than in ductular reaction support malignancy.

entities.variants: Solid tubulocystic iCCA with NIPBL::NACC1 fusion; cholangiocarcinoma with thyroid-like or follicular (thyroid-like) features (overlapping/related)
entities.remarks: Recently described rare iCCA variant in a non-cirrhotic liver, mostly in women; solid, tubular and microcystic architecture with eosinophilic secretions resembling thyroid follicles; bland cuboidal cells; defined by NIPBL::NACC1 fusion; generally indolent.
entities.histo: Solid tubulocystic intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is a recently described, rare variant characterised by a NIPBL::NACC1 gene fusion. It typically presents as a well-circumscribed mass in a non-cirrhotic liver, more often in women. Microscopically, it shows a mixture of solid nests, tubules and microcysts lined by cuboidal cells with eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm and relatively bland, uniform nuclei, and the cystic spaces often contain dense eosinophilic, colloid-like secretions, producing an appearance reminiscent of thyroid follicles (thyroid-like features). Mitotic activity is low. Tumours with this appearance have been reported in the literature under names such as cholangiocarcinoma with thyroid-like features. Behaviour appears to be indolent in most reported cases, but data are limited. The differentials include metastatic thyroid carcinoma (TTF-1, thyroglobulin, PAX8 positive), conventional iCCA, cholangiolocarcinoma, neuroendocrine tumour (synaptophysin, chromogranin) and bile duct adenoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology descriptions are limited; aspirates would be expected to show bland cuboidal cells in microfollicular clusters with colloid-like material, which could suggest thyroid metastasis, so immunostains are essential.
entities.ihc: The tumour is positive for CK7 and CK19 and negative for TTF-1, thyroglobulin and PAX8, excluding thyroid carcinoma, and negative for hepatocellular markers and neuroendocrine markers. The NIPBL::NACC1 fusion is confirmed by sequencing or FISH, and NACC1 immunostaining may show strong nuclear expression in fusion-positive tumours.

entities.entity: Rare histological types of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (adenosquamous, squamous, mucinous, signet ring, clear cell, sarcomatoid)
entities.variants: Adenosquamous carcinoma; squamous cell carcinoma (primary hepatic, also from ciliated foregut cyst or teratoma); mucinous (colloid) carcinoma (often from IPNB); signet ring cell carcinoma; clear cell cholangiocarcinoma; sarcomatoid cholangiocarcinoma and carcinosarcoma; hepatoid carcinoma variants
entities.remarks: Uncommon morphological types of iCCA; squamous and sarcomatoid tumours behave aggressively; metastasis from other organs (lung, oesophagus, stomach, breast) must always be excluded first.
entities.histo: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma occasionally shows unusual histological types that must be distinguished from metastatic tumours. Adenosquamous carcinoma contains both glandular and squamous components, and pure squamous cell carcinoma is very rare and may arise in ciliated foregut cysts, teratomas, hepatolithiasis or hydatid cysts. Mucinous (colloid) carcinoma consists of pools of extracellular mucin with floating tumour cells, usually arising from an intraductal papillary neoplasm. Signet ring cell carcinoma shows discohesive cells with intracytoplasmic mucin displacing the nucleus. Clear cell cholangiocarcinoma has abundant clear cytoplasm, mimicking renal cell carcinoma or clear cell HCC. Sarcomatoid cholangiocarcinoma contains spindle and pleomorphic cells, often with a residual glandular component, and carcinosarcoma has heterologous elements. These variants generally have a poor prognosis, especially squamous and sarcomatoid types. Because metastases to the liver from the lung, oesophagus, head and neck, stomach, breast, kidney and other organs are far more common than these primary variants, a thorough clinical and radiological search for another primary is essential. The differentials include metastatic carcinomas of the corresponding types, sarcomatoid HCC, and undifferentiated carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates reflect the histological type (keratinised squamous cells, mucin with floating cells, signet ring cells, clear cells or spindle cells); cytology cannot determine primary origin, and imaging and clinical correlation are essential.
entities.ihc: Squamous components are positive for p40, p63 and CK5/6; glandular and mucinous components are CK7 and CK19 positive; signet ring cells require exclusion of gastric and breast primaries (CDX2, GATA3, ER, E-cadherin); clear cell cholangiocarcinoma is PAX8 and CA9 negative and HepPar1 negative; sarcomatoid areas retain at least focal keratin. Site-specific markers such as TTF-1, CDX2, SATB2 and GATA3 are used to exclude metastases.

entities.variants: EBV-positive lymphoepithelioma-like cholangiocarcinoma; EBV-negative form (rarer)
entities.remarks: Rare iCCA variant, mostly in Asian women; poorly differentiated carcinoma cells in nests and glands amid dense lymphoid infiltrate; usually EBV positive (EBER); better prognosis than conventional iCCA.
entities.histo: Lymphoepithelioma-like cholangiocarcinoma is a rare variant of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, reported mostly in Asian patients, particularly women, which resembles nasopharyngeal undifferentiated carcinoma. It consists of poorly differentiated carcinoma cells arranged in syncytial nests, cords and small glands, intimately admixed with a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells, often with lymphoid follicles. Most cases are associated with Epstein-Barr virus, demonstrated in tumour cells by EBER in situ hybridisation, while a smaller group is EBV negative and may be associated with mismatch repair deficiency. The prognosis is generally better than for conventional cholangiocarcinoma. The differentials include lymphocyte-rich HCC (hepatocellular markers positive, EBV usually negative), metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma, lymphoma, inflammatory pseudotumour, EBV-positive inflammatory follicular dendritic cell sarcoma and medullary-type carcinomas.
entities.cyto: Aspirates contain abundant lymphocytes with scattered clusters of large atypical epithelial cells, which may be overlooked or lead to a diagnosis of lymphoma or reactive lymphoid tissue; keratin staining and EBER on cell block are diagnostic aids.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for keratins (AE1/AE3, CK7, CK19) and EBER in situ hybridisation, and negative for HepPar1 and arginase-1. The lymphoid infiltrate is mixed T and B cells. Mismatch repair protein staining should be performed in EBV-negative cases. Nasopharyngeal examination may be needed to exclude metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

entities.variants: Combined HCC-CCA (distinct HCC and CCA components, any proportion); intermediate cell carcinoma (cells with features intermediate between hepatocytes and cholangiocytes); cHCC-CCA with stem cell features (WHO 4th ed subtypes: typical, intermediate cell, cholangiolocellular; no longer used as subtypes in WHO 5th); collision tumours (separate tumours, not cHCC-CCA)
entities.remarks: Primary liver carcinoma with unequivocal hepatocytic and cholangiocytic differentiation within the same tumour; diagnosis requires morphology (H&E), IHC supports but does not define; worse prognosis than HCC; reported with percentages of each component.
entities.histo: Combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma is a primary liver carcinoma in which both hepatocellular and cholangiocellular differentiation are present within the same tumour mass, recognised morphologically on H&E. It occurs in the same settings as HCC, including viral hepatitis and cirrhosis, and accounts for a small proportion of primary liver cancers. The HCC component shows trabecular or solid growth of hepatocyte-like cells, sometimes with bile production, and the cholangiocarcinoma component forms glands, often with mucin and desmoplastic stroma, and the two may be intermixed or form separate areas within the tumour, with transition zones. WHO 5th edition recommends reporting the presence and approximate percentage of each component, rather than using the older subtypes (classical, with stem cell features: typical, intermediate cell and cholangiolocellular). Cholangiolocarcinoma is now regarded as small duct iCCA, and intermediate cell carcinoma, composed of uniform cells with features between hepatocytes and cholangiocytes in trabeculae and cords, is considered a distinct but poorly characterised pattern. Collision tumours, in which separate HCC and CCA tumours meet, are excluded. Prognosis is worse than for HCC and similar to or worse than for iCCA, and the tumour is usually not eligible for liver transplantation. The differentials include HCC with pseudoglands or CK19 expression, scirrhous HCC, iCCA with hepatoid features, and collision tumours.
entities.cyto: FNA may show two distinct populations: polygonal hepatocyte-like cells in trabeculae with endothelial wrapping, and glandular clusters of columnar or cuboidal cells with mucin; often only one component is sampled, so cytology frequently underdiagnoses the combined nature.
entities.ihc: The HCC component is positive for HepPar1, arginase-1, glypican-3 and albumin ISH, while the CCA component is positive for CK7, CK19, MUC1 and often mucin stains; stem cell markers such as CK19, EpCAM, CD56 and CD117 may be expressed in transition zones. IHC supports, but does not replace, morphological recognition of both components, as HCC can express CK7 and CK19, and iCCA can express albumin ISH.

entities.variants: Undifferentiated carcinoma (no line of differentiation); undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclast-like giant cells; carcinosarcoma of liver (carcinoma with heterologous sarcomatous elements); sarcomatoid carcinoma of indeterminate lineage
entities.remarks: Rare, high-grade primary liver carcinoma expressing keratins but lacking morphological or IHC evidence of hepatocellular or biliary differentiation; diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out metastases, sarcoma, lymphoma and melanoma; very poor prognosis.
entities.histo: Undifferentiated primary liver carcinoma is a rare, high-grade carcinoma in which tumour cells show epithelial differentiation (keratin expression) but no morphological or immunohistochemical evidence of hepatocellular or biliary differentiation. The tumour consists of sheets of poorly cohesive, pleomorphic, spindle or giant cells, often with extensive necrosis and haemorrhage. Some cases contain osteoclast-like giant cells, and carcinosarcomas contain both carcinomatous and heterologous sarcomatous elements such as osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma or rhabdomyosarcoma. Because undifferentiated tumours in the liver are much more often metastatic, the diagnosis requires a thorough clinical and radiological search for another primary, and immunohistochemistry to exclude sarcomatoid HCC, sarcomatoid cholangiocarcinoma, sarcoma, lymphoma, melanoma and germ cell tumours. The prognosis is very poor. The differentials include sarcomatoid HCC, sarcomatoid iCCA, metastatic undifferentiated carcinomas (lung, kidney, pancreas), SMARCA4- or SMARCB1-deficient undifferentiated tumours, undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma in older children and young adults, angiosarcoma, and melanoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show highly pleomorphic, discohesive malignant cells, sometimes with spindle and giant cells, without features specific to any lineage; cell block immunostains are essential.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for keratins (AE1/AE3, CAM5.2) at least focally, and negative for HepPar1, arginase-1, albumin ISH (usually) and biliary-specific differentiation. A broad panel is used to exclude other tumours: S100, SOX10 and HMB45 (melanoma), CD45 (lymphoma), CD31 and ERG (angiosarcoma), desmin and myogenin (rhabdomyosarcoma), SALL4 and OCT4 (germ cell tumours), TTF-1, PAX8 and others for metastatic carcinoma, and INI1 and BRG1 (SMARCA4) for SWI/SNF-deficient tumours.

entities.entity: Primary hepatic neuroendocrine tumour (NET G1, G2, G3)
entities.variants: Well-differentiated NET grade 1 (Ki-67 under 3%), grade 2 (3-20%), grade 3 (over 20%); primary hepatic NET arising in liver; NET arising in hepatobiliary cysts or bile ducts; vast majority of hepatic NETs are metastatic (separate row)
entities.remarks: Primary hepatic NET is very rare and a diagnosis of exclusion after thorough search for a GI or pancreatic primary (imaging, DOTATATE PET, endoscopy); nested, trabecular or glandular monotonous cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin; graded by Ki-67 and mitoses.
entities.histo: Primary neuroendocrine tumours of the liver are extremely rare, and most neuroendocrine tumours found in the liver are metastases from the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas or lung. A primary hepatic origin can only be accepted after a thorough search for another primary, including cross-sectional imaging, somatostatin receptor PET and endoscopy, and long-term follow-up without evidence of another primary. Microscopically, these well-differentiated neoplasms consist of uniform cells with moderate amounts of finely granular cytoplasm and round nuclei with salt-and-pepper chromatin, growing in nests, trabeculae, ribbons, rosettes or glandular patterns, with a delicate vascular stroma. They are graded by mitotic count and Ki-67 index according to WHO criteria (G1 under 3%, G2 3 to 20%, G3 over 20%). The differentials include metastatic NET (far more common), HCC with trabecular pattern, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, solid pseudopapillary neoplasm metastasis, paraganglioma and epithelioid PEComa.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show cellular smears of monotonous, loosely cohesive cells and rosettes with eccentric round nuclei, salt-and-pepper chromatin and plasmacytoid appearance, which strongly suggests a neuroendocrine neoplasm; Ki-67 can be assessed on cell block, although small samples may underestimate grade. Cytology cannot determine whether the tumour is primary or metastatic.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin A, INSM1 and keratins (CAM5.2, AE1/AE3), and negative for HepPar1 and arginase-1. Ki-67 is used for grading. Site-of-origin markers help search for a primary: CDX2 (midgut), SATB2 (hindgut), ISL1 and PAX8 or PDX1 (pancreas), and TTF-1 (lung). SSTR2A staining supports somatostatin analogue therapy and imaging.

entities.entity: Neuroendocrine carcinoma of liver (small cell and large cell)
entities.variants: Small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma; large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma; NEC arising in IPNB or with adenocarcinoma (see MiNEN); primary vs metastatic (lung)
entities.remarks: Rare, highly aggressive poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma; sheets of small or large cells with high mitotic rate and necrosis; Ki-67 usually over 50%; TP53 and RB1 alterations; metastasis from lung must be excluded.
entities.histo: Neuroendocrine carcinoma of the liver is a rare, poorly differentiated, high-grade neoplasm that may be primary or, more commonly, metastatic, particularly from the lung. Small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma consists of sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm, finely granular chromatin, nuclear moulding, absent or inconspicuous nucleoli, numerous mitoses, apoptotic bodies and extensive necrosis, with crush artefact. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma shows larger cells with moderate cytoplasm, vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli, arranged in organoid nests, trabeculae or rosettes, with high mitotic activity and necrosis. Both have a Ki-67 index usually above 50%, and they are associated with TP53 and RB1 alterations. They may arise in association with adenocarcinoma or intraductal neoplasms. The prognosis is very poor. The differentials include NET G3 (well-differentiated morphology), poorly differentiated HCC or cholangiocarcinoma, lymphoma, small round cell tumours, metastatic small cell lung carcinoma and Merkel cell carcinoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show highly cellular smears of small cells with nuclear moulding, fine chromatin, scant cytoplasm, crush artefact and necrotic background (small cell type) or larger cells with prominent nucleoli (large cell type); cytology is often diagnostic of high-grade NEC with cell block immunostains, though it cannot establish the primary site.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin (often weak), INSM1, CD56 and keratins (often dot-like), with Ki-67 usually over 50%; p53 is aberrant and RB1 is lost in many cases. TTF-1 can be positive in both pulmonary and extrapulmonary small cell carcinomas, so it does not establish a lung origin. CK20 is negative (excluding Merkel cell carcinoma), and CD45 and lymphoma markers are negative.

entities.variants: Mixed adenocarcinoma (cholangiocarcinoma) and NEC; mixed HCC and NEC; mixed NET and adenocarcinoma (rare)
entities.remarks: Each component must make up at least 30% of the tumour; most commonly cholangiocarcinoma with high-grade NEC; aggressive behaviour driven by the NEC component.
entities.histo: Mixed neuroendocrine-non-neuroendocrine neoplasm of the liver is a rare tumour composed of a neuroendocrine component, usually high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma, and a non-neuroendocrine component such as cholangiocarcinoma or, less often, hepatocellular carcinoma, with each component representing at least 30% of the tumour. The components may be intermingled or form distinct areas. The neuroendocrine component typically drives the prognosis, which is poor. Neuroendocrine differentiation in a minority of cells of a conventional carcinoma does not qualify as MiNEN. The differentials include NEC alone, poorly differentiated cholangiocarcinoma or HCC with focal neuroendocrine marker expression, combined HCC-cholangiocarcinoma, and collision tumours.
entities.cyto: Aspirates may show two distinct cell populations, glandular and neuroendocrine, but sampling of only one component is common.
entities.ihc: The neuroendocrine component is positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin and INSM1 with high Ki-67, while the adenocarcinoma component is CK7 and CK19 positive and the HCC component is HepPar1, arginase-1 and glypican-3 positive. The proportion of each component is estimated on H&E and confirmed with IHC.

entities.variants: Sporadic angiosarcoma; associated with vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast, anabolic steroids; paediatric angiosarcoma (formerly type 2 infantile haemangioendothelioma); epithelioid angiosarcoma; patterns: sinusoidal, cavernous, solid spindle, papillary, haemangioma-like; secondary angiosarcoma
entities.remarks: Commonest primary hepatic sarcoma in adults; multifocal haemorrhagic tumour; malignant endothelial cells grow along sinusoids, dissecting liver cell plates, forming cavernous spaces and solid areas; MYC amplification in some; very poor prognosis; biopsy risk of bleeding.
entities.histo: Angiosarcoma is the most common primary malignant mesenchymal tumour of the liver in adults, although it is rare overall. It is associated with exposure to vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast and anabolic steroids, but most cases are sporadic. Paediatric cases, previously called type 2 infantile haemangioendothelioma, also occur. Grossly the tumour is often multifocal or diffuse, forming spongy, haemorrhagic, poorly circumscribed masses with necrosis, and rupture with haemoperitoneum is a frequent presentation. Microscopically, malignant endothelial cells with hyperchromatic, pleomorphic, elongated or epithelioid nuclei grow along pre-existing sinusoids, lining and dissecting liver cell plates, which become atrophic, and they also form anastomosing vascular channels, cavernous blood-filled spaces, papillary tufts and solid spindle or epithelioid sheets. Mitoses and necrosis are common. Low-grade areas may resemble haemangioma, which makes sampling important. Kupffer cells may also proliferate. The prognosis is very poor, with most patients dying within a year. The differentials include cavernous haemangioma (bland, no sinusoidal infiltration), anastomosing haemangioma, hepatic small vessel neoplasm (infiltrative but bland), epithelioid haemangioendothelioma (cords of epithelioid cells in myxohyaline stroma), peliosis hepatis, Kaposi sarcoma, and poorly differentiated carcinoma or HCC in solid epithelioid forms.
entities.cyto: Aspirates are often bloody and paucicellular, and may contain spindle or epithelioid atypical cells, sometimes with intracytoplasmic vacuoles or erythrophagocytosis; epithelioid angiosarcoma can mimic carcinoma. FNA carries a risk of bleeding, and immunostains on cell block are required.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for vascular markers ERG, CD31 and FLI1, and often CD34, with a high Ki-67 index. Epithelioid angiosarcoma may express keratins, which can lead to misdiagnosis as carcinoma unless ERG and CD31 are tested. MYC amplification or overexpression is seen in a subset. HHV-8 (LANA-1) is negative, excluding Kaposi sarcoma, and CAMTA1 and TFE3 are negative, excluding epithelioid haemangioendothelioma. HepPar1 and arginase-1 are negative.

entities.variants: WWTR1::CAMTA1-fused EHE (most); YAP1::TFE3-fused EHE (vasoformative, younger patients); multifocal hepatic EHE with lung involvement; high-risk EHE (size, mitoses)
entities.remarks: Low- to intermediate-grade malignant vascular tumour; multiple subcapsular nodules with capsular retraction, often lung involvement; epithelioid and dendritic cells with intracytoplasmic lumina (blister cells) in myxohyaline stroma, growing along sinusoids and veins with zonal architecture; CAMTA1 nuclear IHC; unpredictable course, transplant option.
entities.histo: Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma is a malignant vascular tumour with a variable course, which often involves the liver in a multifocal pattern, frequently together with the lungs. It occurs mostly in adults, more often women. On imaging, there are multiple subcapsular nodules that coalesce and cause capsular retraction, which can mimic metastatic carcinoma or cholangiocarcinoma. Microscopically the nodules show a zonal pattern, with a hypocellular, sclerotic or myxohyaline centre and a more cellular periphery, where tumour cells infiltrate sinusoids and grow into hepatic and portal vein branches, often forming intravascular tufts. The tumour cells are epithelioid or dendritic (branching), with eosinophilic cytoplasm and intracytoplasmic vacuoles (lumina) that may contain red blood cells, giving a signet ring or blister-like appearance, and nuclear atypia is usually mild. The WWTR1::CAMTA1 fusion is present in most cases, and a minority carry YAP1::TFE3, which shows more vasoformative growth. Tumour size and mitotic activity help predict behaviour. The differentials include metastatic adenocarcinoma or signet ring carcinoma (keratin can be positive in EHE, a pitfall), cholangiocarcinoma, angiosarcoma (more atypia, high mitoses, necrosis), sclerosed haemangioma, epithelioid sarcoma and inflammatory pseudotumour.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show epithelioid or spindle cells with moderate cytoplasm, intracytoplasmic vacuoles, sometimes containing red cells, and myxohyaline stromal fragments; the cells can mimic carcinoma, and vascular markers and CAMTA1 on cell block are necessary.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for ERG, CD31, CD34 and FLI1, and frequently show focal keratin expression; nuclear CAMTA1 staining is present in WWTR1::CAMTA1-fused tumours and is a sensitive and specific diagnostic marker, while TFE3 nuclear staining identifies the YAP1::TFE3 subset. HepPar1, arginase-1, CK7 and CK19 are negative or only focal, which helps exclude HCC and cholangiocarcinoma, and Ki-67 is generally lower than in angiosarcoma.

entities.variants: AIDS-associated (epidemic) Kaposi sarcoma; iatrogenic (transplant-associated); classic; endemic (African)
entities.remarks: HHV-8-driven vascular tumour; hepatic involvement usually part of disseminated AIDS-related disease; portal-based and capsular spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces, extravasated red cells, hyaline globules; HHV-8 (LANA-1) nuclear IHC diagnostic.
entities.histo: Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8-driven vascular neoplasm that involves the liver mainly in patients with disseminated AIDS-related disease or in immunosuppressed transplant recipients, and is rarely the presenting site. Grossly, it forms multiple small, red-brown, haemorrhagic nodules, often along portal tracts and beneath the capsule. Microscopically, it shows fascicles of spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces containing red cells, with extravasated erythrocytes, haemosiderin, plasma cells and intracytoplasmic and extracellular eosinophilic hyaline globules (PAS positive). The lesions are centred on portal tracts and extend into the adjacent parenchyma, and early patch-stage lesions can be subtle, with only irregular vascular spaces in portal tracts. The differentials include angiosarcoma (atypical endothelial cells lining sinusoids), bacillary angiomatosis and bacillary peliosis (Bartonella organisms, neutrophils), peliosis hepatis, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour and other spindle cell tumours.
entities.cyto: Aspirates may yield spindle cells in loose fascicles with blood, which is non-specific; HHV-8 immunostaining on cell block is necessary.
entities.ihc: Tumour cells are positive for HHV-8 LANA-1 nuclear staining, which is diagnostic, and for CD31, CD34, ERG, FLI1 and D2-40. Bartonella immunostaining or Warthin-Starry staining is negative, excluding bacillary angiomatosis, and the low-to-moderate Ki-67 and HHV-8 positivity distinguish Kaposi sarcoma from angiosarcoma.

entities.variants: Classic UESL of older children (6 to 15 years) and young adults; UESL arising in or with mesenchymal hamartoma (19q13.4 rearrangement); UESL with cystic degeneration
entities.remarks: Third commonest paediatric liver malignancy; large, solitary, cystic and solid mass, normal AFP; pleomorphic, bizarre spindle and stellate cells with eosinophilic PAS-positive diastase-resistant hyaline globules in myxoid stroma; entrapped bile ducts at periphery; chemotherapy plus surgery has improved survival.
entities.histo: Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver is a malignant mesenchymal tumour that occurs mainly in older children and adolescents, typically between six and fifteen years, and less often in adults. It presents as a large, solitary, rapidly growing mass, usually in the right lobe, with normal serum AFP, and on imaging it may appear cystic despite being largely solid, because of its myxoid stroma. Grossly, it is a large, well-demarcated mass with solid, gelatinous, haemorrhagic, necrotic and cystic areas. Microscopically, it consists of loosely arranged, highly pleomorphic, spindle, stellate and bizarre multinucleated cells in a myxoid stroma, with numerous mitoses, including atypical forms. Characteristic eosinophilic hyaline globules of varying size are present within the cytoplasm of tumour cells and in the stroma, and they are PAS positive and diastase resistant. Entrapped bile ducts and hepatocytes are seen at the periphery, and extramedullary haematopoiesis may be present. Some cases arise in association with mesenchymal hamartoma, with which it shares 19q13.4 rearrangements. With multimodal therapy, the prognosis has improved considerably. The differentials include embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the biliary tree (younger children, cambium layer, myogenin positive), mesenchymal hamartoma, hepatoblastoma with mesenchymal components, sarcomatoid HCC, malignant rhabdoid tumour and other pleomorphic sarcomas.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show markedly pleomorphic spindle and multinucleated giant cells in a myxoid background, with intracytoplasmic and extracellular hyaline globules; the cytology is suggestive in the right clinical setting but requires histological and immunohistochemical confirmation.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for vimentin, and often for glypican-3, keratins (focally) and CD10, BCL2 and alpha-1 antitrypsin, but lack specific lineage markers; they are negative for myogenin and MyoD1 (excluding rhabdomyosarcoma), HepPar1 and arginase-1 (excluding sarcomatoid HCC), and INI1 is retained (excluding rhabdoid tumour). The hyaline globules are positive for alpha-1 antitrypsin.

entities.entity: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the biliary tree (and liver)
entities.variants: Botryoid embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the bile ducts; embryonal RMS of the liver parenchyma; alveolar RMS (rare)
entities.remarks: Commonest cause of obstructive jaundice due to tumour in young children (usually under 5 years); grape-like polypoid masses in bile ducts with a subepithelial cambium layer of small round to spindle rhabdomyoblasts; myogenin and desmin positive; good prognosis with multimodal therapy.
entities.histo: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the biliary tree is a rare malignant tumour of young children, usually under five years of age, and is the most common tumour causing obstructive jaundice in this age group. It arises from the extrahepatic or intrahepatic bile ducts and forms soft, grape-like (botryoid) polypoid masses within the ductal lumen, with extension into the liver. Microscopically, it consists of small, round to spindle cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scant eosinophilic cytoplasm in a myxoid stroma, with a dense subepithelial condensation of tumour cells beneath the intact biliary epithelium (the cambium layer), characteristic of the botryoid subtype. Rhabdomyoblasts with eosinophilic cytoplasm and cross-striations may be seen. With combined chemotherapy, surgery and radiotherapy, the prognosis is relatively good. The differentials include undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma (older children, pleomorphic cells, hyaline globules, myogenin negative), mesenchymal hamartoma, hepatoblastoma, choledochal cyst and inflammatory polyps.
entities.cyto: Aspirates or brushings show small round to spindle cells, some with eccentric eosinophilic cytoplasm (rhabdomyoblasts), in a myxoid background; immunostains for myogenin and desmin on cell block help confirm the diagnosis.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for desmin, myogenin (MYF4) and MyoD1, often with heterogeneous nuclear myogenin staining in embryonal RMS (diffuse strong staining suggests alveolar RMS, which would prompt FOXO1 testing). Keratins, glypican-3 and hepatocellular markers are negative, and INI1 is retained.

entities.variants: Primary hepatic leiomyosarcoma (from hepatic veins, IVC or portal vessels); leiomyosarcoma of IVC with hepatic involvement; metastatic leiomyosarcoma (uterus, retroperitoneum, GI tract) is more common
entities.remarks: Rare primary hepatic sarcoma; fascicles of atypical spindle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei, mitoses and necrosis; exclude metastasis and GIST; EBV-associated smooth muscle tumours occur in immunosuppressed patients (separate).
entities.histo: Primary leiomyosarcoma of the liver is a rare tumour, arising from smooth muscle of intrahepatic vessels, the hepatic veins or the inferior vena cava, and it is far less common than metastatic leiomyosarcoma from the uterus, retroperitoneum or gastrointestinal tract. Leiomyosarcoma of the IVC can extend into the liver and cause Budd-Chiari syndrome. Grossly, it forms a large, firm, white-tan, whorled mass with haemorrhage and necrosis. Microscopically, it consists of intersecting fascicles of spindle cells with eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasm, blunt-ended cigar-shaped nuclei, perinuclear vacuoles, nuclear atypia, mitotic activity and coagulative tumour necrosis. Epithelioid and myxoid variants are recognised. The prognosis is poor. The differentials include metastatic leiomyosarcoma, GIST (CD117, DOG1), EBV-associated smooth muscle tumour (EBER), sarcomatoid HCC or carcinoma, angiomyolipoma with myoid predominance, solitary fibrous tumour, MPNST and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show cohesive fascicles and single atypical spindle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei and fibrillary cytoplasm; immunostains are required to exclude GIST and other spindle cell tumours.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for SMA, desmin, h-caldesmon and calponin, and negative for CD117, DOG1, S100, SOX10, HMB45, Melan-A, STAT6 and keratins (keratin may be focally positive). EBER is negative, excluding EBV-associated smooth muscle tumour. ER and PR positivity suggest a uterine primary.

entities.entity: Malignant PEComa of liver (malignant epithelioid angiomyolipoma)
entities.variants: Malignant PEComa; malignant epithelioid angiomyolipoma; TFE3-rearranged PEComa
entities.remarks: Rare aggressive tumour in the PEComa family; large size (over 5 cm), infiltrative growth, high nuclear grade, necrosis, vascular invasion and mitoses over 1 per 50 HPF indicate malignancy; HMB45 and Melan-A positive; may respond to mTOR inhibitors.
entities.histo: Malignant PEComa of the liver is a rare tumour in the family of perivascular epithelioid cell neoplasms, which includes angiomyolipoma. It consists predominantly of epithelioid cells with abundant clear to eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, arranged in sheets and nests around blood vessels, with marked nuclear atypia, prominent nucleoli, multinucleated giant cells, frequent mitoses, coagulative necrosis and vascular invasion. Features associated with malignant behaviour include large size (over 5 cm), infiltrative growth, high nuclear grade and cellularity, mitoses greater than one per fifty high-power fields, necrosis and vascular invasion. Some tumours harbour TFE3 rearrangements rather than TSC2 alterations. Metastases may occur in the lungs and peritoneum. mTOR inhibitors are a therapeutic option for TSC-altered tumours. The differentials include HCC, especially clear cell and poorly differentiated forms, metastatic melanoma, adrenal cortical carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, and benign epithelioid angiomyolipoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show large epithelioid cells with abundant granular or clear cytoplasm, atypical nuclei and prominent nucleoli, which can closely mimic HCC; cell block immunostains are essential.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for HMB45, Melan-A and cathepsin K, often for SMA and desmin, and sometimes TFE3 in rearranged cases; they are negative for keratins, HepPar1, arginase-1, glypican-3, S100 and SOX10 (excluding melanoma), and PAX8 (excluding renal cell carcinoma).

entities.entity: EBV-positive inflammatory follicular dendritic cell sarcoma (inflammatory pseudotumour-like FDC sarcoma)
entities.variants: Hepatic EBV-positive inflammatory FDC sarcoma; splenic counterpart; WHO 5th digestive term 'inflammatory pseudotumour-like follicular dendritic cell sarcoma'
entities.remarks: Rare low-grade tumour of liver and spleen, mostly middle-aged women; spindle cells with vesicular nuclei scattered among dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, often with haemorrhage, necrosis, fibrinoid vessels and granulomas; EBER positive; FDC markers (CD21, CD23, CD35) often weak or focal; indolent with local recurrence.
entities.histo: EBV-positive inflammatory follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, previously called inflammatory pseudotumour-like follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, is a rare neoplasm that arises almost exclusively in the liver and spleen, mainly in middle-aged women, and is associated with Epstein-Barr virus. It forms a well-circumscribed, often haemorrhagic and necrotic mass. Microscopically, it consists of spindle to ovoid neoplastic cells with vesicular nuclei, distinct nucleoli and indistinct cell borders, scattered singly or in loose fascicles among a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells, sometimes with eosinophils, epithelioid granulomas and blood vessels with fibrinoid deposits. Atypical cells, sometimes resembling Reed-Sternberg cells, can be seen. Because the inflammation dominates, it is easily mistaken for inflammatory pseudotumour, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour or Hodgkin lymphoma. The behaviour is generally indolent, with local recurrence possible after excision. The differentials include inflammatory pseudotumour (non-neoplastic, EBER negative), inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour (ALK or ROS1 positive), IgG4-related disease, lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and conventional FDC sarcoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show a mixed lymphoplasmacytic population with scattered large spindle or ovoid cells with vesicular nuclei; the neoplastic cells are easily missed, and EBER and FDC markers on cell block are needed.
entities.ihc: The neoplastic cells are positive for EBER by in situ hybridisation, which is the key test, and they express follicular dendritic cell markers CD21, CD23, CD35, clusterin and podoplanin (D2-40), often only weakly or focally, and SSTR2 in many cases; SMA may be positive. ALK and ROS1 are negative, keratins are negative, and CD30 and CD15 are negative or focal, which helps exclude Hodgkin lymphoma.

entities.entity: Other primary sarcomas of liver (synovial sarcoma, MPNST, liposarcoma, fibrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, malignant SFT)
entities.variants: Primary hepatic synovial sarcoma (SS18 fusion); malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour; liposarcoma (well-differentiated, myxoid, pleomorphic); fibrosarcoma; extraskeletal osteosarcoma; Ewing sarcoma (EWSR1 fusion); undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma; malignant solitary fibrous tumour; desmoplastic small round cell tumour (involvement)
entities.remarks: Very rare primary sarcomas; most liver sarcomas are metastases or sarcomatoid carcinomas; molecular tests (SS18, EWSR1, MDM2) and IHC guide classification; exclude sarcomatoid HCC and cholangiocarcinoma.
entities.histo: Primary sarcomas other than angiosarcoma, epithelioid haemangioendothelioma, undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma and leiomyosarcoma are very rare in the liver, and most sarcomas found in the liver are metastases from other sites. Synovial sarcoma, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour, liposarcoma (well-differentiated, myxoid or pleomorphic), fibrosarcoma, extraskeletal osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma have all been reported as primary hepatic tumours. Their histology is the same as at other sites: monophasic or biphasic spindle cell proliferation for synovial sarcoma, fascicles of wavy spindle cells with geographic necrosis for MPNST, lipoblasts and atypical stromal cells for liposarcoma, herringbone fascicles for fibrosarcoma, malignant osteoid for osteosarcoma, and sheets of small round cells for Ewing sarcoma. Malignant solitary fibrous tumour shows hypercellularity, atypia, necrosis and mitoses in a STAT6-positive tumour. Before accepting a primary hepatic origin, sarcomatoid HCC or cholangiocarcinoma, metastatic sarcoma, melanoma and GIST must be excluded.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show the cytological features of the particular sarcoma; cell block material allows immunostaining and molecular testing for defining fusions.
entities.ihc: The panel depends on morphology: TLE1 and SS18-SSX fusion-specific antibody for synovial sarcoma, loss of H3K27me3 and partial S100 or SOX10 in MPNST, MDM2 and CDK4 for well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcoma, SATB2 for osteosarcoma, CD99 with NKX2.2 and FLI1 for Ewing sarcoma, STAT6 for SFT, and desmin with WT1 C-terminal for desmoplastic small round cell tumour. Keratins, HepPar1, arginase-1 and CK19 help exclude sarcomatoid carcinomas, and CD117 and DOG1 help exclude GIST.

entities.entity: Primary hepatic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
entities.variants: DLBCL NOS (germinal centre and activated B-cell types); EBV-positive DLBCL; DLBCL associated with HCV infection; DLBCL in immunosuppressed patients; high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements
entities.remarks: Commonest primary hepatic lymphoma, though primary hepatic lymphoma is rare (secondary involvement is much more common); solitary or multiple masses; associated with HCV, HBV, HIV and immunosuppression; sheets of large atypical B cells; R-CHOP chemotherapy.
entities.histo: Primary hepatic lymphoma is defined as lymphoma confined to the liver at presentation or with predominant liver involvement, without significant nodal, splenic or marrow disease, and it is rare, while secondary involvement of the liver by systemic lymphoma is much more common. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the commonest type of primary hepatic lymphoma, often associated with chronic hepatitis C, hepatitis B, HIV or immunosuppression. It presents as a solitary mass or multiple nodules, sometimes with raised LDH and B symptoms, and imaging may suggest HCC or metastases. Microscopically, sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells with vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli efface the liver parenchyma, with entrapped bile ducts and hepatocytes at the periphery, and necrosis and apoptosis are frequent. Cell of origin classification (germinal centre or activated B-cell type) and testing for MYC, BCL2 and BCL6 rearrangements are performed as in other sites. The differentials include poorly differentiated carcinoma, HCC, metastatic melanoma, Burkitt lymphoma, high-grade B-cell lymphoma, classical Hodgkin lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma and myeloid sarcoma.
entities.cyto: FNA shows a monotonous population of large, discohesive atypical lymphoid cells with scant basophilic cytoplasm, vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli and lymphoglandular bodies in the background, together with apoptotic debris; cytology can strongly suggest lymphoma, and flow cytometry on aspirated material supports the diagnosis, but core biopsy is needed for full classification.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for CD45, CD20, CD79a and PAX5, with variable CD10, BCL6 and MUM1 for cell of origin assignment (Hans algorithm), and high Ki-67. BCL2 and MYC expression are assessed, with FISH for MYC, BCL2 and BCL6 rearrangements. EBER in situ hybridisation identifies EBV-positive DLBCL. Keratins, HepPar1, S100 and SOX10 are negative, excluding carcinoma and melanoma.

entities.entity: Primary hepatic extranodal marginal zone lymphoma (MALT lymphoma)
entities.variants: Hepatic MALT lymphoma; associated with HCV, PBC, autoimmune disease; amyloid-associated variant
entities.remarks: Rare primary hepatic lymphoma; nodular infiltrate of small centrocyte-like and monocytoid B cells with plasma cells, colonising follicles and forming lymphoepithelial lesions of bile ducts; indolent; key differential is reactive lymphoid hyperplasia.
entities.histo: Primary hepatic extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) is a rare indolent lymphoma, associated with chronic hepatitis C, primary biliary cholangitis and other autoimmune diseases. It usually forms a solitary mass and is often discovered incidentally. Microscopically, the tumour consists of a nodular or diffuse infiltrate of small to medium-sized B cells with irregular nuclei (centrocyte-like) and pale cytoplasm (monocytoid), together with plasma cells, sometimes with light chain restriction, and scattered large transformed cells. The neoplastic cells colonise reactive germinal centres and infiltrate bile duct epithelium, forming lymphoepithelial lesions. Amyloid may be deposited in some cases. The prognosis is favourable after excision or local therapy. The differentials include reactive lymphoid hyperplasia (pseudolymphoma), large portal lymphoid aggregates in hepatitis C, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, small lymphocytic lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma and IgG4-related disease.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show a population of small to medium-sized lymphoid cells with plasma cells and occasional larger cells, which is difficult to distinguish from a reactive process on morphology alone; flow cytometry demonstrating light chain restriction supports lymphoma, and core biopsy is preferred.
entities.ihc: The neoplastic B cells are positive for CD20, CD79a and BCL2, and negative for CD5, CD10, CD23, cyclin D1 and SOX11, which helps exclude small lymphocytic, follicular and mantle cell lymphoma. Keratin stains highlight lymphoepithelial lesions of bile ducts, and CD21 or CD23 show disrupted follicular dendritic meshworks. Kappa and lambda in situ hybridisation demonstrates light chain restriction in plasma cells, and IGH clonality testing is positive.

entities.variants: Gamma-delta TCR type (most); alpha-beta TCR type (rare); associated with immunosuppression (thiopurines plus anti-TNF in IBD, solid organ transplant)
entities.remarks: Aggressive peripheral T-cell lymphoma of young men; hepatosplenomegaly without lymphadenopathy, cytopenias; monotonous medium-sized cytotoxic T cells infiltrating hepatic sinusoids (and splenic red pulp, marrow sinuses); CD3+, CD56+, CD4-, CD8- (usually), TIA-1+, granzyme B-; isochromosome 7q; very poor prognosis.
entities.histo: Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma is a rare, aggressive peripheral T-cell lymphoma that mainly affects adolescents and young adults, more often men, and is associated with immunosuppression, particularly combination therapy with thiopurines and anti-TNF agents in inflammatory bowel disease, and solid organ transplantation. Patients present with marked hepatosplenomegaly, fever, systemic symptoms and cytopenias, but without lymphadenopathy. In the liver, monotonous medium-sized lymphoid cells with moderate pale cytoplasm and slightly irregular nuclei infiltrate the sinusoids in a diffuse, single-file or clustered pattern, with relative sparing of portal tracts, and hepatocytes are usually preserved. The spleen shows red pulp infiltration and the bone marrow shows intrasinusoidal infiltration, which can be subtle. Isochromosome 7q is a characteristic cytogenetic abnormality, and STAT5B and SETD2 mutations are frequent. The prognosis is very poor despite aggressive therapy. The differentials include EBV hepatitis and other viral hepatitides with sinusoidal lymphocytosis, T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukaemia, aggressive NK-cell leukaemia, leukaemic infiltration, haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and other peripheral T-cell lymphomas.
entities.cyto: Liver aspirates are not usually used; peripheral blood or bone marrow aspirates may show atypical medium-sized lymphoid cells, and flow cytometry demonstrates the characteristic phenotype.
entities.ihc: The neoplastic cells are positive for CD3 and CD2 and usually CD56, and negative for CD4, CD5 and usually CD8, and they express TCR gamma-delta (TCRdelta immunostain) in most cases, with a non-activated cytotoxic phenotype: TIA-1 positive, granzyme B and perforin negative. EBER is negative, which separates the lymphoma from EBV-associated T or NK cell proliferations. T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies and FISH for isochromosome 7q confirm the diagnosis.

entities.entity: Secondary involvement of liver by lymphoma, leukaemia and plasma cell neoplasms
entities.variants: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (portal-based, granulomas, VBDS); follicular lymphoma; small lymphocytic lymphoma/CLL (portal); mantle cell lymphoma; hairy cell leukaemia (sinusoidal, angiomatoid lesions); Burkitt lymphoma; peripheral T-cell lymphomas; ALCL; acute myeloid and lymphoblastic leukaemia (sinusoidal); chronic myeloid leukaemia; myeloma and plasmacytoma; myeloid sarcoma; systemic mastocytosis (see histiocytic/mast cell row)
entities.remarks: Far more common than primary hepatic lymphoma; pattern of infiltration gives clues: portal (low-grade B-cell lymphomas, CLL, Hodgkin), sinusoidal (leukaemias, HSTCL, hairy cell leukaemia), mass-forming (DLBCL, Burkitt); Hodgkin lymphoma can cause granulomas and paraneoplastic ductopenia without infiltration.
entities.histo: The liver is frequently involved by systemic lymphomas and leukaemias, much more commonly than by primary hepatic lymphoma. The pattern of infiltration provides useful diagnostic clues. Low-grade B-cell lymphomas, such as small lymphocytic lymphoma or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma, usually expand portal tracts with dense monotonous small lymphoid infiltrates, sometimes forming nodules, and must be separated from chronic hepatitis. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma involves portal tracts with Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells in a mixed inflammatory background, and it may also cause hepatic granulomas, idiopathic cholestasis and vanishing bile duct syndrome without direct infiltration. Leukaemias, hairy cell leukaemia and hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma show predominantly sinusoidal infiltration, and hairy cell leukaemia may form angiomatoid blood lakes lined by tumour cells. Aggressive lymphomas such as DLBCL and Burkitt lymphoma form mass lesions. Multiple myeloma may infiltrate sinusoids or form plasmacytomas and can be associated with light chain deposition or amyloid. Myeloid sarcoma forms masses of immature myeloid cells. The differentials include chronic viral and autoimmune hepatitis, EBV hepatitis, extramedullary haematopoiesis, reactive lymphoid hyperplasia and metastatic carcinoma.
entities.cyto: FNA of focal liver lesions may reveal a monotonous lymphoid or blast population, Hodgkin cells in a mixed background, or plasma cells; flow cytometry on aspirated material is valuable, and core biopsy or excision of a more accessible site is preferred for full classification.
entities.ihc: Lineage and subtype-specific panels are applied: CD20, CD3, CD5, CD10, CD23, BCL2, BCL6, cyclin D1, SOX11 and LEF1 for small B-cell lymphomas; CD30, CD15, PAX5 (weak) and MUM1 for Hodgkin cells; CD25, CD103, annexin A1, TRAP and BRAF V600E for hairy cell leukaemia; CD34, CD117, MPO, TdT and CD33 for leukaemias and myeloid sarcoma; CD138, kappa and lambda for plasma cell neoplasms; and MYC, BCL2 and Ki-67 for high-grade B-cell lymphomas.

entities.entity: Malignant germ cell tumours of liver (yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, immature teratoma)
entities.variants: Primary hepatic yolk sac tumour; primary hepatic choriocarcinoma (infantile choriocarcinoma, often with maternal disease; adult); immature teratoma; mixed germ cell tumour; metastatic gonadal germ cell tumours (more common)
entities.remarks: Extremely rare primary liver tumours; yolk sac tumour has very high AFP (overlaps with hepatoblastoma); choriocarcinoma has high beta-hCG and haemorrhagic mass; exclude metastasis from gonads and mediastinum; hepatoid yolk sac tumour mimics HCC.
entities.histo: Primary germ cell tumours of the liver are exceedingly rare, and metastasis from a gonadal or mediastinal primary must always be excluded. Yolk sac tumour, which may occur in children or adults, produces very high serum AFP and shows reticular, microcystic, solid, glandular and papillary patterns with Schiller-Duval bodies and hyaline globules, and the hepatoid variant closely resembles hepatocellular carcinoma. Primary hepatic choriocarcinoma presents as a haemorrhagic mass with very high beta-hCG, either in infants, where it may be associated with placental choriocarcinoma in the mother, or rarely in adults; it shows a biphasic population of syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts with extensive haemorrhage and necrosis. Immature teratoma contains immature neuroectodermal tissue. The prognosis depends on histological type and stage, and these tumours are treated with platinum-based chemotherapy. The differentials include hepatoblastoma (AFP also high, fetal and embryonal patterns), HCC (especially in adults and for hepatoid yolk sac tumour), hepatoid carcinomas and metastatic germ cell tumours.
entities.cyto: Aspirates of yolk sac tumour show loose clusters of epithelial cells with vacuolated cytoplasm and hyaline globules, and choriocarcinoma shows large multinucleated syncytiotrophoblasts and mononuclear cytotrophoblasts in a haemorrhagic background; immunostains and serum markers are needed for confirmation.
entities.ihc: Yolk sac tumour is positive for SALL4, glypican-3, AFP and keratins, and negative for OCT4 and CD30, and it may express HepPar1 in the hepatoid variant, while arginase-1 is often negative, which is a helpful distinction from HCC. Choriocarcinoma is positive for beta-hCG, GATA3, SALL4 (cytotrophoblasts) and keratins. Immature teratoma components express lineage markers such as SOX2 and GFAP in neuroepithelium. Hepatoblastoma differs by nuclear beta-catenin in fetal and embryonal cells.

entities.entity: Atypical hepatocellular neoplasm (well-differentiated hepatocellular neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential, HCN-UMP)
entities.variants: Atypical hepatocellular adenoma (HCA with focal atypia); hepatocellular neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential; borderline hepatocellular adenoma/HCC; beta-catenin-activated adenoma with atypical features
entities.remarks: Descriptive category (not a WHO entity) for well-differentiated hepatocellular neoplasms in non-cirrhotic livers with features between adenoma and HCC (focal reticulin loss, pseudoglands, mild atypia, men, older age, beta-catenin activation); managed by complete resection like low-grade HCC.
entities.histo: Atypical hepatocellular neoplasm, also called well-differentiated hepatocellular neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential, is a descriptive term used for well-differentiated hepatocellular tumours in non-cirrhotic livers that show some, but not sufficient, features of hepatocellular carcinoma, so a confident diagnosis of either adenoma or carcinoma cannot be made. Typical features include focal cytological atypia such as increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio and small cell change, focal pseudoglandular architecture, focal reticulin loss, and occurrence in clinical settings that increase the risk of malignancy, such as male sex, age over 50 years, anabolic steroid use or glycogen storage disease. Many of these tumours show beta-catenin activation. Molecular studies show that a proportion harbour TERT promoter mutations or chromosomal gains typical of HCC. The category is not an entity in the WHO classification but is endorsed in many practice guidelines, and these lesions are managed by complete resection with follow-up similar to low-risk HCC. The differentials include hepatocellular adenoma (particularly beta-catenin-activated), well-differentiated HCC arising in adenoma, FNH and high-grade dysplastic nodules in cirrhosis.
entities.cyto: Cytology cannot classify these lesions; aspirates show well-differentiated hepatocytes with mild atypia, and the diagnosis requires a resection specimen.
entities.ihc: The adenoma subtyping panel (LFABP, CRP or SAA, glutamine synthetase, beta-catenin) is combined with HCC markers (glypican-3, HSP70) and Ki-67; diffuse glutamine synthetase with nuclear beta-catenin, focal glypican-3 positivity and focal reticulin loss are typical. Molecular testing for CTNNB1 and TERT promoter mutations and copy number changes helps refine risk.

entities.variants: Hepatic small vessel neoplasm (HSVN) with GNAQ, GNA14 or GNA11 activating mutations
entities.remarks: Rare vascular neoplasm of uncertain potential (WHO 5th); infiltrative, poorly circumscribed proliferation of small thin-walled vessels lined by bland, hobnail endothelial cells, entrapping portal tracts and hepatocytes; low Ki-67, no MYC amplification; mimics well-differentiated angiosarcoma.
entities.histo: Hepatic small vessel neoplasm is a recently described vascular tumour of the liver in adults, included in the WHO 5th edition, with uncertain but probably low malignant potential. It is typically a small lesion, though it can be larger, discovered incidentally or during imaging for other reasons. Microscopically, it is a poorly circumscribed, infiltrative proliferation of small, capillary-sized, thin-walled vascular channels lined by flat or hobnail endothelial cells with bland nuclei, lacking significant atypia, multilayering, mitoses or necrosis. The vessels infiltrate the adjacent parenchyma and entrap portal tracts and hepatocytes, which raises concern for angiosarcoma. Activating mutations in GNAQ, GNA14 and GNA11 have been described. Complete excision is usually curative, and behaviour is benign in reported series, although follow-up is limited. The differentials include well-differentiated angiosarcoma (atypia, multilayering, high Ki-67, MYC), capillary and anastomosing haemangiomas, and peliosis hepatis.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no established role; aspirates would be expected to contain blood and occasional bland endothelial cells.
entities.ihc: The endothelial cells are positive for CD31, CD34, ERG and FLI1, with a low Ki-67 index (usually under 10%) and wild-type p53 staining. MYC is negative, unlike some angiosarcomas, and GLUT1 is negative.

entities.variants: CNSET with ossification and calcification; CNSET associated with Cushing syndrome (ectopic ACTH); CNSET in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
entities.remarks: Rare tumour of children and young adults, mostly female, in a non-cirrhotic liver; well-demarcated nests of epithelioid and spindle cells in desmoplastic stroma with psammomatous calcification and ossification; CTNNB1 mutations or deletions; WT1 and nuclear beta-catenin positive; low-grade, local recurrence possible.
entities.histo: Calcifying nested stromal-epithelial tumour is a rare primary liver tumour, also known as ossifying stromal-epithelial tumour, occurring mainly in children and young adults, with a female predominance. Some patients have ectopic ACTH production with Cushing syndrome, and associations with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome have been described. It forms a large, well-circumscribed, lobulated, firm mass, often with calcification on imaging. Microscopically, it consists of well-demarcated nests of epithelioid and spindle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and bland, oval nuclei, surrounded by a desmoplastic myofibroblastic stroma, and the nests often contain psammomatous or dystrophic calcification and ossification. Mitotic activity is low. CTNNB1 mutations or deletions are frequent. Behaviour is generally low-grade, with good outcomes after resection, but local recurrence and rare metastases have been reported. The differentials include hepatoblastoma (younger children, high AFP), desmoplastic small round cell tumour (WT1 C-terminal and desmin positive), metastatic neuroendocrine tumour, fibrolamellar carcinoma, and synovial sarcoma.
entities.cyto: Cytology descriptions are limited; aspirates would be expected to show clusters of bland epithelioid and spindle cells with calcific debris.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for WT1 (nuclear), keratins (AE1/AE3, CAM5.2), vimentin, CD56 and nuclear beta-catenin, and often show CD117 or CD10; they are negative for HepPar1, arginase-1, glypican-3, chromogranin and desmin, which helps exclude hepatoblastoma, HCC, NET and desmoplastic small round cell tumour. The stroma is SMA positive.

entities.variants: Benign-behaving SFT; malignant SFT (hypercellular, atypical, necrosis, mitoses over 4 per 10 HPF); SFT with hypoglycaemia (Doege-Potter syndrome, IGF2 secretion); lipomatous SFT
entities.remarks: Rare in liver; NAB2::STAT6 fusion-driven fibroblastic tumour with patternless arrangement of spindle cells, staghorn (haemangiopericytoma-like) vessels and keloidal collagen; STAT6 nuclear IHC diagnostic; risk stratification by age, size, mitoses and necrosis.
entities.histo: Solitary fibrous tumour is a fibroblastic neoplasm of intermediate, rarely metastasising behaviour, which can occasionally arise in the liver, usually as a large, well-circumscribed, firm, white mass in adults. Some patients develop hypoglycaemia due to tumour secretion of IGF2 (Doege-Potter syndrome). Microscopically, it consists of bland spindle to ovoid cells arranged in a patternless pattern with alternating hypercellular and hypocellular areas, thick keloid-like collagen bands, and branching, dilated, staghorn-shaped (haemangiopericytoma-like) vessels. Malignant SFT shows hypercellularity, nuclear atypia, mitoses (over 4 per 10 high-power fields), necrosis and infiltrative borders. Risk stratification models using age, tumour size, mitotic count and necrosis predict metastatic risk. The tumour is defined by a NAB2::STAT6 fusion. The differentials include leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour, GIST, schwannoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma and angiomyolipoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show bland spindle cells, singly and in loose groups, with collagen fragments; the cytology is non-specific, and STAT6 on cell block helps.
entities.ihc: Nuclear STAT6 staining is highly sensitive and specific; CD34 is usually positive, and CD99 and BCL2 are often positive. The tumour is negative for SMA (or focal), desmin, S100, CD117, DOG1, keratins and HMB45. Ki-67 is higher in malignant SFT.

entities.variants: ALK-rearranged IMT; ROS1-, NTRK-, PDGFRB- or RET-rearranged IMT; epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma (RANBP2::ALK, nuclear membrane ALK, aggressive)
entities.remarks: True neoplasm (unlike inflammatory pseudotumour); fascicles of myofibroblastic spindle cells with vesicular nuclei in an inflammatory background of plasma cells and lymphocytes; ALK or ROS1 rearrangement in many; targetable with ALK inhibitors; intermediate behaviour with local recurrence.
entities.histo: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour is a neoplasm of intermediate, rarely metastasising behaviour, composed of myofibroblastic spindle cells with an accompanying inflammatory infiltrate, and it can occur in the liver in children and adults. It must be distinguished from the non-neoplastic inflammatory pseudotumour of the liver. Microscopically, IMT shows three patterns, which may coexist: a myxoid vascular pattern resembling nodular fasciitis, a compact spindle cell pattern with fascicles of myofibroblasts admixed with plasma cells and lymphocytes, and a hypocellular fibrous pattern resembling a scar.
