The spindle cells have plump, vesicular nuclei with small nucleoli and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, and ganglion-like cells may be present. Kinase fusions involving ALK, ROS1, NTRK, PDGFRB or RET are found in many cases. Epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma, an aggressive variant with RANBP2::ALK fusion, consists of round epithelioid cells in a myxoid stroma with neutrophils. The differentials include inflammatory pseudotumour (IgG4-related or infectious), EBV-positive inflammatory FDC sarcoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma, leiomyosarcoma, SFT and GIST.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show spindle cells with plump nuclei in a mixed inflammatory background of lymphocytes and plasma cells, which is non-specific and difficult to distinguish from reactive inflammatory lesions; ALK immunostaining on cell block helps.
entities.ihc: The spindle cells are positive for SMA, often desmin, and ALK in about half of cases (cytoplasmic, or nuclear membrane in RANBP2::ALK cases), with ROS1 and pan-TRK immunostains for other fusions; keratin may be focally positive. They are negative for CD21, CD23, CD35 and EBER (excluding inflammatory FDC sarcoma), STAT6 (excluding SFT), and CD117 and DOG1 (excluding GIST). IgG4-positive plasma cells may be present but do not exclude IMT.

entities.entity: EBV-associated smooth muscle tumour of liver
entities.variants: Post-transplant EBV-associated smooth muscle tumour; HIV/AIDS-associated; congenital immunodeficiency-associated; multifocal tumours (liver, lung, GI tract, CNS)
entities.remarks: Smooth muscle tumours driven by EBV in immunosuppressed patients; often multifocal; bland or mildly atypical spindle cells with intratumoral T lymphocytes and primitive round cell areas; EBER positive in tumour cells; behaviour linked to immune status rather than histology.
entities.histo: EBV-associated smooth muscle tumours occur in immunosuppressed patients, including solid organ and haematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients, people with HIV/AIDS and children with congenital immunodeficiencies, and the liver is one of the most common sites, often with multifocal involvement of other organs such as the lungs, gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system. Microscopically, the tumours consist of fascicles of spindle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and cigar-shaped nuclei resembling leiomyoma or low-grade leiomyosarcoma, often with a characteristic intratumoral lymphocytic infiltrate and areas of primitive round cells. Atypia is usually mild, and mitotic activity is variable. The behaviour does not correlate well with histological features, and outcome depends more on the patient's immune status and response to reduction of immunosuppression or antiretroviral therapy. Multifocal tumours generally represent independent primaries rather than metastases. The differentials include conventional leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma (EBER negative), Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8 positive), inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour and GIST.
entities.cyto: Aspirates show bland spindle cells in fascicles with scattered lymphocytes, which is non-specific; EBER in situ hybridisation on cell block is diagnostic.
entities.ihc: The tumour cells are positive for SMA, desmin and h-caldesmon, and EBER in situ hybridisation shows nuclear positivity in tumour cells, which is the key diagnostic test. HHV-8, CD117, DOG1, S100 and ALK are negative.

entities.entity: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) involving the liver
entities.variants: Non-destructive PTLD (plasmacytic hyperplasia, infectious mononucleosis-like, florid follicular hyperplasia); polymorphic PTLD; monomorphic PTLD (DLBCL, Burkitt, plasma cell neoplasms, T/NK-cell lymphomas); classic Hodgkin lymphoma-type PTLD; WHO-HAEM5 'lymphoproliferative disorders arising in immune deficiency/dysregulation'
entities.remarks: Spectrum of lymphoid proliferations after solid organ or stem cell transplant, often EBV-driven; liver graft or native liver involvement can mimic rejection or hepatitis; graded from reactive-appearing to frank lymphoma; managed by reducing immunosuppression, rituximab and chemotherapy.
entities.histo: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders are lymphoid proliferations that develop after solid organ or haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, as a result of immunosuppression, and most are associated with Epstein-Barr virus. The liver is commonly involved, especially in liver transplant recipients, where PTLD may affect the graft and mimic acute rejection or viral hepatitis. Non-destructive lesions show plasmacytic or follicular hyperplasia, or an infectious mononucleosis-like pattern, with preserved architecture. Polymorphic PTLD shows a destructive infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells and immunoblasts of varying size, often with necrosis, which forms masses or expands portal tracts. Monomorphic PTLD meets the criteria for a specific lymphoma, most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, but also Burkitt lymphoma, plasma cell neoplasms or T and NK cell lymphomas. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma-type PTLD is uncommon. In the liver, a portal-based infiltrate of atypical lymphoid cells with expansion of portal tracts, destruction of bile ducts and sinusoidal spread is suggestive. The differentials include acute T-cell-mediated rejection (mixed infiltrate with eosinophils, duct damage and endotheliitis, EBER negative), EBV hepatitis, CMV hepatitis and recurrent viral hepatitis.
entities.cyto: Aspirates of mass lesions show a polymorphous or monomorphous lymphoid population, and flow cytometry and EBER on cell block support the diagnosis, but histology is needed for classification.
entities.ihc: EBER in situ hybridisation identifies EBV-positive lesions, and CD20, CD79a, PAX5, CD3, CD138, kappa and lambda define the B-cell, T-cell or plasma cell composition and clonality; Ki-67 is typically high in polymorphic and monomorphic PTLD. CD30 and CD15 identify Hodgkin-type cells. Clonality studies (IGH, TCR) are helpful in distinguishing polymorphic PTLD from reactive processes.

entities.entity: Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving the liver
entities.variants: Multisystem LCH with liver involvement (risk organ); LCH sclerosing cholangitis; portal-based LCH infiltrates; BRAF V600E-mutated and MAP2K1-mutated LCH
entities.remarks: Liver is a 'risk organ' in multisystem LCH; Langerhans cells with grooved, folded nuclei and eosinophils infiltrate portal tracts and bile ducts, causing sclerosing cholangitis and biliary cirrhosis; CD1a, langerin and S100 positive; BRAF V600E in about half.
entities.histo: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a clonal myeloid neoplasm of cells with a Langerhans cell phenotype, and the liver is involved mainly in children with multisystem disease, where it is regarded as a risk organ associated with a worse prognosis. In the liver, LCH typically targets the medium and large bile ducts, producing a sclerosing cholangitis that can progress to biliary cirrhosis, sometimes after the active LCH infiltrate has disappeared. Active lesions show portal and periductal infiltrates of Langerhans cells, which are medium-sized cells with abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and characteristic folded, grooved or coffee bean-shaped nuclei, admixed with eosinophils, lymphocytes, macrophages and multinucleated giant cells, and they infiltrate and destroy bile duct epithelium. Later stages show periductal fibrosis, ductopenia, ductular reaction and biliary-type fibrosis with few residual Langerhans cells. BRAF V600E mutation is present in about half of cases, and MAP2K1 mutations in many of the rest, which can be targeted therapeutically. The differentials include primary sclerosing cholangitis, other causes of secondary sclerosing cholangitis, eosinophilic cholangitis, Rosai-Dorfman disease and Erdheim-Chester disease.
entities.cyto: Aspirates of nodular lesions may show Langerhans cells with grooved nuclei and eosinophils, which are suggestive, but cholangiopathic involvement is not sampled by FNA.
entities.ihc: Langerhans cells are positive for CD1a, langerin (CD207) and S100, and often cyclin D1, while they are negative for CD163 (or weak) and BRAF V600E-specific antibody (VE1) is positive in BRAF-mutated cases. CK7 and CK19 assess bile duct damage and ductopenia. CD68 highlights macrophages, and eosinophils are seen on H&E.

entities.entity: Other histiocytic and mast cell neoplasms involving the liver (Rosai-Dorfman disease, Erdheim-Chester disease, histiocytic sarcoma, systemic mastocytosis)
entities.variants: Rosai-Dorfman disease (extranodal hepatic involvement); Erdheim-Chester disease (perirenal and hepatic infiltration); histiocytic sarcoma; ALK-positive histiocytosis; systemic mastocytosis with hepatic involvement (portal fibrosis, portal hypertension)
entities.remarks: Rare; recognise histiocyte phenotypes: Rosai-Dorfman (S100 positive emperipolesis), Erdheim-Chester (foamy CD68+, CD1a-negative histiocytes, BRAF V600E), histiocytic sarcoma (malignant, CD163+); mastocytosis causes portal infiltrates of spindle mast cells, fibrosis and portal hypertension.
entities.histo: Several rare histiocytic and mast cell neoplasms may involve the liver. Rosai-Dorfman disease, a histiocytic proliferation often with MAP2K1 or KRAS mutations, shows large histiocytes with abundant pale cytoplasm and emperipolesis of lymphocytes and plasma cells, which can form portal or nodular infiltrates. Erdheim-Chester disease, frequently with BRAF V600E mutation, shows sheets of foamy histiocytes with Touton giant cells and fibrosis, and the liver may be involved as part of multisystem disease. Histiocytic sarcoma is a malignant neoplasm of large pleomorphic cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, mitoses and necrosis. ALK-positive histiocytosis can involve the liver in infants. Systemic mastocytosis frequently involves the liver, with portal and sinusoidal infiltrates of spindle-shaped or round mast cells, eosinophils and portal fibrosis, sometimes causing non-cirrhotic portal hypertension and ascites in aggressive forms. The differentials include Langerhans cell histiocytosis, haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, storage disorders, granulomatous inflammation, lymphoma and metastatic carcinoma or melanoma.
entities.cyto: Aspirates may show the characteristic histiocytes with emperipolesis (Rosai-Dorfman), foamy histiocytes (Erdheim-Chester) or atypical large cells (histiocytic sarcoma), and mast cells with metachromatic granules on Giemsa in mastocytosis; immunostains on cell block are needed.
entities.ihc: Rosai-Dorfman histiocytes are positive for S100, CD68, CD163 and OCT2, and negative for CD1a and langerin. Erdheim-Chester histiocytes are positive for CD68, CD163 and factor XIIIa, negative for CD1a and S100 (or weak), and VE1 positive in BRAF-mutated cases. Histiocytic sarcoma is positive for CD163, CD68 and lysozyme and negative for CD1a, keratins, CD30 and B or T cell markers. Mast cells are positive for CD117, tryptase and aberrantly CD25 and CD2 in systemic mastocytosis, and KIT D816V mutation testing supports the diagnosis.

entities.variants: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma (commonest; garland necrosis, dirty necrosis); pancreatic and biliary adenocarcinoma; gastric and oesophageal adenocarcinoma; breast carcinoma (ductal and lobular); lung carcinoma (adenocarcinoma, small cell); neuroendocrine tumours (small intestine, pancreas); melanoma (cutaneous and uveal); renal cell carcinoma; GIST and other sarcomas; ovarian and endometrial carcinoma; prostate carcinoma; neuroblastoma and Wilms tumour (children); treatment response in metastases (necrosis, fibrosis; tumour regression grade); sinusoidal (diffuse infiltrative) metastasis with liver failure
entities.remarks: Metastases are far more common than primary liver malignancy in non-cirrhotic livers; the liver is a major site for GI, pancreatic, breast, lung and melanoma metastases; morphology and IHC panels identify the likely primary; report treatment response and margins in resections for colorectal metastases.
entities.histo: The liver is one of the commonest sites of metastatic disease, owing to its dual blood supply and portal drainage of the gastrointestinal tract, and in non-cirrhotic livers metastases are far more frequent than primary liver malignancies. Grossly, metastases are usually multiple, well-circumscribed, firm, white nodules, often with central necrosis and umbilication on the capsular surface, while some tumours, such as breast lobular carcinoma, small cell carcinoma, melanoma and lymphoma, can infiltrate sinusoids diffusely and cause acute liver failure without discrete masses. Colorectal adenocarcinoma is the commonest metastasis seen in surgical specimens, characterised by tall columnar cells forming cribriform glands with luminal necrotic debris (dirty or garland necrosis). Pancreatic and biliary adenocarcinomas form infiltrating glands in desmoplastic stroma and are morphologically and immunohistochemically similar to intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Other common sources include breast, lung, stomach, oesophagus, neuroendocrine tumours, melanoma, kidney, ovary, endometrium, prostate and sarcomas such as GIST. In children, neuroblastoma, Wilms tumour and rhabdomyosarcoma are the main metastatic tumours. After neoadjuvant chemotherapy, resected colorectal metastases are assessed for treatment response by the proportion of viable tumour, necrosis and fibrosis, and the background liver should be assessed for chemotherapy-associated injury such as sinusoidal obstruction syndrome and steatohepatitis. Margin status is reported. The differentials include primary hepatocellular and biliary tumours, combined tumours, and benign mimics such as bile duct adenoma, von Meyenburg complexes, segmental atrophy and inflammatory pseudotumour.
entities.cyto: FNA is widely used for the diagnosis of liver metastases and is often sufficient, especially with a cell block for immunostaining. Aspirates show tumour cells foreign to the liver, often with background hepatocytes, and the morphology suggests the type: columnar cells with dirty necrosis (colorectal), mucinous glandular cells (pancreatobiliary), small cells with moulding (small cell carcinoma), pigmented or epithelioid cells with intranuclear inclusions (melanoma), plasmacytoid cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin (NET), and clear cells with delicate vessels (renal cell carcinoma). Pitfalls include reactive bile ductular cells, mesothelial cells from capsular sampling and well-differentiated HCC mimicking metastatic carcinoma, and vice versa. No dedicated IAC-IARC-WHO reporting system applies to liver FNA.
entities.ihc: Immunohistochemistry is central to identifying the primary site: CK7 and CK20 profile as a first step, CDX2, SATB2 and CK20 for colorectal; CK7, CK19, CA19-9, SMAD4 loss for pancreatobiliary; TTF-1 and napsin A for lung adenocarcinoma; GATA3, ER, PR, mammaglobin, TRPS1 and HER2 for breast; PAX8, CA9 and CD10 for renal; PAX8, WT1 and ER for ovarian serous; NKX3.1, PSA and PSMA for prostate; SOX10, S100, Melan-A and HMB45 for melanoma; synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1 with CDX2, ISL1 and TTF-1 for neuroendocrine tumours; CD117 and DOG1 for GIST; and HepPar1, arginase-1, glypican-3 and albumin ISH to exclude HCC. Predictive markers such as HER2, PD-L1, mismatch repair proteins, and molecular testing (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF in colorectal; EGFR, ALK in lung) may be performed on liver metastases.

entities.entity: Genetic tumour syndromes predisposing to liver tumours
entities.variants: Familial adenomatous polyposis (APC; hepatoblastoma, adenomas); Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and hemihypertrophy (hepatoblastoma, mesenchymal hamartoma, haemangioma, CNSET); trisomy 18 (hepatoblastoma); MODY3 (germline HNF1A; adenomatosis); glycogen storage disease types I and III (adenomas, HCC); hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1 (HCC); PFIC2 (HCC and cholangiocarcinoma in childhood); hereditary haemochromatosis and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (HCC); Alagille syndrome (HCC); BAP1 tumour predisposition syndrome (BAP1-inactivated HCC, iCCA); Lynch syndrome (cholangiocarcinoma); tuberous sclerosis complex (angiomyolipoma); McCune-Albright syndrome (adenomas); Carney complex (PRKAR1A-inactivated fibrolamellar carcinoma); rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome (SMARCB1); DICER1 syndrome (rare); von Hippel-Lindau (hepatic haemangioblastoma, cysts); hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (vascular lesions, FNH-like nodules)
entities.remarks: Recognising a syndrome affects surveillance, family testing and management; hepatoblastoma, multiple adenomas, young-onset HCC without cirrhosis, PRKACA-negative fibrolamellar-like tumours and BAP1-deficient tumours should prompt consideration of germline testing.
entities.histo: Several inherited syndromes predispose to liver tumours, and pathologists play an important role in recognising patterns that suggest a germline cause. Familial adenomatous polyposis greatly increases the risk of hepatoblastoma in young children, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and isolated hemihypertrophy predispose to hepatoblastoma, mesenchymal hamartoma, infantile haemangioma and calcifying nested stromal-epithelial tumour, so these children undergo AFP and ultrasound surveillance. Trisomy 18 and very low birth weight are additional hepatoblastoma risk factors. Maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 3, due to germline HNF1A mutation, causes HNF1A-inactivated adenomatosis, and glycogen storage disease types I and III cause multiple adenomas with risk of HCC. Inherited metabolic diseases, including hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1, PFIC2, hereditary haemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Wilson disease and Alagille syndrome, increase the risk of HCC and, in PFIC2, cholangiocarcinoma. BAP1 tumour predisposition syndrome is associated with BAP1-inactivated HCC and cholangiocarcinoma, Lynch syndrome with cholangiocarcinoma, tuberous sclerosis complex with angiomyolipoma, McCune-Albright syndrome with adenomas, Carney complex with PRKAR1A-inactivated fibrolamellar carcinoma, and rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome with malignant rhabdoid tumour. Von Hippel-Lindau disease can cause hepatic cysts and rare haemangioblastomas, and HHT causes vascular malformations and FNH-like nodules. Histological features of the tumours themselves are those of the sporadic counterparts, but the context (young age, multiplicity, non-cirrhotic liver) should prompt consideration of germline testing and genetic counselling.
entities.cyto: Cytology has no specific role in recognising syndromes; FNA of tumours in these patients follows the same principles as for sporadic tumours.
entities.ihc: IHC can provide clues to germline syndromes: nuclear beta-catenin in hepatoblastoma (FAP and sporadic), LFABP loss in multiple adenomas (MODY3), BAP1 loss (BAP1 syndrome, also somatic), mismatch repair protein loss in cholangiocarcinoma (Lynch syndrome), PRKAR1A loss in fibrolamellar carcinoma (Carney complex) and INI1 loss in rhabdoid tumour. Germline genetic testing is needed for confirmation.
